The Problem o f Proto-Indo-European Glottogenesi s

Stefan Zimmer (University of Bonn, Germany)

ABSTRACT

Traditional reconstruction of Proto-Indo-European (PIE) and its implied

speaker community has been variously identified with the Neolithic

Revolution of ca. 8000 BC, the later Secondary Products Revolution of the

late Neolithic (ca. 4000 BC), or as a much older daughter language of

Nostratic or Eurasiatic. This paper argues for identifying PIE with the more

recent date, posing socio-economic questions as to how PIE may have

emerged as a self-conscious group and how it may have diffused in

subsequent millenia as the familiar Indo-European groups. Problems in

arriving at a definite answer include the lack of an adequate post-pidgin

and creole model for including sociolinguistioc factors in comparative

studies of language families. This study, however, calls attention of a

number of possible models for the diffusion of groups in history.

0. The Problem

When the existence of the Indo-European language family was discovered

about two hundred years ago, scholars almost immediately started to

discuss the historical implications of this finding. The lively, often heated,

discussion has produced an immense secondary literature, and continues

to do so up to this day. In recent decades, American scholars have taken a

prominent part in Indo-European Cultural Studies, culminating in the the

publication of an Encyclopedia of Indo-European Culture (Mallory-Adams

1997). This is a great achievement,1 but many fundamental issues are still

in need of discussion.There is no common opinion on practically any of its

theoretical aspects, and not even on the mere existence of some such

aspects. The key issues lie [26] somewhere between the fields of

Comparative Indo-European Grammar, Archeology, Historical Sociology

and Sociolinguistics. Obviously, an interdisciplinary approach is the only

way towards acceptable models of one or more major social changes in

the prehistory of Europe and parts of the Middle East.

The problem was dramatically posed because of the existence of a large

family of languages, spread out between India down in the South-East and

Iceland in the far North-West, and therefore quite aptly labelled Indo-

Germanique by the Danish geographer C. Malte-Brun (1810: 577).2

1. Ideological Trap s

Consciously or unconsciously following Biblical and Classical modes of

understanding, the spread of a language family could only be understood

as the direct result of the expansion of a small human unit or tribe, by

population increase, conquest and colonisation. So, in parallel with the

work of reconstructing the common ancestor of the historically attested

Indo-European languages, scholars have attempted to locate the speakers

of the numerous reconstructed or postulated languages from the proto-

forms of the different branches such as Germanic, Greek or Indo-Iranian,

over variously posited intermediate levels, like Balto-Slavic, Italo-Celtic, or

also larger units such as North-Western Indo-European, Eastern Indo-

European etc., back to Proto-Indo-European itself.

1 In spite of numerous shortcomings, inevitable in the first edition of any such book,

cf. Zimmer 1999. — References to many names and subjects mentioned in this article are to

be found in the Encylopedia.

2 The English correspondent `Indo-Germanic' first appears in Adam Black's English

translation of Malte-Brun 1810 (Black 1822: 567), cf. Shapiro (1981). Young's `Indo-

European' (Young 1813) is, by the way, not `politically correct' because half a dozen

`national' European languages (Basque, Estonian, Finnish, Georgian, Hungarian, Maltese,

Turkish) and several smaller ones do not belong to the group.

To locate the linguistic communities which necessarily must have used

those `starred' proto-languages in space and time is highly problematical

in the absence of any historical documentation beyond the reconstructed

linguistic items, and in the absence of any theoretical framework other

than the age-old literary topoi of overpopulation and colonisation. All

scholars of the 19th and early 20th centuries, living in the great period of

European and American Imperialism, took for granted [27] the naive

transfer of Darwin's biological theory into social studies. The spread of the

Indo-European languages over large parts of Western and Southern Asia,

practically all of Europe, and then in modern times to the Americas,

Australia and even parts of Africa, was seen as a clear case of the

`survival of the fittest' in the ongoing `struggle for life' of human

languages. With few exceptions, academic scholars did not pay attention

to political implications of their work. Historical linguists used to think of

themselves as pretty safe in their ivory towers, unaffected from the

turmoil of `real life' in the outside world. Franz Bopp, the founding father

of Comparative Grammar, lived in Paris from 1812-1818, but his letters

hardly refer at all to the political turbulence of the time — he spent his

days in libraries or at his desk at home (cf. Schlerath [1989] 2000: 217).

2. Traditional approaches

Indo-European Studies proper, that is Comparative Historical Linguistics,

has always regarded every question that is not purely linguistic as laying

outside its own field or at least as being of secondary interest. Those

scholars who did pay attention to the historical and social implications of

the results of linguistic reconstruction, concentrated on two questions, viz.

Ausgliederung (‚separation‘) and Urheimat (‚homeland‘).

Ausgliederung refers to the reconstruction of the process of gradual

separation of the various linguistic units from the common ancestor and

from each other, with regard to possible relations with each other after the

separation (grouping); the label Urheimat designates the search for the

geographical area where the original language, the so-called Ursprache,

was spoken, a consideration of space usually combined with chronological

considerations. All such attempts of transforming the linguistic

Stammbaum, or genealogical tree model, into an acceptable historical

theory have been - and still are - hampered by the extreme weakness of

any possible argument for one or the other proposed solution.

2.1 On Ausgliederung (separation and grouping)

Usually, argumentation is based on two facts, one doubtless objective, but

of limited time depth, and the other of disputable objectivity and unknown

time depth. The first entails the relative [28] position of the various Indo-

European languages as attested by historical documents, the second the

purely linguistic net of inherited features, partly shared innovations, and

the various isoglosses delimiting divergent developments on all linguistic

levels.

Paradoxically, all documented changes which took place in historically

attested periods are of limited importance in the process of building up a

hypothesis; the burden of proof lies with the correct ordering of

reconstructed features (i.e., their relative chronology) and with the always

difficult, often even utterly impossible, distinction between inheritance

from a common ancestor and parallel development in already separated

branches.

It is a principle that the past in its entirity is not recoverable. This

seemingly obvious, but crucial, point is often neglected. It is not a problem

to draw a map of e.g. the Classical world in 500 BC, indicating the major

languages and sometimes even dialects, but any attempt of a linguistic

map of Europe north of the Alps of the same period would have to

struggle with enormous blanks.

Extrapolation in time backwards from any given situation is, by and large,

mere guesswork. Linguists do not know anything about the population

movements which might have taken place in prehistory (cf. § 3 below for

archeological aspects). Experience shows a number of apparently bizarre

cases such as Tocharian, an Indo-European language of centum type far

away in Central Asia; Brahui, a Dravidian language in Baločistān; Ossetic,

linguistically an Eastern Iranian language, the westernmost of all

members of the Iranian branch, and Baloči, a Western Iranian language,

on the south-eastern border of the Iranian domaine; the Vandals, speaking

an East Germanic dialect in North Africa; the hotly disputed Proto-Bangani,

perhaps the remnant of a centum-language in Northern India,3 not to

mention some curious results of modern colonization.

2.2 The „Original Homestead“

All theories about the Urheimat question are based on some general

opinions about where, when and in what sequence the separation

might have taken place. Three types of linguistic [29] items are taken into

account:

1) the so-called 'linguistic paleontology'

2) loan-words

3) geographical names, mostly river names.

2.2.1 Argumentation based on `linguistic paleontology' goes back to the

founding father of Indo-European Cultural Studies, Adalbert Kuhn, whose

famous article (Kuhn 1845) first dealt with the history of the Indo-Euopean

people.4 He was the first to develop the idea that reconstructable lexical

items of the protolanguage should be proof enough to postulate the

existence of all features they signify in the material, intellectual and

spiritual world of the speakers of that language. This principle has been

used in fervent disputes by scholars from various countries, mostly voting

for their own homeland as the original habitat, or at least near to it. Many

Germans e.g. were convinced that the Indo-European words for `beech'

and `salmon' showed beyond any doubt that northern Germany alone was

3 Zoller's last article (Zoller 2000, with references to earlier publications, but not

mentioning Delmarre (1995) who supports him) contains a devastating answer to the seeingly

more than unfair criticisms of van Driem and Sharma (1996).

4 Pictet's (1859-63) paléontologie linguistique tells of his thinking in terms of `guide

fossils'. In those days, linguists pretended to work `as exactly' as natural sciences do.

the cradle, the beech not found east of Königsberg (today Kaliningrad) in

what then was Eastern Prussia, and the salmon mounting only rivers going

into the North Sea and the Baltic. Many terms have been discussed in this

way,5 and the corresponding publications retain their importance, though

not in the authors‘ original sense as such studies failed to take into

account the fact that designations are quite often transferred to similar,

but different objects. The Proto-Indo-European `beech'-word was used by

the Greeks for a kind of oak, by Iranians in the Caucasus for an elm tree;

the 'salmon'-word probably could be used for any salmon-like fish (see

Diebold‘s 1985 careful study) or even for any fish, as in Tocharian.

Even when a formal reconstruction of a given word is perfectly possible in

all details, the reconstruction of its semantic content is far less secure,

and rarely possible with precision. In the case of the salmon, the decision

hinges on the internal etymology. L salmo belongs to salire 'to jump' and is

therefore clearly a term for 'jumping fish', be it the salmon proper or any

other member of the salmonid class. But Proto-Indo-European *lokso- lacks

any convincing etymology: if it belongs to a word for `red', as

Hoff[30]mann thought (apud Thieme 1951, who adds full argumentation),

it might have arisen as a generic term, so that the Tocharian usage is old

and does not represent a case of generalization.

The older studies further suffer from the fact that their theoretical base is

insufficient. The dispute had already been fought out in medieval

theology. The existence of a denominans (or signifiant, as de Saussure put it)

does not automatically imply the factual existence of a corresponding

denotatum (or signifié). The word `god' is no proof of the existence of a

`Supreme Being'. All human languages and literatures abound with words

and ideas denoting features which do not exist materially, which are

merely imagined, which are dreamt of, wished, feared, unreliably

reported, or simply unknown. Even if all Indo-European languages had a

word for `unicorn', and we could reconstruct the Proto-Indo-European

word in all details, who would ever have ventured to postulate the

`Urheimat' was swarming with unicorns?

5 A very useful overview is provided by Jankuhn (1969).

2.2.2 Loan word studies can be used successfully to detect early trade

relations, as has been done in many cases. Quite often, terms denoting

special objects of trade seem to belong to no detectable source language,

or the direction of the loan is unclear. Why should Proto-Indo-European

*tauro- 'bull' be a loan6 from PSem *ṭawr- and not inversely? Why are not

both a loan from an unknown third language? The danger of rash equation

of similar words is naturally higher when the precise meaning of one or

both items compared are insufficiently understood. A famous example of

the type was OInd paraśú- Gr $ πέλεκυς `axe, hatchet', supposedly a loan $

from Accadian pilaqqu- `id.' which, however, later turned out be something

quite different, viz. either a `distaff' or a `stiletto'.7 One has to [31]

conclude that loanwords are completely irrelevant to movements of

populations or languages. Ketchup is quite an important element in the

North-American-lexicon, but nobody ever took it as a sign for a

noteworthy Malayan component in the ethnic puzzle of the United States

of America.

2.2.3 Names for imposing natural features, such as rivers or mountains,

are notorious for being retained even if the language or languages spoken

by the country's inhabitants changes. The many rivers in England called

Avon (= Welsh afon 'river') are a well known case. America presents us

*teuh2- `to swell'. This implies a metathesis of the laryngeal difficult to account for.

7 Makkay‘s attempt (1998) to back the old idea of a Semitic borrowing in some IE

misquotes of a number of linguistis (e.g. Frisk in fn.9, and Schlerath in fn. 21). Akkadian

pilaqqu, also transcribed pila uḳḳ , means ‚distaff‘ and ‚spinning whorl‘, never ‚axe‘. It is

important to note that Cuneiform Akkadian does not distinguish the two Semitic phonemes

q/ḳ Qof and k Kaf. The word is well attested, as are its Western Semitic cognates with are

consistently spelled with -k- (Kaf), eg. Hebrew pelek, Phoenician and Ugaritic plk, Arabic

falakat. The word is etymologically somehow isolated, the only possible connection is to

the Arabic verbal root flk ‚to be round‘ (uspecifically). The root seems to have been

sometimes confused, by non-Semitists, with the root flq ‚to split, to tear apart‘ - whence

$the erroneous etymological connection to Akkadian pilaqqu ‚distaff‘. That Greek πέλεκυς $and Sanskrit paraśú- are most probably loans from an unknown source (which may well

be the source of Akkadian pilaqqu, etc., also) is still the best possible result of scholarship.

(I am obliged to my friend Josef Tropper, Berlin, for help in Semitics.)

with many other examples, but also with salient counter-examples. (cf.

the types of Chicago vs. Boston). In Greece, many rivers and mountains were

2.2.3.1 For the linguistic prehistory of large parts of Europe, Hans Krahe

was able to elaborate a complex system of river names which, to judge

by their phonological and morphological [32] structure, are too old to

belong to any known Indo-European language. This is what Krahe called

the `Old European hydronymy'. There can be no doubt about the

relevance of Krahe's findings, but the interpretation of the material is

hotly disputed till the present day. These names certainly are vestiges of

older unattested and therefore unknown languages spoken in Europe

before the earliest traces of the various known vernaculars, but nothing

more.

2.2.3.2 Similarly, in a sharply defined region in northern Germany and

parts of the Netherlands, Hans Kuhn had observed not only river names

with special phonetic characteristics, such as *p for Proto-Indo-European

*ku, and a preponderance of the vowel [a], but also a special vocabulary,

mostly belonging to popular speech and lower levels of social discourse,

which displayed the same features. By way of explanation, he postulated

the existence of a former non-Germanic, but perhaps Indo-European

population, which managed to retain its own language long enough not to

undergo Grimm's Law, though finally adsorbed by the surrounding

Germanic dialect groups. This is Hans Kuhn's `North-Western Block'.

2.2.3.3 Objections to Krahe's and Kuhn's Theories

Both Krahe's `Old European Hydronymy' and Kuhn's `North-Western

Block' have met with fierce protests and widely deverging interpretations

of the same materials. It is not possible to go into detail here, but some

basic problems in any such discussion should be raised.

2.2.3.3.1. Proper names are distinguished from appellatives by the fact

that they can be, and quite usually are, used without any reference to a

possible semantic content of the linguistic form. In other words, whereas

a given lexeme is defined by a special correlation of form and content,

based on broad general agreement within a given speech community, a

proper name is by definition nothing but a label attached to one

individual being, human as well as animal or otherwise natural or

supernatural, and therefore liable to be transmitted freely from one

language community to another. An appellative which has become

obsolete i.e. whose meaning is lost, which is no longer understood by the

majority of speakers, can no longer be used without risks of

understanding. No such danger exists for a proper name - it is used

without any problems even if the underlying lexeme is unknown or has no

meaning at all outside its usage as a proper noun, because the name is

obsolete, foreign or simply made up at random. Proper names usually are

not automatically [33] analyzed by its users, and the only grammatical

rules they have to obey, aside deliberate derivations for special purposes,

are phonotactic.

Any argumentation based exclusively on proper names is therefore rather

weak, all the more so as in the absence of a supra-individual meaning, a

distinction between accidental identity or similarity, and regular

sy stematic relationship - i.e. a linguistic or grammatical relation - is

impossible. Krahe's etymologies of those river names are, on the whole,

empty speculations based on resemblances to reconstructed Proto-Indo-

European roots, and his morphological analysis is but one possibility. In

these names it is impossible to distinguish between genuine Proto-Indo-

European roots and foreign words, possibly adapted to Proto-Indo-

European speech habits.

2.2.3.3.2 Of lesser importance, but further weakening all theories like

Krahe's, is the unrecoverable grade of representativity of the presented

material. If the names belonging to an alleged `system' are only a small

part of all names of the same class in a given territory, their statistical

value is of course drastically diminished. The study of river names is

severely hampered by the commonly practized superficial way of

recording present-day names, viz. from existing maps instead of detailed

fieldwork,8 and by the poor historical documentation available for the vast

majority of all these names. According to Hans Kuhn, 75% of the river

names found in the Ruhr Region of Germany do not fit into Krahe's

system, but most of them do fit into his own. The interpretation is open to

debate.

8 I can give an example from personal acquaintance: Two creeks in my home town

Fulda (both obviously belonging to Krahe's `system') are not even mentioned in the relevant

literature: Waides and Ohm. Both have been partly covered in the 18th and 19th centuries,

and therefore do not figure on usual maps.

2.2.3.3.3 These objections are not meant to diminish the importance of

Krahe's and Kuhn's findings. They are perhaps the only linguistic vestiges

of Pre-Indo-European Europe north of the Alps. They provide us with

questions, but give no answers: Both systems have to be discussed

anew, and in a broader perspective than before.

It has convincingly been argued that for large parts of the vocabulary of

e.g. Greek and Germanic, secure Indo-European et[34]ymologies cannot

be given.9 Various explications have been suggested, none of them is

convincing. It is striking to note that Greece takes no part in Krahe's

hydronymy - obviously, the language or rather, languages spoken there

before the arrival of the Indo-European Hellenic language were different

from the language or languages spoken in other parts of Europe. This is a

strong indication that a much greater prehistorical variety of languages

existed in Europe than imagined by Krahe and his followers who postulate

only one single `system' from Northern Spain to Northern Russia. We

should avoid the danger of oversimplification. Documented history shows

clearly enough that the complexity of social features in all societies of all

periods can hardly be overestimated.

3. Archeology and Linguistic s

3.1 One of the fundamental problems, perhaps the most important of

all, in Indo-European Cultural Studies and all similar fields is the big

divide between archeology and linguistics. These two sciences have in

common a wide range of questions about the prehistory of peoples and

regions, but their respective approaches are totally different. Both

sciences have their own methodology and their own terminology. Any

discussion between the two is therefore fraught with misunderstandings,

and the mutual use of hypotheses developed by the other can lead to

absurdities, their misuse by politicians to atrocities ...

What needs to be discussed in more detail is the discrepancy between

9 Neumann‘s (1971) attempt to save the almost pure IE nature of the Germanic lexicon is

hardly convincing. See also Scardigli & Toth (1995).

linguistic and archeological ways of arguing about prehistorical

civilizations. As a linguist, this author is in no position of describing, with

any degree of accuracy, the fundamentals of archeology. What is

expressed is an external view from an adjacent field, a view motivated by

keen interest and sincere admiration for the great achievements of our

colleagues.

Linguists study language which belongs to the mental side of human

existence. Archeologists study material assets of early periods. Both are

working in the field of Geisteswissenschaften (humanities) but from rather

different starting points. Historical [35] linguists, having reconstructed

earlier forms of language, may attempt to find traces of the material

world in those abstract symbolic systems. Archeologists, having classified

and arranged material objects, consider recovering the mind of those

who made and used these objects.

The results of Historical Linguistics are reconstructed linguistic systems or

parts of systems; traditionally, we speak of reconstructed `languages'.

This usage is rather problematic because of the difference between

natural languages and reconstructed languages, commonly overlooked

by non-linguistics.

The results of Archeology are `cultures', typical combinations of

archeological findings which are thought — at least by non-archeologists

— to be remnants of certain specific population units. Consciously or

unconsciously, the tendency still prevails to equate reconstructed

`languages' with archeologically defined `cultures' even if one knows

pretty well that "pots don't speak" and "words are but sound".

3.2 It should be left to archeologists to discuss the problematic nature

of the archeological term `culture'. Linguists, as well as all other non-

archeologists, can only ask for the criteria which decide what is typical for

a given archeological conglomerate of findings. Obviously, it seems very

difficult to agree on objective criteria, and scholarly literature contains

numerous cases where one theory is critized by supporters of another as

being based upon `gross misunderstandings' or purely subjective

choices. Similar situations are, of course, to be found in Historical

Linguistics, and there is no need to go into more detail here. Zimmer

(1994) has commented on the dilemma resulting from the difficult

relation (or better: non-relation) between archeology and linguistics.

Progress in that complex, but fascinating matter may be possible, when

not only the weaknesses of our own methods, but also the questions and

results of other disciplines are taken into account. The first area for

possible collaboration is historical sociology or cultural anthropology. The

second is another branch of linguistics, viz. Pidgin and Creole linguistics.

Why should one look for further partners in a discussion which has

already proven to be rather frustrating? One of various possible answers

obviously is that the former partners have not asked each other the right

questions and that both need fresh support from a third or even forth

perspective. If archeologists and linguists, for lack of mutually acceptable

arguments, [36] cannot agree on a sensible equation of `culture' with

`reconstructed language', one may conclude that neither of them has

developed a model complex enough for consideration from an adjacent

branch of social studies. From a linguistic perspective, the age-old

equation of `language' with `nation' has long been recognized as

unfounded, not only through history but also through scholarly research

of all kinds. A `tribe' or a `nation' can never be defined by language

alone, but classical Indo-European Studies, basing reconstructing on the

genealogical tree model, have usually persisted in this old error and still

cling to it in our times.

3.3 Neither the value of the genealogical tree model nor the

importance of reconstructed languages should, however, be

underestimated. The traditional method of Indo-European Studies is

indispensable and beyond any doubt adequate to the problems studied.

Whoever abandons the notion of `sound law' and `genealogical tree',

looses all the outstanding results of 180 years of scholarly work. But the

amassed knowledge about Indo-European languages covers only partially

the problem involved. Even a complete grammar of Proto-Indo-European

could be only part of the truth. One has to keep in mind that, as Wilhelm

von Humboldt pointed out, language only exists in speaking. All other

forms being secondary abstractions. In other words, reconstructed

`languages' are only models for undocumented languages spoken by

people. This is, of course, not a new defintion, but it takes on new

significance as the traditional equation of a reconstructed or postulated

proto-language with a corresponding proto-population has failed to bear

fruit in discussions between archeologists and linguists in recent years.

The problem is clearest in its Indo-European context. The Indo-European

language family presupposes the former existence of an Proto-Indo-

European language which must have been spoken by a noticeable

population. Yet archeology has been unable to prove that any given

`culture' belongs to the postulated Proto-Indo-European people.

Moreover, of course, the argument could be reversed: Indo-European

linguistic studies have been unable to identify any given archeological

`culture' as being that of the Proto-Indo-Europeans.

Furthermore, modern archeological studies from many parts of Europe

have suggested that large-scale migrations, which used to be adduced in

order to explain the spread of the Indo-European languages, have been

rather improbable in prehistory. [37] To give but one well-known exaple,

archeology sees a thoroughgoing continuity in the prehistory of Greece,

whereas for the linguist, the foreign origin of the (successive groups of)

Hellenic speakers is beyond any doubt. In this contrext the fresh

persepctive proposed, or rather sketched, by Sherratt (1999) offers new

vistas also for Indo-European cultural studies,10 but its importance seems

not yet to be realized by most participants in the (necessarily complex)

interdisciplinary discussion. See further see below para 5.3.

10 Though Sherratt gives only a few basic archeological references, and carefully

avoids citing Indo-European scholarship strictu sensu, it is implicit that some of my earlier

published ideas (e.g. Zimmer 1991, partly raised again here) are at least very well

compatible with his own.

4. New Questions for Indo-European Cultural Studies

Indo-Europeanists have to look for theoretical models of language spread

which are compatible with the results of archeological research, empirical

as well as theoretical. And first of all, one has to start to think earnestly

about the emergence o f the language family. How could Proto-Indo-

European have come into existence at all? For a considerable time, there

have been two types of answer to the question, viz.

A) to reconstruct further backwards - to Nostratic or even back to

Proto-Human, or

B) to abandon reconstruction at a certain point of prehistory, and to

explain vaguely some given language as the result of mixture and/or

mutual assimilation of two or more earlier languages - this is Trubeckoj's

model.

Both types suffer severly from theoretical shortcomings:

Answer A is without any doubt overly optimistic. First, "we cannot

reconstruct ad infinitum", as J. Kuryłowicz wisely said (1964: 58). Because

only preserved features can serve for reconstruction, all losses by

definition being unrecoverable, the relation of reconstructed vs. lost

features becomes smaller and smaller, the further one goes back.

Answer B puts back the basic problem to unknown earlier languages

which are purely hypothetical. It thus lacks any methodol[38]ogy.

Trubeckoj never substantiated his model. In all fairness, one must

acknowledge that in his times, Pidgin and Creole Linguistics were still in

their infancy (see below § 5.2).

5. A New approach

A new start is urgently needed in the vexed question posed by the

existence of the Indo-European family. Language is a social phenomenon:

one therefore has to pay attention to the social conditions connected with

language history in the broadest possible way. Before starting to ask how

a new language emerges, one should ask how new social units come into

existence. This is the old question of ethnogenesis, which up to our own

times, used to be answered by mythological stories. The unprecedented

richness of documentation about all possible aspects of social life which

is available in our days is, of course, still insufficient for many scholars,

but it may indeed facilitate the attempt to build up new, more rational

theories.

One condition for group formation without any doubt was already

important in even the earliest periods of human history: A close unit of

persons is based above all on a group consciousness, not on any other

social, racial, or material criterion. Parallels from documented history

abound, and have often been discussed, mostly under headings such as

`When was England?' (to cite a popular catchphrase of English

historiography)11 or `The early beginnings of the X people'.

Today we still see young `nations' all over the world struggling with

countless obstacles on the way to building up state-wide [39] group

consciousness. Even within established nations, discussion is constantly

rekindled by the arrival of immigrant groups or the emergence of

separatist movements.

5.1 The Impact of Historical Sociology

The German sociologist and ethnologist Wilhelm Mühlmann has

11 England is a particulary interesting example: Anglo-Saxon England consisted of a

number of independent, mutually mostly hostile, kingdoms. If it were the West-Saxons

kings, who finally brought the whole country under their power, the name is taken from the

Angles, not the West-Saxons nor the Saxons in general. Under the Tudor kings, with their

Welsh background, and again after the union with Scotland, a new `British' (originally the

name of pre-Anglo-Saxon Celtic inhabitants of the Isle; earlier still perhaps referring to the

pre-Celtic Picts only) identity was built up to include the whole `Celtic fringe' on the main

island. This attained success, but the attempt to include Ireland failed, for obvious reasons.

There, the dispute unfortunately is still burning in the six counties today. For the English

language, Hines (1998) might be indicated as an example of the vast literature on the topic.

published, time and again, on the mechanisms of the formation of social

units bigger than families, the criteria which constitute such units, and

their definition against neighbouring communities (Mühlmann 1962,

1964, esp. 1985). Mühlmann's findings are, according to the present

author, especially useful for the discussion about emergence and spread

of language families. These include:

1) the various `limitic structures',12

2) the origins of nomadism, and

3) an important theoretical problem called `gap of consistency'.

Brief comments on these three points are intended to clarify and explain

what is meant, and to underline their relevance for the present

discussion.

5.1.1 `Definition' is literally the drawing of a border line, the delimitation

of two items opposing each other; it implies the distinction between `us'

and `the others'. The term `border' usually has strong geographical

connotations in all languages which makes it inappropriate for discourse

about ethnic units. The modern stereotype of `one country, one nation,

one language', sometimes extended to `one religion', etc., has to be

dismissed as a myth, deliberately created for political purposes. If such a

situation ever existed, it was (or is) unnatural. All over the world, before

the rise of modern nationalisms ca. 200 years ago, manifold mixtures of

ethnic units and languages are what anthropologists have documented or

observed. Mühlmann proposed the use of the term `limitic structures'

because it is free of connotations and because it can include the set of

features that differenciate the collective consciousness of any ethnic unit.

Ethnological research has found that the following features express social

affiliation (Mühlmann‘s order here expresses ranking): [40]

- types of clothing and adornment, including tatooing, body painting,

12 `Limitic', a coinage of Mühlmann's, is not to be misunderstood as `limiting'. The

terms basically means `pertaining to limits', as specified in para 5.1.1.

hair style, artificial body deformations

- design and decoration of habitation

- choice and making of tools and weapons, and their use

- language, with special genres in literature

- types of music and dance, musical instruments

- cooking, dishes.

For the linguist, and perhaps for everyone who is not a sociologist, the

low position of language is remarkable. Traditionally, language is

regarded as the first criterion for ethnic (or even national) classification.

This is obviously wrong. With a bit of reflection, one might detect, in

history or the present, numerous cases confirming the relatively

unimportant rank of language in definitions of ethnicity or nationality.

Politically defined nationality is not only characteristic of the United

States of America but also occurs in most countries of present-day

Europe, independent of a citizen's mother tongue.13

5.1.2 `Nomads' play an important role in the history of many nations.

Formerly, nomadism was seen as a stage of social evolution intermediate

between the hunter-gatherer level and sedentary agriculturalism. As

Mühlmann has shown, based on large-scale studies of nomadic societies

all over the world, this is fundamentally erroneous.14 Nomadism

presupposes the existence of sedentary agricultural populations. Nomads

and farmers have multiple economic relations with each other. Nomads

cannot exist without goods acquired from farmers by purchase, exchange

or plunder. Farmers usually buy metal or metalwork or other necessary or

esteemed foreign goods from nomads who are often involved in long-

distance trade. Surplus products of farmers may be sold or bartered to

nomads who either consume or export them. In balance, the nomadic

lifestyle presupposes [41] the existence of a sedentary agricultural

13 Reference to ancient or modern Vielvölkerstaaten [my E dict. translates this term

as `multi-racial states' which seems misleading or even wrong] such as the Hittite or

Achemenid Empires, Austria-Hungary or the Soviet Union, does not further the

understanding of the problem. They might serve as an analogy, showing the utterly complex

structure of allegiances which might struggle with each other even in one single person.

14 Similar views have been expressed by Goodenough (1970).

population, but the inverse is not true. This reflects the socio-historical

background of nomadism. According to Mühlmann (1985: 23), nomads

are `sieved out' from the sedentary population : nomadic societies are

collecting receivers, reception units for all kind of fugitives, homeless and

displaced persons, criminals, adventurers and outlaws.

There are historically documented cases of such communities, which

might almost be labelled `asylum people', such as the `Children of Israel'

or, nearer to our times, the Cosacks15 and Uskoks.16 For all these unstable

groups, Mühlmann proposed the term colluvies gentium , literally 'dregs

of tribes'.17 This very useful term will be important later in the discussion

here.

5.1.3 `Gap of consistency' is Mühlmann's term for the constraint caused

by the discrepancy between theory and practice of ethnocentrism. Most,

if not all members of pre-modern societies are convinced that they

themselves, their own social unit, tribe or people are the only human

beings in any full sense. They are convinced that all others are foreigners,

intruders, or creatures of lesser rank; that the world and its ressources

have been created first of all for their own purposes; and that their own

morals and ways of life are the best of all. In short, only members of

one's own group are properly to be properly called human beings. This is

what we call `ethnocentrism'. Though some aspects may sound familiar

to today's popular mass values, the whole concept is absurd for the

average 21th century cosmopolitan. But the firm existence of such deep-

rooted ideas is shown beyond doubt by a variety of languages.

Indigenous self-designations, which are clearly nothing other than the

15 Since the 15th c., landless (orthodox East-Slavonian) peasants from the regions

between Russia, Poland and Ukraina, fleeing from poverty, hunger and Polish catholic

missionary attempts, penetrated into the steppes at the bords of Dnjepr and Don, establishing

practically independent communities, living from war and plunder in Turkish and Tatar

regions. Later, the Cosacks were instrumental in the Russion colonization of Siberia.

16 Serbs, Croats and Bosniaks fugitives before the Osmanic conquest, the Uskoks settle in

Dalmatia and Istria, fighting the Turks and Venetians. Later, they were resettled by Austrian

authorities in Slovenia as border defending soldier communities.

17 Coined after Tacitus Ann. 2,55 and 14,44 colluvies nationum (similarly Jerome, Epist.

130,6 colluvies perfugarum atque servorum).

speakers' own appellatives for `man, human being' are frequent. Well-

known cases are Esquimau Innuit, Hottentot Khoi, Bushman San, or Native

[42] American self-designations of the type Maidu. A few more are found

among Finno-Ugrian languages: Hungarian Magy-ar, Wogul Mańśi, Ostjak

Moś, Nenzi Samoyed (ny)enyec, Tavgi Samoyed nganasan, Selkup söl'qup, lit.

`man of the earth'. Inversely, the neighbours are called `strangers', as

Wotyak por `Cheremiss', lit. `stranger'.18

Usually, historical, mythological, or religious reasons for such bold

pretensions are forwarded as seemingly obvious explanations, but in

spite of these extravagant theoretical claims of exclusive possession of

full human rights, everyday commerce with members of other

communities is basically unproblematic. The discrepancy between theory

and practice is characteristic for so-called `primitive' cultures.19 On the

one hand, every stranger and everything foreign is suspect, alarming,

dangerous; on the other hand, daily life quite often imposes contacts

between members of different social groups, ethnic units, and the like.

5.1.4 Sociological investigation has shown that all human societies have

developed mechanisms to bridge the gap, to shield against the unknown

powers of the strange, to handle persons and goods of foreign

provenance. These are rituals which allow contacts by creating new

social memberships, which dedicate certain qualities to persons and

things, thereby establishing harmless possibilities of contact. These

rituals necessarily comprise a wide variety of situations. For the history of

an ethnic group, those who permit interrelation with members of other

groups are most important. Many of them can be taken together as

various forms of adoption. For example, occasional strangers may ask to

be allowed to join the community, and kidnapped children or abducted

prisoners of war are often integrated in order to strengthen the own

group or to replace human losses. There is also adoption in order to settle

18 In the same context, we find mocking designations for other people such as Greek

bárbaros, Sankrit mleccha-, Mongol tatar, all originally `stammerer', or Slavonic nemec

`German', literally `dumb'.

19 Note that `primitive' is not used as a depreciatory adjective here — it is to be taken in

its literal sense, belonging to the field of `first, early, primordial'. The term seems

indispensable for the description of only lightly differentiated pre-urban societies.

blood-feuds, as a kind of human compensation. Exogamy also belongs in

this context because it usually leads to mutual [43] commitments and

stable social bonds between the communities involved, preparing the

later formation of nations.

5.2 The Historical Model of Pidgin and Creole Linguistics

Next to anthropology, a relatively new branch of linguistics is to be

considered, which is neither purely theoretical nor historical in the

traditional sense. While Pidgin and Creole Linguistics have existed for

more than 130 years,20 only in recent decades have such studies gained

monumentum.21 In the sixties and seventies, scholarly attention was

most attracted by the pidgin and creole languages of the Americas,

which are based on European colonial languages. In the eighties and

nineties, quite different pidgin and creole languages in Australia, New

Guinea and adjacent regions seem to have become the focus of

attention. I cannot claim competence in the field and therefore ask the

specialists' indulgence for the following attempt to briefly summarize the

principles underlying the Pidgin-Creole process.

5.2.1 Whenever people without a common language meet at regular

intervals, or begin living together, they immediately start to create a

new language in order to fulfill their most urgent communicational

needs. The main strategy used is mutual simplification: Participants start

to drop all linguistic signs felt as redundant, or less important, first of his

or her own language, than of such rudiments of the other's language as

he or she is able to grasp. This is obviously a gradual process governed

by trial and error. The psycholinguistic details are not yet sufficiently

investigated, but it is an indisputable fact that the process works, and

new means of mutual understanding and communication in fact come

20 Its beginning is traditionally reckoned from Van Name (1869-70).

21 The proceedings of the Jamaica Conference 1968 (Hymes 1971) probably mark the

beginning of the new period.

into being in a very short time22 by dint of necessity. This first stage of a

new language is called a Pidgin. Its lexicon is rather restricted,

morphophonemics are very simple, syntax is confined to a few

straightforward types.23

5.2.2 It is probable that in a newly assembled human group of

variegated linguistic background, such as a colluvies gentium, more than

one Pidgin is produced, depending on social conditions. If [44] these turn

out to be stable, Pidgins have two possibilities, namely either to vanish

in favour of the language of a dominating group, or to develop into the

mother-tongue of future generations. In the second case, the emerging

new language is called a Creole language.24 It is characterized by a

strong tendency to develop complex morphophonemic structures quite

rapidly, again under the pressure of the need to communicate in all life

situations of the society which has no other common language. After

about three generations, a fully grown grammatical system may exist,

with every chance of persisting into the future.25

5.3 OIE and the Secondary Products Revolution

Sherratt (1999), with his reflections on a `secondary products

revolution'26 as an economic basis for cultural expansion processes offers

a fresh perspective, also for Indo-European Cultural Studies.27 Renfrew's

thesis that the Indo-Europeans spread agriculture to Europe as part of

the `Neolithic Revolution' (ca. 8000 BC) focuses on developements that

are decidedly too early for PIE. Sherratt‘s ‚Secondary Products

22 According to Hall (1962: 151-156), this is a matter of hours or maximally days.

23 For more details, see Thomason & Kaufman (1988: 167-199).

24 Manessy (1979) stresses the importance of a new group solidarity in the process.

The relevance of this new approach for diachronic linguistics has immediately been seen by

Polomé (1979).

25 Thomason & Kaufman (1988: 48ff., 147-166, 211) insist on the possibility of „abrupt

creolization“, i.e. the emergence of a new language, a creole, without a former pidgin

phase.

26 Such `revoltions' apparently are common in archeological jargon.

27

Revolution‘ (ca. 4000 BC) is thus much more attractive, and perhaps not

incompatible with the result of Indo-European historical linguistics. Its

potential, and as I think great importance seems not yet to be realized

by most participants in the (necessarily complex) indisciplinary

discussion. Sherratt postulates a social dynamics based on new trading

ways or new (luxury) goods to trade. Such dynamics could have

provided a catalyst for the emergence of a PIE community, and a

material base for its expansion — if only, and this indeed should be

stressed, one could find reasonable items. As far as I know, no such new

trade goods could be yet defined either by archeologists, nor by

historical linguists. While possibilities abound, it remains for actual

discoveries to pinpoint them. Such a trading context, once defined,

might well offer the socioeconomic basis for the development of a

pidgin-creole glottogenesis. If such a trade language could be shown to

reflect the reconstructions made for PIE, we would con[45]clude that PIE

arose during the period of trade motivated by the ‚Secondary Products

Revolution‘.

6. A Tentative S olution

Taking into account Mühlmann's theories about ethnogenesis, and the

role of Pidgin and Creole languages in glottogenesis, a tentative solution

for the Indo-European problem as defined above may be sketched in

terms of (1) emergence, (2) diffusion, and (3) mixed group types.

6.1 Emergence

A number of factors must be considered:

6.1.1 Linguistic reconstruction of Proto-Indo-European implies the

existence of a speech community. In view of the absence of any

convincing proposal of attributing an archeological `culture' to this

population group, it is probable that the kernel was rather small.

6.1.2 If Proto-Indo-European is not seen as a branch of `Nostratic' or any

similar superfamily, it is reasonable to assume that it came into being as

the language of a new ethnic unity. Social anthropology and history

suggest the model of a colluvies gentium as the least improbable theory

for the emergence of such a new unit.

6.1.3 The colluvies gentium was a nomadic group consisting of persons

'sieved out', for various reasons, from surrounding cultures, living at the

borders28 of permanently cultivated areas. Its members most probably

came from more than only one such sedentary agricultural community,

and perhaps also from other nomadic groups.

6.1.4 There is a wide range of possible source civilizations, from the

neolithicic farming communities in Eastern Europe to early cultures in

the great valleys of China. However, a number of historical cases

strongly point to eastern origins: all foreign in[46]vaders in the history

(as opposed to prehistory)29 of Europe came from regions east of

Southern Europe and/or north of China:

- the Scythians (Sarmatians) c. 800 B.C.,

- the Alans c. 100 B.C.,

- the Huns in the 4th century,

- the Avars in the 5th and 6th,

- the Turks, including Chazars and Bulgars, from the 6th to the 9th

century,

- the Magyars (i.e. Hungarians) and Petcheneges in the 9th, and finally

- the Mongols in the 13th century.

6.1.5 The possible time span of Proto-Indo-European is delimited only by

a terminus ANTE quem, the first attestation of Indo-European Anatolian

28 This was felt by earlier scholars, e.g. Hirt (1905: 96) for whom is is „self-evident that

the Proto-Indo-Europeans must have lived in a border country“ (my transl.).

29 Note that Sherratt (1999: 270-279) points to eastward expansions in the 4th and

3rd millenia. On his criticism of Nichols (1997 and 1998), see also Justus (2001).

proper names in Akkadian documents from the 20th century B.C. A

terminus POST quem or a tempus AD quem may be guessed at in quite

diverging ways, depending on one's ideas about the time span

necessary for developing a new language, and for the subsequent

dialect splits. There are historical cases of both very rapid and very slow

developments.

6.1.6 The assumption that the ethnic kernel of Proto-Indo-European was

formed by a kind of colluvies gentium implies the creation of a new

language for the new community. No other theory is better suited to

provide a model for this process than Pidgin-Creole linguistics. At

present, this is the only acceptable linguistic model capable of showing

how a completely new language may emerge out of a plausible social

situation.

There is, of course, no possible argument against the application of the

older split model, well attested in history, and thoroughly studied by

historical linguistics, to the prehistory of Proto-Indo-European. But this

would be clearly the weaker hypothesis, simply putting the problem

further back into undocumented protohistory. Among various

conceivable hypotheses, one should opt for that scenario which fits best

into known patterns of social and linguistic develop[47]ments. It has the

advantage of being based on modern sociolimguistic research (cf. also

Thomason & Kaufman 1988).30

6.1.7 Ethnogenesis and glottogenesis are but two aspects of one

complex process, the development of an in-group-consciousness

differentiating one‘s own group from (an)other, probably rival group or

groups. This collective self-consciousness arises in conflict situations

when it is important to know about every other person's relationship to

oneself. One might say, modifying the anthropologist Ernst Haeckel's

famous dictum, that `ethnogenesis is the recapitulation of idiogenesis'.

30 I am grateful to Carol Justus for referring me to this book which is a big step forward

indeed. I must confess that the book had somehow escaped my attention earlier.

There is no `self' without an `other'; no political unity (in the widest

sense) is possible without a common enemy, no religious unity without

competing cults, no linguistic unity without the notion of foreign speech.

In brief, no social unit can exist without a counterpart conceived as being

different. This is common knowledge in philosophy and psychology, but

also quite important with regard to the history of modern nations.

Structurally similar historical processes, though on smaller scale

compared to documented history, must be assumed for earlier, smaller

ethnic units.

6.1.8 The model of the Proto-Indo-European speech community as a

colluvies, as a new type of society with a new type of language, living a

nomadic life outside established sedentary civilizations, provides a

plausible explanation for the enormous dynamism of the Indo-European

language family. A colluvies is formed by persons who are

unconventional, mobile, creative, audacious, perhaps bold, daring or

even simply criminal, but at any rate strong enough to take the risk of a

new beginning. The emergence of a new stable common language is

proof of the success of the new community and inspires its members to

develop far-reaching ideas. Every dynamic community is based on a

common ideology. The earliest very advanced sedentary civilizations of

Antiquity, both the Sumerian and the Egyptian, show rather static

structures with deep hierarchies. Nomadic societies, on the contrary, are

rather egalitarian or at least have only flat hierarches, and are often

quite dynamic.

6.1.9 The basic value of Proto-Indo-European society was free[48]dom .

It may first have meant freedom from old constraints, from persecution,

or from poverty. It must have quickly developed into a comprehensive

view of the social and supernatural world. The rudiments of common

Indo-European religion, law, and social structure which can be

reconstructed on the basis of the oldest Indo-Iranian, Greek and Hittite

texts, point to sharp differences between the Indo-European world and

its neighbours. It is remarkable and symptomatic that an Indo-European

deity, as a rule, is to be adressed with his or her proper name, not with a

general cover term, or with an epithet instead of the name. Indo-

European gods have no secret names; to call the divine name is not

dangerous, to say nothing of taboo (cf. Markey 1985).

Two other values were also fundamental for the Proto-Indo-European

society: hospitality and truth. This is well documented in linguistic and

literary sources, and seems today widely accepted by the scholary

community, so that no further comment upon these two subjects is

needed for the moment.

There was no highly differenciated social hierarchy. There must have

been rich and poor, as everywhere, and affluence gave no doubt

influence, as always, but at least theoretically, all family heads were

equal (cf. Zimmer 1985). They were the only political subjects, they only

were responsible for their family, and they alone may have elected a

chief or king whose power was, however, rather restricted, at least in

time of peace. Is it too bold to imagine a kind of (oligarchic, to be sure)

democracy avant la lettre?

6.1.10 A relatively free, and relatively egalitarian society must provide

for those who are too young, too bold, or too adventurous to comply

easily with the common rules of social life. Proto-Indo-European society

most probably had one or more institutions to cope with exuberant

elements. In later historical sources, similar groups are variously

described as `Jungmannschaft', `war-bands', `fiana', or the like.31 There

may have existed a kind of educational system comparable to the well-

known African age classes of the recent past, some of which lived

outside the main community for specified periods, subsisting from

plunder and hunting. The different literary texts in old Indo-European

languages, or younger folkloristic sources, only show more or less

ritualized remnants. Such satellite roving groups probably became,

under propitious conditions, driving powers of Indo-European expansion.

31 Cf. McCone (1987) and (1995); McCone (1986) is confined to Irish cases.

[49]

6.2 Diffusion / Spread

The spread of a language cannot be regarded as an isolated event.

History shows an abundance of cases that the expansion of a language,

or the implantation of a colonial language in an alloglottic country is,

above all, the result of political changes. Political history is, alas, mostly

based on military victories and defeats, but also on economic

innovations, and sometimes also on the emergence of ideological

powers, such as a new religion or a fresh wave of imperialism. Modern

scholarship attempts to disentangle the complexities of modern history,

politics, economics, societies. The nature of man has not fundamentally

changed over the past 10.000 years. Therefore, one is safe to assume

prehistory to have been fully comparable to history in regard to

complexity, even if, due to low population numbers and relatively simple

living conditions, the complexity of any given feature may have been

considerably lower than in our own times.

Even if a language is intentionally proliferated, this is never done for the

sake of the language itself or the beauty of its literature, but for political

and/or economic reasons. In the early spread of Proto-Indo-European and

of later subsequent intermediate languages, down to the proliferation of

already attested languages, the language seems to have been

propagated rather unintenionally. We call the process of transmitting

Proto-Indo-European or any later Indo-European language to formerly

non-Indo-European speaking populations Indo-Europeanization. Many

types of Indo-Europeanization may have existed, and certainly, there

must have been many cases of, linguistically speaking, unsuccessful

operations.

6.2.1 A first distinction may be possible between quick, large-scale

operations on the one hand, and slow advance of small groups on the

other. The first type is in fact attested by e.g. the Germanic

Völkerwanderung, but hard to assume for prehistorical times. It may be

therefore safer to start with the idea of smaller groups, detaching

themselves from the main community. Such groups may have been

adventurous bands of young warriours seeking fortune elsewhere, or

officially imposed ver-sacrum-type emigrations (see next para) destined

to relieve insufficient living conditions, or else single clan chiefs

wandering away, for whatever reason, with all their families, relatives,

followers and lifestock.

The warband of fierce youngsters may attempt a quick con[50]quest of

a distant agricultural community, living in villages or small towns, or

even the overthrow of the rulers of a foreign city. In any case, they

probably cannot afford long-term wanderings for lack of supplies. If they

succeed, the Indo-Europeanization will have followed Antonio Gilman's

Mafia model (Gilman 1990) or a similar pattern. The newcomers occupy

powerful positions, but have to intermarry and compromize with the

local population, and have only one way of imposing their own language

on their new subjects, namely by creating a kind of `court language',

kept at a formal level by `court poets' with `court poetry', and practised

by bodies of retainers, recruited locally, but of course obliged to speak

the language of their new masters. In many, if not in all, such cases, the

Indo-European language of the new rulers undergoes rapid and massive

changes due to interference by the local language or languages; all the

more so, if the local civilization is technically more advanced, or the local

religious institutions survive practically unaltered. Such a situation may

be seen in the fate of Hittite and the other Indo-European Anatolian

languages.

6.2.2 It is far from certain whether the institution of ver sacrum ever

existed in reality. The custom is described in Classical historical works

and may have been simply a literary topos. According to Latin authors, it

ideally consisted in the dedication of all living beings, born in one

precisely defined year, to the gods in order to placate divine anger. The

animals are slaughtered, the boys and girls, once having reached 21

years of age, are sent away. Greek colonizing enterprises are usually

justified with overpopulation and resulting shortage of food supply. A

similar case is the famous ver sacrum of the Celtic Bituriges reported in

Livy (5,34). King Ambigatus sends away, at the same time, his two

nephews Bellovesus and Segovesus with two such groups with the order

of finding new settlement areas. This is the founding legend of the Celts

in what the Romans called Gallia Cisalpina. It may be useful, however, to

retain the ver sacrum as a possible model of early Indo-European

colonization.

6.2.3 The third model mentioned, that of an entire clan breaking away

and moving towards unknown regions seems to underly the case of the

Indo-Aryans. We may assume that during long wanderings, the nomadic

group became bigger and bigger, by natural reproduction, and also as a

result of attracting single foreigners or other small groups who may have

joined the wandering tribe-to-be. Such groups on the move can indeed

grow very [51] rapidly due to the process known as the `snowball-

effect'.32 Like a small snowball quickly turning into an avalanche, a

wandering clan may become an invading tribe or a conquering people. If

the wandering period is long enough, a strong tradition kernel is formed.

The classical literary case for this procedure is the Children of Israel in

the desert. In the case of the Indo-Aryans, the country finally reached

was void of powerful civilizations, and therefore the imported Indo-

European tradition could continue more or less unaffected to govern the

life of the community in its new settlements. This Indo-European culture

was vigorous enough to incorporate, for a considerable period, many

cultural influences from the various local populations without undergoing

heavy structural transformations. Further expansion in later periods lead,

of course, to quite different situations.

6.3 Mixed group types

32 This expressive term is due to Bernfried Schlerath (1973:20).

Another kind of Indo-Europeanization is that which is carried on by

motley, i.e. ethnically and linguistically inhomogenous groups. These

may be regarded as secondary colluvies gentium with a strong Indo-

European tradition kernel and a considerable admixture of non-Indo-

European elements. According to the German archeologist Hermann

Ament (1986), three elements seem to be constitutive for the

emergence of the Germanic group: the Jastorf culture in Southern

Scandinavia and Northern Germany (whose population probably spoke a

kind of Indo-European), other Iron Age groups in Northern Central

Europe, and Celtic remnants in Southern Germany.33 From the historical

standpoint, this type is best attested in the case of some of the historical

Germanic tribes, such as the Franks and Alamannians who started their

respective existence as bands of robbers on the Roman frontier, invading

the Empire.34 [52]

The linguistic effect of one or more adstrats, combined later, after the

final settlement, with substrats of indigenous populations, is responsible

for the various transformations of the imported Indo-European language

(see e.g. Polomé 1992 and Salmons 1992). In this type, lexical changes

are more prominent than changes in grammatical structures. Grammar

is also affected, but to a lesser degree, perhaps because of the

perseverance of a tradition kernel. One must recall here that several

Germanic poetic formulas retain remnants of the Indo-European poetical

tradition.

7. Outlook

Every branch of the Indo-European family, and perhaps even every

single language, has to be studied on its own in view of possible or

33 For a comprehensive state of scholarship, see RGA vol. 11, 181-438.

34 The Franci, most probably `the free ones', are first attested AD 257 as a band of robbers

in Gaul, constantly augmenting their numbers by fugitive slaves and other roving people

who joined the group. The Alamanni are first mentioned for AD 213; the Byzantine historian

$Agathias (2nd half of 6th c.) explains their name as συγκλύδες `washed together' [NB ≈ $

$colluvies] and μιγάδες `mixed'. Another telling name, first found in Caesar (BG 1,51,2) is $

Marcomanni `men at the frontier'.

probable substratal and adstratal effects.35 Superstrats also exist, but

seem to be of minor relevance for the prehistory of the Indo-European

languages. Every case is different, and historical sources are meagre or

simply do not exist. This is why further comparative studies of a new

kind are needed. It might be possible to compare the respective

grammatical structures with those of the other attested Indo-European

languages, and also the reconstructed Proto-Indo-European, with regard

to possible effects of influence from non-Indo-European languages.

These questions have been discussed many times, but mostly in terms

of inheritance, loss or innovation, within a closed model of internal

development of the language family. I am aware of the fact that

substrate studies are highly controversial in Indo-European academic

circles, not only on account of ideological restraints, but also, because no

common opinion about the details of grammatical (deep) structure of

(Pre-)Proto-Indo-European exists. Future studies along the lines

suggested in this contribution are further hampered by the fact that no

methodology of substratum linguists is generally accepted, and that

arguably the big difference between substratum effects and creolizing

mechanism is insufficiently understood. This article is intended to bring

this and related issues to a wider readership of linguistis in the hopes of

arousing further fruitful interdisciplinary scholarship.

35 A fine example of such a study is Gensler (1993).

A Proto-Indo-European word for ‘spider’?

$Un-weaving the prehistory of the Greek ἀράχνη $

and the Latin arāneus

Stefan Höfler (Austrian Academy of Sciences; University of Vienna)

&

Johan Ulrik Nielsen (University of Copenhagen)

Abstract

$The Greek ἀράχνη and the Latin arāneus ‘spider’ have long been considered cognates, yet $

a convincing etymology is still missing. Based on words for ‘spider’ in other Indo-European

traditions that are predominantly derived from roots and verbs meaning ‘weave’, ‘spin’, and the

$like, we assume that the root at the core of Gk. ἀράχνη and Lat. arāneus had similar semantics. $

Analysing the preform *araksnā as *h₂ŕ̥h₂⁽g̑⁾sneh₂-, we recognize the underlying root *h₂reh₂⁽g̑⁾- $‘weave’ not only in ἀράχνη and arāneus, but also in the Gk. ῥῆγος ‘rug, blanket’ and the root $

$noun ῥώξ ‘a kind of venomous spider’, the continuant of a former agent noun ‘weaver’. $

Keywords

etymology; laryngeal dissimilation; nominal derivation; Graeco-Latin isogloss

https://doi.org/10.5817/GLB2022-1-6

$A Proto-Indo-European word for ‘spider’? Un-weaving the prehistory of the Greek ἀράχνη … $

1. Introduction

$The1 etymology of Greek ἀράχνη ‘spider; spider’s web’ (Hp., A., Arist. etc.), ἀράχνης m. ‘spider’ (Hes., Pi. etc.), ἄραχνος m. ‘id.’ (A. Supp. 887), ἀράχνιον n. ‘spider’s web’ $(Od.+), and Latin arāneus m. ‘spider’ (Plaut.+), arānea f. ‘spider’s web’ (Plaut.+), ‘spider’ (Cat.+) is still a major mystery within the historical grammar of the two languages. The preform underlying these formations can be phonologically reconstructed as *araksnā,2 $with *-aksn- > Gk. -αχν- as in ἄχνη ‘chaff’ (*aksnā) and *-aksN- > Lat. -āN- as in exāmen $‘swarm (of bees)’ (*eks-agsmen).

Within Latin, the expected *arāna was further extended by *-ei̯o- to give arāneus, $arānea. As this suffix usually derives relational adjectives (cf. aurum ‘gold’ → aureus ‘gold-$en’), one could hypothesize that the adjective arāneus ‘of a spider’ (attested in Plin., Col.) was first substantivized as a word for the web of the spider (i.e., arānea ‘spider’s web’ Plaut.+). Such a process can be paralleled not only within Latin (cf. arāneum n. ‘spider’s $web’ Phaed., Plin.) but also in Greek (cf. ἀράχνιον n. ‘spider’s web’ Od.+, probably from an adjective *ἀράχνιος ‘of a spider’). From this, the meaning ‘spider’ (Cat.+) could have developed by metonymy. On the other hand, however, Gk. ἀράχνη has both meanings $‘spider’ and ‘spider’s web’ as well and shows that the metonymy can (arguably, at least) develop in the other direction, too. In addition, the masculine arāneus that only means ‘spider’ is apparently the older variant (cf. Ernout & Meillet 1959: p. 42 s.v. arāneus). In any event, the suffix -eus, -ea is not uncommon in words denoting various animals (e.g., ardea ‘heron’), sometimes small (e.g., clupea ‘a kind of very small river-fish’) and/ or unwanted ones (e.g., tinea ‘larva, grub, maggot’), and in some cases forms with and without -eus, -ea stand side by side (e.g., equulus ‘small horse’ and equuleus ‘id.’), at times with a difference in meaning (e.g., hinnulus ‘young mule’ and hinnuleus ‘young stag or roebuck’) or adding only a slight nuance (e.g., capra ‘she-goat’ and caprea ‘a kind of wild she-goat’). In line with this, arāneus, arānea might originally have meant ‘small spider’ or ‘a kind of spider’ and therefore presupposes a form *arāna < *araksnā.

$Yet any further analysis of the *araksnā that both Gk. ἀράχνη and Lat. arāneus point $to is made unsustainable for lack of obvious etymological cognates.3 This is why some scholars have entertained the thought that Lat. arāneus, arānea is a loan from Greek

We thank the two anonymous reviewers for several invaluable comments and suggestions, which have improved this paper considerably. All remaining errors are our own.

A connection with Gk. ἄρκυς ‘net’ (A.), ἀρκάνη ‘thread with which the warp is intertwined, when they are setting it up in the loom’ (Hsch. α 7271 Latte) is semantically attractive (see sections §2 and §3), but phonologically only possible if both ἄρκυς and ἀρκάνη represent syncopated $forms (< *arak°). A more straightforward solution is presented in section §3.

In support of this scenario, Beekes (2010: pp. 123–124 s.v. ἀράχνη) cites the $narrow distribution of the word within the Indo-European languages5 and the fact that *araksnā “looks non-IE”. The latter point, however, might be contested as *araksnā does not look any less “IE” than a word such as *lou̯ksnā (Lat. lūna f. ‘moon’, OPruss. lauxnos $f. pl. ‘stars’, YAv. raoxšnā- f. ‘light’, etc.; cf. *leu̯k- ‘bright’ in Gk. λευκός ‘white, bright’, etc.), *u̯l̥k̑snā (Gk. λάχνη f. ‘woolly hair, down’ Il.+; cf. *u̯olk̑o- ‘hair’ > Av. varəsa-, OCS vlasъ, Russ. vólos, etc.), or the already mentioned *aksnā (Gk. ἄχνη ‘chaff’ Il.+; cf. Lat. $acus, -eris n. ‘husk of grain; chaff’ Cato+). All these words are interpretable as containing a suffix *-snā- (< *-s(-)neh₂-). This, of course, invites one to review whether *araksnā may be identifiable as an inherited word as well and if the underlying root is found in more lexemes of Greek, Latin, or other Indo-European provenance.

As PIE *s would be expected to devoice a preceding obstruent at any chronological stage of these languages, the final consonant of the root underlying *arak(snā) can be *⁽k̑⁾, *⁽g̑⁾, or *⁽g̑⁾ʰ. When it comes to the initial sequence *ara°, the options are more lim-ited. Latin precludes initial *s-, *i̯-, or *u̯-, so the only viable alternatives are *h₁arh₂°, *h₂erh₂°, and *(h₂)ŕ̥h₂° (more on which below in section §3). Since these elements can be teamed up to an incredibly large number of theoretically possible combinations, it seems nearly hopeless to offer a plausible Proto-Indo-European form based on the etymon’s phonological shape alone. It is therefore wise to turn to the semantics of the words for ‘spider’ in other Indo-European languages first and see what kind of roots these are de-rived from. This will help narrow down the number of possible candidates for the root that underlies *araksnā ‘spider’.

2. ‘Spider’ in Indo-European

Words for ‘spider’ are attested in every branch of the Indo-European language fam-ily, which is not surprising as spiders are found virtually everywhere across Eurasia. However, there is no single reconstructable term for ‘spider’ that is found in two or

$4 Clusters of χ plus nasal in Greek borrowings are rendered as c(h) plus nasal in pre-Classical Latin and develop an anaptyctic vowel. Compare Gk. δραχμή and Lat. drachuma ‘drachm’ (Enn.) or τέχνη and techina $‘trick, ruse’ (Plaut.); see Leumann (1977: p. 103). Accordingly, a West Greek /arákʰnā/ should have been borrowed as *arac(h)una. And even if we assume that this cluster treatment occurred only after the accent-ed syllable and that /arákʰnā/ was borrowed as */árakʰnā/ (with Latin-specific recessive accentuation), the outcome of this would probably have been *aragna (thus Walde & Hofmann 1938–1954 I: p. 61 s.v. arāneus; cf. *deknos > dignus ‘fitting’). The only scenario in which a Greek loan would regularly end up as Latin *arāna is if the input form was *araksnā, which, however, would have to be borrowed from 2nd millennium Greek.

2.1 Isolated formations and borrowings

A couple of Indo-European languages possess words for ‘spider’ that are without good parallels in other Indo-European languages. Old Irish damán allaid ‘spider’ (literally ‘wild calf, fawn’), Modern Irish damhán alla ‘id.’, for example, is difficult to explain semantical-ly, though the motivation may be similar in nature to Mod. Ir. bóín dé ‘ladybug’ (lit. ‘calf of god’) and other words for insects that are named after larger animals.7 The underlying semantic image, though beyond our modern-day comprehension, could possibly also explain Armenian *ernǰak ‘spider’, if derived from erinǰ ‘heifer’ (Ačaṙyan 1971–1979 II: p. 68b; cf. Martirosyan 2010: p. 270 s.v. *ernǰak) by means of the diminutive suffix -ak (as $in cov ‘sea’ → cov-ak ‘lake, pool’; Olsen 1999: pp. 243–244). A comparable case might be $ǰori ‘mule’ and ǰoreak ‘a kind of small locust’ (cf. Martirosyan 2010: p. 789).8

Borrowed terms for ‘spider’ include Albanian merimangë, a loanword from Greek $(cf. Mod. Gk. μυρμήγκι ‘ant’; Orël 1998: p. 257 s.v. merimangë), Classical Sanskrit markat.a-, $the source of which is unknown (cf. EWAia III: pp. 390–391 s.v. markat.a-), and Welsh cop (also copyn, pry(f) cop, pry(f) copyn) which is from English cop (GPC 1967 I: p. 554 s.v. copyn¹, cop²).

2.2 The spider’s body

A couple of languages derive their ‘spider’ words from expressions denoting round objects, inspired by the spider’s spherical body. Old English ātorcoppe, Middle English attercoppe, Modern English (obsolete) attercop, Old Danish ederkoppæ, Modern Danish edderkop, Old Swedish ēterkoppa or -koppe (Bjorvand & Lindeman 2019: pp. 240–241 s.v. eiter; Söderwall 1884–1918 I: p. 228 s.v. eterkoppe (-koppe)) are all evidently from Pro-to-Gmc. *aitra- ‘poison’ and a second member based on *kupp-a- ‘round thing’ (cf. loc. cit.; Falk & Torp 1960 I: p. 180 s.v. Edder; Holthausen 1974: p. 57 s.vv. copp, coppe; Orël 2003: p. 224 s.v. *kuppaz), which is also found uncompounded in the above-mentioned Middle English coppe, Modern English (obsolete) cop, and Middle Dutch coppe (Van Veen & Van der Sijs 1997: s.v. kobbe²).

The naming after its round body has a parallel in Latvian zirneklis ‘spider’, derived $from zirnis ‘pea’ (Karulis 1992: p. 564 s.v. zirneklis), and in Iranian (cf. Sogd. γōndē, $
