Transit to Germanic status would mean shvabi/шваби ----> shvaben) In the search of arguments along the line of Prus-sians’ Slavic past suddenly new arguments appeared also with regard to possible transformation by the Swabians through one of above schemes. In Figures 7, 8 and 9 appear Skalvia, Sklavinia and Skalvinians, and through Table 6, where Old Prussian clans are listed, we can appreciate how close the transcription of their names in their neighbors’ languages comes to our one time assumption. In this segment we’ll add a few facts from the Lexicon mentioned above, and the monography “The German Tribes” /20/. Borrowed from it a map of Pomerania is shown on Fig. 10, to the west of Old Prussia, where we see the settlement Шлаве (Schlawe), which is in direct support to our initial assumption in /17/.

The tribes inhabiting the region are labeled in common as “Pomoranen” (full analog of “Поморийци”), the coastal vil-lages in the neighborhood of Schlawe (Шлàве) carry names that sound rather Slavish, while the adjacent region is called Kraina, a Slavic toponym - please recall about Ukraina!

In above-mentioned monography /20/ several chapters relate to the tribe of Swabians (Schwaben, Ger.) as important com-ponent of the consolidated German nation. One of the chap-ters begins with a proposed transformation suggesting a long evolution of the name (Fig. 11), which - while not necessarily coinciding fully with our proposal - demonstrates similarity of the logic and the overall approach. Since this author had not assumed probable closer kinship and dwelling areals with the Borusci, he did not search for proof about the Swabians as far northeast and so far back in time. As we have already demonstrated such material has been discovered in the Bal-tic realm; moreover, records exist in quantities larger than we ever anticipated - and we have actually not undertaken a truly in depth search...

At this point we will finish with one last, indirect argument. On one of the maps in the Lexicon /19/, which describes the

Fig. 10: Map of Pomerania with Slavic names of the settlements. Most important to us is Schlawe

Fig. 11: A chapter from the monography discussed in the text, related to the Schwabians

![https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/notebooklm/ABzcPv3Qdgf2OlhCKCVrxDByQo7FBweTNnKeF4DL84mzEya4rjUlvoT1Xpx83Hw-lGerue7uizHL0AT8jfk17sk6rZAYdUR5jXj_NBQqJiitCkuYvxOKdqZ1C3SWT1vkSdY8DOqg3hTT=w464-h717-v0](https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/notebooklm/ABzcPv3Qdgf2OlhCKCVrxDByQo7FBweTNnKeF4DL84mzEya4rjUlvoT1Xpx83Hw-lGerue7uizHL0AT8jfk17sk6rZAYdUR5jXj_NBQqJiitCkuYvxOKdqZ1C3SWT1vkSdY8DOqg3hTT=w464-h717-v0?authuser=0)

local dialects in Prussia’s various regions we see an item “Swabian Colony.” In the scant, as in any lexicon, text there are no explanations yet it is clear that this fact fixes the presence in the region of representatives of this (already) German tribe at this mo-ment in history. Interestingly, the domain labeled “Swabian Colony” is relatively very large - larger than most other (‘local”) groups in Eastern Prussia of the time. Without further conjunctions, speculations or information, the appearance of this “colony” ex-actly there is a fact which is stunning at the least (Fig. 12).

One last argument pertaining to the possible protoSlavic past, respectively origin, of the Swabians arose while translating the original lecture /21/. The work regarding the Slavs involved analysis of the variety of ways to transliterate the name. At the time I have postulated as quite possible the transformation

шлави, шлавини ---> слави, славини [s(c/k)lavi], [s(c/k)lavini] ---> [slavi, slavini]

even though the probability, in the lack of hard evidence, did not seem very high (see

in /17/ and the references therein). However, even the translating job offered additional argumentation: If the [Shvabians] (die Schwaben, Ger.) became [Swabians] - not so long ago, and just between two Germanic nations’ languages - why should it be impossible that [Shlavi], [Shlavini] ---> [Slavi], [Slavini]

also had happened, albeit during earlier times, with different transformation periods, and different nationalities of the wit-nesses....*7

The evidence described in the last two segments allows for laying with the highest certainty the claim that the North-North-West vector carrying migrating Proto-Indo-Europeans calling themselves Aryans who had started their journey from the West-NorthWest region of the Circumpontic had contributed most to the formation in the Baltic areal of new tribes. By the time of their settlement on these lands they must have been speaking a version of Proto-Indo-European language (Thracian) whose evolution until the moment of emergence of Old World’s unquestionable hegemon, the Roman Empire, seems to have been minimal, but after that due to the development of communications and the intensified spiritual exchange - unified (and even monopolized) by the Christian Church - marks a speedy acceleration. Parts of thus emancipated (Balto)Slavic tribes must have continued to migrate further west and southwest, others will have suffered administrative influence and at times spiritual pressure. New tribal groups will have been the result, with the examples here fully supporting as really possible the transformation Slavic ---> Germanic (compare now with the schematic on Fig. 4, while not forgetting to account for the approximate character of the time scale; one could proceed analogically with the other “branches”).

***

After the demonstration of above transformation’s degree of veracity, we can return to the issue of trustworthiness - given our limited knowledge about the language - of the claim

PIE = Thracian = proto-Slavic (proto-Slavic-Bulgarian, a.k.a. Old Bulgarian, a.k.a. Church Slavonic)

New additions to the argumentation regarding the relationship “Thracian - proto-Slavic”

In /15,16/ we published considerations regarding the deciphering of some of the few inscriptions from Thracian times. Since these inevitably prompt about the rules of grammar, i.e. point to the “language’s melody,” the continuous systematic attempts for further deciphering of the available texts (in the hope to achieve a final version) lead to comprehending the basics of Thracian’s syntax. To wit, the first attempts to decipher the text onto the Ezerovo ring has led us to

7 All insertions in blue marked with a star are additions to the publication that are not present in the original text in Bulgarian /21/,

Fig. 12: “Swabian colony” in Eastern Prussia. The map is borrowed from /20/ and it illustrates the local dialects. Whichever the reason, the appearance of the root “schwab” in the local terminology manifests an interrelation, in full agreement with our hypothe-sis, as launched in /17/.

Ролистеня с(ъ/и)н Ереня... i.e. На Ролистен, син на Ерен (Ирен; Иреней)... To Rolisten, son of Ireney (Iren; Eren)...

with very pronounced declension forms, whereby the declension ending regarding the first name could suggest - from de-ductive logic and practical considerations - genitive or dative:

Подарен на Ролистен.......... (Gifted to Rolisten) Посветен на Ролистен........ (Dedicated to Rolisten) Притежание на Ролистен... (Belonging to Rolisten)

Continuing the deciphering we arrive to the key question, how would the separate words look like in otherwise the contin-uously engraved script:

ROLISTENEASNERENEATILTEANHSKOARAZEADOMEANTILEZYPTAMIHERAZHLTA  

Here we will display only a couple of the sense-making versions to which we arrived following the crucial conclusion from our previous work, namely that Thracians’ language is the language of the proto-Slavs as well (which in its early stage could be labeled as well the language of the proto-Sloveno-Bolgars). The first version looks like the following:

ROLISTENEA SN ERENEA TI LTEA NHSKO A RAZEA DOMEA N TI LEZY PT A MIH E RAZHLTA  

The interpretation of this version, with sub-variants (and clarifications/assumptions of ours) in brackets , is as follows:

Ролистеня, с(ъ/и)н Ереня ти л(ъ/е)тя ниско и разя домя нъ ти лежи път а мий (на мен ми) е ражъл(и)та

{ а мий (за мен) е раж(ъ)л(ъ/и)та } { а мий (за мен) е раз(ь/йъ)л(ъ/и)та }

The final version of which we estimate the probability of being true no less than 80% is

ROLISTENEA SN ERENEA TI LTEA NHSKO A RAZEA DOMEA N TI LEZY PT A MIH E RAZH LTA   с прочит

Ролистеня, с(ъ/и)н Ереня ти л(о)тя н(ь/йъ)ско (полетя долу, в отвъдното ???) и разя домя нъ ти лежи път (и сега пътят ти е далеч от дома ни) а ми(й/йъ) (на мен ми, за мен) е раз(ь/йъ) л(ъ/а)та

{ лот, вин. пад. лота = съдба, жребий } lot = lot, fate, destiny { лотя = изтеглям жребий } to lot = to try/draw my lot, to face my fate

{ раз(ь/йъ) = сега, един път } ràz (‘) = now; once; one time { разя род. пад. = сега, този път8 } ràzya = now, this time

{ ньско (или нйъско) = вариант на “ниско” n’sko = low

In other words, we arrive at the preferred here version:

ROLISTENEA SN ERENEA TI LTEA NHSKO A RAZEA DOMEA N TI LEZY PT A MIH E RAZH LTA 

Ролистеня, с(ъ/и)н Ереня, ти л(о)тя н(ь/йъ)ско а разя домя нъ ти лезу п(ъ)т а мийь е раз(ь/йъ) л(о)та.

На Ролистен, син на Иреней, ти изтегли беда (извади лош късмет; изтегли лош жребий; сполетя те бедствие; полетя надолу, в отвъдното) и сега (този път = разя) пътят ти е далеч от дома /ни/ (домя нъ ти лезу п(ъ)т = към дома /ни/ не тe води път; към къщи не ти лежи път*), и за мен /това/ е сега /тежък(а)/ жребий/съдба (нещастие).

To Rolisten, son of Ireney, you had bad luck (drew unlucky lot; faced disaster; flew down to the underworld - the kingdom of the dead) and now (this time = ràzya) your road is far from /our/ home (your road does not lead to /our/ home) (and now your road does not lay homewards*) and for me /this/ is now /hard/ lot/fate (bad luck, trouble, unhappiness)

8 Derivatives of this root (раз, transcribed here as raz-) are present in many, if not all, of the Slavic languages: teraz = сега (now) in

In one sub-variant “DOMEA” (домя = house, in declensed form) could in fact represent two words, “DO” and “MEA”: the first one being a preposition analogous to the English “to” or “by”, and the second being the pronoun for 1st person singular in a declensed form similar to the English “me.” DO MEA then would mean “to me,” “by me,” etc. Hence the third line above from the inscription would become “до мя нъ ти лезу път,” which in translation would become “до (към) мен не ти лежи (не те води) път” and “to me leads/lays no road of yours.” Clearly, this exercise supports my point: Thracian = proto-SLAVIC.*

Transitioning now to the Kyolmen inscription below we present the split of the originally continuous text per our preference: this is the text’s first half; the rest we set aside unchanged, for now (for further examination, later on):

EVAR.ZESA SN HNETE SA IGEK. A N BLABAH GN NYASNLETEDNYEDNEINDAKATR.S 

At first glance the inscription reads:

Евар, Зеса с(и/ъ)н й(ъ)нете са игек. А нъ вълавай г(ъ)н (носовката г(^)ъ)9

where й(ъ)нете са игек = намира се отдолу/тук is placed hereunder й(ъ)нете са игек = почива си тук is resting here й(ъ)нете са игек = лежи си отдолу lays hereunder and нъ вълавай г(^)ъ = не безпокой го (погребания) don’t disturb him (the buried) нъ вълавай г(^)ъ = не откривай го (гроба) don’t uncover (the tomb) нъ вълавай г(^)ъ = не повдигай го (камъка) don’t lift (the stone)

Hence the translation sounds as follows: Евар, син на Зес почива тук. И не го смущавай (И не го откривай /изваждай от гроба/) = Evar, son of Zes rests here. And don’t disturb him (And don’t open /take him out of the tomb/)

Without giving up on the suggested translation here we will note only that in order to accomplish it meaningfully into mod-ern (Slavic-)Bulgarian we introduced the obligatory inversion which had impended when abandoning the declensions in our language (in contrast to all other Slavic languages) and their replacement by more extensive use of prepositions. In raw form the translation will sound in the contemporary language of that time (some 2 millennia back !) like this:

Евар, на Зес син намира се отдолу/тук И не смущавай го...

Evar, to Zes son lays/is buried underneath/here. And don’t bother/disturb him...

At the end of this lecture we will offer a hastily designed but by far not improbable solution for deciphering of the inscription on a vessel for cremation residues:

DADALEME

Here we base our suggestion on the following arguments:

1. Under the condition that we have demonstrably proven the anticipated thesis that Thracian language is identical to pro-to-Slavic, the text must be aligned in terms of syntax, and to sound in close harmony with the contemporary Bulgarian; 2. The inscription should suit the theme of a deceased close person (relative, friend...)

It seems to us natural that дадалеме = да жалеме ! (да жалееме, да жалиме)... [da zhaleme] = to mourn. The deliberate pronouncing of the same letter as “d” and immediately after that as “zh” should not bother anybody since in reality the per-son writing the inscription uses Greek characters hence what we denote as “D” in reality is “Delta.10 But if we can substitute “d” with “delta” why can we not substitute with “delta” “zh” as well? Especially given that they each mark two very close in terms of method of creation voiced consonants. Moreover, it is perfectly possible that in the period of time contemporary for $these vessels (pre-Roman epoque on the Balkans) “zhaleme” could have been pronounced “δαλεμε”, before evolving into its $sounding two millennia later. In conclusion, we believe that the translation of the inscriptions on burial residues containing vessels should be:

DADALEME ---> DA DALEME = да жалиме [da zhalime = to mourn]

9 The transcription г(^)ъ we find suitable to express nasal vowels, as suggested earlier in /15,16/. 10 In Greek the sound “d” does not exist, therefore there is as well no letter dedicated to it. At later times, when extensive communication with foreign nations began, introduced was the convention existing to this date, whereby the combination of two other letters is used to denote

Conclusions and Recommendations:

1. The chronological scheme proposed here is a worthwile tool in the exploration of languages’ evolution in the distant past, and its refining must continue. 2. The language of original Aryans’ tribal community, whom we later on identify as Thracians, demonstrates closest similarity to Sanskrit. 3. Thracians’ language had evolved in Slavic-Bulgarian (a.k.a. Old Bulgarian, a.k.a. Church Slavonic), to which until not so long ago had aligned the languages of most Central- and East-European nations, i.e; those in the “Slavic” group within Indo-European type of languages. 4. The thorough, in-depth examination of Veda Slovena would be of greatest importance for Thracian language’s full recon-struction. 5. Obtaining Biblia Bessica (or even just fragments of it) would be of greatest importance for the deciphering of the “bridges” to other Indo-European languages, more precisely those in the Middle East.

Preface

When linguists and philologists first began systematically analyzing the striking parallels among the Indo-European (IE) languages and reconstructing the fea-tures of their prehistoric ancestor, Proto-Indo-European (PIE), they soon realized they were uncovering more than just phonetic systems, words, and phrases. They were also identifying the underlying concepts those terms evoked in the minds of the speakers. Based on the evidence of the IE daughter languages, scholars were able to reconstruct, for example, the word for the domesticated one-toed ungulate, *h₁ék̑u̯os, or the term for the circular object that rotates around an axle,

*kʷékʷlos. But the words for the ‘horse’ and the ‘wheel’ cannot have been part of the PIE vocabulary by accident: they must have also been a part of the real world that surrounded the speakers of PIE. In other words, the reconstruction of the prehistoric language entails the reconstruction of its speakers’ prehistoric reality, a research interest that scholars of Indo-European studies share with specialists in archaeology and anthropology.

Animals and wooden objects are not the only elements that were recovered on the basis of comparative evidence. The rich inherited vocabulary of the IE daugh-ter languages also allowed for the reconstruction of words for social institutions like ‘youthful war band, sodality’ (*kori̯os) and ‘bride price’ (*h₂u̯edh₁-mn(-o)-), of the names of deities belonging to a polytheistic pantheon (e.g., *di̯ḗu̯s ph₂tḗr ‘Father Sky’ and *h₂éu̯sōs ‘Dawn’), of elaborate kinship terminology such as ‘daughter-in-law’ (*snusós) and ‘husband’s brother’s wife’ (*h₁i̯enh₂tḗr), and even of verbal roots that refer to such intricate interhuman actions as ‘to change sides, social class, or ownership’ (*h₃erbʰ- or *h₁erbʰ-) or ‘to demand atonement, punish’ (*kʷei̯-).

The desire to explore these cultural concepts and social institutions alongside linguistic structures led Indo-Europeanists to foster a productive interdiscipli-nary dialogue with experts in archaeology, anthropology, the history of religions, and – especially in the last decade – ‘ancient DNA’. A number of theorized con-cepts which had been reconstructed solely on the basis of linguistic data, such as the practice of patrilocal marriages and female exogamy, have now been con-firmed or further developed thanks to cross-disciplinary research; and linguistic

8 Preface

reasoning has, in turn, quite frequently been able to support or refute hypotheses made by archaeologists, anthropologists, and historians of religion. It is precisely at this intersection of diverse but complementary approaches to the investiga-tion of prehistoric culture and society that the present volume is situated. It seeks to explore the dynamics of power, gender, and mobility, three concepts that are essential for a profound understanding of the historically attested IE-speaking societies and of the prehistoric society reflected by PIE. In a cross-disciplinary fashion, the book combines linguistic, anthropological, and archaeological per-spectives in order to offer a comprehensive analysis of topics ranging from gender roles and female onomastics to power structures and the role of poets as social brokers, from Indo-European legal language and initiation rites to matrimonial practices and age-based social hierarchies. It provides fresh interpretations and new approaches to known material as well as novel explorations and unprece-dented analyses of new data.

The first section of the book, Gender, Power, and Language, deals with gen-der as both a grammatical and a social category, its interplay with language, and with the role that power relations have in shaping them both. Ulla Remmer’s contribution “How (not) to name a woman in Indo-European: The evidence of female onomastics for the status of women in Indo-European societies” discusses naming patterns for women and girls in Indo-Iranian and other Indo-European traditions as evidence for their lower social status compared to men, illustrated by the fact that a woman’s name was often simply a modification of her father’s or husband’s name. Tackling gender as a grammatical category, Stefan Höfler’s chapter “Gender in Indo-European: A synopsis” explores the development of the three-gender system and the origin of the feminine gender in IE, and investigates the role of gender in PIE grammar. In her study “Pan, Pūṣan, and their matrimo-nial functions”, Jil Schermutzki focuses on the long-established etymological and thematic connection between the Greek god Pan and the Indic god Pūṣan, dis-cussing their shared associations with marriage, matrimony, and fertility, which seem to provide further support to Pan and Pūṣan’s common descent from an inherited deity. In “The Charioteer Athena as goddess of warriors: Constellations and their role in the prehistory of Greek religion”, Michael Janda departs from a comparison of Athena’s role in the Iliad with the goddess Aṣ̌i’s in the Avestan tradition, identifying the latter with the constellation Auriga and investigating the origin of Athena in Indo-European starlore as a female charioteer who travels across the sky. Finally, Michael Weiss’s chapter “Quaecumque a Benveniste dicta essent, commenticia esse” is a careful critique of Émile Benveniste’s 1969 book, Le vocabulaire des institutions indo-européennes, probably one of the most cited

9Preface

works of Indo-European linguistics ever published, with special focus on three etymological topics closely linked to either gender or power: the two variants of the Indo-European ‘male, male animal’ word (*u̯r̥s-en- vs. *(h₁)r̥s-en-), the insti-tutions of the Latin cēnsor and cēnsus, and the concept of Latin auctoritās.

The second section, Power, Mobility, and Conflict, is devoted to the power dy-namics that underlie fundamental social institutions, including those linked with spatial and social mobility (such as guest-friendships and patron–client relations), as well as to the conflicts that may arise within them (and the resolution thereof). It explores how these dynamics shape and are shaped by social hierarchies and mobility patterns. Peter Jackson Rova’s Schleicher-inspired study “The wolf, the lamb, and the dog: An Aesopian guide to Indo-European sociology” departs from two Ancient Greek fables and takes them as useful tools to develop a model of Indo-European society that is based on four dimensions, distributed along a hori-zontal axis between domesticity and savagery, and a vertical one between dom-inance and submission. In “On the prehistory of legal language and procedure: Repairing a misdeed in Proto-Indo-European and in Core Indo-European”, José Luis García Ramón focuses on the two possible conceptualizations of the repara-tion of a misdeed attested in the legal lexicon and phraseology of various ancient IE traditions: the misdeed as something that must be ‘repaired, made good’ (likely already PIE), and the misdeed as something that the offender must ‘pay, atone’ for (probably later, Core IE). Riccardo Ginevra’s chapter “Indo-European patrons vs. clients, and the role of poets as social brokers: ‘Leaders’ vs. ‘friends’, and intelligent speakers in the mythologies of Scandinavia, India, and Rome” is devoted to the IE social institution of patron–client relationships, whose power dynamics are investigated through a comparative analysis of Norse, Indic, and Roman myths about ‘intelligent speakers’ (i.e., poets) acting as social brokers or mediators be-tween patrons and their clients. To close the section, Rune Iversen challenges the standard picture of pre-IE Europe as characterized by peaceful societies based on matrilineality and sex egalitarianism in his chapter “The violent Indo-Europeans: Some general thoughts on the martial influence of the Corded Ware on Neolithic societies”, and argues that the violent aspects of early Indo-European societies were already well-established elements in Neolithic Europe.

The third and final section, Mobility, Gender, and Social Structure, explores the ways in which mobility – whether spatial, social, or economic – intersects with gender norms and expectations, examining the resultant impacts on societal organization and hierarchies. This section also delves into the cultural and insti-tutional mechanisms, including initiation rites, that regulate mobility and gender, shedding light on the complex interdependencies that shape the lived experienc-

10 Preface

es of individuals within various IE societies. Mikkel Nørtoft’s chapter “An update on the Corded Ware culture: Formation and spread, social aspects, human–canid relations, and tooth and shell status items” integrates archaeolinguistic and bio-archaeological data to discuss both general social aspects of migrations from the steppe to Europe and human–canid relationships in (likely IE-speaking) Corded Ware societies, challenging, or at least supplementing, the widespread view that wolves/dogs were associated with young male warrior bands. Discussing inher-ited vocabulary pertaining to diverse forms of social relationships, Birgit Anette Olsen’s study “In-laws and outlaws in Indo-European societies: The master of the house and his circles of interest” explores the various strategies employed by aristocratic clan leaders to establish alliances with neighbours and gradual-ly extend their influence, including exogamous marriages, fosterage, patronage, and guest-friendship. Jan N. Bremmer’s chapter “Indo-European initiation: The Greek contribution” is an investigation into how Ancient Greek texts may pro-vide important data for the study of several features of male initiations in IE tra-ditions, such as hairstyles and wandering, and argues for a more differentiated usage of the term Männerbund within IE studies. Finally, Kim McCone’s contri-bution “(Proto-)Indo-European age-based male social hierarchies and groupings: Age-grades, sodalities, coevals, age-sets and the origins of Rome’s curiae (includ-ing the curia ‘senate-house’)” proposes the reconstruction of lifelong associations of coevals (so-called ‘age-sets’) as a prominent feature of Proto-Indo-European society, sets forth the evidence for this social institution in several IE traditions, and discusses the implications of this proposal for the study of linguistic and mythological peculiarities attested in texts from various ancient IE languages.

Focusing on three essential aspects of Indo-European society, namely power, gender, and mobility – of which at least the question of gender, the relations be-tween gender and power, and the role of the unprivileged are still insufficiently investigated – we are here trying to fill a gap in the study of the speakers of early Indo-European varieties and of their world. Extending the perspective from fam-ily structure, which was the overarching theme of the preceding volume in the series, Kin, clan and community in Indo-European society, to a broader scope of social phenomena, it has been our aim to reassess and elaborate on some of the vital questions raised by Benveniste 55 years ago, many of which still await a final answer.

Some of the chapters are based on papers that were originally presented at the online conference Power, gender and mobility: Features of Indo-European society, held on 26–27 March 2021 and organized by several members of the Roots of Europe research group at the University of Copenhagen, namely Adam Hyllest-

11Preface

ed, Benedicte Nielsen Whitehead, Birgit Anette Olsen, Guus Kroonen, Riccardo Ginevra, Simon Poulsen, and Stefan Höfler.

Part I Gender, Power, and LanGuaGe

How (not) to name a woman in Indo-European

The evidence of female onomastics for the status of women in Indo-European societies

Ulla Remmer Vienna

In Indo-European onomastics, gender issues have seldom been in focus.

Under the premise that a name is bestowed by the powerful onto the less

powerful, it is worth investigating female names in opposition to male

names in order to procure information on the social status of women. The

onomastic data of the oldest Indo-Iranian languages, as well as further evi-

dence from other ancient Indo-European languages, imply that the naming

of girls and women was executed with less individualizing intention than

the naming of boys and men. Female names are usually feminized male

names and tend to express the dependence of their bearers on their social

group, family, or husband, suggesting a lower social status of women in

ancient Indo-European societies.

The study of names is an important source of evidence in Indo-European linguis-tics. Even so, the naming of women has rarely received much attention within this field of study, and although one of the founding fathers of Indo-European linguistics, Jacob Grimm, gave a public speech on female names as early as 1852 (published in Grimm 1865), the number of publications on gender-sensitive ono mastics was tiny until the turn of the millennium (notable exceptions being Bechtel 1902, Boehler 1930, Zimmer 1995). This changed in 2002, when a research project was established at the university of Zurich.1 Building on the onomastic publications and standard works of such eminent scholars as Manfred Mayrhofer and Rüdiger Schmitt, it had a considerable output of publications, including the handbook Indogermanische Frauennamen (Stüber, Zehnder & Remmer 2009), with a synopsis of the naming traditions of various attested Indo-European lan-

1 The research project Die indogermanischen Frauennamen was founded by Michael Janda and led by Karin Stüber. It was funded by the Schweizerischer Nationalfonds (SNF; ‘Swiss National Science Foundation’).

16 Ulla Remmer

guages and a survey of reconstructed female names and name types in Proto- Indo- European (PIE), as well as their onomastic morphology.

Various issues in the present paper are presented in detail in Remmer (2006), Remmer (2007), and in the author’s articles on Indic, Iranian, and Germanic in the mentioned handbook. Apart from a few digressions to Ancient Greek, Latin, and Germanic languages, the focus of this paper will be on the data provided by the Indo-Iranian languages and their oldest text corpora. Because of their an-tiqui ty and the amount of surviving archaic texts, this group forms one – though not the only – important pillar for the reconstruction of PIE.2

1 Indo-European and Indo-Iranian preliminaries

As is well known, the PIE language is not directly attested and can only be re-constructed on the basis of its daughter languages. When trying to investigate the onomastics of ancient Indo-European societies we have to rely on the data provided by the literatures and literary remnants of the attested linguistic succes-sor cultures, which, ranging from inscriptions and short texts on administration to poetic texts of valued literature, are diverse and chronologically disparate and cannot be compared to each other easily.

The Indo-Iranian languages are divided into the Indic branch on the one hand, with Sanskrit and its more archaic variety Vedic as its earliest-attested languages, and the Iranian branch on the other hand, with Avestan and Old Persian as the oldest attested languages. These ancient Indo-Iranian languages are phonologi-cally and morphologically still very alike. Moreover, their societies share the lin-guistic feature of using a variant of the term *ā̆r(i)ya- for self-designation,3 which is used also as a lexical element in human names (cf. below).

2 The equally relevant Anatolian languages, among them Hittite and Luwian, will not be considered here, since these languages differ fundamentally from the rest of Indo- European languages, including the striking lack of a feminine–masculine distinction in their grammar. Accordingly Anatolian languages have a different system of gender onomastics, as described by Zehnder (2009, 2010). According to a theory supported by many Indo-European scholars the Anatolian languages branched off from PIE earlier than all other sub-families. When referring to (P)IE excluding the evidence given by the Anatolian languages, some scholars would speak of ‘(Proto-)Core Indo- European’ or ‘(Proto-)Nuclear Indo-European’, others of ‘(Proto-)Indo-Tocharian’ (thus Olander 2019). In this article the term Proto-Indo-European (PIE) will be used for a (model of) reconstruction as implied by the evidence of the mentioned languages minus Anatolian.

3 Vedic ā́rya- (ā́riya-), Younger Avestan airiia-, Old Persian ariya-, Middle Persian ēr,

17How (not) to name a woman in Indo-European

The Old Indic Rigveda, a collection of mostly religious hymns, includes around 500 male names, but only 25–30 female ones. This is only an estimate, since in this prehistoric culture the border between names, epithets and other appellative words is not sharply drawn, making exact counting difficult. The Old Iranian Avesta, a collection of the earliest Zoroastrian religious texts, comprises around 400 male names vs. around 28 female ones, most of them attested within the religious text Yašt 13 in a list of the members of the first community of the Mazda-religion. This cult was established by the prominent religious founder Zo-$roaster, or Zaraθuštra as attested in his own language that we know as ‘Avestan’ $today. Since both the hymns of the Indic Rigveda and the Zoroastrian texts of the Iranian Avesta were transmitted only by oral tradition for centuries, they cannot be dated precisely. Linguistic and historical estimations indicate that they were composed and compiled before or around 1000 bce; however, the oldest textual strata of the Rigveda and the Avesta are definitely older and probably date from approximately 1200 bce.

The second ancient Iranian language, Old Persian, shows a completely different picture as regards its transmission: the inscriptions of the Achaemenid kings pro-vide 47–50 male names of Iranian origin, but not a single female name. Fortunately, many names, among them various female names of Ancient Persia, are attested in texts of neighboring or other contact languages (the so-called ‘Nebenüberlie-ferung’). Most important are, on the one hand, the reports of Greek historians, with their partly florid, tendentious and biased accounts, and on the other hand the cu-neiform clay tablets written in Elamite, excavated in Persepolis, with minimal and sober texts more or less restricted to administrative matters.4 Mayrhofer (OnP) lists a number of 1892 personal names transmitted in Elamite tablets, of which roughly 80% represent names of Old Iranian origin (of the remaining non-Iranian forms the majority is of Elamite origin, cf. OnP 11.3 pp. 304ff.). Only 90–93 entries of OnP are female, a considerable number compared to the rates of the Rigveda and the Avesta, but likewise assuredly including non-Iranian forms. Unfortunately, these non-Iranian names in many cases are hard to identify since, to make things worse, the Elamite version of cuneiform does not adequately convey all aspects of Old Iranian phonology, so that many forms attested on the tablets, though clearly

point to an Indo-Iranian ethnonym *Hā̆r(H)ya- ‘(Indo-Iranian) people’. 4 Published in great part in Cameron (1948) and Hallock (1969). The onomastic material

is treated in Onomastica Persepolitana by Manfred Mayrhofer (1973, here cited as OnP) and Tavernier (2007); the transliterations of the various cited names are taken over from the latter here. For further information on the transmission of Persian and Irani-an cf. Stüber, Zehnder & Remmer (2009: 195ff).

marked as male or female names, are difficult to analyze linguistically, and their exact Persian forms remain unclear. The diagnostic value of this corpus of names and its statistical significance is thus limited to certain issues.

2 Initial questions

At the outset of this survey, two fields of questions arise:

1 What are the differences between names of women and men, and where do they arise? In the following sections, I will contrast the morphology of female names with that of male names and analyze them diachronically. Moreover, I will explore morphological phenomena which are shared by masculine and feminine names but show divergent rates of usage. In ad-dition, I will evaluate whether it is possible to establish differences in the choice of lexemes and in semantics.

2 What evidence do names provide for the status of women in the various Indo-European cultures and in Proto-Indo-European society? It seems worthwhile to investigate the differences between male and female names under the premise that name-giving is an act bestowed by the powerful onto the less powerful. What relations of power can be deduced from a differentiated look on female and male onomastics?

3 Onomastic morphology: ‘Motion’ as the process of grammatical feminization

The prototypical human name in Indo-European is a two-stem full name (in Ger-man: ‘Vollname’), i.e., a compound of two lexical elements; but there are also names consisting of only one lexical stem. In many instances female names differ from male names simply by the use of a ‘motion’ suffix (in German: ‘Motions-suffix’), which transfers a word or a name to feminine gender. In the ancient In-do-European languages there are many pairs of female and male names differing only in the presence or absence of feminine ‘motion’. Accordingly, female names mostly convey the same semantics as male names, as in the two following Greek examples. These compounds, denoting ‘having a manly battle’ and ‘having fallow horses’, reflect the areas of horse- or cattle-breeding and war experience, which are traditionally seen as male occupations:

19How (not) to name a woman in Indo-European

$ Ἀνδρόμαχος m. vs. Ἀνδρομάχη f. Ξάνθιππος m. vs. Ξανθίππη f. $

The origin of ‘motion’ and the rise of the feminine gender is a frequently and hotly disputed issue in Indo-European studies, and it cannot be discussed here,5 but the most common IE ‘motion’ suffixes contain the PIE phoneme *-h₂-. The vast majority of feminine nouns are endowed either with the suffix reconstructed as

*-eh₂- (also found in the two Greek female names cited above), which appears in Indo-Iranian as -ā- (e.g., Vedic Indrasenā́-), or with the suffix *-ih₂- that results in Indo-Iranian -ī- (e.g., Avestan Huuōuuī-).6

Most scholars agree that one of the ‘motion’ suffixes par excellence, *-ih₂-, had the basic function of appurtenance and was used to form derivatives of the meaning ‘belonging to X’. One often cited example is the Greek word for ‘bee’, $μέλισσα < *melit-i̯a < *melit-ih₂-, which was originally an *-ih₂-derivative of the $word for ‘honey’ and meant ‘the honey-ish one’ or ‘the one affiliated with honey’. This basic feature of the ‘motion’ suffix alone suggests that women in PIE society are onomastically defined by their relationship to others, possibly by their group, family, parents, husbands.

4 Onomastic modification: Abbreviations and hypocoristics

Abbreviation is a common feature of onomastic morphology, ubiquitously in use in today’s languages, as shown by examples like Pat for both male Patrick and female Patricia, or Beth and Liz, both abbreviations for the female name Elizabeth. Unsurprisingly, abbreviation also occurs in the onomastics of the early Indo- European societies and turns up occasionally in the many male Indo- Iranian names. In rare instances both name versions are found denoting one and the same person – e.g., the Vedic name Śyāvā́śva- ‘with/having dark horses’, whose bearer on one occasion is called simply Śyāvá-. Strikingly, even within the small sample of Avestan female names, there is a group of forms that appear to be ab-breviated versions of two-stem full names known from male persons:7

In the Old Indic branch, the name turns up already in the Mitanni tablets as Šu-wa-ar-da-ta and in Sanskrit as Sūryadatta-, the latter with the replacement of the first element by the related usual Sanskrit word for ‘sun’.8

Such a pairing of a name attested in its full form in the masculine and as an abbreviated form in the feminine is found also in the onomastics of Ancient Per-sia: next to the Old Iranian female name *Mandanā-, transmitted by Herodotus $as Μανδάνη, there is the male two-stem full name *Ariya-manda-, transmitted by the Greek historians as Ἀριομάνδης. *Mandanā- is most likely a feminine $abbreviation of this name, with the frequent onomastic suffix -ā̆na- (feminine

-ā̆nā-) added on. Both historic persons are members of the Old Persian ruling $dynasties. In fact, Μανδάνη, a Median princess by origin, wife of the Persian king Kambyses I and mother of Cyrus II, is an ancestor of Ἀριομάνδης, known as the $military leader in the battle of the Eurymedon (466/465 bce). The compound name *Ariya- manda- means ‘giving joy to the Aryas or Aryan people’ and is built with the already mentioned word for ‘Indic/Iranian people’ as well as with a form

21How (not) to name a woman in Indo-European

of the Indo-Iranian verbal root *ma(n)d- ‘rejoice, give pleasure’. That this name long precedes the days of Cyrus II is shown by the fact that it is also attested in Indic, albeit in a slightly different shape, as the Rigvedic male name Māndāryá-. This form represents a patronymic formation ‘descendent of *Manda-ā/ar(i)ya-’ which matches the Iranian full name *Ariya-manda- except for the inversion of its constituents.9

So, again, we find this pattern: a woman carries a shortened name that lacks the full linguistic and onomastic information, while the full version is attested among the male names. It is striking that even within the small corpus of Avestan female names a substantial number of shortened names occur, and, furthermore, that both in Avestan and in Old Persian a full male name is found next to its abbreviated female version within one and the same family. These observations suggest that there is a gender variance with respect to the rate of occurrences – that women are called by abbreviated names more often than men.

A further instance of this ‘Mandanā- phenomenon’ with a similar pairing is found in Old Germanic with the lexeme *hlewaz ‘glory’, the Germanic descendant of the synonymous and onomastically very important PIE word *k̑léu̯os. In the standard work Lexikon der altgermanischen Namen by Hermann Reichert (LaN), only two personal names of antiquity are mentioned with this lexeme: the well-known masculine two-stem full name Hlewagastiz, attested on the horn of Galle-hus and one of the earliest known Old Germanic names, and the less prominent female name Chlevvia,10 obviously a feminine abbreviation of either Hlewagastiz or another full name containing *hlewaz.

Hypocoristic versions of names are very frequent in the onomastic systems of ancient Indo-European societies, for both men and women. Suffixes that form hypocoristics often have diminutive meaning and carry affective connotations. One of the most common hypocoristic suffixes in Indo-Iranian is -kā̆- with its variants -akā̆-, -ikā̆-, -ukā̆-. It is attested more often in classical Sanskrit and in Old Persian than in the Rigveda and the Avesta. For instance, the feminine coun-terpart to the Sanskrit male name Chandaka- is found in the Old Persian tradi-$tion as Σανδάκη; suffixal variations are attested as male Σανδώκης and female Σανδαύκη (name of a daughter of Dareios I). $

9 Inversion of constituents is a well-known phenomenon in Indo-European onomastics. $For a more thorough presentation of the group Μανδάνη, Ἀριομάνδης, and Māndāryá-, $cf. Remmer (fc.).

10 Reichert LaN I/ii, p. 547. The female name is attested as Clhevvia in CIL XIII.1882, cf. LaN I/ii, p. 202.

22 Ulla Remmer

Here again the question arises, whether the phenomenon under investigation has divergent rates of usage according to gender. At this point, it is worth con-sidering the Old Iranian names provided by the Elamite cuneiform tablets, since their numbers seem sufficiently high to allow some statistical measuring. The corpus contains names of men and women of various social statuses, including names of common workers as well as high-ranking administrative staff, and even members of the ruling family. As stated above, the interpretation of these name forms is often blurred by the ‘disguise’ of Elamite cuneiform writing. However, short name forms and names with the -kā̆-suffix and its variants can be quite safely diagnosed, even if the lexemes on which the names are built remain unclear in many cases.

A counting of the names of the Elamite tablets listed by Mayrhofer in OnP re-veals that, compared to male names, female names show more hypocoristic forms (most common -akā- and -ukā-), which for the most part consist of only one lexeme. Of the 1892 entries in OnP (pp. 121–258) approx. 90–95 names are clearly marked as female (cf. above). To make a balanced comparison between male and female names, some 40 forms known from the Elamite versions of the subcorpus of Achaemenid royal inscriptions should be excluded, since in these inscription-al texts women are not mentioned. Among the remaining male names (approx. 1760) a search for two-stem full names (i.e., without hypocoristic or patronym-ic suffixes) reveals around 250 forms (14,2%); and approximately 290 masculine forms (ca. 16%) are supposedly built with hypocoristic -ka- and its variants, most of them -(a)uka- and -aka-. Among the female names, the application of the same criteria yields 11–14 assumed full names and no less than 29 names (more than 30%) with a variant of -kā-, again mostly -(a)ukā- and -akā-. These figures seem to suggest that women were much more often called by a hypocoristic name using the -kā̆-suffix. Especially instructive is tablet PF 2038 (Hallock 1969: 629), dealing with the monthly rations of a group of male and female workers, which names 22 women, no fewer than 9 of whom have a name with hypocoristic -(V)kā-.11

Onomastic abbreviation and the use of hypocoristic suffixes is frequently found also among high-ranking people, including members of the royal Persian dynasties and nobility; examples include the woman Iš-ti-in who is mentioned on the Elamite tablets along with her title dukšiš, probably a word for ‘princess’. Her

The likelihood that these names are one-stem names and abbreviations is high. Other possible female hypocoristic forms on this tablet are U-še-ma, Ku-ra-a-za, Su-iz-za und Šá-iz-zí-iš. A one-stem name without suffix is Ba-u-da.

name is a one-stem abbreviation of a full name based on Old Persian r̥šti- ‘spear’ or the equivalent of Avestan ī̆šti- ‘prosperity, wealth’ and suffixed with the hypo-$coristic -inā̆-, which is also found in Βαρσίνη, name of a great-granddaughter of Artaxerxes II. Both Βαρσίνη and the male name of prince Bardiya-/Br̥diya- (second son of Cyrus II) are abbreviations of a compound name like *Miθra-$br̥zā̆nā̆- ‘raising/magnifying (god) Mithra’,12 albeit in two different dialects of Old Iranian. This onomastic compound is found also in Elamite as Mi-za-bìr-za-ka₄ attested as the name of a high-ranking woman, not abbreviated but with $the -kā̆-suffix.13 Σανδαύκη, daughter of Dareios I, was already mentioned. The $freedom with which the -kā̆-suffix was used is illustrated by a Persian queen who was the daughter of Cyrus II and one of the wives of king Darius I. Her name $is given by Herodotus as Ἀρτυστώνη and on the Elamite tablets as Ir-taš-du-na, $both forms pointing to *R̥tastūnā- as the original Persian form, with r̥ta- ‘truth’ as first element. On one tablet (PF 730) the scribe names her Ir-taš-du-na-ik-ka (probably for *R̥tastūnakā-) with the hypocoristic -kā̆-suffixed form, despite the power imbalance between the queen (according to Herodotus the king’s favorite wife) and himself, a clerk of the palace.14

In contrast, in the closely related and more archaic Avestan language, the suffix had pejorative connotations. Among the hundreds of male names it is only awk-ward figures, enemies of the Mazda religion, whose names exhibit the -kā̆- suffix.15 It seems that by calling somebody by such a name one would additionally express that this person is of inferior state in matters of morals and religion. On the list of the truthful followers, -kā̆-suffixed names are almost totally absent, with only one exception: the female name Kanukā-, meaning roughly something like ‘(female) youngster, girlie’. Thus, the only person in the list of first Mazdayaznian believers whose name attests this depreciatory and patronizing element is female. Consid-ering the enormous overabundance of male names attested in Avestan in general (see above), this is a possible piece of onomastic evidence of the lower status of women in prehistoric Indo-Iranian society.

24 Ulla Remmer

5 The name formula: Patronyms and pro-patronyms

In ancient Indo-European societies, filiation or other expressions of origin could be added as a name-like formation: patronyms and pro-patronyms express the descendance from father or grandfather. Women, too, could have patronyms and other filiation expressions, cf. the woman’s name Pā́vīravī- ‘daughter of Pávīru-’ attested in the Rigveda, or names of the structure X-putrī- ‘daughter of X’, com-posed with the lexeme putrī- ‘daughter’. A famous example is provided by the wife of the five Pāṇḍava-brothers in the Mahābhārata, who is far better known by her patronym Draupadī- ‘daughter of Drupada-’ than by her individual name Kr̥ṣṇā-. Occasionally women are onomastically defined as the mothers of their sons, e.g., Sanskrit Bharataprasū- ‘having given birth to Bharata’.

On the other hand, as expected in a patrilinear society, metronyms, i.e., names or epithets revealing the mother’s name, are hardly found. In Late Vedic texts, metronyms are attested in the name of some Brahmin men. These names, called ‘Neo-Metronymika’ by Schmitt (1995: 652b), are of the shape X-putra- ‘son of (the woman) X’, with X being itself a feminine patronym. So, for example, the male name Gautamīputra- means ‘son of (the woman) Gautamī- (= daughter or female descendant of the man Gautama- or Gotama-)’. These neo-metronyms were not built to express reverence towards the bearer’s mother herself but rather, as Paul Horsch (1965: 227–246) explains, to signify that his Brahmin origin was ‘impec-cable’ not only on the father’s but also on the mother’s side. Such a statement was seen as necessary in times when the observance of the strict rules of separation between the castes was felt to be declining.16

6 Family names

Likewise, a name referring to the family of origin can be added, being usual-$ly modeled on the name of a forefather or remote ancestor. Zaraθuštra himself is sometimes referred to with the bipartite name formula Zaraθuštra- Spitāma- ‘Zaraθuštra of the Spitāma family’. In very restricted contexts Zaraθuštra appears $only with his family name, as in the vocative expression Spitama ‘Oh Spitāmid!’. Women can likewise have a family name added to the individual name, as seen $in the case of Zaraθuštra’s daughter Pourucistā- who in one attestation is even $named with a tripartite name formula: Pourucistā- Haēcat̰.aspānā- Spitāmī-. Haē-

16 See also Stüber, Zehnder & Remmer (2009: 153–155) on this matter.

25How (not) to name a woman in Indo-European

cat̰.aspānā- denotes her descendance from the Haēcat̰.aspa-clan which is said to $be closely related to Zaraθuštra (cf. Remmer 2006: 210). $

Besides, in Avestan society, women could be named with their family name $throughout, as seen with Zaraθuštra’s wife, whose individual name is not trans-$mitted: she is known exclusively by her family name Huuōuuī-, which just means ‘member of the Huuōuua- family’. In contrast, her male relatives are named with a bipartite name formula, with the family name added to the individual name: Frašaoštra- Huuōuua- and Jāmāspa- Huuōuua-. In being called only by the family name, the woman Huuōuuī- is granted less onomastic individuality than her male relatives who are known in society with both family name and individual name. A similar, albeit less conclusive, instance of this is the name of a woman called Asa-banā-. Probably also a family name, its masculine form is used as an epithet of two men negatively characterized in a semi-mythological context: Kara- Asabana- and Vara- Asabana-. Since the name Asabanā̆- has no stringent Avestan etymology and its phonology is atypical of Younger Avestan, its origins may lie in either another Iranian tribe or an ethnic group of non-Iranian origin. If so, the name Asabanā- would actually convey the meaning ‘woman of the foreign Asabana-clan’.

This custom of calling women only by their family name is reminiscent of the official naming system in ancient Rome where women were exclusively identified by the nomen gentile (the family name) of their fathers, while male citizens bore the tria nomina (praenomen, nomen gentile, and cognomen). Any girl or woman descending from the gens Iulia was thus compulsorily known by the name Iulia, as in the case of both the daughters of Gaius Iulius Caesar and his adoptive son Gaius Iulius Caesar Octavianus (later known simply as Caesar Augustus). Further identifi-cations, such as Iulia Caesaris filia or Iulia Augusti filia, or the rare and exceptional attestations of female praenomina, however necessary, had no official character.17 The combined evidence of the Avestan female names with Huuōuuī- and Asabanā- on the one hand and the Roman naming system on the other could suggest a ten-dency already in PIE to call girls and women more often by their family name, the rigid Roman system reflecting a unique and extreme development of this tendency.

7 Gamonyms or matrimonial names

When entering into a marriage, one partner often customarily takes over the name of the other; in the vast majority of Western and European cultures, it has

17 Cf. Stüber (2009: 224–230) for details on the female praenomina in Latin and Italic.

26 Ulla Remmer

been the woman who takes on the name of her husband. There is evidence for reconstructing this custom back to prehistoric Indo-European cultures. In Old Indic, matrimonial names could be made simply by ‘motion’, i.e., by transferring the male partner’s name into feminine gender (cf. Hilka 1910: 148), but there are also other ways to form gamonyms (cf. Remmer 2009a: 155). A peculiar process of deriving gamonyms from i-stems is found in Vedic, by which the wife of the male god Agní- ‘fire’ becomes Agnā́yī- ‘wife of Agni’ or ‘Mrs. Agni’. The stem suffix

-i- of the base-word agní- ‘fire’ undergoes a process of lengthening or ‘upgrading’ to a long diphthong -āy- before adding the usual ‘motion’ suffix -ī-. Synchronical-ly, this gamonymic process, attested by few but secure examples, appears strange and archaic; but from an Indo-European viewpoint, it can be subsumed under a securely reconstructed derivational process in PIE, by which adjectives of ap-purtenance were formed based on sonorant-stem nouns. Thus, the female gamo-nyms that ultimately result from this derivational type – again – had the original meaning ‘belonging to (the husband) X’.18

Furthermore, the PIE shape of the diphthong of this adjective of appurtenance probably was *-ō̆i̯-, and in Ancient Greek, female names with the suffix *-ō̆i̯- are $very common – both mythological names like the goddess Λητώ and the Nereid Δωτώ and historical names like the poet Σαπφώ. Obviously, the PIE feminine ga-$monyms in *-ō̆i̯- became frequently used at some early stage of ancient Greek his-tory, hiving off from their original function as gamonyms of male i-stem names to make *-ō̆i̯- an independent suffix for creating feminine hypocoristics and indi-vidualizing formations.19

It should further be noted that such adjectives of appurtenance in *-ō̆i̯- would originally have been both feminine and masculine. Thus, by means of this word formation process, one could theoretically create not only female names but also male ones denoting ‘belonging to’. However, for some pragmatic reason, their use in onomastics became restricted to deriving female names. The explanation that suggests itself is that women had a reduced legal status and were dependent on

18 For a parallel process with u-stems and a detailed presentation of the phenomenon under discussion, cf. Remmer (2007).

$19 Besides this, there is a group of personifications of the type φειδώ ‘thrift’ that seman-$tically emerge from a transition zone between onomastical and appellative formations and can be analyzed in the same way as German personalized abstracts like ‘Frau Spar-samkeit’. The suffix is still productive in Modern Greek, an illustrating example being $μαλάκω, which turned up at the end of the 20th century as the female counterpart of the widespread masculine slang word μαλάκας (roughly ‘weakling’).$

27How (not) to name a woman in Indo-European

their husbands, whereas men, apart from slaves, were free – a fundamental differ-ence expressed here by onomastic morphology.

8 ‘Female’ semantics in women’s names and female Nachbenennung

Another question that deserves attention is whether women’s names show spe-cial or ‘female’ semantics and lexicon. In an article entitled “Frauennamen aus Blumen”, Jacob Grimm (1865) argued for a tendency of female names being built on lexemes of the floral world. Grimm’s material, the basis of his argument, was too recent and barely covered the prehistoric dimension of PIE onomastics; still, several linguists, philologists, and Iranologists have advocated such gender-based interpretations of female names in several past studies of ancient Indo-Iranian onomastics. ‘Feminine’ semantics such as ‘having long eyelashes’ or ‘desiring jewels’ were attached to names that were clearly feminine but not amenable to easy interpretation, and female names were unhesitatingly, but with little cogent reason, translated with feminine semantics. On closer consideration and with today’s knowledge, most examples of these highly individualizing interpretations that ‘play the gender card’, cannot be maintained20 and must be replaced by others that belong to familiar ‘male’ semantic spheres, such as war, virtue, patriotism, horsemanship, and cattle-breeding.

$An example is the name of Hutaosā-, wife of Zaraθuštra’s patron Vīštāspa. $Hutaosā- is revered in Zoroastrian religion for the crucial role attributed to her in $the reformation of Zaraθuštra. For a long time in the relevant literature, her name $was interpreted as ‘having beautiful thighs’, as proposed by James Darmesteter in 1884.21 Since this interpretation was based on a far-fetched and linguistically disputable equation of the second element taosa- with Old High German dioh and English thigh, Mayrhofer justifiably compared taosa- with the Old Indic root $√toś instead and corrected the denotation of the name first to ‘donating well, with $good gifts’ (Mayrhofer 1977: 39f), and later, after a reinterpretation of the mean-$ing of the root √toś, to ‘the one who presses, thrusts herself much’ (Mayrhofer in EWAia I 671f.). However, the Sogdian name γʾwtws ‘driving cattle’, with its $

20 Cf. Remmer (2006: 16–23, 242–246 and, specifically on the Avestan female name form Paēsaŋhanuua-, 180–190).

21 Cf. Bartholomae (1904: 1822). See also Stüber, Zehnder & Remmer (2009: 15–17) on this issue.

28 Ulla Remmer

second element tws- matching taosa-, suggests that the name Hutaosā- may also belong to the semantic sphere of stock farming, and that the compound name $originally meant ‘having good driving’ → ‘driving (cattle, horses etc.) well’ (cf. $Remmer 2006: 132ff). Accordingly, Hutaosā- can be seen as a further example of a feminized name originally deriving from the male sphere and cannot serve as evidence for the existence of female names expressing female features or virtues. Undoubtedly, there are names of the semantic sphere of physical appearance, but they are not at all restricted to an exclusively female ideal of beauty – as seen with the name complex Frə̄nah-, Frāniia- and Frə̄nī- (see section 4 above).

Subsequently in the Iranian world, the compound name Hutaosā- came to be restricted to being used as a female name in remembrance of its prominent Zoroastrian female bearer, comparable to names of female Christian saints in Europe.22 In the Achaemenid dynasty, at least two or three female members are $named with a Persian equivalent, transmitted in the forms Ἄτοσσα by the Greek $historians and Ú-tam-sa-na and Ú-du-sa-na-na on the Elamite tablets. The first $and most famous Achaemenid name bearer, Ἄτοσσα (I), was (like her sister, the already mentioned Ἀρτυστώνη) wife to Darius I and daughter to Cyrus II (cf. $Remmer 2006: 132ff and 2009b: 200f). This makes Hutaosā-, or rather its Persian version, the first attested instance of female ‘Nachbenennung’ (i.e., the naming of somebody in remembrance of another person) in Iranian, but it cannot be used as an argument for female semantics in women’s names.

However, a few other Avestan names deserve some attention in this regard.23 First, there is the already mentioned name Kanukā- which most likely means $something like ‘(female) fresher, girl’. Second, there is the female name Vaδut- $with a peculiar t-stem morphology instead of one of the typical ‘motion’ suffixes. $The lexeme on which the name is built resembles the Avestan word vaδū- (Ved. vadhū́-) ‘bride, young woman’. A third formation, *Jaγrut-, cannot be connect-$ed to an existing word, but with its initial reduplication syllable (ja-), which in nominal morphology sometimes conveys iterative function, it may have meant ‘(woman) who often/usually bears (children)’, i.e., ‘fertile woman’, as opposed to $the well- attested privative compound aγrū- (Ved. agrū́-) ‘not having given birth; $unmarried woman, young woman’. The Avestan appellative compound huzāmit- ‘giving birth easily/having delivered easily’, a derivative of huzāmi- ‘easy delivery’ and likewise a t-stem, fits these interpretations. These three onomastic forms in-

29How (not) to name a woman in Indo-European

deed seem to carry a specifically feminine meaning. However, they do so without any individualizing nuance. Quite the contrary, in fact: the semantics refer to very general aspects of womanhood, namely phases of physical development and fertility. Characteristically, the suffix -t- serves (among other functions) to create designations for female beings, including female animals, in Old Indic (cf. AiGr II,2: 321f §205).

9 Conclusion

Various historical disciplines give information on the status of women in ancient Indo-European societies – history, archaeology, literature, mythology, etc. – and provide evidence that women were not entirely without rights but could have a certain social influence. In the Zoroastrian tradition, for instance, Hutaosā, wife of the ruler Vīštāspa, had a crucial role in the establishment of the Zoroastrian re-ligion. In later Vedic literature, female rishis (sage poets) appear. And as Brosius (1996) has shown, the clay tablets of Persepolis provide evidence that in Ancient Persia, some women had substantial influence in administration and were finan-cially independent and legally responsible. The evidence provided by onomastics, however, does not corroborate the view of an emancipated female part of society in prehistoric times:

- Most female names are feminized male names.
- Women are often named after their family or marriage partner.
- Female onomastic morphology is a specialization of appurtenance morphol-

ogy: women often have ‘dependent’ names (gamonyms or family names).

- Modification of full names (shortening, hypocoristification) occurs more

often than among male names.

- There is little evidence for specific semantics of female names, apart from

very general non-individualizing meanings referring to womanhood and fertility.

These facts show that, compared to men, the naming of girls and women in the ancient Indo-European world was almost devoid of individualization. A gender- based study of names supports the assumption of a patrilinear and patriarchal structure of the ancient Indo-European world and PIE society. Altogether, the evidence which names can provide clearly suggests that women in prehistoric Indo-European societies had a dependent and lower status.
