Gender in Indo-European

A synopsis

Stefan Höfler Austrian Academy of Sciences / University of Vienna

Grammatical gender is one of the most interesting categories in the world’s

languages. Within the prehistory of the Indo-European family, we can dis-

cern a shift from an earlier two-gender system to a three-gender system,

distinguishing masculine, feminine, and neuter nouns. This paper gives

an overview of how this gender distinction plays out in the grammar, ad-

dressing gender agreement in pronouns, numerals, and adjectives. It then

focuses on the origin of the feminine gender, which has been a hotly de-

bated question in Indo-European linguistics for over a century. Finally, the

paper provides an overview of what groups of nouns typically take femi-

nine gender in the Indo-European languages and tries to investigate the

mechanisms behind these assignment rules.1

Grammatical gender is not only one of the most intriguing phenomena in the languages of the world, it is also “perhaps the only grammatical category that ever evoked passion – and not only among linguists” (Matasović 2004: 13). In 2019, for example, the US-based dictionary Merriam-Webster named the non-binary pro-noun they their word of the year,2 catching the attention of many media outlets around the globe, and in 2021, a heated debate over gender-neutral language in the Duden, the preeminent dictionary of Standard German, filled the arts sec-tions and op-ed pages of many German newspapers.

1 This paper was written during the project Of beasts and men. The animals of the Proto- Indo-Europeans, which received funding from the European Union’s Horizon 2020 re-search and innovation program under the Marie Skłodowska-Curie grant agreement No. H2020-MSCA-IF-2018-835954.

2 See https://www.merriam-webster.com/wordplay/words-of-the-year-decade-in-review (19 February 2024).

34 Stefan Höfler

1 A fascinating category

The fascinating thing about grammatical gender is that it has “obvious links to the real world”, namely “in the connection between many grammatical gender systems and biological sex” (Corbett 2014: 1). Compare the following sentences:

(1) She likes apples. (2) He likes oranges.

In these phrases, the pronouns she and he do not just refer to two individuals who like apples and oranges, respectively, they also tell us whether the person referred to is (or is perceived as) a woman (she) or a man (he). The French pronouns elle and il fulfill the same function (Elle aime les pommes. Il aime les oranges.), but unlike their English counterparts3 they also express grammatical gender.

(3) Voilà la table. Elle est pleine de fruits. “Here is the table. It is full of fruit.”

(4) Voilà le feu. Il est très chaud. “Here is the fire. It is very hot.”

The French language has a full-fledged system of grammatical gender, in which every noun belongs to either the masculine or the feminine class. Even though the table (la table) is not a biological female, it is grammatically feminine and therefore requires the use of the anaphorical pronoun elle ‘she’, just as the fire (le feu) is taken up as il ‘he’. Depending on the gender of a given noun, certain other words (determiners, pronouns, adjectives) are required to appear in the correct corresponding form, e.g., La table est pleine ‘the.f.sg table.f.sg is full.f.sg’ (vs. plein ‘full.m.sg’) and Le feu est chaud ‘the.m.sg fire.m.sg is hot.m.sg’ (vs. chaude ‘hot.f.sg’).

For native speakers of French or many other European languages, grammati-cal gender does not seem like a big deal. Kids learn the gender of any noun auto-matically, mostly without questioning this system. Even for speakers of English and other languages that lack a fully gender-based noun classification system, the fact that pronouns can express the biological sex (and/or social gender) of the referent does not appear overly exotic. Yet, there are many languages in which

3 The  feminine pronoun she is sometimes used to refer to ships, churches, islands, or nation states.

35Gender in Indo-European

the biological sex of referents does not find an expression at all in the grammar of the language. For instance, the Finnish pronoun hän can refer to a person of any gender, as can Hungarian ő.

(5) Ő szereti az almát. “He/She likes apples.”

Gender is therefore by no means a universal feature of language. According to The World Atlas of Language Structures, from a sample of 256 languages of the world, 144 (approximately 56%) do not have a gender system (cf. Corbett 2013), including languages as diverse as Turkish, Mandarin Chinese, Maori, Nahuatl, and West Greenlandic. The fact that most European languages do exhibit gram-matical gender in some way or other is directly linked to Indo-European heritage.

2 But what exactly is gender?

Charles Hockett proposed a definition of the term ‘gender’ that still seems valid today:

Genders are classes of nouns reflected in the behavior of associated words. (Hockett 1958: 231)

These “associated words”, i.e., the words that take on different forms depending on the gender of the noun, can be of several different categories. We see gender in pronouns, as in English he/she(/they), which mostly coincide with biological sex, but also in German er/sie/es or French il/elle, used for both biological sex and grammatical gender. Many languages express gender in articles or determiners, as for example French (6) or Czech (7).

(6) la femme le garçon the.f.sg woman.f.sg the.m.sg boy.m.sg la table le feu the.f.sg table.f.sg the.m.sg fire.m.sg

(7) moje dcera můj syn my.f.sg daughter.f.sg my.m.sg son.m.sg moje země můj stůl my.f.sg country.f.sg my.m.sg table.m.sg

36 Stefan Höfler

Another place where we see gender is in adjectives, as for instance in the following noun phrases from Ancient Greek (8) and Middle Welsh (9).

$(8) ὠκέα Ἶρις ὠκὺς Ἀχιλλεύς $swift.f.sg Iris.f.sg swift.m.sg Achilles.m.sg

(9) croen gwynn gwreic wenn skin.m.sg white.m.sg woman.f.sg white.f.sg

Some languages also exhibit gender marking in verbs, as for example Modern Hebrew (e.g., katávt ‘you.f.sg.wrote’ vs. katávta ‘you.m.sg.wrote’); in the Indo- European languages, this is not very common, though.4

The systematic influence of nouns on their associated words is called agree-$ment or concord. In the noun phrases from (8), the adjective ὠκέα ‘swift.f.sg’ agrees with the grammatically feminine Ἶρις ‘Iris’ and ὠκύς ‘swift.m.sg’ agrees with the masculine Ἀχιλλεύς ‘Achilles’. $

(10) et stort hus en stor have ‘a big house’ ‘a big garden’

In the Danish phrases in (10), both the determiner (et) as well as the adjective (stor-t) agree with the neuter gender of hus ‘house’. In en stor have, the common gender noun have ‘garden’ requires a different determiner (en) and a different agreement form of the adjective (stor). Agreement is thus an important compo-nent of morphosyntax in many Indo-European languages.

3 Two genders vs. three genders

Most branches of the Indo-European family attest a three-gender system of mas-culine vs. feminine vs. neuter. This is reflected in the Indo-Iranian branch, in Balto-Slavic, in Greek, Italic, Germanic, Celtic, and – with some idiosyncratic de-velopments – in Tocharian and Albanian (cf. Matasović 2004: 33–72). Armenian has lost all trace of grammatical gender. Most scholars agree nowadays that the three-gender system is inherited from a common ancestor of all these branches. They also agree, however, that this system evolved from an earlier two-gender

4 An exception is the Slavic preterite (e.g., Russian ona znala ‘she knew’ vs. on znal ‘he knew’), which goes back to a construction involving a participle.

37Gender in Indo-European

system (common gender vs. neuter), which some argue is still reflected in the Anatolian branch, as this is widely believed to be the first branch to have split off from the family. In what follows, I will use the term Proto-Indo-European to refer to the proto-language of all Indo-European branches, and Core Indo-European for the stage after the split-off of the Anatolian branch.

The older system that distinguished common gender from neuter is still vaguely discernible through certain characteristics in the inflection of nouns. All neuters, for example, have the same form in the nominative and accusative, while most archaic masculine and feminine nouns bear the ending *-s in the nom. sg. and *-m in the acc. sg.

The exact path from a two-gender system to a three-gender system is still largely a mystery.5 For a long time, Johannes Schmidt’s (1889: 8–9) identification of the feminine morpheme *-ā (i.e., *-eh₂ in laryngealistic terms) with the mor-$pheme found in ‘collectives’ and neuter plurals (e.g., *i̯ugóm n. ‘yoke’ → *i̯ugé-h₂ ‘yokes’ > Vedic yugā́(ni), slightly remodeled in Greek ζυγά, Latin iuga, etc.) was $the accepted opinion among many scholars of Indo-European studies. Building on this premise, the feminine gender was often explained as going back directly to collectives in *-(e)h₂ (cf. Tichy 1993, Fritz 1998, Hackstein 2012, Litscher 2014), which would explain, for example, why feminines in *-eh₂ have an asigmatic nom. sg. and a dual ending *-ih₁.6 In recent years, however, there has been grow-ing skepticism towards this view (cf. Kim 2014, Melchert 2014, Nussbaum 2014, Lundquist & Yates 2014: 2099–2100), not least because the Anatolian branch not only preserves both paradigmatic neuter plurals in *-eh₂ (e.g., Hittite nom.-acc. $sg. *šākuwan n. ‘eye’ → nom.-acc. pl. šākuwa ‘eyes’) and plurale tantum collectives in *-eh₂ derived from common gender nouns (e.g., Hittite alpaš c. ‘cloud’ → nom. $pl. alpēš ‘clouds’ and nom.-acc. pl. alpa ‘cloudbank, mass of clouds’), but also common gender nouns in *-eh₂-, both as abstracts like Lycian arawa- c. ‘freedom’ and as designations for persons of either sex like Lycian lada- c. ‘wife’, kumaza- c. ‘priest’ (cf. Hajnal 1994, Melchert 2014, Sasseville 2018). It is therefore more plausible that there was a continuity from Proto-Indo-European neuters to Core Indo-European neuters, and that the feminine gender originated within the com-mon gender nouns (cf. Luraghi 2009, 2011, 2014). After its first emergence, we have to imagine an intricate set of rules that—by formal analogy and/or semantic

5 For a concise overview of the history of scholarship, cf. Neri & Schuhmann (2014: 1–4) and Lundquist & Yates (2018: 2099–2100). For a detailed account, see Litscher (2018: 33–106).

6 For possible explanations for the asigmatic nom. sg. of *-eh₂- and *-ih₂- stems, see the discussion in Litscher (2015).

38 Stefan Höfler

association—assigned feminine gender to various groups of previously common gender nouns, more on which in section 9 below.

4 Where do we see gender in the Indo-European languages?

In the ancient Indo-European languages, the grammatical gender of a noun can only rarely be guessed based on superficial criteria. As mentioned above, a neuter noun usually has an asigmatic nominative, but some masculine and feminine nouns do, too, be it for phonological reasons (e.g., via Szemerényi’s Law: **ph₂térs ‘father’ > *ph₂tḗr) or in a systematic way (e.g., the Core Indo-European feminines/ masculines in *-eh₂-). On the other hand, one group of neuters is characterized precisely by the fact that they end in *-s in the nom. sg., namely the neuter s-stems (e.g., *g̑énh₁-os n. ‘offspring’), though here *-s is of course part of the suffix and not the ending. Neuters are also distinguished from masculines and feminines by the fact that they are always identical in the nominative and accusative, and some stem types (e.g., heteroclites) are only attested as neuters. When it comes to mor-phosyntactic alignment, neuter plurals in *-h₂ sometimes behave as singulars (the $so-called τὰ ζῷα τρέχει [‘the animals.n.pl run.3.sg’] rule), a pattern that is attest-$ed in Anatolian, Greek, Vedic (rarely), and Avestan. This phenomenon finds an explanation in the assumption that the paradigmatic plural of neuters continues a collective formation that was originally a singular before being reanalyzed as a plural (cf. Teffeteller 2019 and, skeptically, Melchert 2011). Initially, this collective $could be derived from neuters and non-neuters alike (cf. Hittite alpaš c. ‘cloud’ → alpa ‘cloudbank, mass of clouds’ from above; Greek κύκλος m. ‘wheel’ → κύκλα $‘wheels (as a set)’). Apart from taking singular verbal agreement, these collectives are plurals in every Indo-European tradition including Anatolian, which suggests that this reanalysis had already taken place in Proto-Indo-European.

Another area where neuters differ from common-gender nouns is the dual. $While animates take the ending *-h₁e (e.g., *pód-h₁e ‘(two) feet’ > Greek πόδε), $neuters persistently have an ending *-ih₁ (e.g., *h₃(e)kʷ-ih₁ ‘(two) eyes’ > Greek $ὄσσε [*okʷi̯e], Old Church Slavonic oči, Lithuanian akì, Armenian ačʿ-kʿ pl.; with $secondary *-s- Vedic akṣī́, Young Avestan aši). As with the neuter plural, né col-lective, it is thinkable that the form in *-ih₁ was originally derivational. Elsewhere, there is no formal difference between nouns of different genders. They share the same endings.

In what follows, I will focus not so much on the distinction between neuter and common (masculine/feminine) gender, which is an interesting matter in its

39Gender in Indo-European

own right, but rather on the contrast between masculine and feminine and on the origin of the feminine gender in Indo-European.

On the formal side, there is no difference between masculine and feminine nouns. Most stem classes have members of either gender, be it root nouns (e.g.,

*pód- m. ‘foot’ and *bʰŕ̥g̑ʰ- f. ‘hill; stronghold’), thematic stems (e.g., *su̯ék̑uros m. ‘father-in-law’ and *snusós f. ‘daughter-in-law’), or other stem classes like

*-ter-stems (e.g., *ph₂tḗr m. ‘father’ and *dʰugh₂tḗr f. ‘daughter’), i-stems (e.g., *h₁ó/égʷnis m. ‘fire’ and *k̑lóu̯nis f. ‘hip’), or s-stems (e.g., *h₁érh₂ōs m. ‘love’ and *h₂éu̯sōs f. ‘dawn’), to name but a few. The only systematic way to see grammatical gender and the difference between masculine and feminine nouns in the ancient Indo-European languages is through agreement, i.e., through the influence that these nouns exert on associated words. For Core Indo-European, there are only three classes of words that exhibit different agreement forms according to the gender of the corresponding nouns: adjectives (including participles), numerals (only 1–4), and pronouns. But on closer inspection, the picture is a little bit more complicated than it may seem at first glance.

5 Adjectival agreement

When it comes to adjectival agreement in Core Indo-European, we are faced with a paradox. On the one hand, feminine agreement forms with the ending *-eh₂- for thematic adjectives can be reconstructed quite safely based on the ubiquitous $pattern exemplified by Greek καλὴ κόρη, Vedic priyā́ kanyā̀, Latin puella pulchra $‘pretty girl’, Old Church Slavonic dobra žena ‘good woman’, Latvian liela māja ‘big house’, etc. In all these languages, the feminine of the thematic adjective takes on the endings of the feminine *-eh₂- stems and is inflected accordingly (e.g., Latin puella pulchra ‘pretty girl’, gen. sg. puellae pulchrae, acc. sg. puellam pulchram, etc.). Formally, this ending *-eh₂ can be analyzed as *-e-h₂, with *-e- being the thematic vowel of the underlying adjective.

On the other hand, however, Ancient Greek has a considerable number of thematic adjectives ‘of two endings’ or ‘terminations’ that take the masculine set $of endings (i.e., nom. sg. -ος, etc.) when agreeing with both masculine and fem-inine nouns. Compare νῆττα ἥμερος f. ‘tame duck’, ῥοδοδάκτυλος Ἠώς f. ‘rose- fingered Eos’, ἄλκιμος μάχη f. ‘brave fight’, χθών πάτριος f. ‘land of the father’, φωνὴ βάρβαρος f. ‘foreign language’, etc. (cf. Kastner 1967, Höfler 2022a). This peculi-$arity cannot easily be explained as secondary (cf. Wackernagel 1924: 47, Schwyzer & Debrunner 1950: 32, 36, Kastner 1967: 116, Fortson 2004: 119, Matasović 2004:

40 Stefan Höfler

155, Weiss 2020: 213 note 18). Rather, it suggests that the agreement pattern with *-eh₂- for the feminine adjective is a relatively recent development that had not been fully generalized and grammaticalized when Core Indo-European split up. And while Greek is the only language that systematically preserves ‘ungendered’ feminine agreement forms of the thematic adjective, one other language might retain at least a trace of that earlier system: according to Olsen (1999: vi and 35), the Armenian o-stem adjective amowl (amloy, -ocʿ) ‘barren’ goes back to a com-$pound *n̥-putlo- ‘childless’ (cf. Sanskrit a-putra-, Avestan a-puϑra- without a son’). $Since it is only used of women, Olsen argues that its o-stem inflection “supports the view that ‘Adjektiva zweier Endungen’ of the Greek type may in some cases reflect the situation of the proto-language better than the full gender distinction exhibited by Sanskrit” (Olsen 1999: vi).7

A recent origin of adjectival agreement is indeed also suggested by the situation found with athematic adjectives. In principle, the feminine is formed by adding the so-called devī́-suffix *-ih₂- to the stem of the adjective: *pl̥th₂ús ‘broad.m.sg’ $(Vedic pr̥thú-, Greek πλατύς) → *pl̥th₂(e)u̯ih₂ ‘broad.f.sg’ (Vedic pr̥th(i)vī́, Greek πλατεῖα), *u̯éi̯du̯ōs ‘knowing.m.sg.’ (Vedic vidvā́ṁs, Young Avestan vīδuuā̊, Greek εἰδώς) → *u̯idusih₂ ‘knowing.f.sg’ (Vedic vidúṣī, Young Avestan vīθušī, Greek ἰδυῖα). However, the use of masculine (common gender) agreement forms for the feminine athematic adjective is well-attested not only in Greek (e.g., ἡδὺς ἀυτμή ‘pleasant odor’, θῆλυς ἀϋτή ‘women’s battle cry’), but also elsewhere (e.g., Vedic $matíḥ … cā́ruḥ ‘dear thought’, Gothic jah handus is so taihswo was þaursus ‘and his right hand was withered’),8 and some athematic stem classes lack feminine $adjectives in *-ih₂- altogether, for example s-stem adjectives (e.g., Greek σαφὴς ἀρετά ‘manifest virtue’, Vedic nā́rīḥ apásaḥ ‘busy women’).9 $

$In addition, the cognate pair Vedic pī́varī and Greek πίειρα ‘fat.f.sg’ (*píhₓu̯er-ih₂), the feminines of the adjectives Vedic pī́van- and Greek πίων ‘fat.m.sg’ $(*píhₓu̯on-), respectively, suggests that these agreement forms in *-ih₂- were not (initially, at least) derived from the masculine (or common gender) adjective, but

*snusós dʰugh₂tḗr ‘daughter bound by marriage’ with subsequent ellipsis of the head noun (see Höfler 2020: 195 note 53) is correct.

8 Cf. Neri (2003: 158 note 460), Braune & Heidermanns (2004: 120–121). Similarly per-haps in Old Lithuanian, see Stang (1966: 262).

41Gender in Indo-European

rather independent nominal formations,10 and that they only secondarily became paradigmatically conjoined with the masculine (or, common-gender) adjective.11 There might have even been a phase in which formations in *-ih₂- could also supply the feminine of a thematic adjective, as suggested (though not unequiv-ocally) by the Tocharian evidence, where this is the rule, e.g., Tocharian B tapre ‘high.m.sg’ < *dʰubrós and tparya ‘high.f.sg’ < [virtual] *dʰubrih₂ (cf. Kim 2014: 121–124, Hackstein 2012, Pinault 2008: 516-519, Fellner 2014a, 2014b).

Originally, the function of the devī́-suffix *-ih₂- seems to have been to cre-ate derivatives of ‘appurtenative’ meaning (i.e., ‘belonging to X, related to X’), $as in the eponymous example *di̯éu̯- ‘sky’ → *dei̯u̯ih₂- ‘belonging to the sky’ > $‘goddess’.12 Even though Vedic attests a handful of male personal names formed by this suffix (Remmer 2010[2011]), its specialization for creating designations for typically female referents can be already attributed to Core Indo-European, which explains its important role in the implementation of feminine adjectival agreement forms.

The prehistory of the other agreement suffix *-eh₂- or (more precisely) *-h₂- is murkier, since there are several, partly homophonous suffixes containing *-h₂-.

It seems plausible that the latter has a shared prehistory with one of the other *-h₂-’s.

Recent years have seen a growing consensus that there is a connection be-tween the thematic agreement form in *-e-h₂- and the substantivizing deadjecti-val suffix *-h₂- (cf. Nussbaum 2014, Melchert 2014, Kim 2014, Fellner & Gresten-berger 2016: 144–146, Höfler 2022a; skeptically, Litscher 2018: 102–105), yet since $the latter also derives masculine nouns (e.g., Latin scaeuus ‘left-handed’ → scaeua $m. ‘lefty’), the last word has not yet been said on this issue (see Höfler 2022a, 2022b for a discussion).

Taken together, the evidence suggests that the creation of agreement forms for the feminine adjective was a rather recent development in the history of the fem-inine gender, one which presupposes the existence of an already existing agree-ment distinction in other parts of the grammar.

6 Numerals

The other area for which we can reconstruct feminine agreement forms are the numerals from one to four. The words for ‘one’ and ‘two’ follow the pattern seen above in adjectives. The numeral ‘one’ behaves like an athematic adjective: next $to *sém-s ‘one.m’ (Greek εἷς, Tocharian B ṣe) and *sém ‘one.n’ (Greek ἕν), we find the feminine *sm-íh₂ ‘one.f’ (Greek μία, Armenian mi), gen. sg. *sm-i̯éh₂s > *si̯éh₂s (Greek ep. ἰῆς) (cf. Peters 1980: 132 note 80). As with *píhₓu̯erih₂-, the $form *smíh₂, gen sg. *si̯éh₂s may originally have been an independent formation with no specific feminine flavor, which might explain its potential presence in Anatolian, where Hittite šii̯a- ‘one’ looks like a continuant of *si̯eh₂- < *smi̯eh₂- (cf. Kloekhorst 2008: 750–751; and Eichner 2015: 20–21, arguing for a grammatical feminine in Proto-Indo-European). The word for ‘two’, on the other hand, fol-lows the pattern of thematic adjectives, as if from a stem *d(u)u̯ó- to which the dual endings were attached: besides *d(u)u̯óh₁(e) ‘two.m’ (Vedic d(u)vā́, Greek $δύω, Latin duo, etc.) and *d(u)u̯ói̯h₁ ‘two.n’ (Vedic dvé, Old Church Slavonic dvě, $

43Gender in Indo-European

Old High German zwei), we find *d(u)u̯éh₂ih₁ ‘two.f’ (Vedic dvé, Latin duae, Old Church Slavonic dvě).

The more intriguing agreement forms, however, are the ones for ‘three’ and ‘four’, which both exhibit an element *-sr-. Compare *tréi̯-es ‘three.m’ (Vedic tráyas, $Greek τρεῖς, Latin trēs, etc.), *trí-h₂ ‘three.n’ (Vedic trī́, Greek τρία, etc.), and *tisrés $‘three.f’ < *tri-sr-és, attested in Indo-Iranian and Celtic (Vedic tisrás, Avestan tišrō, Gaulish tidres, Old Irish téoir, Middle Welsh teir); as well as *kʷetu̯ór-es ‘four.m’ $(Vedic catvā́ras, Greek [Doric] τέτορες, etc.), *kʷetu̯ór-h₂ ‘four.n’ (Vedic catvā́ri, $etc.), and *kʷéte-sres ‘four.f’ (Vedic cátasras, Avestan cataŋrō, Old Irish cethéoir, Middle Welsh pedeir) (cf. McCone 1993, Harðarson 2014).

The element *-sr- in *t(r)isrés ‘three.f’ and *kʷétesres ‘four.f’ has been iden-tified with a word for ‘woman’, *(h₁)sor-, which is reconstructable on the basis of forms like *su̯e-sor- ‘sister’, Cuneiform Luwian ašrul(i)- ‘female’, and Avestan hāirišī- f. ‘woman’ (cf. Fortson 2004: 120, Pinault 2013, Harðarson 2014, Sasseville & Steer 2022). Interestingly, it is also at the core of the Hittite suffix -(š)šara- that is used to create terms for female persons based on their male equivalents: com-pare Hittite ḫaššu- ‘king’ and *ḫaššuššara- ‘queen’, or Hittite išḫā- ‘master, lord’ and išḫaššara- ‘lady, mistress’, as well as being found in Luwian, namely in Hiero-glyphic Luwian nanasri- c. ‘sister’, and in Cuneiform Luwian nāna-šr-iya- ‘sisterly’ (besides nāni(ya)- ‘brotherly’). The same element, yet in athematic shape -šar, is already attested in the oldest written accounts of Anatolian (and thus, Indo- European) linguistic material, namely in the Old Assyrian tablets from Kültepe/ Kaniš (ca. 1930–1720 bce), which contain a vast number of Anatolian names, many of which end in -šar and denote women, e.g., Ḫapuwaḫšušar, Ḫištaḫšušar, Niwaḫšušar, etc. (cf. Goetze 1954: 354–355, Zehnder 2010: 74, Harðarson 2014: 42).

Thus, we are seemingly dealing with an element that was already present in Proto-Indo-European and was used to derive words denoting female persons. This, however, does not presuppose a feminine gender. A neat parallel for *-sor from a genderless language is the suffix -né in Hungarian that likewise creates $words for the consort of a male officiary (e.g., király ‘king’ → királyné ‘queen con-sort’, pap ‘priest’ → papné ‘wife of a priest’) and is attached to names of men to indicate their wives (e.g., Bartók → Bartókné ‘Mrs. Bartók’, Bartók Béláné ‘Mrs. $Béla Bartók’). Etymologically, it is identical to the noun nő ‘woman’, which makes it aptly comparable to *-sor, *-sr- and its prehistory.

For the numerals *t(r)isrés ‘three.f’ and *kʷétesres ‘four.f’, this leads to the hy-pothesis that these forms were initially used to count groups of girls or women (cf. Oettinger 1986: 126, Hackstein 2010: 52–64, Pinault 2013: 245–246), and that the element *-sr-(es) served as a classifier, i.e., a word or suffix that ‘classifies’ the nu-

44 Stefan Höfler

meral depending on the type of its referent noun. Numeral classifiers are a wide-spread phenomenon in the languages of the world (cf. Gil 2013), and even English knows certain words in which a quasi-classifier can be used to count them (e.g., three head of cattle, two pieces of paper, etc.). Within the Indo-European languag-es, comparable numerals of younger origin are, for instance, found in Old Irish, where they are known as ‘personal numerals’ (cf. Stifter 2006: 231–232, Pinault 2013: 246). A form like Old Irish triar ‘three’ is used exclusively to count men (i.e., ‘three men’) and historically continues Proto-Celtic *tri-u̯irom (with *-uir- being the same element as in *u̯iros ‘man’ > Old Irish fer). The fascinating thing about

*t(r)isrés ‘three.f’ and *kʷétesres ‘four.f’ is thus that they are potential tangible ev-idence for the role of biological sex in the development of the feminine gender.

7 Pronouns

Gendered pronouns are a centerpiece of feminine morphology and are attested in all Indo-European branches except for Anatolian and Armenian.13 A gender distinction between masculine and feminine can be reconstructed for the deictic pronoun *só ‘this.m.sg’ (: *séh₂ ‘this.f.sg’ : *tód ‘this.n.sg’), the anaphoric pro-noun *(h₁)ís ‘he.m.sg’ (: *(h₁)íh₂ ‘she.f.sg’ : *(h₁)íd ‘it.n.sg’), the relative pro-noun *hₓi̯ós ‘which.m.sg’ (: *hₓi̯éh₂ ‘which.f.sg’ : *hₓi̯ód ‘which.n.sg’), and per-haps the interrogative pronoun *kʷís, *kʷós ‘who.m.sg’ (: *kʷéh₂ ‘who.f.sg’ : *kʷíd ‘what.n.sg’). In all these cases, the feminine nom. sg. is derived by adding *-h₂ to the stem of the pronoun. Apart from the intriguing *(h₁)íh₂ ‘she.f.sg’ (Lithuanian jì, Old Church Slavonic ji, Gothic s-i, Old Irish s-í, Vedic iyám < *(h₁)ih₂-om), the most interesting form in this respect is the deictic pronoun *séh₂ ‘this.f.sg’ (Vedic sā́, Greek ἡ, Gothic sō, Tocharian B sā), because it shows that the feminine was derived from the stem of the masculine (i.e., erstwhile common gender) *só, and not from the neuter *tód.

Unlike with adjectival agreement, where the previous usage of masculine (i.e., erstwhile common gender) agreement forms for feminine nouns can still be seen directly in the Indo-European languages (see section 5), pronouns do not show any fluctuation in this regard (cf. Lühr 2014: 168–169). Feminine pronouns

13 However, within the personal pronouns for the first and second person there is general-ly no gender distinction, with the notable exception of Tocharian A, which secondarily developed two separate pronouns of the first person singular (nom./obl. m. näṣ, f. ñuk, gen. m. ñi, f. nāñi); cf. Jasanoff (1989a).

45Gender in Indo-European

for feminine referents are deeply entrenched in the grammar of all Core Indo- European daughter languages that preserve the feminine gender, and are used for female referents even in some languages that have subsequently lost feminine gender and agreement such as English or Danish. This suggests that the gram-maticalization of feminine pronouns had already been fully accomplished by the time of the split-up of Core Indo-European. Indeed, it can also be counted as sup-port for the idea that the very point of origin of the feminine gender lies within pronouns, a word class which is cross-linguistically known to furnish the basis for noun class and gender systems (cf. Corbett 1991: 310).

As such, it is perhaps not wrong to imagine that forms like *séh₂ and *(h₁)íh₂ were either created intentionally to refer to female persons, or were formed for a different reason but repurposed to refer to female persons at some later stage (cf. Kastner 1967: 116, Pinault 2011, Hackstein 2013: 95, Lühr 2014: 193–194, Luraghi 2014: 225–226). Since *-h₂ is found in the ending of the Proto-Indo-European allative (e.g., Hittite aruna ‘to the sea’ < *-eh₂; mēnaḫḫ-anda ‘opposite’ < *méneh₂ ‘to the face (mēna-)’ + anda ‘into’; cf. Nikolaev 2010: 68) and, as a suffix, is used $in deadjectival substantivizations (e.g., *h₂enkuló- ‘bent, curved’ → *h₂énkule-h₂- $‘bent, curved thing’), a process that could be described as ‘determining’, one could postulate some sort of deictic function for *sé-h₂ ‘that one (vel sim.)’,14 which would have designated ‘the other one’ (i.e., ‘the woman’) in a male-centered, pa-triarchal society (though this is little more than idle speculation at this point).15 Be that as it may, at this stage the pronouns *séh₂, *(h₁)íh₂, etc. would have still been grammatically common gender.

It is probably no coincidence that the desinences found in feminine pronouns, *-eh₂ (*séh₂, *hₓi̯éh₂, etc.) and *-ih₂ (*(h₁)íh₂), resemble the suffixes that prototyp-ically create feminine nouns and feminine agreement forms of the adjective. The fact that this correspondence is limited to the strong stem of the pronoun, howev-er, indicates that a one-to-one correspondence is probably the wrong way to think about it. The apparent congruence can be due to an analogical association and subsequent grammaticalization of formerly unrelated morphological material. In any event, the singular oblique of the feminine pronoun contains an element

*-si̯eh₂- (e.g., dat. sg. *té/ósi̯eh₂ei̯ > Vedic tásyai, Gothic þizai, Old Church Slavonic toji) that, when compared to *-sm- of the masculine and neuter oblique (e.g., dat.

14 Compare also the personal pronoun doublets with and without *-h₂: *tú and *tú-h₂ ‘you.sg’ and *h₁ég ̑and *h₁ég̑-(o)h₂ ‘I’. A similar account, though in its details very differ-ent, is presented in Pinault (2011).

15 But compare – if only impressionistically – Catullus’ use of illa ‘that one’ in his poems to refer to the object of his desire.

46 Stefan Höfler

sg. *té/ósmōi̯ > Vedic tásmai, Gothic þamma, Old Church Slavonic tomu), allows an identification with the numeral *sém- ‘one’, fem. obl. *si̯eh₂- (see above) in some way or other.

8 The origin of the feminine gender

The question of the origin of the feminine gender in Indo-European has been one of the most-discussed topics in the history of Indo-European linguistics, and there is still no commonly accepted hypothesis. As mentioned above, there has been a shift in recent years, with more and more scholars abandoning the tra-ditional idea that the feminine gender arose from a reanalysis of collectives, in favor of a more nuanced picture, in which biological sex on the one hand and pronouns on the other play an important role. As a whole, rather than pursuing a monocausal explanation,16 it is preferable to view the emergence of the femi-nine as a gradual process that needed a number of ‘ingredients’, i.e., a number of initially unrelated elements that were present in the language and which together could lead to the establishment of a new noun class. Let’s have a look at these ‘ingredients’.

As mentioned above, perhaps the main component were the pronouns *séh₂ and *(h₁)íh₂ that were ultimately based on the common gender forms *só and

*(h₁)ís, respectively. They were created specifically or came to be used secondarily to refer to female persons. Exactly why this happened, we do not know. It is note-worthy, however, that *séh₂ and *(h₁)íh₂ resemble the suffixes *-eh₂- and *-ih₂-, which are both found in other elements of feminine morphology.

The suffix *-h₂- did not in and of itself have a feminine meaning. Apart from being a ‘primary’ suffix (see above §5), we know it as a ‘secondary’ denominal $suffix that has substantivizing function (*h₂enkuló- ‘bent, curved’ → *h₂énkule-h₂- $‘bent, curved thing’). These formations were initially common gender, as seen in $Anatolian (e.g., Lycian *kumeze- ‘sacred’ → kumaza- c. ‘priest’), and vestigially in masculine ā-stems in Greek (e.g., ταχινός ‘swift’ → ταχίνᾱς m. ‘hare’) and Latin (e.g., scaeuus ‘left-handed’ → scaeua m. ‘lefty’). Nevertheless, recent scholarship $has recognized a connection between *-h₂- as a substantivizing suffix and the feminine agreement forms of thematic adjectives.17 So, it is legitimate to regard

16 Thus also Melchert (2014: 268): “not […] necessary or wise to attempt to explain the rise of the feminine gender in terms of a single factor.”

17 Cf. Nussbaum (2014), Melchert (2014), Kim (2014), Fellner & Grestenberger (2016:

47Gender in Indo-European

the denominal suffix *-h₂- as another factor on the way to the grammatical fem-inine.

The more obvious feminine suffix, however, is the devī́-suffix *-ih₂- (with an asigmatic nom. sg.). As mentioned above, its primeval function may have been to create relational derivatives, which can still be seen in formations like *dei̯u̯ih₂- ‘goddess’ < *‘belonging to heaven (*di̯éu̯-)’ (cf. Remmer 2010: 158 note 1). Unlike for *-h₂-, however, there is overwhelming evidence that *-ih₂- was indeed preva-lent in words denoting women,18 making it a substantial ingredient for the gram-matical feminine (cf. Stüber 2007b, Kim 2014). Apart from lexicalized formations such as *dei̯u̯ih₂- ‘goddess’ and *h₃rḗg̑nih₂- ‘queen’, and feminine adjectives like

*píhₓu̯erih₂- ‘fat’, a cornerstone of formations in *-ih₂- denoting persons of female gender is personal names.

As discussed by Ulla Remmer (this volume), female personal names in many Indo-European traditions typically end in suffixes that continue Proto-Indo- European *-eh₂- and *-ih₂-. Despite being an elusive part of the reconstructable lexicon of Proto-Indo-European (see Stüber, Zehnder & Remmer 2009), names must have been one of the most central elements of every-day life and speech. Female personal names in *-eh₂- and *-ih₂- are therefore arguably another ingre-dient on the way to the attested agreement system.

A further, if perhaps slightly minor constituent were nouns that ended in *-h₂ and denoted female persons. As far as the reconstructable evidence goes, there are fewer of these than we would expect. Many of the prominent lexemes referring to biological females belong to other stem classes: *méh₂tēr ‘mother’, *dʰugh₂tḗr ‘daughter’, *su̯ésōr ‘sister’, *snusós ‘daughter-in-law’, *hₓi̯énh₂tēr ‘husband’s broth-er’s wife’, *su̯ek̑ruh₂s ‘mother-in-law’, *h₂enhₓos ‘grandmother’, etc. In contrast to that, the number of reconstructable appellatives in *-ih₂- is quite low (cf. *dei̯u̯ih₂ ‘goddess’, *h₃rḗg̑nih₂ ‘queen’), and the only stem in *-eh₂- is the rather specif-ic *h₁u̯idʰéu̯eh₂ ‘widow’. There was, however, at least one stem with an ablauting suffix *-(e)h₂- that might have played a considerable role, viz. *gʷén-h₂, gen. sg.

*gʷn-éh₂-s ‘woman’ (continued directly by Old Irish ben, bé ‘woman’, gen. sg. mná; for the details see Jasanoff 1989b), which was the basis of many words denot-ing ‘woman’ in the individual branches (*gʷnéh₂- in Vedic gnā́- f. ‘divine female’, $Old Avestan gənā- f. ‘woman, wife’; *gʷn̥(n)éh₂- in Greek γυνή, Boeotian βανά; $

*gʷeneh₂- in Proto-Germanic *kʷenōn- ‘woman’, Proto-Slavic *ženà, Tocharian B

144–146); see Höfler (2022a) for a detailed discussion. 18 On a few Vedic masculines with devī́-inflection see Debrunner (1954: 407–408), Rem-

mer (2010[2011]: 160–165).

48 Stefan Höfler

śana – see the discussion in Simon, Sasseville & Opfermann 2022), and thus prob-ably a central element. While it is remarkable that abstracts and verbal nouns in

*-eh₂-, which are a large and well-attested group in many Indo- European tradi-tions, are without exception feminine, their role in the emergence of the feminine gender was probably only circumstantial. We will return to them in section 9.

The last ingredient is one of the strongest pieces of evidence for the impor-tance of biological sex in the establishment of the genus femininum as a new noun class, namely the numerals ‘three’ and ‘four’. As outlined above (§6), the feminine forms *t(r)isrés ‘three.f’ and *kʷétesres ‘four.f’ attested in Indo-Iranian and Celt-ic (Vedic tisrás, cátasras, Avestan tišrō, cataŋrō; Old Irish téoir, cethéoir, Middle Welsh teir, pedeir) contain an element *-sr- that can probably be identified with a noun for ‘woman’, and therefore suggest an initial application for counting groups of female persons.

With all these ingredients in mind, the path to the emergence of the gram-matical feminine could be envisaged as follows: initially, there was only one set of pronouns, numerals, and adjectives to refer to all nouns of the common gender, denoting persons of male and female biological sex alike. To designate the spouse (or other female dependent) of a man, a suffixoid *-s(e/o)r- (originating in com-pounds and/or univerbations with a second element *(h₁)sor- ‘woman’) could be used both in appellatives and names; this stage is still reflected in Anatolian (cf. $Hittite išḫā- ‘master, lord’ → išḫaššara- ‘lady, mistress’). The suffix was also used $to count groups of three (*t(r)isrés) and four (*kʷétesres) women, which marked the first grammatical difference in the language structure that was based on bio-logical sex. In the function of creating female consort names, *-s(e/o)r- was lat-er replaced by the suffix *-ih₂- that initially formed common-gender derivatives with a meaning ‘belonging to X’ (e.g., *dei̯u̯ih₂- *‘belonging to heaven (*di̯éu̯-)’ > ‘goddess’) and became more and more restricted to deriving words and names $for wives or female dependents (e.g., *h₂nér- m. ‘man’ → *h₂nēr-ih₂- ‘wife’ > Vedic nā́rī- f., Young Avestan nāirī- f.; Vedic Agní- m. ‘Agni’ → Agnā́yī- f. ‘Agni’s wife’; $see Remmer, this volume).

At some point, the innovated pronouns *séh₂ and *(h₁)íh₂ as well as the nu-meral *smíh₂ (original function unknown) came to be used exclusively to refer to female persons. This was probably facilitated by the fact that a few appellatives and many names denoting women already ended in *-ih₂ and (to a lesser extent)

*-eh₂. At this point, one cannot yet speak of a feminine gender. Even the next log-ical step, the extension of the female pronouns *séh₂, *(h₁)íh₂, etc. to also denote female animals, did not establish a new noun class. The stage we are at now re-sembles the system of Modern English, where the anaphoric pronoun she is used

49Gender in Indo-European

for female persons and animals alike (and where suffixes such as -ess [e.g., actress] can optionally denote biological females).

The crucial moment in the genesis of the feminine gender is when this sys-tem of anaphora was extended analogically to include nouns that did not de-note female persons or animals but could in some other way be associated with these lexemes, for instance by homophonous desinences or semantic association. While prior to this point, a common-gender verbal noun such as *bʰugéh₂ ‘flight’ $(Greek φυγή f., Latin fuga f.) or a common-gender concrete noun such as *h₂i-$h₁/₃séh₂ ‘shaft (of a cart)’ (Hittite ḫišša- c., Vedic īṣā́- f.) would have been referred to by *só ‘this’, it now became possible to use *séh₂ instead. And since *séh₂ was used for nouns that took the numerals *t(r)isrés and *kʷétesres when being count-ed, the next step would be employing *t(r)isrés and *kʷétesres by analogy for tal-lying ‘flights’ and ‘shafts’ as well. The loss of their original, literal meaning (‘three women’ and ‘four women’) in favor of the acquisition of a grammatical function (i.e., counting words of a specific noun class) marks the grammaticalization of the new system. From this point on, it is fair to speak of a new grammatical gender, and more and more nouns joined this class by assignment (see section 9).

When this agreement system had established itself, a logical next step was to create or repurpose formations in *-ih₂- as the feminine agreement form of the adjective. Since these formations were originally substantival, their employment as adjectives probably came about in predicative usage. The origin of the agree-ment form of the thematic adjective in *-e-h₂- is somewhat more obscure, but the fact that it coincided formally with the desinence of feminine nouns in *-eh₂ and the pronoun *séh₂ must surely have helped expand the pattern to the attested uniformity found in most languages (except Greek).

The establishment of a new noun class, endowed with a distinct set of agree-ment forms for pronouns, numerals, and later also adjectives, opened up a whole array of possibilities, a new dimension, which the language began to exploit for making distinctions that previously had been impossible to make (e.g., *h₁ék̑u̯os c. ‘horse (of either sex)’ >> *h₁ék̑u̯os m. ‘stallion’, *h₁ék̑u̯os f. ‘mare’). This will be the topic of the last section.

9 How nouns become feminine

In this last section, we want to look at the various groups of words that acquired feminine gender. Note that under the proposed scenario, there was a continu-ity from common gender to masculine gender, meaning that the former com-

50 Stefan Höfler

mon-gender agreement forms are identical to the later masculine agreement forms (e.g., *só, *(h₁)ís, *séms ‘one’, etc.). It is thus not the masculine gender that is assigned to any given noun, but the feminine gender, i.e., the allocation of a word to the new noun class was an intentional process, governed by specific rules and principles, the most influential of which was biological sex.

If the road map outlined above is accurate, the natural hotbed of the feminine gender was words referring to female persons, such as the already mentioned

*gʷénh₂ ‘woman’, *méh₂tēr ‘mother’, *dʰugh₂tḗr ‘daughter’, *su̯ésōr ‘sister’, *snusós ‘daughter-in-law’, *hₓi̯énh₂tēr ‘husband’s brother’s wife’, *su̯ek̑ruh₂s ‘mother-in-law’, *h₂enhₓos ‘grandmother’, *h₃rḗg̑nih₂ ‘queen’, *h₁u̯idʰéu̯eh₂ ‘widow’, etc. The second sphere were personal names of women and girls, which must have been a central part of everyday conversation, but which are, sadly, almost entirely unknown to us. As a third component of feminine-gender nouns, one can invoke names denot-ing female goddesses: apart from the word for ‘goddess’ itself, *dei̯u̯ih₂, the most prominent female numina are *h₂éu̯sōs ‘Dawn’ and *dʰég̑ʰōm ‘Earth’ (though the latter is never attested as such; see Mallory & Adams 1997: 174). It is conceivable that the appellatives *h₂éu̯sōs ‘dawn’ and *dʰég̑ʰōm ‘earth’ followed suit and were also assigned feminine gender along the way.

The last group for which the feminine gender was an obvious choice were nouns denoting female animals. Most Proto-Indo-European zoonyms were epicene, i.e., they were used for males and females alike (e.g., *gʷṓu̯s c. ‘bovine’,

*h₂ó/éu̯is c. ‘sheep’, *h₁ék̑u̯os c. ‘horse’). Words that exclusively denoted the females of a certain species were rare and—if existent at all—were limited to livestock animals; possible examples include *u̯ak̑(k̑)éh₂ ‘cow’ (Vedic vaśā́-, Latin uacca) and *súhₓs ‘sow’ (if the root etymology as ‘birther’ is correct; cf. Vedic sū́te ‘gives birth’).19 After the rise of the feminine, the erstwhile common-gender epicene animal terms could now be used in the masculine to refer to the male individual and in the feminine to refer to the female individual (e.g., *h₁ék̑u̯os m. > Greek $ὁ ἵππος ‘the (male) horse, stallion’ and *h₁ék̑u̯os f. > ἡ ἵππος ‘the (female horse), $mare’, Old Latin equus fēmina ‘mare’). In some branches, the feminine usage of the former epicene noun became prevalent (e.g., *h₂ó/éu̯is c. ‘sheep’ >> Proto- Germanic *awiz f. ‘ewe’; *gʷṓu̯s c. ‘bovine’ >> Proto-Germanic *kūz f. ‘cow’), which led to the introduction of new words for the males (e.g., Proto-Germanic

*steuraz ‘bull’) and new epicene designations (e.g., Proto-Germanic *fahaz, *skēpa- n. ‘sheep’). The creation of so-called ‘motion’ feminines, i.e., words for female

19 This designation may be due to the fact that sows have considerably larger litters than other domesticated animals.

51Gender in Indo-European

individuals derived from a masculine noun using overt ‘feminine’ morphology (i.e., mostly *-eh₂- and *-ih₂-) is also a post-Core-Indo-European development and happened individually in certain branches (or pre-stages thereof). A forma-tion like *h₁ék̑u̯eh₂ ‘mare’, though suggested by the apparent cognates Vedic áśvā, Lithuanian ašvà, Latin equa ‘mare’, probably did not exist in Core Indo-European. $Greek ἡ ἵππος and Old Latin equus fēmina ‘mare’ preserve the older stage, i.e., $

*h₁ék̑u̯os f. ‘mare’ (cf. Hackstein 2013: 96–98). This is where biological sex as a factor for the assignment of feminine gender

ends. All other groups and categories of words that typically have feminine gen-der in the Indo-European languages owe their assignment to a heterogeneous set of mechanisms (‘gender assignment rules’), many of which are not entirely trans-parent (cf. Matasović 2004: 79–131). While some are based on formal features such as congruent suffixes (see below and cf. Matasović 2004: 136–138), others are seemingly motivated by semantic associations or perhaps animistic beliefs. For instance, there is another group of zoonyms that acquired feminine gender, albeit in a way unconnected to biological sex. The generic word for ‘duck’, for example, *h₂énh₂ti-, *h₂n̥h₂téi̯-, is feminine in most branches (Vedic ātí- f., Greek $νῆττα f., Latin anas f., Lithuanian ántis f., Serbo-Croatian ȕtva f., Old English $ænid f., Old High German anut f., Old Norse ǫnd f.), and it is not quite clear why this is the case. The Proto-Indo-European word for ‘bird’, *h₂éu̯i-, *h₂u̯éi̯- (notably of the same inflectional type20 as ‘duck’) seems to have been epicene (though the direct evidence is limited to Vedic véṣ, víṣ m., Avestan vīš m., and Latin auis f.), $and so do the words for ‘goose’, *g̑ʰáns- (epicene in Greek χήν, feminine in Proto- $Germanic *gans, Lithuanian žąsìs, Proto-Slavic *gǫsь, Old Irish géiss ‘swan’, mas-$culine in Vedic haṁsá-, Latin ānser), and ‘crane’ (epicene in Greek γέρανος, Latin $grūs, Welsh garan, masculine in Proto-Germanic *kranan-, Proto-Slavic *žeravь, feminine in Lithuanian gérvė). The word for ‘eagle’, on the other hand, *h₃érō(n), is masculine throughout (Gothic ara, Old Norse ari, ǫrn, English ern(e), German Aar, Lithuanian erẽlis, Serbo-Croatian òrao, Russian orël, Polish orzeł, etc.). This might give the impression that stereotypical undertones that speakers connected with a certain animal played a role in assigning masculine and feminine gender, respectively (cf. Matasović 2004: 93).

An even more intriguing case is the fox and its different Indo-European desig-nations. In almost all traditions, the generic word is feminine, even if they do not $continue the same etymon. Compare the feminines Latin uolpēs, Greek ἀλώπηξ, $

20 The reconstruction as a proterokinetic i-stem differs from Schindler (1969) and Zair (2011) but accounts best for both Vedic and Latin (see Lindner 2021: 27).

52 Stefan Höfler

Lithuanian lãpė, Latvian lapsa, Proto-Slavic *lisa, Albanian dhelpër, Proto- Germanic *fuhōn- (seemingly more primary than Proto-Germanic *fuhsaz m.). An explanation for this that suggests itself is that the fox was seen as more ‘femi-nine’ than its predatory counterpart, the wolf, *u̯ĺ̥kʷos, which is masculine every-where (cf. Vedic vŕ̥ka-, Avestan vəhrka-, Lithuanian vil̃kas, Old Church Slavonic $vlьkъ, Greek λύκος, Latin lupus, Proto-Germanic *wulfaz, Tocharian B walkwe). $A similar explanation is possible for the feminine gender of words for ‘weasel’ (cf. $Proto-Germanic *wisulōn-, Latin mūstēla, Greek γαλέη, Proto-Slavic *lasica, Ital-$ian donnola, all etymologically unrelated, but all feminine; cf. Bettini 2013), and it may be that the reason many modern-day generic words for ‘cat’ are feminine in traditions unrelated to each other (cf. Albanian mace, German Katze, Rus-$sian kóška, Modern Greek γάτα, Lithuanian katė̃, etc.) is that they received their $gender in ‘opposition’ to the masculine ‘dog’ (cf. Albanian qen, German Hund, $Russian pjos, Modern Greek σκύλος, Lithuanian šuõ, etc.). One could think of $this phenomenon as ‘oppositional gender assignment’, i.e., that in a pair of con-cepts that were semantically related (though this relationship could be manifold), one (the stronger, bigger, more prominent one) was assigned masculine gender, while the other (the lesser, smaller, more delicate one) was given feminine gender. This principle may also be key to understanding why so many different words $for ‘hand’ are feminine (cf. Greek χείρ, παλάμη, παλαστή, Latin manus, palma, $Proto-Germanic *handuz, Old Irish lám, Proto-Slavic *rǫkà, Lithuanian rankà, Young Avestan pərənā-, etc.), with its antipode pód- ‘foot’ being, of course, mas-$culine (Vedic pā́d-, Greek πούς, Latin pēs, Proto-Germanic fōts, etc.). $

An assignment rule of a different kind seems to have operated in tree names. In both Latin and Greek, for example, inherited dendronyms are almost exclu-$sively feminine (even if the Greek word for ‘tree’, δένδρ(ε)ον, is neuter) and it is $plausible that this is a legacy from a common proto-stage. One consequence of this rule is that many Latin tree names are feminine exceptions within their most-ly masculine stem classes (e.g., the o-stems fāgus ‘beech’, laurus ‘laurel’, corulus ‘hazel’, etc.; the u-stems quercus ‘oak’, pīnus ‘pine’; even the word for ‘tree’ itself, the $s-stem arbōs, arbor, gen. arboris); this is mirrored in Greek (the o-stems φηγός f. ‘oak’, λύγος f. ‘chaste tree’, κυπάρισσος f. ‘cypress’; the u-stem πίτυς f. ‘pine’; etc.), $although feminine o-stems are not as rare in Greek as in Latin.21 The reason for

21 In the other branches, this rule was obliterated via the tendency to adjust the gender of a noun to its stem class or the stem class of a noun to its gender, so that feminine o-stems became either masculine (cf. *kóslos f. >> Proto-Germanic *haslaz m. ‘hazel’) or were transformed into ā-stems (cf. *bʰeh₂g̑ós f. >> Proto-Germanic *bōkōn- f. ‘beech’). That this is a recent development is suggested by cognate mismatches such as Lithuanian

53Gender in Indo-European

the consistent feminine gender of dendronyms is unclear;22 it may be related to animistic beliefs about trees, for which one could compare the dryads or tree nymphs in Ancient Greek mythology.

Another feature, typical of all Indo-European languages, is that most non-neu-ter verbal nouns are feminine. This is true for all stems in *-eh₂- (*bʰugéh₂- ‘flight’,

*tomh₁éh₂- ‘cut(ting)’, etc.), *-ti- (*men-ti- ‘thought, thinking’, *g̑enh₁-ti- ‘birth, de-scendance’, *h₃ekʷ-ti- ‘synopsis’, etc.), and root nouns (*bʰúg- ‘flight’, *i̯úg- ‘yoking’, etc.). Again, the reason for this is not obvious, but it has long been known that there is a typological parallel in Hebrew, where many abstract nouns are also fem-inine (e.g., hulédet f. ‘birth’, maḥšaváh f. ‘thought’, ʿaṣmaʾút f. ‘independence’, etc.).

A striking feature of the mentioned types (*-eh₂-, *-ti-, root nouns) is that they are also attested as masculines, but almost exclusively when they refer to male persons. Compare the masculine stems in *-eh₂- (attested in Greek, Latin, Balto-Slavic, Germanic), some residual nomina agentis in *-ti- (e.g., *dʰuhₓ-ti- m. ‘shaker, agitator’ > Vedic dhū́ti-, *teh₂ti- m. ‘thief ’ > Old Church Slavonic tatь, etc.), and many masculine root nouns (e.g., *h₃rḗg̑- m. ‘king’, *i̯úg- m. ‘yoke com-panion’, etc.). The obvious inference from this is that most words in these stem classes would initially have been common gender and have had both the abstract and the concrete meaning at the same time. After the rise of a three-way gender distinction, the concrete meaning (often an agent noun) remained masculine, while the abstract meaning would have been assigned feminine gender. It is con-ceivable that this assignment rule originated in stems in *-eh₂- because of an an-alogical association of the nom. sg. in *-eh₂ with the desinences of the pronouns (most notably *séh₂), which were the nucleus of the feminine agreement system in the scenario outlined in section 8. This analogy led all stems ending in *-eh₂- to acquire feminine gender except for those for which biological sex forbade such an assignment, i.e., stems in *-eh₂- denoting male persons (e.g., Latin scaeua m. ‘lefty’). By semantic association, other abstract noun types of certain stem classes were also assigned to the feminine gender, especially, one could further argue, when such an attribution helped distinguish two meanings (cf. Nussbaum 2014: 304–306). When the abstract noun type was not inherently ambiguous, they re-mained masculine, such as, for instance, the *tómh₁os type (cf. Nussbaum 2017) or verbal abstracts in *-tu-, both of which never (or only secondarily) create agent nouns (cf. Brugmann 1906: 440). For this reason, it is not surprising that stems

béržas m. and Proto-Slavic *bèrza f., Proto-Germanic *berkōn- f. ‘birch’ (pointing to *bʰerhₓg̑os f.).

22 On this question see now Hackstein (2021).

54 Stefan Höfler

in *-tu- are masculine in Vedic (e.g., gántu- ‘way, course’, tántu- ‘thread, string’23), Avestan (e.g., pərᵊtu-/pəṣ̌u- ‘ford’, pitu- ‘food’), Latin (e.g., gustus ‘taste’, iussus ‘or-der, command’), Old Irish (e.g., guth ‘voice’, cruth ‘shape, appearance’), Baltic (e.g., Lithuanian lietùs ‘rain’, Latvian sātus ‘prosperity’), and Germanic (e.g., *liþuz ‘bend, joint’, *wulþuz ‘glory’). Since there were no agent nouns in *-tu-, there was no reason for disambiguation, and thus no feminine gender was assigned to these verbal abstracts. When we do find feminine abstracts in *-tu-, as for instance in $Greek (cf. μνηστύς f. ‘wooing’, δαιτύς f. ‘meal’, etc.), they are explainable through $a secondary implementation of the gender assignment rule “assign feminine gen-der to verbal abstracts” in the individual branch.

A few examples of root nouns may serve to illustrate the process of disam-biguation through gender assignment. On the basis of widespread evidence we $can reconstruct a masculine root noun *h₂nér- ‘manly one, man’ (Greek ἀνήρ, Ve-$dic nár-, etc.). At the same time, however, there is reason to believe that there was $also an abstract noun *h₂nér- ‘vigor’, inferable from the second member °-ήνωρ in ἀγήνωρ ‘having great courage’, and from Vedic nr̥-vánt- ‘strong’ < *‘possessing, $provided with *nr̥-’ (cf. Nussbaum 2022). It seems unsatisfactory to assume that

*h₂nér- ‘manly one, man’ acquired an abstract meaning ‘manliness, vigor’ second-arily, and equally counter-intuitive that *h₂nér- ‘manly one, man’ should be a re-cent concretization of an original abstract meaning ‘vigor’. More appealing is the idea that *h₂nér- naturally had both meanings, i.e., of an adjectival abstract and of a concrete referent, something which is far more common cross-linguistically $than it may seem at first sight (cf. Greek γλεῦκος n. ‘sweetness’ and ‘sweet wine’ $< *‘something sweet’). Once the feminine gender and its agreement system were established, *h₂nér- ‘vigor’, being abstract, was assigned feminine gender,24 while

*h₂nér- ‘manly one, man’ remained masculine (supported by the biological sex of its referent).

A further example is *nék̑-. In the two-gender system, this root noun would have been common gender and united both abstract ‘death’ and concrete ‘dead one’ in itself. A differentiation would only have been possible through context, though there are not many contexts in which the ambiguity would actually have made conversations difficult. In the three-gender system, *nék̑- f. now exclusive-ly meant ‘death’ (unless referring to a female dead person, in which case *nék̑-

23 Vedic vástu- f. ‘brightening, dawning, daybreak’ is exceptionally feminine because the underlying concept of ‘dawn’ (and ‘Dawn’), uṣás-, is feminine.

24 Since the simplex *h₂nér- ‘vigor’ is not attested, we do not know its gender, but compare the adjectival root-noun abstracts *lúk- f. ‘light’ (Vedic rúc- f., Latin lūx f.), *bʰŕ̥g̑ʰ- f.

‘height’ (Proto-Germanic *burgz f. ‘stronghold’, Old Irish brí f. ‘hill’).

55Gender in Indo-European

f. ‘dead (woman)’ would be expected), continued by Latin nex, -cis f. ‘murder’, $while *nek̑- m. was reserved for the meaning ‘dead one’, as attested in Greek νέκες· νεκροί ‘corpses’ (Hsch.). $

A third example is from the root *h₃reg̑- ‘rule’. In Vedic, the root noun rā́ṭ is attested both as a feminine ‘ruling power’ (e.g., iyáṃ te rā́ṭ ‘this is your strength’ VS, ŚB) as well as a masculine ‘king, master’ (RV). Only in the latter meaning do we find cognates outside India, viz. Latin rēx, Old Irish rí, Middle Welsh rhi, all ‘king’. While it is possible that these facts point to a Proto-Indo-European or Core Indo-European root noun *h₃rḗg̑s ‘ruling power’ that was secondarily concretized to a meaning ‘king’ (cf. Weiss 2017), it is also conceivable that the noun had both meanings, ‘ruling power’ and ‘ruler’, right from the beginning, and that the emer-gence of the three-gender system helped distinguish the abstract feminine ‘ruling power’ from the concrete masculine ‘ruler’. Of course, a non-abstract feminine

*h₃rḗg̑s would still be legitimate when referring to a female ruler, which probably explains Gaulish female personals names in -rix such as Biturix (cf. Stüber 2007a) and the rā́ṭ in RV 5.46.8 that refers to a female goddess.

10 Conclusion

The purpose of this paper has been to give an overview of gender as a gram-matical category in the Indo-European languages. Focusing on the distinction between masculine and feminine, its goal has been to illustrate in which areas of the language we can distinguish genders of nouns. I have tried to outline a possi-ble scenario for the emergence of the feminine gender as being the result of and in conjunction with several ‘ingredients’, and not due to a single factor. Finally, I have presented a survey of the groups of words that acquired or were assigned to the feminine gender, including an outline of how this newly established distinc-tion was exploited to differentiate formerly ambiguous words. In sum, I hope to have shown that grammatical gender is indeed an “endlessly fascinating category” (Corbett 2014: 1) that will probably continue to amaze and puzzle generations of scholars to come.
