Pan, Pūsạn and their matrimonial functions

Jil Schermutzki Westfälische Wilhelms-Universität Münster 1

This article is a modest contribution to the study of the two gods Pan and

Pūṣan, who have long been associated with each other. After touching on

the etymological derivation of the two deities’ names and the points of

comparison between them which have been widely accepted in scholarship

so far, I elaborate on the notion of their Indo-European origin by adding a

new perspective: marriage, matrimony, and fertility. The role of marriage is

attested for Pūs ̣an in the Sūryāsūkta, and this article discusses the possible

evidence of the same role for Pan. I summarise by comparing these features,

once again confirming the associations of the deities.

Since the end of the 19th century, the two shepherd gods Pan and Pūṣan have been compared to and associated with each other (cf. West 2007: 281). In this ar-ticle, the hypothesis that they are offshoots of an Indo-European shepherd god is affirmed by adding a new element of comparison. The thesis can be summarised in the words of Calvert Watkins: “In the Arcadian figures of Pan transformed into Hermes = Pūṣan we have to deal with the reflexes of an Indo-European divinity reconstructible both in name and in function” (Watkins 1970: 351). In the follow-ing, however, I will not deal with the transformation of Pan into Hermes; only the mythological connection of the two will be mentioned.

A highly specific common feature of Pan and Pūṣan is the etymological re-lationship of their names, which is generally accepted today. One can discuss whether one wants to trace both back to a paradigm with stem alternation, with $nominative *páh₂usōn (for Greek Πάν) and genitive *puh₂snés (for Vedic Pūṣán-, $gen. Pūṣṇás) or, as Birgit Olsen (2009: 353) suggests, both to a common base form

*puh₂sṓn or, more precisely, *puh₂sh₃ṓn (see also Olsen, this volume). It would be important to know the morphological structure and the naming motif of the

1 I want to use this opportunity to thank Birgit Olsen and the team of the conference Power, Gender, and Mobility. Features of Indo-European Society for giving me the op-portunity to present my results, and to Michael Janda for his guidance and inspiration. I am also very grateful to Patrick Stiles for comments on an earlier draft.

64 Jil Schermutzki

name. Today, one predominantly sees in it a formation with the ‘Hoffmann’ pos-sessive suffix (nom. sg. -h₃ōn) based on an us-stem *páh₂-us-, meaning ‘sheltered domain or pasture’, which in turn would be derived from the Proto-Indo-Euro-pean root *peh₂(i̯)- ‘to protect, shepherd, pasture’ (LIV²: 460). Thus, for Norbert Oettinger, the predecessor of Pan and Pūṣan was a ‘lord of the sheltered domain’ or ‘of the pasture’, which would fit well with the characterization of the two gods (Oettinger 1998: 545–546, 2000: 397; cf. Malzahn 2014: 163).

On the other hand, Michael Janda informs me that in an unpublished dis-cussion piece after Oettinger’s lecture in Erlangen (2000), he pointed out that another Proto-Indo-European root, *pi̯eh₂- ‘to beat’ (LIV²: 481–482), shows a u-extension in the present stem *pi̯éh₂-u- which, in purely descriptive terms, could correspond to the *-u- in the designation of our god – especially since the $two relevant verbs, Greek παίω and Latin paviō (both reflecting *pau̯i̯e/o-), point $to a root extension *peh₂-u- rather than *pi̯eh₂-u-. On such u-presents, see Jens Elmegård Rasmussen’s (2011: 491–497) study. In this case, the Indo-European god would be named after a ‘blow’ he delivers with his whip, something which is en-countered in descriptions of both gods.

1 Comparison of the two deities

In Zeitschrift für vergleichende Sprachforschung 42 (1908), Schulze expressed his $belief that, since Pan’s old name “Παων” had recently been discovered on an in-scription from Arcadia (dat. sg. Παονι), Pan and Pūṣan may share their etymo-$logical heritage (cf. Schulze 1908: 81).

Based on that remark, a series of comparative studies emerged, not only con-cerning the names of the two gods, but also their features. The most striking is their connection to goats. Pan’s association with these animals is represented in his physical appearance, his two horns and goat-like legs:

$ἀμφί μοι Ἑρμείαο φίλον γόνον ἔννεπε Μοῦσα, αἰγιπόδην δικέρωτα φιλόκροτον, ὅς τ ̓ ἀνὰ πίση δενδρήεντ ̓ ἄμυδις φοιτᾷ χορο<γ>ηθέσι νύμφαις (h.Pan. 1–3) $

About Hermes’ dear child tell me, Muse, the goat-footed, two-horned rowdy, who roams about the wooded fields together with the dance-merry nymphs. (West 2003: 198f.)

65Pan, Pūṣan and their matrimonial functions

Pūṣan is connected to goats as well since they are his draft animals, setting him apart from the other gods whose chariots are drawn by horses:

asyā́ ū ṣú ṇa úpa sātáye bhuvó ’heḷamāno rarivā́ṁ ajāśva śravasyatām ajāśva ó ṣú tvā vavṛtīmahi stómebhir dasma sādhúbhiḥ nahí tvā pūṣann atimánya āghr̥ṇe ná te sakhyám apahnuvé (RV 1.138.04)

Will you come near us, for the winning of this (“team” of wealth), you who have goats for horses, who are not wrathful but bestowing—you who have goats for horses, (for the benefit) of those who seek fame? We would turn you hither with praises that achieve their goal, wondrous one, for I do not disdain you, glowing Pūṣan, nor do I spurn your fellowship.2

West (2007: 282) adds that on occasion goats were sacrificed to Pūṣan. The appearances of the two gods are described in similar ways. Pūṣan is said

to be bearded (10.26.7), and while other deities like Indra appear to have beards as well, it is a feature he shares with Pan, who is described as being very hairy and bearded immediately after his birth (cf. h.Pan. 39).

The cult of Pan spread throughout Greece since the 5th century bce. Before that he could only be found in Arcadia, an area known for the nature-bound shepherd lifestyle in its arts and literature. An environment fitting for the goat-like god Pan, who “roams the mountains and climbs the peaks to view the flocks” (West 2007: 282). Pūṣan performs a similar function regarding the protection of cattle. In RV 6.54 this feature expands from livestock to wealth in general and to the role of bringing back lost cattle:

pūṣā́ gā́ ánv etu naḥ pūṣā́ rakṣatv árvataḥ pūṣā́ vā́jaṃ sanotu naḥ pū́ṣann ánu prá gā́ ihi yájamānasya sunvatáḥ asmā́kaṃ stuvatā́m utá mā́kir neśan mā́kīṃ riṣan mā́kīṃ sáṃ śāri kévaṭe áthā́riṣṭābhir ā́ gahi śr̥ṇvántam pūṣáṇaṃ vayáṃ íryam ánaṣṭavedasam ī́śānaṃ rāyá īmahe pū́ṣan táva vraté vayáṃ ná riṣyema kádā caná stotā́ras ta ihá smasi

2 All English translations of the Rigveda (unless otherwise indicated) are taken from Jamison and Brereton (2014).

66 Jil Schermutzki

pári pūṣā́ parástād dhástaṃ dadhātu dákṣiṇam púnar no naṣṭám ā́jatu (RV 6.54.5–10)

Let Pūṣan follow after the cows for us; let Pūṣan protect the steeds; let Pūṣan win the prize for us. Pūṣan, go forth after the cows of him who sacrifices and presses (soma), and of us who praise (you). Let none disappear; let none be harmed, let none get fractured in a hole. But with unharmed (cows) come here. Pūṣan who listens, the take-charge one whose possessions never get lost, him holding sway over wealth do we beseech for wealth. Pūṣan, under your commandment might we never suffer harm. We here are your praisers. (Even) from a distance let Pūṣan place his right hand around (us); let him drive our lost (livestock) back to us again.

In contrast to these good-natured spirits, there are some indications of cruel and mischievous character traits. Panic is one of the key features of the Arcadian god, as the word indicates. He scares the shepherds and the livestock with his whip-lash while remaining unseen, and creates a dreadful feeling of panic just for fun, which puts men and beasts to rout. Pūṣan does not seem to scare for his own enjoyment, but in RV 6.53.5–8 we see a rather cruel handling of a miser:

pári tr̥ndhi paṇīnā́m ā́rayā hŕ̥dayā kave áthem asmábhyaṃ randhaya ví pūṣann ā́rayā tuda paṇér icha hr̥dí priyám áthem asmábhyaṃ randhaya ā́ rikha kikirā́ kr̥ṇu paṇīnā́ṃ hŕ̥dayā kave áthem asmábhyaṃ randhaya yā́m pūṣan brahmacódanīm ā́rām bíbharṣy āghr̥ṇe táyā samasya hŕ̥dayam ā́ rikha kikirā́ kr̥ṇu (RV 6.53.5–8)

Bore around the hearts of the niggards with an awl, you poet. And make them subject to us. Thrust through (them) with an awl, Pūṣan. Seek what is dear to the heart of the niggard. And make them subject to us. Shred them, make them shrapnel—the hearts of the niggards, you poet. And make them subject to us.

67Pan, Pūṣan and their matrimonial functions

The awl that you carry, which impels the sacred formulation, o glowing Pūṣan, with it shred the heart of each one, make it shrapnel.

In RV6.58.1, Oettinger (1998: 545) finds another hint to Pūṣan’s two-faced char-acter.

śukráṃ te anyád yajatáṃ te anyád víṣurūpe áhanī dyaúr ivāsi víśvā hí māyā́ ávasi svadhāvo bhadrā́ te pūṣann ihá rātír astu

Light is your one, sacrificial your other form; you are like the sky during the different halves of the day, because you love all phantasms, you self-important one. Your generosity shall be auspicious here, Pūṣan.3

These are some key features the two deities share apart from their common name. Now I will focus on their function in the matrimonial sphere.

2 Pūṣan

The hymn RV 10.85, widely known as Sūryāsūkta, is an important sūkta in the context of marriage and fertility and reveals the role Pūṣan plays in this sphere. First, we get acquainted with the groom, Soma – not the ritual drink, but the god, associated with the moon. The bride is Sūryā, the daughter of the sun. Their wedding “serves as a prototype of human marriage” (Jamison and Brereton 2014: 1519), which gives us hints about the rituals taking place. It is said that the wooers of Sūryā are the Aśvins led by Agni. Jamison and Brereton interpret this role not as a sexual relationship with the bride-to-be, but as representatives of the groom who go to the bride’s father to negotiate the marriage. What follows is a long pas-sage about other deities and the Aśvins’ chariot that takes the bride to her new house. The narrator of the hymn then declares “the new wife off-limits” (Jamison and Brereton 2014: 1519) and bound to her new husband to have sons and fortune (stanzas 21–26). As we reach the deflowering of the bride, Pūṣan enters the scene to lead her:

pūṣā́ tvetó nayatu hastagŕ̥hyāśvínā tvā prá vahatāṃ ráthena gr̥hā́n gacha gr̥hápatnī yáthā́so vaśínī tváṃ vidátham ā́ vadāsi (RV 10.85.26)

3 My translation, based on the German translation by Geldner (1951–57).

68 Jil Schermutzki

Let Pūṣan lead you from here, having taken you by the hand. Let the Aśvins convey you forth in their chariot. Go to the house, so that you will be mistress of the house. Exerting your will you will announce the ceremonial distribution.

Her former virginity becomes evident by the red marks of blood on her garment and with this affirmation her husband is bound to her. After that, an interesting passage follows, where the power of the wife is described as witchcraft.

nīlalohitám bhavati kr̥tyā́saktír vy àjyate édhante asyā jñātáyaḥ pátir bandhéṣu badhyate párā dehi śāmulyàm brahmábhyo ví bhajā vásu kr̥tyáiṣā́ padvátī bhūtvy ā́ jāyā́ viśate pátim (RV 10.85.28–29)

It [= bride’s garment] becomes dark red. [She = the bride] becomes witchcraft, a noose. She is smeared (with blood). Her relatives are elated; her husband is bound in bonds. Hand over the stained garment; to the brahmins parcel out the goods. She herself has become walking witchcraft: the wife enters her husband.

This passage shows how the sexual act has a mutual influence on the spouses: the groom is usually physically superior, but the bride has witchcraft to “enter her husband”.

tā́m pūṣañ chivátamām érayasva yásyām bī́jam manuṣyā̀ vápanti yā́ na ūrū́ uśatī́ viśráyāte yásyām uśántaḥ prahárāma śépam (RV 10.85.37)

Pūṣan, rouse her, most kindly disposed—(she) in whom humans scatter their seed, (she) who will willingly spread apart her thighs for us, (she) in whom we can willingly thrust our penis.

Pūṣan’s role is now to arouse the wife so she is willing to receive the semen. Sūryā is said to have four husbands after she was conveyed by Pūṣan. The first is Soma, the second Gandharva, the third Agni, who grants the fourth, human husband a long life and splendour along with the wife. Finally, the sūkta concludes with blessings regarding children and prosperity.

In RV 6.55, we find an odd remark about Pūṣan being the lover of his sister and the wooer of his mother. Although incest is not an uncommon theme in mythology, Pūṣan’s relationships to his sister and mother nonetheless seem a little misplaced in a sūkta that mostly focuses on his goat-drawn chariot and his wealth.

69Pan, Pūṣan and their matrimonial functions

A possible explanation could be that an assumed progeny will be prosperous if the mythological parents stem from the same, glorious family.

éhi vā́ṃ vimuco napād ā́ghr̥ṇe sáṃ sacāvahai rathī́r r̥tásya no bhava rathī́tamaṃ kapardínam ī́śānaṃ rā́dhaso maháḥ rāyáḥ sákhāyam īmahe rāyó dhā́rāsy āghr̥ṇe váso rāśír ajāśva dhī́vato-dhīvataḥ sákhā pūṣáṇaṃ nv àjā́śvam úpa stoṣāma vājínam svásur yó jārá ucyáte mātúr didhiṣúm abravaṃ svásur jāráḥ śr̥ṇotu naḥ bhrā́téndrasya sákhā máma ā́jā́saḥ pūṣáṇaṃ ráthe niśr̥mbhā́s té janaśríyam deváṃ vahantu bíbhrataḥ (RV 6.55.1–6)

Come here! Let us two, o child of release, glowing one, together accompany each other. Become the charioteer of truth for us. The best charioteer, with braided hair, holding sway over great bounty, the companion of wealth we beseech for wealth. You are a stream of wealth, glowing one, a heap of goods, you with goats as horses, the companion of every visionary. Pūṣan who has goats for horses let us now approach with praise—the prize-winner, who is said to be the lover of his sister. The wooer of his mother I have spoken to: let the lover of his sister hear us, brother of Indra, companion to me. Let the trusty [?] goats draw Pūṣan on his chariot, him who brings (all) to readiness *with his sharp (goad), they bearing the god.

In contrast to the Sūryāsūkta (RV 10.85) discussed above, where Pūṣan has the function to arouse her for the husband, he himself is said to be the husband of Sūryā in the following stanza.

pūṣā́ subándhur divá ā́ pr̥thivyā́ iḷás pátir maghávā dasmávarcāḥ yáṃ devā́so ádaduḥ sūryā́yai kā́mena kr̥táṃ tavásaṃ sváñcam (RV 6.58.4)

Pūṣan has good lineage from Heaven and from Earth, lord of refreshment, bounteous, of wondrous luster, whom the gods gave to Sūryā, him prompted by desire, powerful, of lovely outlook.

70 Jil Schermutzki

Jamison and Brereton also suggest an allusion to the matrimony of Pūṣan and Sūryā in RV 10.26, another hymn dedicated to Pūṣan.

ādhī́ṣamāṇāyāḥ pátiḥ śucā́yāś ca śucásya ca vāsovāyó ’vīnām ā́ vā́sāṃsi mármr̥jat (RV 10.26.6)

The husband of her who cares [?] [= Sūryā?], (companion) of the gleaming (female [= Dawn?]) and gleaming (male [= Agni, Soma, Sun?]), weaver of garments of sheep [= wool], always rubbing [= cleaning] the garments.

Since most of the hymns do not attest to a matrimonial relationship between Pūṣan and Sūryā it is not very clear how to interpret the last two stanzas. It may be that the passages refer to the connection between these two divinities from 10.85 concerning the wedding night and read into it a legal status, perhaps a met-aphorical one.

3 Pan

Pan, too, appears in the context of wedding and matrimony in passages from ancient texts. As we know from the Homeric Hymn to Pan, the god shares his abode with nymphs,4 though he never has a sexual relation with them. This ten-sion between proximity and distance is reflected in mythology and holds many opportunities for ancient writers.

3.1 Pan in Aristophanes’ Lysistrata

The power of sexuality is an essential theme in Aristophanes’ play Lysistrata. The author describes how in the twentieth year of the Peloponnesian War, 411 bce, the sexual frustration of the warring men was used by the women who were tired of war to put an end to the fighting. The wives, both Athenian and Spartan, withhold their marital duties and through this sexual blackmail eventually manage to restore peace. Even though Pan is only mentioned in a few places, he is the driving force of

$4 It may be noted that the Greek word νύμφη has two meanings: on the one hand, it may $refer to a human woman before her wedding, that is, a bride; on the other, it is also used to refer to the supernatural semi-divine female figures that the term ‘nymph’ is commonly associated with today.

71Pan, Pūṣan and their matrimonial functions

the action, symbolised by the door to his grotto that was reproduced on the stage set (cf. Landfester 2019: 32). In his edition of Lysistrata, Manfred Landfester (2019: 55) notes that the men “must be made voluptuous and horny as Pan [is].”

The protagonist Lysistrata gives an account of how the cult of the shepherd god was celebrated.

$ἀλλ’ εἴ τις ἐς Βακχεῖον αὐτὰς ἐκάλεσεν, ἢ ’ς Πανὸς ἢ ’πὶ Κωλιάδ’, ἢ ’ς Γενετυλλίδος, οὐδ’ ἂν διελθεῖν ἦν ἂν ὑπὸ τῶν τυμπάνων. νῦν δ’ οὐδεμία πάρεστιν ἐνταυθοῖ γυνή, πλὴν ἥ γ’ ἐμὴ κωμῆτις ἥδ’ ἐξέρχεται. χαῖρ’, ὦ Καλονίκη. (Ar. Lys. 1–5) $

[Lys:] Now were they summoned to some shrine of Bacchus, Pan, Colias, Genetyllis, there had been No room to stir, so thick the crowd of timbrels. And now! – there’s not one woman to be seen. Stay, here comes one, my neighbour Calonice. Good morning, friend. (Rogers 1946: 7)

Describing the empty streets where there is no woman to be found, she creates an image that is so very different from a scene that would occur if there was a feast of Pan or Colias or Genetyllis, the latter two being deities from the reproductive and erotic sphere. Instead of emptiness there would be dazzling music from tambou-rines and crowded streets appropriate for these gods or goddesses.

3.2 Pan in Menander’s Dyskolos

Another well-known work of Ancient Greek literature provides us with informa-tion about the power attributed to Pan. In Menander’s Dyskolos, the frame of the story is set by the shepherd god himself when he makes a rich young man, Sostra-tos, fall in love with a young girl who lives with her misanthrope of a father, a farmer named Knemon. The girl honours the nymphs who live with Pan, in order for him to reward her reverence with the possibility of a rich marriage.

Sostratos’ mother, alarmed by a dream in which she saw her son in fetters and commanded by Pan to dig the fields, sacrifices to the god so this situation may turn out for her son’s best interests. The ritual is interrupted by the cook who forgets the pot for the sacrifice; he has to ask Knemon for help, which serves

72 Jil Schermutzki

the comic plot. Some fragments of the text show us how a usual ritual would be held. While not engaged in the ritual, a slave named Daos from the household of Knemon’s stepson Gorgias (half-brother to the girl Sostratos loves) sees some drunken worshippers of Pan dancing and singing outside the shrine (230–233). Sostratos’ mother also orders a hired piper, Parthenis, to play the pipe, because

“one should not approach this god in silence” (Balme 2001: 20). Two other serv-ants, the cook Sikon and the slave Getas, carry the necessary items such as the sheep that is to be sacrificed, rugs and cushions, presumably to make the shrine more comfortable (394, 403). To prepare the sacrifice (i.e., to cook the sheep), some other items are needed, such as holy water and a stewing pot. Balme notes that “the sacrificial knife, barley grains for scattering on the victims head” (Balme 2001: 295) can be added to the items mentioned in the play.

As the story continues, the reader learns that both Pan’s initial curse to make Sostratos fall in love and the sacrifice in his honour lead the man into matrimony with his chosen one. In addition, Gorgias is elevated to be a man of honour by Sostratos’ father and is promised one of his daughters in marriage (843–845).

Both Lysistrata and Dyskolos provide information about the rituals that were per-formed in connection with Pan. What is striking here is that integral parts in-clude music, dance, and alcohol, which puts the mostly female participants into a frenzy. As described in Dyskolos, the rituals held for Pan may have been linked to fertility and/or the covenant of marriage.

3.3 Pan and the Nymphs

In later ancient sources, Pan himself is the protagonist in carnal episodes with nymphs. However, these do not end in fulfilment, but rather with the ruin of the female part. This is a frequent pattern (cf. Borgeaud 1988: 78–79): Pan is filled with lust and approaches the nymph, but she refuses and flees. Either through Pan’s active intervention or by suicide, the nymph dies and is taken up and trans-formed by Gaia.

In Longos’ Daphnis and Chloe, the echoing songs of sailors prompt Daphnis to tell Chloe about the myth of the nymph Echo. As the mortal daughter of a nymph and a human, she is brought up by nymphs and muses. She is very talented at singing and playing the syrinx, and proud of her virginity. Pan is furious because he cannot seduce her, but also jealous of her talents. In his anger, he drives some

73Pan, Pūṣan and their matrimonial functions

shepherds and goatherds insane, so they tear Echo into pieces, scattering her still singing body throughout the world. Since then, she imitates all the sounds that she hears, even the whistling Pan.

$ἄρρενας δὲ ἔφευγε πάντας καὶ ἀνθρώπους καὶ θεούς, φιλοῦσα τὴν παρθενίαν. ὁ Πὰν ὀργίζεται τῇ κόρῃ, τῆς μουσικῆς φθονῶν, τοῦ κάλλους μὴ τυχών, καὶ μανίαν ἐμβάλλει τοῖς ποιμέσι καὶ τοῖς αἰπόλοις. οἱ δὲ ὥσπερ κύνες ἢ λύκοι δι-ασπῶσιν αὐτὴν καὶ ῥίπτουσιν εἰς πᾶσαν τὴν γῆν ἔτι ᾄδοντα τὰ μέλη. (Longus $3.23.2–3)

She [Echo] shunned all males, humans and gods alike, liking her maidenhood. Pan grew angry with the girl, being jealous of her music and unsuccessful at winning her beauty. He afflicted the shepherds and goatherds with madness, and they tore her apart like dogs or wolves and scattered her limbs, still sing-ing, over all the earth.” (Henderson 2009: 132–133)

Another noteworthy myth is Pan and Pitys. The connection between Pan and a pine tree is already hinted at in Daphnis and Chloe where people perform a sacri-fice to Pan under a pine tree. The Geoponica (11.10) tells us about the love triangle between Pitys, Pan, and Boreas, the North Wind. Because Pitys favours Pan, Bo-reas is enraged and kills Pitys. Gaia transforms her into a tree, the pine tree. Her relationship to the two divinities, however, remains the same: as a wreath, her branches crown Pan, but when the North Wind Boreas blows around her, she moans and moans (Owens 1806: 74–75).

In contrast to that, Nonnos’ Dionysiaca tells us that it is again Pan she is flee-ing from because of his obtrusive stalking, and that she disappears into the earth and becomes a tree with “honey-sweet tears” (i.e., pine nuts).

$μέλπε Πίτυν φυγόδεμνον, ὀρειάσι σύνδρομον αὔραις, Πανὸς ἀλυσκάζουσαν ἀνυμφεύτους ὑμεναίους· μέλπε μόρον φθιμένης αὐτόχθονα· μέμφεο γαίῃ. καὶ τάχα δακρύσειε γοήμονος ἄλγεα νύμφης καὶ μόρον οἰκτείρουσα· σὺ δὲ φρένα τέρπεο σιγῇ μυρομένης ὁρόων μελιηδέα δάκρυα κούρης· οὐδὲ γέλως πέλε τοῖος, ἐπεὶ πλέον οἴνοπι μορφῇ ἱμερταὶ γεγάασιν, ὅτε στενάχουσι γυναῖκες. (Nonn. D. 42.259–266) $

Yes, and sing also of Pitys who hated marriage, who fled fast as the wind over the mountains to escape the unlawful wooing of Pan, and her fate – how she

74 Jil Schermutzki

disappeared into the soil herself; put the blame on the Earth! Then she may perhaps lament the sorrows and the fate of the wailing nymph; but you must let your heart rejoice in silence, as you see the honey-sweet tears of the sorrow-ing maid. No laugh was ever like that, since women become more desirable with that ruddy flush when they mourn. (Rouse 1932: 244–247)

The myth of Pan and the nymph Syrinx is also mentioned in Daphnis and Chloe. The nymph Syrinx is a talented singer and is quite merry. One day, Pan takes interest in her, but she refuses his advances. He gets violent and tries to rape the nymph; she flees into the swamp, but Pan follows her. The storyteller, Lamon, Daphnis’ foster father, explains how Pan cuts the reeds and, since he cannot find Syrinx, believes that she is dead. From the reeds, Pan creates an instrument, the varying length of the pipes symbolizing the unequal “love” they felt. And so, the syrinx, the characteristic pan-pipes, was born.

$ὁρμᾷ διώκειν ὁ Πὰν ἐς βίαν. ἡ Σῦριγξ ἔφευγε καὶ τὸν Πᾶνα καὶ τὴν βίαν· φεύγουσα κάμνουσα ἐς δόνακας κρύπτεται, εἰς ἕλος ἀφανίζεται. Πὰν τοὺς δόνακας ὀργῇ τεμών τὴν κόρην οὐχ εὑρών τὸ πάθος μαθὼν τὸ ὄργανον νοεῖ [καὶ] τοὺς καλάμους κηρῷ συνδήσας ἀνίσους, καθότι καὶ ὁ ἔρως ἄνισος αὐτοῖς· καὶ ἡ τότε παρθένος καλὴ νῦν ἐστι σῦριγξ μουσική. (Longos 2.34) $

Pan started to chase her with force in mind. Syrinx started running from Pan and his force. When she tired from running, she hid in some reeds and vanished into a marsh. Pan angrily cut away the reeds, could not find the girl, realized what had happened to her, and thought of the instrument after he had bound reeds together with wax, of unequal lengths just as their love had been unequal. And what was once a fair maiden is now a musical syrinx. (Henderson 2009: 98–99)

Syrinx and Pan are also involved in a premarital ritual that Achilles Tatius depicts in The Adventures of Leucippe and Clitophon. After Leucippe endures a series of adventures amongst men and pirates, Thersander makes a vile comment about pan-pipes and openly doubts Leucippe’s virginity, prompting Clitophon to ask a priest about the background of the remark. The priest now retells the myth of Pan and Syrinx but also mentions a ritual that reveals the status of a girl’s virginity. The girl in question is locked into a grotto, dedicated to Pan. If she is still a virgin, a clear tone from the pan-pipe is heard. If not, the pipe remains silent, a groan can be heard, and the people leave the grotto locked for a few days.

75Pan, Pūṣan and their matrimonial functions

$ὁρᾷς τουτὶ τὸ ἄλσος τὸ κατόπιν τοῦ νεώ. ἐνθάδε ἐστὶ σπήλαιον ἀπόρρητον γυναιξί, καθαραῖς δὲ εἰσελθούσαις οὐκ ἀπόρρητον παρθένοις· ἀνάκειται δὲ σύριγξ ὀλίγον ἔνδον τῶν τοῦ σπηλαίου θυρῶν. εἰ μὲν οὖν τὸ ὄργανον καὶ παρ’ ὑμῖν ἐπιχωριάζει τοῖς Βυζαντίοις, ἴστε ὃ λέγω· εἰ δέ τις ὑμῶν ἦττον ὡμίλησε ταύτῃ τῇ μουσικῇ, φέρε καὶ οἷόν ἐστιν εἴπω, καὶ τὸν ταύτῃ τοῦ Πανὸς πάντα μῦθον. […] ταύτην οὖν τὴν σύριγγά φασιν ἀναθεῖναι μὲν ἐνθάδε τὸν Πᾶνα, περιορίσαι δὲ εἰς σπήλαιον αὐτήν, θαμίζειν τε αὐτοῦ καὶ τῇ σύριγγι συνήθως αὐλεῖν. χρόνῳ δὲ ὕστερον χαρίζεται τὸ χωρίον τῇ Αρτέμιδι, συνθήκας ποιη-σάμενος πρὸς αὐτήν, μηδεμίαν ἐκεῖ καταβαίνειν γυναῖκα. ὅταν οὖν αἰτίαν ἔχῃ τις οὐκ εἶναι παρθένος, προπέμπει μὲν αὐτὴν ό δῆμος μέχρι τῶν τοῦ σπηλαίου θυρῶν, δικάζει δὲ ἡ σύριγξ τὴν δίκην. ἡ μὲν γὰρ παῖς εἰσ έρχεται κεκοσμημένη στολῇ τῇ νενομισμένῃ, ἄλλος δὲ ἐπικλείει τὰς τοῦ σπηλαίου θύρας. κἄν μὲν ᾖ παρθένος, λιγυρόν τι μέλος ἀκούεται καὶ ἔνθεον, ἤτοι τοῦ τόπου πνεῦμα ἔχοντος μουσικὸν εἰς τὴν σύριγγα τεταμιευμένον, ἢ τάχα καὶ ὁ Πὰν αὐτὸς αὐλεῖ. μετὰ δὲ μικρὸν αὐτόμαται μὲν αἰ θύραι ἀνεῴχθησαν τοῦ σπηλαίου, ἐκ-φαίνεται δὲ ἡ παρθένος ἐστεφανωμένη τὴν κεφαλὴν πίτυος κόμαις. ἐὰν δὲ ᾖ τὴν παρθενίαν ἐψευσμένη, σιωπᾷ μὲν ἡ σύριγξ, οἰμωγὴ δέ τις ἀντὶ μουσικῆς ἐκ τοῦ σπηλαίου πέμπεται, καὶ εὐθὺς ὁ δῆμος ἀπαλλάττεται καὶ ἀφίησιν ἐν τῷ σπηλαίῳ τὴν γυναῖκα. τρίτῃ δὲ ἡμέρᾳ παρθένος ἱέρεια τοῦ τόπου παρελθοῦ-σα τὴν μὲν σύριγγα εὑρίσκει χαμαί, τὴν δὲ γυναῖκα οὐδαμοῦ. (Ach.Tat. 8.6) $

You see this grove here behind the shrine. Within it is a grotto that may not be entered by any women except clean maids, and a little within its walls there hangs up a pan-pipes. If this instrument is found as a native institution among you of Byzantium, you will be well acquainted with that of which I speak, but if any of you are less familiar with music of this description, allow me to explain it to you and to tell you the whole story of Pan. […] So it is said that Pan there hung up the instrument, shutting it up in a cave, and that it was his custom to resort there often and play on the pipes. Some time after he made a gift of the whole spot to Artemis, making a compact with her that it should be entered by no woman no longer a maid. If therefore any girl is ac-cused of being of undoubtful virginity, she is sent by public decree to the door of the grotto, and the pan-pipes decides the ordeal for her; she goes in, clad in the proper dress, and the doors are closed behind her. If she is in reality a virgin, a clear and divine note is heard, either because there is some breeze in the place which enters the pipes and makes a musical sound, or possibly because it is Pan himself that is piping; and after a short time the doors of the grotto open of their own accord, and out comes the virgin with a wreath of

76 Jil Schermutzki

the foliage of the pine upon her head. But if she has lied about her virginity, the pan-pipes is silent, and a groan comes forth from the cave instead of a musical sound; the people go away and leave the woman inside. On the third day after, the virgin priestess of the spot comes and finds the pan-pipes lying on the ground, but there is no trace of the woman.” (Gaselee 1917: 402–405)

This ritual, transmitted through literature from the 2nd century ce, reveals the role that Pan plays in the sphere of chastity and matrimony, but also shows his savage nature in dealing with intimate relations.

4 Marriage and fertility

Burkert (1985: 172) writes that “Pan embodies the uncivilized power of procrea-tion which nevertheless remains indispensable and fascinating for civilized life”. As we saw in the preceding section, from the moment the cult of Pan spread throughout Greece,5 he is mentioned in several literary sources and myths within the sphere of sexuality and matrimony. He is associated with nymphs but, as we know from the stories pertaining to them and from the Homeric Hymn to Pan, he does not have a sexual relationship with them and may thus also be character-ised as frustrated. However, when he gets the chance, he becomes uncontrollably $violent and tries to rape the nymphs – what Euripides calls Πανὸς γάμος ‘Panic $marriage’ (i.e., rape). It is impossible for him to enter the bond of marriage and yet, as shown immediately below, he is included and honoured in wedding rituals. In modern Western societies, marriage as a civilised form of sexuality is ideolog-ically opposed to both rape and premarital sex. In ancient Indo-European soci-eties on the other hand, it was not uncommon for marriage to go hand in hand with violence, such as abduction and forced marriage (cf. for instance the Rape of the Sabine Women). As such, it would not be unnatural for Pan to be part of the matrimonial sphere as an embodiment of uncivilised procreative power.

A good piece of evidence for Pan playing a leading role in the marriage ritual is a bowl that was discussed in detail by Alexander Stuart Murray (1902). It is a Megarean bowl, found in Thebes and presumably dating from the 3rd to 1st cen-tury bce (the British Museum dates its production to between 225 and 175 bce).6

5 As West (2007: 281) suggests, Pan first was known only in Arcadia and became promi-nent in other areas in the fifth century bce.

6 See https://www.britishmuseum.org/collection/object/G_1897-0317-3 (27 February 2023).

77Pan, Pūṣan and their matrimonial functions

It shows a scene from the Persephone myth: the daughter of Demeter is abducted by Hades on a chariot, followed by Demeter, Athene, Hecate, and Artemis. The chariot is headed towards the left side of the bowl, into the underworld. The en-$trance to the underworld is symbolised by a stele inscribed ΕΥΣΕΒΩΣ (cf. τῶν εὐσεβῶν λειμῶνας ‘the Fields of the Righteous’ Orph. Fr. 153 Abel). Hermes is in $front of the chariot, between it and the stele, while an odd boyish figure is hiding in reeds on the other side of the stele. Murray interprets this figure as follows:

The arrival of Persephonè in Hades was associated with the Theogamia, and bearing this in mind we at once recognize the boy amid the reeds of Acher-on playing on his flutes as a type of the boy who led the way in marriage pro-cessions […]. But this boy among the reeds, though dressed in the ordinary manner, has two small horns on his forehead. He is therefore a young Pan. Reeds are a natural enough environment for Pan and from his association with nymphs it was perhaps an easy step to connect him with the marriage of Persephonè. (Murray 1902: 4)

So, does this depiction prove a function of Pan as leading the bride? Murray’s de-scription might lead one to answer with a tentative yes, but a few factors give one pause, such as Pan’s position behind the stele (i.e., already in the underworld?) and not in front of the chariot (quasi ‘leading’ it), as well as the lack of more spe-cific features of the shepherd god. It remains questionable whether one can really interpret the figure as Pan leading the bride (i.e., Persephone). Perhaps his po-sition underlines the direction of the procession and goat horns and flutes were iconic enough to make him immediately identifiable. But of course, these are mere presumptions. A more certain hint are the reeds Pan is surrounded by that refer to the story of Syrinx mentioned above.7

To reinforce these presumptions, I am going to compare Pan and Pūṣan in terms of their function in human sexuality and marriage. Both have the ability to arouse a woman; for Pūṣan, this is made clear in the Sūryāsūkta, whereas we learn in Aris-tophanes’ Lysistrata about the ritual dedicated to Pan in which the women reach an orgiastic state. Pūṣan’s role as the leader of the bride is touched upon in the wed-ding song. While this explicit mediating function is elusive for Pan, he very often appears with nymphs, and it is precisely these who, according to their designation,

7 The British Museum also calls this figure between the reeds Pan.

78 Jil Schermutzki

$are the ‘brides’ (νύμφαι) elevated into the semi-divine. Moreover, in Menander’s $Dyskolos, it is to Pan that a sacrifice is made for the success of marriage.

If we now return to Murray’s description of the bowl, Pan is part of the wed-ding procession, but in contrast to the goddesses following the chariot, he is in front of it, already in the underworld, their destination. The question, then, is: how can Pan represent on the one hand unbridled and sometimes crude fervour, and on the other civilised sexuality and marriage, leading the bride into matrimo-ny? Borgeaud summarises this apparent contradiction and the function of Pan in the wedding ritual as follows:

But the meaning of his detachment from the institution of marriage becomes clear only when we see that as patron of everything improper to marriage […], he prepares, introduces, and initiates into marriage. The outcast is from this point of view a founder. One could say much the same of Artemis and the nymphs, although oppositely. Furthermore, just as Artemis, that fierce virgin, is nonetheless also goddess of childbirth, so Pan appears simultane-ously distant from the proper relation between the sexes and, inasmuch as he symbolizes sexual desire, present at the very heart of that relation. To sac-rifice to Pan means to make love; although sanctuaries generally admit only chaste behaviour, his grotto makes a place for furtive unions and welcomes lovers. (Borgeaud 1988: 155–156)

5 Conclusion

As we have seen, there are many parallels between the two shepherd gods Pan and Pūṣan. There is a great deal of overlap not only in their attributes and functions, but also in the etymology of their names.

In this contribution, I have tried to show that, in addition to the already well-established similarities between them, their associations with sexual fertility and their roles in wedding rituals also show a likeness. Since the importance of the Vedic god Pūṣan for the marriage ceremony is established in the Sūryāsūkta (RV 10.85), the focus of this paper was on finding possible corresponding func-tions of the Greek god Pan. Numerous literary and cultic connections between Pan and the ritual of marriage show that similarities to the Vedic god can cer-tainly be found. Since these do not stem from later cultural diffusion, it supports the hypothesis that both Pan and Pūṣan must have a common predecessor, the Indo-European shepherd god *páh₂usō(n).

The Charioteer Athena as goddess of warriors

Constellations and their role in the prehistory of Greek religion

Michael Janda Westfälische Wilhelms-Universität Münster

With Skjærvø’s comparison of the specific Homeric situation of Athena

and Diomedes at the chariot with that of Zarathustra and Aṣ̌i in the Aves-

ta, Windfuhr recognized in Aṣ̌i the mythical transformation of the celestial

Charioteer. And so a new question arises: does Athena also have something

to do with Auriga? In fact, the war goddess wears a goat skin, the famous Ae-

gis, around her shoulders, reminiscent of Capella, the brightest star of Auriga.

This is not the only evidence in favor of an origin of Athena in the night sky.1

1 Athena on the move

Athena, the powerful city goddess of Athens, is the patroness of inventions, crafts and arts. As the goddess of war and warriors, she differs from the bloodthirsty, clumsy Ares in her cool strategy. But it is not only intellectually that she is a very agile goddess. The myth shows her roaring down from Olympus to the battlefield before Troy on her chariot, and in the cult we also see her on the move on her vehicle. How could a goddess enter this domain reserved for men?

2 Goddess and hero at the chariot

In an essay from 1997, published in 2000, Prods Oktor Skjærvø pointed out the similarity between three mythical motif complexes from Homeric Greece, the Iran of the Avesta and the India of the Mahābhārata. I will confine myself in the following to the first two cultures mentioned. The scene takes place on or near a chariot: a goddess meets a hero, praises his beauty and encourages him with her touch. In the fifth book of the Iliad, Athena goes to the battlefield at Troy and

82 Michael Janda

meets the wounded Diomedes, who has just pulled an arrow out of his shoulder (Il. 5.107f., 5.114f., 5.121–126):2

$ […] πρόσθ’ ἵπποιιν καὶ ὄχεσφιν 107 $

$ἔστη […] δὴ τότ’ ἔπειτ’ ἠρᾶτο βοὴν ἀγαθὸς Διομήδης· 114 $

$κλῦθί μευ, αἰγιόχοιο Διὸς τέκος, Ἀτρυτώνη […] ὣς ἔφατ’ εὐχόμενος, τοῦ δ’ ἔκλυε Παλλὰς Ἀθήνη, 121 $

$γυῖα δ’ ἔθηκεν ἐλαφρά, πόδας καὶ χεῖρας ὕπερθεν· ἀγχοῦ δ’ ἱσταμένη ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα· θαρσῶν νῦν, Διόμηδες, ἐπὶ Τρώεσσι μάχεσθαι· ἐν γάρ τοι στήθεσσι μένος πατρώιον ἧκα ἄτρομον, οἷον ἔχεσκε σακέσπαλος ἱππότα Τυδεύς. (Ludwich 1995: I 190f.) $

[…] he stood before the horses and the chariot […] 107

And then Diomedes, good at the war-cry, made a prayer: 114

“Hear me, child of Zeus who carries the aegis, unwearied one! […]” Thus he spoke in prayer, and Pallas Athene heard him, 121

and made his limbs light, his feet and his hands above; and she stood near him and spoke to him winged words:

“Be daring now, Diomedes, to fight against the Trojans, for in thy breast I have put the impetuosity of thy father, the dauntless might, such as the horseman Tydeus, wielder of the shield, used to have.” (Skjærvø 2000: 176)

In the ancient Iranian tradition, the Young Avestan Yašt 17 is addressed to the goddess Aṣ̌i,3 whose name means ‘grant, reward’. She asks Zarathustra, here clear-ly a mythical figure, for his name in Yt. 17.17:

$paiti.staiiata ⁺raθaiia4 $aṣ̌iš vaŋᵛhi yā bərəzaiti uiti vacə̄biš aojana kō ahi yō mąm zbaiiehi. (Hintze 2000: 310)

Good Aṣ̌i the tall stood at/on the chariot [or: as charioteer?],

$ner (1889: 234) and Skjærvø (2000: 176) prefer the emendation ⁺raiθiia.$

83The Charioteer Athena as goddess of warriors

speaking thus with words: Who are you who invoke me? (Skjærvø 2000: 176)

After Zarathustra has made himself known, the following happens (Yt. 17.22):

ā dim usca pairi.marəzat̰ hāuuōiia bāzuuō dašinaca dašina bāzuuō hāuuaiiaca uiti vacə̄biš aojana $srīrō ahi Zaraθuštra $hukərətō ahi Spitama $huuascuuō darəγō.bāzāuš $dātəm tē tanuiie xᵛarənō $urunaēca darəγəm huuaŋhəm yaθa imat̰ yat̰ tē frāuuaocim. $

She stroked him above all around with the left hand and the right, with the right hand and the left speaking thus with words: You are beautiful, Zarathustra, you are well-made, Spitama, you have good calves, long arms. In your body has been placed glory and long well-being for (your) soul, just as I foretold you. (Skjærvø 2000: 176)

Skjærvø (2000: 175) finds five parallels in these two passages:

1 Reference to chariot 2 Proximity of the goddess 3 Stroking of the hero 4 Address of the hero by name 5 Praise of the beauty and strength of the hero

Two caveats are in order. Athena does not touch Diomedes, and Skjærvø (2000: 177) must refer to other actors and passages for this motif in the Iliad, nor does Athena explicitly praise Diomedes’ beauty. She does, however, state that she has $“now” put μένος ‘impetuosity’ (Il. 5.125) into his chest.$

84 Michael Janda

For Skjærvø, the similarities of these motifs in their combination were so characteristic that he considered them to be inherited from the common Indo- European past of both cultures (2000: 175). However, a historical-genetic connec-tion between Athena and Aṣ̌i did not occur to him.

3 Haoma, Zarathustra and the celestial Charioteer

A few years later, Gernot Windfuhr took up Skjærvø’s hypothesis and added it to the picture he had gained of Zarathustra as the mythical priest and, in a cer-tain sense, successor of Haoma, the Avestan god of intoxication. In 2003, Wind-fuhr published a spectacular observation: like his Vedic brother Soma, Haoma is simultaneously the plant and the sap derived from it; he is the sacrificer, the sacrifice and the divine recipient of the sacrifice. And just as Soma is also in the sky, where he is “set in the lap of these heavenly bodies” according to the Rigve-da (10.85.2), Haoma wears a star-adorned belt and resides on mountain tops (Y. 9.26):

$frā tē mazdā̊ barat̰ pauruuanīm aiβiiā̊ŋhanəm stəhrpaēsaŋhəm mańiiu.tāštəm $vaŋᵛhīm daēnąm māzdaiiasnīm. $āat̰ aŋ́he ahi aiβiiāstō baršnuš paiti gairinąm drājańhe aiβiδāitīšca *grauu ūsca mąθrahe. $

Mazda invested you with the (?)5 girdle, the star-adorned, good Mazdayasnian religion created by the spirit, and you have been girded with this on the mountain tops to hold the bridle and sticks of the holy word. (Josephson 1997: 70; cf. Windfuhr 2003: 472)

In the Yašt dedicated to him, Haoma receives a strange offering (Y. 11.4, the sacri-ficial share also in 11.5):

us mē pita haomāi draonō frə̄rənaot̰ ahurō mazdā̊ aṣ̌auua $haŋᵛharəne mat̰ hizuuō hōiiūmca dōiθrəm. $

Righteous Ahura Mazda, [my] father, bestowed upon me, Haoma, a share, both jaws with the tongue and the left eye. (Josephson 1997: 113; cf. Windfuhr 2003: 471)

5 Windfuhr (2003: 472, note 1) understands “parwanya-” (today rather pauruuanīm), as ‘knotted’; conversely, Cantera (2019) understands it as ‘made of tufts of wool’.

85The Charioteer Athena as goddess of warriors

Windfuhr commented on the Haoma sacrifice (2003: 471):

This seemingly disjunct specification, two jaws and left eye, loses its enig-matic nature when sought in the sky: It is the head of Taurus. Specifically, there is a well-known celestial Jaw, which is the V-shaped outline of the Hyades. Inside it is a well-known left eye, which is the lucida of the celestial $Bull, α Tauri, Aldebaran. $

Opposite this “Bull” must then be his divine sacrificer. Windfuhr achieves a bril-liant identification (2003: 472, excluding footnotes):

The specifications “star-adorned” and “mountain tops” support the corre-lation of the sacrificial animal with a celestial constellation. In fact, Taurus stands right in front of the best-known girdle-wearer in the sky, the mighty Orion. To note, Orion does not only wear his own girdle, but also touches the supreme cosmic girdle, which is the Milky Way. The brilliant, and girdled, constellation Orion, then, would appear to be here identified with the radiant apparition of the divine Hauma, facing the head of his sacrificial Bull. The fact that the Avesta seems not to name that most majestic constellation in the sky at all has always been puzzling. The reason appears to be the narrative genre, and the adherence in those texts to astral myths where one and the same constellation may be part of a number of overtly different myths.

The three shining stars of the Orion belt can be reflected in this mythical image. As we have seen, Windfuhr also points to an alternative: the Milky Way could also be meant, since it touches the constellation Orion.

As Windfuhr (2003: 473) puts it, “[t]he divine Hauma-Orion was thus the first hauma-priest”. In his mythical succession we find four fathers who are awarded for their Haoma-service with famous sons, the last of which is Zarathustra. In a later study, Windfuhr (2010)6 asks whether the two personal relationships – be-tween Zarathustra and Haoma in personal succession on the one hand, and be-tween Zarathustra and Aṣ̌i in their meeting at the chariot on the other – can be traced back to a concrete phenomenon of nature. Aṣ̌i’s chariot, on which the god-dess meets the Haoma priest Zarathustra, and on which she also travels in other

6 I am very indebted to Ramiyar Karanjia for a copy (unpaginated) of this important article.

86 Michael Janda

ways, plays a decisive role; for example, she steers the chariot for her brother, the $famous Miθra, in other texts: $

There is only one well-known ‘Charioteer’ in the sky, and that is the constel-lation Auriga. Auriga is astronomically located above Orion, and both are close by Taurus. To note, the constellation Taurus is one of the prominent 12 zodiacal constellations defined by the circle of the ecliptic. Therefore, Aṣ̌i must correlate with the constellation Auriga, which is located above and north of Orion/Haoma-Priest. […] Recognizing the relative positions of the three constellations, it becomes apparent that just as Auriga is above Orion, so Aṣ̌i is above the celestial Haoma-Priest. Thus is explained the hitherto enigmatic and puzzling statement in Yt.17.22 that Aṣ̌i stroked Zarathushtra from ‘above’, thus correlating Haoma-Priest and Zarathushtra. (Windfuhr 2010)

Even before these observations, the Iran of the Avesta was considered a culture whose pantheon – unlike those of the other Indo-Europeans – included astral de-ities in an explicit way. We need only recall the extensive hymn to the star Tištriia (Yašt 8, cf. Panaino 1990/1995), i.e., Sirius in the Canis Major constellation; or the shorter one to the star Vanaṇt (Yašt 21), i.e., Vega in the Lyra constellation.

Skjærvø assumed that the scene between Aṣ̌i and Zarathustra contained a small complex of motifs that reached back over a long tradition to the Indo- Europeans. This seems to be confirmed by Windfuhr’s explanation since refer-ence is made to a basic, unchanging conception of heaven, the neighborhood of the Charioteer and Orion, the most anthropomorphic figure in the sky. We can now ask: what about Athena and Diomedes?

4 The charioteer Athena

It would be interesting to take a closer look at the fifth book of the Iliad, where the great deeds of Diomedes are praised. Over the course of the action, the chariot comes more and more to the fore. Athena and Hera travel on a chariot adorned with gold towards Troy (Il. 5.720–779), where Athena herself climbs into Diome-des’ chariot after she has rudely pushed down the charioteer Sthenelos (5.835f.). With Athena’s help, Diomedes even manages to attack and wound the war god Ares himself (5.841–867). This is a rare case in which a combat is actually fought from the chariot in the Iliad.

87The Charioteer Athena as goddess of warriors

As Walter Burkert recognized (1970: 361f. with note 23 = 1990: 84 with note 23), the epic chariot ride of goddess and hero seems to mirror an older ritual. In Argos in the Peloponnese, the priest of Athena rode on a chariot to a purification ritual together with the cult image of Athena, the Palladion. The etiological narrative recalls a priest, Eumedes, who had once stolen Athena’s cult image and driven it away. Burkert points out the similarity of the names: in Troy, Athena rides with $Διο-μήδης; in Argos, with Εὐ-μήδης. So, it is possible that Homer or one of his $predecessors is not following a momentary poetic idea, but is either poetically transferring a ritual or the event underlying the ritual.

The work of Skjærvø and Windfuhr develops a line of argumentation that we can now pursue without bias. What do we gain if we take the parallel of Aṣ̌i as our basis and see Athena as a divine charioteer, a mythical transformation of Auriga/ Heniochos, the celestial Charioteer? I will limit myself to four points.7

4.1 The Aegis

Seeing Athena as a celestial Charioteer may provide us with an explanation for the strange Aegis that she wears over her shoulder.8 In Homer, the Aegis appears twelve times (for attestations, see van der Valk 1955). The word formation sug-$gests that it is a goatskin: αἰγίς to αἴξ ‘goat’ as νεβρίς ‘fawnskin’ to νεβρός ‘fawn’ – $and accordingly, it is described as having tassels. But it also has miraculous prop-erties: it is described as being ageless and immortal (Il. 2.447) and made of gold (Il. 24.21). As a kind of shield, it protects the corpse of Hector (Il. 24.18–21), but mostly it arouses terror among the people when lifted or shaken by Athena (Od. 22.297+), Zeus (Il. 4.166f.+) or Apollo (Il. 15.321+). Zeus alone bears the epithet $αἰγίοχος, a compound whose second element probably belongs to the root for ‘move’ (⁽*⁾ϝεχ-, PIE *u̯eg̑ʰ-, LIV 661f.) rather than ‘hold’ (ἔχ-, PIE *seg̑ʰ-, LIV 515f.), $cf. LfgrE (I: 251–253) and Janda (2014a: 467f. with literature).

Besides Zeus, the Aegis is worn by his daughter Athena, hanging on her shoulder, and by Apollo. On the upper arm of the celestial charioteer Auriga $shines a star which the astronomy of the classical cultures calls Αἴξ or Capella, $the Goat (cf. Scherer 1953: 124f.). Capella is the sixth-brightest star in the night

7 A more detailed treatment will be provided in Janda (in prep. 2). 8 On the Aigis, see Burkert (2011: 219), Parker (1996), von Geisau (1979), Stengel (1893),

Roscher (1886), Janda (2014a: 460–476, outdated), and Watkins (2000 and 2002: 169– 176) who considers the concept a loan from Anatolia.

88 Michael Janda

sky, the third-brightest in the northern sky. Interpreting Athena as a female charioteer in the sky provides an immediate explanation for the Aegis. Auriga/ Heniochos also carries two little bucks on his hand, as the illustration from the famous Leiden Codex (Leiden Aratea) shows (Hübner 2010: I, plate 1). We owe to Jan Bremmer (1996) an accurate summary of the myth of the goat or nymph Amaltheia, whose horn of plenty was also found in the sky here in this constel-lation.9

4.2 Athena’s birth

Athena has no mother. The myth describes how she sprang from the head of Zeus in full armour. An explanation for this motif presents itself when we understand $Ζεύς in its etymological meaning ‘heaven’ (PIE *Dyḗus, Lat. Iū-piter, Ved. Dyáuṣ): $Athena emerges from the ‘Head of Heaven’. In fact, there is some evidence that the Indo-Europeans knew of a constellation of this name, even if we cannot re-construct its exact designation for the time being. This constellation lies in the immediate vicinity of the Charioteer, so that the celestial succession could be translated into a genealogical one.

$In ancient India the three stars that make up Orion’s three head stars (λ, φ¹, φ² Orionis) were called mṛga-śiras- or mṛga-śīrṣan- ‘Head of the Beast’ (cf. Scher-$er 1953: 155). In Greece, Joseph Fontenrose, in his book Orion: The Myth of the Hunter and the Huntress (1981) has pointed to the close similarity of the Boeotian hunter Orion and Kephalos, who are both described as being lovers of Eos in $different myths (1981: 86–111). Κέφαλος means ‘one who has a (special) head’,10 $and if we see him as representing the same mythological figure as Orion, he may be identified with Orion’s head, and his name forms a neat parallel to the Indian ‘Head of the Beast’.

It thus seems reasonable to posit that the Indo-Europeans knew of a constel-lation they saw as a ‘Head’ in the night sky, and that it was from this ‘Head of Heaven’ that the Charioteer Athena was born.

9 More will be said about these motifs in Janda (in prep. 2 and 4). 10 See Höfler (2020) for more on possessive derivatives of the type ‘having a (special)

body part’.

89The Charioteer Athena as goddess of warriors

4.3 Athena as goddess of war

In an important article, Georges-Jean Pinault (2006) has shown that the Indo- European root *h₁ar- was used in the meaning ‘to attain, acquire, win’ precisely in the sphere of competition. I myself added, among other words, Hitt. arnuwala- to the family of words derived from this root (2014b). Arnuwala- is the ‘prisoner of war’ who is ‘acquired’ and deported from his homeland. I further suggest that two $more nouns also belong here (cf. Janda in prep. 2): the Greek s-stem ἄρος mean-ing ‘harm, damage’ in Hesychius and Hom. ἀρή ‘harm, mischief, ruin’. In the latter $case, things that were ‘acquired’ or ‘won’ in war are seen from the point of view of the defeated. The formal and etymological problems surrounding the name of Ares, the god of war, disappear when one no longer tries to derive all name $forms from a single stem. I suggest that from the s-stem ἄρος the name Ἄρης was formed by internal derivation (cf. ψεῦδος ‘lie’: ψευδής ‘with a lie; lying, false’): Ares is a god ‘who has the booty (and carries it away)’. From ἀρή is formed Ἀρεύς $in the same meaning. Thus, when we encounter a Hermahās Areiās (e-ma-a₂ a-re-ja) in Mycenaean (see most recently Guilleux 2012 with literature), this is perhaps not a Hermes somehow belonging to Ares, but rather Hermes in his familiar role as god of thieves, a Hermes ‘of carrying away’.

It has long been known that Aṣ̌i, the Young Avestan goddess who meets Zara-thustra at the chariot and strengthens him by her touch, owes her name to this root. For Almut Hintze, she is the personified ‘grant’ or ‘reward’ (2000: 74f.). The name of the common Indo-European predecessor of Aṣ̌i can now be traced back to *h₁árti- (with *h₁), and it is possible that this is the same word as the epithet $Ἀρεία borne by Athena in Athens and elsewhere (cf. Burkert 2011: 259, 378). As an $epithet of Athena, it probably refers not so much to her opponent in Homer, the war god Ares, as to the appellative on which his name is based.

4.4 The celestial “Flower”

India has not played much of a role in my discussion so far, and we are missing a goddess corresponding to Aṣ̌i by name. Windfuhr (2010) implicitly assumes that Aṣ̌i is a manifestation of another goddess who also comes along on the chariot and brings abundance to people, namely Ved. Púrandhi-, OAv. Parəṇdi- and YAv. Pārəṇdi-. Her name has recently been explained by Pinault (2016), who brilliantly modified other existing interpretations (cf. EWA II 145f. and Janda 2020: 70) and assumed a verbal compound: Indo-Iranian *pŕ̥-Handhi- consists of a first element

90 Michael Janda

reflecting the root par- ‘to go over, cross over’ and an i-stem related to Ved. án-dhas- ‘flower, soma-plant’ as its second element. The meaning of this compound was ‘carrying the flourishing across’, later developed into ‘promoter of flourishing, plenitude, liberality’, which Pinault interprets as the role of this goddess in con-veying the intoxicating potion, the ‘flower’ par excellence.

$Now, the Greek cognate of ándhas- is ἄνθος, and this noun is the derivational basis of a number of place names like Ἀνθεδών and also Ἀνθάνα in the region $of Thyreatis in the Peloponnese. As early as 1846 Christian August Lobeck (300, $fn. 21) assumed: “Nomina urbium Ἀθῆναι et Ἀνθήνη fortasse idem significant, Florentiam vel Floram” ‘The names of the cities Ἀθῆναι and Ἀνθήνη perhaps $mean the same thing, Florentia or Flora’. I think Lobeck is right. The first nasal $in Ἀνθᾱ́νᾱ may have disappeared by dissimilation, yielding Ἀθᾱ́νᾱ (> Ἀθήνη). $This dissimilation may actually be attested in the writings of Pausanias, where the Anthana in Thyreatis mentioned above is consistently called ‘Athana’ – unless it is merely the name of the famous capital of Attica exerting its influence.

$The base noun ἄνθη is attested in Plato in the meaning ‘full bloom, flower’ (Phaidr. 230b). The name of the goddess belongs here, too: the derivative ἄνθη → Ἀ(ν)θή-νη compares with ἀκμή ‘(highest) point, vigour’ → ἀκμη-νός ‘full-grown’. The charioteer Ἀθήνη possesses ‘full bloom, flower’ or (in a metaphorical use parallel to that predominant for ἄνθος already in Homer) ‘the finest’ and brings $it to men. Frisk (GEW I 28) and Chantraine (DELG 27f.) omit the significant fact $that Homer refers to the goddess 250 times by the name Ἀθήνη,11 which therefore $cannot be derived from the name of the city.

It is thus possible that the Indo-European goddess passed on the – real and onomastic –  possession of *h₂andʰ-, the ‘flourishing’ or ‘finest’, to Purandhi, Parəṇdi/Pārəṇdi and further perhaps to Aṣ̌i (which we do not know) on the one hand, and to Athena on the other.

$The name of the city of Athens – Ἀθήνη, also in the plural Ἀθῆναι – may be based either independently on the same possessive formation *ἀ(ν)θᾱ-νᾱ $‘(the area) provided with blossom’ or – as a collective – on a tribal designation $*Ἀ(ν)θᾶ-ν-ες, which referred to people who inhabited this region rich in flowers (cf. Κρῆτες → Κρήτ-ᾱ). $

11 Overlooked by Leukart (1980: 246, note 27) and Schaffner (2014: 371).

91The Charioteer Athena as goddess of warriors

5 Intoxication in the cosmos: Diomedes and Dionysos

Finally, I would like to discuss the figure of Diomedes12 who, supported by Athe-na, mows down the Trojans in the Iliad. As mentioned earlier, Diomedes possibly has a predecessor, or at least an alter ego, in cult: the Argive priest of Athena called Eumedes. It has always been surprising that Agamemnon – the powerful king of Mycenae, rich in gold – has an independent king, Diomedes, sitting next to him in Argos, only fourteen kilometres away – though of course only a prob-lem if one believes the Iliad to be an accurate historical source.

$In the two compound names Διο-μήδης and Εὐ-μήδης the first elements are immediately clear: Ζεύς, gen. Διός ‘heaven’ and εὐ- ‘good’. The second element, $which is common to both, is less clear. Since Homer, Greek has known the s-stem $μῆδος ‘intention, plan’, always used in the plural μήδεα (related to Armenian mit-kʿ ‘mind, intellect, idea’, cf. Olsen 1999: 69), and next to it the homonym μῆδος ‘genitals’, again always found in the plural form μήδεα, with the short- vowel side forms μέδεα and, less clear, μέζεα. $

Modern research sees Diomedes as a hero who ‘has the plan of Zeus’ (e.g., $Kanavou 2015: 48–50). However, a consideration of all epic attestations of μῆδος ‘intention, plan’ and μῆδος ‘genitals’, as well as the perhaps related verb μέδομαι with its formulaic participle μέδοντες and possible cognates in the Rigveda, $points to the following: the conventional etymological connection with the root for ‘measure’, PIE *med-, Lat. modus etc. (LIV 423), and partly also the determi-nation of the synchronic meaning, must be abandoned. Instead, the Greek words belong with Ved. mad- ‘intoxicate, delight, rejoice’ (EWA II 299f.), from a pre-viously unrecognised Indo-European root *med- ‘enjoy oneself ’ (for details, see Janda in prep. 3).

We thus start from ‘feel pleasure (at), enjoy, become intoxicated’. *Mḗdos-,13 originally a verbal noun ‘pleasure, enjoyment’, becomes concrete as a nomen loci: ‘place where one feels pleasure; genitals’. In parallel, ‘feel pleasure at, enjoy, be-come intoxicated with’ also means ‘desire to do something’ (cf. NHG Lust haben), $whence μῆδος in the sense ‘lust, intention, plan’. A deeper discussion of the verbal $forms here would be excessive, but Figure 1 shows an overview of the fundamen-tal development.

Confirmation is provided, as is so often the case, by collocations and compounds common to Greek and Vedic. For example, the Vedic syntagm náro … mádanti (RV $1.154.4+) ‘men rejoice’ corresponds to the famous Greek woman’s name Ἀνδρομέδα, and the expression śrávo mádanti ‘rejoice in fame’ (RV 5.52.1) to Κλεομέδων. $

$Thus, the meaning of the second members of the names Διο-μήδης and Εὐ-μήδης should be arranged on a semantic scale ranging from ‘pleasure’ to ‘intox-$ication’ to ‘Lust haben zu, planning, intending’. It now becomes apparent how $fruitful it is to follow the path pioneered by Skjærvø and Windfuhr: Διομήδης $‘has the intoxication of heaven’ and thus, and in his relationship to Athena, corre-sponds exactly to the celestial Haoma with his neighbor Aṣ̌i. It is no coincidence that the myth of the Boeotian hunter Orion also tells how he becomes addicted to wine (see for example Renaud 2004: 137f.).

I have not yet named perhaps the greatest of all of Orion’s avatars, Dionysos. In re-lation to Dionysos in particular, it becomes apparent that, in addition to carefully analysing sources, Indo-European studies must reckon with an overlay of astral motifs and names, maintaining a cross-cultural perspective and keeping in mind that epithets can lead to independent figures. A full treatment of the complex and intertwined material would be beyond the scope of this chapter, but I will give a few suggestive connections:

Dionysos is the god of wine because he eternally follows the spherical con-$stellation of the Pleiades, which the Greeks also appropriately named βότρυς ‘grape’ (cf. Scherer 1953: 144f.).14 Paretymologically named ‘doves’ (πέλειαι), the $

93The Charioteer Athena as goddess of warriors

Pleiades bring ambrosia to the father Zeus, as Homer reports (Od. 12.59–65). In $Euripides’ Bacchae (1189–1192), Dionysοs appears as a great hunter – like Orion $

– followed by hunting dogs. On the one hand, the dog-star Sirius appears here in the plural, as an enthusiastic retinue – for Euripides calls the Bacchae and $Maenads ‘dogs’ (κύνες, 731). On the other hand, the dog in the Dionysοs myth is also a hostile ‘wolfhound’, Λυκ-οῦργος (‘who has the deeds of a wolf $’)15 which $according to Homer (Il. 6.130–140) drives the god into the sea. Of course, α Canis $Maioris could be understood as a dog just because it eternally follows the most human-shaped constellation in the sky. Orion himself is thought of as a hunter because the images of escape and pursuit are common metaphors for the move-ment of the stars (Hübner 1998: 144, Berezkin 2005).

$Another ‘wolfhound’ is Λυκοῦργος, the mythical founder of Sparta’s legal and $political institutions, who is conspicuous in being venerated with divine honors, rather than heroic ones like other city founders (Janda 2022a: 108f.). This implies that he should in fact be identified with a god, and given the wolf-like bynames Lykeios and Lykios applied to Apollo, he is the obvious candidate. Apollo is thus a wolfhound, but at the same time an archer who neither wages war nor hunts with his arrows, but sends disease, originally: in the heat of the dog days.16 Apollo is an archer because the straight line of an arrow is seen in Orion:17 the hunter, hunted and hit. The overlay and interweaving of motifs makes Apollo both a wolfhound and archer. His archaic, golden monumental statue on Delos shows him hold-$ing the life-size figures of the Three Charites on his outstretched hand.18 Τρεῖς Χάριτες was also a name of the three bright stars of Orion’s Belt (cf. Boll 1903: $272f.; Hübner 2010: I 37, 43, II 101f.).

Much more material could be added here (see also Janda 2022b and fc.), but I will finish with Calvert Watkins’ supposition (1986 and 1995: 408–413) that the $hero Meleagros does not look after a field (ἀγρός), but after his club. In his name Μελέ-(ϝ)αγρος, the second element has an etymological equivalent in Vedic váj ra- $‘(Indra’s) thunderbolt, club’. In the myth, Meleagros defeats the Calydonian boar, which seems to correspond to the Hyades ‘piglets’19 that form a constellation of their own in the head of the Bull just in front of the gigantic club-bearer Orion.20

94 Michael Janda

6 Conclusion

This expansion of themes and motifs may seem to lead too far into the darkness of the firmament, into an obsolete mythology of nature. But it is clear that we do not want Athena to stand – or rather, drive – alone in the sky. Cumulative evidence is helping us (and will no doubt continue to do so in future studies) bring the Greeks into closer alignment with the rich, ancient cultures of Egypt and Meso-potamia, insofar as at least some of their gods also reigned from the night sky. It is striking to note that among Greeks, Indo-Iranians and probably Indo-Europeans, the celestial charioteer who travels across the sky is a woman, a goddess who combines war, wisdom and abundance in her personality. Myth and cult testify to Athena’s power and mobility – we now see that these qualities derive from the eternal movement of a constellation.
