Quaecumque a Benveniste dicta essent, commenticia esse

Michael Weiss Cornell University 1

Émile Benveniste is one of the best-known Indo-Europeanists of the 20th

century. His fame extends far beyond the field of Indo-European linguis-

tics and his 1969 book, Le vocabulaire des institutions indo-européennes, is

still widely cited by scholars in a variety of disciplines. In this paper I will

show that Benveniste, though undoubtedly a scholar of great erudition and

insight, pursued and promoted an incoherent and unconvincing method

of lexical-cultural reconstruction. His analyses are often undermined by

forced interpretations, a narrow focus on structural oppositions to the ex-

clusion of sociolinguistic factors, and dogmatic assertion. The nonexpert

reader of the Vocabulaire needs to treat the book with extreme caution, not

blind acceptance.

Émile Benveniste (1902–1976) was a great Indo-Europeanist, Iranist, and gener-al linguist. His work in the European structuralist tradition was influential for many later developments in intellectual life, especially in the Francophone world. I don’t intend to examine his work as a general linguist or Iranist or even his Indo- European work on nominal morphology, which is little read today. Instead I’d like to focus on what is probably his most influential work of Indo-European linguis-tics, Le vocabulaire des institutions indo-européennes, first published in 19692 and

1 I hope scholars will not be offended by this title, a joking reference to the famous 1536 master’s thesis of another French scholar, Petrus Ramus (Pierre de la Ramée), Quae-cumque ab Aristotele dicta essent, commenticia esse “Whatever was said by Aristotele is fictitious”. I obviously don’t believe that of Benveniste anymore than Ramée believed it of Aristotle. Sadly a work with such a title may never have existed, but the title is reported in Johann Freig’s life of Ramus prefixed to Ramus’s Praelectiones in Ciceronis Orationes Octo Consulares (1575: 10). I would like to thank the organizers of the confer-ence for the invitation to speak and Sasha Nikolaev for his careful reading and helpful comments. All errors are to be attributed to me.

2 The two volumes were actually released in 1970.

100 Michael Weiss

translated into English by Elizabeth Palmer in 19733 with the title Indo-European Language and Society. When I first entered the field of Indo-European, I was told by somebody, I don’t remember who, that while Benveniste’s works on nominal morphology were outmoded, his work on the lexicon was uniquely valuable and, indeed, this is true. There is no comparable book-length treatment of the cul-turally important vocabulary of the Indo-European languages.4 The book is an insightful masterpiece and repays repeated close readings, but it is at the same time a deeply flawed work. And I don’t mean just that new information has be-come available that Benveniste could not possibly have known, though that, of course, is sometimes true. I mean that the methods that produced the analyses were wrong-headed and that the distinctions that were drawn are patently con-tradicted by evidence available at the time. The role of derivational morphology is rarely considered even by contemporary standards. Of course, one could go back to the works of many earlier scholars of lasting value and find similar faults. For example, Karl Brugmann’s etymological solutions are often misguided.

So why am I picking on Benveniste? Le vocabulaire des institutions indo- européennes has become a standard reference for scholars outside of Indo- European linguistics. Let me quote as exhibit A the first sentence of the preface to a re-issue of the vocabulaire written by the Italian philosopher Giorgio Agamben:5

Émile Benveniste’s Le vocabulaire des institutions indo-européennes is cer-tainly the culmination of twentieth-century linguistics, in both senses of the term. It is here that the nineteenth-century project of comparative grammar had reached its highest point, and, simultaneously, coincided with its end.

I think most people reading this paper will be shocked and amused by this state-ment. Most 20th- and 21st-century linguists, I guarantee, have never heard of

3 Translations from the Vocabulaire are from Palmer. Other translations from French are my own. Translations from the Rig Veda are from Jamison and Brereton (2014). Trans-lation from the Taittirīya Saṃhita are from Keith (1914). Translations from the Atharva Veda Śaunaka are from Whitney (1905).

4 There are the two works by Mallory and Adams (1997, 2006) but they are largely de-scriptive.

5 It’s telling in itself that the preface was composed by Agamben, an Italian philosopher with no particular expertise in Indo-European linguistics that I know of, rather than a practicing Indo-Europeanist. What would philosophers think if I, not a professional philosopher and with only the most superficial knowledge of the field of philosophy as practiced today, claimed that Kant or Nāgārjuna was the culmination of philosophy?

101Quaecumque a Benveniste dicta essent, commenticia esse

Benveniste’s book and those of us who have (I mean Indo-Europeanists) don’t regard it as the culmination in either sense of the term.

Exhibit B: Charles de Lamberterie (1997: 355) wrote of the book:

This work has been read, thought about, and cited not only by Indo- Europeanists but also by historians, prehistorians, sociologists, anthropolo-gists, philosophers, literary scholars to such an extent that it has become in certain circles, with that typically French taste for orthodoxies, an obligatory reference which sometimes bordered on an oracle.6

I perceive here a slight irony about the status achieved by the book in France, even though the overall assessment of the book and its method is glowing. So the goal of this paper is to show that continued reliance on Benveniste’s book impedes our understanding of some of the phenomena he examined and to illustrate common threads in Benveniste’s approach that have led to misanalyses. It’s especially im-portant to problematize Benveniste because his reputation stands so high outside of the field of Indo-European linguistics. Some of the criticisms are from my own earlier published critiques of Benveniste’s ideas, and others are expressed here for the first time. I should also add in defense of Benveniste that his book was intend-ed to be a popularization of a lifetime’s work and often summarizes more detailed treatments of earlier articles.

1 Gender

Let’s begin at the beginning. The first chapter of the Vocabulaire is devoted to the topic of “male and sire”. In this chapter Benveniste tries to bring some order to a vexing problem. In a number of Indo-European languages we have two similar forms with similar meanings in the area of ‘male’, ‘male animal’. Some of these forms begin with a *u̯ and others without. The *u̯-initial forms mentioned by Benveniste are:

6 «  Cet ouvrage a été lu, médité, cité non seulement par les indo-européanistes, mais aussi par les historiens, les préhistoriens, les sociologues, les anthropologues, les phi-losophes, les littéraires, au point de devenir dans certains milieux, avec ce goût bien français des orthodoxies, une référence obligée qui a parfois confiné à l’oracle. » The English version of the Vocabulaire is cited 876 times on Google scholar which is a lot for a book of Indo-European linguistics from the 1960s.

102 Michael Weiss

Ved. vr̥ṣabhá- ‘bull’; Av. *varəšan- (on the basis of the derivatives Av. varšni- ‘ram’, Av. varəšna- ‘male’); Lat. uerrēs ‘boar’; Lith. ver̃šis ‘calf, bull, ox’, Latv. vḕrsis ‘bull, ox’7

The u-̯less forms he considers are:

$Ved. r̥ṣabhá-; Av. aršan-; Gk. ἄρρην (which never has a digamma according $to Benveniste)

Benveniste argues that in Vedic the two forms vr̥ṣabhá- and r̥ṣabhá- are complete-ly interchangeable referring to the ‘mythological bull’ or the ‘male in general’, but $that in Avestan aršan- is used in specific opposition to a word for female, xšaθrī $or daēnu-, e.g., aspa- arəšan- vs. aspa- daēnu-, and that this matches the functions $of Gk. ἄρρην, which is also typically used to distinguish male from female. There-$fore the PIE meaning of *ersen- was ‘male’ in opposition to ‘female’. The Avestan forms with initial v- on the other hand are not characteristic of a special class of beings but an epithet of functional value, i.e. ‘sire’, by which Benveniste means ‘capable of siring offspring, virile’. Thus Avestan has uniquely preserved the PIE distinction between the two very similar forms one meaning ‘male’ and the other meaning ‘sire’.

Let’s assume Benveniste is correct. Most males are potentially sires and all sires are male. Thus any particular male may well be both a *u̯r̥sen- and a *r̥sen-. Is it really likely in a natural language that these two quite similar meanings would be distinguished by a single consonant? Of course, such things may happen since the sound-meaning correspondence is arbitrary, but it would be a remarkable and awkward coincidence.8

But let’s examine the crucial Avestan evidence more closely. Benveniste gives you the impression that aršan- and *varšan- are truly contrasting items in Avestan, but in fact, the v-initial forms are quite rare. The totality of evidence for the v-forms are three related hapaxes: varšni-, varəšna-, and the compound varšni-

7 Benveniste does not mention Ved. vr̥ṣṇí- ‘ram’, ‘strong’ and vŕ̥ṣṇi- ‘strong’. 8 Of course this is not to deny that languages can make a distinction between ‘male’ and

‘sire’, but it seems to me that, in English at least, sire and its female analog dam are not really technical terms of farming. They are both metaphorical extensions of the human terms (sire ultimately from senior and dam(e) from domina). The crucial distinction, which is often marked in the ancient language of husbandry, is that between a castrated and a non-castrated male, but it is certain that neither vŕ̥ṣan- nor r̥ṣabhá- refers to a castrated bovine which in Vedic is probably ukṣán-. See Falk (1982: 176).

103Quaecumque a Benveniste dicta essent, commenticia esse

$haršta-. The form varšni- (derivational chain: *u̯r̥šn- → *u̯aršna- ‘of the *u̯r̥šn-’ → $*u̯(a)ršni- ‘the *u̯aršna- one’, cf. Ved. vr̥ṣṇí- ‘ram’, ‘strong’ and vŕ̥ṣṇi- ‘strong’9) oc-curs in Yasht 17.56 when the heroine of the hymn, Aṣ̌i Vaŋᵛhī, describes her flight from the Turanians and Naotaras. In stanza 55 she takes refuge under the foot of a bull and in stanza 56 beneath the throat of a ram.

$azəm tanūm aguze aδairi pāδəm gə̄uš aršnō barəmāiiaonahe (Yt. 17.55) $Then I hid myself beneath the foot of the bull Barmāyūn.

$azəm tanūm aguze aδairi maēšahe garō yat̰ varšnōiš satō.karahe (Yt. 17.56) $I hid myself beneath the throat of the ram with a hundred horns.

We can see that, contrary to Benveniste, aršnō and varšnōiš are closely parallel in function. Benveniste might have argued that the difference is that gau- ‘bovine’ is epicene whereas maēša- ‘sheep’ has a distinct feminine maēšī- and thus varšnōiš cannot mean just ‘male’, which would be adequately conveyed by the noun itself. But this argument doesn’t hold because Avestan uses the epithet daēnunąm to qualify the explicit feminine maēšīnąm at Āfrīngān 3.7.

The thematic stem also occurs only once, in Nērangestān in a passage regulat-ing how high the firewood should be piled in a ritual undertaking. The answer is

$yaθa varəšnahe kəhrpahe də̄uš (N. 88.2) $like (i.e. as high as) the forearm/shoulder of a varəšna- body

I don’t think we can decide from this minimal context what is actually intended.10 Does it mean as high as a man’s shoulder or as high as the shoulder of a reproduc-tively capable male and would that difference be meaningful?11 The best evidence $for Benveniste’s claim is the name of the fall festival aiiāθrima- fraouruuaēštrima- $varšniharšta- ‘homecoming characterized by the return (of cattle) and the release of rams’ (Y. 1.9). Here it seems that we are talking about male animals in their generative capacity, but it would be equally possible to refer to males in general. When we combine this passage with the one from the Yasht 17 what stands out is

9 The barytone form is exclusively neuter. On the accentuation of these forms see Wid-mer (2004: 153–154).

10 In Afr. 3.5 firewood is to be stacked as high as an ear or a fore-shoulder. 11 I guess we could be talking about the difference between a 13-year-old and an adult, but

would you call a 13-year-old a stud?

104 Michael Weiss

not so much that varšni- means ‘sire’ rather than ‘male’, but that it refers specifi-cally to rams and that meaning matches Ved. vr̥ṣṇí- exactly.

When we examine the aršan- side of the coin we see the picture is also not very clear. In Yasna 65.2, the Ābān Yasht, dedicated to Arədvī Sūrā Anāhita, we read:

$yā vīspanąm aršnąm xšudrā̊ yaoždaδāiti yā vīspanąm hāirišinąm ząθāi garəβąn yaoždaδāiti $

Who enlivens the semen of all males, Who enlivens the wombs of all females for giving birth

– where we seem to have the use of aršan- in a context focusing on generative capacity.

In Old Avestan at Y. 44.8 Zarathustra specifies dasā aspā̊ aršnauuaitīš uštrəm-cā ‘ten mares with a stallion and a camel’ as his priestly reward. The natural in-ference is that the aršan- is not just a male but a male in his generative capacity. Interestingly in Vedic (RV 8.68.18) we find vŕ̥ṣaṇvatī in a dānastuti:

aíṣu cetad vŕ̥ṣaṇvatī antár r̥jréṣu áruṣī svabhīśúḥ káśāvatī

In the midst of these silvery ones there appeared a ruddy female along with a bull, having good reins and a whip.

In later Iranian the v-less forms completely disappear but the v-ful forms are con-tinued as the name of a variety of male animals, e.g., Oss. D. wyrs, I. urs ‘stallion’ (ultimately borrowed by some pathway into Fin. varsa ‘foal’), Sogd. wšn- ‘stallion’, Wakhi wəšəng ‘bull’, Shugni wīrn ‘ram’, Wanji wurom ‘stallion’, Khwar. ʾwšn ‘stal-lion’, ʾwšnycyk ‘young bull’ (see Abaev 1989:125 and Bailey 1979: 296). In MP the word gušn ‘male’ replaces and translates Av. aršan- (asp ī gušn [Zādspram 3.15, etc.]), cf. also Syr. ʔuʃnaʔ ‘stallion’.

Benveniste stakes his argument entirely on Avestan and simply dismisses the Vedic evidence as uninformative, but let’s examine it more closely. In fact, as Te-desco (1945: 95) noted, r̥ṣabhá- is rare in the Rig Veda, occurring only 4 times vs. 178 times for vr̥ṣabhá-. In the Atharvaveda Śaunaka, however, the ratio is r̥ṣabhá- 25 : vr̥ṣabhá- 21 and by my count in the Paippalāda the ratio is r̥ṣabhá- 43 : vr̥ṣab-há- 18. The four Rig-Vedic occurrences of r̥ṣabhá- (6.16.47, 6.28.8, 10.91.14, and 10.166.1) are instructive. First, the forms clearly do not mean ‘male’ as opposed to ‘female’ but specifically the ‘male bull as procreator’. In 6.16.47 and 10.91.14,

105Quaecumque a Benveniste dicta essent, commenticia esse

obviously drawing on similar poetic stock, r̥ṣabhā́s keep company with ukṣáṇas ‘oxen’ and vaśā́s ‘mated cows’. The poets are talking about real sacrificial animals.

ā́ te agna r̥cā́ havír hr̥dā́ taṣṭám bharāmasi té te bhavantu ukṣáṇa r̥ṣabhā́so vaśā́ utá (RV 6.16.47, popular12)

Here to you, Agni, we bring with a verse an oblation fashioned by our heart: let the oxen, bulls, and mated cows be yours.

yásminn áśvāsa r̥ṣabhā́sa ukṣáṇo vaśā́ meṣā́ avasr̥ṣṭā́sa ā́hutāḥ kīlālapé sómapr̥ṣṭhāya vedháse hr̥dā́ matíṃ janaye cā́rum agnáye (10.91.14)

(For him) into whom horses, bulls, oxen, mated cows, rams, once released, are poured out [=offered], for the kīlāla-drinker who has soma on his back, for the ritual adept I generate with my heart a pleasing thought – for Agni.

In 6.28, a hymn dedicated to Indra and the cows, the insistence on the generative power of the r̥ṣabhá- is unmistakable.

úpedám upapárcanam āsú góṣū́pa pr̥cyatām úpa rṣabhásya rétasi úpendra táva vīryè (6.28.8, popular)

Right here is the inseminator: let there be inseminating right here in these cows, right here when the semen of the bull (is here), right here when your virility (is here), Indra.

Only in 10.166.1 do we have r̥ṣabhá- used as a general symbol of masculine power:

r̥ṣabhám mā samānā́nāṃ sapátnānāṃ viṣāsahím

12 “Popular” means that the hymn shows late, popular features according to the classifica-tion of Vedic language by Arnold based on metrical and morphophonological charac-teristics. See Arnold (1905: 22–27).

106 Michael Weiss

hantā́raṃ śátrūṇāṃ kr̥dhi virā́jaṃ gópatiṃ gávām (10.166.1, popular)

Make me bull over my equals, smiter of my rivals, wide-ruling cattle-lord of cattle. (Attributed to R̥ṣabha Vairāja or R̥ṣabha Śākvara, a name probably extracted from the first stanza)

In the Rig Veda we cannot contrast the two terms in close proximity, but in post-RV texts we do find some interesting cases. In the TS 5.7.2.1–2 we read:

tvā́m agne vrṣ̥abháṃ cékitānam púnar yúvānam janáyann upā́gām asthūrí ṇo gā́rhapatyāni santu tigména no bráhmaṇā sáṁ śiśādhi paśávo vā́ eté yád íṣṭakāś cítyāṃcityām rṣ̥abhám úpa dadhāti mithunám evā́sya tád yajñé karoti prajánanāyatásmād yūthéyūtha rṣ̥abháḥ

To thee, O Agni, the bull, the wise, I have come, generating thee ever new; Be our household rites not halting; With thy keen holy power sharpen us. The bricks are cattle, in each layer he puts down a bull (brick); verily in his sacri-fice he makes a pairing for propagation; therefore in every herd there is a bull.

Here the contrast is between the metaphorical symbol of strength, an epithet of the god Agni (vr̥ṣabháṃ) and an actual sacrificial victim (r̥ṣabháḥ). The same contrast is seen at AVŚ 4.24.3–4:

yáś carṣaṇipró vrṣ̥abháḥ svarvíd yásmai grā́vāṇaḥ pravádanti nr̥mṇám yásyādhvaráḥ saptáhotā mádiṣṭhaḥ sá no muñcatv áṃhasaḥ yásya vaśā́sa rṣ̥abhā́sa ukṣáṇo yásmai mīyánte sváravaḥ svarvíde yásmai śukráḥ pávate bráhmaśumbhitaḥ sá no muñcatv áṃhasaḥ

He who is filler of people, bull (vr̥ṣabháḥ), heaven-finder; for whom the pressing-stones proclaim his manliness; whose is the sacrifice with seven priests, most intoxicating—let him free us from distress. Whose are cows, bulls (r̥ṣabhā́sa), oxen; for whom the heaven-finder, sacrificial posts are set up; for whom the bright [soma] purifies itself, adorned with sacred words—let him free us from distress.

Here the god Indra is the vr̥ṣabháḥ to whom the mortal cattle, subdivided into vaśā́sa r̥ṣabhā́sa ukṣáṇo ‘cows, bulls, and oxen’ belong. The post-RV texts also give us some other insights into how the semantic field was divided between r̥ṣabhá-,

107Quaecumque a Benveniste dicta essent, commenticia esse

vr̥ṣabhá-, and vŕ̥ṣan-. As Grassmann (1873, s.v.) noted, vŕ̥ṣan- is the more general word often used adjectivally and when a substantive is applicable to males other than bovids, for example, stallions. Ved. vr̥ṣabhá-, on the other hand, is typically a substantive ‘bull’ though it too can be extended metaphorically to other ani-mals such as a horse. There are by my count seventeen stanzas in the Rig Veda containing both vr̥ṣabhá- and vŕ̥ṣan-. In seven stanzas we get the combination vŕ̥ṣā vr̥ṣabhá- ‘bullish (or bull-strong) bull’ (1.54.2; 1.103.6; 1.177.2; 4.16.20; 5.1.12; 6.44.20; 6.44.21 (2×!)). In post-RV Vedic we find that vŕ̥ṣan- specifically ‘stallion’ contrasts with r̥ṣabhá- ‘bull’ and vr̥ṣṇí- ‘ram’ (TS 7.3.14.1-14):

agnínā tápó ’nv abhavat vācā́ bráhma maṇínā rūpā́ṇi índreṇa devā́n vā́tena prāṇā́n sū́ryeṇa dyā́m candrámasā nákṣatrāṇi yaména pitŕ̥n rā́jñā manuṣyā̀n pha- léna nādeyā́n ajagaréṇa sarpā́n vyāghréṇāraṇyā́n paśū́n śyen-éna patatríṇas vŕ̥ṣṇā́śvān rṣ̥abhéṇa gā́s basténājā́s vrṣ̥ṇínā́vīs

By fire he surmounted fervour, by speech holy power, by a gem forms, by Indra the gods, by the wind the breaths, by the sun the sky, by the moon the Naksatras, by Yama the Pitrs, by the king men, by fruit the flavours, by the boa constrictor serpents, by the tiger wild beasts, by the eagle birds, by the stallion horses, by the bull kine, by the he-goat goats, by the ram sheep.

If Benveniste had chosen to privilege the Vedic evidence over the Avestan he could with equal justice have made the exact opposite case: the v-less forms refer to the male animal as ‘sire’ and the v-forms are the general word form ‘male’ as powerful hero. We could go on and examine the complicated Greek evidence, but it wouldn’t change the essential picture. The distinction that Benveniste argues was the original is not supported by textual evidence when fairly considered. This conclusion is not new. The Benvenistean distinction has been rejected by at least Watkins (1973), Peters (1993), Pronk (2009), and Pinault (2020).

In my opinion, there is no functional distinction observable between the two terms. They both mean basically ‘male’ and sometimes the contrast is between ‘male’ and ‘female’ but other times the focus is on the procreative aspect of male-ness. But if we compare just Indic and Iranian we can observe an interesting dis-tribution. In Indic the v-less forms start off as non-standard. The basic n-stem is not attested at all, but r̥ṣabhá- occurs in late and popular hymns (according to Arnold 1905’s classification) and starts to rival vr̥ṣabhá- in the Atharva Veda. But this upswing of r̥ṣabhá- was only temporary. If we look at the modern descend-ants of the two forms, we find that the v-ful forms are widespread throughout the

108 Michael Weiss

continent,13 but the v-less forms survive only in the Northwest in the Nuristani languages14 and in the ‘Dardic’ languages,15 precisely the area closest to the Iran-ophone world.

In Iranian, on the other hand, the v-less form is dominant in the formal lan-guage of the Avesta and in Old Persian onomastics. The v-ful forms appear rarely and only in latish texts, and, in later Iranian the v-ful forms completely oust the v-less forms. Here it appears that the old standard form has been truly vanquished. Looking at this from the sociolinguistic point of view, the two synonymous terms were polarized in two neighboring speech communities. In the Indosphere the v-ful forms were standard and in the Iranosphere the v-less forms were.

Given Meillet’s dictum (1906: 27) that “le langage est éminemment un fait so-cial”, Benveniste’s relative insensitivity to sociolinguistic phenomena is surprising, but Benveniste explicitly distanced himself from simple-minded applications of Meillet’s approach, writing (1970):

There is correspondence neither of nature nor structure between the consti-tutive elements of language and those of society.16

One can only agree with this, but Benveniste went further, writing:

… we can isolate language, study it and describe it by itself without referring to its use in society or to its relations with the norms and social representations which make up culture. Whereas it is impossible to describe society, to de-scribe culture, apart from their linguistic expressions. In this sense, language includes society but is not included by it.17 (My emphasis)

de la langue et les éléments constitutifs de la société. » The quotation can be found in the reprint Benveniste (1974: 93).

17 «  [D]u fait qu’on peut isoler la langue, l’étudier et la décrire pour elle-même sans se référer à son emploi dans la société, ni à ses rapports avec les normes et les représenta-tions sociales qui forment la culture. Tandis qu’il est impossible de décrire la société, de décrire la culture, hors de leurs expressions linguistiques. En ce sens la langue inclut la

109Quaecumque a Benveniste dicta essent, commenticia esse

The highlighted words seem to me an overstatement. The elaborate and grammat-icalized honorific systems of some languages could hardly be described without reference to social facts. But in this regard Benveniste was much closer to Saus-sure than Meillet (Puech & Radzynski 1988). Saussure wrote (1916: 42–43):

We think that the study of external linguistic phenomena is very productive; but it is false to say that one cannot know the internal linguistic organism without them … Language is a system that knows only its own order.18

If we look at the wider picture, we can observe that the u̯-ful forms are found for $sure in Latin, probably in Greek (γάρρης [i.e. ϝάρρης]· ἄρρης, Hesych. 183; see $Danielsson 1899: 88), Indic, Iranian, Tocharian (TA kayurṣ, TB kaurṣe ‘yak’) and Baltic (Lith. ver̃šis [AP 2] ‘calf, bull, ox’, Latv. vḕrsis ‘bull, ox’, OPr. werstian). The u-̯ $less forms are only found in Greek (ερσενο̄ν [Gortyn, IC IV.72, etc.]), Indic, Irani-$an, and Armenian (aṙn ‘ram’).19 The u̯-ful forms show more than one formation: hysterokinetic n-stem, hysterokinetic i-stem (Lat. uerrēs which cannot continue an n-stem and could theoretically be a match for the Tocharian forms), -ii̯o-stem (Lith. ver̃šis); while the u̯-less forms are only n-stems or derivatives thereof.20 The u̯-ful n-stem forms were, despite their zero-grade root and hysterokinetic suffix ablaut, barytone. These facts taken together suggest that the u-̯ful forms are the only ones that should be projected back to Nuclear PIE and perhaps that the n-stem was originally amphikinetic *u̯érsōn, *u̯r̥sn-és.

société, mais elle n’est pas incluse par elle. » The quotation can be found in the reprint Benveniste (1974: 95–96).

18 « Nous pensons que l’étude des phénomènes linguistiques externes est très fructueuse ; mais il est faux de dire que sans eux on ne puisse connaître l’organisme linguistique interne … La langue est un système qui ne connaît que son ordre propre. »

110 Michael Weiss

I don’t want to venture an etymology for one or both forms – I’m skeptical of the connection with *h₂u̯ers- ‘rain’21 and *h₁ers- ‘flow’ – and I don’t find any of the explanations for how the *u̯-less forms came about completely convincing though I think metanalysis or dissimilation (*u̯r̥sn̥bʰo- > *r̥sn̥bʰo-, cf. *śvitipad- > śitipád- ‘white-footed’ (Debrunner 1938: 171–173) or *u̯r̥sn̥u̯n̥t- (Ved. vŕ̥ṣaṇvat-) >

*r̥sn̥u̯n̥t- (YAv. aršauuant-)??) must be on the right track. To sum up: the underlying presupposition of Benveniste’s study is that there

should be a semantic distinction reconstructible for two distinct forms. This is obviously a good approach, but the evidence flies in the face of any neat solution, and instead of abandoning this approach to consider other avenues of explana-tion, Benveniste chose to privilege one branch, not coincidentally Iranian (n.b. Teeter’s Law).22 But even the evidence of Iranian hardly supports the proposed semantic distinction.

2 Power

2.1 Lat. cēnsor and cēnsus

Benveniste examined some of the key political terms of Roman culture in the book and in particular tried to explain and illuminate the institution of cēnsor and the concept of auctoritās. In Latin we have the nouns cēnsor, a magistrate, and cēnsus, the official act the censor performs. The related verb cēnseō, Ben-veniste says, means ‘estimate, judge, pronounce an opinion’. In Indo-Iranian the comparanda usually cited are Ved. śaṃs- ‘praise’, Av. saŋh- ‘proclaim solemnly’ $and OP θa(n)h- ‘proclaim’. The PIE meaning is traditionally given as ‘proclaim $solemnly’, ‘feierlich sprechen’. But Benveniste is rightly not satisfied with such a meaning. As Thurneysen noted wryly in the TLL (s.v.), “censeo is connected $with Pers. ϑātij, Aves. sąhaiti ‘proclaims’, Sanskrit śámsati ‘declaims, praises’ more $because of similarity of sounds than similarity of meaning.”23 Instead Benven-iste suggests again that Iranian, in this case, Old Persian, has uniquely preserved valuable information about the original semantics of the root. He reviews the

21 This etymology already occurs in the Nirukta 9.21 vr̥ṣabhaḥ prajāṃ varṣati “The bull rains offspring.”

22 Watkins (1976: 310): the language of the family you know best always turns out to be the most archaic.

$23 “[C]enseo: similitudine sonorum magis quam significationis conectitur c. pers. ϑātij, $med. sąhaiti ‘pronuntiat’, ind. śáṃsati ‘declamat, laudat, pronuntiat’.”

111Quaecumque a Benveniste dicta essent, commenticia esse

occurrences of the verb in the Old Persian inscriptions and determines that the verb means not just ‘to say’ but “to assert with authority as being the truth; to say what corresponds to the nature of things; to proclaim the norm of behavior.”24

But it is difficult to judge the necessity of this translation because most state-ments using this verb are by the Achaemenid emperor and as such are invested pragmatically with an authority they would not have if uttered by the average Old Persian speaker. Benveniste makes much of the existence of another verb of speaking gaub- which is used more or less in the negative sense ‘purport, claim’, but this actually weakens the case because it suggests that there is a marked verb of speaking falsely. And if there is a marked verb of speaking falsely and marked verb of speaking that asserts the truth, then what is the Old Persian verb of just $‘speaking’? If we examine one context where θa(n)h- and gaub- occur in close $proximity, it is instructive.

$avaθāšām aθaham: paraitā avam kāram $Bābiruviyam jatā haya manā naiy gaubataiy (DB 3.85–86)

Thus I said to them: Go forth and smite the Babylonian army which claims not to be mine!

You cannot normally assert the truth of an imperative because the meanings of imperatives are not truth-conditional, so Benveniste would have to say that Dari-us is not asserting this in a technical sense but speaking with full authority when he issues the command. Benveniste writes:

Our definition makes intelligible the specialization of sense undergone by censeo, census, censor in Roman institutions. In that he establishes with au-thority a factual truth, the censor proclaims the situation of each citizen and his rank in society.25

But this isn’t compelling. Establishing the factual truth is not what a cēnsor or a cēnsus does. Of course, the cēnsor is in theory truthful, but what he does is establish the value of every citizen’s property. He evaluates. ‘To evaluate’ is the best starting point for the developments we see in the Indo-European languages.

24 « [A]ffirmer avec autorité comme étant la vérité ; dire ce qui est conforme à la nature des choses ; énoncer la norme de conduite. »

25 « Notre définition rend compte de la spécialisation que censeo, census, censor ont reçue dans les institutions romaines. En tant qu’il spécifie avec autorité une vérité de fait, le censor prononce la situation de chacun et son rang dans la société. »

112 Michael Weiss

From ‘evaluate’ to ‘praise’ (as in Ved. śaṃs-) is precisely the pathway behind such an obscure word as PDE praise, via Anglo-Norman French ultimately from Late Latin pretiare ‘put a price on something’. The pathway from ‘evaluate’ to ‘speak’ is paralleled roughly by PDE count ~ recount and PDE tell beside NHG zahlen. It is notable that Benveniste never argues by citing parallels. What semantic develop-ments he regards as probable are ipso facto probable.

Let us examine the Latin facts more closely—and here I am drawing on a joint paper by Benjamin Fortson and myself (Fortson & Weiss 2019); the basic analysis of the forms of the verb and the meanings is Fortson’s. The verb cēnseō has two interesting features. First, it has two related but semantically and syntactically distinct sets of meanings: ‘to assess, tax, estimate, value’, on the one hand, which is frequently found in the passive, e.g., Plaut. Tri. 873:

heus senex, census quom sum iuratori recte rationem dedi Hey old man, I was assessed when I gave a correct account to the assessor.

The other set is ‘opine, deem, judge, vote, resolve, decree, approve’, which is rarely in the passive and is usually followed by an object clause, e.g., Naevius poet. 44 (45):

censet eo uenturum obuiam Poenum. He reckons that the Carthaginian will come there to meet him.

This distribution is watertight in Old Latin though the non-technical sense ‘opine’ is naturally much more common.26 It’s obvious that the first sense is at the basis of cēnsor and cēnsus, as already noted by Varro L. 5.81:

Censor ad cuius censionem, id est arbitrium, censeretur populus. The censor is the one at whose judgment the people are reckoned.

Second, although the first three principal parts are not irregular or surprising, the fourth, which is also the basis for the clearly ancient, derived nominal system

26 Plaut. Capt. 15 uos qui potestis ope uestra censerier “you who can be assessed by census with your own wealth”; Poen. 55–56 Nomen iam habetis: nunc rationes ceteras / Accipite: nam argumentum hoc hic censebitur “Now you have the name of the play. Now receive the other accounts. For this argument will be reckoned here like the census”; Tri. 493– 494 Aequo mendicus atque ille opulentissumus / censetur censu ad Acheruntem mortuos

“The beggar and the richest man are rated equally in the underworld when dead.”

113Quaecumque a Benveniste dicta essent, commenticia esse

(cēnsor, cēnsus, etc.), is cēnsus and not †cēnsitus as one would normally expect for a second-conjugation verb with a perfect in -uī.

Before we move on to suggesting how to interpret this data, I’ll make two ob-servations in passing. First, according to Roman tradition, the cēnsus predates the cēnsor. The first census that we know of was allegedly conducted under Servius Tullius and the census in the early Republican period was not conducted by the censor but by the consuls (Liv. 1.43; D.H. 4.16–9). It was only in 443 bce that the office of cēnsor was created (Liv. 4.8). If we take this account seriously, the origi-nal fact is the cēnsus not the cēnsor. Second, Plautus and later authors are full of examples of the verb cēnseō in the meaning ‘believe falsely’. In Plautus’ Amphitryo 134–135, the classic example of a mistaken identity play, we read:

illa illum censet uirum / suom esse quae cum moecho est. She who is with an adulterer thinks that man is her husband.

If the original meaning was ‘to speak in accordance with reality’ this is a surpris-ing development, though of course it can’t be entirely excluded.

These two features, one semanto-syntactic and the other morphological, can be explained if we suppose that the Latin verb is the conflation of two distinct paradigms in Proto-Italic. The root *k̑ens- made a thematic present, roughly ‘evaluate’. The perfect passive participle (ppp.) of the simple thematic was *k̑n̥stós ‘evaluated, rated’. This would have yielded Lat. *kenstos which, remade under the influence of *penssos ‘weighed’, became *kenssos and then cēnsus. This ppp. is the source of the meaning ‘assess, value’ which prototypically is associated with pas-sive voice. On the other hand, the iterative *k̑onsei̯e- ‘evaluate (comprehensively?) in speech’, where the iterative morphology perhaps emphasized the event-internal plurality of the evaluative act (cf. in this semantic area Lat. tongeō ‘know’ [Enn.], Go. þagkjan ‘to think’), developed the meaning ‘reckon, decree.’ Thus the original Proto-Italic situation was:

pres. *kenseti, ppp. *kenssos ‘evaluate’ pres. *konsēti, pres. ptc. *konsēns, ppp. *konsetos ‘reckon, decide’

Precisely the present participle of this old verb is now attested in Oscan kúnsíf, and its Latin cognate in the plural is the origin of the Latin Dei Consentes, ‘the decreeing gods’. And, to add something we failed to note at the time, the spell-ing cons- is very well attested in the Latin glosses (conset CGL 1.206; consebat CGL 5.184.29, etc.), which can be interpreted as a confirmation of the existence

114 Michael Weiss

of *konsē- predicted by our conflation hypothesis. The old verb *kenseti lent its e-grade to the iterative-causative *konsēti to yield the attested censet. Thus it is Italic that comes closest to preserving the original meaning of this root which was not ‘assert as true’, but ‘evaluate’, and the TochB verb ṣaṃṣtär ‘counts’ (predomi-nantly middle) < *sk̑ens- confirms this old meaning.

2.2 Lat. auctoritās

Benveniste next turns to the problem of the connection between the root of Lat. au-geō and two important nominal derivatives of this root, auctor and augur. He writes:

It would be of interest to find out how the notion of ‘authority’ came to be derived from a root which simply means ‘grow, increase’. Our dictionaries, which translate the verb with this meaning, also define auctor as ‘he who causes to grow, the author’. This definition seems strange and in any case it is inadequate. We are invited to believe that the profound meaning of auctor could be simply traced back to the notion of ‘growth’. This is hardly satisfac-tory. The notion expressed by auctor and its abstract auctoritas is difficult to reconcile with the sense ‘to increase’, which of course is indubitably that of the verb augeo. But is this the primary sense of the verb augere?27

Benveniste doesn’t actually engage with what exactly auctor means and why this is impossible to connect with a meaning ‘to grow’, but he turns instead to estab-lishing what the older meaning of the root might have been in order to explain how that meaning can more straightforwardly explain the meaning of auctor. Ob-viously, a correct approach. He goes on:

Scholars persist in translating augeo as ‘increase’. This is accurate for the classical period but not for the earliest texts. For us ‘to augment’ is equiva-

27 « On voudrait savoir comment il se fait que la notion d’ “autorité” ait pris naissance dans une racine qui signifie simplement “augmenter, accroître”. Tout en traduisant ain-si le verbe, nos dictionnaires donnent auctor comme “celui qui fait pousser, l’auteur”. Cette définition paraît étrange et en tout cas insuffisante. Le sens si profond de auctor serait rapport simplement à celui de “accroître”. Ce n’est guère satisfaisant. La notion de auctor, celle de son abstrait auctoritas se concilient difficilement avec le sens de

“augmenter” que augeo a en effet et qu’il ne s’agit pas de contester. Mais est-ce le sens premier du verbe augere ? »

115Quaecumque a Benveniste dicta essent, commenticia esse

lent to ‘to increase, to make something which existed before bigger’. Herein lies the unnoticed difference from augeo. In its oldest uses augeo denotes not the increase in something which already exists but the act of producing from within itself; a creative act which causes something to arise from a nutrient medium and which is the privilege of the gods or the great natural forces, but not of men. Lucretius often makes use of this verb when he is retracing the genesis of beings in the universal rhythm of birth and death: quodcumque alias ex se res auget alitque “whatever thing gives rise to other things from itself and nurtures them” (V 322); morigera ad fruges augendas atque animantis “prone to engender plants and living creatures” (V 80). In the archaic prayer formulas the Romans also used augere of the benefits they expected from the gods, namely of ‘promoting’ all their enterprises: Divi divaeque … vos precor quaesoque uti quae in meo imperio gesta sunt, gerun-tur, postque gerentur, … ea vos omnia bene iuvetis, bonis auctibus auxitis “Ye gods and goddesses, I pray and beseech you, that whatever has been done, is being done, and shall be done hereafter under my imperium, you shall aid all those things and increase them with good increases’, that is, cause them to prosper (Livy 29, 27).28

28 « On persiste à traduire augeo par “augmenter”  ; c’est exact dans la langue classique, mais non au début de la tradition. Pour nous, “augmenter” équivaut à “accroître, rendre plus grand quelque chose qui existe déjà”. Là est la différence, inaperçue, avec augeo. Dans ses plus anciens emplois, augeo indique non le fait d’accroître ce qui existe, mais l’acte de produire hors de son propre sein ; acte créateur qui fait surgir quelque chose d’un milieu nourricier et qui est le privilège des dieux ou des grandes forces naturelles, non des hommes. Lucrèce met souvent ce verbe en valeur quand il retrace la genèse des êtres dans le rythme universel des naissances et des morts : quodcumque alias ex se res auget alitque “tout corps qui fait naître de soi et alimente d’autres choses” (V 322) ; morigera ad fruges augendas atque animantis “docile à faire naître les plantes et les êtres” (V 80). Et dans les formules de prières archaïques, les Romains désignent aussi par augere le bienfait qu’ils attendant des dieux, de “promouvoir” toutes leurs entreprises : Diui diuaeque ... , uos precor quaesoque uti quae in meo imperio gesta sunt, geruntur, postque gerentur, ... ea uos omnia bene iuuetis, bonis auctibus auxitis (Liv. 29, 27). »

Interestingly, Agamben (2005: 76) actually engages with this claim in his book State of Exception. He writes: “In the section of his Indo-European Language and Society ded-icated to law Benveniste sought to show that originally the verb augeo (which, in the Indo-European area, is significantly related to terms that express force) ‘denotes not the increase in something which already exists but the act of producing from one’s own breast; a creative act’ (Benveniste 1969, 2:148/422). In truth, the two meanings are not contradictory at all in classical law. Indeed, the Greco-Roman world does not know creation ex nihilo; rather, every act of creation always involves something else—

116 Michael Weiss

I have dealt with the meaning of augeō in Latin in a paper from 2011, and I repeat some of my conclusions from that paper here. First, it’s noteworthy that Benven-iste’s examples of the supposedly oldest meaning of augeō don’t actually come from Old Latin. Second, it is not evident that augeō means ‘creates’ in any of these passages. Let’s examine the first Lucretius passage cited by Benveniste in its context (5.318–323):

Denique iam tuere hoc, circum supraque quod omnem continet amplexu terram: si procreat ex se omnia, quod quidam memorant, recipitque perempta, totum natiuo mortali corpore constat. nam quodcumque alias ex se res auget alitque deminui debet, recreari, cum recipit res.

Again, do but behold that which around and above comprehends all the earth in its embrace: if it makes from itself all things, as some declare, and takes them back when they are destroyed, then the whole consists of a body subject to birth and death. For whatever increases and nourishes other things from itself must

formless matter or incomplete being—that must be perfected or made to grow. Every creation is always a cocreation just as every author is always a coauthor.”

The humble philologist must take exception to such generalizations as “the Greco- Roman world does not know creation ex nihilo.” In a passage from De Divinatione 2.37, Cicero discusses whether a sacrificial animal’s heart might just disappear after the animal was slaughtered and examined. Non ergo omnium ortus atque obitus natura conficiet, et erit aliquid, quod aut ex nihilo oriatur aut in nihilum subito occidat. Quis hoc physicus dixit umquam? ‘Haruspices dicunt.’ His igitur quam physicis credendum potius existumas? “Then the creation and destruction of all things are not due to nature, and there are some things which spring from nothing or suddenly become nothing. Was any such statement ever made by any natural philosopher? ‘It is made,’ you say, ‘by soothsayers.’ Then do you think that soothsayers are worthier of belief than natural philosophers?” (Translation H. Rackham, Loeb edition).

Cicero contrasts the view of a natural philosopher (physicus) who denies that anything can pass in or out of existence with the view of soothsayers (haruspices) who had no problem with this idea. The fact that philosophers took pains to deny this belief (cf. Lucr. 1.148: nullam rem e nihilo gigni divinitus umquam “nothing is ever created out of nothing by divine power”) shows that Greco-Roman antiquity did know creation ex ni-hilo. It is not the views of natural philosophers but of haruspices and ordinary speakers that are relevant.

117Quaecumque a Benveniste dicta essent, commenticia esse

be diminished and remade when it receives things back. (Translation W.H.D. Rouse, Loeb edition)

Here Lucretius is arguing for the mortality of the sky (circum supraque quod om-nem / continet amplexu terram). The argument goes that if the sky creates all things from itself (si procreat ex se / omnia) as some maintain, it suffers changes of decrease (when it causes something to grow) and increase (when it receives the matter back into itself). In this passage what is being described is a zero-sum event: what matter caelum re-attributes to another entity is subtracted from it-self only to be reabsorbed when the entity perishes. But more importantly, the Lucretius passage is closely modeled on a passage from a truly Old Latin author Pacuvius (Chryses 86–87, 89, 90–92 R):

Hoc uide, circum supraque quod complexu continet terram. … Id quod nostri caelum memorant, Grai perhibent aethera … quidquid est hoc, omnia animat, format, alit, auget, creat, sepelit recipitque in sese omnia, omniumque idemst pater, Indidemque eadem aeque oriuntur deintegro atque eodem occidunt.

See that which holds the earth around and above in its embrace. That which our people call the caelum and the Greeks aether. Whatever it is, it enlivens all things, forms, nourishes, increases, creates, buries, and receives in itself all things, the same is the father of all. Again and again the same things rise up in the same way afresh and fall back into the same. (My translation)

In the crucial line of Pacuvius we see that caelum’s contributions to life are more finely delineated. It creates all things (creat), and it makes them increase (auget). The fact is that a survey of the use of augēre in Old Latin does not show that the word means ‘create’, but simply ‘increase’ (transitive). In a literal sense it means ‘add to a preexisting entity’. This addition can be in kind, in discreet units, or in a gradient fashion (often of wealth). A thing may be auctus by an event or activ-ity which does not add in kind, but adorns, supports, or favors the pre-existing entity. This may be a concrete thing like an altar, or it may be something more abstract such as a friendship, or an individual’s spirit. The gods may be on oc-casion the source of this favor, but the thing auctus can also be, and quite often is, a negative.

118 Michael Weiss

My point here is not to explain how auctor got the many meanings that it end-ed up getting. Instead I am highlighting a typical working method of Benveniste, which can be summarized as follows:

1 Identify a key word with a problematic etymology. 2 Choose a meaning of the key word that you judge a probable starting point. 3 Find examples of that meaning in texts (don’t worry too much about text

chronology, context, semantic parallels, or phylogenetics). 4 Assert that the problem is thereby solved or illuminated.

There are many, many other debatable claims throughout the Vocabulaire – e.g., *dom- did not refer to a physical dwelling (see Weiss 2017a); *pék̑u- meant ‘move-able wealth’ and not ‘small domestic animals’; the meaning of rēx is related to the Latin idiom regere fīnēs (see Weiss 2017b); ‘orphan’ and ‘heir’ are the same concept (see Weiss 2016b); the two types of sacred, etc. But now it is time to sum up.

Benveniste worked by insight and not systematically. He had a very broad command of the literatures of the early Indo-European languages, but he could be surprisingly arbitrary in singling out what he considered the crucial detail. Benveniste chose Hegel’s epigram “Das Wahre ist das Ganze” for his Origines (Benveniste 1935: 2), but his approach to the institutional vocabulary was frag-mented and unhistorical. Despite his focus specifically on the institutional vocab-ulary of the ancient Indo-European-speaking societies, he had little interest in a sociological or sociolinguistic approach. His search for fine distinctions recalls the search for the Adamic language. Smart people like clever solutions and these can be found in abundance in Benveniste, but sometimes philology and a rigor-ously applied theoretical approach to morphology can go a long way. Benveniste’s Vocabulaire is a classic of Indo-European linguistics and will be read with interest as long as Indo-European linguistics lasts, but it is far from the culmination of our project.

Part II Power, MobILIty,

and ConfLICt

The wolf, the lamb, and the dog

An Aesopian guide to Indo-European sociology

Peter Jackson Rova Stockholm University

By proceeding from August Schleicher’s exercise in representing the char-

acter of spoken Proto-Indo-European through a self-invented fable, an at-

tempt is made to extend the fable as a progymnastic tool of comparison in

terms also of its moral so as to grasp the fundamentals of Indo-European

sociology. Two fables from the Aesopean corpus (“The Lamb and the Wolf

[Perry Index 261]” and “The Wolf and the Well-fed Dog [Perry Index 346]”)

are selected for this purpose in order to create a model consisting of four

parametric slots: that of (1) the pastoral obligations of kingship; (2) the

merits of hospitality and patronage; (3) crime, deception, and prostitution;

and (4) the punitive and martial obligations of wolfish kingship.

The following text is meant as a sketch. Apart from merely ‘scare quoting’ itself as an unfinished proposal, it might also be excused for appearing a bit presump-tuous. Notwithstanding these apparent shortcomings, I hope that the following thought experiment will be received in the same ludic spirit of intellectual curios-ity in which it was conceived.

1 Extending Schleicher’s exercise

In a brief communication to the journal Beiträge zur vergleichende Sprach-forschung auf dem Gebiete der arischen, celtischen und slawischen Sprachen from 1868, August Schleicher presented the result of a first attempt to compose a com-prehensive text in reconstructed Proto-Indo-European: a fable entitled Avis akvā-sas ka “[The] sheep and [the] horses” (Schleicher 1868). Shortly before dying of tuberculosis at the age of 47, the pioneering linguist described this exercise to have been in part a pastime (animi causa), and in part an attestation to the pos-sibility of constructing coherent sentences on the basis of secure cognates. It was by force a rather shoddy piece of work, because the still scarce set-up of recon-

126 Peter Jackson Rova

structed grammar and lexicon – not least the “almost complete lack of particles” (fast gänzliche mangel an partikeln) – did not suffice to translate an extant text (Schleicher 1868: 206).

Schleicher unsurprisingly ended up with a self-invented fable. This rudimen-tary form of narrative had been recognized ever since antiquity as the preferable starting point in a set of exercises (so-called progymnásmata) used by teachers of rhetoric. A fable is typically short and concise, contains familiar words arranged in simple sentences, and conveys a clear-cut moral. If this genre served Schleicher well in his exercise to begin imagining the spoken character of a hypothetical proto-language, it was not so much in consideration of its moral, but rather due to the linguistic facility of the genre. Today, not only has the increasing detail with which reconstructed PIE is conceived drastically changed the current shape of the fable – the comparative endeavour has also reached far beyond the recon-struction of a hypothetical language into the hypothetical culture of its speakers, with new languages and language branches added to the comparative record, the relative chronology of distinct branching events outlined in great detail, contours and relics of IE institutions and poetics explored, and archaeological horizons and migrations taken into consideration.

The time thus seems ripe to take Schleicher’s progymnastic exercise a step further by exploring the fable as a tool of comparison in terms also of its moral, or the succinctness of its content, so as to assist us in imagining a sufficiently ‘real’ society behind the inherited PIE vocabulary. This exercise should not be taken to imply that the two Aesopean fables selected for this purpose did themselves originate in PIE (or perhaps rather Core-Indo-European, see note 2) society, but rather that they can be employed retrospectively as minor units of cultural signif-icance with which to make sense of this hypothetical society. Otherwise put: the two fables become means of exploring the kind of sense that exponents to a given social reality could have made of them.

2 Sociological preliminaries

It is easy to be overwhelmed by the very prospect of imagining an IE society with a clear-cut demography prior to its gradual dissolution from the early 3rd millen-nium bce onwards. Even if the existence of a once flourishing cultural continu-um – roughly coinciding with the flourishing of Sumer during the so-called Uruk period between 4100 and 3000 bce – seems compelling on linguistic grounds, it is necessarily a culture without a history. Unlike the case of Sumer, IE society is an

127The wolf, the lamb, and the dog

abstraction (à la Saussure’s langue) situated outside of the events in which it took shape, unfolded, and dissolved. There are no traces in any historical record of such an aggregate of people, let alone anything to suggest that the ethnic groups eventually identified as Indo-Europeans in modern scholarship ever situated themselves in a shared past beyond the clades now tentatively labelled ‘Anatolian’, ‘Indo-Iranian’, ‘Greek’, ‘Italic’, ‘Germanic’, etc.

IE society belongs in that peculiar borderland between ancient history and prehistory – between historically situated texts and dumb archaeological re-mains – that George Dumézil cleverly referred to as “ultra-history”, intending thereby the most extreme fringe of history towards which a historian might aspire to reach by systematically comparing secondary manifestations of the same apparent prototype (Dumézil 1973: 14). In order not to confuse map and conjecture with real territory and testimony, however, any attempt at imagining such an archetypal class of cultural objects has to resist the idealistic impulse of hypercorrectivity. What we can aspire to do is, at best, to reach for a sense of mutual comprehensibility among linguistically, culturally, and geographically related groups in a period prior to a series of migrations that eventually caused that continuum to dissolve. A similar sense of relative linguistic and sociocultur-al proximity is likely to have prevailed among Semitic-speaking peoples in the Levant during the 4th millennium bce, Germanic-speaking peoples in Central Europe and Southern Scandinavia during the 1st millennium bce and early 1st millennium ce, and Turkic-speaking peoples in Central Asia during roughly the same period.1

I need to clarify from the start that the caption “Indo-European Sociology” is not meant here to suggest the outcome of a modern sociological (Durkheimian, Weberian, Bourdieuan, etc.) approach to a prehistoric speech community. Rath-er, I shall be using the term in its explicit sense, implying thereby that at least a

1 When a given people is attributed temporal primacy in the transmission of certain cultural traits, this position will often pass as a sign of superior status. In order to avoid such confusion, it is crucial to distinguish the evaluative conclusions that come with simplistic (whether imperialistic or diffusionistic) explanations from the fact of cul-tural diffusion itself. It would be pointless to deny that the population of the British Isles around 1600 must be attributed temporal primacy in the transmission of certain cultural traits (including the English language) to other parts of the world as a conse-quence of migrations and colonisation during the following centuries. How one choos-es to delineate and evaluate the unique composition of ‘British culture’ by that period, and the consequences of its global impact, is an entirely different thing. For a lucid take on these issues, see Ginzburg’s response to Lincoln in Lincoln & Ginzburg (2020).

128 Peter Jackson Rova

fraction of this community subscribed to a particular logic of social intercourse (a sociology), just as there would have been an anthropology, a theology, and a cosmology from which to derive prevalent notions about humans, gods, and the world. The reader should not be misled to assume that such principles of valida-tion were commonly endorsed by all. Quite the contrary, they were most likely also principles of subjugation, organized theft, slavery, blood feud, exploitation, and various forms of dehumanization. Considering the impact of 20th-century sociological scholarship on figures such as Dumézil, it would be presumptuous to begin outlining such a sociology afresh. Much of what we already seem to know cannot easily be unlearned. And yet, it seems advisable to resist applying sociological models that are themselves the outcome of advanced modern schol-arship.

Without allowing too much circularity into the argument, however, I believe there is currently enough comparative linguistic and philological evidence at hand to afford a few general assumptions about the socio-economic character-istics of the Core-Indo-European (CIE) speech community, and from which to begin building a more nuanced model.2 IE society was most likely a conglom-erate of patrifocal chiefdoms with an already developed system of stratification and professionalisation. Most strikingly to judge from the best textual evidence, there was a warrior elite and hired ritual professionals. Bovines, horses, sheep, and goats were slaughtered and consumed at communal sacrifices through the patronage of chiefs. These animals also functioned as a kind of currency, both as tokens of accumulated wealth among their owners, and as payment for ritual ser-vices that could likewise increase the prestige of their patrons. Poetry was com-posed in praise of a chief ’s bravery and generosity in a style roughly analogous to the hymns accompanying the cult.

The dynamic of IE religion can be effectively outlined against the background of two interdependent ritual frameworks. As indicated by reconstructed vocab-ulary, these frameworks must have existed in some rudimentary form in PIE so-ciety. They correspond to different yet equally fundamental procedures by which extra-familial relations are created and sustained, namely in symmetrical rela-tionships based on mutual trust and benefit between equals, and in asymmetric relationships between patrons and clients based on the exchange of goods and

2 It seems advisable to proceed from such comparative evidence in addressing the socio- economic characteristics of a CIE (rather than PIE) speech community, because many of the standard lexical, poetic, and anthroponomastic comparanda on the basis of which such characteristics are reconstructed cannot be attested in the Anatolian lan-guages.

129The wolf, the lamb, and the dog

services. The latter relationship requires a certain degree of professionalisation as well as some form of patronage. If ties of hospitality are ritually created, ties of patron-clientage are the preconditioned means to such an end. Without the assistance of hired ritual professionals (on a par with modern party fixers), the hospitable act of social bonding loses its quality of pageantry. Terminological confusion might arise due to the fact that the term client is sometimes used by scholars of religion in its modern sense to denote a ritual customer, that is, some-one who buys the services of a religious specialist. According to the original func-tion of the ancient Roman patron–client system, however, a ritual specialist hired by a patron must be considered a client, because he economically depends on his patron. This is not to say that systems of patronage and hospitality cannot be intentionally confused so as to serve specific rhetorical ends. A critical passage in Pindar’s Nemean 7 (61–63) is suggestive of this operation:

$ξεῖνός εἰμι: σκοτεινὸν ἀπέχων ψόγον, ὕδατος ὥτε ῥοὰς φίλον ἐς ἄνδρ’ ἄγων κλέος ἐτήτυμον αἰνέσω: ποτίφορος δ’ ἀγαθοῖσι μισθὸς οὗτος. $

I am (your [i.e., Thearion’s]) guest-friend. Keeping away dark blame, like streams of water with praises to the man who is my friend I shall bring true fame: for that is the proper reward for good men (trans. Race)

$By laying claims on being a guest-friend (ξεῖνος) of his host and securing his host’s reward in the form of fame (κλέος), Pindar obfuscates the fact that he is not really a guest-friend after all, but rather a client who (with a subtle threat of ψόγος $‘blame’) expects hard currency in return from his patron.

3 The fables

It is now time to introduce the two Aesopean fables, and then to begin consid-ering their suitability in bringing prevalent topics of IE sociology (such as social mobility, gender roles, and kingship, but perhaps most importantly systems of patronage and hospitality) into a comprehensive model. They run as follows:

The Lamb and the Wolf (Perry Index 261) A Wolf pursued a Lamb, which fled for refuge to a certain Temple. The Wolf called out to him and said, “The Priest will slay you in sacrifice, if he should

130 Peter Jackson Rova

catch you.” To which the Lamb replied, “It would be better for me to be sac-rificed in the Temple than to be eaten by you.”

The Wolf and the Well-fed Dog (Perry Index 346) A Wolf, emaciated with hunger, happened to meet a well-fed Dog. After greeting each other, they came to a stand and the Wolf said: “How comes it, do tell me, that you look so sleek? What have you been eating to put on so much flesh? I am much stronger than you, and yet I am starving.” The Dog replied frankly: “The same lot may be yours if you can render like service to a master.” “What is that?” said he. “To be the guardian of his threshold and protect his house from thieves at night. Bread is brought to me without my asking; my master gives me bones from his own table; the servants toss out tidbits to me and whatever dainties anyone has no taste for. In this way my belly is replenished at no pains.” “Well,” said the Wolf, “I’m ready for that all right; at present I have to endure snow and rain, and it is a hard life that I lead in the woods. How much easier for me it would be to live under a roof, and at my ease to sate myself with food in abundance.” “Well then, come with me,” said the Dog. As they were going along the Wolf noticed that the Dog’s neck had been worn bare by a chain. “How did this happen, my friend?” “Oh, it’s nothing.”

“Tell me, please, just the same.” “Because they think me restless, they tie me up in the daytime, to make me be quiet while it is light and keep watch when night comes. At dusk I am unchained and wander about wherever I please.” “Come now, suppose you want to go away somewhere, are you allowed to do so?” “Why no, as a matter of fact, I’m not.” “Well, Dog, go on enjoying the things you praise; I don’t choose to be a king if I can’t be free to please myself.”

A crucial initial observation to be made is that the moral expressed by the wolf in the last sentence of the second fable (“I don’t choose to be a king if I can’t be free to please myself ”) directly addresses the issue of kingship. It is also a statement $reminiscent of the sombre expression attributed to the ‘wolfish’ (cf. Gk. λύσσα [from λύκος ‘wolf $’]) warrior Heracles in Pindar’s fr. 169 (concerning the so-called enigma of kingship: “For it is better to die when possessions are being seized than to be a coward”). Hence, issues of priesthood (= the lamb as the sacrificial victim of the priest) and kingship (= the dog/wolf as king) can be considered inherent in the fables according to their classical rendering.

131The wolf, the lamb, and the dog

4 A synthetic rendering of the fables

A preliminary synthetic representation of the two fables in regard to the tensions between the three actors might be represented as in Figure 1.

What immediate conclusions can be drawn from this graph? There are three kinds of animals involved, one of which is not domesticated; collectively, they represent what in phonetics is sometimes referred to as a bundle of distinctive features: the wolf does not want to be a dog and seeks to devour the lamb, the dog used to be a wolf and seeks to protect the lamb. The dog can thus be positively contrasted with the lamb in the sense that the lamb depends on it for its protec-tion. Hence, the wolf can be said to exist in contradistinction to the lamb and the dog, just as the dog exists in contradistinction to the wolf and the lamb, and the lamb to the dog and the wolf in their respective capacities as protecting and rapacious canines.

There are also references to a priest and a king in the fables. The priest is the preferable killer of the lamb (at least from the lamb’s perspective), whereas the king is the kind of sovereign the wolf does not want to become at the cost of its natural desire for freedom. But what about the empty slot? Could we think of it, perhaps, as being reserved for someone who has been expelled from the domestic sphere, becoming once more a creature of the wilderness? The semi-human, pre-

132 Peter Jackson Rova

ternatural figure of the outlaw, the ostracised member of the in-group, the wan-dering priest, etc. It could be conceived as a slot reserved for someone considered socially dead, who deserves punishment, or has lost all sense of dignity.

And yet, there is also a wilderness into which one may venture voluntarily, and from which one may eventually hope to return according to certain pre-es-tablished principles of periodicity. This transfer accords with the logic of lupine symbolism long associated with the IE Männerbund/Jugendbund institution (cf. Das & Meiser 2002). It is a pattern perhaps most conclusively preserved in the legend of Remus and Romulus according to Ovid’s Fasti as well as in the ancient cultic traditions of the regions of Arcadia and Argolis involving human sacrifice and men’s transformation into wolves (cf. Burkert 1983: 83–134). In a new study, Birgit Anette Olsen (fc.) has brilliantly taken stock of this archaic institution by clarifying the semantics of the IE deverbative nouns *(s)kor(hₓ)i̯os (‘youthful war band’ < ‘host, army’) and *u̯ĺ̥kʷos (‘a marauding, rapacious one’ < ‘wolf ’) as well as by emphasizing the inherited formulaic nature of the legal pronouncement $Hitt. ur.bar.ra-aš ki-iš-ta-at ≈ Ved. vŕ̥ko hí ṣáḥ (“[for] x has become/is a wolf $”).3

The following IE onomastic features can be used to illustrate the ways in which a potentially positive aspect of a chief ’s wolfish persona survived among IE groups, perhaps in reference to an earlier phase in their career as members of a Männerbund/Jugendbund:

$Run. Hlewagastiz4 = Serb. Slavogost ≈ Gk. Κλεόξενος ‘Guest of honour/Hav-$ing famous guests’ PGmc. *Harjagastiz ‘Guest of the war band’ PGmc. *Harjawulfaz (< PIE *[s]kor[hₓ]i̯o-u̯l̥kʷos [?]) ‘Wolf of the war band’ PGmc. *Haþuwulfaz = Eburonic Catuvolcus ‘Battle wolf ’ (?)5 $PGmc. *Hlūþawulfaz ≈ Serb. Vlьkoslavь ‘Famous wolf $’ (cf. Loma 2020: 20) $PGmc. *Hlūþaharjaz ≈ Gk. Κλεόμαχος ‘Battle-famed’ $

3 A similar legal pronouncement wargus sit, albeit involving an etymologically unrelated yet semantically associated lexeme (see below), occurs in the medieval Germanic Salic and Ripuarian laws.

4 A different interpretation of the first member (viz. as belonging to Old Norse hlé ‘pro-tection’) is also possible (quasi ‘providing protection for the guest’ or similar); see most recently Nedoma (2022).

5 Though superficially suggestive, an etymological match between PGmc. -wulfaz and Eburonic -volcus can only be posited at the cost of numerous aberrations from the rules of expected sound change (Anders Jørgensen, p.c.), but see Hughes (2012).

133The wolf, the lamb, and the dog

In coming back to the negative aspects of the wolf, I call attention to the two over-lapping deverbative nouns first discussed in a paper by Jaan Puhvel (1986), “Who were the hurkilas pesnes?”. Puhvel relies here in part on evidence already laid out by Calvert Watkins in an equally groundbreaking paper (Watkins 1975). As can be concluded from these studies, there is comparative textual evidence to sup-port (1) the existence of two verbal roots, PIE *h₁erg̑ʰ-/*h₂u̯erg̑ʰ- (cf. LIV *h₁erg̑ʰ- [IEW 328] and *u̯erg̑ʰ [IEW 1154–1155]), referring to the culturally associated acts $of bestial copulation (cf. Hitt. ark- ‘to mount, copulate,’ Gk. ὀρχέομαι ‘to dance $[lasciviously]’ < ‘to perform coital motions’) and punitive strangulation (cf. Hitt. hurkel ‘hanging matter,’ Anglo-Latin wargus ‘outlaw, criminal [> wolf]’); and (2) $the idea that the male passive subject of such acts (the *h₁órg̑ʰos [≈ ‘fucked one’] or *h₂u̯órg̑ʰos [≈ ‘strangled one’]) typically denotes someone deserving or being $subjected to punishment, whereas the active (virile or strangulating) aggressor (the *h₁org̑ʰós or *h₂u̯org̑ʰós) rather stands free of charge. The two nouns are not just unisonant, but also express notions that tend to overlap in non-trivial cul-tural terms. Gmc. *wargaz originally meant ‘outlaw, criminal’, but eventually ac-quired the additional sense ‘wolf ’ in Germanic. Still, as the Hittite example shows, the hurkilas pesnes (‘men of strangulation’) in the semi-legal text discussed by Puhvel are already associated with the attempted catching of wolves. As for the long-term association of the two nouns, consider the Old Norse curse-formula argr goðvargr once used as an insult against a missionary in a verse ascribed to the 10th-century skald Þorvaldr veili.

5 Outlaws and prostitutes

Another set of interdependent notions should be briefly considered before the cultural message of the dog–lamb–wolf bundle of distinctive features can be con-sidered sufficiently complete. These notions can likewise be seen to shift in pur-port as they circulate within the model.

Tacitus famously reports (Germania 12) how the ancient Germanic laws pre-scribe “cowardly, unwarlike, and bodily heinous persons” (ignavos et imbelles et corpore infames) to be sunk into the mud of the marshes and covered with hur-dles. It deserves notice in this regard that the expression corpore infamis could still be applied to a prostitute (or she-wolf) in late colloquial Latin: prostibulum lupa; quae pretio corpus vulgat cum quoque; corpore infamis.6 As suggested by

6 Weber (1745): s.v. lupa = “jedermans Hure”.

134 Peter Jackson Rova

this admittedly very late example, the significance of corporeal infamy may have acquired a decisively different sense when ascribed to females instead of males.

There is a cruel irony in the fact that prostitutes were the only women in the Graeco-Roman world who had a chance of independently accumulating wealth for themselves (no matter how minimal their chances of success; cf. Pomeroy 1995). A married wife depended completely on her husband and was considered his sexual property. Her only economic security – and the only thing distin-guishing her from a concubine – was the dowry, which her husband would have to pay back to her family should he want to divorce her. The relation between a husband and his wife (or his concubine) is thus vaguely suggestive of a patron– client relationship. In contrast to the concubine, however, a prostitute operating on an open market incurred corporeal infamy and wolfish traits because she belonged to none and everyone. Unlike her manly counterpart the outlaw (the homo sacer, wargus, etc.),7 however, she legally profited from the community in which she was typically treated as an outcast. The Roman case of Acca Larentia (see below) is indicative of how this precarious condition could be positively re-imagined – according to a logic similar to the wolfish Jugendbündler’s socio-po-litical incorporation – as a she-wolf ’s potential ascent to the royal status of a patroness.

It should be added in this context that the prostitute is not just recurrently perceived as a she-wolf, but is also closely associated with dogs and the apotropa-ic killing of dogs as a source of pollution (cf. the Vedic example below).

6 Completing the exercise

Figure 2 is an elaboration of the first graph with further arrows added to indicate potential transfers between the parametric slots, and with new symbolic associa-tions added to the roles of the three animals involved.

There is a light and a dark side to everything in this graph. In the upper left part of the register, the king appears in his role as a shepherd of his people, as a host and a patron in times of peace and prosperity. In the upper right part, he appears instead in his role as a fierce warrior who violently enslaves and expro-priates neighbouring tribes, punishes the transgressor (the violent aspect of the law), and induces potential social collapse. One is reminded here of the duplex

7 The notion of the ‘sacred man’ (in the sense of being accursed and execrable) is a recur-rent trope in archaic Roman and Germanic legal traditions.

135The wolf, the lamb, and the dog

character of Dumézil’s first function to include sovereignty both in its positive, judicial sense of kingship, and in its dark, coercive sense of sorcery. As a slight modification to this sense of contrast, it should be added that the chief can in fact receive the poet’s glory both in his role as a peaceful protector and benefactor of the in-group (cf. the dithematic name Hlewagastiz ‘fame-guest’) and in his role as $a fierce and wolfish figure on the battlefield (cf. *Hlūþawulfaz ≈ Serb. Vlьkoslavь $‘famous wolf ’). A similar logic pertains to the priestly/ritual function in the lower left and right slots in the sense that the priest (or ritual specialist) may either represent a respected member of the community, or a less respectable entrepre-$neurial figure (cf. Gk. ἀλαζών ‘vagrant’) acting as a free player on an open ritual $market. To roam as a poet-sacrificer without a patron’s support is a precarious situation for which we have good evidence in Old Iranian and Old Indic sources, reflecting back on a period in Indo-Iranian prehistory in which a well-established priestly class did not yet exist, but rather groups of competing ritual specialists.
