I am adding the following excerpts from a selection of Vedic, Greek, and Roman sources in order to illustrate how the four parameters can be understood to in-tersect:

$1 → 4 The myth of Lycaon $Plato, in Republic, expounds on the traditional story of the Arcadian king Lycaon as a means to address the dangers of kingship:

What, then, is the starting-point of the transformation of a protector $[προστάτης] into a tyrant? […] The story [of the shrine of Lycaean Zeus in $Arcadia] goes that he who tastes of the one bit of human entrails minced up with those of other victims is inevitably transformed into a wolf. […] [I]s it not true that in like manner a leader of the people who, getting control of a docile mob, does not withhold his hand from the shedding of tribal blood […]? [I]s it not the inevitable consequence and a decree of fate that such a one be either slain by his enemies or become a tyrant and be transformed from a man into a wolf? (Rep. 565d-565e; trans. Shorey)

$2 → 3 Expulsion of the ἀλαζών $Aristophanes (Pax 1039ff.) provides a derisive portrayal of the diviner Hiero-cles, who arrives out of the blue to meddle with a sacrifice to the goddess Eirene (‘Peace’). Hierocles is supposedly attracted by the odour of fat, engages in all sorts of ritual quiddities with the patron, and is eventually driven off with a stick – $without a share in the ‘inward parts’ (σπλάγχνον in 1012) – as a sign of final relief. Hierocles is depicted here in the typical terms of a ‘travelling charlatan’ (ἀλαζών $in 1120). An almost identical scene occurs in Birds 848–1047.

Consider also the following allusion in RV 8.14.14 to a group of legendary Dasyus who are supposed to have used their deceitful sorcery (māyā́-) in order to conquer heaven:

137The wolf, the lamb, and the dog

They who, through their viles [māyā́bhir], were trying to creep [utsísr̥psata $(√sarp)] up and mount to heaven, Indra, those Dasyus did you send tum-$bling down. (RV 8.14.14)

$2 → 3 “Go to hell, whore!” $The poet and playwright Philemon (3rd–2nd c. bce) is quoted by Athenaeus as saying:

The door is open. One obol:8 enter straight: there’s no prudery, no trifle, no insinuations: but as straightforward as you like, in whatever way you $like. You go out: tell her to go to hell [οἰμώζειν λέγε (cf. Ar., Pl. 58)]. She’s a stranger [ἀλλοτρία] to you. (Philemon apud Athenaeus Deipn. 13.25 569e–f) $

$3 → 4 The myth of Acca Larentia and/as the suckling she-wolf $The legend of Acca Larentia is reported (with minor variations) as follows by Livy and Valerius Antias (cf. Howard 1906). The social transformation of Acca Laren-tia affords a few interesting parallels with Pindar’s mercenary muse according to Leslie Kurke’s analysis (1991: 240-256).

[A] she-wolf, coming down out of the surrounding hills to slake her thirst, turned her steps towards the cry of the infants [Remus and Romulus], and with her teats gave them suck so gently, that the keeper of the royal flock found her licking them with her tongue. Tradition assigns to this man the name of Faustulus, and adds that he carried the twins [Remus and Romulus] to his hut and gave them to his wife Larentia to rear. Some think that Laren-tia, having been free with her favours, had got the name of ‘she-wolf ’ among the shepherds, and that this gave rise to this marvellous story. (Livy 1.4.6ff.; trans. Heinemann)

But Acca Larentia was a public prostitute and by that trade had earned a great deal of money. In her will she made king Romulus heir to her property […]; according to some others, the Roman people. Because of that favour public sacrifice was offered to her by the priest of Quirinus and a day was consecrated to her memory in the Calendar. (Valerius Antias apud Aulus Gellius 7.7.1; trans. Rolfe)

8 An obol in classical Athens purchased approximately 3 litres of wine.

138 Peter Jackson Rova

The Roman legend has a few striking features in common with the so far poorly investigated ethnogonic myth of the Gökturks (cf. Golden 2018). Consider, es-pecially, the following passage recorded in the Chinese 7th-century chronicle Zhoushu (“Book of the [Northern] Zhou”; 50.907–08): “Then the she-wolf hid in the mountains. Here, she gave birth to ten sons. When they grew up, they went out of the cave and married women from the outside” (Golden 2018: 299). Apart from recalling the legend of Remus and Romulus, this passage bears a striking resemblance to the mythological beginning of the Old Hittite Zalpa-text (KBo 22.2) with its now convincingly uncovered reference to a male collective of wolves/wolfish marauders (cf. Olsen fc.): “The queen of Kaniš bore thirty sons within one year. She (speaks) thus: ‘What kind of u̯a-al-ku-an [< *u̯elkʷ- $(?) ‘maraud, plunder’ → *u̯ĺ̥kʷos] did I give birth to?’” While the Turkic peoples $of Central Asia must have shared both a past and cultural characteristics with various Indo- European (Tocharian and Iranian) groups in that same region, it is conceivable that they also shared with them certain ethnogonic notions about themselves.

$3 → 1 A prostitute’s son apotropaically killing a dog in royal sacrifice $According to the Vedic ritual manual Āpastambha Śrautasūtra (20.3.11), an apot-ropaic phase in the royal horse sacrifice (aśvamedha) contains a four-eyed(!) dog being led by a prostitute’s son into a body of water. At a given moment, when the dog loses its footing, the Advaryu priest orders the prostitute’s son to “slay” (jahí) the dog.

$The root √han is used here (and elsewhere) as a term for the justified slaying $of foes or the unjustified slaying of friends, but not for the proper sacrificial kill-$ing of cattle. The same applies to the so-called βουφόνια ‘ox-slayings’ celebrated $during the midsummer festival of Dipolieia in Athens. The ritual slaughter was apparently not seen as a regular bovine sacrifice in that it contained numerous acts to make it appear rather as ritualized crime. In the Vedic example above, the killing of a dog in the sacrificial context of a king consolidating his role as $a protector of his people (cf. Plato’s προστάτης above) also involves apotropaic $concerns, such as keeping the community safe from pollution and intrusion. The dog could apparently be evoked both in its symbolic function as a guardian and loyal servant, and in its very opposite role as a source of pollution.

Dogs were apotropaically killed on a regular basis during the ancient Argive $festival of Ἀρνηΐδες ἡμέραι ‘days of the lamb’, which is sometimes referred to as the κυνοφόντις (ἑορτή) ‘dog-slaying (festival)’ (Burkert 1983: 107).$

139The wolf, the lamb, and the dog

7 Concluding Remarks

I should like to end this exercise by indicating a few preliminary conclusions to be drawn from it. By taking my cue from two simple Aesopian fables, I have ended up with a rather complex representation of contrastive slots with a horizontal tension between domesticity and savagery, and a vertical tension between domi-nance and submission.

The first parametric slot focuses on the pastoral obligations of kingship, in-cluding the king’s apotropaic concern with keeping the community safe from pollution and intrusion.

The second slot focuses on the merits of hospitality and patronage, including the happy outcome of communal feasting and other advantages of royal protec-tion, as well as on the sacrificial animal representing the quintessential gift of atonement (a figure of thought still clearly manifest in Christian liturgy).

The third slot focuses on crime, deception, prostitution, and other potentially corrosive and polluting activities understood to deserve exclusion, loss of dignity, and death.

Finally, the fourth slot focuses on the punitive and martial obligations of the wolfish king, who in his capacity as a sovereign potentially threatens to disrupt the social order in his indeterminate state of exception (cf. Agamben 1995). The wolfish king and the beastly outcast can be claimed to occupy the same savage re-gion – the same extra-legal space – through which they are also seen to variously attract and repel each other.

On the prehistory of legal language and procedure

Repairing a misdeed in Proto- Indo- European and in Core Indo- European

Calvert Watkins in memoriam

José Luis García Ramón Köln / AIBL, Paris 1

In the ancient IE traditions, the repair of a misdeed is conceptualized in

two ways:

(1) ‘to make good the misdeed’ (the offender or the offended) is exclu-

sively attested in Hittite (and may be traced back to PIE): the offender

‘repairs’ (šarni(n)k-mi), or ‘gives a reparation’ (šarnikzil- pai-ḫḫi), or ‘expiates’

(šarni(n)k- with telicizing particles) his misdeed, whereas (b) the offend-

ed ‘repairs’ (i.e. ‘makes repair’ : šarni(n)k-), or ‘takes a reparation’ (šarnikzil-

dā-ḫḫi), or ‘avenges’ (šanḫ-mi with telicizing particles) the other’s misdeed.

This conceptualization lives on in Old Latin (noxiam sarcīre, like Hitt. nak-

kuš šarni(n)k-, remodelled as poenam soluere) and residually, limited to the

$reparation by the misdoer, in Greek (βλάβην ἐξιᾶσθαι ‘to heal the damage’) $

and some Germanic languages.

(2) ‘to atone (*kʷei̯-) the misdeed’ (sc. the offender) as against ‘to make

pay it’ (sc. the offended), as attested in Avestan (YAv. cikaiia-ti ‘to atone’ vs

$kaiiaiia-te ‘to make expiate’; Ved. cáy-a-te ‘to punish’) and in Greek (τίνειν, $

$τεῖσαι vs. τίνεσθαι, τείσασθαι). The collocation lives on, with lexical renew-$

al in Latin (luere, soluere) and in other Core IE languages, but not in Ana-

tolian: it may therefore be traced back to Core IE.

By contrast, the exacting of reparation as ‘to seek the misdeed’ (Hitt. kat-

tau̯ātar šanḫ-, OLat. parricidi quaestores …), being residual as against ‘to

seek a reparation’, may be traced back to PIE.

1 It is a pleasant duty to express my gratitude to Hannes Fellner (Wien), Velizar Sadovski (Wien) and Ana Vegas Sansalvador (Köln) for indications and comments, and espe-cially to Riccardo Ginevra (Milano, Università Cattolica) and Craig H. Melchert (North Carolina), as well as Stefan Höfler (Wien), and Birgit Anette Olsen (København), who read the final version, for their suggestions and criticism. Standard works and editions are quoted according to the current conventions. Vedic translations are taken from (or rely on) Jamison and Brereton (2014).

142 José Luis García Ramón

The juridical terminology, as attested in legal texts or reflected in titles of officials in the oldest Indo- European (IE) traditions and, indirectly, in their phraseology, allows us to identify a series of cultural conceptions and social values which un-derlie the procedures in the form as they occur in the written records. These con-ceptions have certainly been codified as legal terminology first in the individual languages, but may be considered as inherited in view of the striking coincidenc-es, both conceptual and even formal, between different traditions as the reflex of their social structures.

Legal terms and phraseology, as attested in the ancient IE languages, do in-deed reflect conceptualizations of matters, which may differ from each other, and ultimately be inherited and even traced back to different prehistorical layers, with the help of comparison and linguistic reconstruction. This is the case of the conceptualization of the reparation of a misdeed in its twofold dimension, as the expiation by the misdoer or the obtainment of a compensation by the offended, and as the seeking of redress by the latter. The expression of the reparation of a misdeed by the misdoer has proven to be inherited on the strength of the cor-respondences between the Latin actiones noxales in the formulation aut noxiam sarcire aut noxae dedere ‘to repair the damage done and to surrender (sc. the offender) for damage’ and the corresponding regulation for compensatory resti-tution as the alternative to the surrender of the offender in Hittite, as it has been shown in the illuminating analysis by Calvert Watkins (1970). On the other hand, the conceptualization of the exacting of a reparation as ‘seeking the misdeed’ is recognizable in institutions of power and social prestige like the Roman quaestor ‘inquirer’, and especially the parricidi quaestores (Fest.), as persuasively pointed $out by Émile Benveniste (1969), or the Athenian ζητηταί. The conceptualization $of the reparation of a misdeed (by its author or by the one who suffered it) in the different languages allows us to state some striking coincidences, which may point to a common Proto- Indo- European (PIE) origin, as is the case for ‘to exact reparation’, and some differences, equally striking, which point to the existence of, at least, two different phases in the evolution from PIE to the Core IE lan-guages.

The present contribution tries to take one more step on the path of Watkins’ analysis and will make the case for two different conceptualizations of the repara-tion of a misdeed, both by the misdoer and by the offended: one of them, [repair, make good  – misdeed], may be traced back to Proto- Indo- European as it is attested in Hittite and lives on in Latin, in Greek, and in other languages; whereas a conceptualization as [pay (i.e. ‘atone’) – misdeed], which is absent in Hittite, is

143On the prehistory of legal language and procedure

attested under different forms and to varying degrees in the remaining languages, and may therefore be traced back to Core Indo- European.

1 Repair misdeed (the offender), repair misdeed (the offended), seek misdeed

The essentials of the evidence for the expression of the conceptualization of (1) ‘repair/amend/make good a misdeed’ (sc. the misdoer), (2) ‘repair/amend/make good a misdeed’ (sc. the offended), and (3) ‘seek the misdeed’ (sc. the offended) may be set forth, for the sake of simplicity, as (1) [repair – misdeed] (sc. the offender), (2) [repair – misdeed] (sc. the offended) and (3) [seek – misdeed] (sc. the offended). In Table 1 an attempt is made to summarize the situation in Hittite, in Latin and in Greek (also in Indo- Iranian), as prominent representatives of Core Indo- European.

A first glance at Table 1 allows us to state a neat difference between Hittite and the oldest languages of Core IE. Hittite conceptualizes repair as make good (šarnink-mi) in both variants: in (1) [offender – make good – (his own) misdeed] the misdoer amends his misdeed, which in some instances is referred to as accomplished (pret.3pl. šarninkir ‘expiated’, with telicizing particle -kan); in (2) [offended – make good – (another’s) misdeed] the action may also be

referred to as accomplished (pret. ‘he avenged’), when expressed by means of šanḫ- (actually ‘to seek’) with telicizing anda, -apa, and -kan, among others. This displays a sharp contrast with Indo- Iranian and Greek, where repair is conceptualized as pay (IE *kʷei̯-) with the misdeed as object, in the framework of a diathetic opposition, namely between (1) [offender – payactive – misdeed] and (2) [offended  – make paymiddle  – misdeed]. Latin and Greek, being as they are Core IE languages, have a special position: they share with Hittite the conceptualization as [make good – misdeed], albeit to varying degrees: Lat. sarcīre ‘to mend’, resarcīre ‘id.’ (and synonyms piāre, expiāre, section 11) is used $for both (1) and (2), Gk. ἐξιᾶσθαι ‘to heal’, and ἰᾶσθαι, ἀκεῖσθαι ‘id.’ only for (1). $The conceptualization as [make good  – misdeed] coexists with [pay  – mis-deed] in Latin (luere ‘to pay’, ‘to expiate’, also soluere), limited to the reparation $by the misdoer, and in Greek, where active τίνειν, τεῖσαι (1) ‘to pay’, ‘to expi-ate’ stands in opposition to middle τίνεσθαι, τείσασθαι (2) ‘to make pay’, i.e. ‘to $avenge’ (section 14).

On the other hand (3) [offended – seek – misdeed], is attested in all lan-guages, and may be understood as inherited, although seek is expressed by lex-emes which do not occur in this collocation in more than one language, with the $exception of IE *i̯eh₂- ‘to seek, strive for’ (Ved. Av. yā- : Gk. ζᾱ-, Att.Ion. ζη- and IE *prek̑- ‘to ask’ (Lat. poscere ‘to demand’ and OP fraθ ‘to punish’). A special case $is Hittite, where the collocation is expressed by Hitt.-Luv. šark- in some nominal forms with the sense ‘to seek redress’ (as against šarnink- in (1) and (2)), as well as by šanḫ- ‘to exact, seek’ (without particle).

2 Hitt. šarni(n)k-mi beside šarnikzil pai-ḫḫi and šarnikzil dā-ḫḫi

Let us turn to the Hittite evidence for (1) [offender – make good – misdeed] and (2) [offended – make good – misdeed] with their variants, and (3) [of-fended – seek – misdeed].

It may be stressed that in both (1) and (2) the collocation with šarni(n)k-mi (and šarni(n)kišk-mi) ‘to repair’ (originally ‘to make whole’) may coexist with the periphrases šarnikzil pai-ḫḫi ‘to give (also ‘to pay’) a reparation’ and šarnikzil dā-ḫḫi ‘to take a reparation’, respectively, which rely on a secondary remodeling of the basic pattern (section 8). On the other hand, misdeed is expressed by a series of terms, which may occur in more than one of the collocations, namely nakkuš- ‘damage, fault’ in (1), ēšḫar ‘blood (sc. of the victim)’ as a concretiza-tion of ‘crime, damage, injustice’ or kattau̯āttar ‘(legal) grounds for a quarrel,

145On the prehistory of legal language and procedure

complaint’2 in all three, AWAT (: uttar) ‘an affair (of blood)’ in (3), as well as šarnikzil- ‘reparation’.3

The existence of a twofold reading of šarni(n)k- ‘to make good’, depending on who is the agent, is recognizable in the abstract šarnikzil- ‘compensation’ which may be both (1) given (pai-ḫḫi) by the offender (to the offended), or (2) taken (dā-ḫḫi) by the offended, or even remain unclear or ambiguous:4

Ad (1) cf. KUB 13.9 ii 3 mān ēšḫanašš⸗a kuiški šarnikzil pii̯an ḫarzi “and if someone has also given (i.e. paid) compensation for homicide …” (protocol, MH/ NS).

Ad (2) cf. KBo 2.6 i 43–46 dUTU-ŠI⸗i̯a⸗z parkunuzzi šarnikzela (var. [šarni]kzelḪI.A) SA È-TI ME-anzi “his Majesty will also purify himself and they will take (ME-anzi) the compensation for (his) house” (oracle question, NH).

The same applies to šarninkuu̯ar ‘compensation’, with ‘gerundival’ gen. šarn-inkuu̯aš ‘for compensation’, e.g. KBo 2.2 iii 33–36 kuiš IKRIBU šarninkuu̯aš (coll.) n⸗an šarninkanzi UL⸗ma kuis šarninkuu̯aš (?, coll.) nu⸗šši zankila[tar SUM-anzi

“what vow is subject to compensation, they will pay compensation for it. And what vow is not subject to compensation, [they shall pay: SUM-] a penalty (zankilatar) to him” (oracle question, NH). Only the context makes clear that it is the offend-ers who have to ‘make good’ (šarninkanzi) the compensation.5

3 Hitt. šarni(n)k-mi ‘to repair’ (the offender) and ‘to expiate’ (with telicizing particles)

The essentials of the evidence for the three collocations and their variants may be set forth as follows.

2 Melchert (1979: 268–270): “not ‘revenge’, but the object of revenge”, “cause of/grounds for vengeance”, “not ‘retribution’, but that for which retribution is demanded”, “grounds for quarrel, i.e. for retaliation”, “grounds for a fight”. Hitt. kattau̯ātar, which relies on

*kattu-/*kattau̯- ‘hostile, evil’, and neuter ‘enmity’ (PIE *k̑ót-u-) has an aequabile in Gk. $κότος (PIE *k̑ót-o-), as their collocations show (García Ramón 2020). $

3 Also šarnikzel … šarninkišk- (frequent in legal texts: CHD 279–280). On the word for-mation cf. Rieken (1999: 482–483).

4 Both possibilities may be assumed in the formula šarnikzil NU.GÁL “there shall be no compensation” in legal texts (once without negation in KBo 6.26 I 22–27 Laws).

5 Ptc. šarninkant- ‘arranged’ (e.g. mān⸗ma⸗aš parā šarninkanza “if it (sc. the festival) is, however, fully arranged” KUB 16.66 obv. 16,30 NH) may be also active cf. šarni]nkan-zan⸗wa⸗za ēš “sei ein Schadensersatzpflichtiger!” KBo 6.2 ii 54 (as per E. Neu apud Haase 1982: 33–34).

146 José Luis García Ramón

The collocation (1) [offender  – make good  – misdeed] is expressed by šarni(n)k- (1a) ‘to repair’ (beside the periphrasis šarnikzil pai-ḫḫi ‘to give repara-tion for (gen.)’), also (1b) ‘to expiate’ (preterital forms, telicizing adverbs and/or particles):

1a ‘to repair’

… nakkuš n⸗at [šarnik]za (KBo 6.2 iv 53–55) (whatever perished in the house … it is) damage, he shall make compensa-tion for it (var. UL šarnikzi, Leges §98, v.l. OS)

kurim[ma]š dam[me]šḫandaš antuḫšaš kattau̯āttar zik⸗[pat] DUTU-uš šarni(n)kiškiši (ABoT 44 i 36–38, MH/NS) You, the Sun-god, make good the complaint of the bereaved and oppressed man (Melchert 1979: 269)

šarnikzel maškann⸗a KUR-e šer šarninkiškimi (Murs. 1 rev. 19–20) I will repair (sc. ‘to you  … my lords’) reparation and atonement for the country (“ich werde [euch … meinen Herren] Ersatz und Sühne wegen des Landes leisten”; tr. Goetze)6

The periphrasis ēšḫanaš šarnikzil pai-ḫḫi expresses the same state of affairs as *ēšḫar šarni(n)k-:

mān ēšḫanašš⸗a kuiški šarnikzil pii̯an ḫarzi (KUB 13.9 ii 3, protocol, MH/ NS) … and if someone has also given reparation for blood(shed)

It must be noted that, although Hitt. pai-ḫḫi ‘to give’ (like kuššani̯a-mi ‘to hire’) is also used for ‘to pay’ in the periphrasis šarnikzil pai-ḫḫi ‘to pay a compensation’, the collocation [pay – misdeed], as attested in Indo- Iranian and Greek, among other languages, is different, and actually not attested in Hittite.7

6 Cf. also KUB 14.14 rev. 13–14 n⸗at ammuqq⸗a IŠTU É-TI⸗YA šarnikzilaz maškanna[z⸗ ii̯a] šarnenkiškimi. “I too will begin to make compensation for it (i.e. the blood guilt for Tudḫaliya) with compensation and a propitiatory gift from my household.”

7 Lycian ttl(e)i- ‘to pay (a fine)’, probably a denominative of *tille- ‘payment’ (*kʷ(e)i- dʰlo- cf. Serangeli 2018: 188–189; Sasseville 2020: 238–239) beside reduplicated tti- ‘pay’ (*kʷi-kʷi-), reflects the concrete sense of the verb, with indication of a material fine as its object, e.g. TL 102.2ff. me ttleiti puwa : aitãta : am̃mãma : qebelija : ẽni : qlahi :

147On the prehistory of legal language and procedure

1b ‘to expiate’

nu⸗kan mDudḫalii̯an kueš kuennir nu ēšḫar apūš šarninkir (KUB 14.14 rev. 9, ritual against the pest, NH/NS) … those who killed Tudḫaliya had expiated his blood(sin) (Tudḫaliya is al-ready dead)

The specific sense ‘to expiate’ is recognizable as the expression of the fulfillment of the action, by means of the preterite (3pl. šarninkir) with the particle -kan, which explicitely telicizes šarnink-.

4 Hitt. šarni(n)k-mi ‘to make repair’ (the offended) and šanḫ-mi (with telicizing particles) ‘to avenge’

The collocation (2) [offended – make good – misdeed] has two variants, ex-pressed by means of (2a) šarni(n)k- ‘to make repair’ (beside periphrasis šarnikzil dā-ḫḫi ‘to take reparation’), and (2b) šanḫ- ‘to avenge’ (mostly preterital forms and/ or with telicizing adverbs and/or particles) with ēšḫar ‘blood’ as object, also with AWAT (: uttar) ‘affair’. This is a special use of Hitt. šanḫ-, which in its usual sense ‘to seek, search’ (non-telic) is constitutive in the collocation (3) [seek – misdeed] (section 5).

2a ‘to make repair’

[mān Š]A mPii̯aššili U mḪaittili [ēšḫar] šarninkuu̯anzi šanḫeškiši [nu KIN(?) N]U.SIG₅-du N]U.SIG₅ § [nu DINGIR-LU]M ēšḫar⸗pat šarninkuu̯anzi šanḫeškiši (KUB 16.77 iii 5–8, oracle question, NH) if you, (O deity), keep seeking (šanḫeškiši) to get compensation (šarn-inkuu̯anzi) for [the blood (ēšḫar)] of Piyaššili and Ḫaitili, let [the KIN(?) oracle] be unfavorable. § [(If), O go]d you keep seeking to get compensation for the murder only

The deity is seeking (2sg. šanḫeškiši) to make good (infinitive šarninkuu̯anzi) his own claim, i.e. to receive compensation for the murder (ēšḫar) of Piyaššili and Ḫaitili: ešḫar šarnink- is the object of šanḫ- ‘to seek’ in this text.

ebij[e]hi pñtreñni “(falls jemand drinnen irgendeinen (Toten) darauflegt), werden acht qebelija Ziegen? als Bußgabe für die Mutter des hiesigen Heiligtums von Pñtre? bezahlt” (Serangeli 2018: 188).

148 José Luis García Ramón

As to the periphrasis with ‘take’ (ME-), cf. KBo 2.6 i 43–46 dUTU-ŠI⸗i̯a⸗z parkunuzzi šarnikzela (var. [šarni]kzelḪI.A) SA È-TI ME-anzi “his Majesty will also purify himself and they will take (ME-anzi) the compensation for (his) house” (oracle question, NH).

2b ‘to avenge’

n⸗apa DINGIR.MEŠ IP]išenii̯aš išḫar šanḫer (KBo 3.1 rev. i 66, Telipinu, OH/NS) … the gods avenged the blood (: death) of Pišenis

n⸗apa DINGIR.MEŠ at[(taš⸗šaš mZidantaš)] ēšḫar⸗šet šanḫer (KUB 11.1 ii 4–5, OH/NS, with duplicate KUB 11.6 i 3–4c) the gods avenged the blood (: death) of Zidanta, his father

nu⸗za ŠA ABI⸗ŠU [ēšḫar (?) EG]IR-an šanaḫta (KBo 3.57 obv. 10–11) and he (Mursili I) avenged [the blood?] of his father

Note the contrast with the construction with the present:

DINGIR.MEŠ BĒLŪMEŠ⸗YA ŠA mDudḫalii̯a kuit ēšḫar EGIR-an šanḫat[teni (KUB 14.14 rev. 9, ritual against the pest, NH/NS) O gods, my lords! Why are you still avenging the blood of Tudḫaliya? (NB: Tudḫaliya is already dead)

nu⸗kan uu̯atten DINGIR.M[EŠ EN.MEŠ⸗YA] apūn AWAT mTudḫalii̯a TUR-RI ANA ABI⸗YA kinun appezz[ii̯az] anda šanḫatten (KUB 14.14 obv. 32–34, Plague prayer of Muršiliš II, NH) You came, O god[s, my lords], and now at last avenged that affair of Tudḫal-iya the Younger on my father

An interpretation of pret. šanḫer, šanḫt(a) vs. pres. šanḫat[teni, šanḫatten with particle and/or adverb in the passages above as ‘sought reparation’ (or ‘revenge’, sc. ‘of the blood’ of Piseniš, Zidanta or Tudḫaliya) is impossible, as all three are al-ready dead at the narration time. This construction of šanḫ- with ēšḫar is a phra-seological one, and totally different from those with akk/ggatar ‘death’ or ḫinkan ‘id.’ (of the enemy), i.e. ‘to seek/plan the enemy’s death’.8

8 For instance, KUB 33.106 iii 33–4 (Ullikummi, OH) nu dKumarbiš ārušuu̯aru⸗pat kuit

149On the prehistory of legal language and procedure

In conclusion, in the construction with adverbs (anda, EGIR-an  : appan) and/or telicizing particles (-apa, perhaps anda … -kan in Neo-Hittite), šanḫ- is lexicalized as a telic pret. ‘avenged’, as the expression of the full achievement of [make good – misdeed]. This is not invalidated by a unique instance of šanḫ- ‘to avenge’ without a local particle, namely impv. šanḫa ‘avenge!’ (KBo 3.23 i 19 zig⸗a SAG.GÉME.ÌR.MEŠ ēšḫar⸗šemit šanḫa “avenge the blood of (your) sub-jects!”), which displays the transitive semantics of imperative and directive ex-pressions.9 The telicizing adverbs and particles,10 attested mostly with preterital forms (3sg. šanḫt(a), pl. šanḫir …) with ēšḫar ‘blood’, AWAT [: uttar] ‘affair’, undo the imperfective force of Hitt. šanḫ- ‘to seek’, actually a lexicalization of the PIE present stem *sn̥-n-h₂- ‘is seeking, trying to reach’ of *senh₂- ‘to reach, attain’,11 which displays the inherited telic character of the verb. In contrast, šanḫ- without particle means ‘to seek, search for’, as attested in other collocations (section 5).

5 Hitt. šanḫ-mi ‘to seek misdeed (: reparation)’

The collocation (3) [offended – seek – misdeed], meaning ‘to exact the repa-ration’ for a misdeed or grievance the offended has suffered is expressed by means of (3a) šanḫ- ‘to seek’ (the common sense of the verb proper)12 with kattau̯ātar ‘ground for retaliation’, also in the periphrasis with šarnikzel ‘compensation’, and (3b) some nominal(ized) appellatives or names formed from šark- (not šarnink-, i.e. the non-infixed variant of the same lexeme (section 6). Two instances of (3a):

dU-ni IGI-anda aggatar šanḫeškizzi “… Kumarbi really seeks the death of the storm god”, KUB 14.1 obv. 2 (Madduwatta, MH/MS) nu tuēl ŠA mMa[dduu̯]att[a ḪUL-lu] ḫinkan šanḫiskit “he (sc. Attarišiya) has always sought your death, Ma[dduwa]tta”.

9 Among others with verbs of visual perception, with 2sg. impv. ‘look!’ (with subject as $agent: Hitt. a-ú, Toch. B pālka, Gk. ἰδέ, Welsh gwel) of lexemes for ‘to see’ (with subject $as experiencer: Hitt. au-/u-ḫḫi, Toch. B pälk-, IE *u̯ei̯d-, *u̯el-, respectively).

10 Craig Melchert (p.c.) points out to me the ‘telicizing’ effect of particles in some atelic lexemes, e.g. š⸗an⸗ap adanzi ‘they eat up’ (of alleged cannibals eating a fat person) or the standard expression anda uemii̯azzi ‘reaches’ (: u̯emii̯a-mi ‘to meet’) in the Maṣat letters (MH), cf. maḫḫan⸗ta kāš tuppianza anda uemii̯azzi “when this tablet reaches you …” (HKM 14: 3–5 et al.).

11 García Ramón (2002: 131–133, 2020: 164–166). 12 Hitt. šanḫ- (without an adverb or particle) means ‘to seek’, not ‘to avenge’, also in oth-

er collocations, e.g. in the myths of disappearing deities, which are not found (CHD Š-164.1a), cf. VBoT 58 I 21–22 pāer dUTU-un šanḫeškanzi n⸗an UL u̯emii̯anzi “they went (and) searched for the Sungod everywhere, (but) they [did] not find him” (OH/NS).

nu⸗za apāš kattau̯ātar šanaḫzi nu apūn UKÙ-an ANA LUGAL innarā kunanna pāi (KUB 13.7 i 17–18) he seeks the complaint for retaliation and delivers that person to the king explicitly to be killed

Hitt. kattau̯ātar šanḫ-, which has a counterpart in the collocations (1) and (2) with kattau̯ātar šarnink- (see above), is equivalent to, or even mirrors, the Akka-dian phraseme gimilan [a]na turri ‘to exact retribution, take revenge’. The collo-cation coexists with the periphrastic expression šarnikzel šanḫ-:

nu mān LIM apadda šer šarnikzel UL kuitki šanḫta (KUB 22.70 rev. 7) and if you, O god, have sought no compensation on that account

6 Hitt.-Luv. šark-: human plaintiffs and vengeful demons

A few nominal forms of different types formed from šark- (obviously the root un-derlying infixed šarni(n)k-, regardless of how the semantics of the variants with-out and with -n(in)- works) do reflect the reading (3) ‘to seek, exact’ (sc. repara-tion). Their referents are both human beings (plaintiffs in the court) and vengeful deities (all Hittito-Luvian):

1 Luvoid šarkant(i)-, in the instructions for the Royal Bodyguards (MH/MS; IBoT I 36, eds. Guterbock & van den Hout 1991), where it occurs repeatedly, refers to participants in a process in the king’s justice court. Their precise status remains a matter of discussion,13 but an interpretation of šarkant(i)- as ‘plain-tiff ’ (“petitioner, person seeking redress”, Melchert 1996: 135), i.e. as connected with šarni(n)k-,14 fits perfectly into the contexts where the term appears, e.g.

m[ā]n šarkatīš⸗ma arta ANALÚMEŠEDI⸗ma našma ANA DUMU.É.GAL [DĪ]NU n⸗aš⸗kan šarkantīn peran arḫa UL paizzi (IBoT 1.36 iii 31–34) If a petitioner is standing there, but the case is against a guard or palace servant, he does not pass in front of the petitioner (CHD s.v.)15

Hitt. šarkant(i)- reflects the lexicalization as ‘plaintiff, demandant’ of an -(a) nt-participle šarkant- ‘the one who exacts (: seeks to obtain) restitution’16 (i.e. with inflection as an -i-stem, as is the rule in the adaptation of Luvian for-mations), and surely refers to the offended, not to the offender.17 In Luvian,

-ant-participles had become unproductive18 and their inflection as -i- stems is due to a misunderstanding and erroneous reinterpretation of forms with i-motion.19

tuma(n)tim(m)a/i- ‘reputed’) is compatible with the character of the sun- goddess.

3 Luv. *šarkiu̯ali- ‘vengeful, seeking retribution’ (from OH?/MS†) occurs as an epithet of dU.GUR-aš ‘Nergal’ (KUB 35.108(+)35.87 iv 14*) and of the nak-kiu-demons (šarkiu̯alieš nakkiu̯eš ‘vengeful spirits of the dead’):

n⸗ašta a]nda šarkiu̯aliaš [nakkiui̯]aš kištanunu[n] (KUB 17.15 iii 4–5 [conj. NS] = StBoT 30: 233) I extinguished the vengeful spirits of the dead

The term is of Luvian origin, adapted as Hittite (cf. karpiu̯āla- ‘furious’ : kar-pi- ‘fury’), and the character of its referents speaks in favor of a sense ‘seeking revenge’ and of a connection with šarkant(i)-, Luv. 𒀹šargašamma/i-.21

4 ?*(𒀹)šargatti- ‘retribution, redress’ (NH†: 2× nom.sg. šar-qa-za in the oracle question KUB 52.34 obv. 5.9) may be recognised as a derivative of šark-:

DINGIR.ME-aš (or .MEŠ!) šarqaza NU.ŠE-du (KUB 52.34 obv. 5 = obv. 9) (If it is) the retribution(?) / anger (?) of the gods (or: … due to the retribu-tion …) let the oracle be unfavorable

The term may be Luvian and adapted as Hitt. šar-qa-za (as a noun in -att- of the type anii̯att- ‘performance’), but also genuinely Hittite (Melchert, DCL: 241; CHD Š- s.v.). It is clear that (𒀹)šargatti- is something unfavorable on the part of the gods, but it is impossible to decide between ‘retribution, redress’ and ‘arousal, anger’.

In conclusion: Luvoid šarkant(i)- ‘petitioner, (the one) who seeks redress’, CLuv. šargašamma/i- ‘vengeful’ and *šarkiu̯ali- ‘id.’, as well as ?*(𒀹)sargatti- ‘retribution, redress’, reflect the collocation (3) [offended – seek – misdeed] (without men-tion of the object) and point to a base form *šark-, which is surely the same as the one which underlies šarnink-mi (and šarnikzil- ‘compensation’).

153On the prehistory of legal language and procedure

7 Summing up: the Anatolian evidence

The collocations (1) [offender  – make good  – misdeed] and (2) [offend-ed – make good – misdeed] and (3) [offended – seek – misdeed] in Hittite have misdeed as the only object (nakkuš-, kattau̯ātar-, ēšḫar-) and the position of verbal predicate is filled by šarni(n)k- ‘to repair’ and šanḫ- ‘to seek’. The seman-tics of both verbs, namely šarni(n)k- (1b) ‘to expiate’ and šanḫ- (2b) ‘to avenge’, is modified by adverbs and telicizing particles. On the other hand, ‘to seek redress’ is expressed by some appellatives formed from šark-. It must be stressed that the collocation [offender – pay – misdeed], with a specific verb meaning ‘to pay’, ‘to atone’ (*kʷei̯- and synonyms) and misdeed (not reparation!) as object, $which is well-attested in the other IE languages (type Gk. φόνον τίνειν/τεῖσαι), is $fully absent from the Hittite texts, where pai-ḫḫi is not attested with misdeed as object: this is a striking difference between Hittite and Core IE which turns out to be crucial from the chronological point of view.

Beside each of the basic collocations there is evidence for a periphrastic ex-pression with šarnikzil- ‘reparation’ (with genitive of the misdeed) as object and a different verb for each of the three basic collocations, namely pai-ḫḫi ‘to give’ (also used for ‘to pay’ in Hittite)22 for (1) , dā-ḫḫi (: ME-) ‘to take’ for (2), and šanḫ- ‘to seek’ for (3). The periphrastic expressions šarnikzil pai-ḫḫi, šarnikzil dā-ḫḫi, $šarnikzil šanḫ-, which imply the transformation [repair – misdeed] → [repa-$ration – of misdeed], may be understood as secondary even if they are already attested in Hittite.

The semantics of the three basic collocations is unevenly represented in the Core IE languages. On the one hand, (1a) and (1b) and (2a) and (2b) live on, to varying degrees and expressed mostly by synonyms, in other languages, es-pecially in Latin (section 11), where, moreover, the PIE roots of sarciō, -īre and noxia are the same as those of Hitt. šarni(n)k- and nakkuš-, respectively. However, the conceptualization of reparation as [repair – misdeed] stands in sharp con-trast with the conceptualization as [pay – misdeed] in these languages, which is well-attested, especially in Greek and, to a lesser extent, in Indo- Iranian as well as in other traditions, albeit only in residual forms. On the other hand, the colloca-tions (3a) and (3b) [seek – misdeed] live on in the Core IE languages in the same form as in Anatolian, albeit expressed by lexemes which mostly differ from one tradition to the other: they do not allow to recognize a contrast between Hittite and the oldest Core IE languages.

22 Like Hitt. kuššani̯a-mi ‘to hire’, as well as Toch. ai- ‘give’.

154 José Luis García Ramón

In what follows, special attention will be paid to the conceptualization of [re-pair – misdeed] as [pay – misdeed] in the collocations (1) and (2) in the oldest Core IE languages, i.e. those which allow to ascertain striking differences with Hittite – and ultimately to propose a chronological sequence. In contrast, the con-tinuity of the collocations that are not specific to Hittite and do not allow to rec-ognize any relevant difference of conceptualization as against Core IE languages, are of no consequence for the reconstruction of chronological phases within IE reconstruction: this is the case for the periphrasis with reparation and give/ take/seek, as the variants of the collocations (1) (2) and (3) with misdeed as object (section 8), and for the collocation (3) [seek – misdeed] (section 9). They may be left out of a detailed consideration, but a short review of the essentials of both may be in order at this point.

8 Periphrastic constructions: continuity and formal renewal in Core IE languages

The periphrastic constructions with [reparation (šarnikzil-) – of misdeed] as their nominal constituent (instead of misdeed) and a verb ‘give’ or ‘pay’, ‘take’, or ‘seek’ have been mentioned above (sections 3–5) as alternatives to the collocations with [repair  – misdeed] and [seek  – misdeed], which actually express the same state of affairs, although their structure is different. Periphrastic (1) [give – reparation  – of misdeed], (2) [take  – reparation– of misdeed], as well as (3) [seek – reparation – of misdeed] rely on the transformation [repair – $misdeed] → [reparation – of misdeed], i.e. are secondary with respect to the $basic collocations (1) and (2) [repair – misdeed], (3) [seek – misdeed], but they are attested already in Hittite, and may thus be traced back to Proto- Indo- European as well. On the other hand, they live on in all other languages, in which their constituents are expressed by different lexemes: reparation is expressed by different terms, equivalents to Hitt. šarnikzil-, reflecting different conceptual-$izations of reparation, among others ‘penalty, punishment’ (Gk. ποινή [: Lat. poena], ζημία, θωιή; OIr. dígal; ON geldr) or ‘fine, reparation’ (ON bót ‘pecuniary $compensation’, skuld : OE scyld, Germ. Schuld ‘debt, payment due’; Toch. B pkelñe ‘requital, amends’ [*‘ripening, cooking’, cf. IE *pekʷ-]), ‘expiation, atonement’ $(OAv. kaēnā-, YAv. ciθā- ‘penance, atonement, ciθāi- ‘expiation’; Lat. piāculum : U. $pihaclo- ‘propitiatory sacrifice’, also ‘punishment’) and, last but not least, ‘adjust-ment’ (Ved. r̥ṇá- ‘duty, debt’, YAv. arəna-* ‘misdeed’: *Hr̥-ná-, *Hár-na- originally

155On the prehistory of legal language and procedure

$*‘adjustment’;23 cf. the semantic parallel δίκη ‘penalty’ from ‘justice, right’). The $continuity of the three periphrastic constructions attested in Hittite in Core IE languages may be shortly exemplified as follows:

Ad (1) [give  – reparation  – of misdeed] (type mān ēšḫanašš⸗a kuiški šarnikzil pii̯an ḫarzi ‘and if somebody has also given compensation for mur-$der …’, section 3): ποινὴν τείσειν Ξέρξῃ τῶν κηρύκων τῶν ἀπολομένων “to pay satisfaction to Xerxes for the death of the heralds” (Ηdt. 7.134.2), οὐδὲ … ἔδοσάν σφι δίκας τῆς ἁρπαγῆς “and did not give them reparation for the rape” $(Hdt. 1.2.3); mi calido dabis sanguine poenas “you will give me reparation with your warm blood” (Enn. Ann. 1.95).

Ad (2) [take – reparation – of misdeed] (type dUTU-ŠI⸗i̯a⸗z parkunuzzi šarnikzela (var. [šarni]kzelḪI.A) SA È-TI ME-anzi “his Majesty will also puri-fy himself and they will take (ME-anzi) the compensation for (his) house”, section 4): cáyamānā r̥ṇā́ni “making pay compensation” (sc. Ādityas: RV II 27.4), r̥ṇa-cít : YAv. arənat̰-caēša- ‘who makes pay reparation’ (cf. section 15); $ἀπετείσατο ποινὴν … ἑτάρων “he made (the Cyclops) pay for his companions” $(Od. 23.312).

Ad (3) [seek  – reparation  – of misdeed] (type nu mān  … apadda šer šarnikzel UL kuitki šanḫta “and if you … have sought no compensation on that account”, section 5): Ved. r̥ṇa-yā́- ‘the one who demands reparation (: punish-$ment)’; αἰτέειν δίκας τοῦ Λεωνίδεω φόνου “… seek reparation for the murder $of Leonidas” (Hdt. 8.114.2); piacula exegit “reclamed reparation” (Liv. 29.18.18), quos illi … poenas ob nostra reposcent effugia “… they will demand due pun-ishment for my flight” (Verg. Aen. 2.139).

To conclude, the periphrastic constructions with reparation as constituent must be kept apart from the original collocations (1) (2) (3), the constituent of which is crucially misdeed, not reparation.

9 ‘To seek reparation’, ‘to revenge’, ‘to punish’: continuity and formal renewal in Core IE languages

The collocation (3) [offended – seek – another one’s misdeed], with misdeed (i.e. ‘offence’, ‘grievance’, ‘blood’ for ‘death’) as nominal component (e.g. KUB 13.7 i 17–18 nu⸗za apāš kattau̯ātar šanaḫzi “he seeks the (complaint for) retaliation”) is, however, scarcely attested in Core IE languages. In contrast, the periphrasis with [seek – reparation (šarnikzel-, also ‘revenge’, ‘compensation’)], as in KUB 22.70 rev.7 nu mān … apadda šer šarnikzel UL kuitki šanḫta “and if you … have sought no compensation on that account”, which expresses the same state of affairs, is commonly used.

Verbs with a meaning similar to šanḫ-, namely ‘to seek, exact, attempt’ (also ‘to avenge’, ‘punish’ with telicizing particles), are formed from different lexemes in other languages, among them IE *prek̑- ‘to ask’ (Lat. posco, -ere ‘to demand’ and $OP fraθ ‘to punish’) and *i̯eh₂- ‘to seek, search’ (Ved. yā 2, Av. yā, Gk. ζᾱ-, ζη-, see $above), which have reflexes in more than one language. In lexemes of this type, $atelic ‘to exact, demand’, whence (→) ‘to research, inquire’, coexists with telic (or $telicized) ‘to avenge’, ‘to punish’, most probably as the result of semantic shifts with the result of a secondary polysemy under conditions which could be deter-mined only case by case.

The evidence for [(offended)  – seek  – misdeed] is still recognizable in the archaic Latin expression parricidi quaestores: Fest. 221M parrici<di> quae-stores appellabantur qui solebant creari causa rerum capitalium quaerendarum, i.e.

“… were called those who were created to investigate capital crimes” (: for capital affairs to be investigated).24 The official who bears the title parricidi quaestor (i.e. the one who obviously quaerit parricidium*, and quaerit res capitales*) holds ju-dicial inquiries of the crimes committed by a parricida, actually the murder of a relative,25 or a homicide (Fest. ibid. si quis hominem liberum dolo sciens morti duit, parricidas esto “if anyone gives to death a free man with deceit intentionally, let him be a parricide”), or a theft or financial fraud (Cic. Leg. 2.9.22 sacrum sacroue commendatum qui clepserit rapsitue, parricida esto “let anyone who has stolen, or taken by force a sacred thing or an object commended to a sacred place be a parricide”). As persuasively pointed out by Émile Benveniste, the term quaerere

Most. 1088 seruos … dare suos mihi quaestioni “give me his slaves for examination”).

10 The basic conceptualizations ‘to repair a misdeed’ (the offender) and ‘to make (the offended) repair a misdeed’ in Core IE languages

The collocations (1) [offender – repair – misdeed] and (2) offended – re-pair – misdeed], as stated for Hittite (sections 3–6), live on, to varying degrees, in the Core IE languages. Lexical matches are limited to Latin (sarcīre : šarni(n)k- ‘to repair’, noxia ‘damage, of noxa’  : nakkuš- ‘damage, harm’), but the phraseo-logical patterns are continued under the form of synonyms or quasi-synonyms, which may be considered as their substitutory continuants (Ersatzkontinuante). A somewhat arbitrary selection limited to Latin, Greek and Old English material,

11 The Latin evidence

The collocations of OLat. sarcīre ‘to repair, amend’ (sarcire est integrum facere Fest.)34 and re-sarcīre (Cato+), perfectly match those of šarni(n)k-, as noxiam sarcīre ‘to make amends for a damage’ and nakkuš šarni(n)k- shows: noxa ‘harm, damage’, noxia ‘damage, misdeed subject to reparation’ (*-i̯ā-derivative *‘related to noxa’)35 and Hitt. nakkuš- ‘damage’ are etymologically connected (PIE *nok̑-/ nek̑- ‘damage’),36 and the same applies to sarcīre (*sr̥k-i̯o/e-)37 and Hitt. šarni(n)k- (remodeled from *sr̥-n-ék/k-), Hitt. Luv. šark- (PIE *serk- ‘to make whole’).38 As

stressed by Calvert Watkins, the collocation stands in the framework of the nox-ales actiones, which have striking parallels in the Hittite procedure according to which a misdeed may be repaired by means of a reparation (Lat. sarcīre, Hitt. šarni(n)k-) or by delivering the offender to the offended for punishment (Lat. dē-dere , Hitt. šui-mi),39 as attested in Gell. 11.18.8 uoluerunt noxiamque ab his factam sarciri “decided that the damage done by them should be made good” (later Dig. $47.9.9.1, §11 aut noxiam sarcire iubetur), and in Pl. Lg. 936d ὁ τοῦ βλάψαντος δεσπότης ἢ τὴν βλάβην ἐξιάσθω μὴ ἐνδεῶς, ἢ τὸν βλάψαντ’ αὐτὸν παραδότω “let $the owner of the one who has injured either fully repair the damage or hand over the one who has himself injured …” (cf. section 12).

The precise correspondence between Hittite and Latin must be inherited, and its archaic, residual character is explicitly confirmed by Festus’ remark on the gradual replacement of the formula noxiam sarcīre by (fully equivalent) damnum soluere ‘to pay the damage’:40 Fest. p.322 Müll. noxiam sarcito, damnum soluito : sarcito in XII. Seruius Sulpicius ait significare damnum soluito, praestato. The gloss indirectly proves that the conceptualization of reparation as ‘to pay’ belongs to a later chronological layer than that expressed by sarcīre (and Hitt. šarni(n)k-), namely ‘to repair, amend’, and not vice versa.

Other instances of sarcīre (and resarcīre) with damnum, detrimentum, infa-miam, iniuriam as object outside the context of noxales actiones speak for them-selves:

1 with offender as the agent:

nulla dubitatio relinquetur quin honore mortui quam uiuo iniuriam fecimus sarciamus (Cic. Phil. 9.4.8) no doubt will remain that we should repair the offence that we made to him when he was alive now that he is dead with honor

Specifically characteristic for ‘to avenge’ (sc. the offended, like Hitt. šanḫ- with telicizing particle, section 4) is the use of synonymous uindicō, -āre ‘avenge, re-venge’, also lexicalized as ‘punish’ (with dolus malus ‘bad treachery’, facinus, nex ‘slaughter’, ‘offense’ et sim.), e.g. Ov. fast. 6.468 quique necem Crassi uindicet ultor erit “there will be an avenger who shall exact punishment for the slaughter of Crassus”.41

13 Evidence from Ancient Germanic languages

$Οld Εnglish bētan ‘to make better, amend, repair’, ge-bētan ‘id.’ (Goth. botjan “ὠφελεῖν”, ON bæta (bót) ‘to repair’, OHG buozzen, Germ. büssen), with deriva-$tive bōt ‘redressing, compensation’, and with synn ‘sin’ and ealle þing ‘all things (sc. all offences)’ as object, reflects the inherited collocation [make good – mis-deed], with the same semantics as attested in Latin and Greek above (sections 11–12):45

þonne sceolan we mid ure anre saule forgyldan & gebetan ealle þa þing þe we ær ofor his bebod gedydon (Blickling Homilies 7, Morris 1874–1880: I 91) when we must with our souls alone make recompense and amends for all things that we have previously done against his commands (tr. Morris)

Cf. also for bōte his synna “for a redressing of his sins” (Bede de Natura Rerum 4.25).

A collocation [make good – misdeed] may be assumed also for ON bæta (bót) ‘to repair, amend’, also ‘redress, adjust a wrong’, in the specific sense ‘to make good a wrong inflicted’ (with or without yfir, and with the offended introduced by við), cf.

hefir þú yfir bætt við mik um þetta bráðræði (Saga Ólafs konúngs Tryggvaso-nar 159) you would thus compensate me for your rash resolve (tr. Sephton)

On the other hand, the legal sense ‘to pay weregild’ of ON bæta (also the expres-sion bæta baugum ‘to pay weregild’, Eb. 174) may reflect a collocation [repair (bæta) – manACC – with compensationDAT] (texts from Cleasby & Vigfusson 1874, s.v.):

Hrafnkell bætti engan mann fé (Hrafnkels saga 4) Hrafnkell paid no weregild whomsoever he slew

Styrr vá mörg víg, en bætti engin (Eyrbyggja Saga 54) Styrr slew many men, but paid for none

45 I owe these references to Riccardo Ginevra (p.c.).

166 José Luis García Ramón

The same collocation may underlie the derivative bót (pl. bætr) ‘redress, remedy’ (sc. for health), also ‘fine, pecuniary compensation’, as attested in the compound vígs-bætr ‘compensation for manslaughter’ (Riccardo Ginevra, p.c.).

In conclusion, the unmistakable evidence for the collocation [make good – misdeed] in a (forcedly limited) selection of Core Indo- European languages (sec-tions 11–13) strongly suggests that further research may enlarge the list of phrase-ological patterns which reflect this conceptualization in different traditions.

14 Vedic ‘to make pay/atone (med. cáy-a-te) the misdeed’, Latin ‘to pay (luere, soluere) the misdeed’

The conceptualization of the reparation of a misdeed in the collocations with [make good] (1) and (2) in Hittite (sections 3–4) and in some Core IE languag-es (sections 11–13) stands in opposition to that with [pay] (IE *kʷei̯- ‘to pay’, ‘to atone’), i.e. (1) [offender – pay – misdeed] and (2) [offended – make pay (also ‘punish, avenge’) – misdeed] respectively, which are well attested in Avestan and especially in Greek (in terms of diathetic opposition, see below, section 15), as well as in Vedic (only med. cáya-te ‘to punish, avenge’) and in a series of residual forms (from *kʷei̯- or from synonyms, e.g. Lat. luere, soluere) in other Core IE languages. The fact that in some languages there is evidence only for (1) [offender – pay – misdeed] (e.g. Latin) or, less frequently, only for (2) [offended – pay – misdeed] (e.g. Vedic) may be traced back to an earlier stage of development, previous to the diathetic opposition between active ‘to pay, atone’ vs. causative middle ‘to make pay, atone’ (as consistently attested and developed in Greek and, less consistently, in Avestan, i.e. as a specific development of both branches), rather than be under-stood in terms of impoverishment of a complex opposition system we can assume for Core IE. Let us shortly recall the evidence from the two languages where only one of the collocations is attested, namely Vedic and Latin.

Ved. cáy-a-te ‘to punish, avenge’46 (media tantum, which has no active coun-terpart †cáy-a-ti), reflects the lexicalization of causative *‘to make pay/atone’, cf.

ná dūḍhyè ánu dadāsi vāmám bŕ̥haspate cáyasa ít píyārum (RV I 190.5cd) to the evil-minded one you do not concede anything of value; you just pun-ish (: make pay) the reviler, Br̥haspati

46 Cf. Gotō (1987: 132–133); Covini (2017: 225–240).

15 Sonderfall Avestan and Greek: ‘to pay/atone the misdeed’ (active *kʷei̯-) vs ‘to make pay/atone the misdeed’ (middle *kʷei̯-)

A special position is that of Avestan and, especially, of Greek, where the pair (1)  [pay  – misdeed] vs. (2) causative [make pay  – misdeed] is expressed by reflexes of IE *kʷei̯- in terms of voice opposition.

15.1 The Avestan evidence

In Avestan the opposition is residually attested, also in terms of different verbal stems, namely (1) cikaiia-ti ‘to pay, repare’ (sc. the misdoer) as against (2) kaiia-iia-te ‘to punish’ (*to make pay’, sc. the offended, like Ved. cáy-a-te):

1 cikaiia-ti

$cikaiiat̰ sūnahe raēšō baoδō.varštahe ciθaiia (Vd. 13.10ij) “il expiera le tort (raēšah-) fait au chien par la peine du baoδō.varšta” (Kellens $1984: 56; cf. also Vd. 7.38, 15.22 et al.)

2 kaiiaiia-te

vīsaiti upāzananąm pairi ākaiiaiiaṇta (Yt. 10.122g) “qu’ils s’imposent d’expier par une vingtaine de pénitences” (Kellens 1984: 56; $also 122c θrisətam ‘thirty’) $

The hapax YAv. arənat̰.caēša- (Yt. 10.35gf), originally ‘who makes pay a repara-tion/something to be reparated’, matches Ved. r̥ṇa-cít- formally. On the other hand, the semantics of obscure YAv. °caēša- surely reflects that of (2) kaiiaiia-te ‘to punish (: make pay)’:49

$arənat̰.caēṣ̌əm viṇdat̰.spāδəm hazaŋra.yaoxštīm xṣ̌aiiaṇtəm (Yt. 10.35gf) $punisher of misdeed (:  that which is to be adjusted), the levier of armies, whose perception is thousandful, who rules as an all-knowing potentate … (“punisher of guilt” Gershevitch 1959: 186–188).

49 Also “Schuld-antreiber” (Wolf), “Schuld rächend” (Klingenschmitt 1980: 143 = Aufsätze 187). The alleged form *caēšəmnō- (Yt. 19.93ef) is to be read as †jaēšəmnō “(als er) im Begriff war, … zu besiegen” (Hintze 1994: 375, 377–379).

15.2 The Greek evidence

In Greek the expression in terms of voice opposition of (1) [offender – pay – $misdeed] (τίνo/ε-, aor. τεῖσαι ‘to pay, atone’, also ἀπο°, ἐκ°, like Av. cikaiia-ti) and (2) [offended – make pay – misdeed] (τίνεσθαι, aor. τείσασθαι ‘to make pay, $avenge’, like Ved. cáya-te, YAv. kaiiaiia-te) is evident since Homer. This is well-at-$tested in minimal pairs with objects like λώβην ‘outrage’ and, especially, φόνον $‘murder’, which is also attested as object of verbs meaning [make good, repair] in Greek and in other languages (e.g. Lat. nex ‘slaughter’).50 Some minimal pairs may illustrate this, e.g.

Τεισιφόνειoς, Pherai, aet.hellen.) and may be assumed for the MN Τεισάμενoς $(Hdt.+, inscriptions) and, most probably, for Myc. qe-ja-me-no /kʷeiamenos/ ‘having taken/received a reparation’ (from *kʷei̯-sa-meno-), after the MN o-pe-to-re-u /Opʰeltorēus/ (PY Ep 704.1 o-pe-to-re-u  , qe-ja-me-no  …): the sense of qe-ja-me-no is confirmed by the explicit indication, exactly in the same position, in PY Ea 805 (H.43): o-pe-te-re-u , e-ne-ka , a-no-qa-si-ja /⁽ʰ⁾eneka anr̥kʷʰasiās/

We can therefore conclude that the conceptualization of ‘repair a misdeed’ as [pay – misdeed] (sc. the offender) as well as [make pay – misdeed] (sc. the offended), may be assumed for Core Indo- European, regardless of the lexemes by means of which it is expressed, and to what extent in the different daughter languages. A series of nominal derivatives of *kʷei̯- ‘to pay, atone’, with different lexicalizations, may be understood as remnants, often isolated disiecta membra of $the earlier situation, among others: ποινή ‘fine’ (cf. the figura etymologica ποινὰς τεῖσαι ‘to pay a fine’, Pi., Hdt.+) and Lat. poena, OAv. kaēnā- ‘atonement’ (Y. 30.8a), YAv. ciθā- ‘punition’, ciθāi- ‘expiation’, also YAv. kaēnan- ‘avenger’ (Yt. 9.18, 15.28), $MIr. cin ‘guilt, payment due’, also ‘crime’.53 The coexistence in several Core IE

171On the prehistory of legal language and procedure

languages of the conceptualization as [pay – misdeed] with collocations which rely on [make good – misdeed] (sections 11–13) and, especially, the fact that in Hittite [pay – misdeed] is not attested (the periphrasis šarnikzil dai-ḫḫi is a differ-ent construction) strongly support the assumption that it was first created in Core Indo- European, and that the conceptualization as [make good – misdeed] may be traced back to Proto- Indo- European.

16 Conclusion

The reparation of a misdeed in its twofold dimension, namely by the misdoer and by the one who has suffered it, is conceptualized in two different ways, namely [make good – misdeed], which is regular in Hittite and is sporadically attested also in some Core IE languages (especially in Latin) and [pay (atone)  – mis-deed], which occurs only in Core IE languages. These conceptualizations dif-fer obviously as to the action of repairing, but share the object [misdeed]: both are expressed in most cases by means of different lexemes and collocations, with the exception of Hitt. nakkuš šarni(n)k- (hapax) and OLat. noxiam sarcīre for ‘to mend the damage’, which constitute a striking, albeit not formally exact, lexical and phraseological correspondence.

The conceptualization as ‘to make good (actually ‘to make whole’) the mis-deed’, both by the misdoer (who ‘repairs’, or ‘expiates’, his misdeed) and the of-fended (who ‘makes repair’, or ‘avenges’, the misdeed made by another) is the only one attested in Hittite, and is expressed by means of a limited series of verbs (šarni(n)k- ‘to make good’, also, with telicizing particles, ‘to expiate’, and šanḫ- ‘to avenge’) and appellatives for ‘misdeed’ (nakkuš-, kattau̯ātar ‘object of revenge’, ēšḫar ‘blood’). The conceptualization is still attested in Old Latin as noxiam sarcīre, an expression in the framework of the actiones noxales (as shown by Calvert Wat-kins, cf. section 11) which, as pointed out by Festus, has been replaced by poenam soluere ‘to pay the damage’, and lives on, limited to the reparation by the misdoer, $in Greek (βλάβην ἐξιᾶσθαι ‘to heal, cure the damage thoroughly’) and Germanic $languages (e.g. OE betan ‘to make better’), among others.

The conceptualization of ‘to repair the misdeed’ as ‘to pay, atone’ (*kʷei̯-) it (sc. the misdoer) is well attested in Avestan and in Greek, as well as, expressed by means of different lexemes in Latin (luere, soluere) and in other Core IE languages. On the other hand, the reparation of the misdeed by the offended is conceptual-ized in Indo- Iranian and in Greek as ‘to make pay, atone for’ (middle: Ved. cáya-te ‘to punish, avenge’), and specifically in terms of voice opposition in Avestan (YAv.

172 José Luis García Ramón

$cikaiia-ti ‘to pay, atone’ vs. kaiiaiia-te ‘to make pay’) and especially in Greek (τίνειν, τεῖσαι vs. τίνεσθαι, τείσασθαι), as shown by minimal pairs with λώβην ‘outrage’ or φόνον ‘murder’, and by other lexemes in Latin and other languages. The concep-$tualization of ‘to repair’ as ‘to pay, atone’ has left traces in a series of nominal de-$rivatives of *kʷei̯- ‘to pay’, such as ποινή ‘fine’ and Lat. poena, OAv. kaēnā- ‘atone-$ment’ or MIr. cin ‘payment due’, also ‘guilt, crime’ among others.

There is no sure evidence for the conceptualization of ‘to repair the misdeed’ as ‘to pay the misdeed’ (sc. the misdoer) and ‘to make pay the misdeed’ (sc. the offended) in Hittite, where only the collocations ‘to give (sc. pay) a reparation (šarnikzil- pai-ḫḫi) for the misdeed (gen.)’ and ‘to take a reparation (šarnikzil- dā-ḫḫi) for the misdeed’ are attested. This strongly speaks in favor of the existence of two chronological layers: ‘to repair the misdeed’ (regular in Hittite, residually attested in some Core IE traditions, especially in Latin) may be traced back to Proto Indo- European, whereas ‘to pay the misdeed’, well-attested in other daugh-ter languages (Vedic, Avestan and, especially, Greek) by means of reflexes of

*kʷei̯-, represents a specific Core-Indo- European development. A different case is that of the exacting of reparation by the victim of the mis-

deed. Its conceptualization is basically the same, albeit expressed by different terms, in all IE languages, namely as [seek – misdeed]: the collocation is, howev-er, only exceptionally attested (Hitt. kattau̯ātar šanḫ-, OLat. parricidi quaestores). The basic collocation has been, in fact, replaced by a periphrastic construction with ‘reparation’ (not ‘misdeed’) as the object: the construction is already attested in Hittite (šarnikzil šanḫ-) and is the norm in other languages (type Lat. poenas $petere, piacula exigere, Gk. δίκας αἰτέο/ε et al.). $

Indo- European patrons vs. clients, and the role of poets as social brokers

‘Leaders’ vs. ‘friends’, and intelligent speakers in the mythologies of Scandinavia, India, and Rome

Riccardo Ginevra Università Cattolica del Sacro Cuore, Milano 1

Structural and linguistic parallels between the Norse myth of Kvasir, the

Indic myths of Agastya Mānyá-, and the Roman legend of Agrippa Menēni-

us allow for the comparative reconstruction of an inherited IE myth, ac-

cording to which inTelligenT (*men-) speakers, i.e., poeTs, had the

role of social brokers (i.e., mediators) between paTrons (called *h₂ens-u-

‘leaders’) and their clienTs (called ‘friends/allies’).

Our reconstruction of the prehistory of Eurasia and of the development of the Indo- European (IE) language family has most recently been revolutionized by a series of important discoveries, most of which would not have been possible without an intensive cross-disciplinary collaboration between, on the one hand, scholars of historical linguistics and Indo- European studies and, on the other hand, researchers working in the fields of prehistoric archaeology and bio-archae-ology. This integrated approach has been quite fittingly referred to as ‘archaeolin-

1 This publication is part of the project “SunSHINE – The Sun-chariot’s Journey Towards the Nordic Sky: on the (Pre-)History of Ideas on Sky, Sun, and Sunlight in Northern Europe”, which has received funding from the European Union’s Horizon 2020 research and innovation programme under the Marie Skłodowska-Curie grant agreement no. 890522.

It is my great pleasure to thank the members of the Roots of Europe research group at the University of Copenhagen, where my project was based, for their support, especial-ly my project’s academic supervisor, Birgit Anette Olsen. For encouragement, discus-sion, and criticism, I am also grateful to Andrea Lorenzo Covini, Matthias Egeler, Dan-ielle Feller, Frog, José Luis García Ramón, Stefan Höfler, Daniel Kölligan, and Bruce Lincoln. Final responsibility remains my own.

The translations, unless otherwise specified, are adapted from Faulkes (1987, Gylfa-ginning), Jamison & Brereton (2014, Rigveda), and the Loeb Classical Library (Greek and Latin sources).

178 Riccardo Ginevra

guistics’ (Iversen & Kroonen 2018) and has led to several important findings, not only concerning the prehistoric migrations of (most likely) IE-speaking nomadic pastoralist communities from the Pontic Steppe to West, Central, and South Eur-asia,2 but also regarding the social structures of these communities (Sjögren et al. 2020). The present contribution employs a closely related approach, which may be correspondingly referred to as ‘archaeopoetics’ (Ginevra 2024), and which combines the comparative analysis of poetic devices and mythological narratives attested in various IE traditions with the research data and interpretative models of prehistoric archaeology and related disciplines, such as cultural anthropology, with the objective of achieving an (archaeologically and anthropologically) more realistic reconstruction of the culture and society of the speakers of prehistoric IE linguistic varieties.

More precisely, the present paper considers textual, archaeological, and socio- anthropological data in a cross-disciplinary fashion to approach the prehistory of a social institution that is still very prominent in numerous human communities (Eisenstadt & Roniger 1984), namely ‘patron–client relationships’ (or ‘relations’; English patronage and clientelism are sometimes used to refer to the same phe-nomenon). Sociologists and anthropologists have defined a set of features that are cross-culturally common for such relations, among which the most relevant to this study are the following:

(a) Patron–client relations are usually particularistic and diffuse. (b) The interaction on which these relations are based is characterised by

the simultaneous exchange of different types of resources – above all, instrumental and economic as well as political ones (support, loyalty, votes, protection) on the one hand, and promises of reciprocity, soli-

darity and loyalty on the other. […] (e) [… A] strong element of interpersonal obligation […] is prevalent in

these relations – an element often couched in terms of personal loyalty

or reciprocity and attachment between patrons and clients – even if these relations are often very ambivalent. […]

(g) Despite their seemingly binding, long-range, almost (in their ideal por-trayal) life-long, endurance, patron–client relations are entered into, at

least in principle, voluntarily, and can, officially at least, be abandoned voluntarily.

2 On the so-called ‘IE Homeland’ problem, see Anthony (2007) and the overview in Olander (2019).

179Indo- European patrons vs. clients, and the role of poets as social brokers

(h) These relations are undertaken between individuals or networks of in-

dividuals in a vertical fashion (the simplest manifestation of which is a strong dyadic one) […].

(i) Last and not least patron–client relations are based on a very strong

element of inequality and of differences in power between patrons

and clients. […] (Eisenstadt & Roniger 1984: 48–49; emphasis added)

The clash between some of these characteristics causes various “paradoxical con-tradictions” to arise within patron–client relationships, including, e.g., “a rather peculiar combination of inequality and asymmetry in power with seeming mu-tual solidarity expressed in terms of personal identity and interpersonal senti-ments and obligations” and “a combination of potential coercion and exploitation with voluntary relations and mutual obligations” (Eisenstadt & Roniger 1984: 49). In other words, even though they are highly hierarchical, the power-structure of patron– client relationships is often combined with an ideology that stresses moral values of friendship and alliance between the two parties; moreover, even though clients willingly enter relations of mutual obligation with patrons, this choice may also later lead to their potential exploitation by the latter and to sharp tensions that may even threaten the relationship itself.

Typologically, patron–client relations are especially “common among chief-doms, societies with institutionalized differences in prestige and power, where some clans or lineages claim a right of patronage over others, usually on grounds of holiness or historical priority in a given territory” (Anthony 2007: 99). Of course, among historically attested Indo- European traditions, patron–client re-lationships most famously occurred within the clan-based society of Ancient Rome (cf. Eisenstadt & Roniger 1984: 52–64), where, to put it most briefly, “[t]he patronus was the benefactor of the cliens, who in his turn was expected to offer his services to the patronus” (Jackson 2016: 171 n. 3). Patron–client relationships have also been reconstructed by linguists and archaeologists as a fundamental feature of the prehistoric chiefdom society of the earliest IE speakers in the Pontic Steppe, where such relationships “regulated the reciprocal obligations between the strong and the weak” (Anthony 2007: 461). This ancient institution may be most synthetically defined as a “way of legitimizing inequality”, as in the follow-ing exemplary quotation:

Proto- Indo- European institutions included a belief in the sanctity of ver-bal contracts bound by oaths (*h₁óitos), and in the obligation of patrons (or

180 Riccardo Ginevra

gods) to protect clients (or humans) in return for loyalty and service. […] In Proto- Indo- European religion generally the chasm between gods and hu-mans was bridged by the sanctity of oath-bound contracts and reciprocal

obligations, so these were undoubtedly important tools regulating the

daily behavior of the powerful toward the weak, at least for people who belonged under the social umbrella. Patron–client systems like this could incorporate outsiders as clients who enjoyed rights and protection. This way of legitimizing inequality probably was an old part of steppe social

institutions, going back to the initial appearance of differences in wealth when domesticated animals were accepted. (Anthony 2007: 342; emphasis added)

Given that patron–client relationships were both “an old part of steppe social in-stitutions” and a very important factor in the later expansion of IE languages (the incorporation of non-IE-speaking outsiders as clients of IE-speaking patrons was a likely cause for progressive language shift, cf. Anthony 2007: 117–120), it would be rather strange if this prominent socio-cultural item – well-attested in various historical IE traditions – did not find any counterparts in our comparative re-construction of prehistoric IE poetic and mythological heritage, especially if one shares Bruce Lincoln’s (1999: xii) view of “myth as ideology in narrative form”.3 The aim of this paper is thus to fill this gap in the research, by arguing for the reconstruction of an inherited IE mythological tradition dealing with the social tensions of patron–client relationships and with verbal art as the best instrument to keep them intact. This reconstruction will be based on a series of structural and linguistic parallels between various texts belonging to three distinct ancient IE traditions: the Norse myth of the Æsir–Vanir conflict and the birth of Kvasir (section 1); the Indic myths of the birth of Agastya Mānya and his mediation in

3 Original emphasis; cf. ibid.: 147ff and passim. As is well known, Lincoln’s more recent work (roughly from Lincoln 1999 to Lincoln 2018) has been highly critical (not infre-quently with good reason) of the comparative reconstruction of IE mythology, even going so far as to reject its validity altogether: the latter view is obviously not compati-ble with the methodology and results presented in this contribution. The present study, however, has been influenced in some respects by Lincoln’s (2018) recent emphasis on “weak comparisons”, i.e., comparative analyses that “(a) focus on a relatively small number of comparanda that the researcher can study closely; (b) are equally attentive to relations of similarity and those of difference; (c) grant equal dignity and intelligence to all parties considered; and (d) are attentive to the social, historical, and political contexts and subtexts of religious and literary texts” (ibid.: 27).

181Indo- European patrons vs. clients, and the role of poets as social brokers

the Indra–Maruts quarrel (section 2); and the Roman story of Agrippa Menēni-us’s mediation in a dispute between Patricians and Plebeians (section 3). The data gathered from the comparative analysis of these narratives will then allow for the reconstruction of an IE myth (section 4) whose main actants may be identified as leaders (i.e., mythological counterparts to patrons), friends/allies (i.e., mythological counterparts to clients), and an intelligent speaker.4 Finally, in the conclusion (section 5), the latter character will be identified as a mythological reflex of a specific and highly important social role within early IE communities, namely that of the skilled professional of oral-traditional verbal art: the poet.

1 Scandinavia: Æsir, Vanir, and the birth and deeds of Kvasir

The first narrative analysed here is the Norse myth of the war between Æsir and Vanir (the two main tribes of gods according to Scandinavian mythology) and of the closely connected birth of the character named Kvasir, the most intelligent of all beings. This tradition is attested in several medieval texts composed in Old Norse: fragments occur already in the so-called Poetic Edda (e.g., Vǫluspá 24), but the plot of the myth is more extensively attested by the following passage of the Prose Edda (section Skáldskaparmál ‘Language of Poetry’), an Old Norse handbook of poetics and mythology written by Icelandic scholar Snorri Sturlu-son (1179–1241 ce).5 Elements that are particularly relevant to the present study are marked in bold here and in all following quotations.

And Ægir went on: “How did this craft that you call poetry originate?” Bragi replied: “The origin of it was that the gods had a dispute with the peo-ple called Vanir, and they appointed a peace-conference and made a truce by this procedure, that both sides went up to a vat and spat their spittle

into it. But when they dispersed, the gods kept this symbol of truce and de-cided not to let it be wasted, and out of it made a man. His name was Kva-

sir, he was so wise that no one could ask him any questions to which he

4 Within this paper, conceptual elements (like leaders, friend/allies, intelligent speaker) that are relevant to the comparative analysis of the narratives are conven-tionally marked with small capitals.

5 A quite different version of the Æsir–Vanir war (with no apparent connection to Kva-sir’s birth) is reported by Snorri himself in chapter four of Ynglingasaga ‘Saga of the Ynglingar’, which, in turn, is part of Heimskringla ‘Earth’s Orb’, a large compilation of sagas authored by the Icelandic scholar.

182 Riccardo Ginevra

did not know the answer. He travelled widely through the world teaching

people knowledge, and when he arrived as a guest to some dwarfs, Fialar and Galar, they called him to a private discussion with them and killed him. They poured his blood into two vats and a pot, and the latter was called Odrerir, but the vats were called Son and Bodn. They mixed honey with the blood and it turned into the mead whoever drinks from which becomes

a poet or scholar. The dwarfs told the Æsir that Kvasir had suffocated in

intelligence because there was no one there educated enough to be able to ask him questions. […] That is why we call poetry Kvasir’s blood or dwarfs’ drink […]”. (Skáldskaparmál G57; tr. Faulkes)6

As is well known, this myth has attracted the interest of a multitude of schol-ars, including Dumézil (e.g., 1941), who most notably analysed the Æsir–Vanir conflict as a dispute between deities of the first two functions (sovereignty and war) vs. deities of the third function (fertility), respectively.7 As is often the case with trifunctional analyses, the validity of this interpretation has been called into question, e.g., by Motz (1996: 103–124), who convincingly showed not only that this partition finds no support in the extant ON sources, but also that the texts rather seem to attest the opposite system of associations (Vanir–sovereignty vs. Æsir–fertility). Furthermore, some recent studies have been highly critical of the current communis opinio that Snorri’s division of the gods in Æsir and Vanir re-

6 Original text: Ok enn mælir Ægir: “Hvaðan af hefir hafizk sú íþrótt er þér kallið skáldskap?” Bragi svarar: “Þat váru upphǫf til þess at guðin hǫfðu ósætt við þat fólk er Vanir heita, en þeir lǫgðu með sér friðstefnu ok settu grið á þá lund at þeir gengu hvárirtveggju til eins kers ok spýttu í hráka sínum. En at skilnaði þá tóku goðin ok vildu eigi láta týnask þat griðamark ok skǫpuðu þar ór mann. Sá heitir Kvasir. Hann er svá vitr at engi spyrr hann þeira hluta er eigi kann hann órlausn. Hann fór víða um heim at kenna mǫnnum frœði, ok þá er hann kom at heimboði til dverga nokkvorra, Fjalars ok Galars, þá kǫlluðu þeir hann með sér á einmæli ok drápu hann, létu renna blóð hans í tvau ker ok einn ketil, ok heitir sá Óðreyrir, en kerin heita Són ok Boðn. Þeir blendu hunangi við blóðit ok varð þar af mjǫðr sá er hverr er af drekkr verðr skáld eða frœðamaðr. Dvergarnir sǫgðu Ásum at Kvasir hefði kafnat í mannviti fyrir því at engi var þar svá fróðr at spyrja kynni hann fróðleiks. […] Af þessu kǫllum vér skáldskap Kva-sis blóð eða dverga drekku […]”.

7 For a concise overview of Dumézil’s multiple publications on this topic, cf. Belier (1991: 192–193 and chapter six in general). Interestingly, Frank (1981) rather argues that this myth originated from Snorri’s misunderstanding of a kenning kvasis dreyri ‘ferment’s blood’ for ‘mead’; this is unnecessary, however, as shown by Males (2020), who con-cludes that “the evidence is sufficient to corroborate the fact that Snorri reported older lore about the mythical genesis of poetry” (ibid.: 159).

183Indo- European patrons vs. clients, and the role of poets as social brokers

flects actual pre-Christian Scandinavian religious beliefs (Simek 2005; Frog 2021). Without engaging further in this complex and ongoing discussion (which is not directly relevant to the scope of this study), the present investigation exclusively deals with the empirical identification of the following six elements in Snorri’s passage which are most relevant for our comparative analysis:

1 Kvasir is the male protagonist of this narrative. 2 He is born from two distinct social groups, the two main lineages of

gods within Norse mythology (at least as attested in Snorri’s works), namely: 2a The Æsir, referred to as ‘the gods’ (guðin) par excellence in our text.

They may be analysed as the group more closely associated with lead-ership and higher status (at least within Snorri’s Edda) for the fol-lowing reasons, among others. Firstly, the Norse supreme god Odin was a member of this group; in fact, he was both the leader of the Æsir (cf. his epitet Ása-konungr ‘king of Æsir’ in the Flateyarbók; Vigfússon & Unger 1860: 26) and the universal ‘patriarch’ (°fǫðr, on which see Ginevra 2020: 7–58).8 Secondly, the ON nom. pl. Æs-ir (sg. Ás-s) is a reflex of the Proto- Germanic noun *ans-u- ‘god; semi-divine ruler’ (cf. Latinized Gothic ans-es ‘semi-divine rulers’, Old English ōs ‘god’, et al.; Kroonen 2013: 30), which in turn reflects the strong stem of the PIE noun *h₂ens-u-/h₂n̥s-u- ‘lord’ (Watkins 1995: 8–9), whose weak stem h₂n̥s-u- is directly attested by Hittite ḫašš-u- ‘king’, but also indirectly by the Vedic derivative ásu-ra- ‘lord’ (Hale 1986; on this term, see sec-tion 2). Thus, ON Æsir most likely originally meant ‘lords’.

2b The Vanir, i.e., the other major clan of Norse gods according to Snorri’s Edda. Only three members of this group are known by name, namely the god Njǫrðr and his two children Freyr and Freyja. After the in-itial dispute mentioned in the passage quoted above, the Vanir be-come allies of the Æsir; this relationship is attested, e.g., by Snorri’s (Gylf. 51) account of the final battle at the End of Time (Ragnarǫk), in which Æsir and Vanir fight side by side against the beings called Jǫtnar. The latter term is often translated as ‘giants’, but it originated from a word meaning ‘eaters’ (PGmc *etuna-) and referred to mythological ‘members of the out-group, strangers’ (who can either be monstrous

8 On the analysis of ON °fǫðr, a frequent second element of epithets of Odin, as the reflex (originally meaning ‘patriarch’) of a PIE noun *ph₂tr-ou̯- ‘older relative on the father’s side’, cf. Ginevra (2020: 9–22).

184 Riccardo Ginevra

‘devourers’ or friendly ‘commensals’, as argued by Jackson 2014) in op-position to Æsir and Vanir, who must correspondingly be considered as members of the same in-group here. Given that Odin, leader of the Æsir, was the Al-fǫðr ‘patriarch of all’ (Ginevra 2020: 23–34), and thus also of the Vanir, the latter may be regarded to have lower status in comparison to the Æsir (cf., e.g., Lindow 2001: 311). The etymology of the term Vanir may support either of these two characterizations: according to one of the most widely accepted proposals, ON Vanir (sg. Vanr) may be analysed as a term somehow related to ON vinr ‘friend’ (Vries 1962, s.v. vanr) and thus connected to their function of allies of the Æsir; alternatively, it may be analysed as a substantivization of the ON adjective vanr ‘lacking’ (pl. vanir) and thus rather linked to their identity as gods of lower status.

The distribution of Æsir, Vanir, and Jǫtnar in the mythological social space may thus be represented as in Figure 1.

3 Kvasir is born from the saliva of Æsir and Vanir, collected and mixed in a vat. This peculiar detail has long been the object of various interpretations by scholars of Norse mythology, none of which has been accepted with any consensus.9

4 Kvasir’s birth is linked to the resolution of a conflict between Æsir

9 See for example Clunies Ross’ (1994: 216–218) interpretation as an instance of pseudo- procreative symbolism (on the latter, cf. ibid.: 150–152). On the cognitive mechanisms that underlie this myth, cf. further Quinn (2010) and Burrows (2019).
