185Indo- European patrons vs. clients, and the role of poets as social brokers

and Vanir, after which the two groups initiate a relationship based on inequality, in which one clan appears to be dominant (see above), but both parties have mutual obligations to one another (e.g., they ex-change hostages in Gylf. 23).

5 Kvasir is associated with intellectual power: he was “so wise that no one could ask him any questions to which he did not know the answer”; elsewhere he is said to be “wisest of all beings” (allra vitrastr in Gylf. 50).

6 He is closely associated with poetry, which originated from his blood and is thus called “Kvasir’s blood” (Kvasis blóð in our text; cf. Kvasis dreyra in Skáld. 3).

To sum up: the Norse myth analysed here features a male character who is born from the bodily fluids, collected and mixed together in a vessel, of a higher-status group referred to as ‘lords’ (reflecting PIE *h₂ens-u-) and of a lower-status group referred to as either ‘friends’ or ‘the lacking ones’. This character, closely associat-ed with both intellectual power and verbal art, is linked to the resolution of a con-flict between these two social groups, whose relationship is based on inequality and mutual obligations. These elements may be summarized as in Table 1.

In the following section, I will argue that these elements find a number of close parallels in the Indic myths of the seer Agastya Mānya.

Feature Represented by

1 Male character Kvasir

2 Born from both: a leaders of higher status Æsir (PIE *h₂ens-u- ‘lord’)

b friends/allies of lower status Vanir (cf. vinr ‘friend’ or vanr ‘lacking’)

3 born from 2a+2b’s bodily fluids collected in vessel Saliva collected in vat

4 Linked to resolution of conflict between 2a+2b Born as symbol of truce

5 Connection with concept mental power Wisest of all beings

6 Association with verbal art Kvasir’s blood = poetry

2 India: Varuṇa and Mitra, Indra and the Maruts, and the birth and deeds of Agastya Mānya

The Indic traditions discussed here are attested in several texts, composed in An-cient India from the 2nd millennium bce onwards (but put into writing much later), which deal with two distinct narratives involving the same mythological character, the supernatural seer (ŕ̥ṣi-) Agastya Mānya: firstly, the episode of his peculiar birth from the mixed seed of two male gods and, secondly, the story of his mediation in a conflict that once arose between the warrior god Indra and his followers, the Maruts.

Fragments of the myth of Agastya’s birth (on which see, e.g., Sieg 1902: 105– 108, Patton 1996: 266–270) are already attested in the Rigveda (RV, the most an-cient collection of Indic religious poetry):

The two [= Mitra and Varuṇa], brought into being at a (ritual) session, aroused by reverences, poured their common semen into a pot. From it

arose Māna [i.e., either Agastya himself or his father]10 from the middle. (RV 7.33.13abc)11

The whole plot, however, is more extensively attested in later texts, such as the following passage from the Br̥haddevatā (composed after the 1st century CE).12

A pair [dvandvam] was born of her [i.e., of Aditi] – Mitra and Varuṇa. Of these two Ādityas, having seen the nymph Urvaśī in the sacrificial session, the seed was spilled. That [seed] fell into a jar of water that stood over-night. Therefore, at that moment, virile ascetics came into being, the two r̥ṣis Agastya and Vasiṣṭha. The semen, having fallen in manifold ways – in a jar, in water, on the ground – the sage Vasiṣṭha, best of r̥ṣis, came into being on the ground; Agastya came into being in a jar, while Matsya of great brilliance, in water. Agastya of great glory, then arose, the measure of a stick (samya). Because of being measured with a measure, therefore he is here

10 Cf. Jamison (2020: ad loc., date of posting: 15 July 2020), Mayrhofer (2002: 70, with further references).

11 Original text: satré ha jātā́v iṣitā́ námobhiḥ / kumbhé rétaḥ siṣicatuḥ samānám / táto ha mā́na úd iyāya mádhyāt.

12 For an overview of the debate on the dating of the Br̥haddevatā, see Patton (1996: 465– 474).

187Indo- European patrons vs. clients, and the role of poets as social brokers

called Mānya. Or because the rṣ̥i was born from a jar, by a jar also measure-ment is made (Br̥haddevatā 5.148–154; tr. adapted from Patton 1996: 267).13

Some details of these two Indic passages have correspondences with the elements (1–3, 5) that occur in the Norse tradition as well:

1 Agastya Mānya is a male character. 2 He is born from two distinct male gods, who together form perhaps

the best-known divine ‘duo’ (dvandvam in the second passage) of Indic mythology, namely: 2a Varuṇa, one of the gods of highest status (“by the side of Indra, the

greatest of the gods of the RV”, as per Macdonell 1897: 22), closely asso-ciated with leadership: he is the deity who “in particular represents the authority of the king” and whose “divine acts […] were often re-flected in the functions of the R̥gvedic king” (Jamison & Brereton 2014: 43). In the RV (e.g., 2.27.10b; 2.28.7b), Varuṇa is called ásura- ‘lord’14 particularly often, at least compared to other gods (Hale 1986: 52), and, according to a widespread hypothesis (at least as early as Darmesteter 1877; cf. Hale 1986: 187, 191), he may be the Indic counterpart of the Avestan supreme god Ahura Mazda. Both Vedic ásu-ra- and Avestan ahu-ra- reflect a -ro- derivative (quasi *h₂n̥su-ro-) of the weak stem of the same PIE noun *h₂ens-u-/h₂n̥s-u- ‘lord’ that also underlies ON Æs-ir, sg. Ás-s, and other reflexes of PGmc *ans-u-. Varuṇa is thus an-other ‘lordly’ character, both by his conceptual associations and by his traditional epithet.

2b Mitra, a god of likely Indo- Iranian date (Thieme 1975), most often

13 Original text: dvandvaṃ tasyāstu taj jajñe mitraś ca varuṇaś ca ha // tayor āditya-yoḥ sattre dr̥ṣṭvāpsarasam urvaśīm / retaś caskanda tat kumbhe nyapatad vāsatīvare // tenaiva tu muhūrtena vīryavantau tapasvinau / agastyaś ca vasiṣṭhaś ca tatrarṣī saṃ-babhū vatuḥ / bahudha patite śakre kalaśe ’tha jale sthale / sthale vasiṣṭhastu muniḥ saṃbhūta r̥ṣisattamaḥ // kumbhe tv agastyaḥ sambhūto jale matsyo mahādyutiḥ / udi-yāya tato ’gastyah śamyāmātro mahāyaśaḥ // mānena saṃmito yasmāt tasmān mānya ihocyate / yad vā kumbhād rṣ̥ir jātaḥ kumbhenāpi hi mīyate // kumbha ity abhidhānaṃ tu parimāṇasya lakṣyate.

14 On the long-debated issue of the meaning of Vedic ásura-, cf. Hale (1986) in general, and in particular p. 52: “(In the family books of the RV,) [a]n asura seems to be some sort of leader who is respected and has at his command some fighting force. […] Such a lord can be either a god or a human, but since the RV is a collection of hymns to gods, ásura- occurs much more often of gods in that text”.

188 Riccardo Ginevra

mentioned as Varuṇa’s friend in the RV, almost never occurring with-out him (Macdonell 1897: 29). Even though Varuṇa and Mitra form a formulaic and ritual pair and share several of their features, the latter is more closely associated with the concept alliance: “[w]hile Varuṇa governs relations in which one person has authority over another, Mi-tra governs relations defined by mutual obligations. These two kinds of relationships overlap with one another, so […] the functions of Mitra and Varuṇa likewise often coincide” (Jamison & Brereton 2014: 43–44; cf. Macdonell 1897: 30). This characterization is further supported by the name of this god, as Vedic Mitrá- is identical to mitrá-, a formation of certain Proto- Indo- Iranian date (EWAia, s.v.), which may mean ei-ther ‘friend’ (if masculine) or ‘alliance’ (if neuter).

3 Agastya is born from the semen of both Varuṇa and Mitra, collected and mixed in a pot. While this narrative device has parallels in the birth stories of other characters (cf. Patton 1996: 264–266), the detail of the pot used as a vessel in which the bodily fluids are collected and mixed is rather peculiar.

5 Agastya is associated with intellectual power: his patronymic or epi-thet Mān-yá- means ‘(child or person) of Mā́n-a-’, a name that may refer either to Agastya’s father or to Agastya himself (see above and fn. 10), and a formation that is identical to the noun mā́n-a- ‘opinion, notion, con-ception’ (EWAia, s.v. mā́na-). The latter may be traced back to *món-o- ‘thought, cognition’, an action noun (of the so-called tómos type) of PIE *men- ‘mental power’, a root also found in, e.g., Vedic mán-tra- ‘poetic for-mula’ and Greek mén-os ‘(mental) power’.

The second Indic narrative discussed here is the myth of Agastya Mānya’s medi-ation in a conflict between Indra and the Maruts (on which see, e.g., Sieg 1902: 108–119), chiefly attested by a series of hymns from the first book of the RV (1.165, 170 and 171) that are traditionally ascribed to Agastya himself. The plot goes as follows:15 Agastya prepares a sacrifice to the Maruts, but Indra, noticing that he is not being offered anything, reaches the sacrificial terrain first and reproaches Agastya, who tries to appease him – in vain.

15 This presentation of the myth broadly follows the one in Jamison & Brereton (2014: 360).

[Indra:] “Now is there nothing? And tomorrow nothing? Who under-stands this (nothing), which is unmistakable (to me)? The thought of an-other can be bewitched and what he expected is lost.” [Agastya:] “Are you

going to strike us down, Indra? The Maruts are your brothers. Make a

proper arrangement with them. Do not strike us down in your confron-tation (with them). […] You are the foremost institutor of alliances, o lord

of alliances [mitrā́ṇām mitrapate dháyiṣṭhaḥ]. O Indra, come to an agree-

ment with the Maruts, and then eat the oblations in the proper ritual or-

der.” (RV 1.170.1–2; 5bcd)16

Understandably afraid of the Indic warrior-god, Agastya thus ends up rerouting his offering towards Indra; at this point, however, summoned by the sacrifice, the Maruts reach the scene, and, in the next passage quoted below (from RV 1.171), Agastya explains to them that their portion has been hijacked by Indra. In the sec-ond quotation (from RV 1.165), a stand-off between Indra and the Maruts takes place, each of them verbally attacking the other with violent accusations and try-ing to appear worthiest of Agastya’s offering: as expected, Indra boasts that the malicious serpent Vr ̥tra could only be defeated thanks to his strength, and no one else’s; the Maruts, in turn, rebuke him by saying that many of Indra’s deeds were actually a collaborative effort.

[Agastya:] “(Then was) I retreating from this mighty one, Maruts, trembling from fear of Indra. These oblations (of soma) were sharpened for you, but we have sent them away. Have mercy upon us!” (RV 1.171.4)17

[Indra:] “Where was this independent will of yours, Maruts, when you tasked me alone to smash the serpent? For I, the powerful and mighty, pos-sessed of might, humbled with my weapons those of every rival. [Leader of

the Maruts:] You did many things when we were there, with our united manly powers (ready) to be deployed, o bull; we shall do many things in accordance with your purpose, o most powerful Indra, when we, o fellow

Maruts, shall wish it. [Indra:] O Maruts, I smashed Vr̥tra with my In-

drian strength, having become mighty through my own rage. Bearing my mace in my arms, I made these all-gleaming waters go easily to Manu.” (RV 1.165.6–8)18

Finally, in the next passage below (also from RV 1.165), the Maruts concede to In-dra that he is indeed the most powerful being, the two parties reconcile and agree to share Agastya’s offering. Correspondingly, in the second passage below from a later source (the Maitrāyaṇī-Saṃhitā), we learn that the recitation of Agastya’s poetry (referred to as Kayāśubhā-Sūkta) is essential for a king who wants to be reconciled with his own rebellious subjects (cf. Amano 2009, ad loc.).

[Leader of the Maruts:] “This is conceded to you, generous one: There is

no one like you known among the gods. Neither one who is born nor

[Indra: ] Even if I am alone, let my force be far ranging (to do) what in my daring I shall now do according to my inspired think-ing, for I am known as the powerful one, Maruts. The praise song here has exhila-rated me, o Maruts, the formulation worthy to be heard that you created for me, o men—for me, (who am) Indra, the bull and strong combatant—for (me), your friend as my friends/allies [sákhye sákhāyas], for me myself by you yourselves. It is just so: Reflecting me here and receiving fame and re-freshments as my irreproachable (warrior band), you, who are to be seen all around with your shimmering colors, have pleased me, and you will please

me now, o Maruts.” (RV 1.165.9–12)19

For the Maruts he should spread a seven-bowl [sacrificial cake] where a

people tries to do violence to a king. The Kayāśubhā[-Sūkta] of Agastya [i.e., RV 1.165.1–15] should be used […]. A seven-bowl [sacrificial cake] is used, because the Maruts are seven, the Maruts are the people [víñ

marútaḥ]; with the portion due to them, he calms them down (those in-volved) (Maitrāyaṇī-Saṃhitā 2.1.8(4): 10,7–11; my translation, based on Amano 2009).20

These texts on the conflict between Indra and the Maruts allow us to identify a few further parallels between Agastya’s myth and the Norse narrative of Kvasir (2, 4, 6):

2 Agastya appears to be close to two distinct parties, a male char-acter and a male social group, namely: 2a Indra, the other god who is most closely associated with leadership

in the RV beside Varuṇa, although in a slightly different way: e.g., “[i]n IV.42, as in the later Rājasūya, the king becomes both Varuṇa and In-dra; that is, as Varuṇa, the king is a judicial authority governing the actions of his subjects, and as Indra, he is a leader in war” (Jamison & Brereton 2014: 43). Within his relationship to the Maruts, he is of course the god of higher status, as both the leader of their war-band and as the mightiest of all gods in general.

2b The Maruts, a group of warrior gods who are Indra’s friends/allies (sákhāyas in RV 1.165.11 above) in his heroic deeds against the serpent Vr ̥tra and other enemies (cf. his epithet marúd-gaṇa- ‘[the one] with the Maruts as troop’), but also his subjects, being gods of lower sta-tus than him. Since Indra is invoked with the epithet mitra-pate “o lord of alliances/friends” (RV 1.170.5b), it may even be possible to re-fer to the Maruts as Indra’s mitrá- ‘friends, allies’, a close lexical cor-respondence with the aforementioned myth of Agastya’s birth from Varuṇa and the god called Mitrá-.

4 Agastya mediates in the resolution of a conflict between Indra and the Maruts, after which the two parties resume their relationship based on inequality, but also mutual obligations: while the Maruts

20 Original text: mārutá saptákapālaṃ nírvaped yátra víḍ rā́jānaṃ jíjyāset / agástyasya kayāśubhī́yam̐ sāmidhenī́ś ca syúr yājyānuvākyā̀ś ca / agástyo vaí marúdbhya ukṣṇáḥ praúkṣat / tā́n índrāyā́labhata / té vájram ādā́yābhyàpatan / tā́n vā́ eténāśamayat / táñ śamáyaty evaíténa / saptákapālo bhavati / saptá hí marútas / víñ marútaḥ / svéna-ivaínān bhāgadhéyena śamayati.

192 Riccardo Ginevra

recognize Indra as their superior, the god is also said to be “establishing himself as the strong one through (the Maruts) bearing their good signs” (RV 1.171.6c supraketébhiḥ sāsahír dádhāno) and the Maruts are described while “chanting their chant, generating Indra’s strength” (RV 1.85.2c árcan-to arkáṃ janáyanta indriyám). The support of the Maruts is thus essen-tial to Indra’s role as the strongest god. Correspondingly, Agastya’s hymns were used in ritual practice for the resolution of a conflict between a king and his rebellious subjects, as attested in the Maitrāyaṇī-Saṃhitā.

6 Agastya is closely associated with poetry: a legendary poet-priest (“one of the great masters of the R̥gvedic tradition”, as per Jamison & Brereton 2014: 360), he is the author of the hymns 1.165–191 of the RV, including the ones discussed above.

The correspondences between the Indic mythology of Agastya and the Norse narrative about Kvasir may be summarized as follows: a male character is born from the bodily fluids, collected and mixed together in a vessel, of one god who is referred to as ‘lord’ (a term reflecting PIE *h₂ens-u-/h₂n̥s-u-) and one who is re-ferred to as ‘friend’. The same character, closely associated with intellectual power and verbal art, has an essential role in the resolution of a conflict between a leader of higher status and a group of friends/allies of lower status, whose relationship is based on inequality and mutual obligations. These elements may be summarized as in Table 2.

In the next section, the elements identified in the Norse and Indic traditions will be shown to have further parallels in the Roman narrative of Agrippa Menēnius.

Feature Represented by

1 Male character Agastya Mānya

Born from Close to

2 Born from and/or close to both:

a leaders of higher status Varuṇa ásura- (PIE *h₂ens-u- ‘lord’)

Indra

3 Rome: Patricians, Plebeians, and the birth and deeds of Agrippa Menēnius

The last tradition to be discussed comprises the Roman accounts of the first con-flict between the two main social groups of early Rome, Patricians and Plebeians. This dispute, according to tradition, took place in 494 bce, not very long after the alleged date of abolition of the monarchy and institution of the Roman Republic (509 bce). It was the first critical moment for the young republican state, which was only able to survive this crisis thanks to the verbal prowess of a great orator called Agrippa Menēnius Lanātus.21 Our earliest attestations of this narrative (cf., e.g., Müller 2006) occur in Livy’s Annals from the Foundations of the City (2.32– 33) and Dionysius of Halicarnassus’s Roman Antiquities (6.83–86), both written in the 1st century bce, several centuries after the supposed date of the episode. It is thus conceivable that the story, even if it had been originally based on histor-ical events (a hypothesis which can neither be proved nor disproved), acquired mythological narrative structures and details during the course of its long oral tradition.

Assuredly no hope was left save in harmony amongst the citizens [concor-

These passages on Agrippa’s birth and deeds allow for the identification of five parallels (1–2 and 4–6) with the Norse and Indic traditions discussed above:

1 Agrippa Menēnius is the male protagonist of this narrative. 2 He is equally close to (pariter carus) and most likely also born from

(see below) the two main social groups of early Roman society: 2a The Patricians, also referred to as the ‘Fathers’ (patres) in our texts.

This group of higher status detained the leadership of the Roman Republic, being the only citizens who were originally allowed to be-come members of the Senate (cf., e.g., Dionysius of Halicarnassus 2.12). Agrippa Menēnius is referred to as “ambassador of the senators to the people” (legato patrum ad plebem) and as a former consul, an office that was exclusively held by Patricians up until 367 bce (when the Leg-es Liciniae Sextiae made it possible for Plebeians to become consuls),25 implying that he is himself both a senator and a Patrician.

2b The Plebeians, also referred to as the ‘people’ or ‘multitude’ (Latin plebs; Greek plē̃tʰos) in our texts. They were the social group of lower sta-tus in Rome, bound to the Patricians by the ideology of the ‘harmo-ny of citizens’ (Latin concordia civium), i.e., the alliance between the two main social groups of Roman society. According to our texts, Agrippa Menēnius was “dear to the plebeians because he was one of them by birth” (quod inde oriundus erat, plebi carum), which, however, contradicts the fact that, having been a consul and senator, Agrippa must have also been a Patrician.

It is thus reasonable to assume that the Roman protagonist Agrippa was regarded as a person born from both Patricians and Plebeians, matching the main character of the Norse myth, the god Kvasir, who was born from

6 Of course, Agrippa Menēnius is also closely associated with verbal art: he is described as an “eloquent man” (facundus vir), who is able to convince the Plebeians to resume their relationship with the Patricians by telling a fable, ‘The Belly and the Members’. This fable was not just some bedtime story for Roman children, but rather a reflex of the deep influence of Ancient Greek (Hellenistic) political thought and rhetoric on Roman culture (cf. Nestle 1927), and thus a further token of Agrippa’s verbal art (on which see also Lincoln 1989: 145–148).

To sum up, the Roman legend of Agrippa Menēnius has several parallels in the Norse myth of Kvasir and in the Indic myths of Agastya: Agrippa is a male char-acter who is (likely) born from two different social groups, a higher-status group associated with the concept of leadership and a lower-status group that is linked to the former by means of an alliance. Agrippa’s family name Menēnius is etymo-logically linked to the idea of intellectual power, and he is able to use complex verbal art in order to heal the fracture between the two social groups, allowing them to resume a relationship based on inequality and mutual obligations. 4 Mythological and linguistic parallels: the Leaders, their Friends, and the Intelligent Speaker

As shown in the previous sections, these IE traditions have a number of parallels in their structure, narrative, and onomastics, allowing for the reconstruction of an inherited mythological tradition that underlies them all. The following ele-ments are shared by all or at least two (when explicitly noted) of the three tradi-tions analysed above:

1 A male protagonist: Norse Kvasir; Indic Agastya Mānya; Roman Agrippa Menēnius.

2 The protagonist is close to and born from two distinct male char-acters or social groups, who together form a well-established tradi-tional pair/partition in each culture: 2a The leader(s): Norse Æsir; Indic Varuṇa and Indra; Roman Patri-

cians. A male character or social group of higher status, associated with leadership and with a reflex of the PIE term *h₂ens-u-/h₂n̥s-u- (Old Norse Æs-ir; Vedic ásu-ra-).

2b Their friend(s): Norse Vanir; Indic Mitra and Maruts, respectively; Roman Plebeians. A male character or social group of lower status, associated with the concept alliance, even by name (Old Norse Van-ir, if related to vinr ‘friend’; Vedic Mitrá- ‘Friend’).

3 The protagonist is born from the bodily fluids (Norse spit; Indic se-men) of both leader(s) and friend(s), collected and mixed in a ves-sel (Norse vat; Indic pot).27 This peculiar detail may be the reflex of a well-known ritual complex, see below.

4 He is associated with the resolution of a conflict between the lead-er(s) and their friend(s) (Norse Kvasir is born as a result thereof, where-as Indic Agastya and Roman Agrippa are agents of the resolution), after which the two parties either initiate or resume a relationship based on inequality but also mutual obligations, i.e., a patron–client relationship (explicitly referred to as such in the texts of the Roman tra-

27 As noted by Matthias Egeler (p.c.), the use of a vessel may be seen as a logically neces-sary element of the ‘mixed fluids’ motif, rather than as a genuinely independent point; this is not necessarily true, however, as the bodily fluids could have been mixed without a vessel too: this is the case, for example, in the Indic myth of the birth of the god Skan-da from the mixed seed of the gods Śiva and Agni in the Sanskrit epic Mahābhārata (13.83–84).

199Indo- European patrons vs. clients, and the role of poets as social brokers

dition). This element supports the hypothesis that, at least within this in-herited mythological tradition, the leader characters acted as a narrative counterpart to the patrons of IE society, whereas the friend characters were the counterpart to the clients.

5 The protagonist is associated with intellectual power: Norse Kvasir is referred to as the “wisest of all beings”; both Indic Agastya’s patronymic/ epithet Mānyá- and Roman Agrippa’s family name Menēnius can ultimate-ly be traced back to the same PIE root *men- ‘mental power’.

6 He is associated with verbal art: in Norse, ‘Kvasir’s blood’ is a poetic periphrasis for poetry itself; Indic Agastya Mānya and Roman Agrip-pa Menēnius are both experts of verbal art (Agastya’s poetry, Agrippa’s rhetorics and fable) who skillfully use it in order to heal the frac-ture between leader(s) and friend(s).28

The numerous parallels between these three IE traditions may be summarized as in Table 4.

Before moving on to the conclusion, three considerations are in order. First-ly, the parallels between Indic leader-characters Varuṇa and Indra on the one hand, and their friend-characters Mitra and the Maruts on the other, do not point to an original identity of any of these characters: even though these gods have similar associations and assume similar roles within these specific mytho-logical narratives, they do not seem to share many other features. Gods are more than characters in a myth, and similar narratives may be attached to different gods, if their characterizations allow it: in this case, an inherited IE traditional narrative involving a pair leader(s)–friend(s) may have been attached inde-pendently to the fixed pairs Varuṇa–Mitra and Indra–Maruts simply because their associations with specific concepts (leadership–alliance, respectively) allowed it. This is not to say that such mythological pairs are interchangeable, but one should keep in mind that the real protagonist of this IE myth is the male char-acter associated with intellectual power and verbal art, whose identity is discussed in the conclusion.

Secondly, the story of Roman protagonist Agrippa Menēnius takes place in 494 BCE, i.e., during a period of the history of Rome which lies at the thresh-old between aetiological myth/legend and actual recorded events; Menēnius may

thus be either a mythological character that has been historicized or an originally historical person who has been conflated with a mythological character. The lat-ter’s name may have originally been only Menēnius (or *Menēnus), as suggested not only by its etymological link with Vedic Mānyá-, but also by the fact that, in Livy’s text, the character is often mentioned with the praenomen Agrippa after the nomen Menēnius (i.e., Menēnius Agrippa), which does not reflect the regular praenomen–nomen–cognomen order (as if one referred to Gaius Iulius Caesar as Iulius Gaius). This may point to some kind of (historical) priority or (seman-tic) salience of Menēnius over Agrippa; however, it is also possible that Livy was just influenced by the onomastic practice of his own time, when Agrippa had already become a cognomen (like Caesar) and was thus mentioned after the fam-ily name (as in Marcus Vipsanius Agrippa). The intriguing detail of the initial Ag- occurring in both Latin Ag-rippa (Menēnius) and Vedic Ag-ástya- (Mānyá-) must remain an open question at the current state of the research, as the formal analysis and etymological history of these names are currently unclear (cf. Ernout & Meillet 1959: 18; EWAia, s.v. agásti-). Given that, apart from their Anlaut, the two names do not seem to have exact formal correspondences, their similarity may be due to chance; alternatively, the parallel may reflect a shared heritage that has been deformed for various possible reasons, e.g., tabooism.

Finally, the peculiar detail of (3), the collecting in a vessel and mixing of the bodily fluids (spit in the Norse myth and semen in the Indic one) of both leaders and friends may have a historical counterpart in the ritual exchanges of bodily fluids – including blood, saliva, and semen – that have been report-ed, e.g., among African, Caucasian, Middle Eastern, and Native North American cultures as part of ceremonies performed to initiate relations of “blood brother-hood and affine relationships of covenanted comradeship or sacrosanct amity” (Eisenstadt & Roniger 1984: 1; cf. Pitt-Rivers 1968: 410 and 1973: 127–128). It is thus conceivable that within prehistoric IE societies the bond between leaders and friends/allies, i.e., patrons and clients, could be combined with such a relationship and correspondingly sanctioned by such a ritual exchange of bodily fluids. Given the “paradoxical contradictions” that are typical of patron–client relationships discussed in the introduction, it is not uncommon for such relations to be combined with ritual friendships: e.g., there are attestations of patron–client amicitia ‘friendship’ in Ancient Roman society (Eisenstadt & Roniger 1984: 61) or patron–client compadrazgo (godfather-hood) in Spanish-speaking communities (ibid.: 75–76).29

29 As noted by Bruce Lincoln (p.c.), Kvasir and Agastya, being the result of the union

202 Riccardo Ginevra

5 Conclusion: the poet’s role as social broker (‘legitimizing inequality’) in prehistoric Indo- European society

As summarized above, the IE myth that may be reconstructed by comparing the Norse, Indic, and Roman traditions involves a main character who not only is (1) male and (2) close to and/or born from both leaders (PIE *h₂ens-u-/ h₂n̥s-u-) and friends, more specifically (3) born from their bodily fluids col-lected and mixed together inside a vessel of some kind; but he is also (4) linked to the resolution of a conflict between leaders and friends that allows them to have a patron–client relationship, as well as (5) associated with the concept intellectual power, expressed by the reflexes of the root *men-, and (6) with verbal art of some kind, which he actively uses to heal the fracture between leaders and friends.

The last elements (4–6) deserve a closer look, as they allow for a possible identification of the prehistoric social category reflected by the ‘intelligent speak-er’ of this reconstructed myth: the poet, the natural protagonist of a narrative that clearly was an aetiological myth about the origin of poetry and verbal art and about their function within (Proto- )Indo- European society. Firstly, the Old Norse passage analysed above explicitly attests that in Scandinavia this traditional narrative could serve as the answer to the question “How did this craft that you call poetry originate?” (see above). Furthermore, linguistic support for this iden-tification comes from the etymological analyses of Agastya’s epithet/patronymic Mānyá- and of Agrippa’s family name Menēnius, both of which may be traced back to the PIE root *men- ‘intellectual power’: this root, referring to the trained minds of poets, was traditionally linked to verbal art in early Indo- European tra-ditions (and thus probably already in PIE), cf. the following quotation by Wat-kins concerning Vedic and Ancient Greek (see also Fortson 1998: 138, West 2007: 33–35, as well as Katz 2018a: 127–129 and 2018b):

Note that the words for the poet’s understanding (manīṣā́) and wisdom (mánma = Old Irish menmae ‘mind’), and the remembering (manvata) the 3×7 secret names of the cow which is Vedic poetics itself, are all derivatives of the root *men- expressing active mental force, thinking, perceiving, re-

between the bodily fluids of males mixed in a vessel without any maternal contribution, exemplify in their very essence the union between two entities more equal in status and power than was the case in any marital or heterosexual union, from the perspective of the patriarchal societies in which these stories were told.

203Indo- European patrons vs. clients, and the role of poets as social brokers

$membering. So too is Greek Μοῦσα (Aeolic Μοῖσα) ‘Muse’, daughter of $Zeus and Mnemosyne ‘Memory’: Proto- Greek *montwa from *mon-tu-h₂, cf. Vedic mántu-, amantú- ‘(un)caring, (un)mindful’. The inspiration of the divine Muse is thus only a personification of the trained mind of the poet. (Watkins 1995: 73)

The interpretation of the main character of this reconstructed myth as a reflex of the prehistoric social figure of the poet allows us to better frame and under-stand his mythological role as a mediator between the leader characters and the friend characters. More precisely, this detail may reflect one of the most important functions of poets in (Proto- )Indo- European society, namely their role as mediators between patrons and clients. On the one hand, poets could praise patrons for their positive impact on the lives of their clients (including them-selves) and use their rhetoric skills to encourage clients to be obedient towards their own patrons, justifying Anthony’s (2007: 342) definition of the institution of patron–client relationships as a “way of legitimizing inequality”. On the other hand, poets could encourage patrons to be munificent to their clients (cf. the quote from Anthony 2007 below) and use their elaborate verbal art to reproach and scold patrons who did not behave generously towards their own clients – e.g., those who did not adequately reward praise poetry (cf. the quote from Watkins 1995 below).

Praise poetry at public feasts encouraged patrons to be generous, and val-idated the language of the songs as a vehicle for communicating with the gods who regulated everything. (Anthony 2007: 343)

The reciprocal situation of poet and patron may have a negative side as well. Generosity leads to praise, but ungenerous payment can provoke blame,

invective, and satire, the “formidable weapon” (Binchy 1940: 69) of poets from India and Greece to Ireland. (Watkins 1995: 75)

As long argued within sociological theory, dyadic figures are latent triangles (Fi-scher 2004: 80; Krämer 2015: 82). In other words, dual social structures such as patron–client relationships often entail a ‘third figure’ who acts as a mediator be-tween the two poles; as noted by Krämer (2015: 81), “[t]hirdness” is the “[n]ucleus of [s]ociality: […] [t]he messenger makes a social relation possible between peo-ple who are distant from one another”. English broker or social broker is the term used by sociologists and anthropologists to refer to the social figure who, just like

204 Riccardo Ginevra

our IE (mythological) intelligent speakers and (historical) poets, not only “mediates between the patron and client and is seen by the others as necessary for a satisfactory outcome”, but also, “[b]ecause of his vital role as intermediary, […] takes on aspects of both patron and client” (Wilson 1990: 163), a detail that is mythologically exemplified in our texts by the double lineage of Norse Kvasir, Indic Agastya, and Roman Agrippa. The (social) broker has also been defined as a person who “bridges gaps in communication between persons, groups, struc-tures and even cultures” and as “a professional manipulator of people and infor-mation to bring about communication” (Boissevain 1969: 380), all descriptions that nicely fit the intelligent speakers Agastya and Agrippa of the Indic and Roman myths analysed above. Thus, according to this interpretation, all three main actants of the IE myth reconstructed above may have had real-life counter-parts in the IE social institution of patron–client relations: the leaders are the mythological counterparts to the patrons; the friends/allies are counterparts to the clients; and the intelligent speakers reflect the social role of the poets as social brokers mediating between the two sides.

As a final caveat, it should be noted that this triadic structure is in no way reminiscent of Dumézilian trifunctionalism. No functional distinctions between leaders/patrons and friends/clients may be reconstructed by means of the comparative analysis of the IE myths: both leaders (1st function ‘sovereignty’ in Dumézil’s theory) and friends are also warriors (2nd function), and neither has closer associations with fertility (3rd function) compared to the other. Finally, the intelligent speaker is not really a member of a different social group, but is actually close to both parties, and even biologically belongs to both (as myth-ologically exemplified by his birth from mixed bodily fluids). The absence of any reconstructable traces of functional tripartition within this IE myth on patron–client relationships is consistent with the fact that the latter are purely hi-erarchical structures, which have no connections with labor functions and which actually display ‘Russian doll–like’ recursion: “[n]ested hierarchies in which cli-ents are themselves patrons of other clients are characteristic of the growth of patron–client systems” (Anthony 2007: 360). Thus, chiefs or communities could be patrons of other chiefs or communities (e.g., the Ancient Greek poet Pindar could have a whole city as patron, cf. Watkins 1995: 61; the Roman Republic was patron to several client states called civitates liberae, cf. Eisenstadt & Roniger 1984: 62–64 and 247–248), while a patron’s clients (regardless of their occupation) could have people of lower status as clients of their own (e.g., poets acted as cli-ents to their human lords, but the latter acted as clients to the gods, cf. Watkins 1995: 70 and passim, Jackson 2016).

205Indo- European patrons vs. clients, and the role of poets as social brokers

To sum up, the comparative analysis of the mythological traditions discussed above allows for the following reconstruction: within early (Proto-)Indo- European society, the role of social broker (i.e., mediator) between patrons (*h₂ens-u- ‘leaders’) and clients (‘friends/allies’) was supposed to be fulfilled by intelligent (*men-) speakers, i.e., poets, ideally conceived as male individ-uals who were equally close to both sides (even biologically so), and thus linked to the resolution of their disputes. The fact that the IE mythological tradition reconstructed here involves three main actants – leaders/patrons, friends/ clients, and intelligent speakers/poets – should not be considered as evi-dence for the reconstruction of functional tripartition in PIE society, but rather as a coherent reflex of how the dual institution of patron–client relationships most likely required the ‘tertiary’ mediation (brokerage) of poets to function properly.

The violent Indo- Europeans

Some general thoughts on the martial influence of the Corded Ware on Neolithic societies

Rune Iversen The Saxo Institute (Archaeology section), University of Copenhagen

This paper wrestles with the old, but persistent, view that the appearance of

Indo- European speaking groups in Europe caused radical changes in so-

cial organization, including the introduction of the idealized male warrior,

increased violence and changed gender relations, replacing matrilineality

and sex egalitarianism with an exogamic patrilocal family structure. The

aim is not to downscale or deny the violent and warring aspects of early

Indo- European societies; instead I argue that these features were not new

but already well-established elements in pre-Indo- European Neolithic Eu-

rope. Hence, my aim is to nuance the view on the impact Indo- European

societies had on Neolithic Europe, not by questioning the violent Indo-

Europeans but the tough myth of the peaceful farmers.

The introduction of early Indo- European dialects has traditionally been related to the arrival of violent hordes of battle-axe–brandishing steppe nomads who im-posed their customs, social organization and language on the resident, peaceful farmers (e.g., Glob 1945: 241–244, 1971: 106–107, Gimbutas 1993). In the somewhat controversial interpretation put forward by Marija Gimbutas, this scenario is fur-thermore linked with highly contrasting family structures, where the sedentary farmers were conceived as matrifocal, matrilineal and sex egalitarian, whereas the intruding steppe nomads were warlike, patriarchal and hierarchical (Gimb-utas 1993: 206). Even though this scenario may appear oversimplified and naïve, it still seems to influence the way we look at the (supposed) introduction and staging of the male warrior and associated social institutions (e.g., Anthony 2007: 236–237 and 364–365, Kristiansen 2009, Kristiansen et al. 2017; see also Mallory 1989: 110–111 for a critical stand).

According to the prevalent steppe hypothesis, Proto- Indo- European developed in the Pontic–Caspian steppe between 4500 and 2500 BC, and early Indo- European spread into Europe via migrations during the early third millennium BC. The

212 Rune Iversen

linguistic spread of early Indo- European is usually associated with the Yamnaya, Corded Ware and Bell Beaker archaeological complexes. Individuals interred with material culture related to the Corded Ware and Bell Beaker archaeological com-plexes seem to inherit a significant amount of DNA from the early third millenni-um BC steppe populations, usually referred to as Yamnaya or steppe ancestry (An-thony 2007, Allentoft et al. 2015 and 2024, Haak et al. 2015, Olander 2019, Egfjord 2021). This process may very well have been partly violent and, as indicated by some DNA studies, male-driven (Goldberg et al. 2017, Scorrano et al. 2021).

The purpose of this paper is not to challenge the idea of the ‘violent Indo- Europeans’ but rather that of the peaceful farmers. If we look at the archaeological evidence from early farming societies in Europe, recent decades’ excavations and interdisciplinary research clearly show that these societies were far from peaceful, but rather warlike. Thus, the overall question I will reflect upon is whether we are overestimating the violent and warring impact of the Indo- Europeanization. First, I will take a closer look at the social structure of the early Indo- Europeans. As Indo- European is a linguistic term, describing a widely spoken language family, I refer to the early Indo- Europeans as those groups who, according to the steppe hypothesis, presumably spoke early Indo- European. Second, I will consider the concepts of violence, war and warfare before I proceed with a discussion of the presence of warfare before and after the Corded Ware, i.e., before and after the supposed introduction of Indo- European traditions into Europe.

1 The social structure of the early Indo- Europeans

The social structure of early Indo- European communities is often described as male-dominated. Linguistically this has been demonstrated by the reconstruc-tion of the Proto- Indo- European vocabulary for kinship terminology, which in-dicates that the Core Indo- European family (i.e., Indo- European minus Anato-lian) was patrilineal and patrilocal (Olsen 2019, 2021). The household seems to comprise the ‘master of the house’ (grandfather), his wife, sons and daughters-in-law, unmarried daughters, and grandchildren. Marriages were exogamous. Based on aDNA and strontium/oxygen isotope analyses of individuals found in Central European Corded Ware and Bell Beaker burials, a similar family structure has been identified as the ruling principle in these societies. Genetic kinship (‘core families’) seems to be central in the social organization, which furthermore ap-pears to have been exogamous and patrilocal (Haak et al. 2008, Sjögren, Price & Kristiansen 2016, Knipper et al. 2017, Mittnik et al. 2019, Sjögren et al. 2020).

213The violent Indo- Europeans

This exogamic and patrilocal family structure provides an essential argument in explaining how steppe ancestry spread through Europe during the early third millennium BC. A genetic study of female and male demographics indicates that the migrations from the Pontic–Caspian Steppe to Central Europe happened over a period of multiple generations and were heavily dominated by males. By con-trast, the earlier Neolithization process shows no evidence of sex-biased admix-ture (Goldberg et al. 2017). In the apparently male-driven migrations from the steppe, exogamy was a necessary mechanism if the migrating males wanted to establish households and communities of their own. That this process was not without potential conflicts can be seen in the Eulau multiple Corded Ware burials, Central Germany, which show lesions caused by stone axes and arrows (Haak et al. 2008, Meyer et al. 2009, Kristiansen et al. 2017: 338). Biological kinship seems to represent the basic structure in the Eulau burials, including a nuclear family. According to strontium isotope analyses, the women appear to be of a different origin compared to the males and children. The most probable scenario is that the buried individuals were victims of a raid carried out by a group of attackers, who presumably belonged to the Neolithic Schönfeld culture, as indicated by a transverse arrowhead found in the bone of a female buried in one of the graves. A proposed reconstruction of the motive relates the attack to the exogamic relations between the Corded Ware group and the local Neolithic communities, where a phenomenon such as ‘honour killing’ might be part of the explanation (Muhl et al. 2010: 120–123, 144–147).

That a similar exogamic and patrilocal family structure existed in other Cord-ed Ware areas is indicated by the vast majority of male graves recorded within the Danish Single Grave culture (local variant of the Corded Ware). Male burials predominate among the single graves with a share of 57% based on the artefacts found in the graves (Hübner 2005: 632–633 fig. 454). Battle-axes, flint axes, ar-rowheads and blades are associated with a right-crouched position interpreted as male burials, whereas amber beads are associated with a left-crouched position interpreted as female burials. Unfortunately, it is often only the contours of the body that are preserved and very few graves contain human bones suitable for anthropological analysis and sex determination. However, anthropological anal-yses carried out on remains from Corded Ware burials in southern Germany and Bohemia confirm these stereotypical gender-differentiated burial customs (Ge-bers 1984: 90–92 and 100, Nausch 1997, Wiermann 2002: 116–117, Hübner 2005: 587 with references, Vandkilde 2006: 410–417). A highly sex-biased distribution is particularly predominant in the early phase (c. 2850–2600 BC), when close to 90% of the Danish graves contain males (Hübner 2005: 632–633 fig. 454). This

214 Rune Iversen

distribution fits a scenario where incoming males established exogamic relations with local Neolithic females who were perhaps buried in the megalithic tombs according to old norms. Despite a general lack of preserved skeletons from the Danish Single Grave culture, a recent study has demonstrated close genetic re-semblance to Central European Corded Ware groups (Egfjord et al. 2021).

One way of explaining the background of the dispersal of male-dominated early-Indo- European–speaking groups from the steppe to Europe during the ear-ly third millennium BC is to consider a certain ‘warrior ideology’, known from early Indo- European myths and poetry. Here dogs and/or wolfs are strongly asso-ciated with death, war, warriors, and in particular youthful war-bands. The term for such ‘brotherhoods’ of young warriors may have been the Indo- European noun *kori̯os. The concept is often referred to as Männerbund/Jungmannschaft or ‘black youth’, which describes a social system that includes war-bands of landless and unmarried adolescent young sons supervised and trained by a senior male. These bands were situated at the edge of ordinary society, where they adopted ‘wolf-like’ predatory behaviour and subsisted on raiding until they were ready to re-enter the tribe as men through cleansing rituals (rites de passage) when reach-ing adulthood. Such groups of young males were highly mobile and willing to take risks by undertaking pioneering migrations to acquire livestock, goods, territory, wives, and personal glory (Anthony 2007: 364–365, Petrosyan 2011, Kristiansen et al. 2017: 39–40 fig. 1, Brown & Anthony 2019: 101 and 110–114 with references).

Archaeological remains of what has been interpreted as a regional centre for the performance of warrior initiation rituals associated with the Indo- European

*kori̯os institution has been unearthed at the Russian Late Bronze Age Srubnaya site Krasnosamarskoe at the middle Volga just east of Samara. The site dates to c. 1900–1700 BC and has revealed winter-season depositions of cut-up remains of at least 51 dogs and 7 wolves, with a significant predominance of male dogs (Brown & Anthony 2019).

As suggested by Kristiansen et al. (2017), the presence of such a warrior-train-ing institution within early Indo- European societies could explain the presumed male-driven migrations from the steppe into Europe that helped create the Cord-ed Ware culture through exogamic relations.

2 Violence, raids and warfare

As seen from the review above, it is to be expected that an institutionalized war-rior ideology was an integrated part of the basic social structure of Corded Ware

215The violent Indo- Europeans

(and Bell Beaker) societies. At first sight, this reconstruction of a violent and war-ring social structure confirms the scenario, mentioned in the introduction, of the peaceful Neolithic farming communities that were overrun by violent Indo- Europeans. However, before we jump to conclusions, we will have to reconsider the image of the peaceful Neolithic and first briefly discuss the concepts of war and warfare in the past.

Conflict, interpersonal violence and fighting seem to be integral elements of human behaviour. The result, in the form of injuries caused by violence, is found on human bones widely distributed across time and space. Single individuals showing lesions, healed or lethal, can tell us something about how violent society was within given periods and geographical areas, but they do not necessarily tell us if war existed or not. The question is: when did aggressions take place on a scale and under circumstances that allow us to define them as warfare? How should we define war, and how can we discern traces of warfare in the archaeological record?

2.1 The concepts of war and warfare

Wars have been the topic of epic poems and historical chronicles from antiquity to the present, describing great battles, fights and sieges ranging from the Late Bronze Age battles of Kadesh and Troy to the decisive battles of World War II. However, among the earliest works that theorize on war and military strategies are those of Chinese general Sun Tzu from around 500 BC (tr. Giles 2014), as well as those of Renaissance historian and political philosopher Niccolò Machiavelli from 1521 (tr. Franeworth 2001). But it is Vom Kriege ‘On War’, the oft-cited work of Prussian general and war theorist Carl von Clausewitz published in 1832–1834 (tr. Graham 2012) which has had the greatest impact on the modern development and conception of war in the West.

According to Clausewitz, war can be defined as follows: “War therefore is an act of violence intended to compel our opponent to fulfil our will” (Graham 2012: 41). Further, war can be regarded as politics carried out with other means, the political view being the object while war is the means (ibid.: 64). Thus, war has a purpose, a political gain. But which factors should we consider in order to define human aggression as war?

Even though most people will know what we are talking about when we men-tion the term ‘war’, it is not easy to define, and most scholars who deal with the concept of war have their own more or less diverging definitions (for an over-view and general discussion, see among others Schjødt 2003). However, some el-

216 Rune Iversen

ements seem to recur in the perceptions of war, namely that it is a social or rather collective act, is violent by nature, is organised in some way and has a purpose. As the American anthropologist R. Brian Ferguson (1997: 337) puts it, “War is a relationship between groups”. Hence, war can be separated from other forms of violence such as the killing of individuals, including homicide, executions, liq-uidations, interpersonal strife, fights, duels and family and intra-group violence.

An important element in the Hungarian peace researcher István Kende’s defi-nition of war is the emphasis on its continuity. War is not a single attack or battle: it has a certain duration, and societies will be in a state of war for shorter or longer periods. Kende has put forward three co-occurring qualifying criteria of war: ac-tive regular armed forces at least on one side, a certain degree of organization on both sides, and a certain continuity between the armed conflicts including a strategic–tactical and organizational coherence (Kende 1971: 6). The Dutch be-havioural scientist Johan M.G. van der Dennen suggests a somewhat different view on the violent aspect of war, as he sees war as a very special category of macro-level violence:

War is a species of the genus of violence; more specifically, it is collective, di-rect, manifest, personal, interpersonal, organized, institutionalized, instru-mental, sanctioned, and sometimes ritualized and regulated, violence. (van der Dennen 1995: 69)

The violent aspect of war can be more or less emphasised in the different defini-tions. If we return to the works of Ferguson, he characterises war as:

[…] organized, purposeful group action, directed against another group that may or may not be organized for similar action, involving the actual or potential application of lethal force. (Ferguson 1984: 5)

The potential use of violence also has parallels in the ethnographic record showing that ritual warfare characterised by formal and arranged battles occur and that these can be fought with few casualties. Such battles can take the form of tour-nament-like face-to-face confrontations between groups that exchange blows or engage in club fights or spear-throwing and arrow shooting (Gat 2006: 122 and 124, Keeley 1996: 63–65, Ember & Ember 2011: 262–264).

Then, was war in one form or another present in early prehistory? Let us take a brief look at two analogies often applied when researchers try to describe the nature and origins of war, namely humankind’s closest relatives the chimpanzees,

217The violent Indo- Europeans

and the ethnographic record concerning mobile hunter-gatherers. Intentional, lethal, and gang-based attacks are common features among chimpanzees as part of inter-group aggressions probably carried out in order to expand their territory. The attackers are predominantly male chimpanzees, as are the victims; however, young infants are often killed during the attacks, probably because they are easy targets. In general, the attackers far outnumber their victims, showing that at-tacks take place when the risk of being killed is low (Mitani et al. 2010, Wilson et al. 2014, Southern et al. 2021).

Ethnographic studies indicate that these patterns are not unique to apes, but also occur among humans as warfare among some mobile human hunter- gatherer groups resembles the so-called ‘chimpanzee model of war’ in three essential as-pects. The model proposes that,

1 chimpanzee groups compete over territory, food and females 2 there is a strong tendency for hostility against members of other groups

and, by cooperating in killing rival groups members, males increase dom-inance and access to food for their own group in the long run

3 intergroup aggression primarily takes place when the killings can be car-ried out at low risk, i.e., when the attackers greatly outnumber their victims

However, elements such as revenge-seeking and parochial altruism, manifested in self-sacrificial or excessively risky behaviour, seem to differentiate human warfare from that of chimpanzees (Wrangham et al. 2006, Wrangham & Glowacki 2012).

As in the cases referred to above, ambushes and raids – understood as surprise attacks by small groups or larger raiding parties, and not battles – are the most common and lethal kind of warfare in many non-state or ‘non-modern’ societies (Keeley 1996: 65–67, Gat 2006: 114–132). However, raids can hardly fit into most contemporary conceptions of war, and it therefore seems reasonable to distin-guish between two main categories of war: ‘simple’ (also referred to as ‘primitive’) and ‘complex’. Simple warfare is often ascribed to small-scale hunter-gatherer and farming societies and is dominated by raiding and feuding, whereas complex war-fare is related to societies with developed political hierarchies and includes battles fought by soldiers under orders from leaders (Wrangham & Glowacki 2012: 8). An intensification of the violence leads from small-scale raids to actual massa-cres, defined as larger surprise attacks with the purpose of annihilating an enemy community including men, women, and children. Massacres have been recorded in several ethnographic cases, even though they seem to occur infrequently (i.e., once a generation) in non-state societies (Keeley 1996: 67–69).

218 Rune Iversen

3 Simple warfare before and after the Corded Ware

If we are to identify traces of warfare in the archaeological record, we must of course critically analyse the available sources and try to differentiate between warfare and other forms of killing, such as interpersonal aggression/dispute, homicide, lynchings, executions or human sacrifices. A high percentage of hu-man remains with traumas may indicate that the injured individuals were vic-tims of warfare, but found individually, whether buried in graves or deposited in, e.g., bogs and lakes, they may equally well represent one of the practices outlined above. In order to differentiate between these two main categories – ‘war-like’ (inter-group armed violence) and ‘judicial’ (intra-group violence; cf. Chenal et al. 2015: 1324) – we need an archaeological context to support either of the inter-pretations.

3.1 Warfare and killings in the Neolithic

One example of a case that shows a violent ending but has not been interpreted as a result of warfare is the famous Tyrolean naturally-mummified man known as Ötzi, who was shot by an arrow and ended up in a glacier in the Italian Ötz-tal Alps (from which the name Ötzi was coined) around 3300 BC. One scenario among others is that Ötzi was chased and killed by a group of attackers (Fleck-inger 2014). Another, but rather different example is the Early Neolithic find from Sigersdal Mose, northern Zealand, Denmark (c. 3400 BC). A lugged flask and the remains of two skeletons of young individuals (probably women) were found close together in a bog, one of the skeletons with a cord around its neck. The find is interpreted as a human sacrifice (Bennike & Ebbesen 1987). A similar exam-ple was found at Boelkilde, on the island of Als, southeastern Jutland, Denmark. Here, two males (c. 16 and 40 years old) dating to the Early Neolithic around 3400 BC were found in a bog, the older with a cord around his neck (Bennike, Ebbesen & Jørgensen 1986). These Early Neolithic individuals represent examples of a practice where single individuals were intentionally killed and deposited in bogs or lakes, probably for sacrificial reasons (for more Early Neolithic human bog finds, see Sjögren et al. 2017; see also Fischer et al. 2024 on the significant life-history of the maltreated and deposited Vittrup man of NW Jutland). This practice is geographically and chronologically widespread and is well illustrated by the renowned Pre-Roman Iron Age (c. 500–1 BC) bog bodies from sites like Tollund, Elling, and Grauballe (Jensen 2003: 176–187).

219The violent Indo- Europeans

However, these categories do not necessarily need to be strictly separated, as illustrated by an ethnographical example from Borneo, where headhunting was practiced by agriculturalists who carried out raids on other villages in order to obtain human heads needed in a variety of ritual practices. Here, raids became the means to obtain cultic objects (the human heads), which were hung up (in archaeological terms ‘hoarded’ or ‘deposited’) in longhouses and subjected to in-tensive ritual attention (Rothstein 2021). The chopped-off heads are often indica-tions of raids even though they could be acquired by other means. Warfare and ritual practices are thus closely intertwined as raids became a necessity for the cult – perhaps the individuals that ended their days in the bogs at Sigersdal and Boelkilde, too, were captured in raids whose sole purpose was to acquire subjects suitable for sacrificial offerings?

Another fusion of warfare and offering is of course the widespread practice of sacrificing (some of) the spoils of war and/or war captives as thank-offerings for success on the battlefield. This practice is well-attested archaeologically, among other places, in the South Scandinavian Iron Age (e.g., Randsborg 1995, Jør-gensen, Storgaard & Thomsen 2003, Holst et al. 2018).

One of the most spectacular victims of interpersonal violence from the Dan-ish Neolithic is the significant bog find of the skeletal remains of a man recovered at Porsmose on southern Zealand (Figure 1). A bone arrowhead has penetrated the nose section, and another has gone through his breastbone. The skeleton has been radiocarbon-dated to the mid-fourth millennium BC (Becker 1952, Bennike & Ebbesen 1987: 101). The remains of a similar violent scenario have been recov-ered during excavation in the Salpetermosen bog in northern Zealand (Figure 2). In this case, a 15-cm long bone arrowhead was found together with human remains of a male aged 25–30 (c. 3600–3500 BC) who had suffered an unhealed blow to the head in addition to an older, healed skull injury. The arrowhead was not logged into any of the bones, but the find context makes it probable that the man was hit by the arrowhead, as no other artefacts were found in relation to the deceased (Jørgensen & Hagedorn 2015). It is not possible to say with certainty whether the men from Porsmose and Salpetermosen were killed in warfare or executed, but it is reasonable to see these cases as the result of lethal attacks that included fighting. The way the arrowhead had penetrated the Porsmose man’s nose section clearly indicates that he was shot from above, perhaps the victim of an ambush (Becker 1952: 30).

Even if these Early Neolithic examples cannot with certainty be related to war-fare, they definitely show that South Scandinavian pre-Corded Ware Neolithic societies were violent, which is also indicated by the presence of weaponry such

221The violent Indo- Europeans

as flint halberds, stone battle-axes, and mace heads (Ebbesen 1988, 1994b and 1998). Furthermore, specialized war arrowheads seem to be part of the repertoire of the ‘sub-Neolithic’ Pitted Ware culture, which overlaps with the early Single Grave culture in the early third millennium BC (Iversen 2016). A study of skull traumas from the South Scandinavian Neolithic in general (c. 4000–1700 BC, i.e., including the Middle Neolithic Corded Ware and Late Neolithic periods) shows injuries in 378 individuals, mainly sampled from megalithic tombs. These inju-ries indicate sex-biased engagements in conflicts, as male samples show unhealed lesions mainly on the left side, suggesting face to face fighting (in the case of two right-handed opponents), whereas the female samples show lesions mainly on the right side of the skull. While significantly more males are marked by healed injuries, the two sexes seem to be equally represented as regards perimortem/ lethal injuries (Fibiger et al. 2013).

3.2 Violence in the Linear Pottery and Michelsberg cultures

Evidence of intentional killing is certainly also present in the archaeological record from Neolithic Europe, as shown by arrowheads embedded in human bones, skulls with multiple traumas and traces of downright massacres (e.g., Thorpe 2006, Schulting & Fibiger 2012, Heath 2017). Before the Corded Ware, we see some spectacular examples from the Central European Neolithic – in particular, the Linear Pottery culture (c. 5500–4900 BC) has provided quite a number of significant cases. Many of these have been mentioned in the literature several times, and I will refer to them only briefly here (see also Golitko & Keeley 2007).

One of the most renowned sites is the mass grave at Talheim in southwestern Germany, c. 5000 BC. The grave pit revealed the remains of 34 individuals – men, women and children representing three generations – who show injuries and de-fects caused by blunt and semi-sharp weapons and arrowheads. The demographic profile of the interred individuals indicates a massacre of a whole community (Wahl & Trautmann 2012). A comparable case from the Linear Pottery culture is Schöneck–Kilianstädten in central Germany. Here at least 26 individuals were killed by blunt force, including cranial trauma and injuries caused by arrows. The general picture indicates that the victims were subjected to torture and mutilation. Again, men, women and children are present, but there is a significant absence of younger women. It has been suggested that this pattern indicates that the younger women were taken as captives (Meyer et al. 2015). A similar demographic dis-

222 Rune Iversen

tribution is shown at the Austrian enclosed settlement Asparn/Schletz, dated c. 5000 BC. The site has revealed the skeletal remains of 67 individuals, found at the base of a ditch, with crania showing multiple traumas. Men, women and children are all represented at this site as well, but with an underrepresentation of females among younger individuals (20–40 years). As with the Schöneck–Kilianstädten site, the lack of younger women has been interpreted as the result of abduction (Teschler-Nicola 2012). The younger women may then in fact have been the main reason for some of these attacks, in which case we may be dealing with a situation of (forced) patrilocal exogamic relations (see also Bentley et al. 2012) comparable to that outlined for the early Indo- European communities above. Of course, other kinds of family structures may have existed within the widespread Linear Pottery culture (cf. Hrnčíř, Vondrovský & Květina 2020).

An even more extensive, but rather different, example is the presumed ritual gathering place of Herxheim in southwest Germany, dated c. 5000 BC, which shows traces of cannibalism, skull manipulations and skulls with healed inju-ries (Boulestin et al. 2009, Orschiedt & Haidle 2006). Yet another category is the presumed systematic execution of a selected group of nine non-local individuals, almost exclusively adult males, found in a Linear Pottery culture mass grave at Halberstadt in central Germany (Meyer et al. 2018). In addition, there were also enclosed sites with V-shaped ditches and palisades, which some scholars see as fortifications and thereby indirect evidence of warfare (e.g., Heath 2017: 17–35, Lull et al. 2015, Keeley & Caben 1989).

The somewhat later central European Michelsberg culture (c. 4400–3500 BC) has also revealed direct traces of interpersonal violence, such as those found in a pit at Bergheim in Alsace, France. The pit contained seven individuals and the fragmented skull of an eighth person, deposited on top of a number of amputated human upper limbs. One of the individuals shows numerous traces of violence including blows to the head. The find is interpreted as the result of armed vi-olence and the amputated arms as trophies (Chenal et al. 2015). In addition to Bergheim, a series of other examples showing violence have been recorded from pits (e.g., Heidelberg–Handschuhsheim) and contemporary enclosure ditches holding large numbers of human remains (Wahl & Höhn 1988, Chenal et al. 2015: 1329 with references; see also Jeunesse 2012).

Examples of intergroup violence are also known from the Globular Amphora culture (c. 3300–2700 BC), as well as from other areas of Neolithic/Chalcolithic Europe, e.g., at Koszyce in southern Poland from c. 2800 BC (Schroeder et al. 2019), Potočani in Croatia from c. 4200 BC (Novak et al. 2021) and Els Trocs in the Spanish Pyrenees from c. 5300 BC (Alt et al. 2020).

223The violent Indo- Europeans

3.3 Violence in Corded Ware societies

The grave mentioned above from Koszyce belongs to the Globular Amphora culture; it dates to c. 2880–2776 BC and is therefore contemporary with the ear-ly Corded Ware. Genetically, the interred individuals are clearly different from the contemporary and neighbouring Corded Ware groups, as they do not have steppe-related ancestry. Whether the expansion of Corded Ware groups was the reason for the massacre is not easy to say, but it has been suggested as a reasonable scenario for the event (Schroeder et al. 2019). Together with the multiple Cord-ed Ware burials from Eulau, Koszyce suggests that the emergence and spread of Corded Ware communities caused violent intergroup conflicts.

Direct traces of violence have been recorded on a series of (usually healed) skulls from the German Corded Ware (including the Single Grave culture). These show a higher frequency of presumed combat injuries on male skulls, compared to their female counterparts, indicating that violence is closely related to males and, from the analysed skulls, often non-lethal (Lidke 2012). Furthermore, there appears to be a correlation between skull traumas, males and the presence of stone battle-axes (but also other stone items such as mace heads, etc.) in Cen-tral German Corded Ware graves. Most of the traumas found on male skulls are located on the left front and top indicating that face-to-face fights between two right-handed opponents caused the injuries. Thus, it seems very plausible that the widely distributed Corded Ware stone battle-axes were actually used in close combat (Wicke et al. 2012, Schwarz 2015; see also Heath 2017: 37–51).

As the skeletal material from the Danish Single Grave culture (Corded Ware) is very rarely preserved, it is not possible to observe whether a similar correspond-ence between skull traumas and battle-axes exists. However, with the emergence of Single Grave societies on the Jutland Peninsula, we see a dramatic increase of more than 900% in the number of stone battle-axes. This trend increases further in the Early Late Neolithic (c. 2350–1950 BC) when flint daggers replaced stone battle-axes as the main weapon and warrior symbol (Iversen 2015: 89–90 and 135–136, 2017: 368–369 with references). Thus, weapons were certainly present in the Danish Single Grave culture and, based on the data from the Central Ger-man Corded Ware, they were also used in combat. Direct evidence of a violent encounter from the Danish Single Grave culture has been recorded in the stone cist burial at Gjerrild, eastern Jutland, which contained the remains of at least ten individuals buried over a period of c. 300 years, from 2600/2500 to 2200 BC. A tanged flint arrowhead had penetrated the breastbone of a male aged 20–30, and two similar arrowheads were found in the cist, one by the right hip of a male aged

It is noteworthy that the two individuals associated with arrowheads and traumas have matching radiocarbon dates and could theoretically be victims of the same or a series of related encoun-ters between Single Grave culture groups (Egfjord et al. 2021).

3.4 Displaying the warrior – the Danish case

I have already mentioned the focus on battle axes and the display of warriors seen, for example, in the Jutland single graves (cf. Hübner 2005: 632–633 fig. 454, Vand-kilde 2006, Kristiansen 2009). The typical (male) grave goods in the early phase (c. 2850–2600 BC) consist of a stone battle-axe in addition to, e.g., a flint axe, ar-rowheads, blades, a pair of amber discs, and a beaker (Figure 3). However, if we

![https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/notebooklm/ABzcPv3ol_zG7UwYWz9lbRl-pOV3ZRNTClhg043ZEzZaJTKz00B-xZaHuaF5F0ttV1JRmGHjYUlUTclBG4CrTXXHgIzRGDKdzdKLt4pzVg5fHGWsEJHZ_H-4XGiZ3rH_thmLu2lSMIWitQ=w1280-h1051-v0](https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/notebooklm/ABzcPv3ol_zG7UwYWz9lbRl-pOV3ZRNTClhg043ZEzZaJTKz00B-xZaHuaF5F0ttV1JRmGHjYUlUTclBG4CrTXXHgIzRGDKdzdKLt4pzVg5fHGWsEJHZ_H-4XGiZ3rH_thmLu2lSMIWitQ=w1280-h1051-v0?authuser=0)

225The violent Indo- Europeans

look at the typical grave goods found in the Early Neolithic (c. 4000–3300 BC) non-megalithic earth graves and dolmens, we find the same range of elements. Though far from frequent, weaponry is present in the form of stone battle-axes, mace heads, and flint halberds alongside flint axes, various flake tools, amber ornaments, and pottery (Ebbesen 1994a: 45, 2011: 283–299; Figure 4). This basic picture is repeated in the late Middle Neolithic northwest Jutland stone-packing graves (c. 3100–2800 BC), which presumably represent wagon burials holding flint axes, pottery, amber beads, and occasionally stone battle-axes (Jørgensen 1977, Fabricius & Becker 1996: 136–195, Johannsen & Laursen 2010; Figure 5). Even though the representation of the warrior figure/persona appears far more integrated and dominant in the early Single Grave period compared to the previ-ous Neolithic phases, we can faintly see a similar conceptualization of the warrior in the Early Neolithic graves.

4 Concluding remarks

In this article, I have tried to nuance the picture of the peaceful Neolithic farmers that were subdued by violent incoming Indo- Europeans. I have done this not by trying to scale down the potential violent nature of early Indo- European societies, but rather by stressing some violent aspects of the pre–Corded Ware Neolithic. I do not find it convincing to argue for a significant increase in violence after the appearance of the Corded Ware. Violence is, and has probably always been, a la-tent feature of human societies that can increase or break out in different regions in certain socially unstable situations.

On the other hand, the scale of violence and its degree of organization has generally increased through time in line with technological advancements, and while interpersonal and intergroup violence certainly occurred in Neolithic and Chalcolithic societies, it most likely took the shape of ‘simple warfare’ (i.e., raids and massacres), or sometimes perhaps even as mock or formalized/ritualized non-lethal battles. The scale of warfare seems to be the same throughout the Ne-olithic, even though we have more sources available (historical linguistics) when it comes to describing the later period concerning early Indo- European societies.

I am generally in favour of the hypothesis that early Indo- European speakers had social structures resembling those described as the *kori̯os institution, Män-nerbund/Jungmannschaft, ‘black youth’ or the like. The presence of such social

Figure 5. Grave goods from stone-packing grave, feature XIII at Vroue Hede II, central Jutland, early third millennium BC: Funnel Beaker pottery, thick-butted flint axes, double-axe–shaped amber bead and double-edged stone battle-axe. After E. Jørgensen (1993: 113).

227The violent Indo- Europeans

organizations provides a reasonable explanation for the relatively rapid dispersal of steppe ancestry across much of Europe during the early third millennium BC. However, in this vivid reconstruction of the violent male-driven Indo- European expansion (which shares many similarities with the appealing story commonly told of Scandinavian Viking raiders in the 8th–11th centuries AD), we must not draw a simplified and idyllic picture of the preceding Neolithic societies. Many of the material, and probably also social-organizational, features ascribed to the Yamnaya and Corded Ware cultures were already widespread in Europe before the steppe migrations (cf. Heyd 2017, Iversen 2019). Perhaps Neolithic societies were even patrilineal, patrilocal and hierarchical long before the steppe influenc-es arrived, as suggested by some genetic studies (e.g., Sánchez-Quinto et al. 2019, Cassidy et al. 2020, Dulias et al. 2022, Fowler et al. 2022).

Pre–Corded Ware Neolithic societies seem to be quite familiar with intergroup violence, raids, massacres and what I have referred to as ‘simple warfare’, and ful-ly capable of carrying them out. This is notably the case with the Linear Pottery culture, where the cranial fractures from many sites seem to be inflicted by stone axes and shoe-last adzes belonging to these early farming communities, indicating that the attackers came from other Linear Pottery culture communities (Golitko & Keeley 2007: 339, Wahl & Trautmann 2012: 84). But violence must not be con-sidered a feature characteristic only of the Linear Pottery culture – it also applies to later Neolithic/Chalcolithic groups targeting, e.g., Corded Ware communities, as clearly illustrated by the Eulau-scenario. Furthermore, even though the display of the warrior figure/persona seems to intensify with the Corded Ware, it was cer-tainly there before, as illustrated by the finds from Early Neolithic burials.
