Part III MobILIty, Gender,

and SoCIaL StruCture

An update on the Corded Ware culture

Formation and spread, social aspects, human–canid relations, and tooth and shell status items

Mikkel Nørtoft Prehistoric Archaeology, Saxo Institute, University of Copenhagen 1

This paper provides an update on general social aspects of migrations

from the Ukrainian steppe in the 3rd millennium bce from archaeology,

DNA, and linguistics. It also provides a quantification of the prestige value

of some tooth and shell status items in the Czech Corded Ware culture.

Furthermore, it raises the issue of currently unconvincing archaeological

evidence that wolves/dogs were linked with young male warrior bands in

the formation of the Corded Ware culture, as suggested by Anthony (2022)

and Kristiansen et al. (2017), showing that dogtooth (and shell) ornaments

were in fact overwhelmingly associated with females in the Corded Ware

culture. Although the paper does not give an exhaustive overview of all the

available data, it attempts to inspire more detailed archaeolinguistic and

bioarchaeological studies into human–canid gender and age relationships

in early Indo- European societies.

As this paper covers a wide range of topics relating to 3rd-millennium BCE steppe migrations in Europe, it is divided into two parts: Part I gives an update on the social aspects of the formation and spread of the Corded Ware culture from an-cient DNA and archaeology, and some notes on how this may inform on Indo- European phylogenetic branching. Part II provides a critical archaeological as-sessment of the role of dogs/wolves in connection with these migrations through dog burials and dogtooth ornaments, especially in relation to a widespread hy-pothesis that young male warriors migrating from the steppe associated them-selves with dogs or wolves.

1 I would like to sincerely thank the reviewers for their constructive comments on the paper, and the Saxo Institute at University of Copenhagen for supporting this interdis-ciplinary research project. The paper was first submitted in 2021 and revised in 2022, and despite some updates and additions during proofreading, some aspects may be somewhat out of date or missing references to sources which have appeared since then.

242 Mikkel Nørtoft

Part I An update on the social aspects of early steppe migrations in Europe and their relation to some Indo- European phylogenetic problems

1 The spread of the Corded Ware culture

In recent years, ancient genomic studies have shown that the genetic landscape in most of Europe changed drastically from being primarily Anatolian Farmer–de-rived in the early Neolithic to being Pontic steppe/forest-steppe–derived in the 3rd millennium bce (Allentoft et al. 2015, Haak et al. 2015, Malmström et al. 2019, Olalde et al. 2018 and 2019, Papac et al. 2021). That the migration underlying this change played a crucial role in the formation of the Corded Ware culture (CWC) had already been suggested previously by linguists and some archaeolo-gists (relatively recently by Kristiansen et al. 2017, Anthony 2017, Chang et al. 2015, Anthony 2007, Mallory 1989), but ancient genomics continues to provide more evidence supporting a connection between these prehistoric steppe migrations and the spread of Indo- European languages. Most recent is the discovery of a hitherto genetically undetected subsequent Late Bronze Age spread of ancestry from Continental Europe to The British Isles and Iberia, supporting linguistic hypotheses of a Proto- Celtic homeland in Central Europe, consistent with the spread of the Urnfield phenomenon and the early Hallstatt culture (Patterson et al. 2022, Olalde et al. 2019). The details and social dynamics of how the steppe migrations happened, their more precise origins, and whether there were several waves of people from the steppe during the 3rd millennium bce is the next part of the puzzle currently under scrutiny (Heyd 2021).

How these questions may affect ideas of the internal structure of the Indo- European language tree and its inter-branch contacts will probably become clear-er in the coming years, but genetics, especially Y-haplogroup patterns, offer sup-port for an internal ‘super-branch’ connecting the Indo- Iranian (R1a-Z93) and Balto-Slavic (R1a-Z282/Z283) branches in their ancestral branch R1a-Z645 in the eastern CWC (Narasimhan et al. 2019, Nordqvist and Heyd 2020).

R1a-Z93–rich groups seem to migrate back east towards the Ural Mountains at a relatively early date (c. 2900 BCE), whence they form the Russian Fatyanovo (c. 2900–2200 BCE), Balanovo (2500–2200 BCE), and Abashevo (2200–1900 BCE) cul-

243An update on the Corded Ware culture

tures2, and subsequently the Sintashta (2100–1700 BCE), Andronovo (1900–1200 BCE), and Srubnaya (1900–1100 BCE) cultures (Nordqvist and Heyd 2020, Antho-ny et al. 2016: 12-19), through which Indo- Iranian languages most likely spread throughout Central Asia and into South Asia (Narasimhan et al. 2019). R1a-Z645 also spread into the East Baltic (possibly in its derived R1a-Z282 form), Southwest-ern Finland, and eastern Sweden (likely via Finland, Holmqvist et al. 2018) during the 3rd millennium BCE (Mittnik et al. 2018, Malmström et al. 2019, Allentoft et al. 2024a and 2024b). Denmark and southern Sweden feature both R1a-Z645 and R1b-L151 (and its descendants R1b-P312 and R1b-U106) during the 3rd millennium BCE, the latter possibly from a second Bell Beaker culture incursion (Allentoft et al. 2024a and 2024b, Malmström et al. 2019, Mittnik et al. 2018). For a graphical overview of steppe-derived Y-haplogroups R1a and R1b, see Figure 1.

A Core Indo- European term for ‘copper’ (or perhaps generically ‘metal’) is preserved in Gothic aiz < Proto- Germanic *ajiz- < Core-IE *h₂áies- (Thorsø 2024, Olander 2024), but no metallurgy and almost no metal has been found in Scandi-navia or Finland, and very little in Northern Europe in general, during the CWC period.3 Metal then reappears in Southern Scandinavia in the subsequent Bell Beaker/Late Neolithic period (Iversen 2015: 108–109, Nordqvist et al. 2012: 8, Lutz et al. 1998: 46–50). The conditions for preserving such a word in Scandinavian CWC communities, assuming they spoke an Indo- European dialect, are there-fore quite poor.

2 The formation of the Abashevo culture west of the Urals has recently, based on similar-ities in metals, burial rites, and ceramics, been suggested to be a product of Bell Beaker and Early Bronze Age culture groups in Central Europe and the Carpathian–Danube region migrating east (Mimokhod 2022). Whether this can be supported genetically remains to be tested. The typical Y-haplogroup R1b-P312 in Bell Beaker culture individ-uals (e.g. Olalde et al. 2018, 2019), is (so far) quite scarce or even missing in Srubnaya, Sintashta (two potential candidate genomes of R1b-M269, ancestral to R1b-P312, are known in this area, one from Sintashta, I0980 at Kammenyi Ambar 5, and one from the contemporary Potapovka culture, I7670 at Grachevka), and the Andronovo complex (Narasimhan et al. 2019). If Abashevo has some relation to Bell Beaker groups, their paternal lineages seem to have been outcompeted in Eastern Europe and Central Asia, where R1a-Z93 became dominant after being introduced in the Fatyanovo–Balanovo culture.

3 Only three small copper finds with secure context are known in Scandinavia, belonging to the later Battle Axe period (after 2600 BCE) in Sweden, and interpreted as Bell Beak-er culture imports (Iversen 2015: 108). A copper disc in a reused long barrow in Rude, eastern Jutland, is seen by some as of Early Neolithic type, but also has parallels in the Bohemian or Swiss CWC (see discussion and further references in Madsen 2020: 35-36, Allentoft et al. 2024a: Supplementary Note 6, 184–185).

This, along with the consecutive spreads of ancestry and Y-haplogroup shifts into Scandinavia may suggest that the arrival of the linguistic ancestor(s) of Ger-manic was more complex than just the arrival of CWC groups (Single Grave/ Battle Axe variants). The early date and close interval (c. 400–500 years) of these incursions into Scandinavia would make it extremely difficult to untangle which of them gave rise to ancestral pre-proto-Germanic. However, the mix of pater-nal lineages in Scandinavia could perhaps reconcile the debate on the phyloge-netic position of the Germanic branch in the Indo- European family tree, having isoglosses shared with both the Balto-Slavic and Italo-Celtic branches (although some of these may be due to later convergence, see discussions by Pronk 2022 and Hansen & Kroonen 2022). Thus, Germanic may have formed as a mixture of sim-ilar Indo- European dialects during the 3rd millennium BCE, one in close contact with a gene pool of pre- or para-Proto- Balto-Slavic speakers (R1a-Z645-branch), and one (later) in close contact with pre-Italo-Celtic speakers (in the West/Cen-tral European Bell Beaker culture, R1b-P151-branch). Core-IE *h₂áies- ‘copper’ into Scandinavia, whether as a singular loanword or along with a second Indo- European incursion into Scandinavia to form (part of) ancestral Pre-Proto- Germanic.

Traditionally, the migrations from the steppe, and early Indo- European soci-ety itself, have been associated with male-dominated society (Gimbutas 1993: 218, Mallory 1989: 123), a male warrior elite (e.g., Vandkilde 2009: 68–70), patrilocal marriage practices,4 and patrilineal inheritance (Olsen 2019, Sjögren et al. 2020, Mittnik et al. 2019). Furthermore, several ancient genomic studies have shown that 3rd-millennium BCE steppe-derived migrations were often male-driven (Pa-pac et al. 2021, Furtwängler et al. 2020, Olalde et al. 2018 and 2019, Goldberg et al. 2017), and high-status graves of some non-local female individuals in Bronze-Age Germany have been linked to female exogamy (Mittnik et al. 2019).

Comparative anthropological evidence of stateless societies across the globe suggests that marriage transfer as some form of payment is more or less ubiqui-tous, especially bridewealth (also, especially formerly, termed ‘bride-price’), but sometimes in combination with dowry (Testart 2013). Simply put, bridewealth is when the groom (or his family) pays to the bride (or her family), while dowry is when the bride’s family pays or gifts to the bride (e.g., in textile form, trousseau5) or to the married couple; in Hindu law, the dowry is owned by the bride (strī-dha-na ‘woman’s wealth’6), whereas in (Roman-influenced) Europe, it was managed by the husband (Testart 2013: 27). Both can exist in the same society, often on a spectrum of social class where either the dowry (typically upper class, urban) or bridewealth (typically lower class, rural) may be the larger payment, depending on which party has more status (Testart 2013). Bridewealth is known in ancient Europe with Germanic tribes (Visigoths, Lombards, Franks), while dowry is his-torically most prevalent in ancient Rome and Greece (e.g., in 6th-century BCE Athens as 10% of the bride’s father’s wealth). Due to the Germanic migrations,

For example, Derksen (2015: 258) describes krienas as “bride-price, tribute which a peasant girl that is getting married must pay to her master”, a definition that fits dowry rather than bridewealth. However, it is difficult to find one clear etymon for ‘bridewealth’ or ‘dowry’ preserved in the majority of the daughter branches, so their Proto- (or Core-) Indo- European age may be questioned, or their fragmentary attestation could be the product of continuously changing customs. According to Anderson (2007: 158), bridewealth is more common in polygamous societies, while dowry is more common in monogamous societies. Mallory and Adams (1997: 123) suggest that, while a possibly shared word for ‘concubine’, *parikah₂, has been attested in Celtic and Iranian,11 and illegitimate children were not unheard of (and could still be heirs under Irish law), early Indo- European society was probably not formally polygamous. If early Indo- European societies were not (formally) polygamous, but rather (mostly) monogamous, we might expect dowry to play a role as well. While Testart shows that dowry was most prominent in state societies, the Greek customs being particularly influential, he also shows that both kušata ‘bride-wealth’ and iwara ‘dowry’ were present in Hittite customs, mostly in the upper class (Testart 2013: 39). While Germanic tribes are known for their bridewealth, it is interesting to note that most of the Germanic attestations for *wetman- seem to suggest a meaning ‘dowry’, rather than ‘bridewealth’. This may, however, simply be because these words were documented after the Christianization of Northern Europe where dowry customs became dominant.

Turning to possible male clans, previous studies have shown a strong bottle-neck in paternal lineages (i.e., Y-chromosome haplogroups) in both the Yamna12 culture (R1b-Z2103), the Corded Ware culture (R1a-Z645 and derivatives), and the subsequent Bell Beaker culture (R1b-L151 and its descendant branch R1b-P312). The R1b-lineages so far both seem to derive from R1b-M269 on the steppe or forest-steppe, and R1a-Z645 derives from R1a-M41713. The exact presence of

248 Mikkel Nørtoft

R1a-M417 on the Eneolithic steppe is still (at the time of writing) a bit of a mys-tery.14 Recently, Anthony et al. (2022: 40) reported that most of their, as yet unpub-lished, male genomes from the Eneolithic Serednii Stih culture (5th millennium BCE) in Ukraine belonged to haplogroups R1a and I, though without specifying which subbranch of R1a. At contemporary Khvalynsk in the Volga region, where instead R1b dominates, only one case of R1a (M459, too basal on the R1a tree to reveal specific steppe lineages) was found. The bottleneck in Y-haplogroups has been suggested to be an indication of blood feud–like competition between males of different patrilineal clans eradicating some male lineages from subsequent gene pools (Zeng et al. 2018). An institutionalized form of such blood-feuding is still known from the Albanian law of Kanun, where dishonour from another clan can be resolved by killing a male member of that clan, and has parallels in Corsica, Northern Caucasus, and Northwestern India (Cara et al. 2015: 181).

Such a scenario for early steppe-derived societies could perhaps explain the bottleneck of Y-haplogroups in these groups (Yamna, Corded Ware, and Bell Beaker) and the mass migrations from the steppe being divided into separate paternal lineages (especially Corded Ware R1a-Z645 being very different from Yamna R1b-Z2103 and Bell Beaker R1b-P312).

However, new CWC genomes (Papac et al. 2021) with some of the earliest dat-ings so far (c. 2900 cal bce) have shown that early Corded Ware–associated males in Bohemia had a range of different R1a and R1b Y-haplogroups, one instance of haplogroup Q, and one (typically Yamna) haplogroup R1b-Z2103. Haplogroup Q is usually associated with West-Siberian hunter-gatherers, but is also found in the Yamna-neighbouring Steppe Maykop culture north of the Caucasus (Wang et al. 2019, Narasimhan et al. 2019) and in a few genomes from Khvalynsk (Anthony et al. 2022). R1a then becomes dominant in the Bohemian CWC only from 2600 bce, but it is not the R1a-Z645 subbranch that dominates here, unlike elsewhere in

14 Previously reported in individual I6561, who was first dated to c. 4000 BCE by Mathie-son et al. (2018) but since redated by C14 to c. 2134–1950 cal BCE. The problematic date was seemingly first discussed publicly in a blog post (Quiles 2019); the new dates were corroborated in a Twitter post by Iain Mathieson on 10 June 2022 (https://twitter.com/ mathiesoniain/status/1535319673662758913) and later updated in David Reich’s reposi-tory of published ancient genomes, AADR, available at https://reich.hms.harvard.edu). The new date of this genome is more reasonable due to its (also later specified) Y-hap-logroup R1a-Z93, derived from R1a-Z645, and otherwise only known from the later 3rd millennium BCE, as well as the mutation for lactase persistence (reported already in Mathieson et al. 2018), which only slowly increases in frequency from the Bronze Age onwards (Wilkin 2022).

249An update on the Corded Ware culture

the CWC. This shows that larger studies focussing on thorough time-transects in one region can completely change the way we understand these migrations, and that the Y-haplogroup bottleneck we thought we were seeing in early steppe-de-rived individuals was not necessarily a steppe migration phenomenon. It rather happened in the transition from early to late Corded Ware, and could be due to selection, social structure, or an influx of non-local males carrying R1a-M417 (Papac et al. 2021). Interestingly, in the Bell Beaker period of Bohemia, R1b-P312 (a sub-branch of the early Bohemian CWC R1b-L151) becomes the dominant lin-eage. It continues well into the Bronze Age (primarily the Únětice culture) along with other lineages, including R1a-Z645, best known from non-Bohemian CWC individuals, as well as typical hunter-gatherer Y-haplogroups, such as I and C and new genome-wide admixture possibly from the northeast, perhaps Poland or the Baltic (Papac et al. 2021). The genetic landscape after the arrival of steppe ancestry in Central-Northern Europe is thus not static, but under constant change from external and/or internal social processes.

The increased and continuous long-distance mobility of especially males across the CWC world has also been suggested archaeologically by Bourgeois and Kroon (2017) and linked to subsequent diffusion of new artefact styles be-tween regions during the Corded Ware period (Furholt 2014). Thus, shifting ar-chaeological trends and genetic changes across Europe during the Corded Ware, Bell Beaker, and Únětice periods begin to unfold beyond static culture-historical categories.

In Papac et al. (2021), all 75 CWC graves in the Central Bohemian cemetery Vliněves were sampled for DNA, yielding 21 genomes that passed quality checks. Of these genomes, only one first-degree genetic relationship was reported, be-tween a father and son lying on each side of the cemetery. Only one other first-de-gree CWC genetic relationship was found in Bohemia, at Obříství, though they were reported more frequently for the later Bell Beaker (at three sites, including multiple links at Radovesice) and Únětice (at five sites) cultures in Bohemia (Pa-pac et al. 2021: Table S4). Although similar dense sampling is needed from other CWC cemeteries, this one case study perhaps suggests that people were not nec-essarily buried together in close family units in the CWC, and that they were still very mobile during this period and connected their families in wider networks. If this is the case, such long-distance networks already in the Corded Ware period and well into the Bronze Age could be supported linguistically by a widespread Indo- European guest-host institution that secured proper treatment when vis-iting distant like-minded families or clans (Nørtoft 2017: 98–99 with references; Anthony 2007: 31–32, 303, 342; Mallory et al. 2006: 269).

250 Mikkel Nørtoft

Some studies using summed probability distribution of radiocarbon dates and/or archaeobotanical data as proxies for activity have suggested a decline in population in Northern, Northwestern and Central Europe during the late 4th millennium BCE, followed by an increase with the appearance of the CWC. How-ever, there is regional variation to this pattern, hinting that some nuances in this decline could be due to population movements as well, and likely also different lifestyles and mortuary expression resulting in different amounts and types of material left behind (Colledge et al. 2019, Kolář et al. 2022, Barnett et al. 2020, Shennan et al. 2013, Hinz et al. 2012). However, a recent study using pollen data and multiple proxies for temperature now estimates a long decline in mean annu-al temperature in the Eastern Carpathian region starting c. 3400 BCE and lasting until c. 2200 BCE from 12 to 9 °C, and with intermediate temperature drops in cycles of 330–370 years at 3400 BCE, 3000 BCE, 2700 BCE, and 2200 BCE. The most pronounced events were at 3000 BCE (1.7 °C drop), and 2200 BCE (3.3 °C drop) (Ramos-Román et al. 2022). The drops at 3400 BCE and 3000 BCE may have been a strong incentive for some communities to abandon farming and rely more on animal husbandry. We see this with the rise of the Globular Amphora culture, the spread of the Pitted Ware culture in Scandinavia (with more emphasis on fish-ing/hunting), and the appearance of the stone packing graves in Jutland with a new herder symbology in the form of cattle burials (Johannsen and Laursen 2010, Iversen 2019, Szmyt 2010, Woidich 2014). Migrant pastoralists from the steppe, such as the early CWC, would be well adapted to this more mobile lifestyle in Central and Northern Europe.

Finds of plague (Yersinia pestis) in Neolithic skeletons dated to after the steppe migrations at first suggested that steppe migrants might have spread this disease around Europe (Rasmussen et al. 2015). However, a later study found plague before the steppe migrations (dated c. 2900 BCE) in Gökhem, Sweden, and suggested that a plague pandemic in Europe could have been an important factor in the decline in population.15 A potential zoonotic transfer and breeding ground for this plague pandemic was proposed to be in the mega-towns of the Cucuteni-Trypillia culture where animals and humans may have lived close to-gether in large numbers, although plague has not been found there yet (Rascovan et al. 2019). Later, others have found a more basal, possibly non-lethal, strain of plague in a hunter-gatherer from Latvia, c. 3200 BCE, the strain emerging al-

15 Further evidence for plague in larger kin groups from the later Scandinavian Funnel Beaker culture groups has recently been forwarded in Seersholm et al. (2024), support-ing the hypothesis of plague as a factor in the Neolithic decline, at least in Scandinavia.

251An update on the Corded Ware culture

ready in the 5th millennium BCE, which could indicate that the earliest plague may not have caused an epidemic but rather happened in independent zoonotic events, in this case possibly from eating beavers or other rodents (Susat et al. 2021).16 The (now) second major strain first described by Rasmussen et al. (2015), and widespread in the 3rd millennium BCE, may have been more dangerous than the basal hunter-gatherer strain, but being pneumonic it probably only caused relatively localized outbreaks similar to modern pneumonic plague, and may not have been a major candidate for the Neolithic decline. The more dangerous flea-adapted bubonic plague (the third known major prehistoric strain) was first found in an individual of the Srubnaya culture in the Volga region c. 1800 BCE (Spyrou et al. 2018), and recently also in Iberia c. 1200 BCE. The flea-adapted and non–flea-adapted strains seem to have coexisted for at least 2500 years until the flea-adapted became dominant (Andrades Valtueña et al. 2022).

With all these social aspects mentioned here, it should be kept in mind that The Third Science Revolution in archaeology, as Kristiansen calls it (most recently in Kristiansen 2022: 4), has rapidly increased the pace of new studies and the ac-cumulation of data on the aspects described here. As exemplified in, for example, the CWC Y-haplogroups, the amount of hunter-gatherer admixture in the CWC, and the role of Neolithic plague, new data regularly makes us change the models of the past, to the effect that most overviews of these aspects become outdated in some details even before they are published, this study included.

2 The origins of the Corded Ware culture – current status

Papac et al. (2021) showed that there was a larger proportion of hunter-gather-er–like admixture (5–15%) in the early Bohemian Corded Ware than previously realized. Working proxy sources for some early non–steppe-like CWC female in-dividuals are found in the Globular Amphora culture, Neolithic (hunter-gather-er–rich) Latvia, Neolithic Ukraine, or even the Pitted Ware culture of Scandinavia. These specific groups may or may not have contributed to the early Corded Ware hunter-gatherer admixture; some as yet unsampled groups with similar ances-try may have been more accurate sources. The Globular Amphora culture does provide a plausible archaeological link, already showing cultural contact with un-sampled groups from the Ukrainian steppe – the pre-/early-Yamna Zhivotilovka

16 Recently, Krause-Kyora et al. (2024, preprint) has shown dogs to be potential interme-diary carriers of plague to humans in Neolithic Europe.

252 Mikkel Nørtoft

group – around the time the first Corded Ware migrants appear in Central Eu-rope (Szmyt 2021, Heyd 2021, Manzura 2016). Single Grave culture genomes from Denmark are now also modelled as having Yamna-like steppe ancestry (60–85%), and 10–23% Globular Amphora-like ancestry, but only minor (3–18%) ancestry from the local Funnel Beaker culture, a composition they also model for CWC genomes across Europe (Allentoft et al. 2024b: 12–13).17

The Zhivotilovka group in Ukraine have burial traditions that resemble typ-ical Corded Ware positions (left-crouched = female, right-crouched = male, al-though the Zhivotilovka individuals have not yet been osteologically sexed), some stone shaft-hole axes (or ‘battle-axes’), and single graves under a kurgan. We do not yet know the genetics of this Zhivotilovka group18 or other, neighbour-ing hybrid steppe-farmer groups from the late Trypillia C2 group (Sofievka/Kas-perintsy/Gorodsk/Vikhvatintsy/Usatove variants). Some were buried with stone hammer-axes, and some with cord-decorated ceramics (also prominent in many steppe groups), which will likely be important for understanding Corded Ware origins (Heyd 2021, Szmyt 2021, Manzura 2016, Kadrow et al. 2010, Szmyt 2010: 184–185). One of these late 4th-millennium bce hybrid steppe-farmer groups, the Usatove culture around Odessa, is described by Anthony (2007: 271, 344–360) as having steppe elites (‘patrons’) in kurgans, and farmer ‘clients’ in flat graves. Patron– client relations are discussed in more detail by Ginevra (this volume).

Although the exact sources of farmer and hunter-gatherer admixture in the CWC have not yet been clearly identified, the Globular Amphora culture seems a

17 Globular Amphora culture genomes are labeled “Poland_5000BP_4700BP” in Al-lentoft et al. (2024a and 2024b).

18 Two genomes from one double grave associated with the Zhivotilovka group were re-cently included in two large preprint articles (Lazaridis et al. 2024 and Nikitin et al. 2024), but they were genetically very different from each other and from CWC ge-nomes and may not be representative for the Zhivotilovka genetic ancestry in general. Lazaridis et al. (2024) did show the North(-west?) Pontic region (“west of ‘Core Yamna’”, and earlier Serednii Stih) to be the most likely source of the steppe component in CWC genomes, but still primarily with different Y-haplogroups (still primarily R1b-Z2103) from those common in the CWC (R1b-L151 and R1a-M417). “The geographical home-lands of the Corded Ware and Yamnaya would … conceivably be in geographical prox-imity to allow for their synchronous emergence and shared ancestry. The Dnipro-Don area of the Serednii Stih culture fits the genetic data …” (24). The study thus supports the general North/Northwest Pontic source area described above and close genetic re-lations between North Pontic ‘Core Yamna’ and the steppe component in the CWC, but still without the ‘smoking gun’ for genetic CWC origins due to their mismatch in Y-haplogroups.

253An update on the Corded Ware culture

promising genetic and archaeological fit, and hybrid variants of the Trypillia C2 and Złota groups may also have been involved, as may Southern Polish Funnel Beaker and Funnel Beaker–related groups. The eclectic Budzhak group of the western Yamna in the Dnister region connecting the Zhivotilovka/North-North-west Pontic Yamna and Globular Amphora cultures, as well as cultures in the Danube and Carpathians, likely reflects prolonged contacts and extensive mobili-ty in this transition zone during the early 3rd millennium bce (Heyd 2021, Ivano-va 2013). This also indicates that the sudden expansion of people from the steppe may have been ‘seeded’ by these interactions both before and during the early 3rd millennium bce (Heyd 2021, Włodarczak 2021). Expansion from the steppe may thus have been about trade as well as raiding, and not necessarily as violent as sometimes portrayed (Barras 2019), although occasional hostilities during this period have also been documented in Europe (Schroeder et al. 2019, Konopka et al. 2016, Fibiger et al. 2013, Haak et al. 2008).

To this we can add that no clear evidence for taking captives has been found in connection with the CWC, and that institutionalized slavery has not been gener-ally suggested before the Early Bronze Age in Central Europe, e.g., in the Únětice culture (Meller 2019: 57, 67).

If we look at the Indo- European vocabulary, no clear Proto- (or even Core) Indo- European word for slavery is reconstructable; most attestations are inde-pendent secondary words in the daughter branches (Campanile 1998: 16-17). However, a few words are still of interest. One such word is *h₂m̥bhi-kʷolh₁o- with the literal meaning ‘moving around’ found in Latin anculus ‘servant’ (only in li-$thurgical contexts), and more commonly ancilla ‘female servant’,19 Greek αμφί-πολος ‘moving around; servant, handmaid’, Mycenaean a-pi-qo-ro /ampʰi-kʷo-$los/, ‘servant’,20 and Sanskrit abhi-cara- ‘servant’.21 Both Greek, Indo- Iranian, and Latin also use this word in a religious or ritual context ‘servant of the gods, priest(ess)’,22 so it may have been the old Indo- European context as well, instead of captives or slaves (Olsen 2019: 157).

19 Latin reflexes of PIE *h₂m̥bhi are ambi- or amb- before vowels, but an- or am- before consonants, with -n- before velars (DeVaan 2008: 37). DeVaan (2008: 41) explains the unexpected -i- in ancilla as derived from a folk-etymological diminutive in the male anc-ulus given a new diminutive for the feminine *ank-elela to Latin ancilla (for hap-lology of -elela to -illa, cf. *septemo-mēmbris ‘of the seventh month’ [in the Roman calendar] to septembris).

20 For the Mycenaean word, see Beekes (2010: 95). 21 Initial laryngeal disappears in Indo- Iranian and syllabic *m̥C becomes Sanskrit aC. $22 Cf. abhicārá- ‘witchcraft’, αμφί-πολος ‘priest(ess)’, Latin anc(u)lare ‘serve the gods’ $

254 Mikkel Nørtoft

Another interesting word in this context is Latin servus ‘(male) servant, slave’, perhaps from a stem *ser-u̯o-. Olsen (2019: 158) tentatively connects this with the homonymous *ser-u̯o/ah₂- (masculine/feminine), used in the same seman-tic realm23 but referring to thievery and raiding, and found in Welsh herw ‘raid (usually cattle), outlawry’ and Archaic Irish serb ‘theft’ from *ser-u̯-ah₂-, and pos-sibly also in Hittite šāru ‘booty’ from an o-grade *sor-u-.24 From the o-grade and zero-grade, we could perhaps add Lithuanian sarióti ‘devastate, loot’ and Latvian sirt ‘loot, raid’ (LIV² 535; Nørtoft 2017: 89). If this connection is to be accepted, ‘raid, loot’ would be the original meaning, and ‘captive, slave’ in Latin would be secondary, understood as the bounty of raiding.

A similar semantic connection could be suggested for another word connected with raiding, Proto- Indo- European *lah₂-(u̯)-/*lh₂a-(u̯)- (with laryngeal metath-esis) seen in Proto- Germanic *launa- < *lah₂u̯-no- ‘reward, recompense’ (Gothic laun, Old Norse laun > Danish løn, Old English lēan, Old High German lōn; Kro-onen 2013: 329), in Proto- Celtic *(ufo)-lawto- < *lah₂u̯-to- ‘property, wealth’ (OIr. fo-lud ‘substance, material, property; equivalent, reason, cause’, Middle Welsh go-lud, Old Cornish wu-ludoc ‘wealth’ (gloss: dives); Matasović 2009: 397–398), in Proto- Italic *luklo- < *lh₂u-tló- ‘seizure, gain’ with dissimilated instrumental

-tlo- suffix and zero-grade in the root (Lat. lucrum ‘material gain, profit’; De Vaan $2008: 349–350), and in Greek (Attic λεία, Doric λᾱίᾱ < *λᾱϝ-ίᾱ < *lah₂u-i̯eh₂- ‘booty’, (ἀπο-)λαύω ‘enjoy’; Beekes 2010: 118, 842). De Vaan (2008: 350) proposes $that this root could be connected with *lah₂-(u̯-) ‘to fight; army’ found in Anato-lian (Hittitie lāḫḫ- ‘military campaign, journey’, Cuneiform Luwian lahhi(ia)- ‘to $travel, campaign’ < *ló/áh₂-; Kloekhorst 2008: 510–511), in Greek (λᾱ(ϝ)ός ‘men, $army’ < *lah₂-u̯o-, Mycenaean ra-wa-ke-ta- /lāw-āgetās/ ‘army-leader’, Phrygian lawagtaei (dative singular) ‘military leader’; Beekes 2010: 832–833; Matasović 2009: 234–235), and, suffixed *lah₂-iko-, in Proto- Celtic *lāyko- (Old Irish láech ‘warrior’; Matasović 2009: 234–235).

Thus the loot, *lah₂-(u̯)-, would be acquired by fighting or raiding, *lah₂-(u̯-) (De Vaan 2008: 350), like the slave *ser-u̯-ah₂- (at least in Italic) would be the cap-tive (or part of the loot along with cattle and other livestock) acquired in a raid

*ser-u̯-ah₂-. In any case, it seems that the vocabulary for raiding is relatively clear, while the vocabulary for slaves or captives is less certain, and at the point of Core Indo- European probably not an institutionalized practice yet, though captives

(Mayrhofer 1986: 91–92, Beekes 2010: 95, DeVaan 2008: 41). 23 And both with a non-trivial e-grade + *-u̯o- suffix (Olsen 2019: 158). 24 An e/o-grade variation also found in *deru̯o-/deru̯ah₂- vs. *doru ‘tree’ (Olsen 2019: 158).

255An update on the Corded Ware culture

may in some cases have been taken in a raid along with livestock. To the semantic field of armies, we can add *kor-(i̯)os ‘army’ in Baltic, Iranian, Celtic, Germanic, and Greek, which has long been connected with early Indo- European warrior bands (Beekes 2010: 732; Kroonen 2013: 211–212, and more in-depth in McCone 1987).

Recently, Kroonen et al. (2022) re-examined Indo- European terminological evidence of agriculture for various stages of Proto- and Core Indo- European. They concluded that the area that archaeologically (and archaeobotanically) best correlates with the quite limited agricultural vocabulary reconstructable for Core Indo- European is the Northwest Pontic region in the late 4th to early 3rd mil-lennium BCE, supporting the Indo- European homeland region discussed above.

A large genetic study on ancient horses has shown that the horses analyzed in CWC (so far) were wild, suggesting that steppe expansions in the early 3rd millennium bce probably did not happen on horseback, although horses may have been domesticated without riding already in the Yamna period (Librado et al. 2021).25 Intensive dairying on the steppe also seems to have started around the advent of the Yamna culture, 3300 bce, roughly contemporary with the adoption of wheel and wagon technologies which allowed people to move farther away from the rivers and deeper into the steppe for pasture. In turn, dairy (a stable and mobile source of food), a mobile lifestyle, and horses in the herd being better at removing snow cover than other livestock (Wilkin et al. 2021: 350) may have enabled a much more stable subsistence, resulting in more successful births and lower child mortality and paving the way for a population boom on the steppe (Wilkin et al. 2021). To sustain such a rapidly growing population, these steppe herders would have had a high demand for new pastures, explaining their rapid expansion from the steppe around 3000 BCE (Heyd 2021: 386).

Overall, this may change the way we have traditionally imagined these mi-grations, with CWC ancestral migrants not riding on horseback. Whether they migrated in search of new pastures to support a population boom, fled from clan warfare and oppression, or were attracted by foreign resources is still an open question, and one scenario does not rule out the other. If people from the Yamna

25 Trautmann, et al. (2023) have shown that some human skeletons associated with the western Yamna culture in the Carpatho-Balkan region show evidence of horseback riding. This does not change the fact that horses from the CWC so far have been genet-ically unrelated to domestic horses on the steppe in the Yamna culture (Librado et al. 2021), but it may open up the possiblity that Yamna riders drove out ancestors of CWC groups (Zhivotilovka?) from the Ukrainian steppe and explain why Yamna and CWC Y-haplogroups are so different.

256 Mikkel Nørtoft

culture were the only groups suddenly riding horses, it may have been a con-siderable power factor to drive other steppe groups away (of which CWC may be the product).26 At the same time, if herd sizes became larger and the steppe (and dairy) more intensely exploited, it is possible that, as a result of a population boom, second sons would have to leave the family to establish themselves in new territory, and perhaps in this regard make a name for themselves.

A prominent institution of making a name for oneself may be indicated by the Proto- Indo- European word(s) for ‘fame’ (as an adjective *k̑lu-tó- ‘famed, fa-mous’, and as a noun *k̑léu̯-os ‘fame’, both from the root *k̑leu̯-, ‘hear’). Much later naming traditions in the historically attested Indo- European daughter branches still show reflexes of the PIE ‘fame’ word(s) as prominent elements, as in Slavic, Greek, Sanskrit, Illyrian, and possibly Germanic if the Gallehus horn’s Hlewa-gas-tiz is interpreted as ‘fame-guest’,27 a particularly prominent compound in Europe (Jackson 2012: 14–15 [Appendix]; also summarized in Nørtoft 2017: 90–100). We should of course not forget the parallel phrase ‘fame imperishable’ in both Vedic Sanskrit and Greek, which could go back to Core Indo- European *k̑leu̯os n̥-dgʷʰi-tom (Watkins 1995: 173–178), a stage of Indo- European (excluding Anatolian) that may coincide with the Yamna period.

It is not so much the presence of this word in reconstructed Indo- European vocabulary that is interesting, but rather how widespread and well-preserved these two particular formations from the same root are,28 as well as its prominent role in naming practices. The best comparison in the PIE vocabulary may be the widespread *h₁/₃nó(h₃)-mn ̥ ‘name’ (whose exact reconstructed form remains a topic of debate), which also sometimes encompasses the meaning ‘fame, renown’ (e.g., Old Irish ainm), or both words combined (Greek, Tocharian, and Sanskrit)

26 We will need much more detailed bioarchaeological studies to determine who had signs of horse riding and who did not in this period, and thus which of these scenarios are most plausible.

27 For a recent argument that Hlewagastiz rather refers to ‘shelter-guest’, see Nedoma (2022). Even without Hlewagastiz, we still have Germanic attestations of the root in comparable contexts: *hleumunda- < *k̑leu̯-mn-to- in OHG (h)liumunt m. (f.), MHG li-umunt m. ‘Kunde, Ruf, Ruhm, Gerücht’, and *hluda- < *k̑lu-tó- in the Merovingian and Carolingian royal names Hlod-ericus, Chlod-ovechus (Wodtko et al. 2008: 425–426).

28 Cognates in Old Irish, Sanskrit, Avestan, Greek, Armenian, Latin, and Old High Ger-man personal names from PIE *k̑lu-tó-, and cognates in Greek, Old Church Slavonic, Latvian, Lithuanian, Sanskrit, Avestan, Old Irish, Tocharian A and B, and Illyrian per-sonal names from PIE *k̑léu̯-os (see examples with references in Nørtoft 2017: 89–90). An o-grade *k̑lou̯-ah₂- with the meaning ‘fame, reputation’ is more widely attested in Baltic and Slavic (Wodtko et al. 2008: 426).

257An update on the Corded Ware culture

(Mallory & Adams 1997: 192). It may be that ‘name’ primarily served a practically necessary function as a label of identity (Mallory & Adams 1997: 390), while ‘fame, famous’ is a more abstract concept, rather useless in a daily practical context. The widespread preservation of this specific root for ‘fame’ – the two formations being attested in a total of eight or nine of the ten main Indo- European branches29 be-tween them, six branches each30 (not attested in Anatolian) – indicates that it was an important part of at least Core Indo- European vocabulary, a prominent fea-ture of early Indo- European culture, and potentially a driving force for long-dis-tance migrations. It may also have been manifested in oral tradition and/or in the long-lasting custom of building very visible kurgans, which we see across most of the Yamna and Corded Ware cultures, as well as in several subsequent periods. At the same time, *k̑léu̯-os ‘fame’ may have had an important function in regulating behaviour, as the word often also had the connotation of ‘reputation, rumour’ – a bad reputation may have travelled fast in the kind of networks and guest-host institutions mentioned above.

3 Conclusion

Above, I have provided an overview of the current understanding of the migra-tions from the steppe throughout Europe in the 3rd millennium BCE, and some of the social aspects in this connection. A few additional hypotheses have been proposed, e.g., that the widespread preservation of a Core Indo- European word for ‘fame, reputation’, along with the search for fame, may have functioned both as a driving factor in the steppe expansions, and as a behavioural regulating func-tion to maintain one’s reputation in connection with a widespread guest–host institution. This set of related hypotheses is still tentative and should be tested further in the future.

*k̑leu̯-. 30 PIE *k̑lu-tó- is reflected in personal names in Old Irish, Sanskrit, Avestan, Greek, Ar-

menian, Latin, and Old High German; while *k̑léu̯-os is found in personal names in Greek, Old Church Slavonic, Latvian and Lithuanian, Sanskrit, Avestan, Old Irish, To-charian A and B, and Illyrian (see examples with references in Nørtoft 2017: 89–90). An o-grade *k̑lou̯-ah₂- with the meaning ‘fame, reputation’ is more widely attested in Baltic and Slavic (Wodtko et al. 2008: 426).

258 Mikkel Nørtoft

Another hypothesis proposed is that the mix of Y-haplogroups R1a and R1b seemingly from different directions in Scandinavia may indicate that the linguis-tic ancestor of the Germanic branch was a mix of similar early Indo- European di-alects perhaps distantly related to Italo-Celtic and Balto-Slavic, respectively. The presence of the Core Indo- European word for ‘metal, copper’, combined with the lack of metal finds in Northern Europe and Scandinavia in the Corded Ware peri-od, may also indicate that the word was introduced into the ancestor of Germanic from speakers in the Bell Beaker culture. Alternatively, the R1b-rich Bell Beaker culture could have introduced the ancestor of Germanic in some form into Scan-dinavia, mixing with an already existing Indo- European substrate introduced by the previous R1a-rich Single Grave culture.31

31 Additional genetic evidence for internal changes in ancestry within Scandinavia after the initial arrival of steppe ancestry with the Single Grave/Battle Axe cultures has re-cently appeared, showing that East Scandinavian/East Baltic–derived Southern Swed-ish genetic components spread to Denmark along with Y-haplogroup I1 around 2200– 1600 BCE (McColl et al. 2024 with supplementary notes), as also suggested in Allentoft et al. (2024b). This would correlate with a range of technological and mythological archaeological elements also found in Indo- European vocabulary, such as wool, spoke-wheeled chariots, domestic horses, and figurative mythologically loaded iconography (Iversen 2024).

259An update on the Corded Ware culture

Part II The dog (or wolf) as a symbol of savage male youth warriors in the Corded Ware culture?

1 Human–canid relations in prehistory

Inspired by Brown & Anthony (2017), and based on accounts in Kershaw (2000), Petrosyan (2011, on traditional Armenian ‘Black Youths’), and others, Kristiansen et al. (2017) and Anthony (2022) have proposed a model for the formation of the CWC which holds that steppe migrations were driven by young male warrior bands identifying as wolves or dogs, progressively roaming further into Europe while raiding and taking local wives.

The remaining part of this study will make the case that the association of ca-nids with male youths remains to be convincingly demonstrated archaeologically in relation to these steppe migrations, and that the presently available data for the CWC rather shows a clear association between canids and females.

The cultural conception of Indo- European wolf-/dog-warrior institutions has been put forward by various scholars during this and the previous century (more recently McCone 1987, Kershaw 2000, Das & Meiser 2002) based on a large body of comparative mythological and ethnographic evidence, and is well attested in various Indo- European traditions. Kristiansen et al. (2017) and Anthony (2022: 67–68) apply it specifically to the formation of the CWC; Brown & Anthony (2017, 2019) apply it to a steppe site in Samara from the early 2nd millennium BCE and, using comparative mythological evidence, project it back to Proto- (or at least Core) Indo- European societies. In this model (as described in Brown & Anthony 2017, 2019), young male boys (c. 7–14 years old) are initiated into a wolf/dog war-rior sodality and live a savage wolf/dog life raiding their surroundings for about four years until they reach adulthood, shed their wolf/dog skin in a wolf/dog sac-rifice, and reenter society. Relating to the formation of the CWC, these wolf/dog warrior bands are suggested to have acted as scouts for steppe relatives to follow, resulting in an actual migration (Anthony 2022: 67–68). Following this model, we would expect to see archaeological traces of this relation between wolves/dogs and boys or men in the CWC. Archaeological evidence for this wolf/dog sodality is suggested by Brown & Anthony (2017, 2019) to be found at the Srubnaya cul-ture site Krasnosamarskoe (c. 1900–1700 bce) in the Samara river valley, Russia, where 51 dogs and 7 wolves were sacrificed in a nearby settlement building, but

260 Mikkel Nørtoft

not buried in the kurgan. Their heads were cut into small, standardised pieces. The fact that the dogs are mostly male (71–90%, depending on certainty), and that a few of the canid bones found at the site are wolf bones, suggests to Brown & Anthony (ibid.) that this is a male-oriented ritual fitting their dog-warrior theme, and that the wolf bones would have symbolized warrior ‘savagery’. However, it should be mentioned that the non-adults (in their study defined as below 17 years old) buried in the nearby kurgan at Krasnosamarskoe were mostly (15 out of 22) below Brown & Anthony’s proposed ‘age of initiation’, and that only one out of the 22 non-adults (a juvenile) has been sex-determined (in this case a male). Further-more, neither the high ratio of male dogs over females nor the practice of eating dogs or opening their craniums, possibly to eat the brain (Bökönyi 1974: 318–320), is necessarily unique in the European Neolithic or Bronze Age. A genetic study on dogs from across Neolithic–Bronze Age Western Eurasia showed that 72% of them were male (a ratio of 23:9 male:female; Bergström et al. 2020: Supplemen-tary Information 11). Even so, the standardised chopping of the dog craniums at Krasnosamarskoe may still be unique.

Anthony (2007: 411) also uses dogtooth pendants found with males in the Sintashta culture as a supporting archaeological argument for the male wolf/dog sodality in Indo- European societies. According to him, dogtooth pendants are numerous in the Sintashta culture, sligthly earlier than the Krasnosamarskoe site, and usually associated with Indo- Iranian speakers (Narasimhan et al. 2019, Kuz’mina 2007, Anthony 2007: 408–411, Bjørn 2022, Grünthal et al. 2022). Antho-ny (2007: 411) exemplifies this with dogteeth (19 pieces) in Sintashta at Kammenyi Ambar (dated 2030–1660 cal BCE; Narasimhan et al. 2019: Supplementary Materi-als 39) in kurgan 4, grave 2. This is a multiple grave with four males (three broth-ers) and one female, all genetically analysed. Two of the three brothers were 3–5 years old, one 3–9 months old, and they had high “West Siberian Hunter-Gather-er” ancestry, making them genetic outliers in the Sintashta culture.32 The fourth boy was also 3–5 years old, and the female was 7.5–12.5 years old (Narasimhan et al. 2019: Supplementary Materials 44, 46, 49). The boys here were thus well below the usual ‘age of initiates’ for Indo- European wolf-/dog-warriors. If, as Anthony suggests, the dogteeth belonged to the boys, and not the girl (only ge-netically sex-determined recently), they are so young that the dogteeth probably

32 Although we should not automatically equal genetic ancestry, culture, and language, this outlier ancestry opens the possibility that the parents of these three brothers may have also had a non-Indo- European cultural and linguistic background, e.g., related to the neighbouring Seima-Turbino horizon.

261An update on the Corded Ware culture

functioned as protective amulets, metaphorical pets, or companions in the after-life, rather than as emblems of wolf-/dog-warriors. Further associations between dogteeth, sex (or gender), and age in the CWC will be treated below.

An interesting parallel to the dog sacrifice at Krasnosamarskoe in the early 2nd millennium BCE may be found in the early Usatove culture of the late 4th millennium bce in the Odessa area of the Northwest Pontic. According to Razu-mov (2018: 62), at least 73 dogs have been found at the Usatove culture settlement Mayaki, interpreted as a ceremonial center with regular dog sacrifices, but they have not been sex-determined. Razumov also mentions possible dog images on a grave stela from a mound at Usatove. Additionally, there are dogs buried in ‘guardian-like’ locations in mounds of seemingly rich human burials (e.g., on pit ceilings or in grave or mound entrances), often with an adult and child buried to-gether, but a clear pattern in the sex or gender of either humans or dogs does not seem obvious in these burials (genetics could determine this further). Razumov notes that dog sacrifices (burials of both whole animals and skulls) and especially dog-like figures painted on ceramics are well known in the neighbouring Cu-cuteni-Trypillia culture with a primarily farming economy.

Further east in the steppes, dog burials are also known from the Dereivka 2 settlement, and paired burials of dogs in separate pits are known from Eneolithic cemeteries on the Dnipro and the Middle Don. Dog figurines have been found in the entrance of the ‘princely’ kurgan 31 of the Novosvobodnaya culture (c. 3000 bce) in the North Caucasus, which also had contacts with the Usatove culture (Razumov 2018, with references). Thus, the guardian-like function of dogs in mortuary contexts may have been in effect in some areas of the steppes as early as the late 4th millennium bce.

Brown & Anthony (2017: 146) mention that the guardian-like theme for dogs is a widespread pan-Eurasian complex also found in the Chukchi and Tungus tribes in Siberia and even in the Americas, hinting at a possible Palaeolithic ori-gin, presumably beginning in Siberia. The afterlife guide (‘psychopomp’) theme for dogs is also known from the Chukchi and Tungus. Archaeologically, Meso-lithic dog and wolf sacrifice has been found in mortuary contexts near Lake Bai-kal and the mouth of the Ishim (Brown & Anthony 2017: 146), while genetic ev-idence has linked Native Americans and East European Hunter-Gatherers, both with ancestors in Siberia, specifically around Lake Baikal (Raghavan et al. 2014, Sikora et al. 2019). The earliest genetically, morphologically, and temporally con-firmed domestic dog (Canis lupus familiaris) bones in Europe are found in the Basque Country, dated to c. 15,460–15,146 cal BCE with several contenders in Italy and Germany; all carry haplogroup C, which has been traced back genetically to

262 Mikkel Nørtoft

22,000–14,000 BCE in Europe during the later part of the Last Glacial Maximum (LGM). Less certain so-called ‘dog-like wolves’, some of which may reflect an in-termediate development between wolves and domestic dogs, have been found from the Altai (from c. 31,000 BCE) to France (from c. 29,000 BCE), and in the East European Plains from c. 25,000–22,000 BCE. Palaeogenetic studies suggest that wolf domestication may have begun slowly already around 39,000–35,000 BCE and accelerated during the LGM (Hervella et al. 2022). Although more work needs to be done to pinpoint the specific origins of dog domestication, it has been shown that the earliest domestic dogs in Europe derived from Siberia (Bergström et al. 2022: 5).33 East European Hunter-Gatherers also derived most of their an-cestry from Epi-Palaeolithic Hunter-Gatherers from Siberia (Sikora et al. 2019). We thus have a genetic link connecting both early hunter-gatherers on the steppe and early dogs to Eastern or Central Eurasia (including Southern Siberia), as well as the afterlife/guardian dog theme, and dog sacrifice in mortuary contexts, similar to that known in the Indo- European world. While it is for now only cor-relation, causation is starting to become increasingly attractive.

In rare cases, CWC males, or their artefact insignia, can be connected with dog burials. One case is grave 148.2.1 at Stará Hora, Kyjov-Netcice in Moravia (find group IIIa–b, middle-late CWC), where the skull of a presumed male (based on the grave goods) of c. 50 years was buried. This individual had remains of a possible dog skull, a battle-axe of calcareous sandstone, a stone flat axe of green schist, a cord-decorated beaker, an undetermined large decorated vessel, a blade of glacial flint, and a pig canine (Šebela et al. 1999: 85, 194). Another case is in a grave of the Danish Single Grave Culture in Esbjerg where a dog is buried in a grave mound with a battle-axe, but without any human remains (Hübner 2005: 1320–1321). And at Nickelsdorf in Krossen, Eisenberg, Germany, two young dogs were buried at the feet of a man (Matthias 1969: 14). Conversely, in Köthen, An-halt, Germany, a dog was buried in front of the face of a left-crouched (indicat-ing female) human (ibid.). Other examples of dog burials include a cave shaft in the Kirschbaumhöhle, Northern Franconian Alps (precise location still secret to prevent looting), where multiple animal and human remains were found. Here, a dog skeleton was found with two human skulls (an adult male and a probable female of late-adult to early-mature age). Both the dog and the two humans were C14-dated to the early CWC (2910–2632 cal bce; Seregély et al. 2015: 226–227, table 3). The dog was determined to be a Canis familiaris palustris (similar to a

33 With a subsequent 5–25% admixture from the Neolithic onwards with origins in anoth-er population related to the Syrian wolf (Bergström et al. 2022)

263An update on the Corded Ware culture

modern Spitz), male, and more than 5 years old, based on its dental wear. Anoth-er dog, not sexed or C14-dated, but certainly a dog, was subadult and less than 5 months old. A neonate or foetus of a third (undated) canid, either dog or fox, was also found. Sheep/goat remains were also found, dating to later periods. All three canids were complete skeletons indicating that they had been brought into the cave whole (Seregély et al. 2015: 226–227).

Other examples of CWC-associated dog burials are known from Linköping, Sweden (the Battle Axe group of the CWC), where an almost complete skeleton of an elderly dog was found together with two human adults, male and female, in typical Corded Ware positions. The dog, like the human female, was lying on its left side, close to the female (Behrens 1964: 50–51). It seems likely that the CWC dog in Linköping was part of the buried family with no ritual connotations. The same could be said for the dog(s) associated with the adult male and probable female humans in Kirschbaumhöhle.

At least three dog skeletons are known from the CWC in Poland. One, found in a collective grave mound in Zakłodzie, Zamość, Lublin, with a bone point sticking out of its ribs, was interpreted as having been killed in connection with the burial of an adjacent human skeleton. A dog burial was also found at Strzyżów, Hrubieszów, Lublin, without grave goods but possibly part of the Corded Ware cemetery,34 lying on its side with the head towards east (Behrens 1964: 38). An-other dog was buried in the primary layer of a mound northwest of the presum-ably contemporary primary human grave in Miernów kurgan 1, grave 4, in the Kazimierza Wielka district, Little Poland Upland. The human buried in this grave was of mature age, male, and lying with the head towards west and on his right side. The grave was dated to the early CWC ‘A-horizon’ based on the grave goods, which consist of a Thuringian amphora and a long flint blade. The dog was also on its right side, but with the head southwards (Włodarczak 2006: fig. 23, fig. 43, 89–90). We could interpret the dog’s placement in the mound – not the grave – as having a guardian-like function, or we could use the male sex/gender of the associated human to support the male dog-warrior model. On the other hand, no battle axe (if interpreting this as a male warrior symbol) was present in the grave. See Figure 2 for a (non-exhaustive) map of dog burials in the CWC and contemporary cultures.

34 Another single CWC dog burial in Strzyżów is mentioned by Behrens (1964: 38), to-gether with two vessels originally attributed to the CWC but later connected with the Bronze Age Mierzanowice period instead (Kołodziej 2010: 143, 168).

264 Mikkel Nørtoft

Dog burials are also known from the partly contemporary Globular Ampho-ra culture, e.g., in Strzelce, Mogilno, Poland, and also in the Złota culture (with mixed CWC and Globular Amphora culture traits) at the Gajowizna cemetery (Behrens 1964: 34–38, Witkowska et al. 2020).

Altogether, for the CWC, we have 7 out of 8 graves with some indication of sex or (mostly) gender determination: 1 female and 4 males in single graves, plus 2 graves with both males and females. From this, there does seem to be a majority of males with dog burials. However, a Chi-squared (goodness-of-fit) test on the 4 males and 1 female shows that the male/female difference is not statistically sig-nificant (p = 0.18, determining signifance at p < 0.05) because the sample size is so small. If we compute the p-value by Monte Carlo simulation with 2000 replicates to correct for the small sample size, the result is even further from significance (p = 0.37, using base R in RStudio). with a presumed male with age determination, it was an unspecified adult and a c. 50 year-old individual. Thus, there seems to be no particular reason to regard these cases as signifying a male initiation of youth warriors rather than just life companions buried with their owner.

In a later pit at Nad Wawrem, Złota, five dog skeletons were placed on three sides around a dismembered human skeleton, likely belonging to the Early Bronze Age Trzciniec culture (Behrens 1964: 38–39).

Other Early Bronze Age examples of dogs in graves include a number of Brit-ish Bell Beaker graves, a Bell Beaker grave in Corderoure, Northern Spain (also with a human skeleton), as well as multiple dog skulls (both whole and broken specimens) in a multiple Bell Beaker grave (19 human skulls), the dogs report-edly being part of the burial ritual (Behrens 1964: 53–54).35 At least 22 Iberian Eneolithic and Bronze Age sites have dog remains in funerary, settlement pit, and special ditch contexts, probably relating to different functions. All three contexts have been found at the same site, Camino de las Yeseras, showing that dogs may have filled multiple social and religious roles in the same community (Daza-Perea 2017).

In a survey by Kołodziej (2010) of animal burials in Central and Eastern Eu-rope in the Early Bronze Age – i.e., after the CWC – 23 cases of dog remains (and one fox) of both sexes and all ages were found, out of 78 animal burials in total, some of them mass burials. In 11 cases there was some possible connection with a human, of which three were in settlement contexts,36 most others in cemeteries or mounds. Dogs were buried three times with an adult female, twice with an adult male (other animals are also found buried with males, e.g., cattle skulls and sheep/

35 A closer bioarchaeological study of these skulls (humans and dogs) might be enlighten-ing for this question.

36 Including Soraksár, settlement features 2, 3 and 4 (c. 5 m apart), at the Botanical Garden in Budapest, associated with the Nagyrév culture who normally cremate their dead. In feature 4, a pit, an adult male was buried, strongly tied up and with his head lying 40 cm lower than his feet. In feature 3 (directly next to the human burial), an adult male dog with a broken skull, three young oxen, many potsherds, and a bone awl were buried with a burnt layer of ash at the bottom. Feature 2 contains seven heads of cattle in an intricate formation, seemingly buried in September or October. The cattle skeletons and the dog skeleton did not seem to have signs of being eaten, but some had broken skulls. The bones of at least five sheep and three pigs were also mixed into the pits. Most of the animal bones were from males, and features 2 and 3 had traces of fire. These were interpreted as human–animal sacrifices after the harvest (Kołodziej 2010: 193–194, 214–215, 226–227, 231–232, 236–238, 266-267).

266 Mikkel Nørtoft

goats, and in one case – Brno-Černá, Únětice culture – a man’s head was placed on top of the dog’s head). In another case, an older male human was buried on top of two dogs and two sheep, and in a third case, a dog was buried after the burial of a woman (25–30 years old) and three children: a 17-year-old female, a 13-year-old male, and a 3-month-old infant (Kołodziej 2010: 159–206, 237, 247–248). This evi-dence does not suggest a male warrior pattern, even after the CWC period.

It has been proposed that animals (including dogs) carefully buried in ceme-teries without humans, but sometimes with ‘grave goods’ typical for the humans in the cemetery, were substitutes for humans whose bodies could not be recov-ered, e.g., if they had drowned or were lost in battle (Kołodziej 2010: 267 with references). This could perhaps explain the quite varied ages and sexes of such an-imals, either to reflect the dead or because they (mostly the dogs) were life com-panions to the dead. The same argument has been made regarding animals bur-ied with humans, mostly dogs (Kołodziej 2010: 268). Cattle is mostly interpreted as a display of wealth for the dead or as food for the afterlife (or the funeral feast, including offerings to the gods), while dogs are interpreted as life companions or a guardian after death, but each case may have different symbolic meanings in the same culture, and we should not assume that these were the same across an archaeological culture (ibid.).

Although much too late to be relevant for the steppe migrations, a grave from the Early Iron Age in a pit complex (pit 284) at Kapitan Andreevo, Southern Bul-garia, is an interesting case. It contains a young genetically male individual (16–18 years old) who was possibly thrown in the pit. His skull was smashed around the time of death, and a dog skeleton lay in the southern part of the pit (Lazaridis et al. 2022: Supplementary Information 101–103).

Most dogs found in the 4th and 3rd millennium BCE were small-to-medium Spitz-like dogs, the CWC dogs being slightly larger than those known from Swiss lake dwellings (Kyselý 2021). Dogs of these sizes would be suitable for hunting small game, for herding in general, and for guarding, mostly by barking at in-comers, but unsuitable for battle or for protecting herds from wolves or bears. In the Hungarian Bronze Age they seem to have been used ritually as foundation sacrifices, while in the Neolithic and Eneolithic, they were rather buried with humans (possibly as companions) or eaten (Gál and Bondár 2022: 49–50). From this, it does not seem straightforward to associate dogs with war as in Brown & Anthony (2019: 101).

In summary, the data does not convincingly show that dog burials around the time of the steppe migrations in Europe were especially associated with males. In the few CWC cases with sex-determination of humans buried with dogs, there is

267An update on the Corded Ware culture

an overweight of males (adult and mature, but too few age-determined graves to rely on), but the sample size is still too small for this to be a significant difference, and we also find cases with both males and females together, indicating that the dog was rather part of the family. In the wider scope, very few cases had any sex, gender or age determination, and the dogs were buried in different ways and lo-cations, which may indicate different roles. Sometimes the dogs are buried in the entrance of the kurgan, perhaps hinting at a guardian-like function, and some-times they are buried close to humans inside the grave, occasionally with what could be families (genetic kinship would help interpret this). Sometimes dogs are buried along with other animals, some of which have been larger sacrifices, with no specific warrior connotations. The most interesting case around the time of the steppe migrations, and the closest parallel to Krasnosamarskoe, is the 73 or so dogs killed at the Usatove culture site at Mayaki. Dog burials vary in frequency over time and geography in later periods, but treating them further would be beyond the scope of this paper.37

2 A prestige measure for grave good categories applied to the Corded Ware culture in Moravia and Bohemia

Before giving a wider overview of dogtooth ornaments, this section will attempt to quantify the prestige value (or ‘exclusivity’) of dogtooth and shell ornaments relative to other categories of grave goods. This is applied here to a dataset of 56 adult CWC graves in Moravia, both scattered graves and smaller cemeteries, as well as 135 adult graves from larger cemeteries in Vikletice and Čachovice (less than 2 km apart), Northwestern Bohemia, and in Vliněves, Central Bohemia. In order to correlate the presence of dogteeth with sex and age, only data from graves with preserved skeletal remains is included. It is important to remember that we can only quantify the material that was preserved, and quantification of any fragile organic grave goods that may have carried important meaning, such as textiles, mats, and baskets, is usually not possible. If females, for example, ex-pressed wealth and status more through textiles than men did, the lack of such preserved material obviously skews the analysis towards more wealthy male

In a previous study (Nørtoft 2022), a sample of 81 graves (all age groups) from two catalogues (Kolář 2011, Šebela et al. 1999) of the Moravian CWC (c. 2700/2600–2200/2000 bce; Kolář 2018, Peška 2021) was collected and quantified in terms of their grave goods and grave-pit depths using eight value and wealth measures. These measures include the depth of the grave pit, estimat-ed meat expenditure, the number of grave good categories in each grave (here called Total number of Object Types, TOT), estimated manufacturing hours of grave goods, the skill required to make them, the distance to the raw material, and the scarcity of the material.

Therefore, an extra measure of the value of grave goods, prestige, was generated by applying the distribution of the TOT measure for each grave good category, visualized in a box-whisker plot specific to each study case/ region; see Figure 3. With this method, we get a better idea of which objects in an assemblage are more exclusive compared to others, and we can compare differ-ences in grave good values between study cases.

Because each grave good distribution gives a spectrum of TOT, we can use the median of each category’s TOT spectrum as the prestige value for each grave good category. Furthermore, we can standardise these values by dividing the TOT median by the top TOT score in the spectrum to get a relative value (ranging from 0 to 1, like Grossmann 2021 normalizes scarcity) comparable between cases with different ranges (Bohemian TOT scores in the range 0–10 and Moravia 0–16 in this example when including graves without grave goods). jects (on the left in the boxplot, e.g., bone beads in Bohemia) which are also rare (although the bone material is not as rare) get a low score (here a 3, normalized 0.3) if they are found in graves with generally few other grave good categories. Using a general scarcity measure for object types (as in Grossmann 2021), bone beads would have gotten a high score even though they’re not found in any rich graves.

Other scarce but locally available objects, such as shell beads (mother-of-pearl/nacre), are primarily found in the upper half of the TOT spectrum, giving a higher prestige value with medians of 6 (normalized 0.6) in Bohemia, and 11 (normalized 0.69) in Moravia.

Extremely rare and exclusive items such as the single gold hair-ring only found in the richest grave on the TOT spectrum (a c. 20-year-old male-gendered individual), gets the highest score with a median of 16 (normalized 1).

The category tooth ornament represents perforated ornaments made primarily from dogteeth, while tooth imitation represents imitations of dogteeth made from the bone of other animals. The latter indicates that the symbolism of dogteeth was so important that they were worth copying using abundant materials, perhaps comparable to faux fur in the modern world. In the Moravian sample of 56 graves, the imitated and real dogtooth pendants are found in the same grave, second highest in the TOT spectrum with a median of 11 (normalized 0.69). In Bohemia, these are a bit lower on the TOT spectrum, with a median of 5 (normalized 0.5). By comparison, another rare dental grave good, boar tusks (worked in two graves and unworked in one grave), usually found with male individuals, are somewhat lower with a median of 7 (normalized 0.44) in Moravia and do not feature in the Bohemian sample. In the Moravian CWC, some boar tusks have traces of metal on them and sometimes appear in graves with other metallurgy tools such as moulds. This suggests that some boar tusks, due to their hard surface, were used as tools for smoothing the surface of metals (Peška 2016). Battle-axes (often termed axe-hammers or hammer-axes in Czech CWC literature) are often inter-preted as a general elite male symbol in the CWC (e.g. Heyd 2004: 197), but in both samples here, they have a lower median than tooth and shell ornaments (6, normalized 0.34, in Moravia; 4, normalized 0.4, in Bohemia)38 and thus appear to have lower prestige value than the typically female-associated dogteeth (fake

38 Removing early CWC-period graves in Bohemia (generally poorer, and where tooth and shell ornaments do not appear) before doing this analysis still resulted in a median of 4 for battle-axes on a sample size of 110 adult graves from Bohemian CWC period II–III.

271An update on the Corded Ware culture

or real) and shell beads. Use-wear studies on archaeological battle-axe specimens from the Netherlands and Denmark, compared with use-wear traces on replicas subjected to various experiments, show that they were not suitable for cutting down trees (unlike edge-polished flint axes), but better for uprooting trees (with matching use-wear traces), and they may have been an integral part of a toolkit for opening the landscape for transport and ploughing. Such opening of landscapes is especially evident with the spread of the CWC in connection with burning down trees, while in the West Frisian CWC settlements on dunes in marshlands, battle-axes are rare. Other experiments showed that using them as weapons (on dead animals) did not show clear use-wear traces, so additional functionality as weapons cannot be excluded (Wentink 2020: 115–126). A use-wear study on two CWC ‘battle-axes’ from Lower Silesia, Poland, found that one of them seemed to have been used for a long time, possibly for woodworking, while the other had unexplained use-wear traces, perhaps partly removed before grave deposition (Kufel-Diakowska and Skuła 2015). Tilley (1982: 14–15) also showed that in the Scanian Battle Axe culture, battle-axes were found more with graves containing fewer than four grave good types (67%) than graves with more than four grave good types (33%), the richest graves in the assemblage having nine grave good types. Fenton (1984), based on experiments, showed that they may have taken a long time to make (c. 20–25 hours, mainly for pecking and drilling the shafthole), but that their manufacture did not require much skill. Altogether, this suggests that battle-axes were neither dedicated weapons nor purely prestige objects, but often utilitarian items – and while they were likely markers of CWC male identity or even a sodality, they were not exclusive, and thus probably not elite symbols.

Mother-of-pearl beads were mostly made of local shells (especially Unio spe-cies) with a mother-of-pearl surface. Perforating and polishing the shell without breaking it may have required a specific technique, and its shiny white surface, hardness, and toughness compared to other shell materials, as well as the time required to make each bead, may have added to their value (Sakalauskaitė et al. 2019, Petzold 2005: 4–5). The perforated and often polished animal teeth (and their imitations) would have taken considerable time to make39 (especially when including their often high frequency in some graves), which may also have affect-ed their perceived value (Petzold 2005: 2, 5).40

39 Typically more than most bone tools with more practical functionalities. Personal bone pins may also have had more symbolic importance (and craft finish) than bone tools (Petzold 2005: 2, 4–5).

40 In the author’s personal experience with wild boar (summer 2021 in Steinzeitpark Dith-marschen), even extracting teeth from an animal skull requires a good deal of effort.

272 Mikkel Nørtoft

It is also important looking at the sex/gender distribution of tooth and shell ornaments. As is well known, Corded Ware gender is, apart from gendered grave goods, primarily marked by a strictly gendered body position and orientation, by which females are buried on their left side (head east), and males on their right side (head west). This holds also for many of the buried non-adults (Turek 2016: 343–348). This pattern generally correlates well with osteological (and genetic) sex determination, and body position in the CWC is often used as a proxy for gender. However, exceptions to this pattern do occur (see Turek 2016 for a discussion on this topic for the CWC, and for counterexamples that challenge traditional binary gender views of the past, especially for non-adults).

3 Description of selected Czech CWC graves with dogteeth and shells

Here follows an overview of Czech CWC graves with dogtooth (and occasional-ly shell) ornaments, including some non-adult graves that were excluded in the quantitative analysis above, and two graves without skeletal remains (in Bohe-mia); in total 81 graves from Moravia and 299 graves from Bohemia, of which 17 graves contained either dogtooth ornaments, dogtooth imitations, or shell orna-ments (see Appendix). In the Moravian sample, one grave contained dogtooth ornaments and shell beads, and three other graves contained shell beads without dogteeth. In the Bohemian sample, three graves contained both dogtooth orna-ments (including wild animal teeth) and shell beads, six had dogteeth and no shell beads, while two contained shell beads without dogteeth. Tooth imitations only appeared in graves with real dogteeth. All graves with dogteeth contained adults, except one child grave in Vliněves, Bohemia (gr. 1423, female left body position and genetically female; Papac et al. 2021), also containing shell beads. No male individuals had dogteeth, but one older male from Moravia (Ivanovice na Hané 4, gr. 810), rich in grave goods (11 on the TOT scale), had three mollusc shells, now unfortunately lost. A brief description of the grave goods from select-ed graves is given here, of which only the Bohemian individuals were examined by forensic anthropologists more recently (Shbat et al. 2009).

- Marefy grave 177.1.1 (Šebela et al. 1999; see Figure 4): Situated on a small hillock and buried into a circular grave pit, this grave contained an individ-ual who could not be osteologically sex-determined (mandible looks female, frontal bone male) or clearly age-determined. However, the body position
