273An update on the Corded Ware culture

(left side with head east) and grave goods indicate a female that is anatomi-cally described as “relatively old” or “elderly” (grave and anthropological de-scriptions in Šebela et al. 1999: 96, 196). In the grave, 375 pendants of dogtooth (incisors, molars, and canines) – all perforated and polished, and estimated to originate from about 89(!) dogs – were laid out in two concentric rings in front of the body. This display of dogteeth is likely to be the highest num-ber recorded across the CWC.41 To this, we can add 57 dogtooth imitations made from bovine bone, 2 unworked bovine teeth, 4 badger canines, and un-der the right thigh, 101 cylindrical bone beads. This grave also had 5,464(!)

41 Only challenged by a female grave in Prague–Březiněves with teeth from 73 dogs; see Kyselý et al. (2019) for a more detailed description of this grave.

Figure 4. Top view of grave 177.1.1 at Marefy. Drawing: Mikkel Nørtoft, based on Šebela et al. (1999).

274 Mikkel Nørtoft

mother-of-pearl (nacre) beads in a heap behind the head, and fragments of 1,700 other shell beads (Unio species), all perforated and polished. Apart from this impressive display, this grave also had the most copper in the whole as-semblage of 81 Moravian graves, with a composite necklace (of 8 spirals) and three composite bracelets of both wire tubes (64 pieces) and sheet copper (24 pieces), as well as copper hair decorations (2 spiral wire pieces). This is a very large amount of grave goods within the CWC in general. The grave also had three amphorae, a, beaker, a jug (all decorated except one amphora), a bone awl, and a flint endscraper.

- Vikletice grave 166/63 (Buchvaldek 1970: 44, 285): This grave contained a young adult individual (c. 20–30 years old) in the primary grave, which was disturbed (including the anatomical position) by the secondary burial of an older child or juvenile (6–18 years old), the few bones (teeth and leg bones) of the latter being mixed with the primary individual. Based on the grave goods, the adult is assumed to be of female gender while the child’s gender is undetermined. Due to the disturbance, several grave goods were displaced, with fragments both at the bottom of the grave and in the grave fill. The grave goods comprised sherds of a beaker (bottom and fill), a small flint drill (among the bones), a fragmented flint blade (in the corner), 36 perforated dog teeth (incl. two fragments), 27 dogtooth imitations in bone (bottom and fill), a sheep/goat tooth, 110 perforated shell beads (bottom and fill), a fragment of a possible marble pendant (under the shell beads), and a bone awl (grave fill). Although the disturbance from the secondary child burial makes the attribution of all the grave goods to only one of the individuals uncertain, the grave goods present partly on the bottom (all but the bone awl) seem likely to be associated with the primary adult grave. No pathological remarks or trauma were reported for these two individuals in a later examination by Shbat et al. (2009).
- Vikletice 67/64 (Buchvaldek 1970: 57, 268–269, 285): A young adult individ-ual (20–30 years old and of undetermined sex), the body lying in a crouched position on its left side, oriented approximately East–West with the head to-wards the East, indicating female gender. Grave goods comprise part of an ornamented amphora, sherds of two or three jar-like vessels, 54 whole drilled dog canines (and 27 fragments), two drilled badger canines, three tooth imi-tations, and a drilled tooth of unknown species. The various teeth were lying in a small heap and in two rows behind the head near the right arm, and a

275An update on the Corded Ware culture

pointy flint blade was behind the head. No caries was detected in the teeth and no pathological remarks or trauma were reported for this individual in a later examination by Shbat et al. (2009).

According to the medical examinations by Shbat et al. (2009), two other indi-viduals buried with dogteeth from this dataset showed possible signs of various trauma and pathologies: Vikletice gr. 12A/63, a young adult female with signs of carcinoma or meningitis, buried with 36 tooth ornaments, of which 11 were from dogs and the rest from fox, otter, badger, and red deer; and Vikletice gr. 140/63, a mature female with possible signs of having survived an infection, buried with a dogtooth, three badger teeth, and seven tooth imitations.

The only clear pattern that appears from the 17 graves with dogteeth and/or shell beads in this study is that they are female (12 out of 17 graves, 70.5%) or sometimes with ambiguous sex/gender traits (3 out of 17 graves, 17.7%), and usu-ally contain an adult (13 out of 17 graves, 76.5%). The two individuals from Bohe-mia described here had no signs of pathologies or trauma. A study on the teeth of some of the individuals in this Moravian sample, from Ivanovice na Hané and Hostice, indicated a high meat intake for some of them (Kolář et al. 2012). Howev-er, estimated differences in meat consumption in the Moravian CWC seem to be non-significant, and CWC and Bell Beaker individuals in Moravia and Bohemia seem to have generally more meat consumption (and perhaps also dairy, at least in Bohemia) than Early Neolithic groups (Kolář et al. 2012: 244–253, Shbat et al. 2009). Higher meat consumption for certain CWC individuals therefore is not a clear marker of exceptionally high status, but at least it shows access to meat, indicating that they are probably not from the lowest tier of their society.

4 Tooth and shell ornaments in the Czech Corded Ware culture

Kyselý et al. (2019) generously provide open data for 72 sex-/gender-determined individuals,42 of which 37 were also age-determined, buried with osseous orna-ments (a collective term for ornaments of tooth, shell, bone, antler, and horn), from all of the Czech CWC. The overall frequency of these ornaments is quite low for children and the oldest individuals, but also low for the few males that

Two extreme outliers (the above-mentioned Marefy gr. 177.1.1 in Moravia and Prague–Březiněves gr. 10 in Bohemia) soar high above the rest, while an intermediate group with almost 2,500 pieces also stands out (Figure 5a). It thus appears that osseous ornaments for females are mostly worn by, or asso-ciated with, individuals in the fertile age. Focusing only on shell beads, the pic-ture becomes even clearer: for males, they are only associated with children less than 10 years old (Figure 5b), and otherwise resemble the general plot. Prague– Březiněves gr. 10 (described by Kyselý et al. 2019) is, in terms of shell beads and dogteeth, the closest comparison to the extremely rich grave in Moravia. Prague– Brezineves gr. 10 is female according to both osteology and body position, and osteologically and typologically dated to the mid-late CWC (find group II–III). It contained at least 412 tooth ornaments (at least 249 drilled) determined to be from 73 dogs, 8,387(!) shell beads (mother-of-pearl), 2 shell discs, fragments of a beaker, an amphora and another undetermined vessel, a flint artefact, and a whetstone (Kyselý et al. 2019).

these may be more prominent with non-adults than the other grave goods (al-though only two examples here; see Figure 5e). They are also found with a few adult males, but those with ‘solar’ decoration are only found with females (Kyselý et al. 2019: 116). In general, the occurrence of these ‘solar’ discs is negatively corre-lated with dogteeth and dogtooth imitations, perhaps hinting at a different func-tion (Kyselý et al. 2019: 106).

Dogtooth imitations were found, and counted, in 34 graves in Kyselý et al. (2019); of these, 18 graves (53%) were from the middle CWC period (if consistent with Find Group II), while only four graves (12%) can be dated to the late CWC (if consistent with Find Group III). The rest are either undated (11 graves) or mid-dle–late CWC (1 grave). Imitations in the middle CWC are primarily found in northwestern Bohemia, and the use of real dogteeth becomes even rarer in the late CWC (Kyselý et al. 2019: 107, 114–116). However, it should be noted that deriv-ing CWC chronology from Find Groups (I, II and III), although often supported by C14 dates, relies on typology, and some temporal overlap is to be expected (Neustupný 2013: 132).

Animal teeth are found in c. 6.7% of all Bohemian and 0.3% of Moravian CWC graves, or 5.3% of all Czech CWC graves (Kyselý et al. 2019: 108); out of the total of 3,719 teeth, 91–95% are dog teeth. Drilled teeth of wild animals are also represent-ed in this dataset, including wolf (4.5%), fox (10%), badger (14.8%), otter (5.6%), wild cat (8%), bear (1%), marten-like species (1%), and domestic pig (4.5%) (per-centages based on table 5 in Kyselý et al. 2019). Out of 88 graves with animal teeth, 87 (98.9%) contained dogteeth (Kyselý et al. 2019: 108).

As seen in Figure 5c, drilled teeth are primarily found with females: of the 39 sex-/gender-determined single graves with drilled teeth, 34 were female (87%), two were male (5%, not shown in the plot since age was not given in the data), and three were ambiguous (8%). Additionally, drilled teeth were found in four double graves (three with a male and a female, one with two females) and 30 graves with an unspecified number of individuals. Of the 34 female single graves, 18 (53%) had age determination (13 adults and five non-adults), of which six (33%) were older individuals (40+) and four (22%) were younger adults (20–39)while three (17%) may have been either older or younger adults (20-59). The five non-adults represent altogether 28% of the graves; three (17%) were infants and two (11%) were juveniles (Kyselý et al. 2019: Supplementary Table).

Individuals with tooth imitations were age-determined in 13 cases, all adults. None of them were determined to be male; ten were female, two had ambigu-ous sex/gender display, and one was undetermined. The highest frequencies were generally found among young adults 20–39 years old (Figure 5d).

280 Mikkel Nørtoft

Shell beads are found primarily with females from 10 years old (Figure 5b). The grave from Marefy 177.1.1, Moravia, soars above the rest in drilled teeth, followed by other extreme examples in Bohemia: Prague–Březiněves gr. 10, Konobrže gr. 35 (2,000 shell beads, 27 drilled teeth, juvenile with ambigious sex/gender), Kon-obrže gr. 37 (1,000 shell beads, 325 drilled teeth, adult female), Prague–Čimice gr. 77 (1,435 shell beads, 200 drilled teeth, female (position) adult), Prague–Bubeneč gr. 72 (1,200 shell beads, 151 drilled teeth, female (position), unknown age), Sule-jovice gr. 96 (1,000 shell beads, 50 drilled teeth, female (position), unknown age) (Kyselý et al. 2019: Supplementary Table).

All in all, the larger dataset from the Czech Republic in Kyselý et al. (2019) shows similar patterns to the more detailed subset of the data compiled by the author. Also, child graves do not have both shell beads and drilled teeth while some adults do have both (Kyselý et al. 2019: 106, 108).

5 Dogtooth ornaments in a broader Corded Ware scope

Petzold (2019), a large study on East-Central German CWC drilled teeth from at least 79 graves, shows that out of 17 dogtooth-bearing graves with anthropolog-ical determination, 76.5% (13 graves) contain females, that 60% (10 graves) are adults and 30% (5 graves) subadults (Petzold 2005: 4, 5). Again, these are compa-rable to the Czech CWC data. Both Kyselý et al. (2019: 93) and Petzold (2005: 4) state that most of the dogteeth were from relatively young dogs, contrasting the predominantly older dogs found at Brown & Anthony’s Krasnosamarskoe.

In Oechlitz, Saale, Sachsen-Anhalt, dogtooth ornaments (mostly canines and incisors) are reported by Menke et al. (2017) in 11 graves (in ten graves also with shell beads, and with amber beads in four graves) out of a total of 158 CWC graves (dogteeth thus found in 7% of the graves), all of them lying in typically fe-male (left-crouched) body position. Most of them were anthropologically female adults under the age of 40 (but mature individuals were also well-represented), except for one male (still left-crouched). Two of the adults were together with a non-adult, and in one instance only a non-adult was found. The number of dogs represented by the teeth in each grave at Oechlitz range from 6 to 18 minimum numbers of individuals, and the teeth were mostly lying in front of the individu-al, sometimes in rows, though other positions similar to those in the Czech data are known as well. Some found behind the head with shell beads were interpret-ed as a possible shawl or back veil–like adornment and compared to similar veils with various inbraided shells, flowers, glass beads, metal plates, grain straws,

281An update on the Corded Ware culture

and cloth strips worn by girls in the child-bearing age in 17–19th-century North-eastern Bulgarian societies. In other graves the placement indicated bracelets or arm rings.

Grave 20055 with a stone slab construction contained a young adult in fe-male body position buried with dogtooth ornaments, fox canines, a copper arm ring, amber beads, and a flint blade, and with a 2–3-year-old child. Some of the dogteeth (canines) may have formed a necklace, and some may have been a shroud for the child (Menke et al. 2017). Menke et al. (2017: 277–278) mention ethnographic parallels in the Solomon Islands where headbands made of shells and dog- or dolphin teeth are used as currency, and even as dowry, which may be relevant for interpreting CWC shells and animal teeth.

We also find a few graves with dogtooth ornaments between Tauber and Steig-wald in South-Central Germany, e.g., in Hopferstadt gr. 12 (56 teeth), Geißlin-gen gr. 1012 (144 teeth and imitations), and Possenheim gr. 10005 (at least 72 teeth from dogs, pigs, and a small ruminant), all three containing adult females (Schussmann 2016: 81–84).

Shell beads and animal tooth ornaments are also found in the CWC of the Little Poland Upland (all from period III, c. 2550–2200 BCE, Włodarczak 2006: 126), judging from the data from 220 CWC graves in Włodarczak (2006: 39, ta-bles 29 and 40). However, the sex/gender pattern for these is different from the other CWC regions mentioned here, and their ornaments are fewer in number. Animal (mostly dog/wolf) tooth ornaments are found, only in single specimens, in four graves (1.8% of the 220 graves):43 two males (three if including arrowheads as a male emblem) and one undetermined child. Shell beads in this region of Po-land are found in 6 graves (2.7%, with a maximum of only 10 shell beads in one grave),44 also mostly with males or undetermined children, one together with a female. So in the later CWC of Little Poland, the data does not seem to contradict the male association of dogs and males following the model by Brown & An-thony (2017; 2019) and Kristiansen et al. (2017), although especially dogteeth are very few in number, but the late CWC date still speaks against these dogteeth as reflecting male dog–warrior bands in the formation of the early CWC, while the early CWC dog burial does not.

43 Książnice gr. 2, Książnice Wielkie gr. 3, Malice Kościelne gr. 14A, and Złota–Nad Waw-rem gr. 90 (Włodarczak 2006: table 40).

44 Kazimierza Mała gr. 79, Książnice Wielkie gr. 6 and 11, Malice Kościelne 14A (incl. tooth ornaments), Mierzanowice, st. 1 gr. 129, Żerniki Górne gr. 85 (Włodarczak 2006: table 40).

282 Mikkel Nørtoft

In the Fatyanovo culture, shell and animal tooth ornaments, including bear teeth (perhaps from their connection with the Volosovo culture), are found pri-marily in female graves. Although species other than bear are not reported, some of them seem smaller and could resemble dog canines (Nordqvist and Heyd 2020: 8, 13, 15).

Animal tooth and shell ornaments are not exclusive to the CWC or the Ene-olithic in general, but they may have conveyed different meanings in different periods. They are also known in the Mesolithic and Palaeolithic, often in female graves, sometimes with children. Petersen (2016) has proposed the interesting hypothesis that the Mesolithic and Palaeolithic examples functioned as protective amulets, especially when found with an adult female (presumably mother) and a child. He also suggests that when these shell and tooth beads lie beside the head and/or shoulders, instead of under the head (previously assumed to be part of a kind of pillow), they may have been protective decoration on a papoose or a ‘carrying strap’.

Indeed, in some female CWC graves these dogteeth and/or shell beads have a similar placement. However, in a few cases, the placement was described and analysed more thoroughly. In Prague–Březiněves gr. 10, the dog canines found behind the head of the deceased were interpreted as having adorned a cap, hood, or headdress. Dog canines and incisors (all perforated at the root) primarily lay in eight rows in the neck and chest area of the deceased and were interpreted as a complex necklace, or perhaps rather sewn directly on to the clothing or to a shroud. Canines, especially incisors (particularly incisivus 3 superior, the largest incisor) were over-represented and cheek teeth under-represented compared to anatomical ratios in living dogs, meaning their appearance in the grave were the product of human selection for specific dogteeth, likely resulting from gradual collection. The shell beads lay spread over the torso, with the highest concentra-tion, seemingly in short rows around the pelvis, probably reflecting the original pattern of shell beads or perhaps a special shell-adorned clothing item (Kyselý et al. 2019: 90–94), so here probably not a carrying strap either.

A similar example can be found in Karsdorf, Saxo Anhalt, gr. 59/59, one of the most furnished of the C14-dated CWC graves, and also the oldest (c. 2750 cal bce, see Behnke 2015). The grave, which contains an adult female with a child placed in the corner, is positioned centrally among the old graves in the cemetery and is suggested to represent the ‘founder generation’ at the site (Behnke 2015: 166, 172). During the excavation of the grave, the concentration of many hundreds of beads was interpreted as a form of ‘backpack’ or ‘carrying strap’, but subsequent analysis of the arrangement patterns of the shell and tooth beads (which had both

283An update on the Corded Ware culture

clustered and more scattered areas in the grave) has suggested that it was rather a shell-decorated woven fabric or leather cover or wrapping for the deceased fe-male (Behnke 2015: 128–133). An individual child’s grave was also found at Kars-dorf in the corner of the cemetery, male judging from the body position, with 111 shell beads (perhaps from a belt) and other grave goods such as flint and ceramics, but no dogteeth. This grave was less furnished than grave 59/59 (Behnke 2005 and 2015: 133).

Petersen’s idea of the papoose or ‘carrying strap’ (in the Mesolithic and Palaeo-lithic material) applies mostly to graves with a woman and child, especially when the child is very close to the female. This is often not the case for the Corded Ware examples, where they are primarily found in individual graves of either an adult or a child. Only three out of 37 graves with age group determination in the Czech CWC dataset from Kyselý et al. (2019) had both one or more adults and a child. In the case at Karsdorf, the child is in the corner of the grave pit, with only some parts of the legs being covered by the shell beads (Behnke 2015: 130), and the shell beads may thus rather be associated with the adult female.

Petersen (2016) also suggests that in the Mesolithic and Palaeolithic examples, the shell beads were probably not prestige objects, but that their primary function was to protect the child from evil, and that the women or children wearing them may have been handicapped, sick, or mentally ill. However, I see no reason why the protective and prestige functions should be mutually exclusive (no evidence for the individuals being handicapped, sick, or mentally ill is given by Petersen).45 A papoose-like wearable, while functioning as a magic protection, could also be an ideal way for mothers to show their wealth and status to others, especially when wearing large amounts of shell beads.

Occasionally, as in the richly furnished Marefy 177.1.1 grave, and in Oechlitz, Central Germany, shell beads are found with copper or amber ornaments, which we would expect to be prestigious objects as well. However, if dogteeth and shell beads were only fashion items, the local availability of the source material would make them relatively easy for anyone to wear. Instead, they are still quite rare – dogteeth are only found in nine out of 299 graves (3%) in the Bohemian sample, and one out of 81 graves (1%) in the Moravian sample – so it may have been a cultural restriction, rather than scarcity or the distance of import of the material, which determined who was buried with them.

45 It should be noted that Petersen does not mention the Corded Ware examples, so this is merely a discussion of whether to apply his ideas from the Palaeolithic and Mesolithic material to the CWC cases.

284 Mikkel Nørtoft

Whether this indicates a specialised ritual function or some other heterarchic function for select females with dogteeth is unclear. While the teeth are suggested to have been collected over a long period of time for at least 12 graves with more than 100 dogteeth in the Czech data in Kyselý et al. (2019), their use-wear var-ies. Some look only slightly worn, suggesting that they were either relatively new or only worn on special occasions, while others show more wear or even repair, suggesting long-time use or perhaps being in circulation over several decades (Menke et al. 2017: 278). Overall their position in graves varies considerably, some positions suggesting that they were decorative parts of hats, hoods, headdresses, pouches, or bags, or that they formed necklaces and wrist or ankle jewellery. In cases where they were more scattered in the grave or in longer rows, they perhaps adorned burial shrouds, blankets, coats, or other clothing with stripes of dogteeth, sometimes in combination with shell beads (Kyselý et al. 2019: 126).

6 Dogteeth and shell beads in cultures neighbouring the Corded Ware culture

Shell beads are also found in Pontic–Caspian steppe societies, and may even be portrayed on a Yamna anthropomorphic stone stela from Utkonosovka north of the Danube delta, interpreted as depicting a female (Mallory 1989: 220). However, for the discussion of the connection between dogs and gender in steppe societies, the focus here will be dogtooth ornaments.

Perforated dogteeth (17 pieces) have been found in the CWC-contemporary Globular Amphora culture at Tangermünde and Frohndorf, both in Mittelelbe- Saale, Germany, although their demographic context is not given (Beier 1988: 39, 155).

Anthony (2007: 362, 364–365) refers to dogtooth pendants/beads in some Yamna graves, especially around the Ingul and South Bug valleys in Ukraine and in Eastern Hungary, in the context of Indo- European warrior bands and their presumed belts. He does not mention sex, gender, or age determination for these graves, but suggests a connection between dogteeth and belts as male warrior symbols because anthropomorphic Yamna stone stelae often have belts carved into them in the same area as dogteeth in graves – although images of dogteeth have not, to my knowledge, been found on the stelae.

In the Usatove culture near Odessa, at the site of Usatove, kurgan cemetery II, kurgan 2, grave 1, an individual was buried with a necklace of 47 teeth from dogs or wolves, lying on its left side with head towards east, a position typical for females (Dergachev et al. 1991: 111–112, Razumov 2018). Again, I could not find any reference to the sex and age of this individual.

On the Lower Dnipro in the Nikopol region near the village Pokrovske at the ‘Storozhevaya Mogila’ kurgan group, kurgan 2 had ten Yamna burials (and two from the Catacomb period), one of which (grave 6, 12 m from the centre of the 30 m wide mound) was a child of unknown gender or sex, buried with sheep/goat bones, various bone items, and drilled dog canines (Chernykh et al. 2014: 14–16).

Frînculeasa et al. (2020: 11, with references) give a brief overview of dogtooth ornaments in the 3rd millennium bce from Hungary (at least sometimes with non-adults), Romanian Yamna (mostly with non-adults), Armenia (Kura Araxes culture), as well as in burial mounds from north of the Caucasus, Ukraine, Bul-garia, and Baden culture graves in Central Europe. Investigating the demograph-ic context for all these examples is beyond the scope of this paper. However, in Șoimești, Romania, the dogtooth ornaments (molars from four different dogs), fox teeth (canines), and Unio shell beads, were found with a woman, probably of

286 Mikkel Nørtoft

high status (Frînculeasa et al. 2020). At Târgșoru Vechi gr. 10 in Prahova, Roma-nia, seven perforated dog and fox canines are found with a four-year-old, and at Glăvăneștii Vechi gr. 17, a two-year-old had a perforated animal molar (Frîncu-leasa et al. 2019).

Dogtooth necklaces have also been found in graves of the Baden culture in Austria (Leobersdorf gr. 1) and Hungary (Mezőcsát–Hörcsögös gr. 7) (Sachße 2010: II 56–57, 65). In a Hungarian Baden culture cemetery at Balatonlelle-Rád-puszta site 67/5, grave 367, a 35–45-year-old woman (also genetically female), C14-dated to 3508–3429 cal BCE, was buried with 16 drilled dog canines (from at least six dogs, and probably more based on variation in sizes) and no other grave goods. Her head rested on a fragmented child’s skull (1–7 years old) of undeter-mined sex, seemingly unrelated to her, although the DNA was poorly preserved, and it is uncertain if they were buried simultaneously. Use-wear analysis showed that the dogteeth had been worn for a long time. Most of the teeth were found at her leg (Gál and Bondár 2022).

Zidarov (2020) mentions 117 finds of dogtooth ornaments from 30 different sites throughout the 3rd millennium bce in western Yamna and the subsequent Cata-comb culture (especially in eastern Ukraine), in Hungary (Kétegyháza), Thrace, Macedonia, as well as in the Early Bronze Age Aegean and in western Anatolia (e.g., Troy I). Usually, the dogtooth pendants or necklaces are found in settlements or house floors, but three grave finds are known in Bulgaria: a Bereketska flat grave, a Goran–Slatina tumulus grave (neither of them sex or age-determined), and a Yamna primary tumulus grave from Mednikarovo–Iskritsa. The latter individual, a 14-year-old female, was buried with 2 dogtooth pendants and 14 silver beads (Panayotov et al. 1995: 95, Zidarov 2020: table 1), thus again, based on the silver, seemingly a high-status female, this time adolescent. For a map of all graves with dogteeth in this study from the late 4th to the 3rd millennium BCE, see Figure 6.

Many of these references to dogtooth ornaments do not mention sex or ar-chaeological gender determination of the buried individuals, and sometimes not age either. Some are non-adults, which makes it difficult to determine sex without DNA analysis. Thus, we rarely get more insight regarding the association with males, or lack thereof, of these dogtooth ornaments.

As seen above, CWC dog (and some wolf) tooth pendants are rather found with adult females along with shell beads (and rarely with young males), primar-ily in Bohemia and Central Germany (7–11% of all graves), but also more spo-radically in Moravia, Bavaria and other German regions, Western Slovakia, and Poland (Kyselý et al. 2019: 121).

287An update on the Corded Ware culture

The practice of wearing dogteeth seems to have persisted in some areas after the Corded Ware period. Gál & Bondár (2022) give an overview of dogtooth (pri-marily drilled canine) ornaments from settlements and graves of the Bronze Age (Maros, Vatya, Encrusted Pottery, Gáta, and Perjámos/Maros cultures), and in the cases where sex or gender has been determined, the individual is female: at Hód-mezővásárhely–Kopáncs (Perjámos/Maros culture, c. 2300–1500 BCE), we find a 16- to 18-year-old girl with “a lavish array of jewellery” comprising canines and incisors of dog, fox, wolf, and cattle, as well as marine shells, faience beads, bronze spiral tubes, and bronze studs, possibly attached to garments or a headdress (Gál & Bondár 2022: 52); and at the Oroszvár cemetery (Gáta culture, c. 2200–1500 BCE), we find dog canines on a woman together with bronze spiral beads, and shell beads (Dentalium species). According to Gál & Bondár (2022, with references), these dog canines symbolised rank and status early on, and during the probably more socially stratified Bronze Age, they symbolised wealth and power.

At the Early Bronze Age Mokrin necropolis in northern Serbia, a female child grave (gr. 55) was found with a handled beaker and a necklace with three perfo-rated canine dogteeth, two cylindrical bone beads, and 12 greenish kaolin beads (Lazaridis et al. 2022: Supplementary information 176–177). We also find dog-tooth ornaments in the Únětice culture in the early 2nd millennium bce, such as the cemetery at Mikulovice, and in the Maďarovce culture in Slovakia (Zidarov 2020, Kyselý et al. 2019: 121–123).

Further, we find the combination of dogteeth and mother-of-pearl beads in Græse, Zealand, Denmark, in a Late Neolithic (2350–1700 bce) grave of a physi-cally “robust” female (Kjær 1910).46

7 Conclusion

This section has critically examined the evidence for a proposed hypothesis of a male wolf/warrior in connection with steppe migrations in the early 3rd millen-nium BCE.

From a detailed subset of Czech Corded Ware culture graves, it has been shown that perforated dogteeth (sometimes in very high numbers) and shell beads appear in the upper half of a grave-good wealth scale (TOT) which is based on the presence of different types of grave goods – higher, in fact, than items like battle-axes, a traditionally suggested elite male sodality symbol. In this sample

46 I would like to thank Jens Winther Johannsen for this information.

288 Mikkel Nørtoft

data, dogteeth and shell beads are mostly found with adult females, and only very rarely with males. Dogteeth are also found in fewer graves than battle-axes, sug-gesting that they may have been a stronger status marker (especially when found in high numbers), despite the fact that both dogteeth and shell beads (mother-of-pearl) were locally available materials. However, when found in low numbers in child graves, they could also have functioned as protective or guiding amulets in life or in the afterlife.

A wider overview of dogtooth ornaments and shell beads (especially from mother-of-pearl), while not exhaustive, shows that these ornaments were clearly associated with females in the Corded Ware culture (CWC) in general, as also concluded by Kyselý et al. (2019), except in the few cases from the Little Poland Upland. While they are also found in steppe societies, their association there with gender, age, and status remains unclear until a proper bioarchaeological study is done on the individuals in these graves. If the CWC is to be seen as reflect-ing an early (Core) Indo- European–speaking culture, it does not seem to reflect the male dog/wolf youth warrior institution or initiation that Brown & Anthony (2019) propose and cannot be connected with the early CWC as Anthony (2022) and Kristiansen et al. (2017) propose. Instead, the CWC dogtooth ornaments (ex-cept in the few graves in the Little Poland Upland) seem to be primarily female status items culturally restricted to relatively few females. However, in most CWC cases, they appear only in the middle-late CWC, and in Poland where the few examples seem to be in male graves, they appear in Find Group III, i.e., probably later CWC, which does not fit the early CWC scout phase mentioned by Anthony (2022: 7, 13, 15–16). There may still be a case for the male dog-warrior model in the CWC if dog graves can be demonstrated to be primarily found with males in the ‘age of initiation’ or older. While there may be a pattern of more males (including one early grave in Poland) than females buried with dogs in the CWC (currently 4 males to 1 female), the sample size is still far too small to be significant. Also, the cases found here are mostly adults, and CWC sites with extensive dog sacrifice comparable to Krasnosamarskoe or Mayaki are not known. In any case, a scout-ing phase model with young males penetrating through Europe before the larger steppe migrations still seems plausible without wolf or dog associations since the earliest phases of the CWC do have primarily male burials, and steppe-related migrations, especially relating to the CWC and Yamna, have been shown genet-ically to often be male-driven, though there are some regional exceptions to this pattern where females seem to have played an equal role (cf. Juras et al. 2018 for the eastern CWC, and Patterson et al. 2022 for the Late Bronze Age migrations to The British Isles associated with the spread of Celtic languages). The Yamna

289An update on the Corded Ware culture

phenomenon (at least North Pontic ‘Core Yamna’) is increasingly seen as a form of male sodality, in part due to having mostly male burials, but also due to their very narrow Y-haplogroup range (almost exclusively R1b-Z2103 so far) and very homogeneous autosomal DNA, and perhaps did not represent a society, but rath-er a select male elite or clan (Anthony et al. 2022: 4, Lazaridis et al. 2024).

The question remains why dogtooth and shell ornaments were seemingly culturally restricted to so few individuals despite their locally available materi-als – were they perhaps a kind of social marker, meant for protection, or (judg-ing from their concentration in the upper half of the TOT scale) indicative of their owners’ prestigious function in society, such as female shamans, midwives, or healers with a certain status? In the cases of children with only a few dogteeth, they could perhaps reflect protective amulets, and in the case of individuals with many dogteeth (especially adults), they could perhaps reflect a ritual function or a special status. Kyselý et al. (2019) make a comparison between the CWC dogteeth and the much later Greek goddess Hekate, who had functions relat-ed to transitions between life and death and was often shown accompanied by dogs, suggesting that dogs were seen as guardians of, or guides (‘psychopomps’) in, the afterlife. If presuming a shamanistic function, it is possible that some children with dogteeth and shell beads had been singled out to follow a path as shamans. A proper bioarchaeological investigation into the health and lifestyle of these children (and the adults) compared with the rest of their society could perhaps illuminate this further.

If CWC shells and animal teeth were used as currency and as part of the dow-ry, and assuming Testart is correct that when bridewealth and dowry coexist, dowry is mostly paid in the upper tiers of society, this is perhaps an independent indication that these CWC females were from richer families. However, we would probably not expect the dowry to go in the grave if the individual’s daughter(s) had been married. So under this logic, the dowry would only go into the grave if the buried woman did not have living daughters to pass on her dowry (or rath-er, her trousseau/strīdhana) to. This specific situation could perhaps also explain why these graves are not the norm in the CWC, and are almost only found with females. The geographical concentration of these ornaments would suggest that this form of dowry was most prevalent in Bohemia and Central Germany and may have become less common after the CWC, perhaps already fading in the later phase of the CWC. The larger dogtooth and shell bead assemblages in a few child graves (although not comparable to the richer adults) could perhaps indicate that such a dowry was accumulated over time from the time of birth of a child in some families. It must be noted that no single explanation fits all the data – all these

290 Mikkel Nørtoft

interpretations require a lot of assumptions and speculation and should be taken with the utmost caution.

Regarding the male dog-warrior model by Brown & Anthony and Kristiansen et al., it is also possible that young male warrior institutions became associated with dogs only after the CWC period. It could perhaps have spread with chariots and horseback riding across the Indo- European–speaking world from around 2000 BCE, connected with the Sintashta, Andronovo and Srubnaya cultures (Librado et al. 2021). This would also be closer to the date of Brown & Anthony’s Late Bronze Age Krasnosamarskoe dog sacrifice site (c. 1900–1700 BCE), if that really reflects male dog-warrior initiations. If this was the case, the similar historical and myth-ological accounts about young male dog-warrior institutions summarized by Ker-shaw (2000), among others, might reflect a cultural, rather than demic, diffusion of the association between male warriors and dogs/wolves during the 2nd millennium BCE, with new, intensified long-distance trading and marriage networks between elites. Such networks – resulting in some of the widely shared Bronze Age social and religious institutions, large-scale wool production, spoke-wheeled chariots, and mythologically loaded figurative iconography – were previously suggested by Kristiansen & Larsson (2005: 364), Kaul (2015), and Iversen (2014; 2024). These seem to better fit many elements in the Indo- European world view from compar-ative mythology and vocabulary (Iversen 2024), perhaps including dog-warriors.

Alternatively, young male dog-warriors may have been present as an institu-tion already in the CWC, leaving almost no archaeological trace (except perhaps in Little Poland, and the four dog burials with males) because they were hidden or marginal groups in a temporary phase of their lives. While this cannot be exclud-ed, it does seem a somewhat ad hoc solution, unless bioarchaeological investiga-tions can establish a predominance of male (human) individuals in connection with dog burials or sacrifices.

To explain the predominantly male sex of 72 sampled dog genomes around Eurasia from the Neolithic and Bronze Age we may consider the possibly very old dog-as-guardian function. If guard dogs in life were predominantly male, it could be that afterlife guard dogs (such as Greek Kerberos, Indic Śarvara, and Old Norse Garmr), were also perceived as typically male.47

47 In a quick, but non-exhaustive, survey in etymological dictionaries (Mayrhofer 1986, 1992, and 1997, De Vries 1957, Beekes 2010, Matasović 2009, and Derksen 2015), the words/names relating to ‘dog of the underworld, dog demon, guardian’ in Greek, Indo- Iranian, Celtic, Germanic, and Baltic were all, at least grammatically, masculine: Ger-$manic Garmr, Greek Κέρβερος, Young Avestan vítūla-, and several masculine names $in Sanskrit: kūrkurá-, sīsara, téka-, balā-bandhaná-, and mandākaka-. Only one word

291An update on the Corded Ware culture

This study does not completely ‘debunk’ the male dog/wolf warrior hypothesis associated with the formation and spread of the CWC. However, it raises some serious problems with its archaeological evidence, and tentatively suggests that its Indo- European mythological evidence may rather belong with a larger array of ideas spreading across Western Eurasia from the 2nd millennium BCE onwards, which calls for further investigations.

In-laws and outlaws in Indo- European societies

The master of the house and his circles of interest

Birgit Anette Olsen University of Copenhagen

The spread of the Indo- European way of life in terms of language and

institutions is intimately connected with the capacity of Indo- European–

speaking populations to establish alliances with their neighbours, there-

by gradually extending their circles of social and military influence. The

strategies employed include exogamous marriages, fosterage, patronage

and guest-friendship. This article investigates the vocabulary of some of

these institutions.

For anyone working with concepts such as ‘Indo- European society’ or ‘Indo- European kinship terminology’, it is necessary to define what exactly they mean by ‘Indo- European’ in the given context. Are they, as is often implicitly done, equalling ‘Indo- European’ with Proto- Indo- European, the common pre-stage of all Indo- European languages, or is ‘Indo- European’ simply used as a cover term for reconstructed stages and attested languages and/or cultures that can be traced back to the speakers of Proto- Indo- European? In the present article, I will use the cover term, though primarily dealing with the stage of ‘Core Indo- European’, here defined as the cladistic node following the separation of first Anatolian, secondly probably Tocharian.

As stated in Olsen (2020: 40), “… kinship terminology mirrors the needs and conventions of society, and obviously, it must make a difference whether we are dealing with the nomadic, pastoral societies of the Pontic–Caspian steppe around 3500 bc, now commonly if not universally identified as the Indo- European homeland, or the somewhat later predecessor of the European and Indo- Iranian populations. In both cases, the features of a patrilocal, patrilineal system are ap-parent … but with the development from a nomadic to a more sedentary lifestyle, we may suspect that it gradually became easier to establish more intimate alli-ances of intermarriage, fosterage and guest-friendships between the individual patriarchal households”.

312 Birgit Anette Olsen

In this perspective, the problem is complex in so far as we have to reckon not only with successive stages of society mirrored by the Indo- European proto- language and its descendants, but also with the diverse non–Indo- European so-cieties these populations must have met and interacted with in the course of their migrations to the west and the east. Thus, the essential question, “who are we talking about?” concerns Indo- European–speaking populations meeting either other Indo- European–speaking groups or one of the multitude of prehistoric in-digenous societies that must have existed in Europe and West Asia.

To take an example, we may now have a basic understanding of the cultur-al meeting between the Corded Ware and Únětice cultures in Central Europe (cf., e.g., Kristiansen et al. 2017; Mittnik et al. 2017). Here everything points to a system of exogamy where the Únětice women were included in the patriclans of the Corded Ware culture, but since both cultures may be traced back to Indo- European–speaking populations from the Pontic–Caspian steppe, the differenc-es in social structure may have been minimal. However, the conditions in other parts of Europe, e.g., Southern Europe or Britain, may well have been fundamen-tally different (cf. Booth et al. 2021), not to mention the populations met by the early Indo- Iranians.

For the indigenous inhabitants of Europe and Western Asia, our sources of information are largely provided by archaeologists and geneticists, while solid linguistic evidence is scarce. Most of the extinct non–Indo- European languages in the relevant areas are practically unknown, and at best, we may rely on the interpretation of substratum relics in Indo- European languages, as exemplified by Guus Kroonen’s investigation of agricultural terminology (cf., e.g., Iversen & Kroonen 2017).

1 The Indo- European language family and social terminology

In order to sift the linguistic evidence of the Indo- European languages chronolog-ically with any certainty, we have to know in which order the individual branches separated from the common mother tongue, Proto- Indo- European, and whether any of them formed intermediate proto-languages. Here again we are met with serious challenges.

There is general agreement among Indo- Europeanists that Anatolian was the first branch to separate from the rest of the language family, even if it may be debated how old and how fundamental the schism was. Most likely, Tocharian split off from the main group as the second member though the evidence for this

313In-laws and outlaws in Indo- European societies

is less certain. However, when we move further on in time and space, the details become more obscure. Figure 1 illustrates one attempt to provide a genealogical tree, but there is no guarantee that this is the final answer.

Two striking features characterize the social vocabulary of the Indo- European languages. First, we are in most cases dealing with transparent, phonologically regular inherited creations structured according to known morphological prin-ciples. Secondly, Anatolian shares very little of the common lexicon in this field, and for Tocharian, as far as we can see at present, almost only the most basic kin-ship terms for ‘father’, ‘mother’, ‘brother’, ‘sister’, ‘son’, ‘daughter’ and ‘grandfather’ have cognates in the other branches, though further research in the field may still uncover new details.1

In Anatolian, there are apparently no continuations of the otherwise ubiq-uitous words for ‘father’ (*ph₂tér-), ‘mother’ (*máh₂ter-), ‘brother’ (*bʰráh₂ter-), ‘sister’ (*su̯ésor-), and ‘son’ (*suhₓnú- or *suhₓi̯ú-). Instead, we find various hypo-coristics, as is usual throughout the world’s languages, e.g., Hittite atta- ‘father’, anna- ‘mother’. The only basic kinship terms where Anatolian agrees with the oth-er Indo- European languages include the word for ‘daughter’, Lycian kbatra, which has cognates in all other branches except Albanian, e.g., Vedic duhitár-, Greek $θυγάτηρ, English daughter. To this we may add ‘grandfather’, Hittite ḫuḫḫa-, re-$lated to Tocharian āwe, Latin avus, ON afi, Armenian haw; and a hypocoristic word for ‘child, son’, *putlo-, continued in Hittite Épulla- ‘children’s house’, Vedic putrá-, Oscan acc. sg, puklum ‘son’. Not even the basic root *g̑enh₁- ‘procreate’,

314 Birgit Anette Olsen

known from numerous terms referring to the paternal lineage, is prominent in Anatolian.2

This again means that either Anatolian accidentally lost all of these terms, which rather seems like too much of a coincidence, or that they are the result of a common Core-Indo- European innovation as another indication of the funda-mental “first split” between Anatolian and the other branches.3 The precise status of Tocharian in this context is difficult to evaluate, but a detailed and precise kinship terminology is one of the features that unite the European branches and Indo- Iranian.4

2 Core-Indo- European family structure

The defining features of Core-Indo- European family structure are patrilineage, patrilocality and exogamy. Heritage in all senses of the word goes from father to son. The father is the procreator, the *g̑n̥h₁tḗr/*g̑énh₁tōr, even on the very highest level where Father Heaven is our common father and procreator/procreator and $father – Vedic pitā́ janitā́, Avestan ząϑā ptā, Greek γενέτωρ πατήρ, Latin pater … $genitor (cf. Jackson 2017: 127–128).

The paternal line is essential, and if a family has the misfortune of not having any sons, all measures are taken to repair this flaw and restore the situation to normality. Thus, there are linguistic indications that at least Germanic, Greek and Indo- Iranian agree on the institution of ‘heritage daughters’ to fill in the gap until such a daughter would give birth to a legitimate heir from the patriclan, and the practice is also known from the Iranians, Armenians and southern Slavs.5 The archaic Greek Gortyn Law Code even gives detailed instructions about which

2 Cf. Serangeli (2020) for a thorough treatment of the Anatolian material. The root *g̑enh₁- is preserved in genzu- ‘lap’ and probably in nekna- ‘son’.

3 Cf. Olsen (2020a: 43–46) for further discussion. 4 The literature on the subject is extensive, but let me just refer to Olsen (2020a) for a re-

cent comprehensive treatment that may be consulted for supplementary discussion and references, Pinault (2007 and 2017) for original interpretations of the overall system, Szemerényi (1977) for an older, excessively etymologizing treatment, and the classic work by Delbrück (1889), whose basic observations still hold true. A recent substantial study of the subject from an anthropological point of view is Milanova (2021), and an interdisciplinary study of two Bell Beaker cemeteries including linguistic argumenta-tion is provided by Sjögren et al. (2020).

5 Olsen (2020a: 91–93) with reference to Wackernagel (1953 [1916]: 6–9) and Scharfe (1964–1965: 266).

315In-laws and outlaws in Indo- European societies

member of her father’s family should be prioritized in the marriage of such a heritage daughter (father’s oldest brother, son of father’s oldest brother, etc.) so as to secure the continuation of the lineage.

This seems to be the only situation where the strict principle of exogamy could be broken. Otherwise, wives were ‘led into marriage’ as indicated by the root *h₂u̯edh₁- (cf. Olsen 2020: 160), with the double meaning of ‘lead, conduct’ $(Avestan vāδaiieiti ‘leads’, Old Irish fedid ‘leads, carries, brings’, Gothic gawidan $‘connect’) and ‘marry’, only used about the groom (Welsh dyweddïo ‘betroth’, Old English weddian ‘marry’, Old Prussian wedd ‘marry’, Lithuanian vedù, Latvian vędu ‘lead; marry [of a man]’). Another well-known linguistic argument in favour of exogamy is the rich and very specific vocabulary for members of the husband’s household that must be attributed to Core Indo- European, no matter how exact-ly these terms are analyzed. Thus, there are specific words for ‘husband’s broth-er’, *dah₂i̯u̯ḗr (attested in Italic, Germanic, Greek, Armenian, Balto-Slavic and Indo- Iranian),6 ‘husband’s sister’, *g̑l̥h₂u- or the like (Italic, Greek, Armenian and Slavic),7 and even ‘husband’s brother’s wife’, *h₁i̯enh₂tḗr (Italic, Greek, Armenian, Indo- Iranian and Balto-Slavic).8

8 Gamkrelidze & Ivanov (1995: 662, Mallory & Adams (1997: 522), Pinault (2005), NIL 204–207, Olsen (2020a: 136–138).

316 Birgit Anette Olsen

These linguistic observations are meaningful if the young brides were tak-en from foreign communities and introduced into patrilocal households. Here they would be in daily contact with their husband’s extended family, including his grown-up brothers with their wives and children and his young, still unmarried sisters. What is more, this general picture is now amply confirmed by archaeolog-ical and genetic data.9

3 The mother-in-law and father-in-law

The head of the Indo- European-speaking family was the *déms pótis, the master of the house, his spouse the *déms pot(n)íh₂ (cf. Pinault 2017a: 337), and conse-quently this couple are the parents-in-law of the incoming bride. On the other hand, the groom also has parents-in-law, and while Core Indo- European has a well attested set of terms for ‘mother-in-law’ and ‘father-in-law’,10 it is worth con-sidering whether these terms refer to the parents of the husband, the wife, or both.

For ‘mother-in-law’, an *-uh₂-stem *su̯ek̑rúh₂s is continued in Latin socrus, $Welsh chwegr, Old High German swigar, Vedic śvaśrū́ḥ, Persian χusru $̄ and Old Church Slavonic svekry. A thematic masculine *su̯ék̑uros referring to the father-$in-law is the basis of Latin socer, Old High German swehur, Greek ἑκυρός, Alba-$nian vjehërr, Vedic śváśura-, Avestan xᵛasura-, and Lithuanian šẽšuras; and of the motion feminine *su̯ek̑uráh₂-, referring again to the mother-in-law, continued $in Armenian skesowr (distant assimilation for *kʿesowr), Greek ἑκυρά, -η, and $Albanian vjeh(ë)rrë.

Most often, it is taken for granted that the original meaning was ‘husband’s parents’,11 but this is more out of a preconceived idea that the husband’s family is of primary importance than based on actual evidence. It is true that the pair is only used about the husband’s parents in Greek, Armenian and Balto-Slavic, i.e., the central-east, but not easternmost part of the Core-Indo- European area.

9 Cf. especially Mittnik et al. (2017) on 4000-year-old grave steads in the Lech Valley, Bavaria, pointing to marked gender-related and social differences. The graves reveal local male lineages of up to five generations with accumulated wealth, whereas rich, unrelated females were of foreign descent. Finally, the site contains a group of males and females with no valuable grave goods and no mutual family ties.

10 Szemerényi (1977: 63–66), Gamkrelidze & Ivanov (1995: 662), Mallory & Adams (1997: 386–387), NIL 672–675, Olsen (2020a: 114–125).

11 E.g., Schulze (1907: 401), Buck (1988 [1949]: 124), IEW 1043, Darms (1978: 7), Mallory & Adams (2006: 215).

317In-laws and outlaws in Indo- European societies

On the other hand, the meanings ‘wife’s mother/father’ are well attested in Italic, Celtic, Germanic, Albanian and Indo- Iranian12 – indeed, the oldest attestations of ‘mother-in-law’ in Italic and Germanic refer to the wife’s mother, just as the only Avestan example of xᵛasura- refers to the wife’s father.13

Hence, it seems more economic to assume that a coherent dialect area consist-ing of the eastern Balkanic languages and Balto-Slavic was subject to a lexical nar-rowing than the alternative, namely that the remaining branches of Core Indo- European went through mutually independent processes of semantic extension.

This analysis is further confirmed by a number of secondary derivatives. The vr̥ddhi derivative *su̯ēk̑uró- ‘brother-in-law’, based on *su̯ék̑uro-, must be the son of the father-in-law, but if this father-in-law exclusively referred to the husband’s father, the brother-in-law must always be the husband’s brother, otherwise known as *dah₂i̯u̯ḗr, which is not the case. The oldest attestation of Old High German swāgur refers to the wife’s brother, though we also find the alternative meanings ‘sister’s husband’, ‘sister’s son’ and ‘husband’s brother’. This may of course be due to semantic extension, but more significantly, similar derivatives in modern Indo- Iranian languages exclusively concern the wife’s family, thus *śvā́śuri- > Kash-miri hahar ‘wife’s brother’ and *śvaśuriya- > Pashai (Dardic) išpairi, also ‘wife’s brother’ (Turner 1962–1966: 737). The linguistic evidence thus suggests that the wife’s family played an important role in the designation of ‘in-laws’ of the oldest generation, and that it may even be appropriate to turn the tables and suggest that the original meaning of *su̯ek̑rúh₂s/su̯ék̑uros was ‘wife’s parents’.

Another unsolved linguistic question is the derivational relationship between the words for ‘father-in-law’ and ‘mother-in-law’, where again some scholars as-sume that ‘father-in-law’ is the primary formation (e.g., Peters 1980: 184, Mayr-hofer 1986: 161–162). It is, however, remarkable that the feminine formation be-longs to a morphologically rare type, whereas the masculine is a simple thematic stem that may easily have been created from the feminine along the following lines:

*su̯ek̑rúh₂- ‘mother-in-law’ $ → *su̯ék̑ruh₂-o- ‘(someone) associated with the mother-in-law’ > *su̯ék̑ru-o- → *su̯ék̑uro- (metathesis preventing hiatus; Olsen 2020: 122). $

12 Out of the two attestations of śvaśrū́- in the Rigveda, one (10.85.46) refers to the hus-band’s mother, the other (10.34.3) to the wife’s (cf. Olsen 2020a: 115–117 for discussion).

13 Yt. 10.116: “Twentyfold is the contract between two friends … eightyfold … –antarə zāmātara xᵛasura – between son-in-law and father-in-law”, cf. Gerschevitch (1967: 131).

318 Birgit Anette Olsen

There are several indications in the individual languages that the mother-in-law is the important member of the pair: Welsh chwegrwn and Russian Church Slavic svekrъ ‘father-in-law’ are modeled on the feminine, Modern Persian xus-rū, the old feminine form, refers to both the mother-in-law and the father-in-law, German Schwiegervater is created after Schwieger ‘mother-in-law’, and the literal meaning of Armenian skesr-ayr ‘father-in-law’ is either ‘mother-in-law’s husband’ (if < *skesowr + ayr) or ‘mother-in-law-father’ (if < *skesowr-a-hayr; cf. Szemerényi 1977: 64).14

$Also in Greek, the irregular final accent of ἑκυρός as opposed to Vedic śváśu-$ra-, whose original status is secured by the contrast-accented vṛddhi formation

*su̯ēk̑uró-, would point to influence from the feminine. Frisk (GEW 1: 478–479) offers a coherent and convincing explanation for these observations: “Auch in anderen Sprachen haben die Namen der Schwiegermutter neue Bezeichnungen $des Schwiegervaters herbeigeführt … Die Oxytonierung in ἑκυρός wird da-$durch leicht begreiflich. Offenbar hat im Leben der alten Großfamilie, nament-lich für die junge Frau … die Schwiegermutter eine wichtigere Rolle gespielt als der Schwiegervater. Die Frage ist somit berechtigt, ob nicht auch idg. *su̯ék̑uros gegenüber *su̯ek̑rṹs sekundär ist”.15

In conclusion, the linguistic data suggest that the mother-in-law had an im-portant function in her own right as the female authority figure of the younger women of the household, while the primary role of the father-in-law was that of master of the house and head of the patriclan. However, while this is all perfectly compatible with the traditional understanding of Indo- European family structure, what may seem more surprising at first sight is the prominent role that originally seems to have been attributed to the wife’s mother in the role of mother- in-law.

14 Cf. also Modern Armenian *skesur-pap “father at husband’s mother”, i.e., husband’s father, and zokʿančʿ-pap “father at wife’s mother”, i.e., wife’s father (Martirosyan 2010: 581).

15 Cf. already Specht (1938: 193): “Da die in die idg. Großfamilie aufgenommene Schwieger-tochter durch Pflicht und Arbeitsbetätigung im wesentlichen mit der Schwiegermutter verbunden war, so ist es auch sprachlich verständlich, daß das verwandtschaftliche Verhältnis zwischen Schwiegertochter und Schwiegervater durch adjektivische Ablei-tung aus dem Begriff *svek̑rṹs wiedergegeben wurde”. I wish to thank Anahita Hoose (p.c.) for pointing out the secondary role played by the father-in-law in medieval Jain literature as an illustration of “a society with a high degree of gender segregation in do-mestic environments” where the daughter-in-law “is totally subordinate to the senior woman of the household, who appears as a much more significant figure in her life than her husband himself ”.

319In-laws and outlaws in Indo- European societies

This leads us to the relation of Indo- European–speaking men to their in-laws. As for the parents-in-law, we first observe that the pair *su̯ek̑rúh₂s/ *su̯ék̑uros can-not be traced further back than Core Indo- European. We do not know the ter-minology in Proto- Indo- European or even Proto- Indo- Tocharian. Secondly, the etymological interpretation is debatable. Usually *su̯e- is assumed to be the stem of the reflexive pronoun,16 but if this is correct, the element *-k̑rúh₂-/-k̑uro- is less clear. A connection with *kruh₂- ‘(outside) blood’, suggested by Linke (1985), does not account for the discrepancy between *k̑ and *k, and quite apart from its doubtful social implications, Pinault’s derivation from an adverbial *su̯é-tk̑-u̯-er- ‘having/taking (others’) child as his (their) own’ (2017: 96) is excessively complicated and necessitates an ad hoc sound change. At first sight, Schwarz’s interpretation of *k̑uro- from *-k̑uHro- as in Vedic śūrá- ‘strong, powerful’ (1992: 405) is more promising as the short vowel might be due to compositional laryn-geal loss (Mayrhofer 1995: 149–150), but this is only possible if the masculine form was primary, contrary to the circumstantial evidence discussed above.

Finally, Szemerényi (1977: 63–66) ventured the idea that the final part of the compound was the word for ‘head’, elaborated by Olsen (2020: 120) with a ten-tative reconstruction *su̯e-k̑rh₂u- > *su̯e-k̑ruh₂- ‘someone with (her) own head (of family)’.17 However, this was no more than a loose conjecture, and perhaps a semantically more satisfactory solution is at hand:

$The root *k̑erh₃- (LIV² 329) is the basis of the verbs Greek κορέννυμι, Lithua-$nian šérti ‘feed, nourish’ and Armenian serem ‘nourish, bring up’, serim ‘be born’, with such derivatives as serownd ‘offspring’ and sermn ‘seed’. From Latin we have the s-stem Cerēs ‘goddess of grain and fruits’ with close morphological parallels in, e.g., Armenian seṙ ‘offspring’, later also ser (Olsen 1999: 85–86), and in Old High German hirso, Old Saxon hirsi ‘millet’ (de Vaan 2008: 109–110). With an s-stem noun and possibly also a stative (‘fientive’) verb (cf. LIV² l.c.), the corresponding adjective could well be a u-stem. While there is no other direct evidence for such a derivative, we may thus consider a compound *su̯e-k̑rh₃-ú- > *su̯e-k̑rúh₃- with the approximate meaning ‘brought up/raised/grown separately’, or perhaps, as suggested by Janus Bahs Jacquet (p.c.), ‘having her own/separate offspring’, bear-ing in mind that the reflexive stem *su̯e- is ambiguous, not only referring to ‘one-self, one’s own’, but also what is ‘by itself, separate’, cf., e.g., Lithuanian svẽčias ‘stranger, guest’. In the latter meaning, it has thus apparently gained ground in a

16 For an alternative segmentation *su̯ek̑-u̯er- with the same suffix as *dah₂i̯u̯ér- ‘brother-in-law’, cf. Mayrhofer (1986: 162).

17 Laryngeal metathesis *h₂u > *uh₂ unless followed by a vowel, cf. Rasmussen (1989: 103).

number of terms for in-laws. For the mother-in-law the suggested interpretation fits nicely, both if we are talking about the wife’s mother, which may have been the oldest meaning, and if we are referring to the spouse of the master of the house. In both cases, the mother-in-law, by the continuous practice of exogamy would have been raised separately from her husband’s clan. If this interpretation is cor-rect, we would originally not be dealing with a feminine *-uh₂-stem, but rather an adjectival u-stem where the sequence *-h₃u- regularly metathesized to *-uh₃- and was then supplied with the nominative ending *-s.

4 Other kinship and social terms with *su̯e-

The reflexive stem *s(u̯)e- ‘self, own’ and ‘own, separate’ abounds in kinship termi-nology. The most obvious example is the word for ‘sister’, *su̯ésor- ‘sister’, whether ‘own woman’ or ‘separate woman’, attested in all branches except Anatolian and Albanian, e.g., Vedic svásar-.18

Apart from this clearly archaic formation, the stem is found in a number of terms either referring to the man’s in-laws or to his associates. As argued by Olsen (2013), the Old High German term for ‘brother-in-law, sister’s husband’, gi-swio (n-stem) should be analyzed as a ‘Hoffmann compound’ (*kom-)su̯(e)i̯-h₃on(h₂)- ‘someone having his own authority, an independent man’,19 where the prefix gi- indicates that we are dealing with one of a group (cf. German Geschwister ‘siblings’), and the Hoffmann element has the well-known function of suffix of domination (cf., e.g., Latin mātr-ōn-a, patr-ōn-us ‘(someone) having maternal/ paternal authority’).

A reconstruction based on Old High German alone may seem slender evi-dence for a Core-Indo- European stem, but its archaic character is confirmed by two secondary derivatives, one masculine and one feminine: Within Germanic, the thematic masculine *swainaz is attested with various meanings, all indicating (young) men of subordinate rank such as Old Norse sveinn ‘boy, servant, thrall, herdsman’, Old English swān ‘man, warrior, herdsman’. Thus, if the *(-)su̯(e)i̯-h₃on(h₂)- is ‘someone with his own authority’, a thematic derivative with the usual appertinentive/adjectivizing function of the thematic

$18 Greek ἔορ has the broader meaning ‘female relative; daughter, niece’. Cf. also Janda $(2000: 159).

19 *su̯i- as the compositional variant of *su̯e- or *su̯ei̯- as in the possessive stems *mei̯no- ‘my’, *tei̯no- ‘your’, *sei̯no- ‘his, her’.

321In-laws and outlaws in Indo- European societies

vowel, i.e., *su̯oi̯-h₃n(h₂)-o-20 (m) > *swainaz, must be ‘(someone) connected with someone having his own authority’, i.e., ‘a subordinate of a free, independent man’.

An even more striking confirmation of the basic stem is a feminine, for which we may mechanically posit a proto-form *su̯oi̯-h₃n(h₂)-ii̯ah₂-, regularly yield-ing on the one hand Armenian kʿeni, on the other Lithuanian sváinė, Latvian svaîne ‘wife’s sister’. This cannot be derived from the above-mentioned masculine

*su̯oi̯-h₃n(h₂)-o-: firstly, the most likely corresponding feminine would be a sim-ple *-ah₂-stem, not an *-ii̯ah₂-derivative,21 and secondly, it would seem rather peculiar to define a ‘wife’s sister’ as a woman connected with a dependent man. Consequently, the original meaning must be something like ‘a woman connected with a man with his own authority’, which may be interpreted in two ways ac-cording to the wife’s sister’s current status, where she is either under the authority of her father or, when she marries, that of her husband. In both cases, we get the notion that the wife’s family, at least in the aristocratic layers of society at the stage of Core Indo- European where this segment of the vocabulary was coined, may well have been of a different ethnicity from that of the husband’s, but that its male members were still free and independent. Most likely, their family structure was also of the patrilocal and patrilineal type.22

A similar line of thought with the stem of the possessive of the reflexive pro-noun underlies Russian svojak ‘sister’s husband’ or ‘husband of wife’s sister’ (but not ‘husband’s brother’), understood as someone by himself, from his own sepa-rate clan, different from that of the speaker, and with his own personal authority.

As argued in Olsen (2013), the striking similarity between Old Norse svilar $‘men whose wives are sisters’ and Greek (Hesychius) ἀέλιοι with the same mean-$

It is true that a proto-form *su̯oi̯nii̯o- would account for Lithuanian sváinis ‘brother-in-law’ (esp.

Derivatives including a suffix *-to- or *-ti̯o- are sufficiently widespread in social $terminology to secure pre-dialectal age. An interesting case is Greek ἔτης, Elian ϝέτας < *su̯etah₂-,24 in Homer most often in the phrase κασίγνητοι τε (ϝ)έται τε ‘brothers and ἔται’ (Il. 6.239, 16.456, and 674 and Od. 15.273). Here the ἔται are $mentioned immediately after the brothers as the most important members of the family, e.g., in such contexts as whose fate a warrior will ask for or who will even-tually take care of his funeral.

Their position in relation to the warriors appears to be higher than that of the $mere comrades, the ἑταίροι, in Il. 7.295: $

This suggests that we are dealing with a group holding an intermediate position between consanguineous brothers and friends and allies in general, i.e., probably ‘male in-laws’, which amounts to the same as ‘allies by marriage’ (cf. also Benven-iste 1969: 330–331). Thus, Frisk’s definition (GEW 1: 581) seems quite to the point:

a phyle’ (cf. also Chantraine 1933: 312). Perhaps the formation is an original col-lective of an adjective of appurtenance based on the stem *su̯e-, with suffix *-to-.

At any rate, a similar derivative, *su̯ōto- or *su̯āto- is the basis of Old Church Slavic svatъ ‘relative by marriage’ (vb. svatiti sę ‘enter an alliance of marriage’; Vaillant 1974: 680) and Russian svat with the double meaning of ‘suitor’ and ‘rel-ative by marriage’, e.g., referring to the relation between the father of the bride-groom and the father of the bride (Vasmer 1955: 586–587).26

Simon Poulsen (p.c.) has suggested that the peculiar and otherwise unex-plained vocalism, *-ō- or *-ā-, may perhaps be interpreted as influence from the word for ‘brother’, and indeed the phraseological connection of the two words in both Greek and Slavic would favour such an idea. From an Old Slavic nominative $brat(r)ъ + *su̯eto- > *svetъ (: Greek ἔτης) it would be possible to change *svetъ $to svatъ after bratъ as a rhyming phrase, after the dissimilation of brat(r)ъ to bratъ, but with preservation of the o-stem inflection of the original stem *su̯eto-. A phraseological unit *bʰráh₂ter- + su̯eto- ‘brother(s) and inlaw(s)’ is likely to be inherited at least from the common predecessor of Greek and (Balto-)Slavic. As $we have already seen, κασίγνητοι τε (ϝ)έται τε is a set phrase in Greek, and the $same is the case of the Polish expression on mi ni brat, ni swat “he is nothing to me”, especially seen in the perspective that swat otherwise only has the secondary meaning of ‘matchmaker’. Thus, the phrase would mirror the hierarchy between consanguineous brothers and in-laws in a society where alliances in war and in peace were of vital importance.

However, even where there are no actual ties of marriage involved, the ele-ment *su̯e- may be used in designations of individuals with an independent status, whether allies or not. For example, an exact match exists between Lithuanian svẽčias, also svetỹs, svẽtis ‘guest, stranger’ (Fraenkel 1965: 950 and 952, ALEW 2: 999–1000) and Armenian kʿecʿ ‘separate’ < *su̯e-ti̯o-,27 with the same structure as derivatives of adverbs of the type Vedic ápatya- ‘descendant’ (apa), nítya- ‘own, native’ (ni).

With the variant *se-, we have Old Church Slavic posětiti, Russian posetit’ ‘visit’, presumably a denominative from an unattested *sětъ < *sēto- ‘guest’ with $unexplained lengthening (vr̥ddhi of *seto- beside *su̯eto-?) and in Greek ἕταρος ‘comrade, companion, friend’ beside the secondary ἕταιρος, ἑταῖρος (after an un-attested feminine *ἕταιρα; the full analogical process is described in GEW 1: 579). $

5 ‘Binding’ in marriages and alliances

Bonds of marriage or loyalty, whether between in-laws or friends and associ-ates, are often derived from roots meaning ‘bind’, notably *bʰendʰ- or perhaps

*bʰendh₁- (LIV² 75 with footnote 1). The important point is the alliance, not the ex-$act relation between the two parties. After the semantic specialization of ἑκυρός in Greek to ‘husband’s father’, πενθερός28 took over the meaning of ‘wife’s father’ (whence also πενθερᾱ́, πενθερή ‘wife’s mother’), as is the case in Homer (Il. 6.170 $and Od. 8.582), but in later texts it is also used about both the ‘son-in-law’ and the ‘brother-in-law’.

Vedic bándhu- is attested as an abstract noun ‘connection, relation, bond, kin-ship’, but it also denotes a ‘relative’, especially on the mother’s side. Thus, in RV 1.164.33, the female counterpart of Dyāus, the pitā́ janitā́ ‘father procreator’, is bándhur me mātā́ pr̥thivī́ ‘my relation, mother earth’.

In Baltic, there seem to be no family ties involved in the relevant derivatives: Lithuanian bañdžius is a ‘friend, comrade; labourer, servant; herdsman’29 and the adjective bẽndras ‘joint, common’ simply denotes a ‘friend’ or ‘participant’ as a noun. A specific reference to military companionship is found in the compound bendra-giñklis ‘brother-in-arms’ (as if *-gʷʰentli-i̯o-).

Finally, one Germanic term has to be mentioned, viz. Old Frisian bōst < *bʰondʰ-st(h₂)u-, or perhaps more likely *bʰondʰo-st(h₂)u- ‘marriage’, probably containing the compositional *-sth₂ú- of the root *stah₂- ‘stand’ (cf. NIL 637–638 with references).30 It is uncertain whether there is a further etymological connec-tion between this u-stem and the Germanic words for ‘cowshed’ or ‘barn’, *bans(t) a-, in Gothic bansts ‘barn’ (i-st.; cf. Casaretto 2004: 453), Old Frisian bōs (with suffix *-to-) ‘cowshed’, Old Norse bass ‘stall in a cow-barn’ etc. The derivational

$28 Perhaps a remodeling of *πενθυρός as a compromise between the externally attested $-u-stem (: Vedic bándhu-) and a derivative in *-ro- (: Lithuanian bẽndras), cf. Olsen (2020a: 124) with references.

29 Cf. Olsen (2019) with references on the suffix. 30 The exact rules for the preservation or loss of compositional *-o- (> -a-) in Germanic

are not quite clear, but at least there seems to be a tendency to syncopate the vowel in Gothic in pretonic syllables, cf. Krause (1968: 71). The initial o-stem *bʰóndʰo- would be an o-grade action noun ‘binding, bond’.

325In-laws and outlaws in Indo- European societies

basis of these words seems to be related to Lithuanian bandà ‘(herd of) cattle’ whose etymological background is disputed (Fraenkel 1962: 34). According to Casaretto (l.c.), the two meanings ‘marriage’ and ‘cowshed’ in Germanic are to be explained as mutually independent derivatives, and Kroonen (2013: 52) even considers them unrelated.

However, it may be worth noticing that a semantic parallel may be found in Vedic gotrá- ‘cow stable’, which in later Sanskrit acquires the meaning ‘family, lineage’ as a testimony of the importance of both herd and family. It is hardly unthinkable that a similar semantic linking occurred to Germanic-speaking pop-ulations, so that an original meaning ‘standing place for the band, herd (of cattle)’ in Old Frisian developed into ‘status of bonding’, i.e., ‘marriage’. At least we may conclude that there seems to be a small series of derivatives of u-and ro-deriv-atives of the root *bʰendʰ- in Core Indo- European, or at least Greek, Indic and Baltic, that specifically relate to social bonds.31

6 The leader and his escort: the root *sekʷ- ‘follow’

In war as in peace, the master of an Indo- European–speaking household was dependent on his group of followers as a patron in relation to his clients. The root used with this semantic shading is *sekʷ- ‘follow, join’ (LIV² 525–26), from which an o-grade ah₂-stem *sokʷáh₂- ‘(group of) followers, escort’ is the basis of numer-ous derivatives in Italic, Germanic, Greek, Indo- Iranian and perhaps Armenian.

$A derivative in *-u̯on- is continued in Greek ὀπάων < *sokʷah₂-u̯ōn ‘a follower’, $already attested in Mycenaean dat. sg. o-qa-wo-ni. The verb corresponding to the $basic ah₂-stem is ὀπάζω ‘chase; make follow, give as a companion’, very frequent in the Homeric poems (cf. also for the semantic scope ἀοσσέω ‘help’ from ‘be a $co-follower’).

From this feminine/collective, a secondary i-stem, *sókʷh₂-oi̯-, originally ‘(someone) belonging to the escort’, is directly continued in Indo- Iranian where the extremely common Vedic sákhāy- ‘friend, companion’, attested 266 times in the Rigveda, typically expresses a mutual relationship, e.g., RV 1.26.3: sákhā sákhye ‘a friend for a friend’ with an exact match in Avestan haxa haš́ē. The stem is further continued in Old Persian haxā-maniš- ‘Achaemenid’, lit. ‘characterized by a follower’s spirit’ (Schlerath 1973: 36). Friends are often described in connec-tion with brothers, thus RV 10.7.3a–b:

agním manye pitáram agním āpím agním bhrā́taraṃ sádam it sákhāyam32 I consider Agni our father, Agni our friend, Agni our brother and our comrade forever

and in the opposite order, RV 5.85.7a–b:

aryamyàm varuṇa mitryàm vā sákhāyam vā sádam íd bhrā́taraṃ vā O Varuṇa, the offence that we have committed against any partner, be he one by alliance or one by custom, or against a brother …

A neuter thematicization of this i-stem leads to the abstract *sokʷh₂-i(i̯)-om > Vedic sakhyám ‘friendship, companionship’, also a very well-attested concept with 157 attestations in the Rigveda and a close cognate in Avestan haxaiia- ‘id.’. Parallel to the basic nouns, sakhyá- is typically connected with bhrātrá- ‘brotherhood’, as $is also Avestan haxaiia- with brāθra-, e.g., RV 4.10.8a–c: $

śivā́ naḥ sakhyā́ sántu bhrātrā́gne devéṣu yuṣme let our comradeship be propitious, our brotherhood, o Agni, (with respect) to you gods

Another derivative is Vedic sakhitvám (n) ‘friendship, companionship’ < *sokʷh₂-i-tuh₂-óm,33 a thematicization of a stem in *-tuh₂(t)-, which would originally have denoted collectives of individuals (cf. the description in McCone 1987 of ‘age sets’ in Latin iuventūs, virtūs, senectūs). Again, the context with ‘brotherhood’ refers to an entire circle of associates of various levels, cf. e.g., RV 4.25.2c–d:

ká índrasya yújyaṃ káḥ sakhitvám kó bhrātrám vaṣti who is eager for the fellowship of Indra, who for the comradeship, who for the brotherhood?

In the masculine, the *-ii̯o-derivative *sokʷh₂-ii̯ós is at least potentially continued in Italic and Germanic, though it is strictly speaking impossible to distinguish between *sokʷii̯ó- from an o-grade action noun *sókʷo- ‘following, escort’ and

*sokʷh₂ii̯ó- from the feminine/collective *sokʷáh₂ (cf. de Vaan 2008: 569–570). The latter has the advantage that the stem in the neuter is already known from Indo-

Iranian. Latin socius thus makes sense as ‘comrade, companion, associate’, especial-ly ‘allied, confederate, someone pledged by a treaty to give support in war’,34 and Germanic *sagja- > ON seggr ‘man, hero’, OS seg ‘man’,35 OE secg ‘man, warrior’.

A close cognate of Vedic sakhitvám is Latin societās ‘fellowship, partnership, alli-ance’, etc. Whereas sakhitvám is a thematicization of an abstract *sokʷh₂i-tuh₂-, soci-etās, as if *sokʷh₂-ii̯o-tah₂-t-, continues a stem with the suffix conglomerate *-tah₂-t-, which is the usual substitution for -tūt- in Latin.36 As the only difference lies in the slightly different derivational basis, an i-stem in Old Indic vs. an ii̯o-stem in Italic, it may not be too daring to assume a common origin. For the original meaning of societās one may adduce an example such as Cic. Rep. 1.49: quod enim est apud Ennium: nulla sancta societas nec fides regni est “for it is said in Ennius: there is no sacred companionship of trust in a kingdom”. As a contrast to the societās as a connection of associates belonging to different groups, we have cīvitās, a similar $formation based on *k̑ei̯u̯o- → Latin cīvis ‘citizen’, denoting a unity of insiders.37 $

Finally, I would tentatively suggest a derivation from this root for the ety-mologically obscure Armenian zokʿančʿ ‘mother-in-law, wife’s mother’, whence zokʿančʿ-pap ‘father-in-law’, cf. pap ‘grandfather’ (Olsen 2020a: 117). As in Greek and Balto-Slavic, a new term was coined when the use of the original skesowr was earmarked for the husband’s mother. Z- is a prefix and preposition, which at least semantically corresponds to *h₂m̥bʰi- (cf. z-genowm : Vedic abhi-vas- ‘dress’),38 so a proto-form *h₂m̥bʰi-sokʷah₂- would be expected to yield zokʿa-, correspond-ing to the Vedic compound verb abhi- + sac- ‘follow, escort’ and the noun abhi- ṣác- ‘follower, escort’.

While the end segment -nčʿ of zokʿančʿ is not quite clear, it is not entirely iso-lated either. A structurally similar adjective anterownčʿ ‘without a master’, is some-how derived from the privative compound an-tēr (tēr, o-st.). Since a suffix -nčʿ is otherwise unknown, we may be faced with opaque compositional forms. As ten-tatively suggested by Olsen (1999: 612), a possible background of -terownčʿ could be a compositional *-i̯o-stem *-h₂onk-i̯o- ‘turning towards, inclined to’ from the root *h₂enk- ‘bend’, added to the o-stem -tēr-, i.e., *-o-h₂onk-i̯o-.
