In most cases, the derivational bases are adverbial forms, but cf. YAv. hunairiiā̊ńc- ‘skillful’ (‘bent/turned towards the arts’, hunara-), which incidentally contains the same element *-h₂ner- as -tēr- (< *ti-ayr) in anterownčʿ. If the suggested analysis of zokʿančʿ is correct, the literal meaning would thus be something like ‘someone (f) turned towards a follower’, where the ‘follower’ would denote the wife’s father.39

7 Inlaws and allies

In the languages where *su̯ék̑uros has been limited to indicate the husband’s father, various new terms were coined for the wife’s father, thus the above-mentioned Greek $πενθερός, the etymologically opaque Lithuanian úošvis (fem. úošvė ‘wife’s moth-$er’),40 Old Church Slavic tьstь (fem. tьsta ‘wife’s mother’) and Armenian aner.41

It seems clear that the in-laws on the wife’s side constituted an essential part of a free man’s circle of alliances. The following passage from the Odyssey (Od. 8.581–586) may serve as an illustration (cf. also Olsen 2020: 123–124):

$ἦ τίς τοι καὶ πηὸς ἀπέφθι το Ἰλιόθι πρὸ ἐσθλὸς ἐών, γαμβρὸς ἢ πενθερός, οἳ τε μάλιστα κήδιστοι τελέθουσι μεθ’ αἷμά τε καὶ γένος αὐτῶν; ἦ τίς που καὶ ἑταῖρος ἀνὴρ κεχαρισμένα εἰδώς, ἐσθλὸς; ἐπεὶ οὐ μέν τι κασιγνήτοιο χερείων γίγνεται ὅς κεν ἑταῖρος ἐών πεπνυμένα εἰδῇ. $

39 Cf. also for the semantic scope Old Irish dám ‘company, escort’ vs. Old Welsh dauu ‘cliens’ and Welsh daw(f) ‘son-in-law, daughter’s husband; sister’s husband; member of a retinue, guest’. The most convincing analysis of these words is a vr̥ddhi derivative

*dōmah₂- (OIr. a-stem)/*dōmo- (W) of the word for ‘house’, ‘those/someone pertaining $to the household’. The alternative comparison with Greek δῆμος ‘land, territory; people’ $from *dah₂i̯- ‘distribute’ is less likely for semantic reasons (cf. LÉIA D-20 and de Ber-nardo Stempel 1999: 524–525 for further discussion).

41 Cf. Martirosyan (2010: 81–82) and Olsen (2020a: 125) for etymological discussions.

329In-laws and outlaws in Indo- European societies

$Did some kinsman (πηός) of thine fall before Ilium, some good, true man, your daughter’s husband (γαμβρός) or your wife’s father (πενθερός), such as $are nearest to one after one’s own kin and blood? Or was it perhaps some com-$rade (ἑταῖρος) dear to thy heart, some good, true man? For no whit worse than $a brother is a comrade who knows what is right

Here the allies in war are listed in three groups according to importance. First $in intimacy and importance is one’s own kin and blood, the αἷμά τε καὶ γένος, including of course the consanguineous brother, the κασίγνητος. The least inti-mate is the friend/associate, the ἑταῖρος. In the intermediate category, comprising πηός, γαμβρός ‘daughter’s husband, son-in-law’ and πενθερός ‘wife’s father’, πηός seems to be the overall category covering both γαμβρός and πενθερός.42 The $primary meaning would thus be ‘kinsman by alliance’, whence only secondarily ‘male relative’ in general.

As for the etymology, Chantraine (2009: 865), while stating that this is a “[t] erme de parenté qui doit remonter à l’indo-européen”, had no positive suggestions; Frisk (GEW 2: 530) was skeptical towards the traditional comparison with Latin parricīda ‘murder of a near relation’ (similarly de Vaan 2008: 447–448); and Beekes’ final verdict (2010: 1187) was simply: ‘‘Kinship term without certain connections”.

$If πηός, Doric πᾱός < *pāsó- does have an Indo- European background, the the-$oretical possibilities would at first sight include *pah₂só-, *kʷah₂só- and *k̑u̯ah₂só-/

*ku̯ah₂só-, none of which gives an immediate clue. However, with the additional possibility of ‘laryngeal breaking’ *uh₂ > *u̯ā in unaccented syllables,43 a pro-$to-form *puh₂só- is remarkably similar to the inherited theonym Πᾱ́ν, Vedic Pūṣā́ $(stem Pūṣán-), which would continue a Hoffmann formation. While Oettinger (1998 and 2000) suggests a reconstruction “péh₂-u̯s-h₃ō(n)”, Olsen (2010: 124–126) ventures to unite the Vedic and Greek forms under a common proto-form *puh₂s -$h₃ónh₂- yielding Pūṣā́ and *pu̯āsṓn > Πᾱ́ν, respectively, thus reducing the need for $analogical levelling in the paradigm. Beside this Hoffmann formation, it would $now be possible to assume a thematic derivative *puh₂só- > *pu̯āsó- > Gk. πηός. $

An etymological connection between a theonym and a term for kinsman by alliance may seem far-fetched. However, in her contribution to the present vol-ume, Jil Schermutzki has highlighted two important, and thus far apparently un-

$42 Cf. LfgrE (2001: 1237) on this passage: “nach der Logik des Satzes ist π. kein Blutsver-wandter, sondern Oberbegr. zu γαμβρός u. πενθερός, also allg. Bez. für alle durch Hei-$rat Verwandten”.

43 Cf. Francis (1970) and Normier (1977 and 1980), modified by Olsen (2009).

330 Birgit Anette Olsen

noticed, similarities between Pan and Pushan, namely their reproductive power and their connection with the wedding ritual. Sexually, both have the ability to arouse women; in terms of marriage, Pushan takes on the important function of leading the bride, and despite his oppositional attitude to marriage, Pan has similar functions in the wedding ritual.

Thus, Pushan is described as the “herdsman of the world”, bhúvanasya gopā́ḥ, in RV 10.17.3, and in the wedding ritual of the Sun Maiden, RV10.85.26a–b, he leads the bride to the wedding:

pūṣā́ tvetó nayatu hastagṛyāśvínā tvā prá vahatāṃ ráthena

let Pushan lead you from here, having taken you by the hand. Let the Asvins convey you forth in their chariot.

Similarly, the shepherd god Pan seems to play a role as the bride leader of Perse-phone, as also discussed by Schermutzki. Consequently, the concept of ‘brides-man, leader of the bride’ seems to have been known at some dialectal stage of Indo- European.

Starting from the fact that the primary function of both Pushan and Pan seems to be that of a shepherd god, it also seems reasonable to assume that the basic root of their common name is derived from the root *pah₂i̯- ‘protect, herd, graze’ (LIV² 460), as argued by Oettinger (1998: 545–546). The semantic connec-tion from shepherd god to ‘bridesman’ is fairly straightforward. As a shepherd leads the herds from one pasture to another, the role of a bridesman or bride lead-er is to secure the safe transfer of the bride from her father’s household to that of her new husband, so if the god *puh₂s-h₃ónh₂- was the divine bridesman, it may not be too daring to suggest that the almost identical formation *puh₂s-ó- indi-cated his earthly counterpart who would in practice be a prominent member of the bride’s family, in other words a ‘kinsman by alliance’. The derivational chains of the two nouns would be approximately as follows:

$*páh₂us- ‘herding’, etc.: us-stem, the type of Vedic tápuṣ- ‘glow’ → 1  *ph₂us-ó- > *puh₂s-ó-44 > Greek *pu̯āsó- > πηός ‘someone herding or $

leading the bride’, i.e., ‘kinsman by alliance’ $2  *ph₂us-h₃ónh₂- > *puh₂s-h₃ónh₂- > Vedic Pūṣā́, Greek Πᾱ́ν ‘leader of the $

$herding’, i.e., ‘shepherd god’ (→ ‘divine bridesman’)45 $

44 Cf. note 17 on the regular metathesis *h₂u > *uh₂. $45 Slightly differently (no ‘laryngeal breaking’ and no inclusion of πηός), Malzahn (2014).$

331In-laws and outlaws in Indo- European societies

This is not to suggest that other types of marriage such as actual abduction were excluded in Indo- European tradition, and if the suggested analysis is correct, the social implications need not go further back than the common prehistory of Indo- Iranian and Greek where the bonds between the two families would have been based on mutual respect and commitment.

8 Avunculate, fosterage and alleged cross-cousin marriage

According to a widespread myth in Indo- European studies, the inherited kinship terminology reveals institutionalized cross-cousin marriage,46 more precisely the practice that in principle a young man should marry the daughter of his father’s sister. The basis of this theory, famously forwarded by Benveniste (1969: 27), is the similarity (but never identity) in several branches of the Indo- European family between the words for ‘grandfather’ and ‘maternal uncle’. However, aside from the obvious principal objection that such a practice would contradict the otherwise consistent principle of exogamy, the alleged arguments in its favour all have false premises. In particular, it is simply not true that the word for ‘grandfather’, Latin avus, etc., only means ‘paternal grandfather’ – the Romans also operated with an avus maternus ‘maternal grandfather’ – so it cannot be deduced that an avunculus ‘mother’s brother’ must be interpreted as a ‘little father’s father’.

In an important study on the institutions of avunculate and fosterage among Indo- European-speaking populations, Bremmer (1976) has presented ample documentation for the intimate relationship of young boys and family members on their mother’s side, particularly their maternal uncle, but in some cases also their maternal grandfather. The evidence includes case stories from Greek, Ro-man, Slavic and notably Germanic and Celtic traditions, and often the relation-ship involved actual fosterage of the boy in the mother’s family. Simultaneously, Beekes (1976) argued against Benveniste that cross-cousin marriages of the type described are particularly characteristic for matrilineal societies, which would definitely not match the Indo- European background. Additionally, cross-cousin marriage is unknown in all archaic Indo- European–speaking traditions.

In general anthropological framework terms, the Proto- Indo- European kin-ship system can be described as a patrilineal system of the so-called Omaha type. One characteristic of such a system is a kinship terminology with ‘skewing’ of the generations, which is reminiscent of the frequent confusion between the words

46 Cf. Mallory & Adams (1997: 133–134 and 370) and Olsen (2020a: 78–80).

332 Birgit Anette Olsen

for ‘grandson’ and ‘nephew’. However, this state of affairs cannot be projected back into the common proto-language.

As already noticed by Delbrück (1889: 403), languages where the old word for ‘grandson’, *népōts, assumed the meaning ‘nephew’, specifically ‘sister’s son’, are the very same as those where the word for ‘maternal uncle’ is derived from the word for ‘grandfather’. This goes for the European branches, Italic, Celtic, Germanic, Baltic and Slavic.

It is important to realize that the terms for ‘maternal uncle’ are not identical, but independent formations, all derived from the ‘grandfather’ word, *h₂au̯h₂(o) s, here in the specific meaning ‘maternal grandfather’. In Italic and Celtic, the basis is an n-stem *h₂au̯h₂o-n- in Latin avunculus, Welsh ewythr, Breton eontr, Old Cornish euitor and Old Irish amnair ‘maternal uncle’ (cf. McCone 1992: 105); the Germanic compound *h₂au̯h₂o-k̑oi̯mo- > Old High German ōheim, Old Eng-lish éam ‘maternal uncle’ has the literal meaning ‘belonging to the home of the (maternal) grandfather’; and in Baltic and Slavic we find the derivatives *h₂au̯h₂i-h₃n(h₂)o- > Lithuanian avýnas and *h₂au̯h₂ii̯o- > Old Prussian awis and Old Church Slavic ujь ‘maternal uncle’.

The semantic extension of the word for ‘grandson’ to the meaning ‘nephew’, especially on the mother’s side, includes from Italic post-Augustean Latin nepōs ‘nephew’, from Celtic Ogam Irish (gen.) niotta and Middle Welsh nei ‘sister’s son’, from Germanic Old English nefa (also ‘stepson’) and Old High German nefo, nevo (also ‘cousin’), and from Balto-Slavic Old Lithuanian neptìs, nepuotìs and Serbo-Croat nećak ‘nephew’. This linguistic mirror image is consistent with the combined tradition of avuncu-late and fosterage that only gradually developed as an areal phenomenon in the European branches, but remained foreign to Indo- Iranian where nápāt- exclusive-ly means ‘grandson, descendent’, never ‘nephew’. When Indo- European–speaking populations became more sedentary it must have been possible to establish more binding relations to the in-laws. And what could be more binding than leaving your young son in the care of their mother’s family, in particular her brother who could fulfil the role of a substitute father figure and see to the boy’s military educa-tion in a way that might even reduce the threat to the integrity and stability of the household that rivalry between brothers under the same roof can bring?

Thus, the description of the maternal uncle as ‘the one connected with the (maternal) grandfather’ would go hand in hand with the identification of the

*népōts as ‘grandson’ seen from the point of view of the boy’s paternal grandfather and his household; and as ‘nephew, sister’s son’ seen from the point of view of the boy’s new warden, the maternal uncle, and his household.

333In-laws and outlaws in Indo- European societies

9 Fosterage

The evidence for fosterage of young boys in the homes of their maternal uncles is sufficiently strong to leave out any doubt, but one may ask if, in the course of time, the alliance between two families by way of fosterage always had to follow this pattern. At least Italic, Celtic and Germanic share the root *h₂al- in the mean-ing ‘nourish’, in the middle voice ‘grow up’ (LIV² 262), cf. Latin adolēscō ‘grow up’, alumnus ‘foster-child’, Old Irish comalt ‘foster-brother, collactaneus’, Middle Irish altra ‘foster-father’, Middle Welsh athrawon ‘foster-uncles’ (with *-awon ‘mater-nal uncle’!) and, e.g., Old Norse ala ‘beget, bring up, nourish’, elska ‘love’.47 At the same time, it is exactly in ancient Rome and in Celtic and Germanic societies that fosterage played a remarkably dominant role.

Besides the established type of fosterage of young, but not infant, boys in their maternal family, it does not seem unlikely that the alternative fosterage by ‘milk kinship’, as known from Arab and Native American societies, was practiced in part of northwest Europe. This implies that a family could adopt infants from friends and allies and thus extend its circle of influence. These infants would be fed and brought up with the family’s own children, and emotional bonds would strengthen the patron–client relation between the two families.48

The institutionalized practice of fosterage is particularly well documented for medieval Celtic and Germanic societies, as described, e.g., by Gerald of Wales (12th c.) and in the Icelandic sagas, and Bradley (1991: 149–154) has highlighted the otherwise somewhat neglected institution of ‘milk kinship’ in ancient Rome.

The following passage from the jurist Gaius (130–180 ad) on the manumission of slaves (Institutiones 1.39) may serve as an example:

iustae autem causae manumissionis sunt, veluti si quis patrem aut matrem aut

The following are proper causes for manumission, for instance, where any-one manumits his father, his mother, his teacher, or his foster-brother.

While part of these traditions may evidently be the result of individual secondary developments, it still seems possible that a nucleus of fosterage by ‘milk kinship’ may go back to a pre-dialectal period.

10 Insiders and outsiders

The possibility of inclusion of members in a household who do not strictly belong to the patriclan is further suggested by the vocabulary relating to family members as well as servants described as ‘insiders’ (cf. Olsen 2020b). Thus, *h₁ni- + *g̑enh- is continued in Pali niyaṃ puttam ‘an in-born son’, while the corresponding Vedic nijá- is used about servant boys, Avestan ni-zəṇta- has the Pahlavi translation $pa xānaγ ‘born in the house’ (Hoffmann 1982: 89–90 and 94, note 45).49 Several $comparable formations are found in Celtic, Greek and Armenian, e.g. *h₁(e)n- $g̑onh₁o/ah₂- > Greek ἔγγονος ‘grandson’, lit. ‘in-born’, Old Irish ingen ‘daughter’ $

11 Conclusion

By now, the basic features of (at the very least) Core-Indo- European family struc-tures are well established by linguistic, archaeological and archaeogenetic data. It was patrilineal and patrilocal, and it followed a strict principle of exogamy. How-ever, following the Indo- European expansion throughout Europe and western Asia, certain features concerning the formation of alliances apparently developed and were accentuated.

First of all, the in-laws, the male members of the foreign bride’s family played an important role in guest-friendship as well as in warfare. They were ‘them-selves’, men with their own authority, but still ‘bound’ by obligations, whether in an actual patron–client relationship or on more equal terms. A man’s broth-ers-in-law and sons-in-law were next only to his own brothers – in the Young Avestan Hymn to Mitra (29.116–117), the contract is described as “eightyfold be-tween son-in-law and father-in-law, ninetyfold between two brothers, hundred-fold between father and son”. Institutionalized fosterage of young boys by their mother’s brother further strengthened the bond between the two families, but it can only be demonstrated linguistically for the European branches of the Indo- European family.

336 Birgit Anette Olsen

Next in line comes the circle of the associates, friends and ‘followers’, also essential in warfare. Perhaps their children were even occasionally included in the patriclans as foster-children, enabling an influential head of family to steadily increase his circles of influence, supporting and protecting the ‘insiders’ against a surrounding world of ‘outsiders’.

Typically such ‘outsiders’ would belong to potentially dangerous and hostile external societies beyond the influence of the master of the house, his family, allies and friends, but there would also have been an element of actual outlaws who had been deliberately expelled from the community and left to their own fate – had ‘become wolves’ – as a consequence of severe transgressions against the commonly accepted rules, without which an ordered society would lose its coherence.50

Indo- European initiation

The Greek contribution

Jan N. Bremmer University of Groningen 1

In this article, I argue for a series of Greek elements, such as age-sets, hair-

style and wandering, that enrich our knowledge of Indo- European male in-

itiation, as presented by Widengren (1969). I also argue for a more differen-

tiated usage of the term Männerbund than is often usual in Indo- European

studies.

Like in most early societies, Indo- European male youths had to advance through various rituals before reaching social adulthood. Recently, we have seen an im-portant study of the vocabulary of physical ‘young adulthood’ (Olsen 2020), but the corresponding rituals have received less attention in recent years. Now, most tribal societies proclaim their young men to be adult at a specific moment in time and effectuate this sudden transition by making the boys pass through a special ritual, initiation, which varies in detail from tribe to tribe and from community to community, but which nevertheless shows a remarkable family resemblance in structure and content all over the world. After this transition, the boys are treated as adults and are expected to behave accordingly. The structure of tribal initiatory rituals usually follows the famous triad delineated by Arnold van Gennep (1909): rite of separation, liminality, and rite of incorporation (rite de séparation, rite de marge and rite d’aggrégation).2

1 This contribution draws heavily on the Preface to Bremmer (2021), but not without abbreviations, additions of overlooked or very recent references, and a change of per-spective. For most Greek passages and themes as well as a bibliography on the scholars mentioned in section 1, see the detailed index in Bremmer (2021). I am most grateful to the editors of this volume for their careful scrutiny of my text.

2 The best survey of tribal initiation of boys and girls is still Brelich (1969: 13–112), to whom I refer for references for the ethnographic practices mentioned in this contribu-tion, but see also Brain (1977 with rich bibliography), Schjødt (2008: 22–49).

344 Jan N. Bremmer

There can be no doubt that of all the Indo- European communities, the Greek world, due to its rich and early literary and epigraphical evidence, has given us the most information regarding initiations, with respect to both myths and ritu-als, whereas the Anatolian, Tocharian and Slavic traditions, for example, have left us virtually no information in this respect. The situation is somewhat better in ancient Rome, where the myths of Romulus and Remus have preserved old tra-ditions; in Persia, about which classical authors have given us numerous details; and in India, where the original structures are often hard to recognise, but per-suasively argued for in studies of the Vedic Vrātyas.3 Among the Indo- Europeans, it is also the Greek world that first received scholarly attention in the study of ancient initiation because of its rich material and long tradition of scholarship. As Widengren (1969) is still the best study of Indo- European initiation, I will take his work as my point of departure, since he overlooked important Greek evidence. Naturally, a detailed investigation of the Greek initiation system would go beyond the limits of an article. Therefore, I will limit myself to a series of elements of Greek initiations in order to illustrate its uniqueness in some ways, but, above all, its importance for reconstructing the Indo- European initiatory rituals. After a historiographical survey (section 1), I will look at: 1. age sets and the contents of early education; 2. fosterage; 3. hairstyle; 4. wandering and groups; 5. defeating a monster; 6. the carrying of a club (German: Keule); 7. the receiving of arms; 8. the wedding (section 2). I will conclude with some final considerations (section 3).

1 Historiography

Modern research starts with Heinrich Schurtz’s (1863–1903) Altersklassen und Männerbünde, published in 1902, which showed the importance of men’s soci-eties and men’s houses for non-European peoples. At the time, although hardly today, the 1908 publication of Primitive Secret Societies by American sociologist and anthropologist Hutton Webster (1875–1955) was also influential, and both books very quickly inspired three studies which, almost at the same time, com-pared the initiatory systems of Crete and Sparta with those of tribal societies.4 What is noteworthy, in retrospect, about these early studies is that they all focused on the Dorian areas of ancient Greece, as if the ethnographic parallels on which they drew had nothing to contribute to a better understanding of other parts of

3 Most recently, Selva (2019: 329–352), af Edholm (2021). 4 Harrison (1912), Nilsson (1912), Jeanmaire (1913).

345Indo- European initiation

Greece. It is also striking in retrospect that they all concentrated on ethnographic, non-Indo- European, parallels. This was the Indian summer of colonialism, and reports from travellers and missionaries were flooding in thick and fast, provid-ing scholars with a wealth of sources on tribal societies, most of which have dis-appeared today. After the First World War, however, such anthropological com-parisons went out of fashion. Classics turned inwards and social anthropology moved away from the kind of big armchair comparisons found in Frazer’s Golden Bough, instead adopting the functionalist paradigm and propagating fieldwork as the correct approach to the study of tribal communities.

Eventually, however, the work of Schurtz and Hutton did start to influence students of other Indo- European traditions. This development began in the late 1920s and early 1930s with German and Austrian studies of Germanic and Scan-dinavian rites of initiation and men’s societies.5 These works were often driven by an idea of Germanic continuity, an over-accentuation of the tie between men’s societies and the dead, and sympathy with the Nazist movement. Yet despite con-veying ideas that are, to say the very least, politically nefarious, these studies can still offer interesting suggestions and associations (Schjødt 2008: 49–52). In the later 1930s, ideas about initiation and men’s societies also began to influence var-ious Scandinavian scholars (Gasche 2016), mainly as a result of their personal contacts with the most influential scholar of this ‘school’, Otto Höfler (1901–1987). These scholars showed the existence of such practices among the ancient Indians and Iranians, although in doing so they perhaps over-emphasized the importance of men’s societies.6 Geo Widengren (1907–1996, cf. Larsson 2021, Gilhus 2023), in particular, long studied the activities of men’s societies, and in 1969 he published a valuable survey of what was known at the time, albeit with an overrepresenta-tion of the Iranian evidence (Widengren 1969). These Scandinavian works also display a certain dependency on Höfler’s idea of secret societies (Geheimbünde) and the importance of the ancestors, neither of which is really that prominent in the Indo- European tradition as a whole. In the case of Celtic communities, by contrast, interest in these topics did not take root until the latter part of the 20th century, although recent decades have seen the appearance of several fine studies that have concentrated in particular on the tales about the boyhood deeds of Cú

5 See especially Weiser (1927), Höfler (1934); for an interesting study of their ideas in their time and place, see Corssin (2010). For a reasonable and, to some extent, rightly appreciative analysis of Weiser’s and Höfler’s use of Tacitus’ Germania, see Meier (1999, with excellent bibliography).

6 Especially Wikander (1938), Widengren (1938: 311–351). Recent evaluations of these studies are found in Ahmadi (2018) and Daryaee (2018).

346 Jan N. Bremmer

Chulainn and of Finn and his fian (Nagy 1985, McCone 198: 101–154, 2012; but note also Rees 1961: 244–258).

The Indo- European studies were not considered by the two notable scholars who still applied the initiation paradigm to ancient Greece in the pre-War period: Louis Gernet (1882–1962) and Henri Jeanmaire (1884–1960).7 Both were rather shy men (the latter even a loner) who spent most of their career working at the margins of French academia, and as a result did not achieve any great influence during their lifetimes. However, unlike in his 1913 study, in 1939 Jeanmaire looked beyond the Dorian areas of Greece in a wide-ranging study of Greek initiation rites. In addition to considering Crete, Sparta and Delphi, he also included Ath-ens in his study by focusing on Theseus. Theseus’ youth is indeed replete with initiatory motifs, such as his education by his mother’s father, his feminine outfit and his sacrifice of a bull,8 his wandering with Peirithoos, the trip to Crete with the battle against the Minotaur, and the return to become king.9 The antiquity of the Theseus myth suggests the early existence of rites of initiation in ancient Greece, plausibly going back into the second millennium BC.

The publication of Jeanmaire’s book at the beginning of the Second World War did not help to spread his ideas or stimulate interest in initiation in Classical circles. Indeed, it was not until the end of the 1960s that Greek initiation again appeared on the scholarly agenda. In 1968, Pierre Vidal-Naquet (1930–2006) pub-lished his article ‘The Black Hunter and the Origin of Athenian Ephebeia’ (1968, 1983: 151–175), in which he argued that the ephebe was a kind of anti-hoplite. His use of the terms ‘cooked’ for hoplites and ‘raw’ for ephebes betrays the influence of Claude Lévi-Strauss (1908–2009), but more crucially, it has been justly argued against him that, instead of a simple opposition between ephebe and hoplite, we should rather think of “the existence of a broad band of youthful status, rather than a polarity between marginal youth and incorporated adult: incorporation and socialisation take place over time” (Ma 2008: 190). Nevertheless, Vidal-Naquet conclusively demonstrated that archaic rites of initiation had survived within Athenian civic practices in fully historical times, even if they had under-gone various transformations.

7 Gernet (1968: 154–171; first published in 1936 as ‘Dolon le Loup’); many references to initiation also in the posthumously published Gernet (2004).

8 See Graf (1979: 14–18), who shows the close connection of Theseus with the life of the Athenian ephebes.

9 Jeanmaire (1939: 228–378), whose analysis is refined by Calame (2018: 69–139). For Jean maire and his book, see Roy (2012), Hugot (2014).

347Indo- European initiation

Vidal-Naquet’s influential position in French academia and his excellent con-tacts with the Anglo-Saxon scholarly world contributed to his article becoming perhaps the most famous modern contribution to the study of ancient initiation. It certainly overshadowed the much more wide-ranging study of Greek male and female initiation by Italian scholar Angelo Brelich (1913–1977). Having already shown an interest in initiation in his earlier books, Brelich went on to publish Paides e Parthenoi in 1969, still the most detailed study of ancient Greek initia-tion, albeit from an ethnographic rather than Indo- European perspective.10 In addition to the now well-studied rituals of Crete, Sparta and Athens, he also per-suasively argued that various Greek religious festivals, such as the Hyakinthia and Karneia, incorporated features of older initiation rituals, albeit reinterpreted

– analyses that have stood the test of time. Gradually, the whole of the Greek world was becoming the subject of studies

of initiation, rather than only the Dorian areas that had been focused on at the beginning of the twentieth century. Although Brelich had cast his net wide, there were still gaps in his survey, but in recent decades, it has been shown that also Macedonia (Hatzopoulos 1994), Boeotia (Huysecom-Haxhi 2015) and Thessaly (Kravaritou 2018) knew male rites of passage.

In the meantime, Fritz Graf, inspired by the warrior exploits of medieval Swiss youths, had also embarked on a series of studies of initiatory rites in Greece, to which he did compare the Indo- European evidence.11 For our purpose, it is im-portant to note his attention to the connection between initiation and certain Greek gods, such as Dionysos, Poseidon and Apollo, the latter especially when worshipped with the epithets Delphinios and Lykeios. This is still a relatively un-explored area, even though the connections of gods like Indra and Odin with the last phase of the rites of initiation have often been observed.

Combining both the ethnographic and the Indo- European approach,12 it seems reasonable to conclude that the proto-Greeks, when arriving in Greece sometime in the early second millennium, brought with them a system of initia-tion that was related to those that have been identified for the ancient Celtic, Ger-manic and Indo- Iranian peoples. In other words, we are speaking of an initiatory system that plausibly reaches into the third millennium, if not earlier.

10 All references to the ethnographic evidence are taken from Brelich 1969: 13–112. 11 Cf. Graf (1979; 1985: 89–90, 219–227, 415–417; 1987; 1993: 74, 107–109; 1999; 2002; 2004;

2009: 103–129). 12 In addition to Widengren (1969), see also the not always satisfactory surveys in Das

and Meiser (2002).

348 Jan N. Bremmer

2 Indo- European initiation: elements for a thick description

Which rites, then, did the early Greeks bring with them? And did they perhaps meet indigenous initiatory rites which they incorporated in their system, or did they develop new aspects of initiation? It is obvious that such questions cannot be answered with any certainty and that our answers can, at best, only strive for plausibility. Moreover, there must always have been variations in the system, de-pending on place and time, war and peace, health and epidemics, etc. We should also be wary of taking later feudalism as our point of departure as in the inves-tigations by Widengren, whose focus on feudalism made him overvalue it in his treatment of Indo- European initiation, especially since he often reasons back from medieval practices. It is unlikely that the invading Greeks – or Indians and Iranians for that matter – had a highly hierarchical society with a court like that of Alexander the Great or the Achaemenid kings. Rather, we should think of chief-tains who were perhaps sometimes powerful, but hardly feudal rulers unless they had taken over older institutions, as clearly happened in the Ancient Near East or developed over time in Mycenaean Greece. Consequently, we should be a bit reticent in our reconstructions and be content with some broad sketches. On the other hand, comparisons of different institutional details can help us to recon-struct older phases, especially if we have examples of these. With these caveats, then, I will briefly discuss various aspects of Greek initiation that will supplement the picture presented by Widengren.

2.1 Age sets and initial training

In many tribal societies, the male youth passed through a system of age sets of varying length. This was also still the case in historical times in Greece (Kennell 2013), where Crete and especially Sparta had reorganised the original system in a militaristic manner, similar to what some native American tribes did.13 Such an age-set organisation seems to have been present among the Iranians and relat-ed peoples as well (Widengren 1969: 36, 91–95), but it is unclear when precisely the actual coming-of-age rituals started. In general, we find that at around 15 or 16, boys began their more adult training, which in Greece comprised weapon

13 See, especially, Lear (2006) about the Crow nation, whose system displayed remarkable similarities with that of Sparta. Nevertheless, their newly constructed rituals still dis-play archaic features (Meier 1998: 142–185).

349Indo- European initiation

skills, running, hunting, singing, dancing and, not to be forgotten, cunning. For Greece, it is also reported that oaths, healing (important for warriors, given pos-sible wounds) and sacrifice were parts of the teaching of Cheiron, the mythical initiator par excellence.

It is difficult to say to what extent all these elements were shared by other Indo- European communities as, up until now, most attention has been given to the warrior aspects of the initiands. Fortunately for us, the Greeks were also ob-servant of the Persians. Herodotus (1.136) mentions that the Persian boys learned horse riding, archery and truthfulness. Strabo (15.3.18), who probably based him-self on earlier sources, adds that they also learn to throw the javelin and glorify the deeds of the gods and the most noble men, and in a neglected passage, Athe-naeus (10.434d) mentions that they learn to dance the same way they learn how to ride horses. In the Rigveda, dancing is of course also an oft-mentioned quality of the Maruts (Widengren 1969: 20), whose connection with initiation has been well known since Wikander’s (1938) classic study. It is obvious from these reports that we are dealing with upper-class boys, as was probably always the case, except for the militarising societies of Crete and Sparta, who mobilised their whole pop-ulation to train for their wars. It may well have been the case that the teaching of religious matters was an old element of the earlier education (de Jong 1997: 446–451): Polybius (4.20.8–9) says of the Arcadians, who were generally consid-ered by the Greeks to be the most conservative amongst them (see also below), that they learned hymns about the local heroes and the gods. Such a teaching of secular and religious material via songs was normal in tribal communities, and this will have been the case among the Indo- Europeans too, albeit developed in varying ways. Chapter 23 of Asser’s Life of King Alfred, where the king’s mother Osburh challenges her sons to memorise poemata Saxonica, may well be describ-ing a similar tradition.

2.2 Fosterage

A complicating factor in our reconstruction of the early stages of Indo- European initiation is the role of fosterage. Widengren rightly dedicated a whole chapter to this institution, which he discusses in detail for the Ossetes, Armenians and Per-sians (Widengren 1969: 64–95). He also notes its occurrence among the ancient Germanic and Celtic peoples, although among the latter the material is much richer than he thought (Kühlmann 2017; O’Donnell 2020). However, Widengren overlooked the oldest Indo- European evidence, which is to be found among the

350 Jan N. Bremmer

Hittites and in Homer, where we hear of heroes being educated not by their own parents but in the house of their maternal grandfather (Iliad 11.221–224), as well as in vase paintings from as early as the seventh century BC showing Peleus hand-ing over his baby son to the Centaur Cheiron (Stark 2012: 150–155). The education of Macedonian elite boys at court is well attested and continued among the Hel-lenistic successors.

According to Widengren (1969: 101), the Indo- European evidence supports his idea, developed from the Iranian material, that “die Erziehereinrichtung sich aus der Erziehung der Jungmannschaft  … innerhalb eines bündlerischen Rahmens zu einer feudalen Sitte entwickelt hat”. However, the Greek evidence does not support the latter, nor does the rich ethnographic evidence for foster-age (Steinmetz 1928: I 1–113), and Greek fosterage did not always develop into a feudal system. Admittedly, fosterage could be used for feudal aims and purposes, but it is not true that it always developed “innerhalb eines bündlerischen Rah-men” (“within the framework of a Männerbund”). In fact, we should distinguish between kinship fosterage, which often took place within the maternal family, as among the Hittites and other Indo- European societies (Bremmer 1976), and alliance fosterage, which helped to bolster feudal relationships, as happened at the Macedonian and Sasanian courts. The case of Achilles, though, is neither an example of kinship nor alliance fosterage. Here, if anywhere, one could think of a “bündlerischer Rahmen”, as the Centaurs plausibly reflected a men’s society that supervised initiations (Bremmer 2021: 45–63, Zarkadas 2021). It seems that fos-terage usually ended when the youths entered their final stage of initiation.14

2.3 Hairstyle

It is unclear how the beginning of the final stage of initiation was dramatised. One would expect some kind of ritual act, but there does not seem to be much evidence for it. We can, however, be pretty certain that a change of hairstyle was part of it: such a change is well attested in the ethnographic evidence and like-ly also applied among the Indo- Europeans. Widengren (1969: 19, 36) has drawn attention to the various hairstyles of Indo- Iranian peoples. Not all his material is relevant, such as his observations about Assyrian soldiers, but he interestingly

14 For the connection between fosterage and the maternal family in Greece, as well as more evidence regarding the ancient Germanic peoples than given by Widengren, see Bremmer (2021: 205–235).

351Indo- European initiation

points to a passage in Faustus of Byzantium (fifth century ad), which mentions that “in the fashion of children, in accordance with the religion and rule of Ar-menia, the youth Artawazd’s head was shaven with a long braid left free” (5.43, tr. Bedrosian). Widengren rightly concludes to a specific hairstyle for the (an?) age set of the male youth in Armenia and compares it to similar hairstyles of the Huns and the Cossacks.15 We do not know Artawazd’s age, but he clearly was not very young, as somewhat later in the text he is described as a “handsome, robust, beardless youth”. It escaped Widengren, however, that Greeks must have had a similar hairstyle at one point, as the Kouretes, the exemplary young men of $early Archaic Greece, had a hairstyle that was called both πλόκαμος ‘braid’ and σκόλλυς, explained by the ancient commentators as meaning the same as κορυφή $‘top, summit’, a hairstyle also associated with other young heroes like Theseus and Hector (Bremmer 2021: 17–20). In an inner-Greek development, the hair, when shaven off at the entry into the last stage of initiation, was often dedicated to riv-ers, who were seen as promoting the growth of youth (Leitao 2003; Pilz 2019). As this hairstyle was adopted at the transition of boyhood to adolescence, the crest of hair was probably shaven at the end of the initiation.

2.4 Wandering and group

A famous passage in Strabo (10.4.21), which he derived from the historian Epho-ros (4th c. BC), relates the pederastic relationship between an aristocratic ado-lescent and a somewhat older youth at the end of the Cretan initiation. Here, I would like to focus on a usually neglected detail of this account. We hear that the upper-class couple spent some time in the countryside feasting and hunting but were also accompanied by the friends of the adolescent, who were evidently lower in rank. This ritual took place in historical times, when Crete was already prop-erly divided up between numerous cities. There certainly was some wild country-side, but it must have been impossible to wander off very far.

Now if we take this combination – initiator/mentor, an upper-class adolescent, the latter’s friends and time spent in the countryside – as a kind of initiatory con-stellation, we can see that we find the same combination in the famous expedi-tion of the Argonauts, where Jason, accompanied by maternal uncles, clearly his initiatory supervisors, and a group of about 50 other adolescents leaves abroad to procure the Golden Fleece, returns and becomes king. This is a myth and thus

15 Other possible examples can be found on Wikipedia s.v. ‘Mohawk hairstyle’.

352 Jan N. Bremmer

dramatised in comparison with the Cretan ritual, but the main elements are all there – in fact, the initiatory background of the Argonautic myth has often been recognised (Bremmer 2021: XVII). The number of his accompanying comrades hardly received any attention in earlier discussions, but Widengren (1969: 88–90, 99) noted that 50 was the standard number for groups of youths in Celtic, Ital-ic, Persian and Slavic traditions. The Argonauts, as well as other Greek exam-ples, show that this number was prevalent in early Greece too (Bremmer 2021: 132–133); it could even explain the origin of the ‘fifty-oared’ ship, the penteconter, which was used for representative and military purposes in the archaic period and later (Bremmer 1990).

The stay outside civilisation could take various forms. In Greek mythology, we also have examples of two males wandering, one slightly older than the other, as in the cases of Peirithoos and Theseus, Pylades and Orestes as well as Silenos and Dionysos. There are striking parallels for such dual wanderings in Germanic traditions, witness the cases of Isung and Vildiver, Ise and Orendel, Eisenhans and Bärenhäuter, Gigas and Hythinus, which all seem to point to motifs of in-itiation, though refracted through different lenses (Bremmer 2021: 102). In the Cretan case recorded by Ephoros we also saw a mentor with an initiand, the latter being accompanied by a group of lower-ranking friends. We may wonder if in myth, epic and fairy tales these friends have not been left out, or if their presence was not simply abandoned in later developments of this motif.

Another form of this stay outside civilisation is wandering. Widengren (1953: 59–62, 1969: 86–92) has noted groups of wandering Iranian and Indian youths, and the Irish fianna spent their youth hunting and roaming the woods. In the earlier Middle Ages the iuvenes, the sons of nobility, were wandering through the countryside, and in Greece we have the example of Orpheus who, with a group of Thracian males, roamed the countryside (Bremmer 2021: 21, 86).16 In none of these cases do we hear of a dual leadership, but it is suggestive of another archaic feature that the Greek expedition against Troy was led by Agamemnon and Menelaos, Rome was founded by Romulus and Remus, the Angles and Sax-ons invaded England under Hengist and Horsa, and the Vandals under Ambri and Assi invaded the island Scadanan, where the Winnili were also ruled by a duo, Ybor and Agio (Origo gentium Longobardorum 1) – not to mention the dual

16 A remnant of initiatory wandering could also be behind the Greek custom sending adolescents as delegates to sanctuaries and festivals to attend, view, and spectate (hence $the word θεωροί) on behalf of the city, as persuasively argued by Rutherford (2004). $Note also Harðarson (2023) for a possible early name of such Indo- European groups of youths.

353Indo- European initiation

Spartan kingship and the two Roman consuls. This deserves further investigation, as it seems absent from the Indo- Iranian traditions (Bremmer 2021: XX). Could it be that this dual leadership developed from the combination of mentor and initiand?17

2.5 Defeating a monster

Jason and his Argonauts must fetch the Golden Fleece, which is guarded by a dragon. The task fits a series of Indo- European traditions in which the hero de-feats a monster before reaching proper adulthood. One only need to think of Oedipus defeating the Sphinx, Theseus the Minotaurus, Perseus Medusa, Sieg-fried the dragon, or Cú Chulainn killing Culann’s dog; Wikander (1941), Widen-gren (1969: 20–21), and Saadi-nejad (2023) have also pointed to dragon-slaying $Indo- Iranian heroes and warrior gods, such as Θraētaona who slays Aži Dahāka, $Kərəsāspa who slays Aži Sruuara, and Indra who kills Vr ̥tra. Given that dragons do not exist, it is clear that these myths and legends dramatise a Kraftprobe ‘trial of strength’. Fortunately, we have a fine example of how to imagine this trial in reality. The Hellenistic author Hegesandros (apud Athenaeus 1,18a) reports that by the Macedonians a man could not recline at dinner – that is, join the adult males – until he had singlehandedly killed a boar during the hunt. Here, I sug-gest, we have a basis for the myths that dramatise the demonstration of strength. Apparently, it was already part of the early Indo- European tradition that one was considered to be a proper adult only after having shown one’s strength by killing a dangerous animal or, as happened among the Germanic Chatti (Tacitus, Germa-nia 31), an enemy – an opponent who became dramatised as a monster in fictional accounts.18

17 It is true that in the mythical/legendary traditions, the dual leadership often consists of brothers, as Riccardo Ginevra points out to me, but this may well be myth/legend intensifying the close connection between the two leaders.

18 Although the Greek evidence is much older, this was also already seen by Weiser (1927: 73–74), whose perceptive study still remains valuable, the more so as it is not ideologi-cally vitiated like Höfler’s work.

354 Jan N. Bremmer

2.6 The club/Keule

Widengren (1969: 61) has argued that the members of Männerbund probably wielded the club as their main weapon. It is true that the club is typical of the Indo- Iranian dragon slayers (Wikander 1941: 76 note 1; Widengren 1969: 19–20), but the matter clearly deserves further investigation, as the Swedish scholars have not looked at this aspect in any detail. Moreover, they could adduce only one passage for the club among the ancient Germanic peoples by comparing the club-bearer in a notice from ad 1091(!) about the familia Herlechini in Ordericus Vitalis (Historia Ecclesiastica viii.19, ed. Chibnall) and overlooked the Irish evi-dence (Hurley 2007). In this case, though, we are lucky and blessed with a new discovery. In 2015, an Arcadian inscription on a bronze tablet that survived in six fragments was published, recording festivals of an almost Panarcadian amphic-tyony. It dates from 475–450 bc and was probably deposited in western Mount Lykaion.19 The inscription, to which we will come back in the next section, plau-$sibly mentions a τέμενος of the hero Areithoos Korynitas (lines 3 and 7), whose $epithet has been convincingly explained as ‘club bearer’ (Mahoney 2020). Now this mythical figure already occurs in Homer, where the old Nestor has an inter-esting tale about him (Iliad 7.132–157). He describes how in his youth he killed a certain Ereuthalion, who had received his armour from Lycurgus when the latter had grown old; Lycurgus, in turn, had gained that armour in his youth by killing

“lord Areithoos, noble Areithoos, whom men and women with beautiful girdles $called by the name Korynetes (‘Club man’)” (7.137–139: Ἀρηϊθόοιο ἄνακτος, δίου Ἀρηϊθόου. τὸν ἐπίκλησιν κορυνήτην ἄνδρες κίκλησκον καλλίζωνοί τε γυναῖκες, $tr. Mahoney) using trickery. The anecdote is one of those vignettes which Homer occasionally gives in the Iliad by referring to little-known sagas from the Greek mainland that most probably derive from sources dating back at least to the time before the Greeks started to emigrate to Aeolia, Ionia and the islands at the end of the second millennium bc.20 In other words, we have here a reference to a mytho-logical Club-man whose tradition must go back to the Mycenaean era.

Now another striking aspect of this legend is that Nestor was very young when he killed Ereuthalion, as was Lycurgus when he slew Areithoos. Clearly, we

19 For text, translation, and commentary, see Carbon et al. (2016, no. 223). For date and place, see Minon (2021).

20 For these vignettes, see Hoekstra (1981: 54–66). Jost (2021) also discusses the case of Areithoos and Lycurgus, but she does not differentiate between pre-Homeric Arcadian heroes and those later appropriated, such as Odysseus and Aeneas, who originally did not belong to Arcadia.

355Indo- European initiation

are supposed to think of the armour and its original hero as living long, long ago, but also that the victors in these battles were very young. We should also note that Lycurgus slew Areithoos with a trick, and in the Arcadian inscription the term ‘complete trickery’ (line 8: Minon 2021: 162–167) also occurs close to that of the $mention of the τέμενος for Areithoos. The connection is probably not arbitrary $as cunning and trickery were a recurring element of Greek initiation (Bremmer 2021: 11, 23). In Homer, the armour of Areithoos has been ‘updated’, as Ereuthal-ion wears his armour on his shoulders, but originally Areithoos must have been armed with a club only, given his nickname. It seems plausible to conclude that the Arcadian inscription suggests a connection between initiation and the wor-ship of the mythical Club-man Areithoos.

There are two more elements to add to this Greek dossier. Firstly, when around the middle of the sixth century bc the Athenian aristocrat Pisistratus grabbed power, our somewhat conflicting sources relate that he requested a bodyguard $consisting of 400 very young men (Diogenes Laertius 1.66: τοὺς νεωτάτους). In $the end, according to Plutarch, it was proposed to give him a group of 50 (see $above) who were ‘club bearers’ (Life of Solon 30.2: κορυνηφόροι). It seems that $club-bearing is associated here with young males who function as a kind of retinue.

Secondly, not only is Heracles’ standard weapon a club, but the biography of this greatest of all Greek heroes is also full of initiatory details, such as his change of name, his upbringing among shepherds, his supervision by educators, his sex-ual activities, his asocial behaviour, his wandering (Bremmer 2021: 107–123), and his fits of madness, which I would now explain as memories of the furor heroicus, albeit reinterpreted in later times when this furor was no longer witnessed in battle. It seems, then, that a club was part of an early stage of Greek initiation and, possibly, also of early Indo- European initiations.

2.7 Receiving arms

In several passages, Widengren has paid attention to the receiving of arms at the end of the initiation. He mainly focused on the girdle and its place in the ac-ceptance into the retinue of the Iranian kings (1969: 22–29), which he connected with the ritual of cingulum dare during knighting in earlier medieval feudalism (1969: 49–50, 60–61).21 Apparently, he was unable to find any early material in

21 Widengren’s analysis is no longer up to date; see Lieberman (2015) for a recent survey of the evidence.

356 Jan N. Bremmer

his Indo- Iranian evidence, just as he could not find any for the entry into the last phase of the initiation. However, he noted that amongst the ancient Germanic peoples “in the midst of the assembly one of the chiefs or the father or relatives equip the youth with a shield and a spear” (Tacitus, Germania 13). The notice shows that the Waffenleihe ‘giving of the arms’ was ritualised, took place, pre-sumably, at the conclusion of the initiation, and was a matter of public concern and importance.

We also find early evidence of this connection between the end of initiation and the receiving of arms among the Greeks. In Thebes, the lover presented his beloved youth with a panoply when he registered as a man (Plutarch, Moralia 761b), whereas the young Cretan aristocrats received a military suit from their lover after the stay with their friends and mentor in the countryside, clearly at the moment that their initial training had come to an end. Moreover, they also received a special piece of clothing to mark the end of their initiation (Ephoros FGrH 70 F 149) and were now called ‘illustrious’ (McClay 2021).

The new Arcadian inscription is also informative in this respect. Among its $prescriptions we find (line 6): κόρϝον, ἐνϝότοι ϝέτει, ἐξάγεν ἀσπίδα, ἀκόντιον, φοινικὶς, ξίφος, Κ[..?... “let a youth, in the ninth year, bring forth: a shield, a small $javelin, red vestments, a sword, […] (unintelligible)”. As has been plausibly ar-gued (Mahoney 2020), we find here the Waffenleihe of the Arcadian youths. How-ever, we should note that the giving of arms is concomitant with a special dress, which will mark out the young men from the socially inferior male Arcadians. This was evidently also the case with the young Cretan aristocrats (above), but it is interestingly also mentioned in regard to Heracles, who received a garment from Athena together with weapons from other gods (Apollodorus 2.4.11), pre-sumably also at the end of his initiation.

The early date of the Arcadian inscription may help us to solve another prob-lem. As we have seen, in addition to the presenting of arms, the inscription also $mentions ‘red vestments’ (φοινικίς), which plausibly were the new, special clothes $of the newly initiated adults. Now, already in the seventh century bc, the first month in Corinth was called Phoinikaios, as we now know from the Antikythera Mechanism, but its name has been unexplained until now. As Greek months are usually named after a festival, the name presupposes a festival Phoinikaia, which will have been ‘supervised’ by Athena, who in Corinth had the epithet Phoinike. Given that the first position in the year would perfectly fit the end of initiation and the arrival of new members of adult society, one may wonder if in Corinth the new adults also received a ‘red vestment’. Athena was closely connected with the Corinthian hero Bellerophon, which would make her appropriate for a di-

357Indo- European initiation

vinity connected with initiation.22 However this may be, it is clear that the early Greeks concluded the initiation of their youth by giving them proper weapons and a special garment.

2.8 Wedding

Lily Weiser (1898–1987) observed that the wedding is usually the concluding stage of the initiation in Germanic Sagen and fairy tales (1927: 71). This is also clearly the case in Greek mythology, where, after the defeat of a monster, Perseus marries Andromeda, just as Oedipus does Iocaste after conquering the Sphinx, and Jason weds Medea after returning with the Golden Fleece. In other words, in these myths there is a common connection between marriage and the end of the initiation. However, Sagen and myths usually focus on a single hero, and they should not be confused with historical reality. As in early Greece the boys were initiated in age sets, it seems likely that they also married in groups. Indeed, we do hear that this was the case in Crete, Samos and the Troad, and the collective marriages of the Danaids and Proitids in myth suggests the antiquity of such mar-riages (Bremmer 2021: XVII). It would seem likely that such collective marriages once took place among the Indo- Europeans, as for Rome we have the legendary wedding of Romulus and his youths with the Sabine maidens, but I have been unable to find other close parallels.23

3 Final considerations

What conclusions can we draw? Looking at the material discussed, it struck me again how difficult it is to evaluate the historical evidence. Although myths and Sagen constitute an important part of our relevant sources, our task is made much more difficult by the fact that there is no straight line from myth to ritual, and we have to continuously keep in mind that narratives have their own laws and logic. Narratives can even contain initiatory motifs without reflecting the whole of the initiatory ritual or focus on specific elements, such as the birth of a hero or his stay in the wilderness. In the end, we should never forget that myths were meant

22 For the evidence regarding the month Phoinikaios, Bellerophon and Athena, see Ziskowski (2019).

23 But see Kim McCone’s contribution to this volume.

358 Jan N. Bremmer

to tell a good story, with which the poets or other narrators had to entertain their listeners and readers, but were not necessarily a true reflection of the ritual pro-cess in historical reality. It is therefore nearly always necessary to compare the ethnographic and historical evidence with the world of myth and Sagen in order to see if the latter simplifies, distorts or exaggerates the actual ritual.

But even with these caveats, my survey clearly shows that the Greek evidence has been wrongly neglected in Widengren’s survey of Indo- European initiation, its wealth of material easily surpassing that of the Indo- Iranian and Germanic sourc-es and being, on the whole, much earlier than that of the ancient Germanic and Celtic peoples. It should also be clear that this brief survey has not exhausted the evidence. More could be said about the education among shepherds (a motif we find quite often in Greece, but also in Persia and ancient Rome, cf. Bremmer 2021: 116–117), the metamorphosis into a wolf (as we hear of in ancient Arcadia), the fu-ror heroicus,24 and other motifs, but those subjects would require a separate study.

Taking all this into account, we can sketch the contours of male Indo- European initiation as follows: after a period at home or being fostered, the youths entered a period of training, the beginning of which was signalled by a change in hairstyle. In the latter part of this period, the youths had to spend a time away from their home area either in more or less egalitarian groups or as part of the retinue of a prince or son of a chieftain. At the end of this period, they had to show their strength and courage by killing a dangerous animal or an enemy. After that proof of their manhood, they received proper weapons and got married.

It is obvious that not all of these parts of the initiation received equal attention in the various branches of the Indo- European world. It is also not wholly clear if all parts were strictly Indo- European or whether some elements were perhaps taken over from the previous population. The Greek evidence raises various ques-tions in that respect. For example, seemingly absent from other Indo- European traditions, or at least not mentioned, a men’s house is an institution well attested $in the ethnographic evidence from Greece: in Crete we find the ἀνδρεῖον, literally $indeed the ‘men’s house’ (Whitley 2018), but a much more widespread form of the $men’s house in Greece must have been the λέσχη, which was closely connected $to Apollo and probably went back to Mycenaean times (Bremmer 2008: 155–168, Marginesu 2001). This is not the only Greek case where we find an element in the initiatory system that has parallels in the ethnographic evidence but not in Indo- European traditions. Another famous case is transvestism, which is fairly

24 For the Arcadian werewolves, see Bremmer (2019: 358–370); the material for the Ger-manic furor heroicus has now been collected by Samson (2020).

359Indo- European initiation

widely attested in Greek myths and rituals, already in the case of Achilles, who was raised as a girl at the court of king Lykomedes of Skyros (another early case of fosterage!) before joining the Greek expedition against Troy (Bremmer 2021: 5, 125–141). One might suspect that both these cases were taken over from the indigenous populations. On the other hand, some elements may have been later Greek developments, such as swimming and pederasty. The former was probably introduced when the proto-Greeks reached the coast of Greece and can be found in various Greek myths and visual representations (Hölscher 2021), but not, as far as I know, in other Indo- European traditions. Pederasty was once postulated by me as an Indo- European tradition in youthful enthusiasm (Bremmer 1980), but it now seems clear that this was a relatively late development in early first- millennium Greece (Bremmer 2021: 177–204).

Last but not least, the use of the term Männerbund, as employed by Höfler, Wikander, Widengren, and others, is confusing and should be reconsidered. We must keep in mind that the stay outside civilisation could lead to different out-comes. The most normal one was probably the return into the community. It is also possible that the youths entered the service of a prince or chieftain for a while, as presupposed by the Argonauts. However, after their return, the partic-ipants of that expedition went home, just as the Greek heroes did after the de-struction of Troy. Such temporary retinues are also attested in Classical literature, for the Celts and ancient Germanic peoples (Bremmer 2021: 241–247). Originally, then, it was especially the youths that were no longer part of the family but had not yet established themselves as head of an independent family, who occupied a marginal position in the tribal societies. In these cases, though, they did not really constitute a Männerbund as a separate organisation within a larger whole.

On the other hand, such a wandering group of youths could also move else-where and become the dominating political factor in an area away from their proper homeland. This seems to have happened with the Near Eastern maryanni, the warrior aristocracy of the Mitanni. The presence of the Kouretes and Molpoi in Ephesus and Miletus as important political groups suggests a similar develop-ment for the Greek colonisation in Western Asia Minor. The Italic custom of the ver sacrum is probably also related to such wandering groups of male youths, but with the difference that the Italic youths were actually prohibited from returning home. Once established as a political factor, each of these groups became a real Männerbund, and their descendants could long retain this political dominance, as we can observe in the Near East, Greece and Western Asia Minor (Bremmer 2021: XV). In the end, it is not implausible to see initiation as a (or the) driving force in the expansion of the early Indo- Europeans.

(Proto-)Indo- European age- based male social hierarchies and groupings

Age- grades, sodalities, coevals, age- sets and the origins of Rome’s curiae (including the curia ‘senate- house’)

Kim McCone Maynooth

This study argues for lifelong associations of coevals termed ‘age- sets’ as a

feature of Proto- Indo- European1 social organisation, taking as its starting

points (a) a PIE social system of three successive age- grades and (b) their

frequent combination with age- sets. After (1) a general introduction and

discussion of methodology, it focusses upon: (2) the junior grade’s ‘wolf-

ish’ bachelor sodalities; (3) age, initiations and other conditions of entry

and exit conducive to the formation of adult age- sets; (4) Rome’s ‘wolfish’

foundation myth and its implications; (5) coevality as an ideal attribute of

sodalities in various IE cultures, the homēlikiē ‘same- age- group’ as a youth-

ful bond maintained into adulthood and old age in the Odyssey, and the

progress of hēlikiai ‘age- groups’ admitted to citizenship together in a given

year through a cycle of 42 successive annual stages in ancient Athens; (6)

the Roman antiquarian doctrine of 30 original curiae, Festus’ statement

that there were actually 35, and a probable original system of age- sets based

on a multiple of 7 like the Athenian hēlikiai. In conclusion (7), the bonds

forged between members of a (P)IE sodality were continued in adult life by

age- sets calculated to enhance their members’ social and military cohesion

and clout.

1 ‘Proto- Indo- European’ is used here in its traditional vaguer sense rather than as a stage specifically including Anatolian and opposed to later CIE ‘Core IE’ excluding it. This, however, is a matter of convenience, not a denial that the Anatolian branch represents a particularly early offshoot.

368 Kim McCone

1 Preliminaries

1.1 Basic (P)IE social structure and associated vocabulary

A case for the Proto- Indo- European social system and associated vocabulary summarised in Figure 1 has been made in three earlier studies. The first (McCone 1987) posited three post- pubescent age- grades along with a dichotomy between a *kori̯os ‘Männerbund, sodality’ of vagrant warlike bachelors likened to wolves and a *teu̯-tah₂ ‘kingdom’ of adult married soldier- farmers who, if they lived long enough, retired from military duty as elders with advisory and judicial functions. The second (McCone 1998) was concerned with the PIE words for ‘king’ and ‘queen’. The third (McCone 2020) posited basic social stratification reflected in a terminological opposition between three upper- class [U] age- grades and generic or lower- class [G/L] counterparts (118–121) integrated by a sacral king (104–115 and 127–130), whose queen was held to be the mortal surrogate of a goddess (160– 163), most likely the radiant and erotic *H₂au̯s-ōs ‘Dawn’ (150–157), bound to him in a hieros gamos or ‘sacred marriage’ (131–138).

1.2 Social structure, ideology and mythology

The nature of much of the evidence adduced below raises the question of the relationship between social structure and mythical or ideological patterns. Ben-veniste (1969: 279–292) maintained Dumézil’s original view that an Indian- style tripartite hierarchy of priests, warriors and farmers/herdsmen was a key feature of PIE social organisation, despite the lack of pertinent reconstructed PIE terms. Meanwhile, Dumézil himself (e.g., 1968: 15) had shifted to the position that “tri-partite ideology” did not necessarily mirror social structure. Thus encouraged, Campanile (1990) declared it an “Indo- European mindset” unaligned with an

“essentially egalitarian society” (40–41) paradoxically presided over by a sacral king (42–49). Schlerath’s (1987) doubts about the feasibility of reconstructing PIE social structure did not extend to mythology, to judge from his argument (Schler-ath 1954) for PIE belief in two hounds attached to the realm of the dead, and his telling criticisms (Schlerath 1995 and 1996) of Dumézil’s model and methods did not rule out the reconstruction of PIE ideology per se.

The uncoupling of mythology and ideology from social organisation creates a false dichotomy because, as the founder of the so-called ‘functionalist’ school of

369(Proto-)Indo- European age- based male social hierarchies and groupings

anthropology put it, “an intimate connection exists between the word, the mythos, the sacred tales of a tribe on the one hand, and their ritual acts, their moral deeds, their social organization, and even their practical activities on the other” (Ma-linowski 1926: 11). This principle is retained by the ‘structuralist’ approach pi-oneered by Lévi-Strauss, but with a crucial caveat against assuming “that a full correlation exists between the myths of a given society and its culture” and “that whenever a social pattern is alluded to in a myth this pattern must correspond to something real and attributable to the past if, under scrutiny, the present fails to offer an equivalent” rather than presenting “the pattern of a nonexistent society, past or present” (Lévi-Strauss 1978: 203–204). Consequently,

it is always rash to undertake, as Boas wanted to do in his monumental Tshimshian Mythology, “a description of the life, social organization and re-ligious ideas and practices of a people … as it appears in their mythology” … The myth is certainly related to given facts, but not as a representation of them. The relationship is of a dialectic kind, and the institutions described in the myths can be the very opposite of the real institutions. This will always be the case when the myth is trying to express a negative truth. (Lévi-Strauss 1978: 172)

The first citation is from Lévi-Strauss’s study of “four Winnebago myths” (1978: 198–210), one of which contradicts actual Winnebago norms. The second is from his celebrated analysis of the Tshimshian (British Columbia) “story of Asdiwal” (1978: 146–197), which points out that the Tshimshian rule of patrilocal residence with the husband’s kin after marriage is contravened by the hero: Asdiwal was not only born where his widowed mother lived with her widowed mother but also
