However, she

identifies the purpose of the incident as being the assertion of Diancecht as the

supreme god of healing, and to define the limits of medicine. This is made clear when

he successfully frustrates his daughter Airmed’s attempt to classify the herbs that

grow when her immensely gifted brother is buried. The text says that ‘herbs three

hundred and sixty-five, according to the number of his joints and sinews, grew

through the grave’. This reference to three hundred and sixty-five is most likely of

cosmological significance, mapping the body of Miach onto the year, so that

humanity provides the measure of time as well as the shape of the physical universe.

Diancecht, however, ‘came to her, and he confused the herbs, so that noone knows

their proper cures’. 39

This frustrates Airmed’s desire to preserve something of her

brother’s skills through the use of the herbs that grew from his body.

During the battle that concludes the text Diancecht’s powers are shown to be

considerable, in that he is able to revive the dead warriors of the Tuatha De Danann so

that they continue to fight and their enemies the Fomhoire are defeated. This ability to

raise the dead also appears in the Mabinogion story ‘Branwen’, where a magical

cauldron will revive dead warriors who are thrown into it.

Conclusion

Archaeology also provides evidence of the place of healing in Celtic religious life.

Water sites were frequently regarded as entry points to the supernatural world, and

excavations at a number of such sites have yielded much in the way of religious

artefacts. Most famous of these shrines is the Roman Baths at Bath (formerly Aquae

Sulis) in the south-west of England. This site, distinguished by hot springs, was

dedicated to the Celtic healer goddess Sulis, whom the Romans associated with

Minerva (Greek Athena). Among the artefacts recovered are curse tablets, requesting

the goddess’ assistance in the getting of revenge against enemies. A less well-known,

but equally deserving, site is the sanctuary of the goddess Sequana at the source of the

Seine, where nearly two hundred wooden figures have been recovered. It is believed

that these were deposited by worshippers and supplicants who were asking the

goddess for cures. 8 These sites provide evidence for the piety of ordinary members of

society.

Because the body was, for the Indo-Europeans, the fundamental model for the

universe, health and healing had wide-ranging cosmological consequences. Gods

were injured and healed or not healed, and could die, and the inevitability of human

death was a constant theme that was examined in a variety of related mythologies

over several millennia. These varying views of illness and wellness, life and death,

were enduringly meaningful to people, until in the early medieval period missionaries

of the new religion of Christianity converted the Welsh, the Irish, and the

Scandinavians to the religion of the one god.

### **Early Indo-European**

### **weapons terminology**

Abstract. Nineteenth-century scholars saw the world of the Indo-Eu­ ropeans in false dichotomies of pastoralism vs. agriculture, patriarchy vs. matriarchy and warriors vs. victims; slowly, but surely, archaeolog­ ical and linguistic research are dispelling these myths. A comprehensive examination of the lexica of the IE languages reveals that many alleged weapon terms have no reliable IE etymology. Those that do, show that the distinction between tool and weapon was not sharply drawn. Others show typological features of non-IE origins. The majority of IE weapons evolved during the Bronze Age from agricultural implements and ev­ eryday tools. Rather than appearing on the scene as armed barbarians, the Indo-Europeans and the pre-IE populations of Eurasia were engaged in a Bronze Age weapons race in which the use of weapons became increasingly important for cultural survival. The task ahead of us will be to define the conditions in which this arms race became a necessity.

In 1929, Edward Sapir declared his admiration for the skill of Indo-Europeanists by proclaiming that ''In the course of their detailed researches, Indo-European linguists have gradually developed a tech­ nique which is probably more nearly perfect than that of any other science dealing with man's institutions." (1929:207) It is challenging to compare this assessment of the results achieved by Indo-European scholarship with the judgment of J. Fraser who only three years earlier dismissed the entire enterprise with these words: ''I cannot see any

### **means by which the Linguistic Palaeonotologist, if he applied ... the**

method which he does apply to the reconstruction of the Indogermans, could fail to arrive at conclusions which we . . . would see to be ludicrous.'' ( 1926:268) The untoward arrogance of Fraser's negative assessment is perhaps the result of his knowing the ''the method which [the Indo-Europeanist] does apply to the reconstruction" so imper­ fectly. Where he demonstrates Linguistic Palaeontology for his read­ ers, he shows only the most amateurish grasp of the subject. The standard means of distinguishing loanwords-phonological tagging by means of anomalous phonemes or alien phonotactics, morphological identification of native words by means of moribund categories, and

224 WORD, VOLUME 44, NUMBER 2 (AUGUST, 1993)

flagging innovations by geographical distribution-are all unknown to him; moreover, Fraser committed the cardinal error of mistaking lex­ icon for language; that is, he assumed that the investigation focuses on vocabulary rather than grammar. His particular collection of pseudo­ scholarship would be of little interest were it not for the effects of Tylor's Law: "A once established opinion, however delusive, can hold its own from age to age without reasonable reference to its origin." (Tylor, 1891).

There are still writers who believe that Indo-Europeanists have claimed to reconstruct words which show a culture marked by false dichotomies such as pastoral versus agricultural, patriarchal versus matriarchal and martial versus pacific. Despite its obvious absurdity, the Wehrmacht interpretation of prehistory still colors discussions of Indo-European origins. It is high time to reexamine the evidence in light of actual scientific practice, not the ramblings of Fraser. 1 A good place to start, I feel, would be weapon terminology, for it is here that the allure of the Wehrmacht model is greatest.

The archaeological record shows that over the course of the Bronze and Iron Ages, weapons became more prevalent. The linguistic evidence indicates a similar proliferation of weapon terms. Buck's Dictionary of Selected Synonyms in the Principal Indo-European Lan­ guages devotes a whole chapter, some forty-eight pages (1949:1370-1418) to warfare. A closer examination of these terms indicates that many are limited to small geographical settings, may be used of non­ military tools, or are marked by open sonorities and their failure to obey the Indo-European root structure constraints formulated by Meil­ let one hundred years ago. That is, these words are regional innova­ tions or loans from non-Indo-European sources. Let us then review the evidence for Indo-European warfare and weapons.

1. Armed conflict. The linguistic evidence shows that, like all peo­ ples, the Indo-Europeans did participate in some type of organized armed conflict. The root Y qer- [P 615] is attested in a simple thematic noun, (Lith kdras 'war, army' and OP kdra- 'people, army' < *qor­ o-), 2 where it reflects the military aspect of the populace, 'members of the raiding party'. A more widely attested derivative, *qor-jo-, (Mir cuire 'troop' [also in Gaulish -corii], PG *xarijaz 'host, army' [ON herr, OE here, OS hari, Go harjis]; and Lith kdrias) along with Greek a compound, KOLpO-j.L

The Indo-European Religious Background of the Gygēs

Tale in Hērodotos

Ethan M. A. Rite

The first “short story” included in the Histories of Hērodotos narrates the rise of the

Mermnad dynasty of Lydia through an act of assassination and usurpation by their founder,

Gygēs.1 To make a long tale short, the Lydian king Kandaulēs, being obsessed with his wife,

contrives to show her naked to his bodyguard Gygēs. After catching him in the act, the queen

confronts Gygēs and forces him to choose between murdering his master or being killed himself.

He takes the former option and establishes himself and his descendants as rulers of Lydia up to the

time of Kroisos. In the commentary of Asheri, Lloyd, and Corcella, this story is characterized as a

“court tale,” but is further analyzed neither with respect to its oral-historical background nor its

motivic structure.2 This paper will argue that the Gygēs narrative reflects a far more ancient, Indo-

European ideology representing the sovereign power as a goddess wedded to the sovereign himself

in a sacred marriage.

What is the Sacred Marriage?

As employed in this article, the term “sacred marriage” refers to a meme in the religions of

ancient Europe and West Asia which metaphorically cast good rulership as a harmonious wedding

between the king, the representative of his people, and the earth, personified as a female divinity.

The origin of this concept is readily apparent, as the successful maintenance of civilization depends

upon an ecological balance between the human population and all other organisms, on whom they

rely for nourishment and whom they, in turn, feed and cultivate. Chief among the king’s functions

was the maintenance of justice, not just between members of the tribe, but also between mankind

and the wider cosmos.3 Here the goddess is also involved, as she represents not simply a patch of

dirt, but the generative process, literally “nature,” which links all creatures in the cosmic hierarchy.

The legitimacy of a given ruler was linked to the health of the generated world, which was thought

to flourish under a just king and wither under a despot.4 Thus, divinized nature conferred upon the

mortal king his right to rule, and for this reason she is herein labeled Sovereignty.

The information used in this article concerning the sacred marriage in Indo-European-

speaking Anatolia and in non-Indo-European cultures of the Near East will largely come from The

Mother of the Gods, Athens, and the Tyranny of Asia, which analyzes Kybelē as a Near Eastern

divinity incorporated into Greek religion through contact and conflict with Anatolian civilization.

Evidence for the existence of the sacred marriage as a concept in the wider Indo-European

MA: Harvard University Press, 1920), 1.7–12; David Asheri, Alan Lloyd, and Aldo Corcella, Commentary on

Herodotus Books I–IV, eds. Oswyn Murray and Alfonso Moreno (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2007), 81. 2 Asheri, Lloyd, and Corcella, Commentary on Herodotus, 81. 3 M. L. West, Indo-European Poetry and Myth (New York: Oxford University Press, 2007), 421–24. 4 West, Indo-European Poetry and Myth, 421–24.

Rite, “The Indo-European Religious Background of the Gygēs Tale in Hērodotos” || 2

linguistic and cultural clade will be drawn from Indo-European Poetry and Myth, a comparative

study of Indo-European literature and religion with respect to shared concepts and motifs, as

opposed to strict linguistic heritage.

Mark Munn cites appearances of the sacred marriage as a topos in Sumerian literature as

early as the Third Dynasty of Ur.5 The presence of sacred marriage in Mesopotamia at the end of

the third millennium B.C.E. and in Proto-Indo-European is significant, as the Indo-European

family was likely at a very early stage of diversification at that point. The coeval attestation of the

topos in civilizations as separate as the city-states of Mesopotamia and the pastoralists of the

Eurasian steppe suggests that it was not diffused from one to the other. It is likely that Near Eastern

and Indo-European traditions of the sacred marriage form part of a wider, Eurasian religious

ideology with probable origins in a culture or cultures that flourished prior to the coalescence of

the Indo-European dialect continuum.

Literary and linguistic evidence for the Indo-European ideology of sacred marriage comes

from several branches of the Indo-European family. It is particularly rich within the Anatolian

branch, of which Lydian is itself a member. Beyond Anatolia, figures representing Sovereignty or

some of her functions are found in stories from the Celtic and Hellenic subfamilies, as well as in

Sanskrit. What follows is a review of the reflexes of Sovereignty found in those sub-branches of

Indo-European, which will enable their shared characteristics to be identified and a Proto-Indo-

European ideology of Sovereignty and the sacred marriage to be outlined. In addition,

archaeological evidence will be used to illuminate the ritual execution of the sovereign that formed

a key part of this ideology within Indo-European cultures. Finally, an analysis of the story of

Gygēs’ usurpation as told by Hērodotos and others will reveal its connection with the Indo-

European concept of Sovereignty and highlight internal evidence for its origin in myth rather than

“pure” history.

Kybelē – Sovereignty in Anatolia

In his study on the Mother of the Gods, Mark Munn analyzes the eponymous goddess, who

provided the justification for the sovereign’s power in the Phrygian and Lydian kingdoms of late

Bronze Age and Archaic Anatolia. The Mother of the Gods, also called Kybelē, was a chthonic

fertility deity associated closely with wells, springs, and mountains.6 Shrines to her were carved

into cliff faces with nearby water sources across the Phrygian domain, manifesting her

$identification with the physical landscape of the kingdom.7 The goddess’ very name, Κυβέλη, is $

plausibly derived from the Phrygian word for “mountain,” making her the “Mountain Mother.”8

In traditional Phrygian narratives Sovereignty is portrayed as a mortal woman who bore

the archetypal king Midas and, on account of her piety, received divine honors from him after her

death.9 From such tales, Munn extrapolates an archetypal “life history” for Kybelē. She begins her

career as a virgin and goes on to become the bride of the king and mother of his son before dying,

after which she is divinized.10 In Munn’s interpretation, Kybelē was “assimilated to the role of the

consort herself” and her life narrative was continually reenacted across generations through the

5 Mark Munn, Mother of the Gods, Athens, and the Tyranny of Asia (Berkeley: University of California Press, 2006),

132–33. 6 Munn, Mother of the Gods, 84–87. 7 Munn, Mother of the Gods, 75–77. 8 Munn, Mother of the Gods, 120–25. 9 Munn, Mother of the Gods, 79–85. 10 Munn, Mother of the Gods, 99.

Rite, “The Indo-European Religious Background of the Gygēs Tale in Hērodotos” || 3

ritual pairing of the Lydian tyrant and his concubines, the favorite of whom bore his successor and

thus became Sovereignty.11

The progression of Sovereignty through a life cycle shows that she was not a static, timeless

divinity, but instead embodied nature as a generative process which the king was obligated to

maintain, and which would, in turn, uphold his rule.12 The support given by Sovereignty to loyal

kings was not just abstract, but practical, because Kybelē also had a martial function. Her ritual

music accompanied Lydian military campaigns and was said to have been appropriated by the

Spartans for their own marching music.13 Munn cites stories from Polyainos in which the

processional rites of Kybelē provide the occasion and cover for acts of conquest, and he recounts

a tale from Nicholas of Damascus in which her sacred artifacts instill “god-sent terror” in the

enemies of the ruling house of Miletus.14 In the religious mind of Archaic Asia Minor, Kybelē was

not a metaphor, but a real manifestation of the sovereign power bestowed on the monarch.

Medb – Sovereignty in Ireland

In Indo-European Poetry and Myth, M. L. West writes that in ancient Ireland, as in Lydia,

the king was legitimized via marriage to a personification of the physical turf of his kingdom who

also represented the sovereignty over that particular land.15 Máire Herbert analyzes one such figure

– Medb, the mythical queen of Connacht and heroine of the Táin Bó Cúailnge – in more detail.

Like Kybelē, Medb is reputed to have taken a succession of kings as husbands, no fewer than nine,

according to West.16 Herbert interprets Medb’s serial polyandry as symbolizing the continuous

need for good rulership and the inconstancy of power,17 which in turn explains Medb’s agency in

choosing her spouse. In one narrative mentioned by Herbert, she abandons one of her husbands in

favor of a “young man who was active in protecting her province” whom she made king instead.18

Although not discussed by Herbert, it merits mention that Medb performs an even more

active martial role than Kybelē. While there is historical evidence that Kybelē’s insignia were

carried before campaigning armies, in the Táin Medb is depicted instigating and commanding the

armed cattle raid of the title. The action starts after she decides to go to war over possession of a

famous bull, the Donn Cuailnge, in order to make the value of her property greater than that of her

husband Ailill.19 On the warpath, she commands the mustered hosts of her kingdom and rides in a

chariot like her husband and other elite warriors.20 Medb even enters combat and gravely wounds

the hero Cethern.21 In her role as not just a war, but a warrior goddess, Medb dramatically portrays

Sovereignty pursuing the polity’s imperative to protect and extend its hegemony.

Pallas Athēnā – Sovereignty in Greece

When surveying examples of the Indo-European sovereignty goddess, the unique figure

from Greek literature noted by West is Basileia, who features in Aristophanes’ Birds as a

representation of “Zeus’ power, wisdom, and justice.”22 However, it is not difficult to posit that

there is a sovereignty goddess among the better-known Greek deities. Pallas Athēnā is presented

in the role of Sovereignty in the epic tradition and there is linguistic evidence that this was once

her function.

Although she is not the wife of any king, mortal or divine, in her role as guardian and

mentor of Homeric kings Athēnā performs a similar function to Medb in the Táin Bó Cúailnge.23

To give just a few examples, she stays Akhilleus from slaying Agamemnōn at the inception of

their storied conflict24 and later sets the iconic blazing nimbus about his head to terrify the Trojans

despoiling the dead Patroklos.25 She strengthens Diomēdēs before his aristeia26 and, recalling

Medb, acts as his charioteer and companion in wounding Arēs.27 Throughout the second Homeric

poem she is Odysseus’ special (and sometimes literal) mentor and (micro)manages his

homecoming. In her own words to Odysseus, “[I am] she who always stands by you in all trials

$and guards you” (ἥ τέ τοι αἰεὶ ἐν πάντεσσι πόνοισι παρίσταμαι ἠδὲ φυλάσσω).28 $

Likewise, in her patronage of Athens she assumes the role of Sovereignty looking after the

well-being of her territory. In Book 8 of the Histories, Hērodotos recounts that when the Athenians

evacuated their city at the approach of the Persians under Xerxēs, the goddess deserted the

acropolis along with her sacred snake.29 Later, a female apparition – surely her in the mind of a

pious Athenian – incites the attack of the Greek fleet at Salamis, bringing about final salvation.30

If Athēnā’s name was in origin an epithet, it is possible that she was once simply called

$Παλλάς. Robert Beekes writes that “Athena’s epithet Παλλάς, άδος … is isolated, among the $

$Greeks in Thebes (Egypt), it functions as a sacral term for ‘girl.’”34 Thus, Παλλάς seems to have $

$originally been a doublet of παρθένος, with the meaning “virgin” or “maiden.” It is interesting that $

$παλλάς appears to be the root of παλλακή, the term used for the concubines of the Lydian sovereign $

from among whom the avatar of Kybelē was chosen,35 suggesting a likeness between the two

divinities.

Furthermore, in Homer, Athēnā is described as the mother of Erekhtheus, the progenitor

$ancestor of the Athenians, whom the “grain-giving field bore” and she herself nurtured (ὅν ποτ’ $

$Ἀθήνη θρέψε Διὸς θυγάτηρ, τέκε δὲ ζείδωρος ἄρουρα).36 Athēnā’s cult in Greece appears to date $

back at least to the palatial civilizations of the Middle and Late Bronze Age. A goddess associated

with militaria and the royal palace is attested in artwork even in Minoan times and an a-ta-na po-

ti-ni-ja, possibly “Lady Athēnā,” is mentioned in Linear B texts from Knossos.37 This author

postulates that the Homeric passage is a reference to Athēnā as a telluric goddess and supposes

that in the deep past Athens was thought to have its own “Maiden” who ritually wedded the king

before becoming mother of his heir, as did Kybelē in Anatolia. With the demise of Mycenaean

sacred kingship and the rise of democracy, the Maiden of Athens was left a perpetual virgin.

Mādhavī – Virginity and Royalty in India

Sanskrit literature contains the figure of Mādhavī, the daughter of the high king Yayāti in

the Mahābhārata. Mādhavī is a royal virgin who, like Medb and Kybelē, supports princely

lineages through the bearing of legitimate heirs. She bears sons to four different kings, thus

ensuring the survival of their respective dynasties.38 These children go on to save their grandfather,

Yayāti, after he allows his superhuman rectitude to be marred by the vice of pride and thereby falls

from the celestial paradise.39 Unlike Kybelē, Mādhavī is not shown progressing through a life

cycle, but she is “gifted with renewable virginity,”40 which enables her to couple with multiple

princes and remain a virgin after each one, just as each successive tyrant of Lydia enacted the ritual

of sacred marriage with a virginal concubine. While Mādhavī is not an earth goddess who must be

cultivated and appeased, the Mahābhārata does elsewhere propound the near-universal ideology

associating a righteous king with prosperity for the land he rules.41

The Ritual Gift and the Mead of Sovereignty

In tales from the Celtic-speaking peoples, the union of the male sovereign with Sovereignty

was formalized by the “proffering of a drink,” often mead, “by [the] bride to her groom.”42 The

$34 Robert Beekes and Lucian van Beek, Etymological Dictionary of Greek (Leiden: Brill, 2010), s. v. παλλακή. $35 Munn, Mother of the Gods, 100–02. 36 Homer, Iliad, 2.547–48. 37 Paul Rehak, “Mycenaean ‘Warrior Goddess’ Revisited,” Aegaeum 19 (1998): 236–38. 38 Jaan Puhvel, Comparative Mythology (Baltimore: Johns Hopkins University Press, 1987), 258–59. 39 Puhvel, Comparative Mythology, 259–60. 40 Puhvel, Comparative Mythology, 258. 41 West, Indo-European Poetry and Myth, 422–23. 42 West, Indo-European Poetry and Myth, 416.

ritual drink motif is exemplified in the origin myth of the Greek colony of Massalia, founded in

Gaulish territory in what is now southern France. In the tale, a native princess of Gaul, in

accordance with the local custom for selecting a husband from among many suitors, offers a drink

to a Greek settler, who is thus legitimized as the founder of the colony.43 The same motif is attested

later in an Irish work from the 11th century, in which the “Sovereignty of Ireland,” portrayed as

the wife of Lug, the chief god, “offers the drink of sovereignty” to a succession of rulers.44

M. L. West writes that the ritual gift of a beverage was a “Celtic marriage custom signifying

the couple’s mutual consent to the union.”45 However, after reviewing a number of courtship tales

from India, Greece, Persia, Germany, Latvia, and Scythia, as well as the Gaulish example above,

he concludes that, within the context of nuptials between mortals, the more common gift from the

bride was a garland of flowers.46 In light of this, the beverages in the tales above connote the sacred

marriage specifically and are not simple wedding presents.

A deep relationship between the ritual drink and the sacred marriage is revealed by

linguistic comparison. West analyzes the name “Medb” as a reflex of *medhu, the Proto-Indo-

European term for “mead.”47 The word *medhu is also ancestral to the Sanskrit name Mādhavī.48

Puhvel explains the shared name of Medb and Mādhavī as an adjectival patronym built on the term

for mead, which he understands as signifying by extension “libation” or “sacrifice.”49 The name

of the goddess would thus mean “of the libation,” explicitly associating Sovereignty and the mead

given to a prospective king with his duties as officiant at rites of sacrifice. The ritual drink not only

functioned as a gift formalizing the sacred marriage, but also emblemized the sacral role of the

sovereign. The association of mead with sovereignty goddesses in languages as distantly related

as Sanskrit and Irish suggests that this motif was present and productive in Proto-Indo-European

culture.

King Sacrifice and Threefold Death

In his sacral office, the Indo-European king served both as priest and victim. Obtaining the

favor of divine Sovereignty granted the earthly ruler ideological legitimacy and sometimes even

miraculous intervention against his political foes. However, this relationship was not at all one-

sided. In myth, the Irish Medb was firmly in control of her choice of consort and could expel an

inferior king for a better ruler. There is evidence that when the land did fall into the hands of a

wicked monarch, very real punishment was meted out to such an abusive husband. The sacrifice

of a failed sovereign is associated with a topos called the “threefold death” – typically by hanging,

stabbing, and drowning – which appears in executions of rulers throughout Indo-European lore.

An archetypal instance of the threefold death is seen in the fate of Agamemnōn in the Greek

epic cycle. A cruel and unjust man in Homer’s telling, the lord of Mykēnai is murdered shortly

after his homecoming by his wife Klytaimnēstra and the younger surrogate lord she has taken in

his absence.50 In Aiskhylos’ rendition of the tale, the slaughter is famously carried out by ensnaring

43 Herbert, "Goddess and King," 265; West, Indo-European Poetry and Myth, 435. 44 Herbert, "Goddess and King," 269–70 45 West, Indo-European Poetry and Myth, 416. 46 West, Indo-European Poetry and Myth, 433–36. 47 West, Indo-European Poetry and Myth, 416. 48 West, Indo-European Poetry and Myth, 416; Puhvel, Comparative Mythology, 261. 49 Puhvel, Comparative Mythology, 260–61. 50 Miller, “Royalty and Mythology,” 110.

the king with a net in his bath before stabbing him to death.51 This method of execution is heavy

with symbolism, as each of the three methods corresponds to a different class of society in Indo-

European trifunctional ideology. The net, a fisherman’s tool, used to entrap the king represents the

third order, associated with fertility and subsistence.52 The blade represents the second order, the

military class, and the washbasin – metaphorically a libation vessel – represents the third order, the

priesthood.53 Aiskhylos portrays Agamemnōn’s death as a sacrifice merited by his offenses against

each of these three social orders. His sins are the sacrifice of his own daughter – a sin against the

priestly order, the tremendous waste of human life on the plains of Troy – a sin against the martial

order, and the avarice inherent in sacking Ilion and going to war over possession of a woman – a

sin against the agricultural order.54 In offending against all three estates of the realm, Agamemnōn

has upset social and cosmic order and thrown away his right to kingship.

The removal of unsatisfactory kings is documented among the Germanic peoples of

northern Europe. West reports that the Burgundians were ascribed the custom of deposing their

ruler “if the nation fares ill in war or if the earth gives poor crops,” while the early medieval Swedes

were alleged to have sacrificed their kings after a bad harvest.55 The threefold killing of a Germanic

king is described in the Old Norse Gautrek’s Saga. In one episode from this tale, King Vikar and

his warband encounter contrary winds while on a raid and must drop anchor.56 Divination reveals

that a sacrifice to Odin – a god associated with sovereignty among the Germanics – must be chosen

from among the crew by lot, which lot falls to the king.57 At the instigation of Odin himself, the

king’s retainer Starkad arranges what appears to be a mock sacrifice, using a reed in place of a

spear and tying a calf’s entrails to a young pine branch to serve as a noose.58 King Vikar suffers

Starkad to place the mock-noose about his neck, deeming it safe.59 However, when Starkad stabs

the king with the reed it is immediately revealed as a spear, the noose transforms into a stout rope,

and the pine branch sprouts into a mighty bough, hoisting the king’s perforated body high into the

air.60

There is archaeological evidence that such sacrifices were carried out at certain times in

the remote past. Throughout Ireland, items of royal regalia, e.g. chariot components and golden

collars, have been found deposited in bogs on the boundaries of old regional political units, such

as baronies, parishes, and counties.61 These finds are thought to have been ritually buried after

royal investiture ceremonies.62 Several of the infamous Iron Age “bog bodies” were likewise found

along these political boundaries, indicating that they also were involved in royal ritual.63

Two well-preserved specimens, Oldcroghan Man and Clonycavan Man, are especially

instructive. These two men were evidently of the elite and enjoyed a cultivated lifestyle free from

manual labor and furnished with exotic luxuries before their decease.64 Both the corpses displayed

damage from violent trauma: Clonycavan Man suffered several blows to the head and

disembowelment, while Oldcroghan Man was stabbed, beheaded, mutilated, and cut in two at the

waist.65 Although it has been suggested that these sacrifices were elite hostages, the removal of

Oldcroghan Man’s nipples has been taken as the mark of a failed king sacrificed to Sovereignty.66

Oldcroghan Man represents an exceptionally strong candidate for a victim of threefold death, as

his arms were found tied with osiers, completing the trio of binding, stabbing, and submersion.67

Iron Age bog bodies executed in like fashion to the Irish examples have been found in Denmark,

England, and the Low Countries, corroborating the account of ancient Sweden and giving vivid

reality to the fate of King Vikar.68

The Indo-European Sovereignty

Based on the comparative evidence surrounding the Anatolian Kybelē, Celtic Medb,

Hellenic Pallas Athēnā, and Mādhavī in Indic Sanskrit, it is concluded that Proto-Indo-European

speakers conceived of the sovereign power within their tribal kingdoms as a female divinity. Like

Kybelē, Medb, and Athēnā, this divinity personified the physical territory under the control of the

king, who was mythopoetically her husband. Three reflexes of Sovereignty – Mādhavī, Kybelē,

and arguably Pallas Athēnā – had their virginity renewed for each successive king that they

coupled with, suggesting that their Proto-Indo-European equivalent was thought to pass through

the life cycle of a mortal being and that living royal consorts adopted her persona or function in

ritual and narrative.

The prosperity of the entire people was thought to rest on the king’s treatment of his bride,

and bad kings could be disposed of and replaced. The decommissioning of a failed sovereign was

a violent ritual attested historically, archaeologically, and in literature which archetypally took the

form of a threefold killing. Each element of the threefold death by hanging, stabbing, and drowning

corresponded to a social class and thus was symbolic punishment for a particular failing of the

ruler. The ritual drink motif in Ireland and the association of Medb and Mādhavī with mead

suggests that the sacred marriage was formalized and the king vested with his office by the ritual

imbibing of a beverage. The militarism of Kybelē and Medb and the protective role of Pallas

Athēnā indicate that their prototype had similar associations and may have been invoked as

intercestrix in time of war.

The Sovereignty of Gygēs

As stated at the beginning of this article, it can be argued that the archetype of the Indo-

European sovereignty goddess is instantiated within the Histories. In his telling of the Gygēs story,

Hērodotos twice associates Kandaulēs’ wife with sovereignty by his choice of words. This first

occurs when the queen presents Gygēs with the choice of dying or murdering Kandaulēs and

seizing power. She expresses the latter option with the words “take both me and the kingship of

$the Lydians” (ἐμέ τε καὶ τὴν βασιληίην ἔχε τὴν Λυδῶν), using the τε καί construction to pair herself $

with the rulership as a single unit.69 The second instance appears when, having killed Kandaulēs,

$Gygēs “took both the woman and the kingdom” (ἔσχε καὶ τὴν γυναῖκα καὶ τὴν βασιληίην).70 The $

queen is inextricably linked to the rulership of Lydia and Gygēs could not have taken one without

the other.

An obvious trait of Sovereignty displayed by the Lydian queen is her agency in choosing

a consort and her leadership in organizing the coup against Kandaulēs. The day after she is

$displayed naked before Gygēs, she assembles retainers (τῶν οἰκετέων τοὺς μάλιστα ὥρα πιστοὺς $

$ἐόντας ἑωυτῆ, ἑτοίμους ποιησαμένη)71 and summons her victim (ἐκάλεε τὸν Γύγεα),72 all on her $

own initiative. Rather than killing Gygēs outright for his crime, which one would expect, the queen

allows him the alternative of taking the scepter for himself. Like the Irish Medb, the queen of

Lydia is custodian of the sovereign power and can bestow it upon any man she pleases. Her motive

is unclear, but perhaps she was impressed by Gygēs’ moral uprightness in rebuking Kandaulēs for

his obscene demand. Given that he is employed as a bodyguard, it is likely that Gygēs is younger

and physically stronger than Kandaulēs, so maybe she perceives him to be more energetic and

better capable of governing. That the queen has no obvious reason for choosing Gygēs specifically

as ruler suggests that the tale is ultimately a post hoc interpretation of historical events through a

mythic framework.

The queen also demonstrates agency in choosing the hour and venue of the assassination,

$which is to be carried out “while he is asleep” (ὑπνωμένῳ) and “from the same spot where he $

$presented me naked” (ἐκ τοῦ αὐτοῦ μὲν χωρίου ... ὅθεν περ καὶ ἐκεῖνος ἐμὲ ἐπεδέξατο γύμνην).73 $

It is a fitting irony that the king’s death should come about at the same place and time as his mortal

offense and recalls some of the symbolism of king sacrifice in Ireland. The remains of Oldcroghan

Man were disposed of along the border of his kingdom, where ritual offerings were likely deposited

at his investiture years before.

Although the specific offense committed by the disgraced monarch – exposing his queen

before another man – is novel, the crime remains a violation of the natural order which he is

obligated to uphold. When begging his master not to make him view the naked queen, Gygēs

$describes the deed as ἀνόμων, literally “lawless.”74 The laws in question are those laid down by $

$the ancestors, the “fair things invented by men long ago” (πάλαι δὲ τὰ καλὰ ἀνθρώποισι $

$ἐξεύρηται).75 By breaking the sacred customs established by his forefathers, Kandaulēs fails in his $

fundamental role as king, meriting capital punishment. Furthermore, his immoderate desire for his

wife’s body betrays a self-interested attitude to his prerogatives as ruler directly contrary to the

kingly ideal of generosity and impartiality.

In his analysis of the traditions concerning Gygēs, Munn recognizes the function of the

queen in Hērodotos’ story as an avatar of Sovereignty. However, he connects her with Aphroditē

and the Near Eastern iconographic motif of the “Naked Goddess,” an exhibitionist representation

of the deity variously known as Inanna, Ishtar, and Ashtarte who demonstrates numinous erotic

power as a sign of divine favor.76 The quintessentially Indo-European crux of the tale – the ritual

destruction of an unjust sovereign – is neglected by Munn.

Although the execution of Kandaulēs is not a complete threefold death, it nonetheless does

partake of the archetypal immolation of an Indo-European king. Kandaulēs is dispatched by

stabbing, which is associated in the trifunctional scheme with the second function, that is, the

$military class.77 It will be recalled that Gygēs is one of his lord’s bodyguards or αἰχμοφόροι, that $

$is, “spear-bearers” (οἱ τῶν αἰχμοφόρων Γύγης).78 While he has generally violated his moral $

obligations as a king, by forcing Gygēs to partake of his crime Kandaulēs specifically offends

against a member of the second order and thus merits the corresponding penalty.

Like the threefold death, the motif of the ritual gift does appear in the Gygēs story, again

in a modified form. The Lydian queen does not bestow upon Gygēs a ritual beverage or even a

floral garland. Instead, she gives to her new consort a dagger, with which he will slay his master

$(ἐγχειρίδιον δοῦσα).79 This brief passage is rich with symbolic meaning, as the weapon $

encapsulates the essence of Sovereignty – the absolute power of life and death over the subject. A

more blatant sign of her blessing and approval is difficult to imagine. The queen’s bestowal of the

dagger has a deeper connection with the ritual gift motif. As mentioned above, the mead embodied

by Medb and Mādhavī betokens the king’s role as sacrificant. Gygēs indeed fulfills this function

by dispatching the incumbent sovereign according to the prescription of the trifunctional ideology.

A hint of the mythic nature of the tale Hērodotos tells comes from the name he gives to the

$unfortunate Heraklid dynast. In Ch. 7, he explains that Kandaulēs was dubbed Μύρσιλος by the $

$Greeks (Κανδαύλης, τὸν οἱ Ἕλληνες Μυρσίλον ὀνομάζουσι).80 However, he consistently uses the $

$name Κανδαύλης thereafter. Whatever Hērodotos thought that word meant, it likely was not the $

given name of any Lydian ruler. Asheri et al., relying on somewhat antiquated sources, explain the

name as a ritual title connected with a “cult of the dog.”81 H. Craig Melchert rejected this

$interpretation, instead translating it as “overpowering.”82 In another analysis, Κανδαύλης is an $

adjectivized form of the Carian word for “king,” loaned into Lydian due to the former’s high status

$in the Late Bronze or Early Iron Age.83 The name Γύγης has also been suggested to be Carian, $

derived from a word meaning “ancestor.”84 Calling the ruler in the tale “king” or “kingly” and the

dynastic progenitor “ancestor” smacks of a mythic mode of storytelling rather than strict history.

The Sovereignty of Gygēs beyond Hērodotos

Outside of the Histories, the Gygēs narrative appears in the works of a few other early

Greek writers, whose treatments likewise suggest the mytho-historical nature of their subject. At

the conclusion of his story, Hērodotos states that Arkhilokhos of Paros wrote an iambic poem

about Gygēs, and a fragment seemingly from that composition survives today. Analyzing the

poem, Jenny Strauss Clay observes that the language in which Gygēs addresses the queen seems

Conclusions

It is always possible that Gygēs did become king of Lydia in precisely the manner described

by the historian. However, considering the characteristic blending of myth and historical fact

throughout the Histories, Hērodotos is plausibly recounting a tale put out by the Mermnad dynasty

to justify their seizure of power.92 Munn proposes that the story of Ankhīsēs coupling with

Aphroditē was promoted by the Mermnads to legitimize their rule as divine in origin.93 The tale of

Gygēs could likewise be propaganda, in which a more “normal” palace coup instigated by a

disgruntled retainer was reinterpreted through the framework of an ancient Indo-European myth

and thereby ascribed to the will of the Lydian Sovereignty herself.

The evidence adduced above for this latter theory is plentiful. First, Hērodotos’ diction

identifies the queen with the kingdom, as does the ideology of the sacred marriage. Like

Sovereignty in other Indo-European traditions, the Lydian queen is vested with the power of

deposing one sovereign and choosing his successor. Significantly, the murder of Kandaulēs, like

those of Agamemnōn and others, is a sacrifice orchestrated to punish his specific crimes against

society. True to her prototype, the queen confirms Gygēs in his new office via the bestowal of a

token. Finally, the names Hērodotos gives to his characters befit mythic archetypes more than

historical individuals. Although the alternative versions of the tale contemporary with Hērodotos

are poorly preserved, they likewise evince language appropriate for myth.

Several lines of evidence have gone unexamined in this article, principally for want of

space and time to treat them. The author has read of Hittite iconographic evidence for rites

concerned with the sacred marriage and expects that Hittite ritual texts would shed light on the

Anatolian tradition of sacred marriage ideology, of which Lydian partakes. Like the Sovereignty

figure discussed above, the aśvamedha horse sacrifice which marked the inauguration of a king is

attested in Hatti-land, Ireland, and India, but has been excluded from this essay as beyond its strict

scope. These fields are quite open to the ploughshares of future investigation.

From Etymology to Conceptual Metaphor Theory: $Ancient Greek θνῄσκω ‘to die’ $

and the metaphor DEATH IS DEPARTURE in Indo-European

Riccardo Ginevra

1. Introduction: Etymology and Cognitive Semantics1 As is well known, the English term etymology most commonly refers to “the branch

of linguistics which deals with determining the origin of words and the historical development of their form and meanings” (OED, s.v. etymology, n., 5.). The past two centuries of linguistic scholarship have seen this discipline develop impressively, especially thanks to the so-called ‘Comparative Method’, by which historical linguists are able to identify and analyze parallels between languages belonging to the same language family, and even to reconstruct features of their common parent language (if unattested). Among other things, this has led to the publication of methodologically well-grounded etymological dictionaries for Classical languages like Ancient Greek (AGk) and Latin, as well as for several further languages belonging to the Indo-European (IE) language family, such as Sanskrit (and its archaic Vedic variety), Old Irish, ancient Germanic languages (such as Old English, Old Norse, and Old Saxon), and Hittite. The numerous correspondences between these and other IE languages allow for the reconstruction of features of their prehistoric ancestor language, conventionally called Proto-Indo-European (PIE), including

1 This contribution stems from my 2022-2023 appointment as ‘Associate in Hellenic Studies’ at Harvard University’s Center for Hellenic Studies within the framework of the project ‘Concise Inventory of Greek Etymologies’ (project leader: Olga Levaniouk). I would like to thank the editors of this volume, Chiara Fedriani and Irene de Felice, for kindly inviting me to contribute; I am also grateful to José Luis García Ramón for valuable criticism and discussion. Final responsibility remains my own.

The translations of Ancient Greek and Latin passages are adapted from those of the Loeb Classical Library; other translations are adapted from van Buitenen 1975 (Mahābhārata), Eggeling 1885 (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa), Faulkes 1987 (Gylfaginning), Graf and Johnston 2007 (OF 474), Gray 1982 (Cath Maige Tuired), Hoffner 1983 (KBo 4.8), Hoffner 1998 (KBo 22.178 ii 3-7 + KUB 48.109 ii 4-8), Jamison and Brereton 2014 (Rigveda), Larrington 2014 (Atlamál, Hávamál, Helgakviða Hjǫrvarðssonar, Vafþrúðnismál), Marold 2017 (Vǫlu-Steinn), and Whitney 1905 (Atharvaveda).

112 Riccardo Ginevra

features of formulaic and figurative language (see, e.g., Watkins 1995; West 2007; García Ramón 2021).

$While the etymological link between words like AGk πατήρ, Latin pater, Sanskrit $pitár-, Old English fæder, all meaning ‘father’, is relatively obvious, easily allowing for the comparative reconstruction of a common PIE ancestor *ph

2 tér- ‘father’, the

situation is often more complicated on the semantic side: during their adventurous history, words frequently undergo peculiar semantic changes, some of which may appear completely unmotivated to a modern eye. As already noted by Sweetser (1990: 9) in her volume From Etymology to Pragmatics, however, “certain semantic changes occur over and over again throughout the course of Indo-European and independently in different branches across an area of thousands of miles and a time depth of thousands of years”.

This is precisely the case for the etymology of $ AGk θνῄσκω ‘to die’ from the $reconstructed PIE root *d'enh

2 - ‘to run off ’, a non-trivial semantic shift that has been

subject to criticism, but finds countless parallels in AGk itself and in other IE traditions. The aim of the present contribution is to discuss this etymological problem in order to show that “a cognitive semantics that allows for metaphorical mapping within the conceptual system can explain such facts straightforwardly” (Sweetser 1990: 9). To this end, after briefly reviewing the formal aspects of this etymology in Section 2, a series of AGk and IE parallels for the shift from ‘to run off ’ to ‘to die’ will be set forth in Section 3. In Section 4, this semantic tendency will be shown to $have a counterpart in a peculiar phraseological pattern attested by θνῄσκω and by $several further verbs in AGk and other IE traditions. In Section 5, this and various further AGk and IE items of figurative language will be argued to result from a complex interaction of several cognitive processes, such as metaphor, metonymy, and image schemas. The results of the study will then be summarized in Section 6.

$2. Formal analysis: AGk θνῄσκω ‘to die’ and PIE *d'enh $2 - ‘to run off ’

The etymology of $ the AGk verb θνῄσκω ‘to die’ and of $ its lexical family (which

$includes, e.g., the noun θάνατος ‘death’ and the adjective θνητός ‘mortal’) is still a $matter of debate (see, e.g., Beekes 2010: 533-534; Chantraine 1999: 422-423; Frisk 1960-1972: 652-653). According to a proposal advanced by Hollifield (1978: 180-182) and accepted in the standard etymological dictionary of IE verbal roots, the $Lexikon der indogermanischen Verben (LIV2: 144-145), the verb θνῄσκω must be traced $back to a PIE root *d'enh

2 -, whose basic semantics may be reconstructed as ‘to run

off ’ (as per García Ramón 2018: 150; LIV2: “sich in Lauf setzen, sich davonmachen”). Among this root’s verbal reflexes in other IE languages are Vedic Sanskrit dhánv-a-ti ‘to flow (of the ritual drink, soma), to run’ (Gotō 1987: 178-180) and Old Persian danu[v-a-tiy ‘to flow’ (with the river Nile as subject), both being

$is unlikely to be inherited, in contrast to its aorist ἔ-θαν-ον and perfect τέ-θνα-µεν. $This finds support in the fact that in the Iliad the aorist (37x) and the perfect (33x) $occur far more frequently, whereas the present θνῄ-σκω is very rare (5x) and confined $(with a single exception, 2.106) to the first (3x) and last (1x) books of the Iliad, whose linguistic features point to their belonging to a later layer of composition (chronologically closer to the Odyssey), as proposed already by Monro (1891) and most recently (by using computer-based Quantitative Authorship Analysis) by $Bozzone and Sandell (2022: 39; 42-43). The present θνῄ-σκω is very rare in early $Greek epic in general, being otherwise exclusively attested 2x in the Odyssey (8.526; 12.22), compared to 41x for the aorist and 24x for the perfect, and 1x in the rest of the epic corpus (Works and Days 116) compared to 4x for the aorist (3x in the Works and Days and 1x in the Homeric Hymn to Hermes) and 3x for the perfect (all in the Shield).

Thus, although in what follows the present will be used to generically refer to the $lemma θνῄσκω ‘to die’ (standing for all the verb’s forms) according to the current convention, it should be kept in mind that the present θνῄσκω was most likely a late $innovation created at a time when the inherited aorist and perfect already existed. $As for the noun θάνατος ‘death’ and the adjective θνητός ‘dead’, they are often $regarded as two reflexes with different accentuation (as per Rix 1992: 73) of the same verbal adjective *d'n ʘh

3. Comparative Semantics: Vedic Sanskrit pra dhánva-ti ‘to pass away, die’ and the semantic shift from SELF-MOTION to DEATH From a semantic perspective, the formal analysis detailed above requires that the

meaning of $ θνῄσκω ‘to die’ in (1) is the result of $ an euphemistic use of a verb originally meaning ‘to run off ’ for ‘to die’ (LIV2: 144 n. 1 “Euphemismus ‘weglaufen’ fuɻr ‘sterben’”). This semantic development, which has been criticized as “possible, but not wholly convincing” (Beekes 2010: 534), is actually directly attested for a reflex of the same PIE root in another IE tradition, namely the Vedic Sanskrit cognate verb dhánva-ti: this verb, which in earlier passages from the Rigveda (RV) still means ‘to flow; to run’ as in (2) with optional pra ‘forth’, in post-Rigvedic texts always occurs with the latter preverb and with the meaning ‘to pass away, die (of fires, of winds, of human beings)’ (Gotō 1987: 179), as in (3).

(1) $ […] ὅς τε πεφεύγοι / ὅς τ> ἔθαν> ἐν πολέµῳ […] (Il. 21.609-610) $ ‘who had escaped and who had died in the fight’

(2) prá pavamāna dhanvasi / sóma índrāya pā*tave (RV 9.24.3ab) ‘You run forth, self-purifying Soma, for Indra to drink’

(3) sa yam ágre ‘gníṃ hotrā*ya prā*vrʘṇata sa prādhanvad (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 1.2.3) ‘Now that Fire whom they at first chose for the office of Hotri priest passed

away’ These two passages clearly reflect two different “semantic frames”, here

understood as “script-like conceptual structure[s] that describ[e] a particular type of situation, object, or event along with its participants and props” (Ruppenhofer et al. 2016: 7): while in (2) dhánvasi ‘you run’ evokes a semantic frame (A) SELF-MOTION among whose core elements are a SELF-MOVER (‘you’) and a DIRECTION (pra ‘forth’), in (3) prā*dhanvad ‘passed away’ evokes a frame (B) DEATH whose only core element is a PROTAGONIST (sa ‘he’). The historically-attested diachrony of Vedic Sanskrit (pra) dhánva-ti may thus be modeled as in Table 1.

The semantics of $ AGk θνῄσκω ‘to die’, being a reflex of $ the same PIE root, may have resulted from a similar diachronic process. This hypothesis may find support in the fact that in early Greek prose it is very common (as noted in LSJ: 199; 802) to encounter, in place of $ θνῄσκω, the synonymous ἀπο-θνῄσκω (especially in the $present, aorist, and future tenses). This formation is of $ course prefixed with ἀπο-, a $preverb with various functions, whose literal sense ‘away’, however, fits into the DIRECTION slot of the SELF-MOTION frame. Rather than having “completive” or “culminative” function (with a corresponding meaning ‘to die completely’), as it is $often assumed (see e.g. Chantraine 1999: 422), the preverb ἀπο- in ἀπο-θνῄσκω may $have retained its spatial value here, as convincingly argued by Méndez Dosuna (2008): $it is thus at least conceivable that the semantics ‘to die’ developed first within ἀπο-θνῄσκω ‘to run away’, and that this innovative meaning later spread to the simplex θνῄσκω, if $ indeed it originally meant ‘to run’. In archaic epic poetry, however, the $simplex θνῄσκω ‘to die’ is attested much more frequently (147x) than the prefixed ἀπο-θνῄσκω (4x), and is thus unlikely to be the result of $ a secondary development. It may be easier to just regard the existence of these two variants as possible evidence that the semantic frame DEATH attested for both terms may have developed, similarly to what happened to their Vedic cognate (pra) dhánva-ti, from a SELF-MOTION frame, $whose DIRECTION element could be either implicit (θνῄσκω) or overtly expressed (ἀπο-θνῄσκω), as shown in Table 2. $

Table 2: Reconstructed semantic diachrony of $ AGk θνῄσκω and ἀπο-θνῄσκω. $

A diachronic development of this sort is likely to result from semantic narrowing from a synchronic situation of polysemy, such as that attested for several AGk verbs

The semantic development from SELF-MOTION to DEATH finds correspondences in the lexicon of other IE traditions as well (on which see, e.g., Giannakis 1998: 585-597). Apart from the exact Vedic etymological parallel discussed above, the following three etymologies exemplify this diachronic tendency:

- the Old Irish verb baïd ‘to die’ in (6) is currently analyzed as a reflex of the same PIE root *gu ʢeh

Just like that of $ AGk θνῄσκω, these semantic shifts from SELF-MOTION to DEATH $

are the likely diachronic result of an earlier synchronic situation of polysemy such as the one of $ AGk βεβᾶσι, with its literal sense ‘they have gone (away)’ and its $figurative sense ‘they have died’. This situation also finds several IE parallels, as exemplified by the Germanic cognates of $ Young Avestan iriθ-iie-iti ‘to die’ itself: the $reflexes of Proto-Germanic *līþ-a- ‘go (away), pass’ include not only simple SELF-MOTION verbs such as Gothic leiþan ‘to go (away)’ and Old English līðan ‘to go, sail’, but also polysemous verbs like Old Icelandic líða, which beside its literal SELF-MOTION semantics ‘to go, move, pass’ may also be used with figurative DEATH semantics: see, e.g., the use of the past participle liðinn ‘gone’ for ‘dead’ in (9). Further SELF-MOTION verbs that display a similar polysemy in early Germanic traditions include, among others:

- Old Icelandic ganga fram ‘to go forth’, whose past participle framgenginna ‘gone forth’ means ‘dead’ in (10);
- Old Icelandic fara ‘to go, travel’, whose preterite fór ‘is gone’ stands for ‘is dead’ in (11) (this and the previous example are from ONP, s.vv.);

To sum up, semantic parallels both within AGk itself and in further IE traditions support the analysis of $ θνῄσκω ‘to die’ as a verb originally evoking SELF-MOTION (in $an outward DIRECTION): ‘to run (off, away, forth)’. But where exactly did dead people run off to in AGk and other IE languages? A first clue is provided by another variant of $ θνῄσκω, namely κατα-θνῄσκω, a formation attested 25x in archaic epic, prefixed with a preverb κατα- that also had several functions in AGk, but whose literal $meaning was clearly ‘down(wards)’: if $ κατα- still retained its spatial value here, as $argued by Méndez Dosuna (2008: 250-254, with a critical discussion of the often-$assumed “intensifying” interpretation), κατα-θνῄσκω may thus have originally had a $literal meaning ‘to run down(wards)’ – into the Netherworld.

4. Comparative Phraseology: the construction [X – GO – to REALM OF THE DEAD] Phraseological data helps us further in identifying the downward GOAL towards

which the dead may have run in AGk. An important piece of evidence is provided by a golden leaf from Hipponion (Southern Italy), dated around 400 BCE: in (13) $θνῄσκω ‘to die’ is used as a SELF-MOTION verb with an implicit subject referring to a DEAD person and an overt GOAL εἰς Ἀΐδαο δόµ"ς ‘(in)to the houses of $ Hades’, which, as is well known, refers to the REALM OF THE DEAD.

(13) $Μναµοσύνας τόδε ἔργον, ἐπεὶ ἂν µέλλ#ισι θαν$σθαι / εἰς Ἀΐδαο δόµ"ς εὐ%ρεας $

[…] (Graf and Johnston 2007: 4; OF 474.1-2 Bernabé) ‘This is the work of Memory, when you are about to die to the well-built house

of Hades’ This peculiar use of the verb has been analyzed by Luppe (1978: 24) as a

brachylogic expression of the type of $ ἀνίστασθαί ἐς Ἄργος “get up (and go on) to $Argos” (Eur. Heracl. 59-60). In view of the etymology of $ θνῄσκω as a reflex of $ PIE *d'enh

2 - ‘to run off ’, however, this passage may rather be interpreted as a fossil

occurrence of the original SELF-MOTION semantics of $ θνῄσκω within a $phraseological collocation [X – GO – to REALM OF THE DEAD]. Within the field of Comparative IE Phraseology (on which see, most recently, García Ramón 2021), phraseological collocations identify fixed combinations of words and meanings that underlie several phrases in one or more IE traditions (in the latter case allowing for the reconstruction of inherited IE collocations). The phraseological collocation [X – GO – to REALM OF THE DEAD] is attested in a number of Homeric passages with several prototypical AGk verbs of SELF-MOTION:6

- $The verb βαίνω ‘to go’ (or rather its suppletive forms βαίην ‘may I go’ in (14) and βήτην ‘they two went’ in (15)) is used in (14) with a GOAL δόµον Ἄιδος εἴσω ‘into the house of Hades’ – closely resembling εἰς Ἀΐδαο δόµ"ς in (13) above – and in (15) with a GOAL εἰς Ἔρεβος ‘to Erebus’. $
- $The verb εἶµι ‘to go’ (participle ἰόντα ‘going’) is attested with a GOAL εἰς Ἄιδός $‘to (the house) of $ Hades’ in (16); its prefixed variant κάτ-ειµι ‘to go down’ (infinitive κατ-ίµεν) is used in (17) with a GOAL expressed by the same formula δόµον Ἄιδος εἴσω ‘to the house of $ Hades’ of (14).
- $The verb ἔρχοµαι ‘to go’, occurs in (18) with a GOAL Ἀίδαο δόµους ὑπὸ κεύθεσι γαίης ‘to the house of $ Hades beneath the depths of $ earth’; its variant κατ-έρχοµαι ‘to go down’ (actually its suppletive aorist participle κατ-ελθόντ>), occurs in (19) with an overt GOAL Ἄϊδος εἴσω ‘to (the house) of $ Hades’.

Phraseological collocations may in turn be understood as the formal side of “phraseological constructions” (Ginevra 2021a, 2023), i.e., phraseological “form and meaning pairings” (as per the definition of “construction” in Goldberg 2006: 3) whose function is to evoke specific frames. Both the peculiar use of $ θνῄσκω in (13) $and that of several AGk verbs in (14)–(19) evoke simultaneously the frame SELF-MOTION with its core elements SELF-MOVER, GOAL, and (sometimes) DIRECTION, as well as the frame DEATH with its single core element PROTAGONIST, supporting the identification of a common underlying phraseological construction [X – GO – (DOWN –) to REALM OF THE DEAD], as shown in Table 5.

Table 5: Semantics of [X – GO – to REALM OF THE DEAD] in AGk.

As most recently argued by Heide (2022, with an overview of previous

scholarship), this peculiar detail reflects a Norse belief in “ancestor mountains” as REALM OF THE DEAD, with exact parallels in Sami traditions (“a largely shared tradition, developed in interaction”; Heide 2022: 55). Old Icelandic deyja, however, is also used as a SELF-MOTION verb in at least one further passage that does not mention mountains nor seems to reflect Sami influence, namely (22) from the Eddic poem Vafþrúðnismál, where the verb deyja is constructed with the locative adverb hinig ‘there’ as overt GOAL,9 also referring to a REALM OF THE DEAD, the underworld Niflhel. As in AGk, these Old Icelandic passages attest to the use of deyja within a construction [X – GO – to REALM OF THE DEAD] that occurs with verbs of SELF-MOTION as well, see, e.g., the occurrence in (23) with an overt GOAL til heliar ‘to Hel’ (the main name for the Norse REALM OF THE DEAD) of ganga ‘to go’, whose variant ganga fram ‘to go forth’ for ‘to die’ was discussed above in (10).

Of course, the same construction occurs in other ancient IE (and probably non-IE) traditions as well, e.g., in Epic Sanskrit, where the event of DEATH may be evoked by SELF-MOTION verbs like Sanskrit gam- ‘to go’ with an overt GOAL referring to the REALM OF THE DEAD, such as yamakṣayam ‘(into the) abode of Yama’ (Sanskrit lord of the dead) in (24). In an earlier, Vedic Sanskrit passage (25), the variant construction [GHOST/SPIRIT – GO – to REALM OF THE DEAD] is attested with the aorist injunctive guḥ of Sanskrit gā- ‘to go’, a reflex of the same PIE root *gu ʢeh

2 - ‘to

$go, stride’ that underlies AGk βεβᾶσι ‘they have gone’ and βαίην ‘may I go’ in (4) $and (14) above, supporting the etymology of Old Irish baïd ‘to die’ in (6) from this very root.

(24) mā gamaḥ sasutāmātyaḥ sabalaśca yamakṣayam (Mahābhārata 2.20.21) ‘Don’t go into Yama’s abode with your sons, your ministers, and your troops!’

(25) mo sv eṣām asavo yamaṃ guḥ (Atharvaveda-Śaunakīya 18.3.62) ‘May their life-breaths not go to Yama’

Cases like that of $ AGk βεβᾶσι and Old Icelandic ganga (fram) above suggest the $

following generalization: verbs that synchronically attest a polysemy between a literal sense ‘to go’ and a figurative sense ‘to die’ also tend to be used within the phraseological construction [X – GO – to REALM OF THE DEAD] evoking DEATH. Thus, the occurrences within this very construction of $ AGk θνῄσκω ‘to die’ in (13) $and Old Icelandic deyja ‘to die’ in (20)–(22) suggest the following diachronic development for these verbs: as verbs that could be used within a phraseological construction [X – GO – to REALM OF THE DEAD], we expect the ancestors of $ θνῄσκω $and deyja to have been polysemous verbs with literal SELF-MOTION semantics that could also be used absolutely with a figurative sense ‘to die’, which at some point became their primary semantics after the loss of the literal SELF-MOTION semantics. To sum up, phraseological parallels in both AGk and other IE traditions support the analysis of $ θνῄσκω ‘to die’ as the reflex of $ a verb originally evoking SELF-MOTION semantics. The comparative data allow for the reconstruction of an inherited phraseological construction [X – GO – to REALM OF THE DEAD], occurring both $with verbs like θνῄσκω and with verbs that display polysemy between literal SELF-$MOTION and figurative DEATH semantics, a stage that, as argued in the previous section, most likely preceded semantic shifts like that of $ θνῄσκω ‘to die’. While it $would be tempting to propose that the polysemy arose by influence of the phraseological construction or vice versa, it is safer to simply interpret these two phenomena as interconnected instantiations of the same underlying con -ceptualization of DEATH, whose details are examined in the following section.

5. Comparative Poetics: the conceptual metaphor DEATH IS DEPARTURE in AGk and other IE traditions The frames (A) SELF-MOTION and (B) DEATH that are evoked simultaneously by

the polysemous verbs of Section 3 and by the phraseological construction [X – GO – to REALM OF THE DEAD] of Section 4 may be understood (as per Croft and Cruse 2004: 15) as the two domains of a metaphor DEATH IS (OUTWARD) SELF-MOTION (TOWARDS THE REALM OF THE DEAD), within which the source domain (A) SELF-MOTION metaphorically maps its structure onto the more abstract target domain (B) DEATH. As clear from the findings of Comparative IE Poetics (on whose integration with Conceptual Metaphor Theory see Ginevra 2021b), however, these are not isolated and peculiar euphemistic idioms: they instantiate a larger, well-known (see, e.g., West 2007: 388) metaphoric system, which also underlies independent, but clearly related phraseological constructions such as [X – LEAD – Y – to REALM OF THE DEAD] for KILLING, attested not only in AGk texts like (26), but also, e.g., in Sanskrit and Old Icelandic ones like (27) and (28), respectively.

(26) $αἲ γὰρ δὴ ψυχῆς τε καὶ αἰῶνός σε δυναίµην / εὖνιν ποιήσας πέµψαι δόµον Ἄιδος $

$εἴσω (Od. 9.523-524) $ ‘Would that I were able to rob you of soul and survival, and to send you to the

house of Hades’

(27) bhīmaḥ saptaśatān vīrān anayad yamasādanam (Mahābhārata 6.50.73) ‘And Bhima then led seven hundred heroes to the abode of Yama’

(28) sendoð systr Helio, / slícs ec mest kennomc (Atlamál 56.9-10) ‘You sent my sister to Hel, that upsets me most’

While this construction [X – LEAD – Y – to REALM OF THE DEAD] for KILLING

is an independent linguistic item, it also clearly reflects the same basic metaphoric conceptualization of DEATH as MOTION that underlies the construction [X – GO – to REALM OF THE DEAD]. In a study of AGk death metaphors in the Iliad and the Odyssey, Horn (2020: 171) has identified Homeric expressions in which DEAD characters are said to GO to the REALM OF THE DEAD (such as those examined in Section 4) as instantiations of the widespread (and probably universal) conceptual metaphor DEATH IS DEPARTURE, a mapping that Lakoff and Turner (1989: 10-11 and passim) have recognized to underlie a number of common English euphemistic phrases dealing with the event DEATH:

to speak of someone, after a serious operation, as being “still with us” is to say he is alive, with the “still” suggesting the possibility of imminent departure. Someone who

126 Riccardo Ginevra

is “at Death’s door” can be spoken of as “slipping away.” If a patient’s heart stops beating and a doctor gets it started again, the doctor can describe this as “bringing him back.” And if a doctor, after an operation, emerges from the operating room and says “We lost him,” then we know the patient died, because something that is lost is absent. (Lakoff and Turner 1989: 2; my emphasis) The DEATH IS DEPARTURE metaphor clearly underlies the semantic phenomena

$discussed in Section 3, i.e., verbs like θνῄσκω for which a polysemy between literal $‘to go/run (away)’ and figurative ‘to die’ is attested or may be reconstructed, whereas the construction [X – GO – to REALM OF THE DEAD] rather seems to instantiate its variant DEATH IS GOING TO A FINAL DESTINATION (Lakoff and Turner 1989: 7-8). While the link between these two metaphors is an intuitive one, an integrated approach that combines the findings of Comparative Poetics with Conceptual Metaphor Theory and other frameworks and notions from Cognitive Semantics allows us to understand better the inner structure of the conceptualization processes that underlie both the data discussed so far and further linguistic items analyzed below.

First, the concept of DEPARTURE may be modelled by means of the image schema10 Center-Periphery, which has been described by Johnson (1987: 124-125) as follows: since “our world radiates out from our bodies as perceptual centers from which we see, hear, touch, taste, and smell our world”, correspondingly “at a certain distance from this perceptual center our world “fades off ” into a perceptual horizon which no longer presents us with discrete objects”. Just like many other image schemas, the Center-Periphery schema “shows itself not only in the structure of my perceptual field but equally important as a structure of my social, economic, political, religious, and philosophical world”. Therefore “some things, events, and persons […] are more central to my interactions”, whereas “others are relatively peripheral at a given point in time”: for instance, “one’s spouse, lover, or friend are more central forces in my interactional world”. The event DEPARTURE, i.e., MOTION FROM A SOURCE, may thus be represented by means of a Trajector that moves away from a well-defined Center towards an indefinite Periphery, as in Figure 1.

10 As first formulated within the framework of cognitive linguistics by Mark Johnson (1987: 29), human thought and (correspondingly) language make use of a limited number of fundamental spatial schemas (“embodied image schemata” in Johnson’s terminology): these are “recurrent pattern[s], shape[s], and regularit[ies] in, or of, [our] ongoing ordering activities”, which “emerge as meaningful structures for us chiefly at the level of our bodily movements through space, our manipulation of objects, and our perceptual interactions”.

Figure 1: Center-Periphery image schema and event DEPARTURE.

Besides the AGk examples mentioned by Horn (2020: 171) – such as (15) above, repeated below as (29) – and the AGk and IE linguistic items discussed above, the conceptual metaphor DEATH IS DEPARTURE is instantiated by a number of further figurative expressions in AGk and other early IE traditions: an overview of at least some of them may help us identify the Center and the Periphery of the figurative MOTION that underlies the semantic development of $ IE verbs like AGk θνῄσκω ‘to $die’.

A first relevant mapping attested in AGk sources is the one between DEATH and ABDUCTION or MARRIAGE (Burkert 1972: 289 and fn. 27; Rehm 1994; Giannakis 2017): in (30)–(31) from Euripides’s tragedies, a woman who dies is said to marry Hades, the lord of the dead, while in (32)–(34) from the Anthologia Palatina, the untimely death of a woman is conceptualized as her being abducted by Hades – often with the intent of marrying her as well. As argued elsewhere (Ginevra 2021a: 187-189), these interconnected metaphors must be understood in the light of the cultural context in which the texts are embedded: within AGk culture, it was possible to associate a woman’s marriage with her abduction, or at least with her relocation, because social norms required the wife to relocate from her father’s household to her husband’s one. Thus, the metaphors DEATH IS ABDUCTION BY THE DEATH-GOD and DEATH IS MARRIAGE WITH THE DEATH-GOD may be interpreted as two variants, licensed by the female gender of the deceased, of the same metaphor DEATH IS DEPARTURE TOWARDS THE REALM OF THE DEAD evoked by the construction [X – GO – to REALM OF THE DEAD] in (29).

wed her’ The English metaphors of the type DEATH IS DEPARTURE are often construed

with an element (such as a first-person pronoun) referring to the deceased’s kin (or dear ones in general) as the point of departure (e.g., still with us and we lost him). Correspondingly, in the AGk metaphors above Hades is said to abduct a woman from her companions or from her husband’s embrace. This allows us to formulate more precisely our metaphor as DEATH IS DEPARTURE FROM ONE’S DEAR ONES, identifying the latter with an element of the Center from which the deceased moves away, as shown in Figure 2.

Figure 2: Metaphor DEATH IS DEPARTURE FROM ONE’S DEAR ONES.

131From Etymology to Conceptual Metaphor Theory

A further relevant modulation of the metaphor DEATH IS DEPARTURE actually involves a complex and well-known11 network of figurative expressions attested in several IE languages, within which the opposite concepts of LIGHT and DARKNESS were employed to refer to the WORLD OF THE LIVING and the REALM OF THE DEAD, respectively. The following are the main mappings of this system (as summarized in Ginevra 2021b, combined with further examples from Ginevra 2019), exemplified by passages in Old Icelandic (45), Vedic Sanskrit ((46), (55), (56), (58)), Latin ((49), (54)), Old Saxon (50), and of course AGk (all others).

The last mapping (3c.) TO MAKE HEALTHY/SAFE IS TO LEAD BACK TO THE

LIGHT AWAY FROM EVIL, exemplified by (57) and (58), is not usually included in the treatments of this system, but, as argued in Ginevra (2021b), it serves the important function of showing that within this network TO BE IN THE LIGHT did not just stand for the plain condition of BEING ALIVE, but rather for the broader condition of BEING ALIVE, HEALTHY AND SAFE, a prototypical and idealized conceptualization of the experience BEING ALIVE that, following Lakoff (1987: 68-76), may be referred to as its “Idealized Cognitive Model” (ICM).12

As proposed in Ginevra (2021b), this complex system of figurative expressions may be analyzed by means of what Lakoff (1993: 222-223) referred to as the “Event Structure Metaphor”, according to which “States are locations (bounded regions in space)”, “Changes are movements (into or out of bounded regions)”, and “Causes are forces”. The ontological correspondences making up this metaphorical system may be summarized as in Table 8 (from Ginevra 2021b: 174).

While the metaphoric architecture of this network is clear, the link between, e.g.,

the concepts LIFE and LIGHT that lies at its foundation must be rather analyzed as a metonymic connection. As argued in Ginevra (2021b: 175-176), this figurative system arises from the metaphoric elaboration of a Part-for-Whole metonymy “Co-Present Subevent for Complex Event” (Kövecses and Radden 1998: 52), namely TO SEE (THE LIGHT) FOR TO BE ALIVE, attested in several IE traditions (see Dunkel 1993:106-108), including AGk as in (59), Vedic Sanskrit as in (60), and Hittite as in (61). This metonymy allows for a better understanding of $ the name Ἅιδης and several $further terms referring to the REALM OF THE DEAD in AGk (Ginevra 2021b: 171-172): according to one possible analysis (cf. Beekes 1998: 17-19), the disyllabic stem $Ἄϊδ- (directly attested by the genitive singular Ἄϊδ-ος in (19) above and the dative singular Ἄϊδ-ι in (62) below) may reflect *n $ʘ-u ʢid-, a root noun of PIE *u ʢeiʢd- ‘to see’ (LIV2: 665-667) prefixed with *n ʘ- ‘not, un-’ and thus meaning ‘not-seeing’ or ‘un-seen, in-visible’, closely matching the frequent usage of $ terms such as ζόφος ‘darkness’ in (63) or σκότος ‘shadow’ in (64) to refer to the REALM OF THE DEAD in $AGk sources.

the father will go to the bed of his son. […] Son will betray his father’ All the metaphors discussed in this section may thus be argued to elaborate on a

Part-for-Whole metonymic conceptualization of the State BEING ALIVE as a Complex Event comprising several habitually Co-Present Subevents, including (but not limited to) BEING IN THE COMPANY OF ONE’S DEAR ONES, BEING UP ON THE EARTH, and SEEING THE LIGHT OF THE SUN. This basic metonymy for BEING ALIVE has a basis in everyday human experience: the quite abstract concept LIFE is indeed a complex phenomenon comprising these and several further concrete situations.

Once this experience-based metonymy is elaborated by means of the ‘Event Structure Metaphor’, however, a metaphoric mapping is established between the State BEING ALIVE and an essentially fictive Location WORLD OF THE LIVING (an idealized conceptualization of the INHABITED WORLD), a bounded region in space that is correspondingly construed as a Complex Location made of Co-Extensive Sublocations WITH ONE’S DEAR ONES, UP ON EARTH, and IN THE LIGHT, which, as shown in Table 9, map onto the respective Co-Present Subevents of BEING ALIVE, namely BEING IN THE COMPANY OF ONE’S DEAR ONES, BEING UP ON THE EARTH, and SEEING THE LIGHT OF THE SUN.

Table 9: Mapping between State BEING ALIVE and Location WORLD OF THE LIVING.

138 Riccardo Ginevra

entails that a person who is within the WORLD OF THE LIVING must also simultaneously be WITH ONE’S DEAR ONES, UP ON EARTH, and IN THE LIGHT. By means of the elaboration of the metaphor, the bounded co-extension of the fictive Location and Sublocations is carried over to the Complex Event and its Co-Present Subevents: now, a person who is ALIVE must also simultaneously BE IN THE COMPANY OF ONE’S DEAR ONES, BE UP ON THE EARTH, and SEE THE LIGHT OF THE SUN. This is clearly a coercion resulting from the metaphoric mapping, as these Event and Subevents are not necessarily simultaneous in everyday human experience: for some people BEING ALIVE does not imply SEEING or BEING IN THE COMPANY OF ONE’S DEAR ONES, and speleologists exploring the underground do not automatically stop BEING ALIVE just because they stop BEING UP ON THE EARTH.

By the Center-Periphery image schema, the fictive Location WORLD OF THE LIVING (WITH ONE’S DEAR ONES, UP ON EARTH, IN THE LIGHT) is automatically identified with our well-defined experiential Center. As shown in Figure 5, this Center must necessarily be opposed to a Periphery, which by definition is a distant and vague region of space that must be located at the opposite end of the image schema, i.e., AWAY FROM ONE’S DEAR ONES, DOWN BELOW THE EARTH, IN THE DARKNESS. These are construed as further Co-Extensive Sublocations that are combined into a fictive Complex Location REALM OF THE DEAD, which by the ‘Event Structure Metaphor’ maps onto the State BEING DEAD.

Figure 5: Construal of REALM OF THE DEAD as Periphery of WORLD OF THE LIVING.

Finally, as shown in Table 10, the ‘Event Structure Metaphor’ prompts several further mappings between the source domain and the target domain: Movements map onto Changes (2a. and 2b.) and Forces map onto Causes (3a., 3b., and 3c.).

139From Etymology to Conceptual Metaphor Theory

Table 10: Mappings of TO BE ALIVE within the Event Structure Metaphor.

As already noted by Lakoff and Turner (1989: 8; cf. also 121), the metaphor DEATH IS GOING TO A FINAL DESTINATION is “an instance of CHANGE OF STATE IS CHANGE OF LOCATION”. As argued in this section, however, the (2b.) mapping of the Movement GO INTO THE REALM OF THE DEAD onto the Change of State DIE (BECOME DEAD) also coincides with our metaphor DEATH IS DEPARTURE (FROM ONE’S DEAR ONES UP ON EARTH IN THE LIGHT), whose conceptual structure may now be image-schematically represented in more detail as in Figure 6.

STATE: BE ALIVE (DEAR ONES, UP ON EARTH, SEEING)

1b

LOCATION: BE IN THE REALM OF THE DEAD (NO DEAR ONES, DOWN BELOW EARTH, IN THE DARKNESS)

STATE: BE DEAD

2a MOVEMENT: GO TO THE WORLD OF THE LIVING (TO DEAR ONES, UP ON EARTH, INTO THE LIGHT)

CHANGE OF STATE: BE BORN (BECOME ALIVE)

2b

MOVEMENT: GO TO THE REALM OF THE DEAD (AWAY FROM DEAR ONES, DOWN BELOW EARTH, INTO THE DARKNESS)

CHANGE OF STATE: DIE (BECOME DEAD)

3a FORCE-DYNAMIC ACTION: LEAD TO THE WORLD OF THE LIVING (TO DEAR ONES, UP ON EARTH, INTO THE LIGHT)

CAUSATION PROCESS: BESTOW LIFE (MAKE ALIVE)

3b

FORCE-DYNAMIC ACTION: LEAD TO THE REALM OF THE DEAD (AWAY FROM DEAR ONES, DOWN BELOW EARTH, INTO THE DARKNESS)

3c FORCE-DYNAMIC ACTION: LEAD BACK TO THE WORLD OF THE LIVING AWAY FROM REALM OF THE DEAD
