Figure 6: metaphor DEATH IS GOING AWAY FROM THE WORLD OF THE LIVING INTO THE REALM OF THE DEAD.

This analysis is intended to be valid for all the synchronic phenomena analyzed

in the previous sections, including the behavior of SELF-MOTION verbs that are figuratively used in the sense ‘to die’ (discussed in Section 3) and the phraseological construction [X – GO – to REALM OF THE DEAD] (treated in Section 4). Given that, as argued above, these phenomena are closely linked with the semantic shift from PIE *d'enh

2 - ‘to run off $’ to AGk θνῄσκω ‘to die’, the latter may be understood as a $

diachronic result of a synchronic conceptualization of DEATH AS DEPARTURE, a metaphoric mapping that is likely universal, but may at the very least be reconstructed for PIE on the basis of the evidence set forth in this contribution.

6. $Conclusion: Ancient Greek θνῄσκω ‘to die’ and the conceptual metaphor DEATH $IS DEPARTURE The results may be summarized as in the following points.

(1) $AGk θνῄσκω ‘to die’ and its lexical family (including θάνατος ‘death’ and θνητός $‘mortal’) may be traced back to a PIE root *d'enh

2 - ‘to run off ’, which is also

attested, e.g., by Vedic Sanskrit dhánva-ti ‘to flow, to run’ and Old Persian danu[va-tiy ‘to flow’.

(2) The reconstructed development from the SELF-MOTION semantics of PIE *d'enh

2 - to the DEATH semantics of $ θνῄσκω has a historically-attested parallel in $

its Vedic Sanskrit cognate dhánva-ti, originally meaning ‘to flow; to run’ in earlier texts, which always occurs in later texts with the preverb pra ‘forth’ and with $semantics ‘to pass away, die’. This and the parallel with AGk ἀπο-θνῄσκω, whose $literal meaning may originally have been ‘to run away’, allow for the hypothesis that ‘to die’ developed from an earlier meaning ‘to run off, away, forth’ (the $DIRECTION being either overt, as in ἀπο-θνῄσκω, or implicit, as in θνῄσκω). This $reconstruction is supported by several parallels in AGk, where verbs that synchronically have SELF-MOTION semantics may simultaneously evoke the frame

141From Etymology to Conceptual Metaphor Theory

DEATH and thus have a figurative sense ‘to die’, as in the case (among others) of $βεβᾶσι ‘they have gone’ (implicitly ‘away’), figuratively ‘they have died’, in A. Pers. $1003. Further correspondences in other IE traditions not only attest to a diachronic tendency of verbs that originally evoke SELF-MOTION to undergo a semantic shift to ‘to die’, as exemplified by Old Irish baïd ‘to die’ (PIE *gu ʢeh

2 - ‘to

$go, stride’, cf. AGk βεβᾶσι) and Old Icelandic deyja (PIE *d'euʢ- ‘to run’, cf. AGk θέω ‘to run’), but also provide a number of $ parallels for the synchronic polysemy between SELF-MOTION and DEATH semantics, as in the case of Old Icelandic líða, literally ‘to go, move, pass’, but figuratively ‘to die’, in Helgakviða Hjǫrvarðssonar 42.6 (et al.).

(3) In view of the etymology of $ θνῄσκω as a reflex of $ PIE *d'enh 2 - ‘to run off ’, the

use of $ AGk θνῄσκω ‘to die’ with a GOAL εἰς Ἀΐδαο δόµ"ς ‘to the house of $ Hades’ in OF 474.1-2 may be interpreted as a fossil occurrence of the original SELF-MOTION semantics of $ θνῄσκω within a phraseological construction [X – GO – to $REALM OF THE DEAD]. This construction is attested by several SELF-MOTION $verbs in AGk sources, such as βαίην ‘may I go’ in Il. 24.244-246 (GOAL δόµον Ἄιδος εἴσω ‘into the house of Hades’) and βήτην ‘they two went’ in Il. 16.326-327 (GOAL εἰς Ἔρεβος ‘to Erebus’). A close IE parallel for the use of θνῄσκω in $this construction is provided by Old Icelandic deyja ‘to die’, which is used as a SELF-MOTION verb in passages like LdnHauksb 23.28 (GOAL i Þoris biorg ‘into mount Þórisbjǫrg’, a so-called ‘ancestor mountain’), instantiating a construction [X – GO – to REALM OF THE DEAD] that is also attested with Old Icelandic verbs of SELF-MOTION such as ganga ‘to go’ in Atlamál 97.7-8 (GOAL til heliar ‘to Hel’). Further IE parallels may be identified, e.g., in Sanskrit, which attests the construction [X – GO – to REALM OF THE DEAD], e.g., with gam- ‘to go’ in Mahābhārata 2.20.21 (GOAL yamakṣayam ‘Yama’s abode’). Given that the construction [X – GO – to REALM OF THE DEAD] is often associated with polysemous verbs that attest a figurative DEATH sense besides their literal SELF-MOTION semantics, a similar phase of polysemy may also be hypothesized for the ancestors of $ AGk θνῄσκω, Old Icelandic deyja, and Old Irish baïd ‘to die’, $followed by a semantic narrowing that led to a complete loss of SELF-MOTION semantics.

(4) Synchronic phenomena like the polysemy between SELF-MOTION and DEATH semantics and the construction [X – GO – to REALM OF THE DEAD] must ultimately be analyzed as instantiations of the DEATH IS DEPARTURE metaphor, which results from the combined interaction of the following cognitive processes (not necessarily in this order):

- A Part-for-Whole metonymy ‘Co-Present Subevent for Complex Event’ allows

BEING ALIVE to be conceptualized as a Complex Event which comprises several habitually Co-Present Subevents, such as BEING IN THE COMPANY OF

142 Riccardo Ginevra

ONE’S DEAR ONES, BEING UP ON THE EARTH, and SEEING THE LIGHT OF THE SUN.

- This basic metonymy is elaborated by means of the ‘Event Structure Metaphor’, prompting a metaphoric mapping between the State BEING ALIVE and a fictive Location WORLD OF THE LIVING, identifying a bounded region in space that is made of Co-Extensive Sublocations WITH ONE’S DEAR ONES, UP ON EARTH, and IN THE LIGHT, which map onto the Co-Present Subevents of BEING ALIVE, namely BEING IN THE COMPANY OF ONE’S DEAR ONES, BEING UP ON THE EARTH, and SEEING THE LIGHT OF THE SUN.
- As, by the Center-Periphery schema, the location WORLD OF THE LIVING (WITH ONE’S DEAR ONES, UP ON EARTH, IN THE LIGHT) coincides with our experiential Center, it is correspondingly opposed to a distant and vague Periphery, which by definition must be located AWAY FROM ONE’S DEAR ONES, DOWN BELOW THE EARTH, IN THE DARKNESS: these Co-Extensive Sublocations are combined into a fictive Complex Location REALM OF THE DEAD that by the ‘Event Structure Metaphor’ maps onto the State BEING DEAD.
- Finally, the ‘Event Structure Metaphor’ prompts the mapping between the Change of State BECOMING DEAD (DYING) and the Center-to-Periphery Movement GOING AWAY FROM THE WORLD OF THE LIVING (WITH ONE’S DEAR ONES, UP ON EARTH, IN THE LIGHT) INTO THE REALM OF THE DEAD (AWAY FROM ONE’S DEAR ONES, DOWN BELOW THE EARTH, INTO THE DARKNESS), a mapping also known (more briefly) as DEATH IS DEPARTURE.

The cognitive processes that lie at the foundation of the DEATH IS DEPARTURE metaphor in AGk and other IE traditions are summarized below in Table 11. Understanding the internal structure of these processes and the way they combine with each other allows us to support the etymology of $ AGk θνῄσκω ‘to die’ from $PIE *d'enh

2 - ‘to run off ’ by placing it within a larger framework of figurative

expressions and conceptualizations attested in AGk, Latin, and several further IE traditions. At this stage of research, it is not possible to attach this semantic network to specific reconstructed roots, as etymological correspondences never seem to extend to more than two traditions (with the sole exception of the PIE root *gu ʢeh

2 -

$‘to go, stride’ of, e.g., AGk βεβᾶσι, Old Irish baïd, and Sanskrit gā-). The best way to $account for the fact that the synchronic semantic associations and diachronic semantic shifts discussed in this contribution “occur over and over again throughout the course of Indo-European and independently in different branches across an area of thousands of miles and a time depth of thousands of years” (Sweetser 1990: 9) is thus to reconstruct these metaphorical mappings and metonymic links as (probably universal, and thus all the more likely) inherited features of the PIE conceptual system.

From giants to the universe. Ancient creation myths

Flash article n. 9, May 2022

By Massimo Fongaro

The myths of ancient civilizations are populated with giants: they are primordial beings who lived before

the creation of the universe. They look like monsters, or animals, even men, and have colossal dimensions.

This is not a detail because at some point something happens: the giants die and the world is created with

their bodies. This model of creation runs through various religious traditions, from the Europe of the Vikings,

to the Greeks, passing through India to China and till Japan.

But they were not isolated and independent inventions. There was a place and a time when an ancient

civilization developed this model of world creation starting from giant beings. This happened in Mesopotamia

between the third and second millennium before our era.

We will take a journey among the giants of antiquity and reconstruct the archetype of the myth; a lot of

blood will flow; in the end, however, the universe we know will be born.

My research is inspired by the work of Giovanni Semerano, the Italian philologist who indicated the origin

of European culture in the ancient civilizations of Mesopotamia. See Semerano, Giovanni 1984-1994. Le

origini della cultura europea, Olschki Firenze, 4 vol. with two etymological dictionaries of Greek and Latin.

Summary

From the lands of the Vikings the giant Ymir

Purusa, the giant made man

How many giants among the Indo-Europeans!

The giant Pangu creates the Chinese universe

A Kami is purified and the universe is born

The journey of an archetype

At the beginning of all things there is Sumer

2

From the lands of the Vikings the giant Ymir

Scandinavian mythology tells of the giant Ymir, the first to be born at the beginning of time in the

Ginnungagap:

"There was in ancient times, where Ymir lived,

Nor sand nor sea, nor icy waves;

the earth did not exist, nor the sky above,

'it was a chaotic abyss, and the grass nowhere ” (Poetic Edda).

The Ginnungagap was the cosmic abyss present before creation; in the north there was ice with the eleven

Élivágar rivers at its center, in the south the heat. Ymir was born from the frozen rivers Élivágar and his

dimensions were enormous enough to cover the whole earth with his body. While Ymir slept, her sweat

spawned the race of giants, hideous and evil. Under his left arm a man and a woman were born and from his

legs a son with six heads was born.

One day the God Odin and his brothers killed Ymir and drowned all the giants in his blood. Then they used

Ymir's body to create the universe. From his flesh formed the earth, from his blood the ocean, from his bones

the mountains, from his hair the trees, from his brain the clouds, from his skull the skies and from his

eyebrows the middle kingdom in which lives humanity, the Midgard.

Finally the sons of Borr took the sparks from the Múspellsheimr and scattered them through the

Ginnungagap creating the stars and the light to illuminate the sky and the earth.

Reference

Orchard, Andy (translator) 2011. The Elder Edda: A book of Viking lore, Penguin Classics.

3

Purusa, the giant made man

In the Indian religious tradition, the process of cosmic creation is centered around the sacrifice of the

primordial man Purusa. He self-immolates so that the universe can come into being and with this act man

becomes part of the cosmic process through which God creates the world.

In the hymn of the Vedas RV X 90 it’s described the formation of the world from the body of primordial

Man, which is so vast that it covers and overflows from the earth: "A thousand heads has the man, a thousand

eyes, a thousand feet; encircling the Earth on all sides, it surpassed it by the width of ten fingers ” (Verse 1).

Later it is told how the gods performed the sacrifice of Purusa to create living beings: “Using Man as their

oblation, the Gods performed the sacrifice. […] From here came the creatures of the air, the animals of the

forest and those of the village; […] Hymns and melodies were born ” (verses 6-10).

Then castes are born: “His mouth became the brahmin; his arms became the prince-warrior, his legs the

common man who practices a trade. The humble servant was born from his feet ” (verse 12).

Finally the elements of the physical world are created: “The moon was born from his mind; the sun came

into being from his eyes; from his mouth came Indra and Agni, while from his breath the wind was generated.

Air gushed from her navel; from his head the sky unfolded, the earth from his feet, from his ears the four

directions. This is how the worlds were organized ” (verses 13-14).

How did the process of creation begin? According to Vedic thinking, there is no real beginning or real

place, because everything that exists is eternal. And we can only represent it by symbols. The first of these is

the infinite expanse of primordial waters where creative energies are concentrated; in the Brahmana we

read: “In the beginning, verily, this world was water, nothing but a sea of water. The waters longed, "How

can we spread?" They inflamed their ardor, doing just this gesture with fervor. Gathering their own creative

energy they warmed up and a golden egg was produced ”(SB XI, 1,6,1).

The golden egg, or golden germ, is a second symbol and represents the unity of God. To manifest, the

divine must sacrifice itself and therefore break the original unity so that the universe can become visible. All

this is summed up in the Aitareya Upanisad, which describes the creation of the universe by Atman: "It

thought: here are the worlds. Now I want to create the guardians of the worlds. Bringing him out of the

waters, It fashioned the cosmic man. And hatched it. After he had hatched it, his mouth opened like an egg:

from the mouth arose the word, from the word fire. The nostrils opened: from the nostrils came the breath,

from the breath the wind. The eyes opened: from the eyes the sight arose, from the sight the sun. The ears

became open: hearing rose from the ears, the cardinal points from hearing. The skin opened: from the skin

arose the hairs, from the hairs the herbs and plants. The heart was opened: from the heart the thought arose,

4

from the thought the moon. The navel was opened: from the navel arose the apana, from the apana death.

The virile member was opened: from the virile member arose the sperm, from the sperm the waters" (Ait.

Up. 1, 1, 3-4).

In analogy with RV X, 90, primordial man is the means by which creation is realized: his huge body is

dismembered and the individual parts form the elements of the cosmos and civilization. So Purusa is not only

the first man, he is also the personal aspect of reality. Furthermore, in the verses of the Aitareya Upanisad

we encounter the symbol of the cosmic egg: the mouth of the Purusa opening like an egg pronounces the

word creator. We will also find the symbol of the cosmic egg in the Chinese myth of creation.

References

Panikkar, Raimundo, 2001. The Vedic experience: Mantramañjarī. An anthology of the Vedas for modern

man and contemporary celebration, Motilal Banarsidass.

Swami Gambhirananda (translator), 1958. Eight Upanishads, with the Commentary of Sankara, Vol. II:

Aitareya,Mundaka,Mandukya & Karika,and Prashna, Vedanta Press & Bookshop.

How many giants among the Indo-Europeans!

Through comparative mythology, scholars have found in various Indo-European religions other creation

myths centered on the sacrifice of a primordial being and have reconstructed elements of a Proto-Indo-

European cosmological dissection and creation.

For example DQ Adams and J.P. Mallory comment on the myths of Ymir and the Vedic Purusa; then they

cite the Old Irish Tain which culminates with the dismemberment of a mythical bull that constitutes Irish

geography; this model of cosmogonic dissection is also found in the Old Russian Stic or golubinoj knig ("Poem

of the king of the dove"); then in Celtic and Germanic traditions (Emsig's Frisian code) in which the body of

Adam is made up of elements of the physical universe.

The Greco-Roman traditions present the myth of Atlas. In the Metamorphoses Ovid tells how the god

becomes a mountain: “The giant's beard and hair become forests, his shoulders and hands in yokes, his head

on top of the mountain and his bones in stone. Then, enlarging everywhere, he grew out of all proportion

5

(this was the will of the gods) and the whole sky with its innumerable stars rested on him " (Metamorphosis

4,655-662).

Also in the Orphic tradition we find some fragments that tell of the creation of the world. We speak of

Orpheus: "For him, water was the principle of all things, and from the water mud was formed, and from both

the dragon animal was born, with a lion's head attached and in the middle an aspect of divinity, named

Heracles and Kronos. This Heracles generated an extraordinarily large egg, which, being full, by the violence

of those who generated it, was broken in two by rubbing. The top half became Uranus and the bottom half

the Earth; a double-bodied god proceeded from it ” (DK 1 B 13).

Finally in the Middle Persian Skend Gumanlg Wizar of the 9th century AD. tat describes how the physical

world derives from the body of the evil demon Kunl, whose skin becomes the sky, his flesh the earth, his

bones supply the mountains and his hair becomes the implant.

A really nice roundup of giants. Adams and Mallory argue that among the Indo-Europeans the central

aspect is the notion of sacrifice (of a brother, a giant, a bovine, etc.). The relationship between sacrifice and

cosmogony was not only that of a primordial event, but the whole act of sacrifice could be seen as an eternal

creation of the universe in which the elements were continually recycled. ... The sacrifice therefore

represents a creative re-enactment of the initial cosmic dismemberment of a victim and helps to restore

material matter to the world [Adams, Mallory 1997).

But are we really sure that this pattern belongs only to alleged Indo-European peoples? As we will see,

the theme of creation starting from a huge being is also found in the ancient mythologies of China and Japan;

their tradition is certainly not Indo-European, so to explain it we will have to broaden our historical and

geographical horizons.

References

Adams, D.Q.; Mallory, J.P., 1997. Encyclopedia of Indo-European Culture, Taylor & Francis.

For the Fragmente der Vorsokratiker edited by Herman Diels and Walther Kranz see

The Texts of Early Greek Philosophy: The Complete Fragments and Selected Testimonies of the Major

Presocratics, by Daniel W. Graham (Author), Cambridge University Press; 1st edition2010.

6

The giant Pangu creates the Chinese universe

Pangu or P'an Ku, is a giant of Chinese mythology, protagonist of the creation of the world. The earliest

mentions of this myth are found in Taoist literature and the tradition reconstructs its history as follows.

At the beginning of time there was nothing and the universe was featureless and formless. Some scholars

even speak of a flood. This primordial state merged into a cosmic egg and within it the opposing principles of

yin and yang were perfectly balanced. Pangu slept inside the egg for 18,000 years and then woke up and

came out of the egg. Pangu is usually depicted as a primitive, furry giant with horns on his head.

At this point Pangu began to create the world: he separated yin from yang with one blow of his giant ax,

creating the earth (murky yin) and the sky (clear yang). To keep them apart, Pangu stopped between them

and lifted the sky. He grew for another 18,000 years and eventually every part of his body transformed: his

breath became wind, fog and clouds; his voice, thunder; his left eye, the Sun; his right eye, the Moon; its

head, the mountains and the ends of the world; his blood, rivers; its muscles, fertile land; the beard, the stars

and the Milky Way; its fur, bushes and forests; his bones, precious minerals; his bone marrow, precious

jewels; his sweat, rain; and the fleas of his fur carried by the wind became animals.

The similarity with the Indian conception is also striking for the element of the cosmic egg. The egg

represents the original unity of the world in which heaven and earth are still undivided and close to each

other. The separation and creation of the visible world takes place thanks to Pangu, the giant who sleeps in

the egg and who at a certain point wakes up. When the egg is split in two, the shells form the sky and the

earth; but to complete the creation it is necessary that the body of Pangu, in analogy with the Vedic Purusa,

divides and that the parts are transformed into the elements of the cosmos.

Reference

David Leeming, Margaret Leeming, 1994. A Dictionary of Creation Myths, Oxford University Press.

7

A Kami is purified and the universe is born

The Kojiki is the main collection of traditional Japanese mythology and tells the birth of the universe and

all the Kami, the spiritual essences, of the ancient Japanese religion. Even here in beginning there is an empty

universe in which the kami live; two of them, Izanagi and Izanami, are the protagonists of the creation of the

world.

After Heaven and Earth came to light Izanagi and Izanami's first gesture was to create Japan. The two

deities went to Ame-no-ukihashi, the floating bridge of heaven, starting to scrape the ground with their spear;

when they resumed the launch, some mud poured into it giving rise to the first island: Onogoro-Shima ("the

island that formed itself"). Later the two deities created eight other large islands, which became Japan.

Then the two deities left the Kingdom of Heaven and established their new home on Earth. From their

union were born the god of the sea O-Wata-Tsu-Mi, the god of the mountains O-Yama-Tsu-Mi, the god of

trees Kuku-no-chi and the god of wind Shina-Tsu-Hiko.

The birth of the last god, the fire god Kagu-tsuchi, cost Izanami his life. Izanagi, angry, killed his son and

went down to hell with the intent to lead his partner back home; upon his arrival, however, the god

discovered that his wife had fed on infernal food and had become an evil demon. Izanagi escaped to the

surface and Izanami remained in hell becoming its terrible queen.

Back on Earth, Izanagi wanted to wash off the filth that had covered him and performed a purification

rite. He dived into a river and blowing his nose gave rise to the god Susanoo (Susa-no-wo), lord of the storm;

from his right eye was born Tsukuyomi, deity of the Moon and from the left one Amaterasu, goddess of the

Sun who will become the mythical ancestor of the imperial family.

In the Japanese myth, cosmogony proceeds in various stages until the last act of Izanagi's purification,

with which the three kami are born from the eyes and nose of the god. In this case there is no sacrifice but a

ritual act. However, the parallel with the giant Pangu is remarkable and a cultural loan from China is evident.

Reference

Donald L. Philippi, 1968. Kojiki ; translated with an introd. and notes, Tokyo University of Tokyo Press.

8

The journey of an archetype

The creation myths seen so far all follow the same conceptual scheme:

1. before the creation of the universe there is an undifferentiated and chaotic state in which all things

are mixed together and not yet distinct;

2. the nature of this primordial cosmos is water in its various forms (ice, abyss, ocean, river);

3. creation begins with the separation of the constituent elements of the universe, first of heaven and

earth, and subsequently with the generation of the other elements of the world;

4. the parts of the cosmos are derived from the dismemberment / division of a giant being, which can

be an egg, an animal, a man or a god.

This pattern is present in all the myths from East to West that we have seen beyond the variants expressed

by the individual religious traditions. Now the question is whether there is a historically documented myth

that represents the archetype that inspired all other myths. And the origin cannot be Indo-Europeans,

because the model of creation studied here goes beyond its geographical boundaries; furthermore, the

reconstruction of the language and culture of the Indo-Europeans is theoretical and there is no written

documentation of the PIE proto-Indo-European language, nor evident historical traces of the alleged Indo-

European people.

But it is not necessary to invent new theories, because halfway between Europe and Japan there is a vast

cultural area, the Middle East, in which very ancient civilizations flourished: first the Sumerians, then the

Akkadians, the Jews, the Hittites, the Assyrians and the Persians; and of all these civilizations we possess

extensive historical documentation, both written and archaeological. I believe that the conception of cosmic

creation starting from huge beings was born in Mesopotamia between the third and second millennium BC,

and that it subsequently spread in all directions, reaching even very distant places.

The model of the myth is exposed in the Babylonian creation poem Enuma elish, which is the result of a

millenary elaboration following the encounter between the Sumerian and Assyrian-Babylonian civilizations.

We too will start from the beginning of this story.

9

At the beginning of all things there is Sumer

The Sumerian civilization, which prospered between 2900 and 1900 BC, presents the oldest written

records of humanity. The first examples of writing, the cuneiform engraved on clay tablets, date back to 3100

BC. but the first literary and mythological texts were born starting from 2600 BC. We can find in the texts

that have come down to us various structural elements of our archetype.

The first element is the theme of the existence of an undifferentiated primordial state that precedes the

separation of heaven and earth: from a text by Nippur: "Heaven and earth were linked to each other

(forming) a whole, they had not yet married; the moon was not yet shining, darkness was everywhere”

(Clifford 1994). There is no mention of the nature of this primordial state, but it constitutes the original and

undifferentiated unity that precedes the creative action.

The second element is the theme of the separation of heaven and earth which marks the beginning of the

cosmogonic action. At the beginning of the myth Inanna, Gilgames and the Underworld the cosmogonic

operation begins with the separation of heaven and earth: "When heaven was separated from earth, when

earth was separated from heaven; when An took heaven for himself, when Enlil took earth for himself”

(Kramer 1979). The idea of separation of heaven and earth, An and Ki, is by no means taken for granted in

archaic thinking as it presupposes a splitting of the living space. The act of creation, in fact, breaks the original

unity, homogeneous and undifferentiated, and allows for the ordering of the multiple elements of existing

reality.

Water as a cosmogonic principle is the third structural element we encounter. Together with the sky An,

earth Ki and mountain Kur, in Sumerian mythology water is one of the fundamental principles of the cosmos

over which reigns the god Enki, the lord of the abyss of the abzu waters; with the reform of King Sulgi, during

the third dynasty of Ur (2100 BC), in the hymn dedicated to him we read that the god of wisdom Enki assumes

primacy over the other gods: "Magniloquent Lord of heaven and earth, sublime by nature, father, Enki,

begotten of the bull, which the seed of the wild bull gave birth, well-liked by Enlil, the Great Mountain,

beloved of the holy An ... sublime dragon that is in Eridu, whose shadow covers heaven and earth … Your

lofty house is built on the Abyss, its (load-bearing) columns are those of heaven and earth ” (Kramer, Maier

1989).

The history of Mesopotamia was by no means linear. The Sumerians coexisted with other peoples of

Semitic origin who arrived in the region starting from 2400 BC: first the Akkadians, then the Amorites and

then the Assyrians; these peoples assimilated and reworked the Sumerian religious heritage according to

their mentality and summarized their knowledge in the Enuma elish, which represents an extraordinary

synthesis of Mesopotamian thought. Compiled in its final form towards the last centuries of the second

10

millennium BC, the poem Enuma elish celebrates the god Marduk, the protective deity of Babylon who with

Hammurabi (1792-1750 BC) became the political and cultural capital of the entire Middle East.

The poem opens with the description of the events concerning the time when not even the gods were

generated, and the only living beings were Apsu, the abyssal fresh water and Tiamat, the water of the sea:

“When on high no word was used for heaven,

Nor below was firm ground called by name,

Primeval Apsu was their progenitor,

Matrix-Tiamat was she who bore them all,

They were mingling their waters together,

No lea was packed together, no canebrake matted close.

When no gods at all had been brought forth…” (Foster 1993, I).

So the abyss of cosmic waters is made up of the mixture of two opposite principles: Apsù -, the masculine

principle, and Tiamat - the feminine principle. Then follows the generation of various deities including Enki,

the wisest, who kills Apsu and then generates the hero of the poem, the god Marduk.

After ups and downs Marduk assumes supremacy over all the gods, but in exchange he must defeat

Tiamat and her army of monsters. The god prepares and after an epic battle he manages to defeat her. At

this point he creates the universe using Tiamat's corpse:

“The Lord calmed down, he began inspecting her carcass,

that he might divide the monstrous lump and fashion artful things.

He split her in two, like a fish for drying,

half of her he set up and made as a cover, heaven.

He stretched out the hide, assigned watchmen,

them he ordered not to let her waters escape.

[…] the foam of Tiamat, Marduk created […]

he compacted (the foam) and made it billow as clouds.

To raise the wind, to cause rainfall,

to make mists steam, to pile up her spittle (as snow?),

he assigned to himself, put under his control.

he set down her head, he heaped di[rt] upon it,

he opened underground springs, they filled up with water.

From her eyes he let the Euphr[ates] and Tigris flow out,

11

he stopped up her nostrils, he left ... he heaped up distant mo[unt]ains from(?) her dugs.

Waterholes he drilled through her to flow out into pools.

He coiled up her tail and tied it as "The Great Bond” (of heaven and earth), […] Apsu beneath his feet. He

set her crotch as the brace of heaven,

having spread [half of] her as a cover, he established the earth.

[After] he had completed his task inside Tiamat,

[He re]leased his net, let all (within) escape,

he created the ... [ ] of heaven and earth, tightening the connection between them” (Foster 1993, IV-V).

The Enuma elish presents the archetype of creation with all the structural elements that we have

identified: the undifferentiated unity at the beginning, the water, the appearance of a primordial being and

its sacrifice with the formation of the universe. In the Babylonian myth, Tiamat is split in two like a fish to be

dried and with its parts the sky, the earth and the other elements of the world are formed. Furthermore, the

poem describes Tiamat (mother ocean) as an enormous, immense being, with monstrous and indomitable

strength, so that the character of titanism al so belongs that is found in the other examined above: Ymir,

Purusa , Atlas, Pangu and Izanagi are all colossal beings.

The Babylonian model of creation is the oldest and most documented since the Enuma Elish dates back

to the second millennium BC, while the other giants belong to religious traditions of the first millennium BC.

or later. I therefore think that the model has spread from the Middle East to the West and East through

migrations, conquests, trade. Then the different cultures have reworked it according to their own

characteristics, while preserving the basic scheme.

12

European myth

Bournemouth University 2018

Abstract

Skyscapes, Landscapes, and the drama of Proto-Indo-European myth

By John Michael Grigsby

Following the work of Larsson and Kristiansen’s ‘The Rise of Bronze Age Society’ (2005) that

utilised Indo-European myth to shed light on the iconography of Bronze Age Scandinavian art,

this thesis postulates a similar relationship between Proto-Indo-European mythology and the

ceremonial sites of the British Neolithic, arguing both, at root, share a derivation from

astronomical imagery, which suggests the ’skyscape’ was as important to the builders of these

monuments as the ‘landscape’, if not more so.

The mythological material utilised in this study is reconstructed using extant comparative Indo-

European literature and is based on comparative linguistic reconstructions, while the

archaeological data is taken from 55 sites (50 henges or associated circular timber structures,

and 5 passage graves). The hypothesis that such structures are oriented on astronomical events

is tested, with specific case studies explored in detail (Stonehenge, Avebury henge, the

Sanctuary, Woodhenge, Thornborough, Bryn Celli Ddu, Barclodiad y Gawres and Yeavering).

The analysis demonstrates a concentration of alignments on the rising and setting of certain

stars within the Milky Way (those of Cassiopeia and Crux) on or around the Winter Solstice, on

the rising and setting of Orion, and with the rising of the sun as it crosses the Milky Way around

the start of May. These alignments often utilise local landscape features such as hills (or

artificial mounds) and rivers and are linked to ritual deposition of cattle remains – all facets that

can be explained in terms of the Proto-Indo-European cosmology reconstructed within this

thesis, which, it is argued, is ultimately of Neolithic Near Eastern pedigree.

This thesis not only provides evidence of a Neolithic ‘shaping mythology’ that Richard Bradley

in his ‘On the Significance of Monuments’ (1998) suggested might lie behind the form and

function of ritual sites, but also suggests that astronomical symbolism (especially concerning the

Milky Way) was at the heart of both this Neolithic myth and the rituals performed at such sites.
