There are multiple analogous references in the Heavenly Questions poem in the Elegies

of Chu:

洪泉極深何以窴之

地方九則何以墳之

河海應龍何畫何歷

鯀何所營禹何所成

The floody abyss was extremely deep—

How did [Yu] fill it in?

Nine were the regions of square earth—

How did he pile them up?

What did the respondent dragon draw on the ground?

Where were the lakes and rivers channeled off?

What was it that Kun had managed? What was it that Yu completed?44

Both Hawkes and Mair translate the third line cited here as two separate clauses with

either “winged dragon” or “respondent dragon” as the subject of the first clause, and seas and

rivers as the subject of the second, rather than what would seemingly be the more straightforward

reading of a dragon of the rivers and seas.45 Anne Birrell instead translates, “Over the rivers and

seas what did the Responding Dragon fully achieve and where did he pass?”46 Whereas Mark

Lewis has “the Responding Dragon of the rivers and the seas, / What did it completely pass

through?”47 Regardless of the differences, the close link between Yu and the dragons and waters

is quite clear.

There are also the fragments of an ancient deluge myth in the Shu Jing. Henri Maspero

claims that the so-called deluge legend is in fact, a myth of primeval waters, in which The Lord

of Heaven sent a minister to put the earth in order. After the first minister failed, a second

minister was dispatched, who succeeded in making the earth fit for mankind. This hero-god

44 Victor Mair, ed., Columbia Anthology of Traditional Chinese Literature (New York: Columbia University Press, 1994), 375. 

45 David Hawkes, The Songs of the South (Reading, U.K.: Penguin, 1985), 128. 

46 Anne Birrell, Chinese Mythology: An Introduction (Baltimore: Johns Hopkins University Press, 1999), 148. 

47 Mark Lewis, The Flood Myths of Early China (Albany: State University of New York Press, 2006), 40.  

became the prime ancestor and taught mankind cultivation.48 Maspero describes four later

versions of the myth, here paired with the theses of Fontenrose (see Appendix A for the details):

(1) Kun made dikes to hold back the waters and thus was killed by the Celestial Lord. Yu

sprang from his corpse, and was told to set the world in order. He vanquished clouds and

rain on Rain-Cloud Mountain, and, importantly, no longer attempted to dam the waters.

(Ths. 3A, 3B, 10A).

(2) Gong Gong, a dragon-like monster, ruled the earth. After a failed attempt, he was

defeated by a second heavenly minister. In his flight he caused a flood. (Ths.

5A,8A,7F,4A)

(3) Nü Gua put the world in order at a time when there was a giant flood (often coupled with

2) (Ths. 4D, 4C)

(4) Chi’ih yu, apparently a river god, pursued the Yellow Emperor, who employed a winged

dragon to fight him. In his fight, the dragon gathered waters and flooded the earth. (Ths.

2E,7F)49

Fontenrose claims that the Chinese might have followed a similar path as the Hebrews, in

that a newer religious idea, namely Confucianism, shaped traditional myths and excised

traditional elements of them. In this case, the Lord of Heaven was moved and raised to a position

where he could not be considered in relation to the chaos. The vital corollary is that the world no

longer begins in watery chaos; the flood as it appears is more limited in scope. Consequently, as

the hero is sent to free the earth from the waters, the fundamental act is reduced from creation to

cultivation.

Further evidence for this extensive euhermerism is provided by Boltz in a discussion of in

a key text related to the Gong Gong myth, the Yao Dian 堯典 in the Shang Shu 尚書. The reason

for this remarkable lacuna in previous comparative literature may be a seeming mistranslation by

James Legge of Gong Gong, the name of a dragon-like creature, as simply “Minister of Works.”

As he translates:

48 Henri Maspero, "Légendes Mythologiques Dans Le Chou King" 1924, Édition complétée le 25 octobre 2004 à Chicoutimi, Québec. 

49 Ibid. 

帝曰 “疇咨若予采？”歡兜曰 “都！共工方鳩僝功。”帝曰 “吁！靜言庸

違，像恭滔天。”

"The emperor said, "Who will search out for me a man equal to the exigency of

my affairs?" Hwan-tow said, "Oh! there is the Minister of Works [Gong Gong],

whose merits have just been displayed in various ways." The emperor said, "

Alas! when unemployed he can talk; but when employed, his actions turn out

different. He is respectful only in appearance. See! the floods assail the

heavens."50

While Legge explains in his notes that Gong Gong appears in the next book as a criminal,

he nonetheless states that it is the name of his office, as in the next book (Shun Dian [舜典])

“Shun calls Ching to the same.”51 Boltz to some degree follows a similar but more extensive line

of reasoning when he (citing personal communication from Professor Paul L-M Serruy) suggests

that the first character of Gong Gong may be derived from hong 洪 and thus be appropriate

translated as “flood worker.” Boltz also attempts to reconstruct the name of Gong Gong’s son as

presented in the Zuo Zhuan and Tian Wen Keng found in Mencius, claming that all are

semanticizations of an original etymon meaning ‘wanton disorder.’

Boltz also cites a few of many passages related Gong Gong in the Huainanzi and Liezi,

for instance:

顓 頊 嘗 與 共 工 爭 矣 … 共 工 為 水 害 ， 故 顓 頊 誅 之

Zhuan once battled with Gong Gong ... Gong Gong brought about a watery

catastrophe, and for this reason Zhuan Zhu executed him (HNZ 15.1–2)52

Interestingly, in this passage Gong Gong is explicitly associated with water in contrast to

fire. There are also passages from the Shan Hai Jing 山海經 suggesting a conflict between an

official of Gong Gong’s and Yu:

An official of Gonggong [no. 314] is called Minister Liu. He has nine heads and

50 James Legge, Chinese Classics, vol. 3, (London: Trubner, 1861–1872), 23–24. 

51 Ibid.  

52 Huainanzi 15.1 – 2. I have amended Boltz’s translation in William G. Boltz, "Kung Kung and the Flood: Reverse Euhemerism in the Yao Tien," T'oung Pao 67, nos. 3–5 (1981) to refer to a “watery catastrophe” instead of a flood, since there is the contrast between this and the fire in the preceding line. 

consumes the sustenance provided by nine mountains. The tracks of his collision

with the landscape became lakes and streams. Yu the Great killed Minister Liu.53

Additionally, he mentions a statement regarding “a Mountain Where Yu Attacked the

Land of Gonggong,” in the entry on Gong Gong in the Shan Hai Jing.54

These additional pieces of evidence, even if late, bolster the case of Boltz and Fontenrose

that, that, in the words of Boltz, the original forms of these myths are “buried under layers of

orthodox Juist (=”Confucian”) euhemerizing interpretations, even to the point where seemingly

seminal characters, such as Gong Gong, do not appear at all in the versions given us by Mencius,

or are transformed into uncooperative officials.”55 Given that according to Shaughnnessy,

scholarly consensus has the Yao Dian emerging at during the late Zhou dynasty, this

euhemerization must have taken place at an early date.56

Boltz concludes with a strong but optimistic statement:

If the Greeks can be said to have mythologized their history, the Chinese

historicized their mythology. Through detailed analyses of the pre-Han texts we

can try to reverse this process, and uncover a fair part of a buried mythological

tradition that has lain for centuries under heavy layers of interpretation and

reinterpretation based on the prevailing doctrines of the dominant Juist

orthodoxy.57

These sorts of interpretations, relying on all of cryptic statements in the early poetic

record, euhemerized historical records like the Yao Dian, and whatever mythic fragments

available elsewhere, indicate that there is an analogous combat myth in the Chinese record in

which dragons served much the same function as in Indo-European poetry and myth.58 However,

53 Richard Strassberg, A Chinese Bestiary: Strange Creatures from the Guideways Through Mountains and Seas (Los Angeles and Berkeley: University of California Press, 2002), 176 (s. 244). 

54 Strassberg, Bestiary, 215 (315). 

55 Boltz, "Kung Kung and the Flood,” 141. 

56 Edward Shaughnessy, “Shang Shu” in Michael Loewe, ed., Early Chinese Texts: A Bibliographical Guide (Society of Early China, 1993).  

57 Boltz, “Kung Kung and the Flood,” 142. 

58 The Book of Changes is indisputably a rich source not covered here due to lack of space. Edward Shaughnessy (“Composition of the ‘Zhou Yi’” [Ann Arbor, Mich.: University Microfilms International, 1983]) discusses the figure of the dragon in the first hexagram fairly extensively (it can be in a watery abyss or flying), yet states that,

the nature of the euhemerization and the more extensive textual tradition could also indicate that,

like the Semitic tradition, something was also preserved regarding the original regulative notion

of the dragon.

These also shed light on various other attempts to find the origins of the Chinese dragon.

For example, M. W. de Visser claimed the Chinese dragon has at least two antecedents, the

Indian Naga by way of Buddhism and another form that potentially originated within China (or

at least pre-dated the Buddhist conceptions). These Naga reside in “waters of the world of men”

and have among them great lords, which when they feel insulted, bring calamities of various

kinds on humans.59 While the Nagas are not mentioned in the Vedas, they belong to Indian

popular belief and were extended by brahaminic religion. Though there is also no mention of the

Nagas in the Jataka tales (and presumably anything else which belongs to the earliest strata of

Buddhist texts) eventually they are represented by the Mahayana school of Buddhism as gods of

rain.60 Unlike later Western counterparts they are “beings wholly dependent on the presence of

water and much afraid of fire, just like the dragons in many Chinese and Japanese legends.”61

However, even if a substantial part of later dragon images derive from both indigenous folk

traditions in China or non-Buddhist Indian traditions brought over along with Buddhist

influence, the very early dates of the evidence considered necessitates some sort of transmission

of mythological frameworks that pre-dates their Warring States redaction.

The evidence presented indicates that the foundational myth of the Chinese state is a

combat myth including a hero and dragon. Like Indo-European and Semitic counterparts, the

dragon is associated with watery chaos brought to an end by a hero’s intervention. Like Semitic

counterparts, this dragon appears to have had some sort of unperformed regulative function that

necessitated the combat. Other related themes, like the interplay between fire and water, also

appear to be present in various elements and very likely relate back to Indo-European ideas of

                                                                                                                                                                                   contrary to tradition, it most likely originates in and refers to the movement of a constellation over the seasons. Although some aspects of his presentation seem likely, his strongest proof is an unsourced diagram of the changing of star positions that he created himself. He does not consider the possibility of the relation of this dragon to other dragons or to related combat myths.  

59 Hardy, Manual of Buddhism, cited in de Visser, Gruenwedel, Buddistiche Kunst in Indian, 2, p. 187, cited de Visser 4. 

60 de Visser, Dragon in China and Japan, 10, 17. 

61 de Visser, Dragon in China and Japan, 13. 

fire, just as with also frequently occurring sexual metaphors.62 Indeed, although the evidence at

this stage is merely suggestive, it may be that all of the different components of the combat

myths outlined by Maspero derive from a single myth that was gradually obscured and replaced

by Ruist orthodoxy. However, although various elements are clearly found throughout the Indo-

European tradition, there is not enough evidence to say for certain that this is originally an Indo-

European myth. Elements which seem to be preserved better in Levantine traditions may indicate

to a near-Eastern origin, as suggested by Fontenrose.

This process is also suggestive insofar as detailed study of a single mythological theme

including aspects in other cultures indicates the various ways in which a myth might be

transformed or obscured given on the disposition of the people, and likely includes an

explanation for why China never developed an indigenous tradition of epic poetry including

these mythological elements—her original mythological tradition was so obscured that later

poets were unable to recover the original “creative” aspects. Thus, this situation is just what

Maspero noted, citing the numerous attempts of generations of Chinese scholars to excise

mythological elements from the Yao Dian:

Le lien établi entre Kong-kong et l'inondation saute aux yeux, avec la répétition

de la formule « les eaux débordées assaillent le ciel ! » [像恭滔天], et les érudits

chinois n'ont pu manquer de le voir ; mais dans leur désir d'éviter la conclusion

déplaisante que le Chou king fait allusion à une légende mythologique, ils se sont

efforcés de trouver des explications ; les diverses écoles en ont imaginé de

différentes suivant les époques ... Mais, tandis qu'en ce qui concerne les légendes

grecques, ce mode d'interprétation évhémériste est abandonné depuis longtemps,

pour la Chine on continue trop souvent à s'en servir, et à affirmer, contre tout bon

sens, que toute cette mythologie est de l'histoire dégénéré.63

In attempting to untangle this mess of threads, we hope that the fire of the intellect serves

its purpose in preventing new Hydra heads from arising from the mess of the Gordian knot—a

problem potentially arising every time the Occident meets the reputedly unfathomable Orient—

62 There is not space here to discuss the torch dragon 燭籠 of the Heavenly Questions or the fire frequently associated with Yandi 炎帝 (another staple of combat myths), nor the possibility that Huangdi was originally also a dragon.  

63 Maspero, "Légendes Mythologiques Dans Le Chou King" (digital edition). 

potentially leaving in its wake a multiplicity of categories that serve to further obscure rather

than elucidate. Though there is a history here of systematic neglect and misinterpretation such

that formative elements linger in obscurity, this is hardly unique to the Chinese. As examined, a

similar situation continues to exist with respect to passages in the biblical Psalms that continue

to serve as an inspiration despite a long history of misleading translations. Undoubtedly

numerous other works of this type in the Indo-European tradition have been entirely lost or are

only partially reconstructed due to their dependence on oral tradition and unfavorable

circumstances. At least from the perspective of contemporary mythographers, Confucius may

have been doing the myths a favor by serving to ensconce the mythical sage kings in popular

memory. Though certain elements have been indisputably lost or corrupted, many have also

been retained that likely would be entirely lost. Thus, even if the emphasis was changed from

creation to wall-erection and cultivation, this may nonetheless have been a source of culture and

societal inspiration. As Stephen Owen notes in his study of Chinese poetry, there is a link

between the idea of creation and poetic creativity modeled on this act.64 This allows the poet’s

act to be both mimetic and creative; it is mimetic with respect to an original creative act, and

creative via inspiration through it.

64 Stephen Owen, Traditional Chinese Poetry and Poetics: Omen of the World (Madison: University of Wisconsin Press, 1985), 82. 

Appendix A: Common Themes Identified by Fontenrose

1. The Enemy was of divine origin.

1A. He was son of the primordial mother: chaos demoness or earth goddess.

1B. He was son of a father god: chaos demon or deposed father god or ruling father god

1C. He had a wife or female companion of like origin and character

2. The Enemy had a distinctive habitation.

2A. The feature of geographical correspondence: The Enemy lived in a region in which myth

tellers were wont to place the dwelling of monsters and demons in general

2B. He lived in cave, hut, or tree.

2C. He occupied a god’s temenos.

2D. He was guardian or spirit of a spring.

2E. He lived in sea, lake, or river.

3. The Enemy had extraordinary appearance and properties

3A. He was gigantic

3B. He had nonhuman form: most often that of a snake but also lizard, crocodile, scorpion, fish,

hippopotamus, boar, lion, wolf, dog, horse, bull, eagle, vulture, hawk, etc.; sometimes a

mixed form of various combinations of bestial and human members

3C. He had several heads, arms, legs, etc.

3D. He sent death by fire, glance, or breath; fire from his nostrils, mouth, or eyes, death-dealing

glances from eyes or countenance, poison-laden breath from nostrils or mouth

3E. He could change his shape at will.

3F. He was a death spirit, evil demon, specter, rising from the lower world.

3G. He was wind, flood, storm, plague, famine, draught

4. The Enemy was vicious and greedy.

4A. He plundered, robbed, murdered, made war

4B. He was a despotic ruler or master who oppressed his subjects and imposed tribute.

4C. He carried off the young of man an beast.

4D. He was gluttonous, devouring whole herds, and a man-eater.

4E. He was a lecher and ravisher, demanding that maidens be offered to him.

4F. He commanded a road and killed travelers upon it, often in a contest that he forced upon

them.

4G. He blockaded rivers or springs to keep men from water; or he drained rivers in his thirst

5. The Enemy conspired against heaven.

5A. He wanted to rule the world.

5B. His mother or wife or female companion incited him.

6. A divine Champion appeared to face him.

6A. The weather god or sky god went forth to fight him.

6B. It was his first exploit; he was then a boy or youth.

7. The Champion fought the Enemy.

7A. The Champion, using his favorite weapons, fought and killed the Enemy.

7B. He had to use numerous missiles; for the Enemy was formidable, or had an invulnerable

hide.

7C. The other gods were panic stricken; they appeased the Enemy or fled.

7D. The Camion’s sister, wife, or mother helped him.

7E. The Champion was helped by another god or hero.

7F. The Enemy fled during the combat.

7G. The combat was the central encounter of a gigantomachy.

8. The Champion nearly lost the battle.

8A. He suffered temporary defeat or death.

8B. The Enemy removed a potent organ from his body or took a potent object from him.

8C. The Enemy overcame him after luring him to a feast.

8D. The Enemy’s consort seduced the Champion to his destruction, or entered into a liaison with

him (Venusberg theme).

8E. The dead champion was lamented.

9. The Enemy as finally destroyed after being outwitted, deceived, or bewitched: he was

especially susceptible to lures of (a) food and (b) sex; he was easily taken in by (c)

disguise; (d) magic was employed against him.

10. The Champion disposed of the Enemy and celebrated his victory.

10A. He punished the Enemy, even after killing him, by imprisoning him in the lower world or

under a mountain, or by mutilating or cutting up or exposing his corpse.

10B. He celebrated his victory with a banquet and other festivities; he was cheered by god and

men.

10C. He was purified of blood pollution.

10D. He instituted cult, ritual, festival, and built a temple for himself.65

65 Fontenrose, Delphic Myth, 9–11.

P On April 23 25, 2015, rebro School of Theology hosted the conference The Words of the Prophets, their meaning and history of reception— with special focus on the book of Isaiah and the Twelve Prophets with generous support from the Swedish Research Council. The conference brought together seventeen scholars from ve different countries who offered papers and responses, a selection of which are published in this volume. We would rst like to thank our colleague, Dr. Lennart Bostr m, who orchestrated the conference which proved to be a great success. We also take this opportunity to thank all the participants who gave valuable input, in particular Dr. Bo Krister Ljungberg, Prof. G ran Eidevall, Prof. Fredrik Lindstr m, and Dr. Bla enka Scheuer, who offered responses to the main papers.

For this volume, we have selected a number of excellent contributions by leading scholars from Great Britain, Finland, Norway, and Sweden, which all focus on different aspects of the book of Isaiah, its history, theology, and reception. It is our hope that these studies will shed new light on the book of Isaiah, which is arguably one of the most complex and yet also central books in the Hebrew Bible, as re ected in its rich history of interpretation to this day.

Finally, we are very grateful to Miriam Cantwell, Assistant Editor of Bloomsbury T&T Clark, to Duncan Burns who helped us with copy editing and indexing, and to the series editors Claudia V. Camp and Andrew Mein for accepting the volume in the esteemed Library of Hebrew Bible/Old Testament Studies and for seeing it through to publication.

P On April 23 25, 2015, rebro School of Theology hosted the conference The Words of the Prophets, their meaning and history of reception— with special focus on the book of Isaiah and the Twelve Prophets with generous support from the Swedish Research Council. The conference brought together seventeen scholars from ve different countries who offered papers and responses, a selection of which are published in this volume. We would rst like to thank our colleague, Dr. Lennart Bostr m, who orchestrated the conference which proved to be a great success. We also take this opportunity to thank all the participants who gave valuable input, in particular Dr. Bo Krister Ljungberg, Prof. G ran Eidevall, Prof. Fredrik Lindstr m, and Dr. Bla enka Scheuer, who offered responses to the main papers.

For this volume, we have selected a number of excellent contributions by leading scholars from Great Britain, Finland, Norway, and Sweden, which all focus on different aspects of the book of Isaiah, its history, theology, and reception. It is our hope that these studies will shed new light on the book of Isaiah, which is arguably one of the most complex and yet also central books in the Hebrew Bible, as re ected in its rich history of interpretation to this day.

Finally, we are very grateful to Miriam Cantwell, Assistant Editor of Bloomsbury T&T Clark, to Duncan Burns who helped us with copy editing and indexing, and to the series editors Claudia V. Camp and Andrew Mein for accepting the volume in the esteemed Library of Hebrew Bible/Old Testament Studies and for seeing it through to publication.

On the Homelands of Indo-European and Eurasiatic: Geographic Aspects of a

Lexicostatistical Classification

Alexander Kozintsev Museum of Anthropology and Ethnography, Saint-Petersburg, Russia

In memory of my teacher Leo Klejn

The matrix of pairwise lexical matches between 106 actual and reconstructed languages belonging to 22 taxa in The Global Lexicostatistical Database was subjected to various dimensionality reduction techniques. The results, combined with the geographic approach, gave rise to a new reconstruction of the dispersal pattern of filial Eurasiatic groups, termed Scenario 2. Unlike the previously outlined Scenario 1, which placed the IE, Uralic and Indo-Uralic homelands in the area east of the Caspian Sea, not far from the presumed common Eurasiatic homeland, Scenario 2 locates the latter in a much more easterly area between Lake Balkhash and the Altai. With regard to proto-IE, Scenario 2 is an extension of Scenario 1 back in time and space, adding a very long initial stretch of the westward expansion of Indo-Hittite across most of western Central Asia. The routes by which the remaining Eurasiatic branches (Uralic, Yukaghir, Chukotko-Kamchatkan, Eskaleut, and Altaic) are supposed to have spread from their last common homeland, on the contrary, are much shorter that those envisaged by Scenario 1. Which of the two scenarios is preferable is hard to say because both refer to relatively late stages of the Eurasiatic macrofamily. The distance separating the place of its origin from that of its split is unknown.

Introduction In my first study published in this journal (Kozintsev 2018) and in a later article in Russian based on a larger sample of languages (Kozintsev 2019a), I used a two-dimensional (quasi-spatial) model to test hypotheses about the southern adstrate in proto-IE.

1 The test was based on the assumption that the two

1 The studies were based on the matrix of lexical matches between the

languages in the Global Lexicostatistical Database, derived from 50-word lists

122 Alexander Kozintsev

The Journal of Indo-European Studies

most closely linked members of Greenberg’s Eurasiatic macrofamily – IE and Uralic (see Kassian et al. 2015) – should be equidistant from the third, non-Eurasiatic family. If the assumption does not hold, this would signal either unequal evolutionary rates or adstrrate. Of the four models tested (Northwest Caucasian, Northeast Caucasian, Kartvelian, and Semitic), only the latter one showed significant asymmetry in the distribution of lexical matches, the difference between IE and Semitic being significantly smaller than between Uralic and Semitic. Because no such asymmetry was observed in the other three models, the hypothesis of inequality of evolutionary rates in IE and Uralic was rejected and the alternative hypothesis of a Semitic adstrate in proto-IE was accepted. Admittedly, the supposed adstrate is quite small – just 1-2 words. One of them, denoting ‘horn’ (IE *ker-, *kr-no- / Semitic * arn-) may be a loan, whereas the second parallel, referring to the first-person nominative singular pronoun (IE *egoH vs. phonetically quite dissimilar Akkadian an ku, Northwest Semitic * anVkV, Egyptian jnk, Berber *nakk-), if not accidental, may be due only to a remote common origin and to what Eugene Helimski (1982: 24–25) termed “areal-genetic ties” – preservation of cognates in adjacent dialects and languages. Small as it is, the IE versus Uralic asymmetry in the Semitic model is highly significant because both IE and Uralic are represented by several languages (12 and 8, respectively), and the variation within these families is small. Contacts between IE and Semitic have more than once been demonstrated with regard to cultural vocabulary (see, e.g., Illi -Svity 1964; see also Gamkrelidze & Ivanov 1995: 769–773; Dolgopolsky 1987; Shevoroshkin 1987; S. Starostin 2007/2000; 2007/2001–2002). Many of these parallels, however, were stigmatized as chance coincidences or Wanderwörter (Diakonoff 1985; Kassian 2010: 426). It is more difficult to discard the parallels relating to items from the short (50-word) list consisting of thoroughly sifted basic terms, which are

(http://starling.rinet.ru/new100/trees.htm, last accessed October 28, 2018). I am deeply thankful to George Starostin, Alexei Kassian, and Mikhail Zhivlov for the generous permission to use their unpublished data. I thank Mikhail Zhivlov and Václav Bla ek for their highly useful comments.

On the Homelands of Indo-European and Eurasiatic 123

Volume 48, Number 1 & 2, Spring/Summer 2020

borrowed very rarely. The fact that even such words reveal a very weak but statistically significant asymmetry between IE and Uralic in the Semitic model deserves attention. On the basis of archaeological, genetic, and linguistic facts, I tried to demonstrate that proto-Anatolians had migrated to Asia Minor, not from the Balkans, but from the east and that therefore the standard version of the Steppe Theory

2 is

implausible (Kozintsev 2019a, 2019b; see references therein). I placed the Indo-Uralic homeland east of the Caspian Sea and associated it with the Mesolithic cultures of that region. These were ancestral to two Neolithic cultures – Kelteminar, which had influenced the early Neolithic of the eastern Ural and western Siberia and was attributed to proto-Uralic-speaking groups by Valery Chernetsov (1960); and one of the early farming cultures of southern Turkmenia and northern Iran, possibly associated with Indo-Hittites, as Colin Renfrew (1987: 192) and Peter Bellwood (2012) believed. In line with Johanna Nichols’ early view (1997, 1998), I postulated the primary westward spread of IE from that locus, caused by the transition of one of the early farming groups to seminomadic pastoralism. The spread, however, likely occurred, not by two routes (the northern one to the Western steppe, the southern to the Near East), but only by the southern mountainous route along the Elburz. An additional fact supporting this scenario is that, judging by reconstructed PIE terms for topographical features, the Indo-Hittites, at some stage of their history, lived in a mountainous terrain, moreover, that the mountain was perceived as a “mighty cliff reaching to the sky”; in addition, there was a sea or large lake nearby (Gamkrelidze, Ivanov 1995: 574–577; Dybo 2013). As the authors conclude, this eliminates the steppe as a primary homeland. Three secondary IE migrations to the Western steppe across the Caucasus were reconstructed – two in the 5

th

millennium BC (Khvalynsk ancestors and Darkveti-Meshoko), and one in the 4

th millennium BC (Leilatepe–Maykop)

2 The traditional term ”Kurgan Theory” is misleading because there are

reasons to believe that the Kurgan tradition was introduced to the steppe from the southern Caucasus (see Kozintsev 2019b for a summary of facts).

124 Alexander Kozintsev

The Journal of Indo-European Studies

(Kozintsev 2019a, 2019b). While all the three resulted in the spread of IE dialects to the steppe, only the earliest and the easternmost migration, from northern Iran or Azerbaijan to the Volga, appears to have been accompanied by appreciable gene flow. However, both the Semitic and the Northwest Caucasian adstrate (Bomhard 2019) were apparently introduced to the steppe IE – the ancestor of all IE branches except Anatolian – by two other, more westerly migrations.

3

The primary task of the present study is to examine the eastern ties of IE, which unambiguously point to Siberia and even the Far East. Apart from IE, Greenberg’s Eurasiatic macrofamily (Greenberg 2000, 2002), or Nostratic macrofamily in the narrow sense, includes Uralo-Yukaghir (some linguists believe IE and Uralic to be daughter families of Indo-Uralic), Turkic, Tungusic, Mongolic, Korean, and Japonic, all of which are sometimes included in the Altaic macrofamily, Eskaleut, Chukotko-Kamchatkan, and language isolates such as Ainu and Nivkh. The exclusively eastern ties of IE within Eurasiatic preclude the idea that the IE homeland was located west of the Ural Mountains or the Caspian Sea. This is all the more true with regard to the Uralic homeland, and, given the affinities between IE and Uralic, their primary homelands can’t be far apart. Do all these facts prevent us from placing the IE homeland in western Central Asia (Nichols 1998; Sver kov 2011; Kozintsev 2019a, 2019b), where, in my view, both the Uralic and the Indo-Uralic homelands could be located as well? And, if the location is correct, where should we place the homeland of the Eurasiatic proto-language? One of the few scholars who have explored the implications of the Eurasiatic (specifically eastern Siberian) affinities of IE was Michael Fortescue (1998). In line with Johann Schmidt’s (1872) wave theory but without mentioning it, he regarded Eurasiatic as a mesh of languages stretching as far east as Chukotka. In his view, ties of IE with this mesh were areal and resulted from the eastward expansion of Afanasievans (Tocharians?), whose language had converged toward Siberian,

3 Kortlandt (2019), following Anthony (2019) now believes that the adstrate

was Northeast, not Northwest Caucasian; see also Björn 2017: 135–136.

On the Homelands of Indo-European and Eurasiatic 125

Volume 48, Number 1 & 2, Spring/Summer 2020

specifically ‘Ural-Altaic’ languages (Fortescue 1998: 183, 196). Sixty years earlier, the idea of IE having converged toward ‘Turanian’ languages was advanced by Nikolai Trubetzkoy (1939), whom Fortescue does not mention and who, unlike him, explicitly cited Schmidt as his predecessor.

4

Can Trubetzkoy’s and Fortescue’s ideas about the ‘convergence’ of IE toward Siberian languages be entertained at present? If so, one must revisit the role of Afanasievans, resp. Tocharians, in this process. If not, one must think about the placement of the Eurasiatic homeland.

Materials and methods As in my previous study (Kozintsev 2018), the distance matrix, taken from the Global Lexicostatistical Database, is derived from the preliminary 50-item wordlists, compiled by G. Starostin et al. and available at http://starling.rinet.ru/new100/ trees.htm (accessed November 10, 2019). The sample selected for this study, however, is much larger. It relates to 106 actual and reconstructed languages belonging to 22 taxa, both polytypic (families) and monotypic (language isolates)

5 and

representing not only Greenberg’s Eurasiatic macrofamily except Ainu and Nivkh, which are absent in the database, but virtually the entire Nostratic macrofamily even in the broad sense. Also included in the sample are North Caucasian languages, unrelated to this macrofamily but possibly exhibiting areal ties with some of its members:

1. Indo-European -- Hittite, Tocharian, Old Indian, Iranic, Greek, Armenian, Albanian, Baltic, Slavic, Germanic, Latin, Celtic.

2. Uralic – Baltic-Finnic, Saami, Mordvinic, Mari, Permic, Ob-Ugric, Hungarian, Samoyed.

4 Fortescue’s frequent mentions of waves refer to migrations, not to the mesh-

like ties between languages, as in Schmidt’s and Trubetzkoy’s theories. 5 The number of taxa is arbitrary because, as the dendrogram shows, they

don’t have the same rank (http://starling.rinet.ru/ new100/eurasia_long.jpg, accessed November 10. 2019; see Figure 2). For instance, Yukaghir might as well be lumped with Uralic, whereas Turkic, Mongolic, Tungusic, Korean, and Japanese could be merged into Altaic. The rank of Berber is much lower than that of other Afroasiatic branches, etc. Taxonomic intricacies, however, will not concern us here.

The Journal of Indo-European Studies

3. Yukaghir. 4. Turkic. 5. Mongoli . 6. Tungusic. 7. Korean. 8. Japonic. 9. Eskaleut:

9.1 Eskimo – Yupik, Inuit. 9.2 Aleut.

10. Chukotko-Kamchatkan – Chukchee, Itelmen. 11. Dravidian – Brahui, North Dravidian, South Dravidian,

Telugu, Gondwan, Kolami-Gadba. 12. Kartvelian – Narrow Kartvelian, Svan. 13. Afroasiatic:

13.1. Semitic – Akkadian, Northwest Semitic, Arabic, modern South Arabian, Ethiosemitic.

13.2. Middle Egyptian. 13.3. Berber – Eastern Berber, Tuareg, Zenaga, Northern

Berber. 13.4. Chadic – Tumak-Somrai, Lai, Kera-Kwang, Mokilko,

The statistical elaboration of the matrix of pairwise lexical matches between languages was carried out by means of the PAST package (Hammer et al. 2001). The underlying model was two-dimensional (quasi-areal). In this model, the position of points in multivariate space is projected onto the plane, providing a possibility to study not only the vector of temporal changes, as in the genealogical model, but spatial vectors as

Figure 1 shows the two-dimensional projection of all languages in multivariate space. Greenberg’s Eurasiatic

128 Alexander Kozintsev

The Journal of Indo-European Studies

(without Ainu and Nivkh) is clearly delimited. 6 Nostratic in the

broad sense includes also Kartvelian, which may be marginally related to Eurasiatic, and Dravidian, which is definitely outside it. The Afroasiatic macrofamily occupies a very separate place, although being linked to Nostratic on a very deep level (http://starling.rinet.ru/new100/eurasia_long.jpg). The fact that Omotic appears to be closely related to Cushitic supports the idea that they are sister families (Militarev 2005a; Bla ek 2013) or members of a single Sprachbund (G. Starostin 2014: 660) rather than the view of Omotic as the earliest branch of Afroasiatic (Bender 1997), supported by the results of cluster analysis.

7 The special status of Ongota, which the cluster

analysis shows to be a sister branch of Omotic (ibid.; see also Militarev 2005b; G. Starostin 2013: 226–228), is visible on the two-dimensional projection as well. The pattern generated by the quasi-areal model generally agrees with the results of cluster analysis of the same data (see link above) and the conclusions of the Moscow comparativist school (see, e.g., G. Starostin et al. 2016). But the two-dimensional projection highlights certain details that are invisible under the genealogical approach, for instance the geographic gradients (see below). Some MST edges may be random. This may be true with regard to a single edge (9.0%) connecting Omotic (specifically Yemsa) with Northeast Caucasian (specifically the reconstructed proto-Nakh). This appears to be an artifact of the MST method, which does not allow for isolated taxa of any rank (North Caucasian is precisely

6 In version 2.17 of the PAST package, which I used, the shortest path connects

the points (languages) not on the plane, where their configuration is distorted, but in the original multivariate space generated by the similarity matrix. In version 3.0 and newer ones, the path is evaluated on the plane (I thank Øyvind Hammer, who has explained this in a personal letter to me). Because this causes a considerable loss of information, and the results are markedly worse, sometimes disagreeing with the traditional classification of languages, I recommend using the 2.17 version or the 4.01 version, see https://folk.uio.no/ohammer/past/ (accessed November 10, 2019). 7 The two-dimensional projection lends even less support to the radical idea

Rising to the family level, we can compare the arrangement of families under four models – genealogical (http://starling.rinet.ru/new100/eurasia_short.jpg, Figure 2), unrooted network (Figure 3), network rooted by the most isolated family – Northeast Caucasian (Figure 4), and quasi-areal (Figure 5). In the three latter cases, instead of using reconstructions, the occurrences of lexical matches between separate languages were averaged for each pair of families. The mean occurrence of matches within a family was taken for 100% (the diagonal element in the matrix of within-family comparisons), and the non-diagonal elements, measuring the internal cohesiveness of a family, were ignored.

Figure 4. Network, rooted by Northeast Caucasian, showing the relationship of families based on frequencies of lexical matches according to the Global Lexicostatistical Database. Ka, Kartvelian; Dr, Dravidian. See Figure 3 for other abbreviations.

As Figures 1–5 show, within the Eurasiatic macrofamily, five Altaic families (Turkic, Mongolic, Tungusic, Korean, and Japonic) are opposed to a macrofamily that includes IE, Uralo-Yukaghir, Chukotko-Kamchatkan, and Eskaleut. I will call the latter macrofamily ‘Indo-Siberian’ for want of a better term. Figures 3 and 4 show that languages within each of the two macrofamilies, Indo-Siberian and especially Altaic, are united

The link between Kartvelian and Tungusic in Figure 5 (10.0%) appears as random as that between Dravidian and Aleut. Admittedly, ties of the same magnitude connect members of the Afroasiatic macrofamily such as Semitic and Cushitic (9.1%), on the one hand, Omotic and Chadic (7.1%), on the other. But in these cases geographic proximity favors genetic affinity. The tie between Mongolic and Northwest Caucasian (6.0%) is apparently an artifact of the MST method, the more so because at the level of separate languages (Figure 1) Northwest Caucasian has no ties with any Eurasiatic family. It is less easy to ignore the edge connecting IE with Middle Egyptian (6.5%). My previous analysis has shown IE to have

Obviously, in the light of modern knowledge, three homelands, namely IE, Uralic, and Altaic, must be shifted in the eastern direction.

spanning much of the northern part of Eastern Eurasia and going first from west to east (IE – Uralic – Yukaghir – Chukotko-Kamchatkan – Eskimo), then from north to south (Eskimo – Japonic), and finally from east to west (Japonic – Korean – Tungusic – Mongolian – Turkic). Importantly, all links in this chain are relatively strong, ranging from 13-14% between IE and Uralic, between Yukaghir and Chukotko-Kamchatkan, and between Eskimo and Japonic to 24-29% between the five Altaic families. The only exception is Aleut, which is connected with Eskimo (31%) and, unexpectedly, with Dravidian (8%). This connection is weaker than that between Aleut and Chukotko-Kamchatkan (13%), but registering the latter edge would result in a cycle (Aleut – Chukotko-Kamchatkan – Eskimo – Aleut).

Discussion

In the previous study (Kozintsev 2019b) I associated the primary IE dispersal center with the early farming cultures of southern Turkmenia or northern Iran, and the primary Uralic dispersal center, with the Neolithic Kelteminar culture, distributed southeast of the Aral Sea and known to have influenced the Neolithic cultures of the southern Urals and western Siberia. The premise of both these assumptions was that the IE homeland must lie south of the Uralic homeland and not far from it. According to this hypothesis, which I will call Scenario 1, IE spread from its primary center westward along the southern Caspian coast toward Anatolia and then northward across the Caucasus to the steppe, whereas Uralic spread in the opposite direction – to Siberia. Previously I didn’t look at other branches of Eurasiatic. Yukaghir can be viewed as the eastern extension of proto-Uralic, originating in Siberia, or as an independent branch stemming from broadly the same center as Uralic. It is more difficult to reconstruct the trajectories of the two remaining branches – Chukotko-Kamchatkan-Eskaleut and Altaic. If the topology of the Eurasiatic tree (Figures 2 and 8) is correct, then they had separated from the common Eurasiatic stem before IE and Uralo-Yukaghir diverged. If this happened in western Central Asia, then their speakers had to undertake extremely long journeys to reach their final destinations. Admittedly they had enough time for that, as the age of both the eastern branches may be of the order of 10 thousand years according to lexicostatistical estimates.

9 But isn’t it possible to minimize the

total length of migration routes connecting filial Eurasiatic homelands with the last common homeland? The immediate impulse that arises when one looks at the dense network of ties between Eurasiatic families (Figure 7), at the geographically stretched Indo-Siberian cluster (Figure 8),

9 Sergei Yakhontov (1991) estimated the age of the Nostratic macrofamily

sensu stricto (without Afroasiatic or Dravidian) at about 15 thousand years, whereas Pagel et al. (2013) speak of 14.5 thousand years if their Eurasiatic tree, which includes IE, Uralic, Altaic, Chukotko-Kamchatkan, and Eskimo as principal members, and Dravidian and Kartvelian as peripheral members, is rooted with proto-Dravidian, and 15.6 thousand years if it is rooted with proto-Kartvelian.

On the Homelands of Indo-European and Eurasiatic 137

Volume 48, Number 1 & 2, Spring/Summer 2020

and at the huge spatial gap separating Uralic from Yukaghir (Figures 7–9) is to move both proto-IE and proto-Uralic further east. As far as Uralic is concerned, this doesn’t present any problem. First, it is connected with the very easterly positioned Yukaghir either by origin (Collinder 1940; Nikolaeva 1988) or by contacts (Rédei 1999). Biological evidence, relating to highly informative cranial traits (Kozintsev 1992), favors the idea of a genetic affinity between Uralic speakers and Yukaghirs. Second, the further west from central Siberia one moves (Samoyed – Ugric – Finno-Permic), the shallower the differentiation (Janhunen 2009). This regularity becomes even more apparent if Yukaghir is added as the earliest and the easternmost branch. Third, the typological similarity between Uralic and Altaic languages is hardly incidental given their geographic adjacency (ibid.). Note, however, that the taxonomic divide between Indo-Siberian, to which Uralic belongs, and Altaic is rather sharp (Figures 2, 8) and the MST method reveals no direct connection between the latter two families (Figures 1, 5, and 9). Indo-European presents a much more serious problem. While Fortescue’s idea that the Afanasievo (supposedly proto-Tocharian) migration to the Altai-Sayan region may have caused the split, if not between Uralic and Yukaghir (1989: 196) then within Uralic is worth being considered,

10 his belief that

this migration accounts for the Eurasiatic affinities of IE is untenable. First, the analysis of lexical ties between IE and Uralic demonstrates that the straightest route connecting these two families in multivariate space passes between Ugric and Hittite whereas Tocharian is quite distant from that route (Kozintsev 2018, Figure 12). Second, having split off from the Repino-Yamnaya tribes and taken a distant journey to eastern Central Asia, the Afanasievo people hardly retained ties with their kin on the Western steppe. It is even less likely that they ever returned, so even if they were responsible for late proto-IE loans in proto-Uralic or proto-Altaic, this cannot account either for the Indo-Uralic elements in Hittite (Kloekhorst 2008) or for

10

The former idea disagrees with the conclusions of the Starostin school, who date the split between Uralic and Yukaghir to the mid-7

th millennium BC and

the separation of the Tocharian branch to the early 4 th

millennium BC. But the disintegration of Uralic broadly coincides with the latter date (I thank Vaclav Bla ek for this remark).

138 Alexander Kozintsev

The Journal of Indo-European Studies

the Eurasiatic affinities of IE in general (Greenberg 2000, 2002). In sum, Trubetzkoy’s and Fortescue’s rejection of the genetic approach in favor of the areal alternative is unfortunate whereas the idea that proto-IE had spread westward from Central Asia or Siberia either by way of migration (Uhlenbeck 1937) or by way of diffusion (Nichols 1997, 1998) remains valid. Two facts prevent us from shifting the IE homeland even further east or northeast. One is that the distance from the source of the adstrate, whether North Caucasian, Semitic, or both, should not be too large, otherwise the gap that we seek to minimize merely changes its position from easterly to westerly. As regards the possible Semitic adstrate, the fact that Ongota, Omotic, and Cushitic appear to be the earliest branches of Afroasiatic (Figure 8) might indicate a northeast African rather than Levantine homeland of this macrofamily and thus a relatively late arrival of Semites in the Levant. This would make it more difficult to accept the idea of contacts between IE and Semitic in that area or in Mesopotamia (Kozintsev 2018, 2019). The alternative explanation, proposed by Alexander Militarev, is that the Afroasiatic homeland correlates with the Natufian and/or post-Natufian culture of the Levant (Militarev & Shnirelman 1984; Militarev 2009) whereas the isolated position of South Afroasiatic languages (Cushitic, Omotic, and Ongota) is due to a separate migration across the Bab-el-Mandeb rather than across the Eastern Mediterranean as in the case of North Afroasiatic African languages – Egyptian, Berber, and Chadic. Under Militarev’s scenario, Semites, speaking a North Afroasiatic language, remained where their ancestors had lived. This view is supported by lexicostatistical calculations suggesting that proto-Semitic was spoken in the northern Levant as early as the fifth millennium BC (Kitchen 2009). The second fact with which one has to reckon is that the proto-IE vocabulary points to a mountainous region with a sea or large lake nearby (see above). If we abandon the southern Caspian coast (Kozintsev 2019b) and attach greater weight to the Eurasiatic (i.e., easterly) ties of IE and Uralic, what might the alternative be? Apart from the Aral Sea, which is remote from any mountains, there are two large lakes east of the Caspian Sea – Balkhash and Issyk-Kul. The former is partly saline, the latter fully saline; both can be stormy and thus sea-like. Issyk-Kul adjoins the majestic peaks of the Tien-Shan.

On the Homelands of Indo-European and Eurasiatic 139

Volume 48, Number 1 & 2, Spring/Summer 2020

Those of the Dzhungar Mountains (Dzhungarian Alatau), towering south of Lake Balkhash, while less gigantic, are still impressive. Also, this lake is larger and closer to Siberia, where the Uralic homeland has been traditionally placed (Hajdú 1964; Napolskikh 1997: 132; Janhunen 2009).

11

Geographically, given the Siberian ties of IE (see Figures 7–9), this area appears more suitable as a prospective IE homeland than the area southeast of the Caspian Sea. Let us discuss the implications of shifting both the IE and the Uralic homelands further east (Figure 10). In view of a very feasible proposal, made by Sergei Yakhontov (1991), to locate the homeland of Nostratic sensu stricto, which is basically the same as Greenberg’s Eurasiatic, close to that of the centrally positioned proto-Uralic, it is possible to place not only the IE and Uralic homelands, but also that of all Eurasiatic languages between Lake Balkhash and the Altai, in an area that includes the Upper Irtysh drainage. I will call this hypothesis Scenario 2 (Figure 11).

12 Apart from the

central position of Uralic, Yakhontov mentioned common

11

Attempts to place the Uralic homeland in Eastern Europe, made by certain Finnish scholars on the basis of alleged early loans (Koivulehto 2001; Kallio 2015), are refuted not only by linguistic (Helimsky 2001; Janhunen 2009; Kortlandt 2018) and mythological facts (Napolskikh 2012) but also by genetic data unambiguously pointing to Siberia as the source of the Uralic migration(s) to Europe (Napolskikh 2012; Saag et al 2019). Only the latest and the westernmost among the filial Uralic homelands – Finno-Permic – appears to have been located west of the Urals. The overwhelming evidence favoring the Siberian ties of IE makes the search for the Uralic homeland in Europe all the more futile. 12

Bomhard (2018: 312, map 5b) locates the homeland of Eurasiatic languages between the Aral Sea and Lake Balkhash. On that map, however, only three branches of Eurasiatic are shown – IE, Uralic, and Altaic, but not Yukaghir, Chukotko-Kamchatkan or Eskaleut. In addition, the trajectory of the Altaic migration, which passes north of Lake Baikal on Bomhard’s map, disagrees with the available facts. Evidently, the speakers of proto-Altaic took a much more southerly route, migrating eastward along the corridor between the Mongolian Altai and the Tien Shan (Figure 11). This may account for the fact that Altaic is opposed to all other Eurasiatic branches (Figures 2–4, 8–10). However, the proto-Altaic landscape reconstructed by Dybo (2013) – “steppe with hillocks and large rivers with seasonal floods, but no sea or lake” – apparently refers to the last Altaic homeland, Manchuria. In the case of proto-IE, the reconstructed mountainous landscape with a sea or large lake nearby may refer to any of the two hypothetical homelands – early (between Lake Balkhash and the Dzhungar Mountains) and later, southern Caspian (Kozintsev 2019b).

Nostratic words for snow and ice as well as the generic term for ‘berry’, *marja (Illi -Svity 1976: 43–45, No. 282), suggestive of a forest environment. In his view, the Nostratic homeland was situated in the southern Urals or in the adjoining regions such as the Volga drainage and western Siberia. However, a continental climate with frosty winters is likewise typical of the area encircled in Figure 11, and forests covering the Altai piedmont in the eastern part of this area abound with berries.

Figure 10. Map showing the presumed homelands of protolanguages, and trees based on frequencies of lexical matches (http://starling.rinet.ru/new100/eurasia_short.jpg, accessed Octo-ber 9, 2019). Compared to Figure 8, the IE and Uralic homelands are shifted eastward; the location of other homelands is the same. See Figures 3 and 4 for abbreviations.

The premise of both scenarios is that the Uralic homeland was situated close to that of IE, north of it. The facts on which Scenario 1 is based (Kozintsev 2019b) suggest that the migration routes taken by Indo-Hittites passed via the southern Caspian coast and Caucasus to Anatolia and to the steppe. I see no reason to discard those facts. However, in Scenario 2, which, with regard to IE, is an extension of Scenario 1 back in time, a long initial stretch is added to that route, crossing entire western Central Asia. Under Scenario 1, the only advantaged branch is IE because the journey which its speakers had to take from their presumed homeland is short relative to the journeys destined for all other Eurasiatic branches. The situation with

On the Homelands of Indo-European and Eurasiatic 141

Volume 48, Number 1 & 2, Spring/Summer 2020

Scenario 2 is the opposite: the route which the speakers of IE are supposed to have taken may appear unduly long, but if the eastward migrations of proto-Yukaghirs, proto-Chukotko-Kamchatkans, and proto-Eskaleuts are considered, this solution can be viewed as a reasonable compromise, the more so because Uralic doesn’t have to spread first eastward to Siberia and then westward to Europe. As regards Kartvelian, if its Eurasiatic affinities receive additional support, it would be easy to imagine another westward migration route paralleling that of IE.

B, Chukotko-Kamchatkan and Eskaleut; C, Altaic; D, North Afroasiatic including Semitic; E, Kartvelian; F, North Caucasian. The topology of the unrooted tree representing the five principal branches of Eurasiatic (IE, Uralic, Yukaghir, Chukotko-Kamchatkan-Eskaleut, and Altaic) is the same as in the rooted tree (Figure 10), except that Altaic is the earliest branch, not the sister branch of Chukotko-Kamchatkan-Eskaleut.

In contrast to the situation with the Transcaspian locus of IE, Scenario 2 makes it rather difficult to find archaeological support for either the more easterly homeland of IE or for the first stretch of its westward expansion. These facts must

142 Alexander Kozintsev

The Journal of Indo-European Studies

concern much earlier periods than those which feature in Scenario 1 – possibly not only the Mesolithic but also the Upper Paleolithic

13 . Moreover, it is not clear whether in this case one

can speak of a single migration, of a demic diffusion spanning many centuries, or indeed of language spread with little or no gene flow. If the earliest IE dispersal route passed across southeastern Kazakhstan, as Scenario 2 implies, then one piece of information may be worth mentioning. This area was the focus of fieldwork by the German-American-Kazakhstanian archaeological project in recent years. The earliest occupation levels of the Dali settlement – a site located ~150 km southeast of Lake Balkhash in the immediate vicinity of the snowy peaks of the Dzhungar Mountains, precisely on the presumed migration route – date to the Early Bronze Age (2705–2545 cal BC). Excavations have revealed an economy based on sheep and goat (domesticated in the Near East) and cattle breeding, and the cultivation of millet, apparently introduced from China (Hermes et al. 2019). The genomic analysis of a female parietal bone from those levels indicates a larger share of the West Siberian Hunter-Gatherer component such as that found in the Botai horse-breeders and a smaller share of the component relating to early Iranian farmers and those from southwestern Central Asia such as Geoksyur and Sarazm (Narasimhan et al. 2019, Supplementary materials: 241, 243). The Dali individual is rather similar to those from the Yamnaya burials at Kumsay, western Kazakhstan, dating to ~3000 BC (they, too, reveal an Iranian farmer component), although it differs from them by displaying an East Siberian tendency (ibid.: 233, 235, 236, Figure S 31).

14 However, the Yamnaya culture had never spread to

southeastern Kazakhstan (but see Mertz & Mertz 2010 for data on Yamnaya migrations to northeastern Kazakhstan), so the

13

In the latter case, one should remember that large parts of Siberia and Central Asia were submerged in proglacial lakes, the history of which has not been reliably reconstructed (Mangerud et al. 2004). 14

Although the ADMIXTURE analysis, on which Figure S 31 is based, does not show the Iranian farmer component, a more sensitive method, qpAdm, does reveal it (p. 243). If Early Bronze Age Dali is modeled as a mixture of Botai with Geoksyur or Sarazm, the former component is estimated at 77–78%, the latter, at 22–23% (I thank David Reich for the clarifications).

On the Homelands of Indo-European and Eurasiatic 143

Volume 48, Number 1 & 2, Spring/Summer 2020

parallel between Dali and Kumsay must have another explanation. None of these individuals resembles Afanasievans. The Dali specimen is much too late to have direct relevance to the IE homeland issue. What matters, however, is that the early Iranian farmer component had been introduced to southeastern Kazakhstan no later than the first half of the third millennium BC neither by the Yamnaya people nor by the Afanasievans, but by people from Iran or southwestern Central Asia (possibly together with the domesticated sheep and goat). If so, could it have been present there much earlier? Which means: could the ancestors of the Dali people be a sought-for link between the populations of Siberia and those of Iran/Turan, and eventually of the steppe (Khvalynsk – Yamnaya)? Could their genetic shift in the East Siberian direction mirror their geographic position near the point where the western and the eastern branches of Eurasiatic diverge?

Conclusions The two-dimensional (quasi-areal) model combined with the traditional genealogical model and the geographic approach offers a useful tool for reconstructing language relationship and, indirectly, population history. The application of these methods to Eurasiatic languages has resulted in the second scenario of Eurasiatic (and, respectively, IE) dispersal, placing its center in eastern Central Asia. This is an alternative to the first scenario, outlined in my previous study, where this center was placed in western Central Asia mostly on the basis of archaeological and genetic evidence. With regard to IE, Scenario 2 is but an extension of Scenario 1. With regard to other branches of Eurasiatic, Scenario 2 may appear preferable to Scenario 1 because it minimizes the total length of migration routes. But this applies only to the time after the split of common Eurasiatic. Because we don’t know the routes the speakers of proto-Eurasiatic had to take before they had reached their last common homeland, wherever it was situated, making a choice between the two scenarios is impossible. Both alternatives appear to be viable working hypotheses.

Heroes, Kings and Monsters in a Cave Under the Mountain

(Indo-Europeans and the Caucasus)

Yaroslav Vassilkov Museum of Anthropology and Ethnography (Kunstkamera)

Saint-Petersburg yavass011@gmail.com

The paper begins with the unique motif of the “Wheel of Time Revolving in an Underground Cave” that appears in both the Indian Mah bh rata and the Armenian epic “Daredevils of Sassoun”. This is followed by a review of stories about characters confined or asleep inside a cave from the Caucasus, the Balkans and Central/Western Europe. Certain episodes from the Indian epics Mbh and R m ya a are for the first time recognized as belonging to the same circle of plots and motifs. In all stories of characters imprisoned or sleeping in a cave, time passes in a peculiar way, divided into cycles by the constant repetition of specific events. The author suggests that all these myths and legends are based on the strong link in human consciousness between the image of a cave and the mytho-ritual complex of ideas: “birth – death – rebirth”. The similarity between stories of this type in Caucasian and Indo-European traditions may be explained by contacts between Indo-Europeans and Caucasians at different times, starting from the period of Proto-Indo-European linguistic unity.

The Wheel of Time/Fate in a Cave (India – Armenia) The comparative analysis of the Indian Mah bh rata (Mbh) and the Armenian epic Sasna c er (“Daredevils of Sassoun”) (Vassilkov 2019) has, among other similarities, revealed a unique and impressive image common to both traditions. In the Mbh (Mbh1. 3.147-151, 166-168, 172-173)

1 the young

Brahmin, Utta ka, penetrates through a fissure into a large cave in the underground world of Snakes (n galoka) where he sees a

1 All Mbh references are to the Critical edition (Mah bh rata 1933 – 1966.)

The Journal of Indo-European Studies

large wheel with 360 spokes and 24 “joints” (parvan) 2 or just 12

spokes 3 , which constantly revolves turned by six boys. There

are also two young women making a cloth on a loom; they continuously interlace the warp with black and white threads of weft

4 . The epithet defining the word for ‘warp’ (tantram) is

vi var pa , translated by J.A.B. van Buitenen (1973: 52) as ‘colorful’ but may also be understood as ‘having universal form’, ‘representing the whole universe’

5 . This meaning is in

line with the last part of the verse Mbh 1. 3.151, from which we learn that the two divine weavers in the process of their work “cause to turn round and round” not just the threads but all the worlds and all living beings within them. Later Utta ka’s teacher explains to him that the wheel he saw is the Wheel of the Year with its 12 spokes (months), and the six boys are the six seasons ( tu)

6 . The Wheel of the Year is

an aspect of k lacakra, the Wheel of Time, popular in the epic image representing K la “(cyclical) Time”, the highest principle of the heroic world view. K la’s “turns” (paryaya) predestine all events in the world and the destinies of humans. The orders of K la are fulfilled by two epic gods who control fate: Dh t (Dh t ) – the ‘Placer’, “Fixer (of destiny)’ and Vidh t (Vidh t ) – the ‘Apportioner’ or ‘Disposer’. It is not surprising that Utta ka’s teacher sees in the two female weavers the forms of these two gods

7 . However, it can hardly be doubted that these

two women are by origin the ancient Indo-Aryan and Indo-

caturvi atiparvayoge a yat kum r parivartayanti // (Mbh 1.3.150) The word parvan has another meaning: ‘fortnight’ i.e. “half a month”. 3 tatra ca may cakra d a dv da ram (Mbh 1.3.168A).
