Heroes, Kings and Monsters in a Cave Under the Mountain 447

Volume 48, Number 3 & 4, Fall/Winter 2020

European goddesses of fate, usually spinners or weavers 8 . In

Indo-European traditions such goddesses tend to be linked with the underworld like, for example, the Hittite goddesses I tu taya and Papaya who spin and ply the thread of the king’s life in the underworld; the South Slavic sudzhenitse, goddesses of fate who sometimes live in mountain caves; the witches (successors of the ancient Norns) who tell Macbeth his destiny in a cave (Act IV, Scene I), etc. But it is the Wheel of Time revolving in an underground cave that is most important to us here. Turning now to the Armenian parallel, we are unfortunately unable to quote a particular text neither in Armenian, nor in English translation. The epic “Daredevils of Sassoun” continued even in the 20

th century to be transmitted

orally as a multitude of tales and their variants. The motif of the Wheel of Fate in a cave is absent in both the collated text published in 1939 under the title “David of Sassoun”

9 and in the

volume of recorded oral tales translated into Russian (Armyanskij narodnyj epos 2004). My only source is the book of the eminent philologist, folklorist and historian of literature Manuk Abeghyan (Abeghian 1899) who in turn quotes from a rare version of the tale of Mher the Younger, recorded and published by another Armenian philologist and folklorist,

8 Cf. e.g., West 2007: 379-385. It is noteworthy that M.L. West when

demonstrating the presence of the goddesses of Fate who spin and weave human destinies in IE mythological traditions of Europe and Anatolia remarks: “…there are no spinster Fate-goddesses in the Vedas” (West 2007: 379, 380). However there is a verse in the first of two Wedding hymns that form the 14

th Book of the Atharvaveda ( aunaka):

y ak ntann avayan y ca tatnire y dev r ant n abhito 'dadanta / t s tv dev r jarase sa vyayantv yu m t ’da paridhatsva v sa // “The goddesses (dev ) who spun (y ák ntan), who wove (avayan), who spread out [the cloth], who stretched on both sides the ends, may those goddesses clothe you with [life until] old age! As one having long life [now], put on this garment!” (AV 14.1.45). The Gobhila G hyas tra (2.1.18) elucidates the ritual context in which this verse ought to be pronounced: the husband, in the course of the wedding ceremony, had to put on his wife a new garment which had not yet been washed, with the verse: “The goddesses who spun, who wove”, and so on. 9 This popularized text in its Armenian and Russian versions (David Sasunskij

1939. served for many decades as the basis for translations and literary renderings of the Armenian epic in other languages.

448 Yaroslav Vassilkov

The Journal of Indo-European Studies

Bishop Garegin Srvandztiants (1874: 134). Here is a quotation from M. Abeghyan’s book (translated from German):

In contemporary Islamic Persia the notion of Fate is connected with arkh – the heavenly wheel and falak – the sky with its circle of planets. The Armenian

bakht ‘destiny; happy lot’, often used since old times, is an Iranian loanword. However, in Armenian dialects nowadays falak or, more often,

c’arkhi falak is also used in the sense of the Wheel of Fate. The latter is usually perceived as being separate from the heavens. This view finds its best expression in the tale of Mher (Srvandztiants 1874: 134), the mightiest among the heroes of the epic Sasna c er, “The Heroes of Sassoun”. He is sequestered together with his horse, in a mountain cave

10 near the

city of Van. It is believed that all the treasures of the world are hoarded together inside; also standing there is c’arkhi falak, the Wheel of the World, or the Wheel of Fate which incessantly revolves apportioning humans their destinies. Mher is watching this wheel fixedly. When it stops, he will leave the cave and destroy the world. (Abeghian 1899: 51)

The description of a wheel by Utta ka that he saw in the underworld (Mbh 1.3.150) is nothing but a variant of the “Year riddle”, well-known from the Vedas (RV 1.164. 11-14, 48; AV. 9.9.13; 10.8.4,5) and the Epic (Mbh 1.3.64-65; 3.133.21-22). The concept of the year revolving as a wheel and returning constantly to the same point is implied in some formulas of the Greek epic, and this gave M.L. West grounds to suggest that the “wheel of the year” image may be derived from Proto-Indo-European (PIE) mythology (West 2007: 371). In Iran the wheel of the year/time became more tightly linked to the concept of Fate and was placed in heaven, probably influenced by Babylonian astrology. In Zurvanism, Spihr, the wheel of the

10

Mher the Younger, a fighter against evil and injustice, defies his father's will. The father then puts a curse on him. The earth can no longer bear the weight of Mher and his horse, therefore the hero has to retire to a cave in the Rock of Van.

Heroes, Kings and Monsters in a Cave Under the Mountain 449

Volume 48, Number 3 & 4, Fall/Winter 2020

starry firmament, is the Body of the highest God, Zurvan (Time); through Spihr and the signs of the Zodiac the destiny of humans, fixed by Zurvan, is apportioned on earth (Zaehner 1972: 111, 161). This is the source of the concept of arkh-i

falak, a heavenly "roulette" that determines human destiny in the later Persian tradition. The Armenian image of the Wheel of Time revolving in a cave stands in sharp contrast with Iranian ideas and has parallels nowhere else except India. There is a choice of possible hypothetical explanations for this Indo-Armenian parallel. Firstly, we may see in both cases the image of the underground wheel of Time/Fate as a survival from the PIE period. However, the “Year riddle” that uses the image of the wheel implies acquaintance with the spoked wheel which was unlikely during the period of PIE unity

11 . We may

also assume that this image in both traditions was inherited from the period of the Greek-Armenian-Indo-Iranian dialect group postulated by many authors

12 (Godel 1975: 132; Schmidt

1980: 39; Mallory 1989: 155; Clackson 1994: 202; Gamkrelidze & Ivanov 1995: 463, 543, 330-350 [Fig. 2]; Watkins 2001: 57; Mallory & Adams 2007: 73 [Fig. 5.2], 79; Schmidt 2007: 38ff; Martirosyan 2013: passim; Kim 2018: 247, 248, 263, 264). However, in light of our present knowledge this conjecture cannot be supported by any arguments. In this article I put forward, and shall try to substantiate, another explanation. The image of the Wheel of Time revolving in a cave might have emerged in India and Armenia due to parallel development from a very archaic mythological concept shared by both traditions. I am referring here to the strong associative link between the image of a cave and the perception of time as a sequence of cycles. This idea, very old and widespread, was however realized in a particular circle of folklore motifs and plots almost exclusively by the Caucasian and Indo-European traditions. Below is a list of stories about characters chained/confined/sleeping in caves from these traditions. Time in all these stories passes in an idiosyncratic

11

The spoked wheel (of a chariot) appeared first in the Middle Bronze Age period, ca. 2100–1700 BCE, at Sintashta in the southern Urals region (Johnson 2017: 340). 12

These branches of Indo-European shared some later innovations absent in other, “peripheral”, Indo-European dialects.

450 Yaroslav Vassilkov

The Journal of Indo-European Studies

way: it is divided into cycles by constant repetition of specific events. The list naturally begins with the tale of Mher because the story of his seclusion in the Rock of Van indicated the direction for my research. Heroes or Monsters Confined in Caves (The Caucasus)  Mher, according to many variants of his tale, is a positive

figure, defender of Sassoun from its enemies. His seclusion is voluntary, which is why he, unlike chthonic characters imprisoned in a cave

13 , does not intermittently struggle to

get out, but there is a regularity of another kind connected with his sojourn inside. Every year on the Holiday of Roses (Vardavar, the Transfiguration) and on Ascension Day he appears on horseback to discover whether or not the earth can hold him again (see Footnote 10).

 The image of another Armenian epic hero, King Artavazd is ambivalent. On the one hand he is a wise ruler, defender of the country, fighting demonic neighbours. In other versions he himself is partly demonic (a vishap). Cursed by his father (like Mher), he was kidnapped by evil spirits (k aj) while hunting and locked in a cave in Mount Ararat. The "vicious" Artavazd tries to break his chains and get out of the cave to destroy the world while two dogs lick or gnaw at them. By the year’s end the chains become very thin, but before New Year’s Day (or every Saturday), on leaving to go home, the Armenian blacksmiths strike the anvil with hammers three times and the chains regain their strength (Abegyan 1948: 54-56).

 The story of Artavazd has a parallel in Iranian mythology with which it may be genetically linked. I am referring to the Iranian myth of a dragon A i Dah ka and its quasi-

13

As we shall see, a character confined in a cave is sometimes a mythic figure: chthonic monster, enemy of the gods or unsuccessful pretender to the throne of heaven. In some cases, he may be the highest god himself, whose power is temporarily usurped by a demonic antagonist. An epic hero as defender of his tribe or nation is as a rule characterized positively, though he may be put in a cave as punishment for challenging a higher god/God or for open rebellion; so he still retains some features of a chthonic monster and his nature is ambivalent (as in the case of Artavazd). Quasi-historical, legendary kings asleep in a cave under a mountain usually possess only positive qualities.

Heroes, Kings and Monsters in a Cave Under the Mountain 451

Volume 48, Number 3 & 4, Fall/Winter 2020

historical transformation into a human king in the epic legend of King Za k. After defeat, depending on the version, either in dragon or human form, he is locked in a cave in the Demavend (Dam wand) mountain where he must stay until the end of Time. The chained Za k tries to break his fetters, causing earthquakes (Carnoy 1917: 265-266, 320-323; Hinnels 1985: 39-40, 54, 68, 114-117). It is worth noting that the leading role in the revolt against the tyranny of Za k is played by the blacksmith K ve (Daryaee 1999).

 The Georgian hero Amirani is locked in a cave and chained to a pole as a punishment for his struggle against God. Once every seven years the cave opens and Amirani is visible inside. A dog weakens his chain by licking it, but on Passion Thursday or Christmas Eve the blacksmiths (enemies he had sworn to destroy) strike the anvil with their hammers and the chain becomes thicker again. In another variant from East Georgia, Amirani shakes the pole, but at the moment he is ready to pull it out, a wagtail lands on it. Amirani strikes the top of the pole with a hammer, the bird flies away and the pole stands firm (Chikovani 1966: 111-112; Hunt 2012: 353-354).

 In a similar way a Wagtail regularly destroys the attempts of Abryskil, the God-fighter of the Abkhaz epic, to break his chains. In another version a dog and a cat lick at his chain, but an old witch who is guarding the hero in the cave interferes. She says to the chain: "Be strong again!", and the chain becomes strong (Gartskiya 1892: 34-38; Dirr 1922: 242-246; Olrik 1922: 167-168; Dzhapua 2003: 110-111, 327, 335; Hunt 2012: 349-350). A bird also appears in the Adyghe tales of the chained Old Man, which feature blacksmiths as well (Colarusso 2002: 168-169; Dzhapua 2003: 114; Hunt 2012: 355-356). There are other Caucasian versions of the same story (Miller 1883: 101-102, 105, 107-108; Berezkin & Duvakin n.d., motif C33: Caucasus–Asia Minor).

452 Yaroslav Vassilkov

The Journal of Indo-European Studies

Heroes or Monsters Confined in Caves or on Rocks (The Balkans and Central Europe) Another region where similar motifs can be found is the Balkans.  Here the Serbian Marco Kralevich who stays in a cave has

a lot in common with the Armenian Mher. The difference is that Marco is a historical figure. He is definitely a positive character, therefore nobody tries to keep him confined. He sleeps in the cave and will leave of his own accord in due course (Hartland 1891: 218). Remarkably, Marco, like Mher, goes out of his cave on certain holidays.

 Another Serbian character, King Dukljan or Dukljanin, is a demonic figure and adversary of God. Dukljan is chained and constantly gnaws on his chains, and each year around Christmas time nearly breaks free to destroy the world. But then Gypsy (Romani) blacksmiths strike the anvil with their hammers, and the chains become thick again (Kulishich et al. 1970:122).

 In Albanian folklore, a devil is tied to a rock by a huge chain. He gnaws on the chain during the year, and by Holy Saturday the chain grows almost thin enough to snap, but on Holy Sunday Christ comes and fastens the devil to the rock with a new one (Miller 1883: 114).

 The famous Greek myth of Prometheus may be viewed as a Balkan variant of the story about a chained hero. Many scholars have studied the myth of this rebellious Titan against the background of its numerous Caucasian parallels (Miller 1883; Olrik 1922: 253-262, 272, 288; Chikovani 1966: 54-52, 67-71; Charachidzé 1986; Hunt 2012: 330-333; Duvakin 2018). In the Chechen story of Pkharmat (Kuryuko in the Ingush version), the hero who stole fire from heaven and brought it to mankind, the god Sela punished Pkharmat by chaining him to a mountain. Each morning Ida, the king of birds comes to the hero and pecks at his liver (Hunt 2012: 343). This story is so close in its structure to the Prometheus myth that influence of Greek myth via printed books in Russian may well be suspected. However similar stories are known to many other ethnic traditions of the Caucasians. There is, for example, an Adyghe legend about the Nart hero Nasran

Heroes, Kings and Monsters in a Cave Under the Mountain 453

Volume 48, Number 3 & 4, Fall/Winter 2020

who brought fire stolen by the gods back to men. The god Paqua chained the hero to the summit of a mountain and ordered his giant eagle to tear Nasran’s chest and drink his blood (Colarusso 2002: 159-163). In the Kabardian (East Circassian) tale the hero, having disclosed a secret belonging to Tha (God) is chained to Mount Elbrus, and every day a black kite comes to peck his heart (Miller 1883: 101-102; Dirr 1922: 241-242). According to David Hunt, forty-five different “Prometheus” legends have been identified in the Caucasus (Hunt 2012: 330). All this allows us to suggest that the Prometheus myth in the Caucasus has an autochthonous origin, or that Caucasians’ contacts with the Greeks (or other Indo-Europeans) occurred much earlier than Russian literary influence. A feature specific to all Promethean stories is the regularity most clearly presented by the Greek myth: every day a vulture or eagle comes to the hero chained to a pillar in the Caucasian mountains and tears at his liver. During the night the liver grows again, and in the morning the torture begins anew (Graves 1955: 145).

One more region where stories about a chained monster or hero can be found is Central Europe.  Bavarian blacksmiths strike the anvil three times on the

eve of St. Jacob's day at the end of June, because by that day the devil, chained to a rock, had almost sawn through his chain. Before holidays in the Tirol, blacksmiths did the same to secure Lucifer's chains, stopping him breaking free and destroying the world (Miller 1883: 114).

 A pre-Christian variant of these views was preserved in Germany. In some villages the blacksmiths strike the anvil three times to keep inside the terrible wolf chained behind nine iron doors (Miller 1883: 114). The wolf is certainly none other than the Ancient Scandinavian mythic Fenrir who will succeed in freeing himself at the time of Ragnarök. Another similar character is Loki, the trickster in Norse mythology, punished by the gods for his role in engineering the death of Baldr. Loki is bound and left to writhe beneath the mouth of a snake which drops its venom onto his face. His wife Sigyn sits with a bowl to catch the drops, but each time she goes to empty it, the

454 Yaroslav Vassilkov

The Journal of Indo-European Studies

poison falls on Loki again. His writhing causes earthquakes (Ellis Davidson 1981: 37, 38).

The King Asleep in the Mountain (Central and Western Europe) Widespread in Central, Northern and Western Europe are legends based on “king under the mountain" or " king asleep in the mountain" motif (D 1960.2 in the Stith Thompson’s Motif-Index). Such are stories of Frederick Barbarossa, Karl the Great, Heinrich the Fowler, Otto the Great, Holger the Dane, King Arthur and other Germanic and Celtic kings and heroes (Krappe 1935: 77-78). Each of them is a national hero who sleeps until the day the country needs him to save or restore it to greatness. They stay in a cave of their own will and do not regularly attempt to get free, but a remarkable regularity of a different kind can be observed.  Once in a hundred years Karl the Great (Charlemagne)

asks a shepherd if ravens still fly round the mountain. When they cease flying and the king's beard can twist three times round the table where he sits, he will leave the cave and join the last battle between good and evil (Grimm 1835: 537-538; Hartland 1891: 213-215). Similar stories were told about Friedrich Barbarossa.

 Every year on Christmas Eve an angel appears before Holger the Dane who sits in a cellar under the Kronborg castle in Elsinore, and the hero asks him: What is going on in Denmark, is everything all right? And the angel says: "Yes, everything is all right, you may sleep on".

 In the legends of King Arthur and many others (e.g., Robert the Bruce, king of Scotland, or Earl Gerald of Mullaghmast, an Irish hero, [see Hartland 1891: 207-212]) we find the same recurrent pattern: a shepherd or an angel regularly visits the king under the mountain, and the king asks him whether it is time for him to come out.

* * *

Heroes, Kings and Monsters in a Cave Under the Mountain 455

Volume 48, Number 3 & 4, Fall/Winter 2020

All the examples cited above indicate that the time in the cave is not linear but cyclic. Regularly, the chain becomes thinner every year, but on the eve of a holiday everything goes back to square one. The mountain splits open regularly on an appointed day, and the hero goes out to look at the world, or a shepherd visits him and answers his questions. The time in the cave is a series of cycles following one after the other. We may call this an example of “eternal return” or describe it by a poetic metaphor of the “Wheel of Time revolving in a cave”. It can therefore be suggested that when the Wheel of Time actually appears in the Armenian and Indian epics, it is a result of a parallel poetic interpretation of some very archaic views linked with caves. Whether the image of the cave is indeed linked with the idea of “eternal return” or the concept of time understood as a series of cycles can be verified if we introduce material from the two great epics of India, the Mah bh rata and the R m ya a, never before used in this connection. Indian Epic Characters in Caves

 There is for example the story of Para ur ma, a brahmin-warrior (Mbh 3.115.1–6; 117.16–18). Having exterminated all k atriyas (the warrior class), he retires to the Mahendra mountain for good. The word "cave" is absent in the texts, but where else can a hermit live on a mountain? Moreover, he is hidden, nobody can see him. But on the 8th and 14th day of each lunar month he makes his appearance to other hermits and pilgrims who gather especially to catch sight of him. Hundreds of years after the time of Para ur ma’s heroic deeds, the main heroes of the epic, the P ava brothers, visit the mountain on the eve of the 14th day and meet him in the morning during their pilgrimage around India. The regularity with which Para ur ma makes his appearance deserves attention.

 There is one more episode: (Mbh 1.189.9-26) Indra encounters the great God iva in the guise of a handsome youth playing a game of dice with P rvat at the top of a mountain in the Himalayas. In addressing the unrecognized "youth", Indra boastfully calls himself "king of the gods" and "master of the universe", but iva

456 Yaroslav Vassilkov

The Journal of Indo-European Studies

paralyses him and moves the mountain aside. Underneath is a cave in which four of the former Indras, i.e. kings of the gods in previous epochs, are kept imprisoned. All of them were punished like the present Indra, for the sin of pride. iva orders the present Indra to join them. All five are to be confined to the cave and sleep there until they are born on earth in the guise of the five P avas. It is only after they have performed great deeds that they will be allowed to return to the celestial world. Notably, the rulers of the five consecutive world epochs enter the cave one after the other. Also remarkable is the fact that iva features here as Lord of Time, because the game of dice in the epic is mythically linked with the cycle of seasons and time in general

14 .

 In the 12 th

book of the epic, ntiparvan, there are two conversations between Indra ( akra) and the asura, Bali, the defeated former "Indra" (Mbh 12. 216-217, 220). Bali, having assumed the aspect of a donkey

15 , is chained in a

cave. Indra has come to humiliate his predecessor, but Bali stays calm and tells Indra of the almighty Time whose cycles (pary ya) determine everything in the world. Bali speaks of thousands of Indras who came before the

14

See e.g., Mbh13. 42.25; 43.5, where the image of six seasons ( tava ) playing dice clearly serves to illustrate the cyclic nature of Time. 15

It seems that the defeated “king of the gods” (or pretender to this title) who assumes the aspect of an animal is a common Indo-European, or at least Graeco-Aryan marginally retained motif. In one Greek myth, when the son of Tartarus, the monstrous giant Typhon, seized power on Olympus, the gods fled in terror to Egypt, where they assumed animal forms: Zeus became a ram; Apollo, a crow; Ares, a boar and so on. Sometime later Zeus in his own form fought Typhon and was defeated and confined to a cave. Released by the gods, Zeus fought Typhon again until he hurled Mount Aetna on top of his enemy. Typhon was thought to have remained under the mountain, which was shown by a fire that from time to time issues forth from the mountain’s cone (Graves 1955: 134). According to the Mah bh rata (3. 175-178), the mortal king, Nahu a, through his unprecedented sacrifices and austerities obtained sovereignty over the whole universe, i.e. became an Indra, king of the gods. At first a pious and benevolent ruler, he later became inflated with pride and insulted the heavenly Brahmins. They cursed him, and Nahu a was hurled down to earth where he had to live in a cave having assumed the form of a huge predatory snake (boa).

Heroes, Kings and Monsters in a Cave Under the Mountain 457

Volume 48, Number 3 & 4, Fall/Winter 2020

present one and tells him that he is bound to lose his power with the next turn of Time.

 There are also parallels to the motif of a character asleep in a cave in Indian epics. In the R m ya a Kumbhakar a, a brother of R ma’s demonic antagonist R va a, is a dreadful monster and voracious cannibal. Together with his brothers, he practices severe austerities (tapas) to attain power. Eventually the highest god Brahm appears to fulfill their wishes. When it is Kumbhakar a’s turn to ask Brahm for a reward, the gods fall into panic, since if the gigantic monster obtains additional strength, he will be able to devour all living things in the universe. Therefore Brahm orders the goddess of Speech, Sarasvat to enter Kumbhakar a’s body and change the words in his mouth into a formulation that suits the gods better. When Brahm asks Kumbhakar a what kind of reward he would like to receive, the monster replies reluctantly: “My wish is to sleep for a great number of years”. Ever since then Kumbhakar a has slept in a cave for six months at a time, after which he eats voraciously for one day, and then goes back to sleep again (R m ya a 7. 10.31-41 [Valmiki 2017]; Mbh 3.259.28; Adhyatmar m ya a 7.2.20-22 [Adhyatmar m ya a n.d.: 336]).

 Another demonic epic character, asura Dhundhu, has so much in common with Kumbhakar a that he is directly compared with him in the text of the Mah bh rata (Mbh 3.195.26: kumbhakar am iv ‘param ‘like another Kumbhakar a’). Dhundhu performs great austerities and obtains from Brahm the reward of being invincible to Gods, D navas (Asuras), Yak as, Gandharvas and R k asas. However, Dhundhu was still unable to overcome and kill his greatest enemy, Vi u. The demon then goes to a desert (“a sea of sand known as Ujj naka”) and begins practicing a unique form of austerity, with the obvious aim of destroying Vi u and devastating the worlds. He goes underground and sleeps there, deep in the sand, waking up and beginning to breathe at the end of every year. Then the whole earth begins to tremble, Dhundhu’s breath raises clouds of sand and shrouds the sun, and the sparks and flames from his fiery breath

458 Yaroslav Vassilkov

The Journal of Indo-European Studies

spread far around (Mbh 3.193.14-22; 195.1-33). E.W. Hopkins keenly remarked that Dhundhu “thus appears to be as much of a volcano as the Sicilian giant” (Hopkins 1915: 49), i.e., probably, Typhon under Mount Aetna mentioned in Footnote 16. Another parallel is provided by Iranian A i Dah ka and Za k under the mountain Demavend.

Each of the Indian epic episodes summarized above contains a motif of cyclic repetition which can be presented by the following chart:

Name Character Text Regularity Para ur ma hero Mbh emerges on the 8

th and 14

th of

each month Indras kings of the

gods Mbh replace their predecessors in a

position and then appear one by one in the cave under a mountain

Bali former king of the gods

R m. locked and chained in a cave, tells Indra about the inevitable change of rulers in the universe due to the “turns of Time”

Kumbhakar a monster Mbh wakes up in his cave for one day every six months

Dhundhu monster Mbh wakes up and moves underground at the end of each year

It can therefore be concluded that Indian epic material supports our proposition: as soon as the image of a cave appears in connection with a mythic or epic character it is associated with time-cycles, “turns of Time”. To explain this I can only suggest that all stories of characters imprisoned or sleeping in a cave are based on the strong link between the image of a cave and the mytho-ritual complex of ideas: “birth – death – rebirth” (Toporov 1992), deeply rooted in human consciousness

16 .

16

In the mythological worldview of hunter-gatherers, which revealed itself for the first time in the Upper Paleolithic cave art, the soul of an animal killed by

Heroes, Kings and Monsters in a Cave Under the Mountain 459

Volume 48, Number 3 & 4, Fall/Winter 2020

Indo-Europeans and the Caucasus The association of the cave with cyclical time and the mythological complex of “birth-death-rebirth” seems to have been shared by all branches of humankind. It found its expression in cave burials and also the construction in various parts of the world of artificial ‘caves’ under artificial ‘mountains’ for the bodies of rulers or religious leaders inside, sometimes mummified

17 . But stories of imprisoned mythical

monsters or heroes and kings sleeping in caves waiting for their time to emerge, based on the same association, have a more restricted distribution. They were recorded almost exclusively in the Caucasus or territories to the East and West of this area inhabited by speakers of Indo-European languages. If a story belonging to this circle is recorded within a non-Indo-European tradition outside the Caucasus, it is generally a borrowing

18 .

a hunter returns to the spirit world or to the Master/Mistress of animals in order to be reincarnated in an animal of the same species (Ingold 1986: 243, 246-247; Vitebsky 2006: 262-263; Witzel 2011; Willerslev at al. 2014: 7). In the ritual practice of hunter-gatherer societies, the central role was played by communication with the world of animal spirits with the aim to ensure rebirth of the killed animals. The world of animal spirits was often located in a cave (Eliade 1972: 42; Heyden 2005 [1987]: 1468; Lewis-Williams 1997: 328). There is probably also evidence of practices to ensure rebirth in burials of animals and humans found in ancient caves. The cave was understood as a place where birth, death and rebirth endlessly rotated. Moreover, “since Paleolithic times caves have been preferred places for many rites of passage” (Heyden 2005 [1987]: 1470; Levy 1948: 37-39, 49, 53; Eliade 1972: 46-48, 50-52, 101, 134-136), which connects the caves with the rotation of stages of life and age classes. All this could be conducive to forming a close association in the consciousness of humans between the cave and the notion of time cycles. 17

Their range is not limited by the pyramids of Egypt or Central America, but includes everything from the megalithic passage tombs of the British Isles like Newgrange, great burrows (kurgans) of the Eurasian steppe, and the earliest st pas of India to the present-day mountain- or pyramid-form cavernous mausoleums of embalmed Communist leaders. Even these latest monuments retain in their symbolism a vague idea of resurrection (cf., e.g., Tumarkin 1997). 18

E.g., in the Kirghiz epic Semetei, son of Manas, does not die but retires to a cave, “where his immortality is shared by his white falcon and faithful horse” (Zhirmunskij 1979: 218). This exceptional case may be explained by the influence on the warriors’ lore and epic tradition of the Turks from the culture of their Iranian-speaking predecessors in the Eurasian steppe (cf., e.g., Rozwadowski 2004: 11).

460 Yaroslav Vassilkov

The Journal of Indo-European Studies

Tales about heroes, kings and monsters in a cave under the mountain may be called a specific common legacy of Caucasians and Indo-Europeans. The only way to explain the origin of this common legacy is to assume that it is a result of long-term cultural contacts between Caucasians and Indo-Europeans. A broad distribution of stories about characters confined or sleeping in a cave in various Indo-European traditions excludes the possibility that such contacts could have taken place in connection with any single historical episode of an Indo-European speaking people’s penetration into the Caucasus (Scythian migrations over the Caucasus to the Middle East, the Greek colonization of the Black Sea coast etc.). We should sooner relate the initial phase of these contacts to a prehistoric period when the ancestors of the IE speaking peoples constituted a linguistic and cultural unity. The majority of linguists at present are inclined to assume that in the Late Neolithic and Early Bronze periods the Proto-Indo-European (PIE) language had contacts with Proto-North-Caucasian (PNC), or one of its two (Northwest-Caucasian and Northeast- aucasian) branches, though there is no real agreement on the nature of these contacts

19 . There is also no

common opinion about the region where such contacts could take place, however the generally accepted locale is in the region to the north of the Greater Caucasus mountain range

20 .

19

J. Colarusso derives PIE and Northwest Caucasian from a common proto-language: Proto-Pontic (Colarusso 1992; Colarusso 2019). A.R. Bomhard sees in the PIE the result of the imposition of an Euroasiatic/Indo-Uralic language on “a population speaking one or more primordial Northwest Caucasian languages” (Bomhard 2019: 11). According to F. Kortlandt, the PIE had been originally an Indo-Uralic language which was transformed due to the contacts with not Northwest, but Northeast Caucasian (Kortlandt 2019). S.A. Starostin (1985; 1988 [= Starostin 2009]) argued for massive lexical borrowings by PIE from NWC in situation of their direct contact. R. Matasovi finds many examples of borrowing between PIE and NWC in the works of Starostin, Colarusso and Bomhard inconclusive, but demonstrates at the same time exclusive areal-typological parallels in phonology and grammar between PIE and North Caucasian which lead him to conclude that “PIE was, indeed, in contact with languages of the northern Caucasus” (Matasovi 2012: 24-25). 20

Deviations emerge in connection with alternative hypotheses of the IE homeland. S. Starostin, following the ideas of T. Gamkrelidze and V. Ivanov (Gamkrelidze & Ivanov 1995 [Russian edition – 1984]), thought that contacts

Heroes, Kings and Monsters in a Cave Under the Mountain 461

Volume 48, Number 3 & 4, Fall/Winter 2020

It is at this place and time, we suggest, that stories about characters confined or retired in caves in the process of cultural contact would become for the first time the shared property of Indo-Europeans and Caucasians

21 .

The high concentration and exceptional variability of plots and motifs under discussion in the Caucasus permits the suggestion that their place of origin must be established here, in the mountains, while the Indo-Europeans who came into contact with the Caucasians somewhere in the northern foothills, were the "receiving side". Linguistic contacts between Indo-Europeans and Caucasians continued after the disintegration of PIE. I am tempted to make a reference here to my own paper (Vasilkov 1994) written after several summer seasons on an archaeological expedition at the Novosvobodnaya (Klady) site in Adyghea. A comparison of the Novosvobodnaya funeral rite with the building of a tomb under a barrow ( ma na), described in the Late Vedic atapatha-Br hma a (13.8.1-4 [ atapatha-Br hma a 1900: 421-440]), has revealed a striking parallelism. A typical Novosvobodnaya tumulus with a chamber-tomb inside reveals such a large number of correspondences that it may be regarded as a physical illustration of the Vedic description. Parallels with certain elements of Novosvobodnaya art and its mythological motifs were found in ancient Greek, Indian and Iranian traditions. This gives us some grounds to suggest that the language of the

between PIE and PNC could have taken place only to the south of the Caucasus in the hypothetical Anatolian homeland of both PIE and the North Caucasian languages (Starostin 1985: 89). A group of scholars (Kassian 2010: 425-427; Duvakin 2018; 2018a) looks for the contact zone in the Balkans where an IE homeland had been first localized by I.M. Diakonov (1985). 21

Recently E.N. Duvakin in a comparative study of a group of “Promethean” motifs (Duvakin 2018; Duvakin 2018a) made a similar suggestion: folklore parallels between Caucasian and Ancient Classical (Greek and Latin) mythological traditions may “reflect the relationships between early Indo-European and North Caucasian-speaking tribes which are supported by lexical evidence”. The only difference with my approach is that E.N. Duvakin, following A. Kassian (2010), locates the zone of these early contacts in the “Carpato-Balkan area”.

462 Yaroslav Vassilkov

The Journal of Indo-European Studies

Novosvododnaya culture belonged probably to the above-mentioned Greek-Armenian-Indo-Iranian dialect group

22 .

Linguists have traced some borrowings from the North Caucasian languages in separate IE languages, descendants of the PIE: Hittite, Proto-Greek, Proto-Italic, Proto-Indo-Aryan, Iranian and Eastern Iranian (Nikolaev 1985; Kullanda 2012). Archaeologists believe that (Proto-) Iranians were neighbors of North Caucasians from very early times (2

nd mill. BC, if not

earlier [cf. Chlenova 1984]). They and other IE-speaking tribes on many occasions could have penetrated from their hypothetical original or secondary homeland in the western region of the Eurasian Steppe across the Caucasus into Asia Minor and the Middle East. Those scholars who locate the IE homeland in the Near or Middle East argue for migrations across the Caucasus in the opposite direction (see e.g., Gamkrelidze & Ivanov 1995: 811-814; Kozintsev 2016; Reich 2018: 120; Wang et al. 2018: lines 647-551; Kozintsev 2019: 345-348, 352-354 [Fig. 1]). Of special importance are results of a recent paleogenetic study (Wang et al. 2018) which reveal that the Caucasus Mountains were not an insurmountable barrier, but rather a corridor or bridge to human population movements in prehistory. There is clear archaeological evidence of intensive intercultural contacts via the Greater Caucasus in the Late Bronze and Early Iron Age periods (Skakov 2011: 124). The migrations of Scythians over the Caucasus to the Middle East and Asia Minor prove that the corridor was open in historical times too. Indo-Europeans who penetrated repeatedly into this mountainous region could become acquainted with new versions of stories about characters chained/confined/sleeping in caves, and make their own creative contribution to the ancient legacy they shared with the peoples of the Caucasus.

Acknowledgement I should like to record my deepest gratitude to Rosemary Babichev who substantially improved my English.

22

The language of the Maykop culture proper in the opinion of some scholars was most probably (Proto-) North Caucasian (Kassian 2010: 427; cf.: Starostin 1985: 89; Antony 2007: 297). Therefore I hope that it is not too bold to imagine that the Novosvobodnaya-Maykop symbiosis could be a bilingual society similar to the Sumero-Akkadian, Hittite-Hattic or Hurro-Aryan in Mitanni.

How to pull a wagon in Indo-European

Vedic īṣā́- ‘shaft’, áyate and ī́yate ‘speeds’, and a new old root for ‘move (a vehicle)’

Abstract: This paper discusses the formal relationship between Hittite ḫišša- c., Vedic īṣā́- f. < *h₂ihxséh₂ ‘shaft (of a cart)’ and the s-stem *h₂éih̯x-os > Slovene ojẹ̑ n., gen. sg. ojẹ̑sa ‘shaft (of a cart)’. It is claimed that the underlying root $*√h₂eih̯x $‘pull, move (a vehicle)’ accounts for substantives such as Lith. íena f. ‘shaft’ and PGmc. *airō- f. ‘oar’ and can also be seen as the basis of the two Vedic verbs áyate ‘speeds’ and ī́yate ‘speeds (on a chariot)’, the discussion of which constitutes the main body of this paper. Finally, $*√h₂eih̯x $is further specified as $*√h₂eih̯₂ $and equated with the root that underlies Ved. yā́ti ‘rides, moves, travels’, Lith. jóju, OCS jadǫ, Toch. B iyaṃ.

Keywords: verbal morphology, morphosyntax, nominal derivation, schwebeablaut, etymology, Vedic philology

In memoriam Chlodwig H. Werba (1955–2019)

1 Introduction As is well known,1 Hittite ḫišša- c. forms an almost perfect equation with Vedic īṣā́-f. (RV+). Both words denote the ‘drawbar’ or ‘thill’, i.e., the shaft that connects a vehicle to the yoke or harness of the draft animals. If there is only one horse or ox, a pair of shafts is needed. As a word denoting an essential part of a tangible artifact with a potentially datable origin, the ‘shaft’ word has received much attention in the discussion of the dating of the proto-language and the determination of the Proto-Indo-European homeland.2

1 The connection was first mentioned publicly by Sommer 1949: 161 and has since been included in every etymological dictionary. 2 Cf. Anthony 2007: 35f.; Anthony & Ringe 2015: 203f.; Pereltsvaig & Lewis 2015: 172; Sherman Morris 2017: 66.

The Hittite word is attested only in the singular: acc. sg. ḫi-iš-ša-an (NS), dat.-loc. sg. ḫi-iš-ši (MS; OH/NS; NS), ḫe-eš-ši (NS).3 The earliest attestation is found in the Old Assyrian texts of Kültepe/Kaneš (19th–18th c. BCE) in the loanword hiššannum, with °-n(n)- being a commonly found “extension” for loanwords also present in tuzzinnum ‘army’ vis-à-vis Hitt. tuzzi- c. ‘id.’ (cf. Dercksen 2007: 30–35). Vedic īṣā́- f. appears twice in the Rigveda as a simplex (both times in the singular)4 and once as the second member of the bahuvrīhi ékeṣa- ‘having one shaft’.5 A dual form īṣé ‘pair of shafts’ is attested in the Atharvaveda (PW: s.v. īṣā́-).

Both words can be traced back to a pre-form *h₂ihxséh₂‑.6 The root-final la-ryngeal can be of any color if one assumes that intervocalic *Vh₂sV (just as is commonly accepted for *Vh₁sV and *Vh₃sV) assimilated to Hitt. VššV.7 The recon-struction of the oxytone accent is based on Ved. īṣā́- alone as there are no plene written endings of ḫišša- to confirm this, nor is there a plene written †ḫi-i-iš° to refute it. According to Kloekhorst (EDHIL: 72), however, the Hittite geminate can only be explained as the product of an assimilation of *h₁ or *h₃ plus *s before the accented vowel, which presupposes an oxytone formation as the source of ḫišša-, too. Finally, while it is true that ḫišša- need not continue a formation in *-eh₂‑ and could equally well be traced back to a thematic masculine *h₂ihxsó-, this option seems unattractive—at least for now—in view of Ved. īṣā́-, itself an *‑eh₂‑ feminine.

Therefore, a reconstruction *h₂ihxséh₂‑ (common gender, later feminine) is a safe bet within the parameters of the comparative method.

2 Formal analysis of *h₂ihxséh₂‑ The form *h₂ihxséh₂‑ can be further segmented as *h₂ihx-s-éh₂‑ when another piece of related material is added: Modern Slovene preserves an s-stem ojẹ̑ n., gen. sg. ojẹ̑sa ‘thill, shaft (of a cart)’8 that is the regular continuant of a neuter *h₂éih̯x-os, a form that—by all appearances—is closely related to *h₂ihx-s-éh₂‑.9 Exactly how the relationship between *h₂ihxséh₂‑ and *h₂éih̯xos is best explained is a question that has not received much attention in the literature.10 On the surface, their relationship looks derivational, yet, strangely, both the continuants of *h₂éih̯x-os and its apparent derivative *h₂ihx-s-éh₂‑ denote the exact same thing, viz. the ‘shaft (of a cart)’, a situationwewould perhaps not immediately expect if wewere dealing with a base and its seemingly exocentric derivative. To account for the endocentric meaning of *h₂ihx-s-éh₂‑, it might be worthwhile to explore two other possibilities (neither of which will lead to a successful result) before returning to the analysis as a derivative.

2.1 Remodeling or extension

On the one hand, one could think of *-eh₂- as a mere functionless remodeling or extension of the consonant stem,11 of a kind similar to what one might recognize in Gk. $φυγή, $Lat. fuga ‘flight’ vis-à-vis the synonymous root noun Gk. $φύγ- $(seen in $φύγα-δε $‘to flight’), or in Gk. $γενεά $f. ‘race, family, offspring’ next to the s-stem $γένος $n. ‘race, offspring’. But this route is unappealing for several reasons. For one thing, one wonders why the remodeling was based on the double zero-grade stem of *h₂éih̯x-os that was characteristic (if at all) only for the instr. sg. of this

noun class.12 It is also unclear why the functionless enlargement suffix would be *-eh₂- (and accented no less) and not the thematic vowel *-o‑. Thirdly, if it were a plain remodeling, why did the gender shift from neuter (*h₂éih̯x-os) to common gender/feminine (*h₂ihxséh₂-)? In addition, neither for Gk. $φυγή $and Lat. fuga ‘flight’ nor for Gk. $γενεά $f. ‘race, family, offspring’ is a remodeling or an extension the preferred (or even a valid) explanation.13 Gk. $φυγή $and Lat. fuga ‘flight’, for example, just seem to belong to a class of verbal nouns in *-éh₂- with a zero-grade root that might originally (that is, as a type) have been derived from root nouns (see Nussbaum 2017: 258), but that can be regarded as an independent word-formation type in its own right.

2.2 A reinterpreted inflectional form

As an alternative one could hypothesize that *h₂ihx-s-éh₂‑ is a former inflectional form of the s-stem that got reinterpreted as a common gender and later feminine *-eh₂-stem. Such a reinterpretation of a case form might be compared to the Latin plural oculī ‘eyes’, which is probably a neuter dual in origin (*-o-ih₁ > Lat. -ī) that after the loss of the dual got reinterpreted as a masculine plural (*-oi̯ > Lat. -ī) and led to the backformation of a masculine nom. sg. oculus ‘eye’ (replacing a neuter *okʷelom, a derivative of the neuter root noun *h₃okʷ- ‘eye’).14 A Vedic example of a secondary ā-stem may be doṣā́- f. ‘darkness, night’, presumably a backformation from the instr. sg. doṣā́ ‘in the evening, at dusk’ (by far the most common case form of this word in the RV) that itself is probably an inherited s-stem instr. sg. *deu̯-s-éh₁ ‘at the sinking (sc. of the sun)’ (for which one can compare the very common Homeric formula $δύῃ/δύσετό τ’ ἠέλιος $‘and the sun sinks/sank’).

A candidate for the reinterpretation of *h₂ihxséh₂‑ as a new nom. sg. that comes to mind is the nom.-acc. pl. of an athematic neuter, the case ending of which is universally reconstructed as *-h₂. However, based on the evidence of the daughter languages, we would expect a neuter s-stem nom.-acc. pl. to surface as *h₂éih̯x-os-h₂ > *h₂éih̯x-ōs (cf. *mén-ōs > nom.-acc. pl. OAv. manā̊ ‘thoughts’) or *h₂éih̯x-es-h₂ (cf. *ǵénh₁-es-h₂ > nom.-acc. pl. Gk. $γένεα, $Lat. genera), but certainly not as *h₂ihx‑s‑éh₂ with a double zero grade in the base and with what would have to be interpreted as an otherwise nonexistent full grade of the plural ending *-h₂.

In addition, there is nothing that points to a plural origin of *h₂ihxséh₂‑ which simply means ‘(one) shaft’.

2.3 A derived collective

If a functionless remodeling and a reinterpreted inflectional form can be dismissed, we are leftwith the option of seeing *h₂ihx‑s‑éh₂ as a derivative of *h₂éih̯x-os. Aprima facie promising path with the potential not only to account for the ablaut reduction in *h₂ihx‑s‑éh₂ and the (apparent) full grade *‑éh₂‑, but also possibly to explain the lack of an exocentricmeaning in the derivative *h₂ihx‑s‑éh₂would be to interpret the formnot as an inflectedplural but rather as anold collective.15 FollowingNussbaum (2014a: 290–292; 2017: 257f.), the creation of collectives typically consists of two derivational steps: (a) the formation of a denominal possessive adjective (e.g., with *-ó-) and (b) its substantivization with *-h₂-. Compare Gk. $φρᾱ́τηρ $‘clansman’ $→ $(a) $*φρᾱτρ-ό- $‘having/consisting of clansmen’16 $→ $(b) $φρᾱ́τρᾱ $f. ‘clan’ (*‘clansmen as a collective’). Since originally the denominal suffix *-ó- led to a reduction of the ablaut grades in the base word (e.g., *(h₁)réu̯dʰ-os n. ‘redness’ $→ $*(h₁)rudʰ-s-ó- ‘having redness’ > Lat. russus ‘red(-haired)’; see already Persson 1893: 271), the double zero grade in *h₂ihx-s-éh₂‑would not be an obstacle, it would even be expected. The putative full grade *‑éh₂-would then not be a full grade at all, but rather *-é-h₂- (i.e., the thematic vowel plus *-h₂-).

But the interpretation of *h₂ihxséh₂‑ as a collective runs into at least two prob-lems. For one thing, the collectives (and ‘delibatives’; seeNussbaum2014a: 277–288) that the abovementioned bipartite process creates typically show recessive accent with respect to the underlying adjective (cf. Höfler 2020: 192–194). Compare Gk. $φρᾱ́τρᾱ $f. ‘clan’ (from above), or Gk. $ἀήρ $‘mist, haze; air’ (< *h₂usḗr ‘morning thing’) $→ $*h₂usr‑ó- (cf. Ved. usrá- ‘matutinal’) $→ $Gk. $αὔρα $f. ‘a cool breeze, the fresh air of morning, morning mist’ (< *h₂úsreh2- delibative ‘a bit of mist/air’) (cf. Nussbaum 2014a: 297), or *méu̯k-os n. ‘slime’ $→ *muk-s-ó-→ $*múkseh₂- > $*μύξη $>> $μύξᾰ $Gk. $μύξα $f. ‘(a bit of) mucus, slime’.17 The apparent counterexamples against this rule can be explained differently.18 And even if one is skeptical towards this accentua-

tion rule and believes that there also existed oxytone derived collectives in PIE,19 or if one concedes that a former recessively accented collective **h₂íhxseh₂‑ acquired an oxytone accent secondarily (perhaps in analogy to the verbal nouns in *-éh₂- of the type Gk. $φυγή, $Lat. fuga ‘flight’ or Gk. $τομή $‘cutting’, Lat. toga ‘covering’), there is an almost insurmountable obstacle left. If *h₂éih̯x-osmeant ‘shaft’ (Slov. ojẹ̑), a collective based on this s-stem should denote something like ‘ensemble of shafts’ or ‘shafts as a collective’. However, as seen above, a cart typically either has one shaft (for a team of draft animals) or two shafts (for a single draft animal), reflected in the exclusive use of the continuants of *h₂ihxséh₂‑ in the singular (Hitt. ḫišša-), and singular and dual (Ved. īṣā́-), respectively. The interpretation of *h₂ihxséh₂‑ (whose continuants both mean ‘(one) shaft’) as a former collective is therefore not only counterintuitive, but it is also difficult to argue for in the first place, as these shafts naturally, so to speak, only came as solitary items or in pairs, but not in anything that would justify the use of a collective. In sum, *h₂ihxséh₂‑ does not lend itself to the analysis as a functionless remodeling or extension of *h₂éih̯x-os, nor can it be a former inflectional form of the s-stem or a derived collective.

2.4 A substantivized adjective

To be sure, there are not many alternatives left for the formal analysis of *h₂ihxséh₂‑, and themost promising option does indeed also depart from a denominal adjective *h₂ihx-s-ó-. The relationship of *h₂ihx-s-ó- to its base *h₂éih̯x-os would be the same as in the pairs *(h₁)réu̯dʰ-os n. ‘redness’ (Gk. $ἔρευθος $n.) and *(h₁)rudʰ-s-ó- ‘having redness’ (Lat. russus ‘red(-haired)’), or *léu̯k-os n. ‘light’ (Ved. rókas-, Av. raocah-) and *luk-s-ó- (Ved. rukṣá- ‘bright’). Under this account, too, *h₂ihxsé-h₂‑ is to be analyzed as a substantivization of this adjective. However, the deadjectival suffix *-h₂- does not only derive collectives and delibatives (as in Gk. $φρᾱ́τρᾱ $f. ‘clan’ and $αὔρα $f. ‘a cool breeze’ from above), but it also creates plain nominalizations of an underlying adjective.20 Compare *h₂enkuló- ‘curved’ (Gk. $ἀγκύλος $‘id.’ with Wheeler’s Law) $→ $*h₂énkuleh₂- ‘curved thing’ (Gk. $ἀγκύλη $f. ‘bend of the arm;

(a ‘delibative’); cf. Höfler 2020: 194 n. 51. 20 Cf. Nussbaum 2014a: 306; Kim 2014: 115–118; Melchert 2014; Höfler 2020: 192–194.

noose, thong’, PGmc. *anhulōn- f. ‘strap, thong’ as in ON ál f. ‘strap, belt’, OE ōl-þwang, etc.21).

In terms of semantics, neuter s-stems derived from a verbal root ‘X’ could func-tion not only as plain action nouns (‘the act of X-ing’) but also (if only secondarily) as nomina instrumenti ‘thing on/with which one X‑es, thing related to X‑ing’. This can be seen with the root $*√sed $‘sit down’ that forms an s-stem *séd-os n. with a meaning ‘sitting down’ (as in Skrt. sádas + $√kar $‘sit down’) as well as ‘the thing on which one sits down’ (as in Ved. sádas- n. ‘throne, residence’, Gk. $ἕδος $n. ‘seat, stool’), or with $*√u̯eǵʰ $‘move from A to B’ and the s-stem *u̯éǵʰ-os n. ‘moving from A to B’ (unattested,22 but the virtual source of the infinitive Lat. uehere) and ‘the thing on which one moves from A to B’ (as in Gk. $ὄχεα $n. pl. ‘chariot’ Hom., Pi. for $*ἔχεα; $cf. $ἔχεσφιν· ἅρμασιν $[Hsch. $ε $7613 L-C], see Panagl 1982). It seems feasible to take the s-stem *h₂éih̯x-os n. as a similar case, with an original meaning of both ‘the act of X-ing’ (unattested) and ‘the thing with which one X-es; the thing used for X-ing’ (Slov. ojẹ̑ ‘shaft’).

In linewith examples suchas *sék-osn. ‘cutting’ (Lat. secusn. ‘sex’ < *‘division’) and *sək-s-ó- ‘cutting, cut’ (subst. in Lat. saxum n. ‘(carved) rock’; Nikolaev 2010b: 199), we can surmise that the denominal adjective *h₂ihx-s-ó-was derived from the s-stem in its function as an action noun and had ameaning ‘having (or: facilitating) the act of X-ing’. A substantivization of this adjective could naturally lead to an instrument noun (‘the thing facilitating the act of X-ing’), and there are indeed good parallels for such a process, as for example PGmc. *sahsa- ‘knife’ > OE seax, OHG sahs, ON sax (a substantivization of *sək-s-ó- ‘having (or: facilitating) the act of cutting’), or the derivational chain *pélh₂-(o)s n. ‘cover(ing)’ (Gk. $°-πελας $n. ‘skin’; denominal verb Umbr. pelsa- ‘bury’; cf. Weiss 2010: 305) $→ $*plh̥₂-s-ó-‘covering’ $→ $*pĺh̥₂seh₂- ‘the thing facilitating the act of covering’ (Hitt. palaḫša-/palḫša-/ c. ‘a garment for women; a cloth covering’, PItal. *palasā > Lat. palla f. ‘women’s garment; a curtain’; cf. Höfler 2018: 130f.).

The only caveat with this interpretation is that a nominalization with *‑h₂-as the substantivizing suffix still ought to display a retraction of the accent (cf. *pĺh̥₂seh₂- > Hitt. palaḫša‑, Lat. palla, and *h₂énkuleh₂- > Gk. $ἀγκύλη, $PGmc. *anhulōn- from above). So either a hypothetical **h₂íhxseh₂‑ received the oxytone accent secondarily by analogy, or *h₂ihxséh₂‑ is not a *‑h₂-substantivization of the likes that we see in *pĺh̥₂seh₂- and *h₂énkuleh₂-, but rather formally an originally oxytone adjective that was nominalized through the ellipsis of a head noun (‘rod’,

This would be comparable to Gk. $στρωμνή $f. ‘a bed spread or prepared; bed, couch’ that can be analyzed as an adjective $*στρωμνός $‘provided with spreading material’ (derived from $στρῶμα $n. ‘anything spread or laid out for lying or sitting upon’) that once stood in a syntagmawith $εὐνή $f. ‘bed’ or $κλίνη $f. ‘couch’ (cf. Höfler 2020: 194f.). In that case, *‑h₂- in *h₂ihxsé‑h₂‑ would not be a substantivizing suffix, but rather a determiner or an agreement marker of some sort.23

Alternatively, one could assume that in the oldest layer of *-h₂-substantiviza-tions, the suffix was not added to the thematic vowel of the underlying base (*-ó-$→ $*-e-h₂-) but rather replaced it (*-ó- $→ $*-h₂-), much like in several well-known cases of *-i-substantivizations such as *n̥bʰr-ó- ‘wet’ (cf. Ved. abhrá- n. ‘cloud, rainy weather’) $→ $*n̥bʰr-i- ‘moisture’ (Lat. imber ‘rain’), or *h₂eḱr-o- ‘pointed’ (Gk. $ἄκρος $‘topmost’) $→ $*h₂ó/éḱr-i- ‘pointed thing’ (Lat. ocrism. ‘rugged mountain’, Gk. $ὄκρις $m./f. ‘jagged point’, $ἄκρις $f. ‘hill-top’; cf. Schindler 1980: 390; Nussbaum 1998a: 523), and *-u-substantivizations such as *bʰeh₂n-o- ‘bright’ (OIr. bán) $→ $*bʰeh₂n-u-‘brightness’ (Ved. bhānú-, Av. bānu- ‘ray of light’; cf. Nussbaum 1998a: 527; Nuss-baum 2014b: 235f.), or *dm̥s-ó- ‘dense’ (Lat. dēnsus) $→ $*dóms-u- ‘denseness, dense thing’ (OIr. dus ‘thicket’; cf. Höfler 2015: 228f. n. 26). In these forms, the thematic vowel of the underlying adjective is substituted with the nominalizing suffixes *-i-and *-u-, respectively. Since these formations sometimes exhibit an apophonic in-dependence vis-à-vis their bases (*h₂eḱro- : *h₂ó/éḱri-; *dm̥só- : *dómsu-),24 which means that the derived *-i- and *-u-substantivization behaves apophonically just like a primary i- and u-stem, one could argue that a derived *-h₂-substantivization initially inflected just like a primary, i.e., proterokinetic *-h₂-stem of the type *gʷén-h₂, gen. sg. *gʷn-éh₂-s ‘woman’ (> OIr. bé, ben, gen. sg.mná), namely *h₂éih̯xs-h₂, gen. sg. *h₂ihxs-éh₂-s (cf. Kümmel 2017: 287; Kümmel 2021: 198f.).25 In the sameway as the weak stem allomorph *gʷn-éh₂- served as the basis of a new nom. sg. in some languages (Ved. gnā́- f. ‘divine female’, OAv. gᵊnā- f. ‘woman, wife’), one could

(on váṅkri-f. ‘rib’); Vine 2006: 154f. (on Lat.mōnsm. ‘mountain’); Weiss 2013: 347 (on OIr. fáir, MW gwawr ‘dawn’). 25 This might explain why the attested *-h₂-substantivization type does not only regularly show a retraction of the accent, but sometimes also exhibits the introduction of new ablaut grades in the base (e.g., *tm̥hx-s-ró- ‘dark’ [Lith. tim̃sras,West Aukšt. tìmsras ‘dark red’] $→ $*témhxsreh₂- ‘darkness’ or ‘dark thing’ [Ved. támisrā- ‘the dark, a dark night’, Lat. tenebrae f. pl. ‘darkness’]; Höfler 2020: 193), which might be a systematic reflex of the older pattern. analyze *h₂ihxséh₂- (Hitt. ḫišša-, Ved. īṣā́-) as the generalized erstwhile weak-stem allomorph of *h₂éih̯xs-h₂. The advantage of this scenario is that the generaliza-tion of the strong stem allomorph *h₂éih̯xs-h₂ >> *h₂éih̯xs-eh₂ (compare *gʷén-h₂ >> *gʷén-eh₂ in PGmc. *kʷenōn- ‘woman’, PSlav. *ženà) could be recognized in YAv. aēša f. sg. (?) ‘shaft (?)’, PBalt. *aisā (the putative source of Finn. aisa, Eston. ais ‘shaft, pole’).26 However, it would be difficult (though not impossible) to account for the fact that Vedic and Avestan continue different stem allomorphs of the un-derlying *-h₂-stem, implying a Proto-Indo-Iranian paradigm that still had ablaut (cf. Kümmel 2021 for more potential examples). It is peculiar (but not out of the question) that Hittite independently decided to generalize the same stem as Vedic. While there is no a priori reason to doubt the equation Hitt. ḫišša- = Ved. īṣā́-, it must be stressed that Hitt. ḫišša- could also continue a suffixless substantivization of the adjective *h₂ihx-s-ó- ‘having (or: facilitating) the act of X-ing’, i.e., a thematic *h₂ihxsó- c. (without *-h₂-) ‘thing facilitating the act of X-ing’, which would make a Proto-Indo-Iranian ablauting *-h₂-stem again a valid possibility. Yet, YAv. aēša is ambiguous and can also be a dual ‘pair of shafts’ (see Katz 1983: 119), and the source of Finn. aisa, Eston. ais, too, can be a masculine PBalt. *aisas. The underly-ing form *h₂eih̯xso-, then, would be a derivative of *h₂ihxséh₂- or *h₂éih̯x-os rather than a direct continuant of the former (see 5.1).

2.5 Conclusion of the formal analysis

The exact prehistory of *h₂ihxséh₂‑ is therefore ambiguous, but the most plausible scenario seems to be that PIE had an s-stem *h₂éih̯x-os n. (Slov. ojẹ̑) thatmeant both ‘the act of X-ing’ and ‘the thing with which one X-es’ (> Slov. ojẹ̑), and a derivative (viz. substantivized adjective) *h₂ihxséh₂‑ ‘the thing facilitating the act of X-ing’ (> Hitt. ḫišša-, Ved. īṣā́-), and that both terms were used to refer to the shaft of a cart. The logical next step is to ask what ‘the act of X-ing’ was and, therefore, what the underlying root $*√h₂eih̯x $meant.

3 The Root $*√h₂eih̯x $Except for a nominal root *ei-̯, *oi-̯ ‘Stange, Deichsel’ (‘shaft’) in IEW: 298, recon-structed on account of Ved. īṣā́- and some of the nominal forms discussed below

26 See Katz 1983: 117 for a discussion of the meaning and morphology of YAv. aēša and Kümmel 2017: 287 for cognates in the other Iranian languages (including Modern Persian xēš ‘yoke, plow’).

and in theAppendix, I amnot aware of any attempt to find a verbal root for ourword family.27 Yet, words denoting the ‘shaft of a cart’ are very often derived from roots or verbs with a very specific semantic profile, with themeanings ‘draw, pull’ (compare English drawbar) playing a prominent role: for example, OHG ziotarm./n., MHG zi-eter, Germ. dial. Zieter < *teudra- (cf. Engl. tether) are from a root $*√deu̯ $‘pull, drag’ (variant of $*√deu̯k $as per IEW: 221; meaning as in trini boues unum aratrum ducent ‘three oxen will pull a single plow’ CatoHist. 103), and Germ. Deichsel < $*þenχslō $<< *tenk(h)sleh₂‑ and Lat. tēmō, -ōnism. < *tenk(h)smōn‑ (see Weiss 2020: 199) are both derived from a root $*√tengʰ $‘to pull, draw’ (IEW: 1067; LIV² Add.: s.v.) that is also the basis for verbal formations used in vehicle-related contexts like, e.g., YAv. 3pl. mid. $ϑaṇjaiiā̊ṇte $‘pull (a cart)’ (in Yt. 19.44 tē mē vāṣ̌əm $ϑaṇjaiiā̊ṇte $‘they [= the horses] pull my cart’). The semantic link between the ‘shaft’ and a root that means ‘pull, draw’ is quite obvious since the shaft is the connection between the body of a cart and the draft animals that pull it. If one assumes that the root $*√h₂eih̯x, $too, had a meaning ‘pull/move’ (or specifically ‘pull, move (a vehicle)’), one can easily accept that the s-stem *h₂éih̯x-os bore the double meaning of a nomen actionis ‘pulling, moving (a cart)’ and a nomen instrumenti ‘the thing used for pulling/moving’ or, more precisely, ‘the thing by means of which the draft animal(s) pull(s)/move(s) the cart’ (Slov. ojẹ̑ n. ‘shaft’). And indeed, a meaning ‘pull, move’ accounts for several nominal formations that seem to be derived from such a root.

3.1 Nominal Evidence Other than *h₂éih̯x-os and *h₂ih̯xséh₂-, as well as words derived from either of them (for which see the Appendix), there are a couple of formations that are interpretable as independent ‘primary’ derivatives (i.e., derived—seemingly at least—directly from the root).

3.1.1 Baltic ‘shaft’

The first set of derivatives is attested in Baltic: Lith. íena f. ‘shaft’ (virtual *h₂eih̯xneh₂-), Lith. íelaktis f. (plus variants) ‘shaft of a (wooden) ox plow, iron shaft of a plow’, Latv. ielukši pl. (plus variants) ‘shaft of a cart’ (quasi *h₂e/oi(̯hx)-l°), Lith. áilis (var. ailė) ‘club, stick, spindle for spreading fishing nets, stick to which a net is attached’, Latv. ailis (var. aîle) ‘part of a fish-weir to which fishing baskets

27 “[T]his word [i.e., the ‘shaft, thill’] is not derived from any known verb root” (Pereltsvaig & Lewis 2015: 172).

How to pull a wagon in Indo-European 93

are attached, handle of a net, a pole that is used for moving heavy objects’ (vir-tual *h₂e/oi(̯hx)-l°), Latv. ilk̃ss f. (plus variants) ‘shaft of a cart or sledge’ (virtual *h₂i(hx)-l°).28 At least Lith. íena f. < *h₂eih̯xneh₂- seems to follow a quite common inherited model of deriving instrument nouns, namely with full grade of the root and a *-neh₂- suffix, as evidenced by *ié̯h₃s-neh₂- ‘thing used for girdling’ > Gk. $ζώνη $f. ‘belt, girdle’ (Il.+), Ved. rā́snā- f. ‘girdle’ (with analogical r-; cf. EWAia: 2, 450), Prasun yāsẽ.29 Its basic meaning must have been ‘thing used for pulling’. The precise derivational prehistory of the remaining formations is somewhat obscure and a largely inner-Baltic question; their common semantic denominator, however, is that they all refer to either the shaft of a cart (ielukši, ilk̃ss) or of a plow (íelaktis), or a pole that is either used for moving fishing nets or other heavy objects (áilis, ailis), which certifies a connection with our root for ‘pull, move’.

3.1.2 Germanic ‘oar’

ON ár f., Elfd. åra f., OE ār f., ModE oar reflect a PGmc. *airō- f. ‘oar’ (already Lidén 1897: 64). This *airō- is also regarded as the source of the Finnish loanword airo with the same meaning. The form itself is best analyzed as a formation in *-reh₂-and thus probably a substantivization in *-h₂- of a ‘deverbal’ *-ro-adjective, the likes of which can be seen in other nouns referring to nomina instrumenti such as Gk. $ἕδρᾱ $f. ‘chair, stool, bench’ (: $*√sed $‘sit’), or Germanic *feþrō- f. ‘feather’ (: $√pet $‘fly’) as in ON fjǫðr, OE feðer, Germ. Feder. We can therefore reconstruct *h₂e/oih̯xreh₂-.30 The oar is used for propelling or steering a boat by pulling the handle and passing the blade through the water, which makes a connection with $*√h₂eih̯x $‘pull, move’ seem attractive. Themotivation behind the word can either be the pulling (of the oar) or the thus-achievedmoving of the boat.31 It can be counted as circumstantial evidence for this etymology that other words for ‘oar’ are derived

from semantically comparable roots, like OCS veslo n. ‘oar’ (from *u̯eǵʰ-slo-) or Lat. tōnsa f. ‘oar’ (from tendere ‘pull’).

3.1.3 Conclusion of the nominal evidence

All the abovementioned nominal formations can be neatly explained by assuming a root $*√h₂eih̯x $with a meaning ‘pull, move’. However, none of the formations definitively requires the assumption of ameaning ‘pull, move’, as all thewords refer to objects of wood and could be subsumed under a different semantic denominator (‘rod’, ‘wood’, etc.). Corroboratory evidence for an actual root $*√h₂eih̯x $‘pull, move’ would have to be supplied by verbal continuants with a meaning close to the one hypothesized above. And indeed, two Vedic verbs may be best explained as going back to such a $*√h₂eih̯x $‘pull, move’.

3.2 Verbal Evidence

To present these pieces of evidence it will first be necessary to outline a scenario of verbal morphosyntax, including some—certainly not unjustified—speculations about a couple of hitherto differently interpreted verbs.

3.2.1 The morphosyntax of *h₂eih̯xeti ‘pulls’

Let us assume that our root $*√h₂eih̯x $formed an active thematic present *h₂éih̯x-e-ti ‘pulls, moves’ comparable to *u̯éǵʰ-e-ti ‘moves (a thing)’ (continued by Ved. váhati, Lat. uehit) that was prototypically used with a draft animal as its subject (just like Ved. váhati, Lat. uehit).

(1) a. OXNOM ox

CARTACC cart

*h₂eih̯xeti pull.3sg.act

‘The ox pulls the cart.’ b. Ved. ráthaṃ … ā́ yám áśvāsaḥ suyújo váhanti

‘White horses drew the chariot.’ Curt. 3.3.11

Starting from the assumption of a root meaning ‘pull, move’, each of the steps (1) to (3) arose naturally as a result of the previous step, backed up by the morphosyn-tactic behavior of Ved. váhati and Lat. uehit. It is within this framework that we are now able to recognize the middle *h₂éih̯x-e-toi̯ ‘moves, rides’ in the Vedic verb áyate ‘speeds’.

3.2.2 Vedic áyate ‘speeds’

There is good evidence for a medium tantum Ved. áyate in a meaning ‘speeds’ (Gotō 1987: 95 ‘dahineilen’; LIV²: 233 ‘eilt dahin’), even though the formations that

Gotō 1987: 92–97; LIV²: 233).34 The former interpretation is certainly possible and in many cases indeed inevitable. The clearest Rigvedic examples of a subjunctive stem áya-are inflected in the active (i.e., just like éti ‘goes’).

(4) áyāma dhī́vato dhíyah ̣ ‘Let’s go to the visionary thoughts of our visionary poet’ RV 8.92.11a

(5) mártaś cid vo nr̥tavo rukmavakṣasa úpa bhrātr̥tvám ā́yati [= ā́ ayati] ‘The mortal also will draw near to brotherhood with you, you dancers with brilliants on your breasts.’ RV 8.20.22ab

In fact, virtually all Rigvedic instances of an active áya- (15 in total, by my count in GRA⁴: s.v. $√i, $Stamm II. áya- and aya-) can be interpreted as a subjunctive of éti.35 It is only the middle forms (6 finite and 2 participial forms) whose formal analysis and semantic interpretation have been amatter of debate.36 Some of these forms also present several philological problems, which is why it will be useful to discuss them one by one. It will become clear from this examination that their identification as a subjunctive of éti and/or a medium tantum thematic present from $√i $‘go’ is less attractive than identifying them as forms of a separate verb áyate ‘(is moved); speeds’.

3.2.3 The participle áyamāna-

A couple of occurrences do not allow an interpretation as a subjunctive. The most evident example of a non-subjunctive formation is the present participle áyamāna-(2× RV) that clearly points to a present stem áya-, traditionally seen as a thematic verbal stem from the root $√i $‘go’.

(6) mánojavā áyamāna āyasī́m atarat púram ‘Going at the speed of thought, it [= the fine-feathered (falcon); S.H.] crossed the metal stronghold [=sky?].’ RV 8.100.8ab

(7) nīcā́yamānaṃ [= nīcā́ áyamānaṃ] jásuriṃ ná śyenáṃ ‘as he [= the horse Dadhikrā; S.H.] makes his way downward like a famished falcon’ RV 4.38.5c

In one instance the participle refers to a falcon, in the other to a horse that is likened to a falcon. While the use of éti in connection with birds is not entirely unknown,37 it would be a remarkable choice to employ a participle of a purported verb áya- ‘go’ twice in exactly the same avian context in which a high speed is either explicitly mentioned (máno-javāḥ ‘fast as a thought’) or implied (jásuriṃ ná śyenáṃ ‘like a famished falcon’). On the other hand, a translation ‘speeding’ for áyamāna- fits both instances nicely.38

3.2.4 The imperfect āyata

Turning to the finite non-subjunctive forms, there are two instances of an aug-mented imperfect 3rd pers. sg. āyata. In both cases, an intense or vigorous move-ment is implied.

(8) yád devā adáḥ salilé súsaṃrabdhā átiṣṭhata | átrā vo nŕ̥tyatām iva tīvró reṇúr ápāyata [= ápa āyata] ‘When, o gods, well clasped to one another, you stood there in the ocean, then the bitter dust [=spray] dispersed from you, like (the dust [=sweat?]) of those dancing.’ RV 10.72.6

3.2.5 sám + áyate

In the following two instances, forms of áyate are employed with the preverb sám. In both cases, the subject are (groups of) warriors (náraḥ kr̥tádhvajaḥ ‘men with hoisted banners’, víśaḥ ‘clans’) that clash together in battle. The forms are 3rd pl. samáyante and sám … áyanta, respectively.

(10) yátrā náraḥ samáyante kr̥tádhvajo yásminn ājā́ bhávati kíṃ caná priyám | yátrā bháyante bhúvanā svardŕ̥śas tátrā na indrāvaruṇā́dhi vocatam ‘[W]here men with hoisted banners encounter each other in battle, where nothing dear occurs, where the beings regarding the sun have fear – there, Indra and Varuṇa, speak for us!’41 RV 7.83.2

(11) sáṃ yád víśó ’yanta śū́rasātā ugráṃ nó ’vaḥ pā́rye áhan dāḥ ‘When the clans clash together at the contest of champions, give us mighty help on the decisive day.’ RV 6.26.1cd

Because of the evident parallelism of the two passages, it is preferable to interpret the náraḥ kr̥tádhvajaḥ ‘men with hoisted banners’ in (10) as belonging to two (or more) different armies that charge upon each other,42 rather than as referring towar comrades gathering under one banner,43 even though a meaning ‘come together’ cannot be ruled out entirely. The associated verbal forms bhávati and bháyante in (10) identify samáyante as a present indicative and thus (according to the communis

40 Compare Geldner’s translation “ging von euch heftiger Staub weg” and “die (…) Keule fuhr auf ihn los”. 41 Translation according to Witzel apud Stuhrmann 2016: 1. Compare Geldner: ‘Wo die Männer mit aufgesteckten Bannern aneinander geraten, in der Schlacht, wo nichts Liebes geschieht, wo alle Geschöpfe, die das Sonnenlicht schauen, Furcht bekommen, in dieser seid unsere Verteidiger, Indra und Varuna!’ 42 The passage refers to the Battle of the Ten Kings. 43 So apparently Jamison & Brereton (JB): ‘Where superior men gather together with their banners set, in a contest where there is nothing at all to love, where living beings, seeing the sun, become afraid, there speak for us, Indra and Varuṇa!’.

opinio) as belonging to a thematic present stem áya-. Things are different for áyanta in (11), which is traditionally interpreted as a present subjunctive of éti (thus GRA⁴: s.v. $√i; $Hoffmann 1967: 258 n. 295; Gotō 1987: 95). In fact, according to Hoffmann (apud Joachim 1978: 40) and Gotō (1987: 95), it is precisely the subjunctive sám … áya- and its seemingly justified use in the reciprocal middle (‘come together’) that, after a reinterpretation as an indicative—supposedly already tangible in samáyante in (10)—caused the emergence of themedium tantum thematic stem áya-.44

While I remain skeptical about the assertion that a reinterpretation of the subjunctive of sám … áya- ‘come together’ could lead to the genesis of a new uncompounded present stem áya- that in most of its occurrences has a specific meaning ‘speed’,45 this account offers a seemingly valid explanation for themiddle inflection of éti ‘go’, a verb that is otherwise an activum tantum. In the interpretation and the translations given just above, the ‘menwith hoisted banners’ and the ‘clans’ ‘encounter each other’ or ‘clash together’, respectively. One could therefore argue, as done by Gotō (1987: 95), that themiddle voice, unaccounted for (from a semantic perspective at least) in the abovementioned participle áyamāna- (6) and (7) and the imperfect āyata (8) and (9), actually does find a justification in (sam-)áyante in that it conveys the reciprocity of meaning (‘encounter each other’, ‘clash together’). Compare the seemingly parallel pair tíṣṭhanti ‘stand’ and (sam‑)tíṣṭhante ‘stand against each other’ (janāḥ … saṃtasthānāḥ ‘peoples that confront each other’ RV 10.42.4a).46

But such an interpretation would find support only if (sam-)áyante were an oppositional middle with reciprocal semantics, standing beside an active sam-éti with a transitive meaning ‘meet (someone); clash against (someone)’. However, the active sam-éti ‘go, come together; come to, lead to’ never takes a direct object; when it is construed with an accusative, the latter has directional value (as, e.g., in RV 3.54.5b devā́m̐ ácchā path(í)yā kā́ sám eti ‘What is the pathway that leads to the gods?’). It is questionable, therefore, whether one can really speak of a ‘reciprocal’ meaning of sám … áya- ‘come together; clash against each other’. In addition, the

44 An alternative account marshaled by Joachim (1978: 40), explaining áyate as an intransi-tive formation based on factitive inóti, is refuted by Gotō (1987: 95) as less likely (“[w]eniger wahrscheinlich”). 45 This hypothesis does not take into consideration that sám … áyanta, the only alleged sub-junctive attested in this meaning, with a secondary ending cannot easily be reanalyzed as an indicative, in which we expect a primary ending -ante. To be sure, a reanalysis would have been possible in a hypothetical 3rd sg. subjunctive sám … áyate, but a singular subject is difficult to justify with the meaning ‘come together; clash against each other’. 46 Compare Geldner: “Menschen […], wann sie […] aneinandergeraten sind”; differently, however, Jamison & Brereton (JB): “peoples, taking their stand […] together”.

100 Stefan Höfler

active participle of sam-éti is also attested in the sense ‘clash together’ once in RV 2.12.8a krándasī saṃyatī́ ‘the two war-cries, clashing together’,47 a passage close to both (10) and (11), which shows that no middle voice was needed to convey the intended meaning. There thus seems to be no semantic motivation for the use of the middle voice in sám … áya‑, which makes an important cornerstone in Hoffmann’s and Gotō’s hypothesis lose its explanatory force. The idea of sám … áyanta expressing reciprocity should therefore be abandoned.

Thealternative scenario is that sám…áyanta is not auniquemiddle subjunctive of sam-éti but rather belongs to a verb áyate. The apparent ‘reciprocal’ meaning would thennot be a result of themiddle inflection, but rather due to the preverb sám that can mean both ‘together (as one)’ (e.g., RV 9.73.1a srákve drapsásya dhámataḥ sám asvaran ‘In the jaw (of the pressing stones) while the droplet was blowing its blast, they sounded in unison’) and ‘together (against each other)’ (e.g., RV 5.34.8a sáṃ yáj jánau sudhánau viśváśardhasau ‘When the two wealthy peoples with all their troops (clashed) together’; compare also janāḥ … saṃtasthānāḥ ‘peoples that confront each other’ from above).48 If amedium tantum verb áyate had a meaning ‘speeds’ (which the abovementioned examples all point to), it is all but expected that sam-áyante would mean ‘speed against each other’ or, for that matter, ‘speed together/alongside each other’ if one prefers to interpret the náraḥ kr̥tádhvajaḥ as belonging to one banner.49 While it is true that the form sám … áyanta would then not be interpretable as a subjunctive of sam-áyante, it must be pointed out that it is not even certain that the form needs to be a subjunctive—it may well be a present injunctive. The use of the injunctive in yád sentences with a prospective meaning

47 Compare Geldner: ‘zwei Schlachthaufen, wenn sie aneinander geraten’. 48 Compare JB: “peoples, taking their stand […] together”. This is more felicitous than to assume reciprocal meaning for sam‑tíṣṭhante as there is no transitive sam‑tíṣṭhanti. 49 This view is supported not only by sam-éti itself (cf. krándasī saṃyatī́ from above), but also by at least two other motion verbs: on the one hand by drávati ‘runs’ (drávanty asya vājíno ná śókā ‘His flames run like prizewinners’ RV 4.6.5c) and its likewise active counterpart sáṃ … drávanti ‘run against each other, clash’ in RV 6.75.11cd: yátrā náraḥ sáṃ ca ví ca drávanti tátrāsmábhyam íṣavaḥ śárma yaṃsan ‘Where men clash and separate, there will our arrows provide shelter for us’, and the medium tantum vártate ‘rolls’ (suvṛ́d rátho vartate dákṣiṇāyāḥ ‘Rolling easily, the chariot of the priestly gift rolls on’ RV 10.107.11b) and sáṃ … vártante ‘roll against each other’ in RV 4.24.4cd sáṃ yád víśó ’vavr̥tranta yudhmā́ ā́d ín néma indrayante abhī́ke ‘When the ī́ clans have rolled together, just then do those on the one side seek Indra at the moment of confrontation’. Compare Geldner: ‘Wenn die streitbaren Stämme aneinandergeraten sind, dann verlangen die einen im entscheidenden Augenblick nach Indra.’
