has parallels (see Hettrich 1988: 351f.),50 so there is no syntactic condition that requires a subjunctive.

What this means for the interpretation of (10) and (11) is that both forms can be satisfactorily explained as belonging to a verb sam-áyante with a meaning ‘move against each other’ and/or ‘move alongside each other’ (samáyante a present indicative, sám… áyanta a present injunctive). The alleged ‘reciprocity’ of meaning is not due to the middle inflection, but rather caused by the preverb sám. But even if sám … áyanta can no longer be seen as a subjunctive of sam-éti, one must acknowledge that the corresponding use of the present participle of the latter in RV 2.12.8a krándasī saṃyatī́ ‘the two war-cries, clashing together’ shows that áyate does not necessarily have to belong to a different root but could still be analyzed as a thematic present of $√i $‘go’.

Before discussing the remaining two instances, let us take stock: of the ex-amples discussed so far, two attestations of a participle áyamāna- and two of the imperfect āyata all referred to vivid motion, and two instances of sám + aya- to the movement of armies. In all six passages, a meaning ‘speed’ presented itself as a plausible translation, yet none of the examples really called for a separation of the respective verbal forms from the root $√i $‘go’. An analysis as a thematic present from this root seems possible, even if the consistent middle voice is somewhat surprising vis-à-vis the consistent active voice of éti. None of the forms referred to vehicles. With that in mind, let us tackle the last two instances of áyate.

3.2.6 sám + ayante + ā́

The first of the two is a 3rd pl. ayantewith two preverbs sám and ā́, which results in a slightly different meaning compared to sám + áyate alone. It will be worthwhile also to quote the preceding stanza to give the context in full.

(12) ā́ vāṃ rátham purumāyám manojúvam jīrā́śvaṃ yajñíyaṃ jīváse huve | sahásraketuṃ vanínaṃ śatádvasum śruṣṭīvā́naṃ varivodhā́m abhí práyaḥ || ūrdhvā́ dhītíḥ práty asya práyāmani ádhāyi śásman sám ayanta ā́ díśaḥ | ‘I summon your chariot with its manywiles, swift as thought, with speeding horses, and worthy of the sacrifice, in order for us to live—

50 “Es steht nichts der Deutung imWege, daß […] der Injunktiv für die Zukunft angenommene generelle Sachverhalte bezeichnet” (Hettrich 1988: 352). The use of another injunctive dāḥ (in hortative meaning; cf. Hoffmann 1967: 262) in the main clause is a coincidence.

102 Stefan Höfler

the winning (chariot) of a thousand banners, bringing hundreds of good things, obedient to command, and creating wide space—toward (our of-fered) enjoyment. At its [= the chariot’s; S.H.] journey our lofty insight has been aimed at your praise. (Our praises, going) in (all) directions, converge (upon you).’

RV 1.119.1–2ab

The subject of sám ayanta ā́ [= sám + ayante + ā́] in the last line is not obvious, which has led to a variety of diverging interpretations of this passage. The verb is evidently a 3rd plural present indicative, but no plural noun immediately presents itself as a possible subject. The hymn, dedicated to the Aśvins, opens with a sum-mons to their chariot, which is described with a series of attributes in the first stanza. The second stanza starts by mentioning the ‘lofty insight’ (ūrdhvā́ dhītíḥ; nom. sg.) that has been aimed (ádhāyi; aor. pass. 3rd sg.) at the Aśvins’ praise (śásman; loc. sg.) during the chariot’s journey (práty asya práyāmani; loc. sg.), and then something (pl.) goes/speeds together (sám ayanta; pres. mid. 3rd pl.) in all directions (ā́ díśaḥ; acc. pl.). But what is this something?

Grassmann (GRA⁴: s.v. diś f.) interprets díśaḥ as a nom. pl. instead of an acc. pl. and thus as the subject of the verb (roughly ‘the directions go together toward …’). However, he adds the comment “bildlich, d. h. von allen Seiten kommtalles herbei”, which does not inspire confidence syntactically or semantically. Witzel & Gotō take the same line and interpret díśaḥ as a nominative: ‘Der emporgerichtete Bedacht ist bei seiner (des Streitwagens) Ausfahrt auf das Verkünden gerichtet. Zusammen sollen die Himmelsrichtungen kommen.’ It is unclear, however, what exactly ‘the (cardinal) directions shall come together’ means. It is, therefore, preferable to interpret díśaḥ as an acc. pl. in a directional meaning, not least because of the parallelism to the pāda end patáyanti ā́ díśaḥ ‘fly to (all) directions’ of RV 10.64.2b. In their translation, Jamison & Brereton (JB) (see above) understand the subject to be an implicit ‘our praises’, based (as it seems) on the loc. sg. śásman ‘praise’ of the previous clause. This reading, however, does not seem self-evident either. They also supply a participial ‘going’ for ā́ díśaḥ ‘in (all) directions’, while the direction of the main verb sám ayante ‘converge’ is another supplied ‘upon you’. Geldner’s translation (‘Das emporgerichtete Nachdenken ist bei seiner Ausfahrt auf euern Preis gerichtet. Nach allen Seiten gehen meine Gedanken.’) is identical in its identification of the constituents in the first clause to theWitzel & Gotō (2007) and Jamison & Brereton (JB) translations, but supplies ‘my thoughts’ as the subject of the main verb (based on dhītíḥ sg. ‘Nachdenken’?). Again, such a conjecture is not self-evident.

A different and to my mind quite plausible alternative has been proposed by Pooth (2019: 32). In his translation, the plural subject of sám ayanta ā́ comprises

How to pull a wagon in Indo-European 103

the three topics of the preceding clause: the chariot (asya [sc. ráthasya]), the insight (dhītíḥ), and the praise (śásman). He translates ‘zusammen (sc. Andacht, Loblied, Wagen) gehen sie (allesamt) hin in die (alle) Himmelsrichtungen’, which amounts to ‘together they (i.e., insight, praise, chariot) go in all directions’. This does indeed furnish an attractive reading and is in line with other instances of verbs with an unexpected plural number in the Rigveda, for which the logical subject is best analyzed as a combination of the topics of the preceding clause. Compare, for example, the surprising plural verb pīpáyanta in RV 1.181.5c, which is accounted for in an ingenious way by Jamison (2021b: 173 ad RV 1.181.5) by assuming that the “plural subject of this verb […] includes both Indra’s pair of fallow bays (c) and the Aśvins’ tawny lead horse (a)”.

Another factor that might corroborate this reading of the verse lies in the combination of the preverbs. If ā́ is understood as indicating the direction of the verbal action (namely díśaḥ ‘to (all) directions’), then sám cannot convey the meaning ‘against each other’ thatwe sawabove (RV 5.34.8a sáṃyáj jánau sudhánau viśváśardhasau ‘When the two wealthy peoples with all their troops (clashed) together’), nor can it easily mean ‘together in one place’ (whence ‘converge’) as this is virtually contradicted by ā́ díśaḥ ‘to (all) directions’. Instead, sám needs to be read as ‘together as one’ and therefore implies that the subject of the verb be understood as a combination of two or more of the aforementioned topics.

The interesting thing for our purposes is that in this interpretation, the chariot is one of the logical subjects of the verb ayante and therefore the first instance where it is specifically used in vehicle-related context. ‘At the chariot’s journey our lofty insight has been aimed at your praise. Together, the chariot, insight, and praise speed in all directions.’ With that in mind, it becomes even plausible to interpret some of the already discussed verbal forms in a similar manner: for the participle áyamāna- (said of a horse and of a falcon), a meaning ‘speeding (like a horse/chariot)’ becomes an attractive translation, and for sám + áyante (said of náraḥ kr̥tádhvajaḥ ‘men with hoisted banners’, víśaḥ ‘clans’), we could easily envisage an underlying meaning ‘speed against each other (on chariots)’, as this was the preferred type of warfare in the Rigvedic accounts (e.g., RV 10.103.4cd prabhañján sénāḥ pramr̥ṇó yudhā́ jáyann asmā́kamedhy avitā́ ráthānām ‘Shattering the armies, pulverizing them, conquering in combat, be[, Br̥haspati,] the helper of our chariots’).

But even if it is the case that the middle áyate in all these attestations is best translated as ‘move vigorously, speed (of/on a chariot)’, it cannot be excluded that the underlying verb is a thematicmedium tantum from the root $√i $‘go’ (quasi *h₁éie̯-toi)̯, as one could still imagine that this thematicmiddle developed an idiosyncratic meaning ‘speed (on/of a chariot)’ (even if this requires a certain amount of good

104 Stefan Höfler

faith).51 The smoking gun needed to argue for the analysis of áyate as *h₂éih̯xetoi̯ ‘moves’ would be either an instance of áyate in a mediopassive meaning ‘is pulled, is moved’ or an instance of (*)áyati in an active sense ‘pulls, moves’.

3.2.7 áyate ‘is pulled, is moved (?)’

The last Rigvedic instance of áyatemight in fact preserve the mediopassive mean-ing ‘is pulled, is moved’. Unfortunately, the passage in question (RV 1.127.3) is notoriously difficult. Our verb appears twice at the end of the stanza.

(13) sá hí purū́ cid ójasā virúkmatā dī́dyāno bhávati druhaṃtaráḥ paraśúr ná druhaṃtaráḥ vīḷú cid yásya sámr̥tau śrúvad váneva yát sthirám niḥṣáhamāṇo yamate nā́yate [= ná ā́ ayate] dhanvāsáhā nā́yate [= ná ā́ ayate] ‘Because he, shining upon the many with his radiant might, becomes the overcomer of deceit— the overcomer of deceit, as an axe is an excellent striker of wood— at whose attack even the staunch aborts and whatever is solid, like the trees, going forth to conquer, he will hold his place, [ná ā́ ayate]— with his conquering of the wastelands, [ná ā́ ayate].’ RV 1.127.3

Traditionally, the verb is identified as ayate, the present indicative of áya-, the purported thematic present stem of the root $√i $‘go’ in a meaning ‘speed’. Geldner, for example, translates the last two pādas as ‘Siegreich läßt er sich lenken, geht nicht durch; von dem Bogensieger gelenkt geht er nicht durch’ (i.e., ‘does not bolt’), while Witzel & Gotō render the passage as ‘Siegreich übertreffend, wird er sich hinlenken. Er eilt nicht hierher. Auf dem trockenen Land ersiegenden (Weg) eilt er nicht hierher.’ (i.e., ‘does not speed hither’). Both translations employ a meaning for áyate that is in line with the other attestations of the verb (i.e., ‘move vigorously, speed’).

Jamison (2021b: 61 ad RV 1.127.3), however, argues conclusively on hymn-internal grounds that the verb must have a meaning “as a quasi-passive ‘be

51 Cf. Joachim 1978: 40: “Vor allem aber fällt auf, daß [áyate] auf eine Art der Fortbewegung beschränkt [ist], bei der eigentliches Gehen mit den Beinen keine Rolle spielt”.

moved’ ”, namely “going forth to conquer, he will hold his place, he will not be moved—with his conquering of the wastelands, he will not be moved”.52 This, of course, is perfectly in line with our reconstructed meaning of *h₂éih̯xetoi̯ ‘is moved; moves’. Yet, Jamison (followed by Pooth 2019: 21–26) takes ayate as a present subjunctive of éti, parallel to the aorist subjunctive yamate (see footnote 52). This is not obligatory, however, as an indicative ‘is not moved’ seems equally valid (but see below footnote 62).

Support for Jamison’s idea that ayate allows an interpretation as a (quasi-)pas-sive could be provided if there was evidence for an active counterpart with a mean-ing ‘moves, pulls’. Such a verbal form might be attested in a 2nd sg. in RV 8.2.40, in a difficult-to-interpret dānastuti53 (40–42), in the linemeṣó bhūtó ’bhí yánn áyaḥ. Grassmann (GRA⁴: s.v. $√i) $analyzes the form as a 2nd person subjunctive of éti but tags it with a question mark, presumably because this would make yán (yánn in sandhi) a present participle of $√i $‘go’ and not a conjunction, leaving the accented verb without justification. The stanza in full reads:

(14) itthā́ dhī́vantam adrivaḥ kāṇvám médhyātithim meṣó bhūtó ’bhí yánn áyaḥ ‘O possessor of the stone—him whose insights are to the point, Medhyātithi Kāṇva, since you, having become a ram, led (him) to (goods)—’ RV 8.2.40

Jamison (2021d: 13 ad RV 8.2.40), following a conjecture proposed by Geldner and taken over by Oldenberg, reads yánn áyaḥ (despite the Pada-Pāṭha’s yán | áyaḥ) as yán náyaḥ (yád in sandhi), which requires no change in the Saṃhitā text. This would make the whole verse a subordinate clause (introduced by yád) and thus account for the accented verb náyaḥ ‘you led’. However, as Jamison admits, this proposal is not without difficulties, as it “has the yád uncomfortably late in

52 “Most tr. (and Old[enberg]) take the point of yamate nā́yate to be that though Agni is victorious, he doesn’t go further: he stays in his hearth. See, e.g., Re[nou] “ ’(Bien que) triomphant, il tient (les rènes), il ne va pas (plus loin).” But the preverb níḥ ‘forth’ (with $√sah $only here and in the root noun niṣṣáh-) seems to presuppose motion (hence my ‘going forth to conquer’), and certainly most treatments of Agni victorious depict him laying waste to his surroundings, as in the immediately preceding two pādas and in the following verse 4. The notion that Agni is suddenly showing self-restraint here seems contrary to the message of the context. I therefore take yamate as meaning not ‘hold himself back’, but ‘hold/keep his place’ (against counterattack) and ā́yate (/ayate) as a quasi-passive ‘be moved’. Medial forms of $√i $are rare enough that a consistent meaning to such a stem is hard to determine, and though some forms of áyate probably belong to a thematized stem (Gotō 1987: 92ff.), the parallelism with the root aor. subj. yamate here strongly suggests that our form is also a subjunctive (to the root pres. éti) and thus further separated from the thematic indicative forms. I therefore think that the somewhat idiosyncratic meaning I have attributed to the form is plausible, esp. as a negated semantic twin to yamate.” (Jamison 2021b: ad RV 1.127.3). 53 On the linguistic features of this genre, see most recently Pinault 2019.

106 Stefan Höfler

its clause” and therefore violates an observation going back to Hale, according to which “only one constituent can precede the yá-form” (Jamison 2021d: 13 ad RV 8.2.40).

Alternatively, yán could be the present participle (nom. sg. m.) of $√i $(thus GRA⁴) and áyaḥ the 2nd sg. present injunctive of a conjectural (*)áyati ‘moves’. The line would then translate to ‘O possessor of the stone—him whose insights are to the point, Medhyātithi Kāṇva, you, having become a ram, moved (him) going forth to (heaven)—’54 and would constitute an example of our verb in its ANIMALNOM VERBACT construction (quasi *h₂éih̯xes ‘you pulled’). However, such an interpretation requires a considerable leap of faith and even if yán is analyzed as a participle, a conjecture yán náyaḥ ‘led (him) going forth’ remains a valid option, provided one explains the accent of the verb as a secondary intrusion in the tradition.

3.2.8 Conclusion on áyate ‘speeds; is pulled, is moved (?)’

All the abovementioned examples can be ascribed to a present áyate ‘speeds’. However, if one believes that a thematic present stem derived from $√i $‘go’ could develop this meaning and interprets the “quasi-passive” ná ā́ ayate of (13) differ-ently, there is no pressing need to reconstruct a separate root for áyate, and this might be the more economical solution after all. One would still need an account for the consistent middle inflection, but various explanations are thinkable (if not necessarily entirely convincing).

On the other hand, the interpretation of these forms as belonging to a sep-arate root, viz. PIE $*√h₂eih̯x $‘pull, draw’, could be substantiated if the root had another, and this time unequivocal, present stem avatar in Vedic, with a meaning comparable or identical to that of áyate ‘speeds’. Ideally, the contexts in which this verb was used would be even closer in semantics and phraseology to the scenario outlined for *h₂éih̯x-e-toi̯ ‘is pulled, moves’ above. And indeed, this avatar is most likely found in the verb ī́yate ‘moves, speeds (of or on a chariot)’.

54 See the discussion of this passage and references to it in later texts in Feller 2004: 135–137 with n. 26.

How to pull a wagon in Indo-European 107

3.2.9 Ved. ī́yate ‘moves, speeds (of or on a chariot)’

Alternative present stem formations (“Mehrfachpräsentien”; Joachim 1978) are not only very common in Vedic; they can also be reconstructed for PIE (see passim in LIV²). For instance, next to the thematic present *u̯éǵʰ-e-ti ‘moves (a thing)’, middle *u̯éǵʰ-e-toi̯ ‘moves, is moved’ we can reconstruct an i‑reduplicated thematic present *u̯i-u̯ǵʰ-e-ti, attested in Ved. ū́hati ‘pushes’. Such a pairing is indeed not infrequent; compare *h₂éǵ-e-ti (Ved. ájati ‘drives’, YAv. azaiti, Gk. $ἄγει, $Lat. agit) and *h₂i-h₂ǵ-e-toi̯ (Ved. ī́jate ‘drives’), or *pét-e-ti (Ved. pátati ‘flies’, YAv. pataiti, Lat. petit) and *pi-pt-e-ti (Gk. $πῑ́πτει $‘falls).’55

In line with that, we can project a pair *h₂éih̯x-e-toi̯ ‘is pulled, moves’ (Ved. áyate) and *h₂i-h₂ihx-e-toi̯ ‘is pulled, moves’. In fact, just like *h₂éih̯x-e-toi̯ (Ved. áyate), this form *h₂i-h₂ihx-e-toi̯might live on in Vedic, namely in the verb Ved. ī́yate whichmeans ‘moves, speeds’. But unlike áyate, ī́yate is very often used specifically for the movement of or on vehicles. In the following examples, (15) corresponds to CARTNOM VERBMID, and (16) to PERSONNOM CARTINSTR VERBMID. An active *ī́yati is not attested.

(15) samānáyojano hí vāṃ | rátho dasrāv ámartyaḥ | samudré aśvinéyate [= aśvinā ī́yate] ‘For your immortal chariot, (always) taking the same route, speeds upon the sea, o wondrous Aśvins.’ RV 1.30.18

(16) prabodháyantī suvitā́ya devī́ | uṣā́ īyate suyújā ráthena || ‘The goddess awakening (the world) for good faring, Dawn speeds with her well-yoked chariot.’ RV 4.14.3cd

In an influential article, Insler (1972: 96) stressed the verb’s “application to the movement of horses (particularly runners), chariots or their wheels, and the wind”, and goes on to say: “When ī́yate is employed to describe the movement of a god— such usage constitutes the majority of occurrences of the verb in the RV—the movement usually takes place through the use of horses or chariots, or is compared to them” (Insler 1972: 97).56

55 Cf. LIV² Add.: s.v. *pet- for the updated reconstruction of the root without a final laryngeal and n. 5 (with reference to Panagl) for the length of the Greek reduplication vowel (but see already Schwyzer 1968: 648). 56 It is used with the subjects rátha- ‘chariot’ (RV 1.30.18; 1.141.8; 4.31.14; 5.18.3); cákra- ‘wheel’ (RV 1.30.19; 8.22.4), rathī́- ‘charioteer’ (R 3.3.6); it is used in connection with harnessed horses (RV 4.45.6; 5.55.1; 6.39.4); it is construed with the instr. sg. ráthena ‘with a chariot’ (RV 4.14.3), or with the loc. sg. ráthe ‘on a chariot’ (RV 6.59.5).

108 Stefan Höfler

Traditionally, ī́yate has been explained in two different ways. In LIV²: 233 s.v. $*√h₁ei̯ $‘go’ n. 12, it is analyzed as an “Innerved. Intransitivbildung zu inóti” (following Insler 1972). However, if it was an inner-Vedic creation based on inóti, one wonders why Ved. inóti ‘impels, sends’ (*‘makes go’) and ī́yate ‘moves, speeds’ do not showany semantic or phraseological overlap. This is also clear from Insler (1972: 102) where he admits that the “single point which can be raised as an objection to the combination of ī́yate and inóti (…) [is] that the subjects of ī́yate are different from the objects of inóti”.

Werba, on the other hand, to whose memory this paper is dedicated, connects ī́yate with the root of Ved. yā́ti ‘rides’ (Werba 1997: 407 with older literature; cf. also Joachim 1978: 138f.),57 Lith. jóju, OCS jadǫ, Toch. B iyaṃ, that is reconstructed as $*√ie̯h₂ $‘dahinziehen, fahren’ in LIV²: 309f. but as $*√h₁ie̯h₂, $i.e., an extended variant of $*√h₁ei̯ $‘go’, by others (e.g., Werba 1997: loc.cit.). In that case, our ī́yate would reflect an i‑reduplicated thematic present *h₁i-h₁ih₂-e-toi.̯ The pairing of an i‑reduplicated thematic present with a root present (*h₁ié̯h₂-ti) of the same root is less common than that with thematic presents (*u̯éǵʰ-e-ti, *h₂éǵ-e-ti, *pét-e-ti). Rix & Kümmel (LIV²) list one secure example, namely *gu̯hén-ti ‘slays’ (Hitt. kuenzi, Ved. hánti, YAv. jaiṇti) and *gu̯hi-gu̯hn-e-toi̯ (Ved. jíghnate ‘slays’), while four secure examples of i‑reduplicated thematic presents are paired with root aorists, and three already mentioned ones (*u̯i-u̯ǵʰ-e-ti, *h₂i-h₂ǵ-e-toi,̯ *pi-pt-e-ti) with plain thematic presents. The identification of ī́yate ‘moves, speeds’ as *h₂i-h₂ihx-e-toi̯ ‘is moved, moves’ might therefore seem preferable.

3.2.10 Ved. yā́ti ‘rides’

On the other hand, one cannot fail to recognize the striking semantic similarity between Ved. ī́yate ‘moves, speeds (of or on a chariot)’ and Ved. yā́ti ‘rides, moves, travels’ and its cognates Lith. jóju ‘ride horseback’, OCS jadǫ ‘travel’, Toch. B iyā- ‘travel, lead’, A yā- ‘travel’. If there was a PIE root for the movement of or on a vehicle, it most certainly was the one underlying Ved. yā́ti and its verbal congeners, to which are traditionally added the nominal formations OIr. á ‘chariot’ (root noun *(h₁)ié̯h₂-s?) (cf. EDPC: 434.), Ved. yā́tar- ‘charioteer’, yā́na- n. ‘vehicle; journey’, yā́ma- m. ‘id.’, yā́man- n. ‘motion, course’, Lat. iānusm. ‘arched passage, doorway’, OIr. áth ‘ford, passage’ (*(h₁)ie̯h₂-tu-).58 It seems like an immensely

57 Mayrhofer in EWAia: 2, 408 s.v. YĀ¹ “Hierher RV ī́yate ‘eilt’ […]?”. 58 Cf. IEW: 296; EWAia: 2, 408 s.v. YĀ¹; de Vaan 2008: 294 s.v. iānus; Zair 2012: 109. Gk. $ὥρα $f. ‘season, year, etc.’ and its congeners do not belong here (see Nikolaev 2010a: 19–49, 305–310).

strange coincidence that a root $*√(h₁)ie̯h₂ $and an overtly similar root $*√h₂eih̯x $both meant ‘move, ride, travel (on/of a vehicle)’. This raises the obvious question of whether we are perhaps dealing with one and the same root.

Combining the evidence, it seems possible to reconstruct the yā́ti-root as $*√h₂ie̯h₂ $and the áyate-root as $*√h₂eih̯₂, $i.e., as two roots that only differ in the posi-tion of the vowel *e.59 This apparent instance of Schwebeablautmight seem strange at first glance, but it has evident parallels in other roots with an underlying struc-ture $*√CI̯EH. $The evidence suggests that they metathesize to *CEI̯H when a vowel follows (Rix 2003: 366–375). Compare $*√gʷie̯h₃ $‘live’ in the root aorist *gʷ(i)ie̯h₃-t > Gk. $(ἐ)βίω $‘lived, survived’, present *gʷie̯h₃-u̯° > Gk. $ζώω $‘live’, *gʷ(i)ie̯h₃-t° > OAv. jiiātu- ‘life’ versus $*√gʷeih̯₃ $in subj. *gʷeih̯₃-e/o- > Gk. $βέομαι $(fut.) ‘will live’, *gʷóih̯₃-o- > Ved. gáya-m., OAv. gaiia-m. ‘life’, PSlav. *gȍjь ‘abundance; peaceful life’,60 or $*√ḱu̯eh₁ $‘swell’ in *ḱu̯eh₁-tró- > Ved. śvātrá- ‘strengthening; strength’ versus $*√ḱeu̯h₁ $in *°ḱeu̯h₁-e/o- in Ved. perf. subj. śūśávāma ‘we shall be swollen’ (RV 1.166.14a), and the s-stem *ḱéu̯h₁-os > Ved. śávas- n. ‘strength’, OAv. sauuah- n. ‘prosperity’.61

Our root variants follow the same distribution: $*√h₂ie̯h₂ $appears in the athematic root present *h₂ié̯h₂‑ti > Ved. yā́ti, as well as in the nominal forma-tions *h₂ié̯h₂-s > OIr. á ‘chariot’, *h₂ié̯h₂-tōr > Ved. yā́tar- ‘charioteer’, *h₂ie̯h₂-n° > Lat. iānus ‘arched passage, doorway’, *h₂ie̯h₂-t° > OIr. áth ‘ford, passage’, while $*√h₂eih̯₂ $shows up in the thematic present *h₂éih̯₂-e-toi̯ > Ved. áyate and in the s-stem *h₂éih̯₂-os > Slov. ojẹ̑, ojẹ̑sa n.62 Formations that seemingly contradict this distribution, viz. *h₂eih̯₂-n° > Lith. íena f. ‘shaft’, *h₂e/oih̯₂-r° > PGmc. *airō- f. ‘oar’, can easily be explained as being based on the prevocalic root variant at a later stage, perhaps in semantic analogy to the verbal stem *h₂éih̯₂-e/o- or the noun *h₂éih̯₂-os, or may exhibit Schwebeablaut as a concomitant feature of the

Ozoliņš 2015: 142f.; LIV²: 339f. s.v. *ḱu̯eh₁- n. 1; Neri 2017: 336. Another possible example is $*√stie̯h₃ $‘be(come) stiff’ as in Ved. ní ṣṭyāyatām ‘shall become stiff’ (< *stie̯h₃-ie̯/o-; see LIV²: 603 s.v. ?*stie̯H-), Gk. $σῶμα $n. ‘body, corpse’ (< *stié̯h₃-mn̥) vs. *steih̯₃-V- in Gk. $στέαρ $n. ‘hard fat’ (< *stéih̯₃-r̥). It would certainly be worthwhile to go through the material systematically and address apparent counterexamples (e.g., Hitt. zēari ‘is cooked’ from *kʷie̯h₁-or or *tie̯h₁-or?). In any event, the distribution rule might be the reason for the remarkable absence of full grades in roots of the virtual structure $*√CReI̯HC $(e.g., $*√sreih̯xg̑/g $‘be(come) cold’, $*√kneih̯xd $‘itch, smell’, $*√bʰreih̯xk $‘bristle’, $*√bʰreu̯hxg̑/g $‘enjoy, use’; see LIV²: s.vv.): the root-final consonant would automatically trigger the $shape*√CRI̯eHC, $but since *CRI̯- (e.g., *sri-̯, *kni-̯, *bʰri-̯, *bʰru̯-) was an illicit syllable onset, the zero grade surfaced instead. 62 One could even hypothesize that áyate (in ná ā́ ayate, example (13) above) < *h₂éih̯₂etoi̯ is the regular subjunctive of yā́ti, parallel to Gk. $βέομαι $: $ἐβίω $‘live, survive’.

110 Stefan Höfler

substantivization of the adjectives *h₂ih₂-nó- and *h₂ih₂-ró-, respectively.63 Similar explanations also account for the unexpected root variants in Av. $gaēϑā- $f. ‘living being; world; possessions’ (*gʷeih̯₃-t°), and in Ved. śávīra- ‘strong’, Gaul. PN $Καυαρος, $MIr. coar ‘hero’ (*ḱeu̯h₁ro-).

One last problem must be addressed with regard to the root present *h₂ié̯h₂-ti and its relation to Ved. yā́ti ‘moves (on a vehicle)’, etc. It is perhaps a bit surprising that this formally active verb does not have the transitive meaning ‘moves (a vehi-cle)’ that is expected in such a formation, but rather the anticausative semantics ‘moves (of/on a vehicle)’ in all the daughter languages, which we might expect instead in a verb with middle inflection. However, no middle forms are attested; *h₂ié̯h₂-ti (or at least its continuants) seems to be an activum tantum. The scenario outlined above with an active verb meaning ‘moves (a vehicle)’ (OXNOM CARTACC VERBACT) and a middle counterpart meaning both ‘moves (of a vehicle)’ (CARTNOM VERBMID) and ‘moves (on a vehicle)’ (PERSONNOM CARTINSTR VERBMID) is what is familiar to us from Vedic and Greek and what is therefore often projected back to PIE (as was done in section 3.2.1 ).

However, the situation that an activum tantum verb functions both as a transi-tive and as its own oppositional anticausative (called “labile syntax” by Kulikov (2012: 27); cf. also Malzahn 2014: 97–100), is reconstructable on ample evidence not only for thematic verbal stems, such as the -ya-presents Ved. ríṣyati ‘injures; is in-jured’, púṣyati ‘makes prosper; prospers’, but also for athematic stems (cf. Malzahn 2014: 99 with references), such as the root aorist Ved. áśret ‘spread (tr.); spread (intr.)’. Our *h₂ié̯h₂-ti ‘moves (a vehicle)’ and ‘(a vehicle)moves’ and ‘moves (on a ve-hicle)’ might attest this causative alternation also for root presents. In that scenario, the latter two meanings, i.e., ‘(a vehicle) moves’ (CARTNOM VERBACT; e.g., yā́ti in RV 1.157.3ab arvā́ṅ tricakró madhuvā́hano rátho jīrā́śvo aśvínor yātu súṣṭutaḥ ‘Let the three-wheeled, honey-bearing chariot of the Aśvins with its swift horses, which is well-praised, journey near’) and ‘moves (on a vehicle)’ (PERSONNOM CARTINSTR VERBACT; e.g., yā́ti in RV 7.75.6c yā́ti śubhrā́ viśvapíśā ráthena ‘[Dawn] drives, the resplendent one, with a chariot entirely ornamented’) would have been general-ized early at the expense of unattested *h₂ié̯h₂-ti ‘moves (a vehicle)’ (ANIMALNOM CARTACC VERBACT).

What is not surprising is that the evidently younger formations *h₂éih̯₂-e-toi̯ > Ved. áyate and *h₂i-h₂ih₂-e-toi̯> Ved. ī́yate showmiddle inflection in themeaning ‘(a vehicle) moves’ (see above examples (12) [ráthas etc.] … sám ayanta and (15) ráthas … ī́yate) and ‘moves (on a vehicle)’ (see above examples (10) náraḥ samáyante [sc. ráthena?] and (16) uṣā́ īyate … ráthena), which is of course in line with the

63 On this type see in the Appendix section 5.1.

How to pull a wagon in Indo-European 111

pattern that becomes productive in the prehistory of Vedic. The single instance of Ved. áyaḥ ‘you moved (tr.)’ (the subject beingmeṣó bhūtáḥ ‘you, having become a ram’) might be a remnant of the oppositional transitive *h₂éih̯₂-e-ti ‘moves (tr.)’ in the construction ANIMALNOM OBJECTACC VERBACT. On the other hand, Tocharian could reflect a stage somewhere in between since Tocharian A yā- is attested with active and middle inflection as ‘travel’, while Tocharian B iyā- it is an activum tantum with “labile syntax”, attested at least once in a meaning ‘lead (sth.)’ (cf. Malzahn 2010: 92, 537).64

The alternative to this scenario, namely that the root $*√h₂ie̯h₂ $had intransitive semantics ‘move (intr.)’ right from the start, is not as attractive since the nominal formations are a little less easily accounted for by assuming such an underlying meaning. After all, the shaft is a vital device for putting the cart in motion, and not just any mobile part of the cart, and the same is true for the oar and the boat.

4 Conclusion In this paper, I argued that *h₂ihxséh₂‑, the source of Hittite ḫišša- c. and Vedic īṣā́- f. ‘drawbar, thill, shaft (of a cart)’, is a derivative of an s-stem *h₂éih̯x-os, preserved in Modern Slovene ojẹ̑ n., gen. sg. ojẹ̑sa ‘thill, shaft (of a cart)’. Based on other words for ‘shaft’, the basic meaning of *h₂éih̯x-os was assumed to have been both that of a nomen instrumenti ‘thing used for pulling, moving (the vehicle)’ (Slov. ojẹ̑) and of a verbal noun ‘pulling, moving (the vehicle)’. This s-stem served as the basis of a denominal adjective *h₂ihx-s-ó‑ ‘having (i.e., facilitating) the pulling, moving (of the vehicle)’, subsequently substantivized (in one way or another) as *h₂ihxséh₂‑ ‘the thing that facilitates the pulling,moving (of the vehicle)’ or ‘the thing bymeans of which the draft animals pull, move the vehicle’. A search for additional evidence for a root $*√h₂eih̯x $‘pull, move (a vehicle)’ started with nominal formations in Baltic (e.g., Lith. íena f. ‘shaft’) and Germanic (PGmc. *airō- f. ‘oar’) and led to the Vedic verb áyate ‘speeds’ < *h₂éih̯x-e-toi,̯ the traditional analysis of which as a subjunctive of éti ‘goes’ and/or a thematic present of the root $√i $‘go’ was challenged by a philological examination of all Rigvedic occurrences of the verb. As it turns out, all instances fit a basic meaning ‘speeds (of/on a chariot)’, with a single occurrence

64 This is taken by Malzahn (2010: 537) as evidence for a denominal origin of Toch. B iyā-, A yā- from *h₁i(i)̯eh₂- ‘going’. Note that Hackstein’s explanation (1995: 23 n. 27) as a reduplicated *ii̯i(̯e)h₂- is no longer possible under the updated reconstruction of the underlying root, but one could envisage a likewise reduplicated *h₂ih₂i(̯e)h₂-, whence (with dissimilation) *h₂ii(̯e)h₂- > Toch. B iyā-, A yā-.

112 Stefan Höfler

perhaps pointing to a mediopassive ‘is moved’. As an even better semantic match, Ved. ī́yate was recognized as another avatar of the root, representing a thematic i-reduplicated present *h₂i-h₂ihx-e-toi.̯ This verb refers to a movement that “usually takes place through the use of horses or chariots, or is compared to them” (Insler 1972: 97), which perfectly alignswith the root semantics set up for $*√h₂eih̯x $‘move (a vehicle)’. Thismeaning is also traditionally reconstructed for the vehicle-movement root par excellence, $*√(h₁)ie̯h₂ $‘move, travel, ride’ (Ved. yā́ti, Lith. jóju, OCS jadǫ, Toch. B iyaṃ), that is uncannily similar to the root $*√h₂eih̯x, $underlying áyate and ī́yate. The apparently most plausible scenario starts from a single root $*√h₂ie̯h₂ $and a Schwebeablaut variant $*√h₂eih̯₂, $whose distribution follows a rule likewise visible in other roots of a structure $*√CI̯EH: $when followed by a consonant, the root shows up as $*√CI̯EH $(e.g., $*√gʷie̯h₃ $‘live’ in *gʷ(i)ie̯h₃-t > Gk. $(ἐ)βίω $‘lived, survived’; $*√ḱu̯eh₁ $‘swell’ in *ḱu̯eh₁-tró- > Ved. śvātrá- ‘strengthening; strength’); when followed by a vowel, however, it appears in the shape $*√CEI̯H $(e.g., $*√gʷeih̯₃ $in *gʷeih̯₃-e/o- [subj.] > Gk. $βέομαι $[fut.] ‘will live’; $*√ḱeu̯h₁ $in *ḱéu̯h₁-os > Ved. śávas- n. ‘strength’, OAv. sauuah- n. ‘prosperity’). This accounts neatly for the attested distribution of $*√h₂ie̯h₂ $in the root present *h₂ié̯h₂-ti (Ved. yā́ti, Lith. jóju) and several nominal derivatives (OIr. á ‘chariot’, Ved. yā́tar- ‘charioteer’, Lat. iānus ‘arched passage, doorway’, OIr. áth ‘ford, passage’) versus $*√h₂eih̯₂ $in the s-stem *h₂éih̯₂-os and the thematic verb *h₂éih̯x-e-toi̯ > Ved. áyate ‘speeds’.

The root underlying both the ‘shaft’ words *h₂ihxséh₂‑ (Hitt. ḫišša-, Ved. īṣā́-) and h₂éih̯₂-os (Slov. ojẹ̑), as well as the Vedic verbs yā́ti, áyate, ī́yate and their congeners is therefore the new old root $*√h₂ie̯h₂ $‘move (a vehicle, on a vehicle)’.

5 Appendix: Other terms derived from *h₂éih̯₂-os or *h₂ih₂séh₂-

A couple of formations in the Indo-European and Uralic languages can be analyzed as (borrowings of) secondary derivatives based on either the s-stem *h₂éih̯₂-os or the *-eh₂-stem *h₂ih₂séh₂-, identifiable by the (former) presence of an *‑s- and a meaning equal to or derived from ‘shaft (of a cart)’. As these formations are not immediately relevant to the discussion of either *h₂ih₂séh₂- or the meaning of the underlying root, they are presented here in the Appendix.

How to pull a wagon in Indo-European 113

5.1 YAv. aēša, Proto-Baltic *aisas or *aisā ‘pole, shaft’

As mentioned above (end of section 2.4), the form underlying both YAv. aēša and Proto-Baltic *aisā (whence Finn. aisa, Eston. ais ‘shaft, pole’) could be *h₂eih̯₂seh₂-, i.e., the generalized strong stem allomorph of a formerly ablauting *-h₂-stem *h₂éih̯₂s-h₂, gen. sg. *h₂ih₂s-éh₂-s. Ved. īṣā́- (and Hitt. ḫišša-?) would then continue the generalized weak stem allomorph*h₂ih₂s-éh₂-. However, the Young Avestan form is a hapax (V 14,10) and is interpreted by Katz (1983: 119) as either a nom. sg. f. of an ā-stem ‘(one) carriage pole’ or as a nom. du. m. of an a-stem in the meaning ‘two carriage poles’.65 The source of Finn. aisa, Eston. ais ‘shaft, pole’ can likewise be both *aisas or *aisā. As such the form can also be analyzed as a vr̥ddhi forma-tion (cf. Kümmel 2021: 199 n. 21).66 Formally, the basis for this derivative can be either the *-eh₂-stem *h₂ih₂séh₂- or the s-stem *h₂éih̯₂-es-. Derived from the former, we would expect a vr̥ddhi formation*h₂eih̯₂s-h₂-ó- ‘related to the shaft’, parallel to *h₃nebʰ-eh₂- ‘nave, navel’ (Ved. *nabhā- in PN nabhāka- and the patronymic nābhāká-, YAv. nabā- in nabā-nazdišta- ‘navel-nearest’ = ‘closely related’; EWAia: 2, 14; Kümmel 2021: 192–194) $→ $*h₃nēbʰ-h₂-o- ‘belonging to the navel, nave’ (YAv. nāfa- m. ‘umbilical cord; family’ with -f- < *-bʰ-h₂‑; Arm. aniw ‘wheel’; Kümmel 2021: 196).

Based on an s-stem, vr̥ddhi formations in Vedic are usually derived from the synchronic oblique (cf. áyas- n. ‘iron’ $→ $āyas-á- ‘made of iron’), but one could argue that at a much earlier stage they were based on the weakest stem allomorph with a double zero grade (which would have been at home in the instr. sg., see above, fn. 12), so *h₂ih₂-s- $‘shaft’→ $*h₂eih̯₂s-ó- ‘related to the shaft’. A comparable case might be *u̯ét-os ‘year’ (Gk. $(ϝ)ἔτος) $: *ut-s- (cf. CLuw. ušša/i- c. ‘year’ < *ut-s-ó-‘having [the duration of] a year’) $→ $*u̯ets-ó- ‘of this year’ (Ved. vatsá-m. ‘calf, young, child’ < *‘born this year’). To be sure, Ved. vatsá- is commonly seen as a possessive derivative of the word for year (see Nussbaum 1986: 117; EWAia: 2, 495). However, possessive derivatives of words for ‘year’ tend to take on themeaning ‘havingmany years; old’ (cf. Lat. uetustus; uetus, -eris; annōsus; English yeared, German bejahrt, etc.), while relational or genitival derivatives are attested in precisely the meaning ‘one year old’ seen in Ved. vatsá-, namely: Gk. $ἐνιαυτός $‘year’ $→ ἐνιαύσιος $‘yearly; of a year, one year old’; $ἔτος → ἔτειος $‘yearly; of one year, yearling’. See also Vine 2009: 216 with a different formal analysis but the same semantic foundation.

65 Kümmel (2021: 198 n. 20) points out that it can also be the dual of an athematic stem. 66 The meaning of Modern Persian xēš ‘plow, yoke’ and its congeners (cf. Kümmel 2017: 287) might corroborate the analysis as a vr̥ddhi formation (‘belonging to the shaft’ vel sim.), but it could also point to simple metonymy (e.g., ‘plow shaft’ > ‘plow’).

114 Stefan Höfler

Alternatively, one could account for YAv. aēša and Proto-Baltic *aisā, *aisos starting from the adjective *h₂ih₂-s-ó- ‘having (or: facilitating) the pulling, moving (of the vehicle)’ that was identified as the basis of *h₂ih₂séh₂- in section 2.4. The underlying formation could then be a substantivization of this adjective with the introduction of a new e-grade in the base (i.e., *h₂éih̯₂s-o-/-eh₂- ‘the thing facilitating the pulling, moving (of the vehicle)’), comparable to formations such as *tm̥hx-s-ró- ‘dark’ (Lith. tim̃sras, West-Aukšt. tìmsras ‘dark red’) $→ $*témhxsreh₂-‘darkness’ or ‘dark thing’ (Ved. támisrā- ‘the dark, a dark night’, Lat. tenebrae f. pl. ‘darkness’; see above, fn. 25). Other substantivizations of this kind show a new o-grade in the base,67 as, e.g., *mr̥-tó- ‘mortal, dead’ (Ved.mr̥tá-, Av.mǝrᵊta-, Gk. $βροτός) → $*mórto-m. ‘mortal one’ (Ved. márta-m., GAv. maṣ̌a-m., Gk. $μόρτος· ἄνθρωπος. θνητός $[Hsch. $μ $1688 L-C]), which makes a formation *h₂óih̯₂s-o-/-eh₂-‘the thing facilitating the pulling, moving (of the vehicle)’ another possible way to account for YAv. aēša and Proto-Baltic *aisā, *aisos. In addition, Komi vož, Udmurt vaiž ‘carriage pole, thill’ point towards a Proto-Finno-Permic *ɔ́̄iš̯V that—according to Katz 1983: 118—was borrowed from Early Proto-Indo-Aryan *ɔ́iš̯ɔ- or *ɔ́iš̯ā-. The latter evidence corroborates both the barytone accentuation of the pre-form as well as the PIA vowel *ɔ that can be from PIE *o (*h₂ó- or *h₃ó-), perhaps favoring the analysis as an o-grade substantivization.

However, Katz’s confidence in reconstructing an exact Proto-Permic preform for this etymon is not sharedby other scholars of Finno-Ugrianhistorical phonology. Holopainen (2020: 627–629), for example, points out that the vowel correspon-dence between Komi vož and Udmurt vaiž (vajiž̬) is irregular and that establishing the precise input form with any degree of certainty is therefore difficult (also ac-knowledged by Katz (2003: 252 n. 50)), even though there can be little doubt that the donor language indeed was (a variety of) Proto-Indo-Aryan. In addition, Junt-tila (Junttila 2016: 218f. followed by Holopainen 2020: 628) proposes an alternative scenario for Finn. aisa, Eston. ais ‘shaft, pole’ according to which the source was not a Proto-Baltic *aisā, *aisos, but rather a neuter plural *ajesā (the counterpart of Proto-Slavic *ojesa, nom. pl. of *oje ‘shaft’ > Slovene ojẹ̑) or a backformed thematic neuter nom. sg. *ajesa(n) (for which Junttila compares OCS kolo n. ‘wheel’, nom. pl. kolesa, whence a new nom. sg. in Russian kolesó n. ‘wheel’), with contraction of *-aje- to *-ai- in the common predecessor of Finnish and Estonian similar to *ajeka > Finn. aika ‘time’ (as per Hyllested 2014: 161–166). The Finno-Ugric evidence is

therefore ambiguous and can unfortunately not be used to support or refute any of the proposed analyses of YAv. aēša.

5.2 Mordvinic Erzya ažija and Moksha ažjɛ ‘pole, shaft’

According to Katz (1983: 120f.), Mordvinic Erzya ažija and Moksha ažjɛ ‘thill, pole’ (both from Proto-Mordvinic *ažja) continue a Proto-Finno-Permic *ăiš̯já, which Katz (1983: 121f.) identifies as a borrowing from early Proto-Indo-Aryan *aiš̯iɔ̯-with a root vowel that can only go back to a PIE *h₂e- qua *h₂eih̯₂sio̯-.68 Based on the seemingly ‘new’ full grade in the first syllable, Katz analyzes this as a vr̥d-dhi derivative of *h₂ih₂séh₂‑, referring to Darms 1978: 31 for examples in which such derivatives are formed by suffixation of *-io̯- to a base in *‑eh₂-. However, the formation *h₂eih̯₂sio̯- could formally also be interpreted as a simple *-io̯- deriva-tive based on the s-stem (viz. *h₂eih̯₂-s-io̯-).69 As the suffix *-io̯- creates relational adjectives, the meaning of such a derivative would be ‘related to the thill’ and would thus match the aforementioned examples. Alternatively, the *-io̯- deriva-tive could also be based on the formation that underlies YAv. aēša (see 5.1). But as above, Katz’s Proto-Finno-Permic reconstruction might be overly optimistic (Sampsa Holopainen, p.c.) and — as Katz himself admits in a later publication — the early Proto-Indo-Aryan donor form can not only be *aiš̯iɔ̯- but also *ɔiš̯iɔ̯- (cf. Katz 2003: 252 with n. 47).

5.3 Gk. $οἰήϊον $n. ‘crossbar of a rudder’, Att. $οἴᾱξ, ‑ᾱκος $m. ‘handle of a rudder’, Ion. $οἴηκες $m. pl. ‘treenails’

Yet another formation may lie at the core of Gk. $οἰήϊον $n. ‘crossbar of a rudder’ (Hom.), Att. $οἴᾱξ, ‑ᾱκος $m. ‘handle of a rudder; tiller, helm’ (S., E., A., Pl.), Ion. $οἴηκες $m. pl. ‘treenails on the yoke of a team of mules’ (Il.).70 They are derived in an unremarkable way from a PGk. *oih̯os or *oih̯ā. The two suffixes Ion. $‑ήϊον $(< *-ēu̯iio̯-) and $-ηκ-, $Att. $-ᾱκ- $(< *-āk-) are typical for instrument nouns and attach to different kinds of base words. Compare $κήλων $m. ‘swing-beam (for drawing water)’

68 If the interpretation of the Mordvinic evidence is correct, this would be additional evidence for a root initial *h₂ (but see below at the end of Section 5.2). 69 On the formal side compare Ved.mátsya-m., YAv.masiia- ‘fish’ from *mad-s-io̯- ‘related to water’ (cf. Lat.madēre ‘be wet’). 70 See Katz 1983: 119f. with n. 11 and Janda 1995: 7f. for the exact meaning of the Greek words $οἰήϊον, οἴηκες, οἴᾱξ.$

116 Stefan Höfler

and $κηλωνήϊον, $Att. $κηλώνειον $‘id.’, or $τροπός $‘twisted leather thong (with which the oar was fastened to the thole)’ and $τρόπηξ $‘handle of an oar’.71

Since the (typically stern-mounted) steering oar of a boat resembles the pole of a cart in form and (at least figuratively) in function, a metaphorical transfer of an old word for the latter to designate the former is quite conceivable.72 The $οἴηκες, $on the other hand, are long wooden nails according to Katz (1983: 119f.), attached to the sides of the yoke (and/or shaft?) to restrict the movement of the draft animals, a function he claims they share (in part at least) with the shafts of a two-shafted thill. Whether it was this similarity of purpose, a perceived similarity of appearance (the $οἴηκες $being ‘small poles’), or the fact that these treenails just very broadly belonged to the harness of a draft animal in general, a formation somehow derived from or related to ‘shaft’ seems the likely source.

From a formal point of view, however, the underlying *oih̯os/*oih̯ā cannot be equated with the vr̥ddhi derivative *h₂eih̯₂s(h₂)-ó- reconstructed earlier on the basis of YAv. aēša, PBalt. *aisas/*aisā, nor with the *‑io̯- derivative *h₂eih̯₂sio̯- set up for Proto-Indo-Aryan *aiš̯iɔ̯-, as this would leave the o-vocalism in Greek unexplained. Unless one chooses to reconstruct the root with an initial *h₃ as $*√h₃ie̯h₂ $(despite the evidence discussed; see footnote 6), the formation underlying Gk. $οἴᾱξ, οἰήϊον $must have a different origin.73 A possible source could be the o-substantivization *h₂óih̯₂s-o-/-eh₂- ‘the thing facilitating the pulling, moving (of the vehicle)’ that was invoked above (5.1) as an alternative preform of YAv. aēša and Proto-Baltic *aisā, *aisos.

A different account was initiated by Eichner (apud Peters 1980: 95 n. 43; ac-cepted by Katz 1983: 120). He reconstructs a prepositional compound “*o-HiHs-o-” (i.e., *hxo-h₂ih₂s(h₂)-ó-) with ameaning ‘situated at the thill’, the second element be-ing either the *‑eh₂-stem *h₂ih₂séh₂- or the s-stem *h₂éih̯₂-es-.74 This compound type with *hxo-° as its first member is rare, yet guaranteed by the well-known example

71 See Peters 1980: 94f.; Lidén 1897: 63 for more examples. 72 “Die Ruderpinne kann man tatsächlich als Deichsel des Schiffes bezeichnen, mit der die Fahrtrichtung bestimmt wird” (Kurt 1979: 147). For more parallels of the ship-as-a-plow metaphor see Janda 1995. 73 No explanation in EDG: s.v. $οἴαξ $(“The base of the Greek words $[οἴαξ $and $οἰήϊον] $was an old s-stem PIE *h₂(o)iH-s-, reflected in thematicized Skt. īṣā́ [f.] ’pole, shaft’ and Hitt. ḫišša- ’id.’, which both point to a zero grade. The origin of the Greek o-grade is unclear.”). 74 For the intervocalic loss of the laryngeal and subsequent samprasāraṇa (*hxoh₂ih₂só- > *hxoih̯₂só-, whence *hxois̯ó- by Saussure’s Law?) compare *suhx-ihxno- ‘porcine, piggish’ > *su̯ihxno-(PGmc. *swīna- ‘pig’, OCS svinъ ‘of pigs’, Latv. svīns ‘dirty’, Lith. svýnasm. ‘pig pen’) and, perhaps, *bʰuh₂-ihx-tu- > *bʰu̯-ihx-tu- (Gk. $φῖτυ $n. ‘shoot, scion’; cf. $φύομαι $‘grow’ < $*√bʰuh₂). $See Peters 1980: 290 n. 243; Neri 2019: 50; Vine 2021; Nikolaev 2021: 24 n. 11.

How to pull a wagon in Indo-European 117

*hxo-h₂u̯i-̯ó- ‘what is with the bird’ > ‘egg’ (Gk. $ᾠόν, $Lat. ōuum, etc.).75, 76 Examples of compounds with other adverbs as their first member and a concomitant full ‘zeroing out’ of the nominal second member are well-attested: *h₁enu-h₂p-ó- (Ved. anūpá- ‘situated at the water’; cf. áp- f. ‘water’), *h₁enu-pn̥th₂-ó- (Ved. ánupatha-‘following the road’; cf. pánthā- m. ‘path’), *h₁epi-pd-ó- ‘following on foot’ (Gk. $ἔπιβδᾰ $f. ‘the day after the festival’; cf. $πούς, ποδός $m. ‘foot’), or *(h₁)en-ḱr(h₂)-ó-‘situated in the head’ (Gr. $ἴγκρος $‘brain’; Cf. $κάρᾱ $n. ‘head’).77

To be sure, the reconstruction of such a compound *hxo-h₂ih₂s(h₂)-ó-might seem gratuitous when one can just as easily equate the base word of Gk. $οἴᾱξ, οἰήϊον $with the form underlying YAv. aēša, PBalt. *aisas/*aisā under a preform *h₂óih̯₂s-o-/-eh₂-, i.e., an o-grade substantivization of the denominal adjective *h₂ih₂-s-ó-. This would comply with the principle of entia non sunt multiplicanda. However, there is a hint—subtle as it may be—from the semantics of Greek $οἴᾱξ, οἴηκες, οἰήϊον $that might indicate that these derivatives are indeed based on a meaning ‘situated at the shaft’, while YAv. aēša, PBalt. *aisas/*aisā, both simply denoting the ‘shaft, pole’, are not. As mentioned above, neither $οἴᾱξ $and $οἰήϊον $nor $οἴηκες $refer to the ‘shaft’ directly or metaphorically, but rather to a wooden element (a crossbar/handle and treenails, respectively) that we can imagine was attached to a larger piece of equipment (the rudder or steering oar and the yoke or shaft, respectively). This might be interpreted in such a way that the under-lying formation *oih̯os/*oih̯ā did not simply denote the ‘shaft’ itself but rather some structure attached to it (so e.g. ‘situated at the shaft’), thus corroborating the reconstruction of a prepositional compound *hxo-h₂ih₂s(h₂)-ó-.

This account has been challenged recently by Zair (2011), who arrives at a reconstruction *h₂óu̯-i-/*h₂éu̯-i- (‘bird’; homophonous in PIE [though in no daughter language] with the word for ‘sheep’) and *h₂ōu̯-i-̯o- (‘egg’; a vr̥ddhi derivative based on the [unattested] strong stem *h₂óu̯‑i‑), which has again been challenged by himself (Zair 2022: 309–311), now opting for an acrostatic stem *h₁ou̯-i-/*h₁au̯-i- (but see Melchert 2022 for the lack of clear traces of o-grades in a-roots). On Indo-European Cosmic Structure: Models, Comparisons, Contexts

JOHN SHAW ABSTRACT. It is observed that relatively little has been published in the field of Indo-European cosmology in relation to the output of comparative mythology as a whole. Lyle’s comprehensive scheme of cosmological structure is reviewed in the light of Georges Dumézil’s work, and sources are examined. On the basis of comparisons from Indic, Iranian, Greek, Anatolian, Celtic and Germanic traditions an alternative triad is suggested for the visible world. Both systems are examined and compared in terms of explanatory power; issues of geographical distribution; the likelihood of cultural contact with neighbouring ancient civilizations, e.g., Mesopotamia; change and development in Indo-European over the millennia before written texts; comparisons across the Indo-European linguistic area; and applications to other aspects of the cultures studied. On the basis of what has survived in the various language groups, an attempt is made to explain the differences between Lyle’s system and the one outlined below. The proposed model is extended to include Allen’s “ fourth function” that deals with what is beyond or outside of the tripartite cosmos, providing a system intended to outline an earlier Indo-European vertical cosmic structure, as expressed in later literatures and iconography. KEYWORDS: Indo-European, cosmology, Indo-European cultural contacts, cosmic structure Considering the number of publications that have appeared on various aspects of Indo-European (IE) comparative mythology, it is noteworthy how little discussion has been devoted to how the proto-Indo-European culture associated with that mythology conceived of the cosmos and its structure (Lyle 1990: 6). The reason given is that “a clearly reconstructible cosmology for proto-Indo-European eludes us, although there are certain major widespread patterns that suggest

58 John Shaw

elements, possibly conflicting, of early IE cosmological systems” (Mallory and Adams 1997: 130). Recently, various systems have been suggested, relating, not surprisingly, to concepts well known to ethnologists and anthropologists. Gamkrelidze and Ivanov (1995: 405, 749) posit a cosmic tree in three sections, consisting of upper, middle and lower worlds, along which all of creation, animate and inanimate, is distributed. The same idea, though with reservations as to its ultimate Indo-European origins, is examined by West (2007: 345-7), who draws attention to Vedic, Germanic and Greek traditions of a cosmic tree or pillar, to which we may add a possible Celtic parallel (Shaw 2007: 257); West (op. cit.: 346) notes, however, that the motif may have been borrowed from northern Asia. HEAVEN – ATMOSPHERE – EARTH Bearing in mind the pervasiveness of his tripartite ideology within the Indo-European world, and the expectation that it would “dominate speculation on the macrocosm and microcosm”, Georges Dumézil has had remarkably little to say on the cosmos.1 His specific contribution has been to describe the vertical construction of the cosmos for Indo-Iranian as being tripartite, where the second (warrior) function is situated between heaven and earth (1995: 78).

Lyle (1990: 7-25) demonstrates how the tripartite ideology developed by Dumézil may be extended beyond the social plane and applied to concepts of space. Her approach has the advantages of ready application to diverse aspects of IE culture, and the flexibility of being able to reconcile dyadic, triadic and quaternary aspects of the IE system with that originally proposed by Dumézil. Lyle takes Dumézil’ s social triad priests – warriors – food producers as the level of the mesocosm, and describes the macrocosmic scale by the triad heaven – atmosphere – earth (op.cit.: 7). The greater part of Lyle’s discussion concerns the horizontal dimension, and she observes how concepts of space within a tripartite ideology can be integrated with cardinal directions, colours, sacrificial animals, etc. In addition to the hierarchy of three functions, she suggests a fourth, a trivalent goddess associated with all three functions and therefore on the vertical plane with the three levels of the cosmos.2 On the basis of comparisons

On Indo-European Cosmic Structure 59

from Roman and Indic traditions, her fourth function has a specific place in the hierarchy, located between the second and the third functions. In terms of her vertical description of the cosmos, this places the fourth (female) function between the atmosphere and the earth, which she defines as the “earth excepting its surface – the world below” (Lyle 1990: 22). In support of the placement of her fourth function in the hierarchy she cites the passage from the Homer’s Iliad 15.187-93, where Poseidon recounts how he, Hades and Zeus had cast lots for the three parts of the world, and were assigned in that order the realms of “ the grey salt sea” , ” the dark gloom-ridden” and “ the wide heaven in the aether and the clouds”; with the earth (Gea fem.) along with Olympus remaining common to all.3
